Jake Brigance is back and it’s about time! The year is 1990 and the place is Clanton, Mississippi. It has been five years since Jake Brigance represented Carl Lee Haley. Now, Jake is asked to represent sixteen year old Drew Gamble, accused of murdering his mother’s boyfriend Stuart Kofer, a cop on the local police force who Drew and his sister claimed were abusing their mother. This is a case that no one wants, for good reason and yet, after being appointed by the Court, Jake defends it to the best of his ability, regardless of the backlash or the consequences. A brilliantly plotted, taut legal thriller that includes compelling characters and a myriad of prevalent issues all of which make for a truly thrilling read. This courtroom thriller kept me on the edge of my seat throughout and completely delivered. Published on Goodreads on 10.25.20.

4.0 stars —- “A Time for Mercy” is the 3rd Jake Brigance novel from John Grisham. I wasn’t a big fan of the last Grisham book I read and was hoping that this one would be back up to his usual high standards. After not being able to read for a week due to COVID issues, I breezed through this very well written and interesting novel in just 5 days. “Mercy” tells the story of a 16 year old boy who is charged with capital murder after killing his mother’s abusive boyfriend, who just happens to be a cop. When Brigance is appointed to be the boy’s attorney for trial, the small town turns against Jake (much like they did in “A Time to Kill”)and Jake has to try to overcome long odds to get his client a fair trial. Grisham does a great job of creating compelling, believable characters that make the novel an interesting read from start to finish. Grisham also does a great job of interjecting humor and sarcasm throughout the book that at rimes is laugh out loud funny. The only weakness was Grisham’s courtroom scenes were lacking, especially when he made Brigance into super-lawyer and the prosecutor a bumbling idiot who was unable to ask a single intelligent question on cross-exam due to the traps and scripted answers Jake had prepared his witness with before trial. Also, the Judge’s rulings were legally wrong time and again which also aided Jake considerably. Other than these slight irritations, the book was good from start to finish and I would highly recommend.

I was really feeling fortunate to have an opportunity to read best-selling author John Grisham’s latest legal thriller, thanks to Netgalley.com. Unfortunately the book did not live up to my expectations for a number of reasons. The third and final volume starring defense lawyer Jake Brigance starts off powerfully as we are plunged into the death of a blind-drunk abusive police officer by one of his terrified victims. The setting is the same sleepy, insular stereotyped Mississippi community we have experienced before, peopled with ignorant bigots, a few colorful characters with good hearts and our hero Jake. Unfortunately as soon as Jake shows up in the story the drama is dialed back. As usual, Jake wants no part in taking on the defense of the accused, the traumatized adolescent son of a woman who was the victim of frequent domestic violence at the hands of the now dead cop, Stu Kofer. Jake is still suffering money problems and hasn’t overcome the horrors he faced from local enemies as a result of his previous big court victory. The prospect of having to defend the killer of a police officer with a stellar reputation understandably brings back all of Jake’s anxiety and fears, but his mentor, the judge in the case, applies pressure and Jake reluctantly takes the case. Grisham now goes into formula mode. Every chapter is padded with paragraphs about such minutia as Jake’s healthy breakfast choices and descriptions of daily routines that add pages but not value to the story. The worst example though is his course in Courtroom 101. Since this is the third in a legal series it seems fair to assume most of his readers will know the basics of courtroom procedure. The addition of all this superfluous explanation slows down the story and condescends to Grisham’s readers. The best part of any legal thriller is, of course, the questioning of the witnesses and seeing the strategy of the lawyers unfold. Perry Mason used to do this every week when he delighted his viewers with a surprise that confounded Hamilton Burger and won the day. Well, there was a surprise in this story too, but the reader learns it early on, and the only question is when Jake is going to spring it on the prosecution. And if you are looking for a powerful ending that ties up all the loose ends and sends Jake happily into the sunset, I’m afraid you are going to be disappointed. Frankly I think Grisham was tired of Jake. The writer must have had a three book deal to tell Jake’s story, but really he didn’t seem worth the effort. There was no passion in the man, little humor and not even much personal struggle, except for the constant worry about paying his bills. I’ve got a suggestion if he ever feels tempted to write about Jake again. Relocate him from this caricature of a sleepy southern town and let him be a real lawyer.

The opening of this book grabs the reader and does not let go. It is Grisham at his finest. The story is about domestic violence and all its ramifications. In many ways the story is a heartbreaker. The plot is interesting and the characters are colorful. There is enough racial tension and legal drama to keep the reader on edge. The story follows the real-world disagreements about domestic violence and what happens when the children victims fight back. I think the book could have been a bit shorter. If you enjoy a legal thriller, you will want to read this book. I read this as an audiobook downloaded from Audible. The book is nineteen hours and fifty-nine minutes. Michael Beck does a good job narrating the book. Beck has narrated many of the Grisham books.

What a weirdly unsatisfying book (not to mention deeply problematic - more on that at the bottom of this rant). I've read plenty of JG over the years, and have come to expect a level of clunky exposition, even clunkier dialogue, and mostly-wooden characters. But the counterbalance to those shortfalls is an old-fashioned potboiler, with a great central character, one or two interesting collaborators, and a web of intrigue that you know will be untangled by the penultimate chapter...you just can't quite see how. This book was a big letdown on all those fronts! First, it's not remotely clear who Jake Brigance is anymore - he does at least a dozen things throughout the book that are craaaazy unethical, to the point where you wonder if this is going to be a low-key Breaking Bad situation (which would be cool!), but then not a single one of those things gets addressed in any meaningful way. And while some old faces float in and out to say some wise words, the only new, interesting character - a Scotswoman who runs a children's criminal defense non-profit - mostly just sits around and marvels at Jake's supposed (but entirely unapparent) brilliance. Aside from the deceased abusive cop, JG doesn't seem to have the stomach to make anyone a "bad guy" (the prosecutor's a nice dude, the cops are respectful, even the thuggish family of the deceased are just acting out of anguish), so there's no real tension as the trial date nears. Meanwhile the B and C plots - a secondary big-dollar civil trial, and a profoundly unethical and gross adoption scheme by Jake and Carla - just sort of meander along, distracting from the heart of the story, and then are resolved, with no tension or conflict, in the final pages. But most frustrating was the centerpiece trial finale which was, simply, a dud. The big drama of the trial is explained in detail a quarter of the way through the book, then discussed ad nauseum (as in "gee whiz, when X happens, that's really gonna create some big drama at trial!"), then it plays out exactly as the characters imagined. There's a lengthy section about jury selection, but virtually none of the "dream jurors" get picked, which makes the arrival of sudden jury drama in the final pages all the more disorienting. All told, I did pick up steam in terms of grinding through this thing when the trial began, but it was the most dissatisfying trial sequence I can recall among the dozens of JG books I've read over the years... I'm a firm believer in assessing books on their own terms - JG is not a literary giant, he just writes good old fashioned thrillers. But even on those terms, this book was a hot mess! ***Finally, I wanted to make sure to unpack this book from a "good read" perspective first, before getting into the messed up politics, because even setting aside the latter, it is decidedly NOT a good read. But there is a subplot - a 14 y/o girl is raped, impregnated by the rapist, and then (along with her indigent, desperate mother) is urged to/coerced into/forced into having the baby in order to (a) benefit her brother's trial, and (b) allow the main character to adopt the baby - that is fucked up and not even a little okay. I could see a scenario where all those things actually come to pass, where the sticky politics of Mississippi circa 1990 lead the characters to do the things they do - but since JG seems no longer able to write with any level of nuance or human insight, it lands like some Handmaids Tale horseshit.***

What a terrific read! The last book I read by Grisham was Gray Mountain, back in 2014, so it’s been quite some time. I have others published after that one but I was not excited to read them as I was with this one, especially because “A Time To Kill” is one of my top 5 by this author, and as I loved “Sycamore Row”, I could not wait to put my hands on this one. I was not disappointed. I enjoyed every minute. Grisham is a great storyteller. I do recommend this book.

Another Great Grisham 3 1/2 Stars. I am very much a Grisham fan. I usually rate 5 stars all the way because of the nonstop action. However, this story starts out with a incredibly bloody beginning in Mississippi and starts a long slow decent to an unsatisfying ending. The plotline is repeated try to many times. It is my guess would that at least 100 pages of repetition could have been trimmed awe would not have missed anything. In the end, it was a good story but not great. I will let the reader make a choice on the recommendation.

Back to another Grisham. This features Jack Brigance who apparently was the lawyer in Grishams first novel. I enjoyed the character of Brigance and those around him. He defends a young boy who killed the thuggish policeman living with his mother and sister. A statute change meant that in two States you can be convicted of the murder in first degree of a policeman even if they are not on duty. Jack covers another civil case as well. He is ‘persuaded’ by a Judge to represent the boy. Bringing the hatred of the town on him as well as a savage beating. The story is fast paced and I found it difficult to put down. Now I have finished I move onto the latest Jack Reacher that I have been saving.

The long wait between instalments is absolutely worthwhile! Jake Brigance returns, representing 16-year-old Drew Gamble, accused of murdering his mother's boyfriend Stuart Kofer, a local police officer, who was not on duty but in small-town Clanton, Mississippi, 1990, this does not matter and Drew finds himself facing the gas chamber. Drew and his sister claim they and their mother are being abused by Kofer. Brigance finds himself embroiled in a deeply divisive trial as Drew's court-appointed attorney, but there is backlash, controversy and significant consequences to his representation of the boy (personal, financial and social). Grisham is a master storyteller. The slow-burning plot is filled with legal drama, damaged characters and a cornucopia of issues, making for a fantastic read. The courtroom scenes kept me turning pages late into the night. Definitely written with another book in mind and I can see this one being made into a movie!

Typical Grisham A fan of the first Jake Brigance book, A Time to Kill, I had high hopes. Instead of something unique, Grisham chose to mimic the story switching out the black adult, Carl Lee for a 16 year old boy and the child with a sexy but useless mother. Paced well, it's hard not to be engaged with the characters in spite of the similar plot. It's not Grisham's best but for fans of Jake Brigance might be worth reading.

This is the third book in the Jake Brigance series by John Grisham and it seems like the author has his mojo back. I really enjoyed the two previous books in this series but have been a little disappointed by some of the authors latest offerings so it was good to have normal service resumed. Jake Brigance is back in a murder trial that nobody wants, defending Drew Gamble who is accused of murdering a local deputy. The case is stirring the local citizens of Clanton, Mississippi, leaving them looking for justice and the death penalty following the murder of their local deputy. . Although it is with reluctance that Jake accepts this case he is a lawyer who seeks truth and justice at all costs, never sidestepping decisions that may put him and his family in danger. Many in Clanton want a swift trial and the death penalty, but Brigance sees it another way. Once he learns the details of the case, he realises he has to do everything he can to save sixteen year old Drew. I always enjoy court room drama and there was plenty in this novel to keep me happy. Excellent characters and good plot written by a master storyteller. John Grisham specialises in legal thrillers and this is well worth reading.

“… the mad glow in his eyes told her this was their last fight. This was the moment he would finally kill her.” In the eyes of his fellow officers and fellow townspeople, Stuart Kofer is a long-term model police officer and the finest sheriff’s deputy that Clanton, Mississippi, has ever seen. Late night and after his work hours tells a dramatically different story. Kofer is a sloppy, violent drunk who routinely beats his wife and step son, Josie and Drew Gamble, senseless, topping off his alter ego’s malicious conduct by assaulting and raping his fourteen year old step-daughter. After a night of particularly heavy drinking and a resulting vicious beating, Drew picks up Kofer’s service weapon and puts a bullet through Kofer’s left temple as he lay passed out on his bed in an alcoholic stupor. The resulting charge of first degree murder takes 16 year old Drew Gamble out of the juvenile court system and places him into the docket as an adult facing a capital trial and the prospect of execution by the state. A TIME FOR MERCY is most decidedly NOT a suspense thriller. From first page to last, it is a legal procedural that describes in heartbreaking (and, if I may say so, rather lengthy) detail the minutiae of the capital trial of a young man who readers will almost certainly believe is innocent as a matter of self-defense. Southern USA small town politics; mental illness; domestic violence and sexual assault; alcoholism and drug abuse; poverty; the difficulties of a small legal practice financing an extended defense for a case forced upon him by the state judicial system; police corruption; and the blue wall of silence make A TIME FOR MERCY an interesting, if somewhat less than compelling or page-turning novel. Admittedly a long way from John Grisham’s best work but an entertaining novel nevertheless that fans will enjoy. Paul Weiss

I haven’t read a John Grisham novel in over a decade. I don’t have anything against the guy. In fact, at one point, I read a bunch of his novels, starting with “The Firm”. It was okay. I really liked “The Client” and “The Runaway Jury”, but I didn’t really like “The Chamber”. I thought “A Painted House” was great. I thoroughly enjoyed his nonfiction work “The Innocent Man”. My favorite novel of his, though, was “A Time to Kill”. It should be noted that every one of these books (with the exception of “The Innocent Man”) was made into a movie. Some were actually decent. Of course, I saw them all, usually after reading the book. I distinctly remember liking the film adaptation of “A Time to Kill”, starring Matthew McConaughey, Samuel L. Jackson, and Sandra Bullock. Was it better than the book? I honestly can’t recall, it’s been so long since I read it. (The book was published in 1989.) Here’s the point, assuming I have one: I haven’t read a Grisham novel in a very long time. I kind of stopped reading Grisham, for no good reason, really. I just found other things to read. So, recently I picked up “A Time For Mercy”, published in 2020. It is a sequel, of sorts, to “A Time to Kill”. The main character, attorney Jake Brigance, reluctantly takes on a case involving the shooting of a police officer. He doesn’t want the case, and no good defense attorney would, for one main reason: In Mississippi, in 1990 (when the novel takes place) shooting a cop is virtually an automatic death sentence. The state had some of the most stringent laws regarding violence toward police. (We won’t talk about how NOT stringent the laws were regarding violence BY the police. That’s an entirely different subject…) The shooter was a 16-year-old living in the police officer’s house. The boy named Drew Gamble admitted to shooting the officer. Practically catatonic when the first responders arrive, Drew willingly goes to jail, but there is clearly something not right about the boy. His mother and sister (who also live in the house) share a heart-rending, disgusting story of a highly abusive—-verbally and physically—-man who, despite being a highly decorated police officer and well-liked in the community, was a mean and vicious drunk. Beatings were regular occurrences. Jake doesn’t want the case because he has good standing within the community. He’s actually friends with most, if not all, the local police officers. All of that will more than likely change when the people of Ford County find out he is defending the cop-killer. Unfortunately, he also knows that he may be the only attorney in the state who could provide the best defense for this kid. “A Time For Mercy” is courtroom drama at its absolute best, mainly because the drama doesn’t confine itself to just the courtroom. Grisham’s knowledge and experience about what goes into a court case in Mississippi in the early-1990s makes for an incredibly believable novel, populated with very real people. All of the characters—-even the ones you aren’t supposed to like—-are sympathetic. It’s hard not to compare Grisham’s defense attorney with another well-known DA, Michael Connelly’s “Lincoln Lawyer”, Mickey Haller. They couldn’t be more different in terms of personality and likability (Jake is a strong family man with good Christian values. Mickey sucks at adulting in almost every way, except in the courtroom.), but both are excellent lawyers. (Also interesting bit of trivia: both characters have been played by Matthew McConaghey in films.) I think it’s about time I start reading more Grisham.

Il Tempo della Clemenza (original title A Time for Mercy) is definitely a big book, since it consists of 522 pages, but it must be said that it can be read quite easily, even if certain long descriptions could be definitely shorter. On the other hand, it's a Legal Thriller and where lawyers are involved, it's by definition a bit heavy. The protagonist is Jake Brigance, previously the protagonist of other books by John Grisham, and on this occasion, Jake is engaged as defense attorney for Drew Gamble, a sixteen-year-old accused of the murder of his mother's partner. To complicate matters, the murdered man was a deputy sheriff, and therefore the whole course of events will be very complicated for Jake. The plot unfolds in a very linear way, without major twists, but the pace is always quite high and Grisham's writing style is very nice as usual. Beyond the story of Drew and his family, in the book Grisham inserts a good amount of food for thought on today’s America, for example the use of weapons, or the law on the death penalty, but also racial discrimination still present in certain states or the different interpretation of the law depending on the state in which you are. It is therefore a book that beyond the central story can also be a good starting point for chats with friends. Three stars well deserved.

Can a Killer Go Free? asks the tagline on the cover. Well John Grisham doesn't tell us - without spoiling the ending, it doesn't reach a satisfactory resolution. After a long, laboured build up which lacks much tension, the book comes alive when we eventually get to the trial, where Grisham is at his best - but then peters out with a flat ending. There's also some dubious bending of adoption laws amongst other things - safe to say honest lawyers and judges are hard to find here. Diverting, but not one of his best.
Started out strong, dragged on in the middle, trial was very entertaining but finished unsatisfying.
Grisham is my auto read/buy list. I don’t always like them but I do love the Brigance trilogy. This one was a slow burn tense read that ended up being really satisfying.

The law works in mysterious ways - at least in small-town Mississippi courtrooms in 1990. And they're laid out here for all to read and enjoy as local attorney Jake Brigance takes on two very different high-stakes cases. One could earn a ton of money for his struggling practice; the other could get him killed. The golden goose case pits Jake against a giant railroad company he alleges was negligent in keeping crossing lights in good repair. The result was a horrible accident that happened - or so Jake needs to prove - because the lights weren't working. Needless to say, the railroad attorneys insist they were working just fine. As the book begins, it looks as if the railroad may be willing to offer a substantial cash settlement with Jake's client - thus allowing Jake to pay his bills as well as those he's racking up defending the client in his other case - one he got [ahem!] railroaded into taking on by the local judge. It is that case that gets the lion's share of attention. A 16-year-old boy has been charged with the cold-blooded murder of his mother's boyfriend. The case is complicated by the fact that the dead guy was a local deputy sheriff - albeit one with a nasty temper and a penchant for getting drunk. Under state law, the boy can and will be tried as an adult; many, if not most, of the town's residents (and most certainly the victim's family and his fellow officers) are fervent in their belief that he deserves the death penalty. The more Jake learns, though, the more he believes the charges against his young client aren't warranted. Readers, of course, learn the details of what really happened as well as how Jake and his legal cronies are working out their courtroom strategy. Suffice it to say it's a real treat to follow along - or at least it was for me. I have to say I wasn't totally thrilled with the way things turned out even though it probably was for the best, but I'm encouraged that there is plenty of fodder for the next book in this terrific series (this is the third). Many thanks to the publisher, via NetGalley, for allowing me to read and review it.

This is a book that just begs for 4.5 stars. The first chapter pulls you in and Grisham never lets up after that. A very good courtroom drama that has plenty of excitement and witticisms. If you like Grisham you will like this tale. Recommended.

It has become one of my annual late Fall rituals. The leaves are falling. College and Pro football are in season, which means it is time to open the new John Grisham novel, “A Time for Mercy”, and re-visit the law in action in the south. And on a personal note, it also an opportunity to get the bad taste of Grisham’s weak Spring outing, “Camino Winds” flushed out of my system. As I through myself into the first chapter, I remembered almost instantly why I love reading Grisham so much. He is a masterful storyteller. He pulls you from the first sentence, sets the scene, and grabs your full immersion in his story. Simple things become interesting and legal issues provide complex and emotional moral stories that pull on your heart strings. That is the case (no pun intended) as Grisham returns to his most established protagonist and underdog winning lawyer, Jake Brigance. It is 1990 in Clanton, Mississippi, where he is finally finding peace for him and his family following the aftermath of his getting a not guilty verdict for Carl Lee Hailey five years previously (as told in “A Time to kill” one of Grisham’s first novels), a man who killed his ten-year-old daughter’s brutal rapist. Now, jake is faced with another explosive and political conflict when he finds himself being pushed by the circuit court justice to take on another impossible case. Not being able to say no, Jake finds himself being appointed as the defense attorney for Drew Gamble, a scared and shy sixteen-year-old who looks more like twelve. Drew is in big trouble. He has been charged with killing a local deputy, with which he, his mom, and sister lived with. Because the victim was a member of local law enforcement and his family strong members of the local community, the gossip and negative reaction are heavy and fierce. Many citizens want swift justice in favor of invoking the death penalty for the teenager. And that anger and frustration gets pointed at Jake and his family as he tries to honor his commitment to defend the young Drew. To make matters worse, the more Jake digs into Drew’s and his family situation, he finds there is more to the story which could serve to inflame the town even more. Before long jake finds his career, family, and financial security will all be at risk as he tries to what he believes is morally right… I purposely tried to pace my reading of this book, to extend and savor the experience. Still, I devoured every page, every challenge that Jake faced, and the legal conflict that comes from small town politics and emotions. This book was like a date that you never wanted to end because you were so mesmerizingly in the moment. I hesitate to share anymore of the plot or characters because I don’t want to take away anything from anyone’s own reading experience. This one is best enjoyed without knowing anything more than what is on the book cover. “A Time for Mercy” radiated the masterful Grisham storytelling that we’ve come to know and love. His descriptions are brief, focused, and vivid. His dialogs are sharp and flow like a Robert B. Parker Spenser novel at its best. More importantly. Like Stephen King, Grisham is a pure in heart storyteller, and his storytelling skills are pretty flawless – smooth and flowing prose with no wasted or unnecessary words, a constant focus on moving the conflict forward. I am probably not the first, not the last, to claim that Grisham is our modern-day William Faulkner of American fiction. Overall, this is an excellent book, a page-turner from beginning to end, with one exceptional issue regarding the ending that I struggled with. The plotting is crisp and tight, moving from scene to another smoothly and effortlessly. The key elements and plot twists are revealed one steady step at a time, like the peeling of a ripe onion, not too fast and not too slow, building to a strong climax that delivers a solid pay off. There’s something about this one too that feels more personal for Grisham. His characters, politics, religious practices, southern history, and legal processes are intertwined into the tapestry of one of his richest stories in a beautiful and masterful way. Grisham projects himself through his protagonist, Jake Brigance, an authentic down to earth, flawed hero, trying his darndest to make the world a better place. As readers, we cheer him, walk with him, and want to be him. As for my one issue, I need to tread gently so as not to spoil anything for my fellow readers. For 434 pages this was a 5-star rating for me and some of Grisham’s best writing. However, the last 30 pages reflected a developing habit that has arisen in his recent books over the past few years (including “The Reckoning” and “Camino Winds”) for endings that feel inconclusive, thrown together, and even depressing. It’s hard to be specific without giving away details that could impact the reading experience, so I will describe it this way. There are two major cases that Jake is working on and after the emotional roller-coaster reading experience, one of them pretty much ends up where it started and the other one sort-of gets taken care in a brief scene or two that leaves you shaking your head and thinking WTH? I may be the only one who struggled with these structural issues, but the outcome for me is a 4-star rating rather than a 5-star. I fully accept that my thoughts on the last 30 pages will more than likely put me in the minority of viewpoints with the millions of readers who will love this book, and that is okay. That does not take away from my belief that “A Time for Mercy” is well-worth the reading the experience. It fully is. Thank you, John, for giving me one of my favorite Fall season experiences. Hopefully, I’ll see you again next year…

I've always maintained and I've always will that if you read one book by John Grisham, you read them all. The same, naturally, goes for this book too. And it is not something that I say out of spite or to criticize or to highlight any other disadvantage. On the contrary, I like Grisham's books and I've read almost all of them. And they are really good. But, at the same time, the aforementioned "read one - read all" means that I probably won't ever in the future rate any of them 5*, simply because of lack of surprise element or something that could be regarded as very unexpected and truly novel. As for this book - while I don't think it is the best book by Grisham, the main character Jake Brigance is probably my favorite person in Grisham's works. He's nice, good-hearted, pretty simple, with a strong sense of duty and honor and generally easy to relate to. So, I actually do not have much to add to. Those how read at least a few books by this author already knows what to expect and they (probably) won't be disappointed with this book, too. And those who haven't read anything by Grisham, well.. First of all, I guess they're in for quite a jolly legal roller coaster in a deep, rural south. Second - why would anyone start from book nr. 3? Go and read A Time to Kill, which probably is the best book (Well, at least one of top-3 for sure) by Grisham, and book nr. 1 in the series at the same time. I'm not gonna reveal any plot here, but it is an easy to read book that caries a sound social criticism at the same time. Certainly, some aspects strike me as too pious or even too bigoted in this book, but I just guess that it had been a standard norm in the rural south back at 1990. As usually, 4 solid *.
Can't go wrong with a Jake Brigance novel by John Grisham! A Time For Mercy is the 3rd book in the series and it's an excellent read! I highly recommend the audiobook!

It’s been a while since I last read a John Grisham book, but I thoroughly enjoyed picking up this one. I particularly liked A Time to Kill and it was great to revisit those characters. The compelling court case in the story, once again handled brilliantly by Jake, made it a delightful read. If you enjoyed the first two books in the series, you’ll definitely love this one. I also noticed there’s a fourth book that I’ll need to read soon.

A Time for Mercy is the newest addition to John Grisham’s fine vigilante series featuring lawyer Jake Brigance. As someone who likes to grab my baseball bat after a few Budweiser’s and police the mean streets of my town until I pass out in the middle of my neighbor Lou’s well-manicured lawn, I can truly appreciate the take the law into your own hands approach Grisham takes with this series. And let me be clear, you do not have to be an active vigilante yourself to enjoy these books, maybe you just always wanted to join the Guardian Angels but (like me) you discovered that sadly all your berets were green. Or maybe you are getting up there in years and unable to rundown those high school punks spray-painting poorly proportioned genitalia on parked cars without throwing out your back. A Time for Mercy starts with young Drew Gamble shooting his Mom’s extremely drunk boyfriend (a Clanton police officer) in the melon after another violent beating. Drew and his sister believe Mom is dead and are traumatized by repeated abuse. The police arrest Drew and the case seems cut and dry. I mean you can’t just kill everyone who injures you, right? You have to work through the system, call the police, and seek help, right? Oh contraire, my frere! In Grisham’s odes to killing those who wrong you, it is never that simple. Lawyer Jake Brigance swoops in and soon works at finding ways to make the jury as well as us readers (even those of a more liberal leaning) outraged at the thought that this poor 16 year old could be convicted for simply shooting an unarmed and passed out man. Like a passive aggressive mother trying to get her slovenly teenager to put down the X-Box controller and do his chores, Grisham manipulates the story like a pro: Drew, while 16 years of age is smaller than Gary Coleman’s Arnold Jackson, The state wants to put him to death—no jail sentence for this kid, the dead boyfriend is an unremittent creep, an abuser with a history of violence that has historically been given a blind eye by his fellow cops and bosses. Grisham is a strong writer. The story is suspenseful and quick moving. As a reader I only paused to emit the occasional outraged grunt or hiss. While I may not agree with the flagrant lawlessness that Grisham endorses with these stories I was swept away by the nail-biting court room action. A fun and light read.
Loved the courtroom drama! Disappointed with the ending.....

The book opens with a violent scene that sets the scene for the rest of the book. The place is Clanton, Mississippi. Thetine. 1990. Jake Brigance finds. Himself pressed into taking a case to defend 16 year old Drew Gamble. The prosecution is asking for the boy to be tried as a adult and seeking the death penalty, as Drew shot a deputy sheriff. But there is a lot more to the story of the Gamble Family, mother Josie, sister Kiera and Drew and what happened with deputy sherrif Stuart Kofer. This is the third book in the series featuring Jake Brigance. I had not read the middle book and wasn’t overly impressed with the first one but the premise of this story sounded interesting. I found this a thought provoking and extremely readable novel. Interestingly it takes till about three quarters of the way though the book to get to the actual trial, the rest is lawyers playing the chess game of the law trying to score points and out think the other lawyer’s moves ahead of time. I found this interesting although sometimes it does seem less about getting at the truth than outwitting the other lawyer. Many people in the community are not happy with Jake for representing Drew and Jake pays the price for that in more than one way. While I enjoyed this and it maintained my interest particularly once it got to the trial, I wasn’t thrilled with some aspects of the ending. Maybe that’s the reality but it just felt a bit unsettling. Still a good read.

3.5 This book was not boring and was a quick read, and when all is said and done, it can be said that it is a decent legal thriller. Taken alone, that would be fine. Only this is a legal thriller by John Grisham and is in the trilogy of A Time to Kill and Jake Brigance. The so called Legal Bar is, and should be, set higher. We should expect it to be. “Decent” is not on this proverbial yardstick. The story was okay, pretty predictable, and the ending was rushed. There was so much more that could have been done to make this of the caliber expected of this writer, and in this line of one of the most popular novels of all time. Would anything come close to what we would expect from a follow up to “A Time”? Yes, I have to believe that Grisham can write it. Is “Mercy” it? Not even. 3.5 – may be generous. My humble opinion, and because I think that much of Grisham.

Fantastic plot. John Grisham is a master at translating the complexities of the courtroom into a language that is both comprehensible and appealing to laypeople like myself. Big issues—great for conversations about domestic abuse, alcohol abuse, and children who, in self-defense, commit heinous crimes. “The facts are what they are and we can’t change them.” Good shit! 🙌🏼

This new release is the third book in Grisham’s Jake Brigance trilogy that began with A Time To Kill in 1989. Set in 1990 it’s an old school Mississippi courtroom drama and as expected for me it was a nostalgic if somewhat dated read. It starts out strong with the murder of an abusive policeman at the hands of the abused and then an exciting courtroom drama ensues? How is Brigance going to pull off a win for his client here? Sadly there’s not much satisfaction of that question and the books ending is both mediocre and incomplete. Color me disappointed especially after reading 460 pages. 3 stars

I was hooked on courtroom dramas early, from reading To Kill a Mocking Bird (a school project requirement which I kicked and moaned about but ended up entranced by) and watching the film 12 Angry Men (made in the year I was born) persuaded to do so by my dad and still one of my favourite films. Though I’ve found some of Grisham’s output patchy I do believe he’s written some of the best courtroom scenes I’ve come across since. Here he’s back with a third episode featuring lawyer Jake Brigance, following up A Time to Kill and Sycamore Row. Jake is based in a small town in Mississippi and when a fourteen year old boy, Drew Gamble, shoots and kills his mother’s bullying and abusive partner it seems that he’s doomed to take a long walk to a short drop (actually it’s a gas chamber at this point in the state’s history, but the result is pretty much the same). The death penalty for a minor? No problem here. But of course there’s much more to the case: there are mitigating circumstances and some actions are open to interpretation in terms of timing and motivation. However, will any of this be enough to save the boy? Well, one complicating factor is that the man he killed was a law officer – that’s guaranteed to go down badly with the jury in this Bible Belt town. There are other complications too, mainly stemming from the fact that Jake is struggling for money. He hasn’t got too many other cases on his books and his biggest potential money earner, his banker, has just hit a major problem. He’s invested big in the case and he’s about to see it all disappear down the drain. With a measly $1000 payment for all of his efforts on Dew’s case it’s possible he could go bankrupt before the trial is over. I loved the everything about this one: the characters are terrific, the story is believable and the legal arguments complex but persuasive. And Jake’s oratory at key moments in the trial is just brilliant. I listened to an audio version of this book read superbly by American actor Michael Beck. Perfect!

I honestly don't remember reading a book of more than 600 pages before. It's a true testament to Grisham's ability to keep a reader glued to the pages that I finished in just three days. I can't say this is his best. Others will, but I felt there was too much side business going on that really didn't help move the plot along. The main plot, the murder of a police officer, is strong and carried my attention to the last page. Each time the train left the tracks, I wondered if it was just to make the book longer. As usual, Grisham's characters are superb. Even without the customary inner thoughts, it was easy and clear to know what the characters were thinking. You will fall in love with the two children. Say no more. The lead character - Jake - has been in two previous books by Grisham. I don't recall the second one, although "A Time To Kill" was amazing. Several word choices become apparent and overused, the reason I couldn't in good conscience rate this one five stars. "Eased" is used so often in five successive chapters that I was wondering if the author's thesaurus was stuck on that page. I like Grisham's writing and have admired it for many years. If you've read everything else by this author, than this book is a requirement. If John Grisham is unknown to you, don't start here.

Easy to read and it kept my attention for the most part but it was way, way too long. About 150 pages too long. I keep reading John Grisham’s books, but sadly, I can only recommend his very early books. And the icing on the cake for this so-so book was the author’s note at the end. Basically he says that he’s too lazy to make sure that all the laws he’s writing about, are in fact, correct. What? That’s not just lazy, but in my opinion, disrespectful of the legions of readers who have put him up on the pedestal he sits on today.
Jake is back! This story starts out red hot and keeps on cooking all the way to the very end. THIS kind of fun writing is why I read John Grisham. ATFM is 4 and 3/4 stars easily.

I really enjoyed this third book in the Jake Brigance series. I didn't read the book jacket because I wanted to go in blind, and I'm glad I did. I knew from the start where it was going, but there were some surprises along the way. The only downsides for me were that it didn't have the same depth with the side characters as usual and that there was a lot of repetition with the law procedures, like picking the jury, for example. We got that in all 3 Jake books, which wasn't necessary. I really like the ending, and I like that there are unanswered questions. Overall, I'm glad I finally got to read this book, and I would definitely read more Jake books and more Ford County and/or Clanton books. I recommend this book to people who enjoyed A Time to Kill and/or Sycamore Row and to people who like legal thrillers. Trigger warnings: domestic abuse, rape, discussion of abortion

Well, I made it through my "big 3" authors who usually publish this time of year. If I had to rank their tales in terms of plot, readability, etc. first prize would go to Michael Connelly, second to Lee Child and his brother's Reacher installment and bringing up the year would be this one by Grisham. The story seemed to plod in places, got repetitive, and there seemed to be a great 300 page novel struggling to get out of a 476 page tome. But, the biggest disappointment was to have the book end with so many loose threads. Train suit? Personal suits? Follow-up to the main trial? County reimbursement suit appeal? Bill collector suits for the client's mother? Just a whole lot left hanging out there! Maybe an attempt to emulate the discontinuity of real life - but frankly, I read to get a bit more wrap up than real life. Bits of the Grisham brilliance here but frankly I think is one of his disappointing efforts.
This was an interesting topic. What do you do??? The ending opens a can of worms for the next book.

A Time for Mercy by John Grisham #2021Reads #MayReads “I can’t believe you would represent a killer like that Jake. I thought you were one of us. xxx ‘Gotta have a lawyer, Helen. You can’t put the boy in the gas chamber if he doesn’t have a lawyer. Surely, you understand.’ xxx ‘...I can’t imagine doing that for a living, representing killers and child rapists and such.’ ‘How often do you read the Constitution?’ ‘...the Constitution, as interpreted by the Supreme Court, says that a person accused of a serious crime must have a lawyer. And that’s the law of the land.’ With Grisham being one of my favorite authors, I have to admit, I was anticipating a great novel. While A Time for Mercy is a reasonably good story, it isn’t that spectacular. A Time to Kill and Sycamore Row, its predecessor books, still reign the best among the ‘Jake Brigance books.’ A Time for Mercy started out strong, but dragged on in the middle by overwhelming the readers with too much information. The trial part was very enthralling but the ending was predictable. There’s also too much repetition of the story from the previous books, for instance, Jake kept on reminiscing how her Paralegal, Portia Lang got to work for him (she’s the daughter of Lettie Lang from Sycamore Row). I believe one of Grisham’s goals in this book is to show the growth of Jake in the legal profession, but sadly, I don’t buy it. Instead, the readers see Jake as a less emphatic lawyer who could be mistaken as a salesman. However, the readers get to see a more compassionate lawyer in Lucien, I quote: “Being fearless, unafraid to take unpopular cases, fighting like hell for the little people who have no one to protect them. When you get the reputation as a lawyer who’ll take on anybody and anything—the government, the corporations, the power structure—then you’ll be in demand. You have to reach a level of confidence, Jake, where you walk into a courtroom thoroughly unintimidated by any judge, any prosecutor, any big-firm defense lawyer, and completely oblivious to what people might say about you.” Verdict: No mistrial. 3/5 stars. FN: I really had high hopes for this book. The title is very timely since I was reading this when my grandmother passed away, her nickname was, Mercy (Mercedes Villena). I miss her so much; WE miss her so much.

It's 5 years after the Carl Lee Hailey trial brought Jake Brigance to prominence in 'A Time to Kill.' Now Jake is back and taking on a case that proves equally, and costly, to defend. Drew Gamble is a 15-year-old who finds his mother lying dead in the living room of the home belonging to her boyfriend, Deputy Stuart Kofer. His mother, Josie, has had a strenuous relationship with Stu, who constantly beat her and her kids, Drew and Kiera, her 14-year-old daughter. But Josie has had a life of hard rocks, never able to support herself, five-and-dime jobs, and no place to live. Shacking up with a deputy in the city of Clanton, Mississippi seemed like a good thing if it meant having a roof over their heads. All she had to do was keep wearing tight-fitting jeans and giving Stuart sex whenever he wanted it. Until it was not enough. Believing Stuart would now kill his sister and him; Drew does the unimaginable. He kills Deputy Stuart Kofer with his own gun, in his own home, and while he was passed out, lying drunk on his own bed. Justifiable homicide? Capital murder? The electric chair? Life imprisonment? Nothing is off the table and Judge Noose has no one who wants the case. Especially a capital murder case the county will only pay chicken-feed wages to the lawyer facing long hours of work on a case that is sure to bring down the townsfolk against him. Good luck with finding a reasonable jury and even more luck receiving a change of venue from Judge Noose. After being strong-armed into defending Drew Gamble, Jake's passion and desire to be seen as a successful trial lawyer kick in. He assembles his team to put together a defense of young Drew in hopes of keeping him out of prison and going to the electric chair. But the evidence against young Drew is overwhelming. The prosecution has the gun in evidence, the boy's confession, along with his fingerprints. Not to forget how the town of Clanton is in an uproar over Jake Brigance handling the defense. His successful win 5 years earlier over the Carl Lee Hailey trial did not win him points with the city white folk, who do not want to see a young boy off the hook from murdering a popular city deputy. Will Jake be able to defend his young client and keep him out of prison and the electric chair. Will he get paid for his work, which is a concern considering his mounting debt and struggling law practice. With time running out, Jake and his team are going to need a lot more than a good defense. They are going to need mercy. I've got to catch up on the Jake Brigance series. I've read 'A Time to Kill,' but missed 'Sycamore Row' and the 4th book in his series. I loved the movie and would like to see Matthew McCaughey and the rest of the cast return to their roles. They were so convincing. Naturally, the author's tongue and cheek writing keep you turning the pages. John Grisham is a gifted writer, and I am certain you will enjoy this book as much as I have, if not more. Keep on reading!

"I was thrilled to see that this latest Grisham was a legal thriller. Grisham is a talented writer across the board, but his legal tales are my favorite. And this latest may well be the best of them! The plot is gripping and the execution is simply fantastic. The behind the scenes machination of a trial are fascinating. As is the actual trial. Grisham's own background as a lawyer adds so much to his books. Jake is a great lead and the supporting cast brings back supporting characters from the previous two books. Time and place are brought to life with detailed descriptions. And then there's the loaded question - is murder ever justified? I chose to listen to A Time for Mercy. The reader was Michael Beck and his narration was perfect for this title. He has created many Southern accents/drawls for the myriad cast of players. Each is just a little bit different and it's easy to know who is speaking. He also does the female/child voices very well. His interpretation of the book is simply wonderful. Beck uses his voice to wonderful effect, capturing the emotions of the characters and the action of the plot. I've said it before and I'll say it again - I become so much more immersed in a story by listening. Five stars plus for this one! I hope we see more of Jake.

John Grisham never disappoints when he writes from the court room. Everyone’s favorite lawyer Jake Brigance returns with a heart breaking story. Coming off of a big win that not everyone agreed with Brigance is looking forward to not having a bullseye on his back. It this is short lived when he is chosen to defend a young boy who has killed a crooked cop. This book will have you hooked from page one and it is heart breaking. Jake has been the best lawyer since 1989 and I was glad to read another story based on him. Hope Grisham continues to allow us to follow Jakes cases! A TIME FOR MERCY is a must read this October

Jack Brigance is a Lawyer in this sensational courtroom drama. He was in previous novels written by Grisham. This story takes place in Clayton, MS and is about 16 year old Drew. He is involved in what happened to his mom’s boyfriend. His sister testifies about the night in question during the trial and her experiences the boyfriend. Riveting, Suspenseful, Gripping! 4 stars!
Interesting enough, but I didn't think it was one of Grisham's best.
Grisham is a master storyteller. I love that Jake and all his family and friends are back. This one will make a great movie, too.
An enjoyable, twisty read. John Grishan is a master of the legal thriller.

I absolutely love Grisham’s books, and Jake Brigance is a complex, engaging character who has endured since “A Time to Kill.” Talking about white people voting: “Lazy? My people vote like hell...they’re tireless, relentless voters. The vote early, often, all day long, late, absentee, with real ballots, stuffed ballots, fake ballots. They vote dead people, crazy people, underage people, convicted felons who have no right to vote.” Sound familiar? What about”We treasure life and can all agree that it is wrong to kill...Why do so many white people love the death penalty?” As always, this Grisham book, although set in 1990, is once again so current. Bravo.

This book was wonderful. I read the audio. Now I have a feeling I may need to go back and read A Time To Kill. I remember reading and seeing the movie A Time to Kill, but the names of the folks in A Time For Mercy remind me of a TTK so much that it may be worth a trip down memory lane. I would try the audio this time instead of the paperback. Grisham is still a master storyteller, but it took a bit too long to actually get to the trial. It was never boring and it didn’t drag, but at some point I began to wonder whether there would even be a trial. I am definitely looking forward to the movie.

My goodness, can John Grisham write a good book! I absolutely loved "A Time to Kill" and "Sycamore Row". I assumed this book would be great as well. And I was right, because this book is fantastic! That being said, this is my least favorite book in the trilogy, despite it getting a near perfect rating, but I'll explain that in a few paragraphs. This book is different because it doesn't really deal with race relations like the first two books did. However, the feeling of anger and visceral reaction that this book elicits from the audience is just as palpable. The whole discussion of the Death Penalty is just so well demonstrated. The book doesn't have any superfluous fluff, even though it has a case that I thought at the beginning would be just filler. The first two books were almost exclusively about one case, while this book is primarily about one case, but has another one hiding in the background. What this book does so well is make me, someone who is pro-law enforcement and pro-death penalty actively root against both in this book. Very impressive for an author to make me root against my morals. This book also has some really tender moments between the characters that I loved, and a wonderful pro-life message. The circumstances behind the conception of one character are certainly horrible, and yet Grisham lays out a compelling case for life without actually arguing it. Some of the characters argue it, but Grisham simply lets the story unfold, and it naturally presents this pro-life angle that I really liked, especially since it dovetails nicely with the whole death penalty discussion. As always, the laws and procedures of courtrooms frustrate me. The whole point is to get context and information, and yet they are constantly limiting it in some contest to see who can get the most objections and least out of the witnesses. My only problem really with the book comes to its ending. I thought that the endings for books one and two were masterful. Book two's ending was a little frustrating, but still masterful. Here, I can't really explain why I dislike it without going into spoilers, but lets just say I don't like the way Grisham resolves everything.... That being said, overall this is a top-notch novel. I cannot wait to read more John Grisham books in the future (next on my shelf is "The Runaway Jury"). But for now, I give "A Time for Mercy" a 9.5 out of 10!

So disappointing, as I loved Time to Kill years ago. The book felt hastily/sloppily written (overuse of the passive voice and lots of paraphrasing and “tell” instead of “show” moments) and extensive use of flat, undeveloped, and/or token characters. The most glaring problem to me, though, is the covert (and sometimes overt) sexism. Women are frequently described in terms of appearances (vs. descriptions of male character’s successes/actions...was it really necessary to describe how Libby looked, or to include Jake’s perspective that she is *almost* attractive...gross!), and any successes women enjoy (as with Portia’s character) are *because* of male support/assistance. Carla (who is a teacher with her own profession) is often found in the kitchen, preparing food or coffee for the men, dismissively does “girl stuff” (p. 297), and hangs on the fringe of Jake’s team and only knows about courtroom/legal affairs “because she was married to a criminal defense lawyer” (p. 354). The Gambles are also treated as token poor people in need of saving by the strapping Brigance, rather than as actual human beings. Won’t even get into issues of race or the abortion debate and how the Brigances pressure the poor, poor Gambles into taking on their perspective on abortion. Ugh. However, I will give it to John Grisham that he knows how to write courtroom scenes. This was the (only) highlight of the book for me.

J. D. Robb (pseudonym for Nora Roberts) infuses murder, suspense, and drama in Encore in Death , a well-written futuristic police procedural set in New York City featuring Lieutenant Eve Dallas with the NYC police department and set around 2061. Celebrity couple Eliza Lane and Brant Fitzhugh throw a party on the night before Brant is scheduled to leave for New Zealand. He is producing and starring in a movie being filmed there while Eliza is set for the role of a lifetime on Broadway. Eve Dallas arrives after Brant toasted Eliza, fell to the floor, and died. The drink that killed him was originally intended for Eliza. Which of them was the target? With over 200 guests, staff, and servers, it’s not going to be easy to identify the killer. Time spent with Eve, Delia (Eve’s partner), Roarke (Eve’s husband), and Eve’s colleagues is always entertaining. The main characters are compelling and three-dimensional. Eve’s need to serve and protect comes through in every book, but the underlying impetus for this is best understood by reading this series in order. As always, the interactions between Eve and Roarke are enjoyable and bring a different facet of Eve’s personality to light. Several of the recurring police characters play significant roles in this book, and readers get to see a bit of their private lives. I also enjoyed seeing Delia take on more responsibility in this story line. The prose is well-written and engaging. The plot is thought-provoking and tragic. While this book has some action, it is mostly a police procedural. Robb usually manages to weave humor in her novels, providing some much needed levity to offset some of the more serious and grim aspects of the story. The humor manages to bring out Eve’s personality. Everything from phrases she doesn’t understand, to her reactions to the loud clothing worn by her colleagues and to a candy thief make her more relatable. The author brings strong characters, great plots, wonderful relationships, and excellent pacing to the series. Woven through the novel are threads of caring for others, friendship, relationships, ego, glamour, careers, leadership, and trust. Overall, this novel was a twisty tale with great characterization that kept me turning the pages. If you enjoy engaging near-future police procedurals, then I recommend this series. This is the fifty-sixth book in the In Death Eve Dallas series and I have read all of them up to this point. I can’t wait to read the next book in the series. St. Martin’s Press and J.D. Robb provided a digital ARC of this novel via NetGalley. Opinions expressed in this review are completely my own and are not biased in any way. Publication date was February 7, 2023. This review was originally posted at Mystery and Suspense Magazine. ---------------------------------------- My 4.88 rounded to 5 stars review is coming soon.

IMHO this is the weakest of the series... and I'm so very sorry to say it!!! I love this series and all the characters, but most of all I love the crimes and the reasons behind them. Here, unfortunately, the crime was and the whys were really, really weak! Also the way Eve got her clues was fortuitous to say the best! I hope the next one will be better... I really hope...

3.5 stars: There was too much slow build in the middle, but once things started moving, I couldn't stop reading. This is an interesting take (IMO) on THE MIRROR CRACK'D FROM SIDE TO SIDE by Agatha Christie in terms of its premise

This is book 56 in the in Death series and it remains good which is pretty amazing given how long it has been out. This one wasn’t the best in the series in my opinion but I did still enjoy it. I think my favorite part was Roarke giving the armor to Dallas’ squad for an anniversary present. This was the moment when they truly fit. This one took longer to get into than most. Dallas is called to the murder of an actor at a party that he and his wife had thrown for their friends. The mystery was ok, but wasn’t the twistiest I had seen. I did like the connections to the long past mystery, it was interesting. Overall I gave this one 4.5 stars which I rounded up because I do love the characters and this series overall so much.

I really liked this one!! At a big, exclusive party, someone is poisoned. Its cyanide. Roarke outdoes himself with his gift to Eve on their anniversary!! I always think to myself ‘wow, time surely moves slowly in their universe!’ Glad of it!!

3.5 stars "We compromised, and still do, though that doesn’t always come easy for us. Love doesn’t hang on conditions, but marriage bloody well hangs on compromise.” Book 56 guys. Each time I finished a book in this series, it always feel like I've accomplished something. And I actually did enjoy this one far more than I expected, despite having a certain actor/actress element being a big part of it. The case was also a pretty straightforward with a few little twists and many lies. As always, the characters were the stars of the book, while the police procedural thing comes second. Nothing much happened, characters-wise, but still it's like coming home. I guess I was just in the perfect mindset for this one.

56 books in and I still really enjoy this series. Still love the narrating style of the audio book. It's a really fast read. This time, Eve, Peabody, Rourke, and the rest of the crew are investigating the poisoning death of an A-list star. It's fascinating the different angles that Eve has to navigate to solve the murder. As an avid reader of the series, I also really enjoy the running gags - like Jenkinson's ties and the thief who keeps stealing Eve's hidden candy bar in her office.

Standard, below par Eve Dallas book. Well written and formulaic, but the story fails to stand the test of logical reasoning in the central scene. This is the one where Eve intuits who she thinks the killer is. That chain of thinking is weak and hinges purely on "instinct". If investigators everywhere used their "instincts" like that, God help the innocents who get caught in the cross-fire. There's a deliberation about the writing in the first chapter leading upto the murder and Eve's introduction, it looks like it was "bolted on" with thinly buried clues, purely to substantiate the eventual killer. It seems like the author wrote herself into a dead-end, then used the investigators "instinct" to force fit another central character into the role of the killer and finally edited in a bunch of cues and clues in the first chapter to tie it together. Like a recipe with salt sprinkled on instead of cooked in.... its not bad, but its missing something in terms of smoothness and flow. This book is the straw that breaks my personal value for money equation - the reason I stop reading JD Robb, 20 years after I started, with "Seduction in death" in 2002. The quality of the writing is still great, still very visual; but the characters have stopped resonating... I suppose its fair to say that this series and this author isn't relatable anymore. I guess, I've finally outgrown her. Good bye. Thank you for 20 years of good books. It was nice while it lasted!

I enjoyed this book so much! JD Robb/Nora Roberts always produces a readable, interesting book. The last 2 JD Robb books, while addressing important issues, were really too much for me to handle due to subject matter. I'm so happy that she has returned to a less traumatic murder, at least for the reader. Our favorite characters progress a bit in their lives; their interactions are amusing and endearing. The victim in this book is a well-loved actor who is poisoned at a party and there are a number of suspects. The story read well, there are enough twists and turns to keep things interesting and of course there are Dallas, Rourke and Peabody. I am just so relieved that this book was fun and terrific.

More of the same but passed the time listening. The crime was easily solved though I’ll admit wavering there somewhat, I was always strong with my initial guess. That along with no character development made a soft read. Nothing to write home about. Probably a 3 for this series but still better than some 3 star books I’ve read, so I’ll round up. Narrator was good as always.

3.5 rounded up The gang’s all back as Eve Dallas and co investigate the poisoning death of a theatre actor. Full of all the trademark wit and humor we love (I mean does it ever get old listening to Eve botch colloquialisms?) Great on audio too narrated again by Susan Ericksen. This was another entertaining murder mystery and the 56th instalment in the series even if not too much plot-wise happens to the main cast of characters other than another Eve and Rourke wedding anniversary. Long-time fans of the series are sure to be entertained!
I thoroughly enjoyed this 56th book in J.D. Robb's "In Death" series!

I obviously love this series if I’ve stuck around for 56 (!!) books. I love the near-future setting, I love the procedural setup, but most of all, I love the characters. By 56 books in with the same core cast, I know these people intimately. They feel more real to me than some people I know in real life. I also love the episodic nature, how each case is self-contained to a single book, while we get to see how the lives of the central cast are progressing and changing from book to book. This particular story deals with the celebrity world. When a hugely beloved actor dies of cyanide poisoning at the party he was throwing with his equally famous actress wife, Eve has to determine which half of the power couple was truly the intended target as she weaves through this world of glitz and glamour and long-held grudges. Just because you’re famous doesn’t mean you aren’t willing to get your hands dirty for revenge’s sake if opportunity presents itself. I found the central story of this particular installment a bit lackluster in comparison to some other books in the series. However, I readily admit that this is due in large part to the fact that I am in no way enamored with the celebrity realm. I see what Roberts was doing with this installment, though. The past few books have dealt with heavy, dark, disturbing content, and this provided a bit of a breather for both the reader and the characters. Even if I wasn’t deeply invested in the case, there were a few interesting twists, and I’m always incredibly happy to catch up with the characters.

Brant Fitzhugh has fallen to his death, and quite naturally, his widow is traumatized. She is certain he was murdered but cannot imagine why. Detective Eve Dallas is on the case. Was he the intended victim, or was his wife Eliza the actual target? Cyanide poisoning in a glass of champagne was the cause of death. Brant was well-liked. His death makes absolutely no sense. He was happily married. Both Brant and Eliza are in the entertainment business. With the harmony in their marriage, their schedules were usually in sync. However, Brant has a project that will take him away to New Zealand for six months. Eliza will be playing a role in a revival of successful play on Broadway so she cannot travel with Brant. In the case of the In Death series, Nora Roberts has written it under her pseudonym, J. D. Robb. I just love her books and have read every single book in this series, including the two that follow, Payback in Death and Random in Death . Everything about this book is wonderful. Whether the drama of discovering who murdered Brant, to Eve and husband's Roarke's amazing relationship, from Eve's relationship with her coworkers, most notably, Peabody, this book packs a wallop. Then I love Eve's sense of humor, and her level of snark, and how she often wonders aloud why certain phrases are what they are - like why is a driveway called a driveway. With a delightful mystery, great characters, solid intrigue and a conclusion that one might not expect, this book definitely rated a solid five stars. Many thanks to St. Martin's Press and to NetGalley for this ARC for review. This is my honest opinion.

I realize my opinion will not be popular but I was not impressed with this book. I love the series but every once in a while I feel like there is a sub par entry and this is one. First of all, the method of murder is redundant. Exact same scenario as used in a previous book. The author could have at least made up a new poison. Its the future; invent something. Too many poorly developed supporting players also. I didn't care about any of them. I will admit that the twist of the hiding place for the poison at the end did make me like the character of Sylvie more. That was a good plot twist. There was also a part where Roarke references a certain HBO show and says that he thinks Eve would like it. I found this very unbelievable for the character as that show has many, many triggers in it that a victim of child abuse/rape/incest like Eve would NOT enjoy and he would know this. There is no way he would suggest she would like it. I just didn't think the book flowed well and there were too many redundant plot points very similar to previous books. I found it boring. There was literally no action in it. Roarkes anniversary present to Eve was also very predictable; anyone who pays attention to the books knows he has been working on that. Below average offering for this series. The case is so-so and takes a long time to resolve even though I suspected who the killer was from the beginning. Pretty good! It wasn't a favorite, but a solid entry to the series.
3.5 stars - Crime/Mystery/Futuristic/Police Procedural

Save your money.... I have purchased every book in the Death series by Nora Roberts. Boring This is the last JD Robb book I will be spending hard earned money on. This one dragged for me and I was pretty sure who the murderer was early on. All caught up! so grateful because I can take a break!

Reading a new In Death story is like coming home, like wrapping myself in a soft warm blanket and sinking into its comfort. Sure, I first came to these stories for the mysteries, and I still thoroughly enjoy the clever plots, the imaginative crimes and motives, and the riveting conclusions. But the characters—Eve, Roarke, Peabody, McNab, etc—and the interactions between them appeal to me at least as much as those crimes and investigations. Eve questioning common sayings never fails to amuse me just as I always have to concede she actually has a point. We do say a lot of weird things without ever questioning them (unless our name is Eve Dallas 😊). And, as always, Robb delivered. The crime was imaginative and the investigation riveting. The cast of secondary characters was colourful and fascinating. If I missed anything in this story, it was an update on the house Peabody and McNab are renovating seen through Eve’s eyes. I also wouldn’t have minded Mavis and Leonardo making an appearance in this story. But apart from that, I just lost myself in this tale. The pages almost turned themselves and I found it next to impossible to put the book down. 56 books in, I’m still not getting bored with this series and I have a hard time imagining I ever will. In fact, the only other thing I want to add here is: is it September yet? (view spoiler)

I have all of 'death in' books, a lot of them in hardback. However I think the author has strayed from what I particularly want - the personal bits of the story. I love to read about Roarke, Mavis, Peabody, Feeney, Nadine, even Somerset. The latest books have, at best, a passing reference to them. I have always preordered the hardback version, even starting to read it on the way home as so excited. The last half dozen or so books are such a disappointment that this time I decided to read it online - I have all the others as hard copy but I guessed I wouldn't re-read this book. I am so glad that I didn't pay almost £20 for this book. Yes, it was okay BUT I sussed out the killer pretty quickly. Wouldn't have worried about this fact but I personally read these books mainly for the interaction between Eve and her friends and colleagues. To be honest a computer could have written this one. A 'plot' (which was fine), but then only a passing reference to Peabody, Mira, Somerset, etc, bit of romance with Roarke but absolutely no comparison to her earlier books - which by the way I often re-read because they were brilliant. So disappointed with this but although I will not continue to blindly buy this series I will definitely continue to re-read the earlier books which were absolutely brilliant!

56 books...who would've ever believed that a series could run that long? Thing is, I have enjoyed each and every one. Some more than others, but that doesn't matter. What matters is JD Robb/Nora Roberts can write! She has created characters that I love dearly & look forward to checking in with. Even better, she remains true to these characters, doesn't fold under the pressure of people who want "more this, more that, she should have a baby bullsh*t". For that, I am extremely grateful. There have been other series, with strong, interesting female leads, that other authors have just ruined by turning them into whiny, weak, weepy, miserable women who sleep with anyone and everyone because "that's what women do" or "that's what's expected of them" or whatever lame excuse they come up with, and it's complete and utter rubbish! Book 57 comes out in September, and I cannot wait!

Mystery - Police procedural After 56 books in the series, there isn't much left to say. These characters are like old friends that you visit a few times a year. This book mostly features Eve, Roarke and Peabody. The other players are still around, but don't feature in this story. Eve is called in after an A-list celebrity dies at a party. He drinks a cocktail that seems as if it was intended for his wife and dies of cyanide poisoning. The rest of the novel is really a police procedural of Eve following up and clearing every possible avenue to reveal the murderer. This was another very solid addition to the series.

While this is typical Eve Dallas - catch a high profile case, investigate thoroughly, step on lots of toes, then throw in sides of Roarke, Peabody, and Co - the drama of the movie stars was different enough and so entertaining it was worth bumping to the top of my book pile.
I didn’t finish this book. “Life is too short to finish books you’re not enjoying”- Goodreads podcast.

When a mega vid star dies of cyanide in the middle of a party by sipping the drink of his mega Broadway star wife, Eve is called in to unravel the clues and bring the murderer to justice. Only, most of the suspects are actors who lie for a living. Not being sure who the intended victim was, Eve and her team have to explore all the angles. Brant Fitzhugh didn't have enemies. Even his ex-wife loved him. Eliza Lake, however, wasn't that nice. She was demanding, a micromanager, and a perfectionist. She had an obsessed fan and a number of bitter rivals. And the drink was made for her. I enjoyed this story very much. I liked the way the police tracked down the evidence to find the real culprit. I love the way Eve interacts with her team of dedicated homicide detectives. Her relationship with Peabody is growing to be more of a relationship between equals with each book. I also love seeing Eve's relationship with Roarke develop as the series progresses.

Encore in Death by J.D.Robb is the 56th book in the In Death series. A party held by celebrity couple Eliza Lane and Brabt Fitzhugh sees Brant die after toasting his wife with a champagne cocktail laced with cyanide. Another brilliant book in the series. Eve and Roarke's relationship continues to grow and Peabody's decorating plans develop further. I love catching up with all the characters and this book sees Roarke Industries presenting the homicide squad with lightweight protective garments to aid in their safety. The candy thief again makes a particularly sneaky strike. A superb mystery expertly solved by Eve and her team.

Once again, the author has woven the world of Dallas and Roarke with a mystery that keeps you guessing and you might get it right, but you might not! I often have it figured out, but I got tripped by a red herring that I thought the author was leading you away from! I love the witty banter, the interpersonal relationships and the well wrapped mystery that is always presented in these books. The narration is so freaking fabulous that you forget that you are listening to a book instead of standing amongst the characters listening to them carry on a conversation. I absolutely love this series and it remains my number one favorite must listen series of all time!

Twists and Turns Abound In This Installment! Eve Dallas novels are my comfort reads, and this one didn't disappoint! It had a very unexpected plot, and a lot of twists and turns to find out who wound up doing the heinous murder. I definitely wasn't expecting the reveal on that front! The characters were very engaging, and I could swear that they were right in front of me, as if they were playing parts in a movie! The pacing was a bit off for me, as it moved slower than I'd like, but all in all, it was a great read!

Usually, I'm all pumped to read a new Eve Dallas Book, but not so much in the recent past. There's a sameness to the plot of the story, practically no fillers or side stories. I would have given this one 2.5 if I was able to.

Another fantastic instalment In the magnificent In Death series this sci fi crime thriller series is absolutely phenomenal to read, I love the characters of Eve, Roarke, Summerset, Galahad, Peabody, mcnab, Baxter, true heart, Mira, Whitney. I loved how in every book takes us on a journey alongside Eve as age follows clues and leads to capturing criminals and bringing them to justice. This series is highly entertaining and enjoyable books to read. Successful actors and husband and wife Eliza Lane and Brant are hosting an A list filled party for Eliza’s latest achievement she’s doing a revival of the play upstage which she originally played the daughter character which boosted her to stardom twenty five years earlier but the party ends in tragedy after the toast Brant collapses to the ground dead. Roarke helps Eve with her case and discover the cyanide connection to Eliza the nephew of Eliza’s Staff who is a metalworker artist, Debra is found dead from cyanide poisoning and keep it quiet to not alert Eliza of their suspicions, they interview Tyler the artist who admits Eliza has been in his studio and was alone for a few moment’s because he’s working on a piece for her, he checks his cyanide and notices some missing, they visit Sylvie and check the room Eliza was staying in and finds a vial of cyanide hidden in a toy teapot in her grandchild playroom horrified by this tells Eve that Eliza wasn’t happy that Brant was going away for six months to produce a movie instead of staying and supporting Eliza as she does the upstage revival.
