** The Stephen King Goodreads Discussion Group is doing a re-read of his works from the beginning to the end. It’s been a long time since I have really immersed myself in Uncle Stevie’s world, but a rate of a book a month, I am all in. My goal is to read and review each one with as much honesty and reflection that I can give. ** Background – “Holly” was originally published in September 2023 as a Scribner hardcover. Length-wise - my original hardcover lists it as 449 pages and my Kindle lists it as 454 pages. Plotline – This continues the story of Holly Gibney, one of King’s most unique and empathetic characters ever. Holly is currently the owner and lead investigator of Finders Keepers Investigations Agency. When it the book begins, Holly is having a tough time. Business is tough in the early post-Covid world. Her partner, Pete Huntley, is sick with Covid. Her Uncle Henry is suffering from dementia and living in an elder care facility. And her selfish and more-than-complex, mother, Charlotte, has just passed away. Holly is just trying to get through the funeral services and keep her business afloat. Then Holly receives a call from a very desperate woman named Penelope Dahl. Penelope’s daughter, Bonnie, has gone missing in medium-sized college town. For some reason Holly cannot turn away from helping her and agrees to look into Bonnie’s mysterious disappearance. While Holly begins her investigation, we are introduced to some of the faculty members of Bell College of Arts and Sciences. Living nearby are Professors emeritus, Rodney and Emily Harris. Both are very successful academic stalwarts, Rodney teaching Life Sciences and Emily teaching English Literature. They have been married for many years, examples of respectability and devotion. Although semi-retired, they have some unique habits and deadly secrets that they are hiding from everyone. The problem for Holly is that their secrets may somehow tie to her search for a mother’s missing daughter. What Holly doesn’t know is that Rodney and Emily are very smart, conniving, and have a dark side… What Holly does discover is that Bonnie is not the only person to go missing in the same area… The question is why? Who is taking them? And more importantly, can Holly connect the dots before she becomes the next victim? Thoughts and Reflections – Let me say right up front, I really enjoyed this book. The plotting, pacing, and tension throughout worked well for me. There just didn’t seem to be any slow spots or wandering too far off on unnecessary paths. For me, King had everything mapped out structurally well – a major mystery leading the way, along with several supporting sub-plots that involving Holly, Jerome, Barbara, and Pete, that all intertwined together in a very well delivered reading experience. It started as a slow boil laying the groundwork and background, heated up throughout the middle, and then delivered a strong climactic ending over the last 80 pages that left me with a very satisfied and happy reader. This novel reminded me a lot of King’s prior Bill Hodges trilogy in many ways. Those books introduced Holly as a minor character, and as King has often stated, she subtly took over and grew into an interesting and uniquely dysfunctional lead character. This book was similar to those in style, plotting, rhythm, and character development. I found the murder mystery to be interesting and compelling, but not for the usual reasons. The guilty party (or parties) are given away early in the book, but the driving factors for committing the crimes are the focal point that drives the mystery. In addition, the bad guy(s) are not super strong villains, but King makes them crafty and ferocious in their own exclusively disturbed ways. The way King lays out this story and then peels the onion throughout the entire book, and even into the epilogue, makes this worthwhile reading. What really makes it work for me, is that King delivers situations and moments that challenge and stretch Holly, forcing her to become stronger and heroic in her own ways. She has become our quiet example and hero as she follows her intuition, develops personal indomitable spirit, and refuses to surrender to the bad things in life. King’s use of Holly’s mother’s death and their conflicting relationship history provides a symbiotic connection and motivation in her ongoing investigation. One feeds the other and vice-versa. For me, Holly really comes across in this book as a combination of the television characters of Columbo and Monk, but then she breaks the model into one that is her absolutely her own. I also enjoyed Jerome and his sister, Barbara’s storylines regarding their writing and publishing successes, and especially Barbara’s mentoring and support from the poet, Olivia Kingsbury. I really connected with Olivia’s freewill personality and frank demeanor. We all want someone like her in our lives to talk to and help motivate us when we need it the most. In addition, Penelope (Bonnie’s mom) had to be one of the most annoying and selfish side characters I have ever experienced. However, she was desperately needed to move the plot forwards in several key moments. Yet, she was a large pain to deal with. And I cannot forget dear old Roddy and Emily Harris. As a nutritionist, Roddy seems to have never met a type of meat that he doesn’t like. As for Emily, she is a beast. A self-centered, psychotic who brings on a whole new level of bat-crap-crazy. She makes Annie Wilkes (from “Misery”) sound somewhat sane and rational. Just saying… Now let’s deal with the elephant in the room. There have been a lot of concerns and criticisms expressed about the numerous Covid and Trump references in the book. I saw a lot of negative feedback regarding the abundant use of these topics in social media. It seems that there are those who were turned off by them, especially with King’s public dislike of Trump. I am not going to take any sides on that and just respect that everyone has their own opinion. I will just speak for myself and say that I get what King was trying to do in using the time of Covid and strong political conflicts as integral elements of his story. The challenge is that using a very polarizing situation and divisive time in our country also unfortunately makes us relive conflicting issues and deep emotions that we really want to have moved on from. Painful issues that we would prefer to see in the review mirror and not have to live through again. For some readers, this may cause a less than enjoyable reading experience, and even potentially border on bad memories. Do I think King used some of his political references too much? Maybe… Probably… And I can see others being sensitive to that. Again, each person has their own opinion and I respect that. I won’t argue or disagree. For me personally, I didn’t let the references or comments take away from the story being told and will wisely I will leave it at that. P.S. There was a specific chilling moment that I loved so much. I will call it a combination “Dexter” TV show / slash / “Misery” Annie Wilkes moment. That should be enough of a clue to those who have read the book (if not, just ask me in a message and I will share it). Other Notes – “Holly” is the sixth book or novella that features the character of Holly Gibney, and King has publicly mentioned that he is working on another novel with her in the lead role. That book will hopefully be published in the next year or two, depending on the publisher’s schedule. Overall – As mentioned fairly extensively above, I enjoyed this book quite a bit and give it a strong 4 star read. I am also not surprised to hear that King is working on another “Holly” novel. He just cannot let go of her. And truth be told, neither can I. Bring on the next Holly adventure! I cannot wait.

Hot damn! Is there ANYTHING Uncle Stevie canNOT turn into a horror novel (with or without a supernatural element)?! Holly, the now boss of "Finders Keepers" and successful PI, is hired by the mother of a young woman that has been missing for a while since the police are no help. But it's the middle of the pandemic so things are all a little ... skewed ... and Holly doesn't have her full team to help her either. This is made all the more dangerous when considering who her adversaries are this time. Not gonna spoiler more, but whether or not there is a supernatural element doesn't really matter with Uncle Stevie on the job. The meticulous modus operandi and veritable depravity were flabbergasting. However, as usual, it was more than the actual adversaries that made me shudder while reading this story: everyone had something to hide and many people were just so ... mean. A very mundane word nevertheless describing perfectly what is wrong with so many people. Prideful stupidity supposed to mask inadequacy but really only highlighting it and just how bad some people are. As fans know, the most shudder-inducing aspect of any SK story is not the fictitious part but the real-life cruelty humans are capable of. From the casual cruelty of on-the-fly comments to emotional abuse to physical violence. And don't get me started on how sick so many people are (about everything from religion to "race" to nutrition to sexuality or younameit). Of course, then there is the shock of actual (view spoiler). That was very nicely done although I was a bit puzzled that we had gotten so much information from the get-go. Believe me, though: it didn't mar my enjoyment at all and it didn't reduce the suspense either. The unease is as much part of the story as punctuation. A little preventive message to anyone reading this: If you're part of the host of Karens trying to denounce Stephen King for having included comments on Covid and Trump, don't bother spewing your nonsense here. I'm vaxxed, I can personally attest to Covid not being like any other flu, Trump is so inadequate (regarding EVERYTHING) that he deserves nothing BUT ridicule, and I will simply delete your comments and not give you any floor for your tantrums. Also: grow up. Funny how you call others snowflakes when it is you yourself who acts the most like one. There. Now back to the book. As you can tell from the disclaimer above, there has been a rabid response to this book. People have down-rated it, maybe even without having read it. I don't know and I don't care. I have read the book and can tell you that it is my second-favorite of the modern ones (the favorite being The Outsider). Now, that doesn't mean too much considering the quality of SK's writing, but it might give you a good idea. Detailed, suspenseful, highly atmospheric, with fantastic characters and great worldbuilding.

I always learn something from King’s books. In “Holly,” I learned that even though you are in your eighties, you can still have a huge impact on other’s lives. It’s not’s too late to take up new things like remodeling your basement or find a passion for food preparation and cooking. ;) “Holly” is a straight up crime novel – none of King’s signature supernatural in this tale. We follow a well-known King character – Holly Gibney. She has appeared in “If It Bleeds,” “End of Watch,” “Finders Keepers,” and originally in “Mr. Mercedes.” In prior books, Holly is depicted as a bright, shy, but courageous character, with OCD and some emotional baggage. She is a strong character and carries the novel. I mean this book has no mysterious supernatural element. There is plenty of creepiness and evil, but nothing paranormal. There is little mystery either, as the narrator is omnipotent, and we see both sides of the equation play out. The action is light, although there is a healthy parfait of suspense. The villains are fairly typical these days – racist and narcissistic psychopaths. The twists and turns are fairly limited for a crime novel – I was never shocked about a turn of events (although the crimes are certainly shocking). I also didn’t enjoy the fact that it was set during Covid-19, who wants to relive that! So, let’s summarize, little mystery, no paranormal, light on action, no big revelations, and it dragged me back though living the pandemic. But guess what, I still enjoyed it. Why, King’s character building is top notch here. Holly is as real a character as you’ll find, and the side characters are strong and unique. King pulls us deep into Holly mind, and that makes for good storytelling. There’s also a bit of nostalgia, connecting back to the past novels that Holly was in. Basically, King makes you like his characters, then lets your root for them, and finally puts them in peril. It works. Four blood dripping stars for this suspenseful detective novel. In my opinion, it’s doesn’t crack his top ten, but if you enjoy deep character development, you’ll eat-up this book.
Phenom. Can’t wait for the next installment

"Just when you think you've seen the worst human beings have to offer, you find out you're wrong. There is no end to evil." Some characters and settings in a story are the equivalent of a cozy blanket, that is what this book felt like to me. Comforting, yet horrifying in equal measure. Be forewarned....If you think you've seen some outlandish dietary plans, just wait till you meet Emily and Rodney Harris.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ In Holly, the master of horror returns to his signature blend of psychological horror and suspense, crafting a chilling narrative that delves into the complexities of evil and the human psyche. The story centers around Holly Gibney, our beloved character (please Steve, don´t kill her in the next book 😭) As Holly embarks on a perilous investigation, the narrative unfolds with a palpable sense of dread, revealing the dark underbelly of society and the insidious nature of obsession. The villain is meticulously crafted, embodying the kind of malevolence that lingers long after the last page is turned. Personally, I give a fuck people who said that this is one of the most political expose from our dear author. Guys, every speech, story, book, and narrative has political involvement, and COVID was (is?) a perfect trigger to express a lot of shit, so, this is a book and not a campaign declamation. Whatever. What sets Holly apart is King’s exploration of trauma and resilience. The characters are deeply flawed yet relatable, each battling their own demons while confronting an external horror that threatens their very existence. King masterfully intertwines personal struggles with the overarching narrative, offering a poignant commentary on the darkness that resides within us all. As the tension mounts, the story becomes a relentless descent into fear, leaving readers breathless and haunted. King’s ability to evoke dread and empathy simultaneously is a testament to his mastery of the genre. Anyway, this is a harrowing tale that explores the depths of evil and the strength of the human spirit, Holly is a gripping and unsettling read that will resonate with fans of King’s darker works. Long live the King!!

4.5 stars The Bill Hodges triology is one of my favourite things King has ever written. Holly is one of the main reasons why I love that series so much. So when I found out she was getting her own full-length novel, I couldn't have been more excited. Was I disappointed? Definitely not! Holly is a grizzly, dark detective novel. It's tight, it's compelling, and it's too the point. The opening chapter had me hooked from the very first word. I very much enjoyed delving deeper into Holly's character and her wider relationships. Does she still have her quirks? Absolutely, but I don't find these as annoying as other people seem to. The plot of this book is excellent. It's a true classic detective story with a brutally gripping storyline that hooked me until the dramatic close. The only reason I couldn't give this book a full five-star rating was because of covid. While I totally understand King's reasoning to set this book during the pandemic, I found the references tiresome and didn't find they contributed a lot to the overall story. Nonetheless, this book has lots of classic Kingisms, which constant readers will no doubt be on the hunt for. For existing Holly fans, this book will definitely delight and hopefully be able to convert a few Holly naysayers, too. Highly recommend.

Holly, Stephen King When I heard that Stephen King was writing a book about Holly I was so excited. Readers of his Mr Mercedes trilogy, The Outsider and Let It Bleed, will have been following along with Holly Gibney’s journey, from a woman who lived at home with her mother and was scared of the outside world, to a woman who is now running a successful business, pretty much on her own. In Holly, we learn so much more about this much loved character. She is loving through a pandemic, which is causing her no end of anxiety with masks, shaking hand and sanitiser. She has just lost her mother, with whom she had a very complicated relationship. Her business partner, Pete is out with Covid and she is grieving. She needs something to take her mind off her mother and what she learns after her death. So she takes in a missing persons case. What at first looks to be a simple case, turns into anything but easy. One missing person leads Holly to discover many others, all with similar stories. Of course it is dangerous, but Holly beat Brady Hartsfield, she can do anything. Ok, King fans, this is dark and seriously messed up. It was stomach churning at times, everything that we have come to expect from this author. If you are not ready for a book set smack bang in the middle of the pandemic, give this a miss. There is a lot of Covid talk, a lot of political talk. For me, it fit with the story and didn’t bother me. Each to their own. I loved that we also saw Jerome and Barbara back again, getting on with their lives after the horrific events in If It Bleeds. The combination of these 3 characters working together made me smile. It was just so nice to back in this world again and I hope that the author will continue to give up more in the future. A massive thank you to Hachette Australia for sending me this book. It was one that I started straight away and took my time with. Throughly enjoyed it. Holly is out now.

I’m just gonna say it: Stephen King’s “Holly” is the best damn novel I’ve read this year, and I’ve read some damn good ones. It took a few months of being on a waiting list at the library to finally get it, and when I did, I think I literally devoured the thing in two days. It’s that frickin’ good. Holly Gibney has quickly become my new favorite detective and, I daresay, my first ever literary crush. I’ll be honest: I used to chuckle and roll my eyes when I’d read about my fellow Goodreads friends crushing on a character in a book. I mean, I’ve become emotionally invested in a lot of characters over the years, but I don’t think I could honestly say that I’ve crushed on one. Until now. Holly is a badass. She’s also funny, super-smart, socially awkward, and vulnerable as hell. It’s also been fun to see her character evolve, from the timid neighbor in “Mr. Mercedes” with no confidence, to the brilliant Sherlock-Holmesian detective of “The Outsider”. In “Holly”, she has a lot of stuff going on in her life. Her mother just recently passed away, and she has conflicting feelings about it, because while she loved her mom, they didn’t always get along. When the estate lawyer drops a bombshell on her, Holly is forced to see her mother in a new light, and it’s not necessarily a good one. It’s also deep into the pandemic, July 2021. Covid-19 has taken the lives of several people she knows (her mom being one), and her partner at the Finders Keepers Detective Agency, Pete, is sick in the hospital with it, despite being double-vaxed. Living through the pandemic has been tough on Holly—-a germaphobe long before it was cool—-but she’s managed to endure. And thrive. She’s finding out that she’s tougher than she ever thought, which is good, considering her new case. The mother of a young girl who has gone missing hires Holly to find her. Not a lot of clues, but Holly is good at seeing things other people miss. After just a few days of digging, Holly suspects that she may have stumbled on to a serial killer in her own neighborhood. She has, but they are not at all what she—-nor the reader—-expects. I can’t in good conscience say more. I can say that I’m well aware of all the whiny bitching people have made over this book, and here’s my two cents: If you believe that the pandemic is a hoax, you are a fucking moron. If you are an anti-vaxxer, you are a fucking moron. If you are of the belief that the shutdowns, masks, hand-sanitizing, social distancing, and all the other inconvenient stuff that we had to endure during the last three years were a personal affront, worthless, or a violation of your civil liberties, YOU ARE A FUCKING MORON. Okay, I’ve said my peace. (It’s been building for a couple years now.) Thanks for letting me vent…

Holly is a very good detective story, with some very suspenseful sequences and clever twists and turns. The character is still delightful and fascinating despite the developments and changes she's undergone in the previous adventures in which she's been involved, as are most of her friends and associates. While it's a straight crime story with no supernatural element, King liberally sprinkles some references for his Constant Readers throughout the novel: for example, on page 29 Holly tells her client that she's willing to take payment via Master or Visa or personal check, but not Amex, because they're difficult to deal with. (If you don't remember the commercial King did back in the '80s, look on YouTube.) On page 37 the missing girl's mother tell Holly that she was a prom queen in high school, but no one dumped a bucket of blood on her. Or on page 193, the numerals in the street address add up to 19... you get the idea-- lots of Easter Eggy fun bits. As has been noted by most people posting comments, it's a very political novel set in 2021, and King shows his frustration at the reality of basic healthcare precautions and procedures being reduced to declarations of political affiliation. While I agree with almost all of what he espouses, I did think that the prevalence of the philosophy detracted from the flow of the story. Near the end of the book, on page 442, he makes some puissant observations on the nature of evil which illuminate his ideas about the differences in supernatural horrors and human wickedness, which should mollify readers expecting or desiring a supernatural element. He observes that the human kind is worse, because it comes from within rather than any outside that could be blamed. It's a captivating book, and King is still the master storyteller he always was. I hope Holly has another case to solve soon.

Not a fan. 90% political talk. King should’ve left it alone as a short story. I know a lot of people like Holly, but she’s too self righteous for me. Was only going to give it 1 star but Olivia’s character deserves a star all her own.

The story line wasn’t bad if it wasn’t for all the covid and politics talk this book would get better ratings and more interesting to read. Its clear Stephen King is a pro Vaccine/ Biden supporter, while bashing everyone that has an apposite point of view in this novel.

SK has taken a liking to crime stories the past 15 years or so. He may have been a master writer long before that, it doesn’t mean a writer can’t get get better at it. I think SK has gotten better at writing crime since he first introduced Holly in mr. Mercedes. One thing SK has always done well was write characters that are easy to become attached to. He gives everyone he writes about enough room to expand and feel real. There was a fair bit about Covid and recent politics in this one. It’s not often to see this from SK. He has made his opinion of these matters clear long before this book. I found that that it wasn’t heavy-handed enough that it would take away from the story, no matter what your opinion on these matters are. Give that crime fiction isn’t my preferred kind of story. I’m happy to read this and SK proves that he still has it, and is always worth returning to.

3.5⭐️ Where to begin??? 😂 Okay… This was good. It got there for me… but let’s start at the beginning…. The Mr Mercedes trilogy is one of my favorite trilogies ever. When the first book came out I was so excited. That book felt DIFFERENT from other Stephen King books, but in a fun way. I was excited to read about a serial killer and detective story from King. And who emerged from that trilogy as one of the most unlikely likable characters ever??? Holly Gibney! I adore her, and her story. So here we have her own book! I was excited. This story tells the tale about a woman who comes to Holly (who is at this time running a very successful private investigation company, “Finders Keepers”) to find her missing daughter, Bonnie. We know from the beginning who most likely took her. A very creepy elderly couple who has really turned to the dark side! 😳 Can Holly find the missing girl before it’s too late?! You’ll have to read and find out! At this point, let me address the elephant in the room. This book takes place during the unfortunately very real covid pandemic. Mr King wrote this book during the pandemic. King, like many of us, has very strong feelings about the pandemic, and our leaders who were responsible for the decision making during the pandemic, and how we as humans responded to the pandemic…. And King was very angry. Listen… I get it. I worked the covid pandemic as an acute care nurse in its entirety. I was tired, I was angry, I was frustrated. I still have nightmares about the patients I lost. It was HORRIFIC. King has earned his spot in the literary world and he’s allowed to write whatever he wants and however he wants. I just felt like… his anger towards how the pandemic was handled really caused an overshadowing of Hollys story. Especially the first half of the book. I’m not saying I agree or disagree with his feelings. I’m just saying from a readers point of view, his anger took me out of his story. Again- I’m not saying his anger isn’t warranted… I understand… but I just feel like I missed out on some of Hollys story. I will say the second half was a little less politically driven and the story was able to get told. And I did enjoy the creepiness of the murderous couple! We got there… it just felt like a scenic route. 😂 sort of like this review… 😉

I absolutely loved reading this and I've loved Holly since the beginning. Which for me was The Outsider because I accidentally read that first having no knowledge of the Bill Hodges trilogy. I was less enamored with Holly this time around and I felt a little sad about it. I think this has to do with being so familiar with her and all her eccentricities over the previous five stories with her as a character. I still really enjoyed reading this one! Jerome and Barbara were awesome as always! The two villains were evil and detestable. I thought King did a great job with them! I've seen so many readers bitching and moaning about all the COVID and BLM stuff. None of that bothered me at all! I didn't feel like it took anything away from the story. This was written during the height of all that so of course it's going to play a part in the overall story. I always say this and it bears repeating here: why become an author if not to write and say whatever the hell you want?! I know I would if I was an author. Overall I thought this was a great story! It was suspenseful and thrilling especially towards the end. Holly was a total badass as always. It's impossible not to root for her and impossible not to love her! Maybe we'll get to see her again before it's all said and done!
Stephen King writes good books and bad books. This is one of his worst. I can’t believe I actually read the entire book.

4.5 ⭐️s My second time through the Hodges | Gibney series and this is still a standout entry. These books have gotten me through a particularly difficult time in my life this time around and I am so thankful that they exist. For that reason, this becomes a somewhat flawed review because I am biased towards the value they hold in my life. Sure, they aren’t perfect, and this has as many flaws as any other book in this series, but damn do I love them. Why You Should Or Shouldn’t Read It You should. It’s weird. It’s fun. It’s gross. It’s just a good procedural, detective story, choosing to leave behind some of the supernatural elements that started to drag down some of the middle portion of the series to me. So that was a welcome return to good ol’ crime noire type of storytelling Themes There is no end to evil. It comes in all forms and from all sources One Thing That Will Stick With Me Parfaits

Spending more time with King's beloved heroine, Holly Gibney, was a delight. She's center stage in this stomach-turning detective thriller that takes a long, hard look at aging and the horrifying lengths one octogenarian couple will go to in an effort to keep time from catching up to them. COVID is very prevalent in this novel. The subject itself didn't bother me, but the number of references to masks or lack of masks and vaccinated versus non-vaccinated became a distraction and slowed the urgency of the narrative. Jerome and Barbara Robinson also get their moment in the spotlight, but more for their writing success than their skills as investigators. I really enjoyed their subplots. They helped balance the sickening behavior of the villains.

It took some time for me to complete this Novel, since it didn't engages me initially with the story. Penny Dahl mother of missing Bonnie Dahl reaches out to Holly a private investigator of Finders keepers. Holly who had lost her mother during the Covid pandemic agrees to take the case but it leads to a serial killers with more than one missing person but what really happen to them. I can see Olivia character leads some how to find the killers but it was dragged a lot like a sloth. How a old couple could be such a creepy and cannibalistic, living in their own world. Wonder how some time few more Knowledgeable people are walking to a mislead path. Overall a creepy detective novel.

Five star all the way … loved every page of this was hooked and a nice easy read though not quite as nice due to Covid, abductions and cannibalism but this is what Stephen king is a master for highly recommend this book and so glad it won awards last year

Near Dark spent a lot of time talking about the past. I know that the author is capable of better. The novel also lacks the consistent mind-boggling action that i've come to expect in Scot Harvath novels. Hopefully the next novel in the series will be straight-forward and action-packed.

Maybe I've just outgrown this genre, but I could barely finish this book. It was, honestly, just boring. And also silly - guy is literally trying to drink himself to death over the very recent murder of his wife and then two seconds later he's falling for the stereotypical female sidekick. It just felt trite and formulaic and not suspenseful at all. I was an avid Mitch Rapp fan until Mills ruined that series. I've read a few of Thor's books in the hopes they would come close to Vince Flynn's writing, and I'm always disappointed. Just not for me.

Intense SPY Thriller! CIA operative Scot Horvath races against time to catch his wife's killer and save himself from assassination in this high-stakes thriller full of suspense. This is a great read with well-rounded characters and should have five stars except Thor rushed the ending like he had to get out the door for a camping trip to the Poconos which is coincidentally how I feel right now finishing up draft 1 of my second book!

Scot Harvath is in bad shape mentally, drinking to forget the devastating personal losses he suffered in the prior book, Backlash. He is lured outside a bar to fight two thugs as part of an assassination attempt, which fails only because his team arrives in time to save him. When he finds out a close Norwegian friend was tortured to death to get to him and someone has put a $100 million bounty on him, he decides to bust out of his funk. Eventually, he meets up with the female Norwegian prodigy of the dead man (Solvi), and their relationship starts to smolder. (Harvath's code name is Norseman from having bedded so many SAS flight attendants.) Things seem to point back to Russia, but it's a feint.

For whatever reason, I've missed the last couple of books in the Scot Harvath series - as in did not read. Not long after I started this one, I realized I've missed them like I miss long-lost friends. As Celine Dion sang, "It's all coming back to me now" - and I've vowed not to make the same mistake going forward. What that boils down to, in book review terms, is that I absolutely loved this one. Maybe it's because I saw a less gung-ho, more circumspect Harvath, still reeling from events that happened in previous books. There was plenty of action, but it didn't seem as rough as usual, and I sensed that Harvath's heart wasn't really in it. Besides that, the author's sometimes lengthy diatribes against some issue or other were noticeable to me in their absence. Quite honestly, all that made this book more interesting to me, but I'll venture a guess that die-hard fans might not be quite as enthusiastic. My husband - also a fan of this series - just started reading this one, and I'll be interested to get his take. As it begins, Harvath is drowning himself in his sorrows (more accurately, in substantial quantities of alcohol) in Key West when he gets bad news; a beloved colleague has been tortured and murdered. The news gets even worse: apparently, someone is offering an almost unbelievably high bounty on his own head - to be paid to the first player to achieve success. Over his years working for the Carleton Group, which functions as a more clandestine CIA, Harvath has accumulated no shortage of enemies. But is it possible that the two bad news scenarios are somehow connected? Enter beautiful and well-skilled Norwegian agent Solvi Kolstad, also a protogee of Harvath's murdered colleague and an intelligence agent, who is on the warpath to find the man's killer. What's more, she wants to hook up with Harvath and put their heads together (with a hint that a few other body parts might be shared as well somewhere down the line). The trick, you see, will be ferreting out the colleague's murderer (and, depending on who that is, who ordered the hit) while avoiding the bounty hunters who will do almost anything to snuff out Harvath for good. The sometimes bloody trail takes him and Solvi to a few countries and a few narrow escapes and culminates, I must say, in an ending that's satisfying to some characters but not to others. The conclusion to my review is a non-conclusion; I have no idea from whence my copy came. Most of the books I read I get as advance review copies from publishers via NetGalley, but this one - a hardcover edition - simply showed up in the mail with no accompanying documentation. I have a vague recollection of entering some kind of giveaway - possibly from Bookish First - but thus far I haven't been able to confirm it. So for now, all I can say is whoever you are, I thank you very much.

A Thriller? I’ve read all 19 books in the series, so I felt confident purchasing this one. Chapter 11 made me stop and post this review, something I would normally never do without finishing the book. The writing here is slow, dry and boring; lots of exposition, more like historical non-fiction than a rollicking action thriller.

I had an amazing opportunity to read an early copy of Brad Thor's next Scot Harvath release scheduled for July '20, NEAR DARK. I've read every book since Lions of Lucerne and developed into a HUGE Thor fan. At this point in Brad's career, he's in the enviable position where just about anything he writes will be received by an eager, paying crowd. At the risk of guessing a writer of his position might sooner or later fall into a pattern of repetition and 'call one in', I would be dead wrong. His novels continue to evolve and improve with each release. Hard to imagine NEAR DARK could improve on last summers smash hit, BACKLASH. But it does. What Brad does this time is put you directly in the agony of Harvath's existence--the loss of so many loved ones in his inner circle crushes the will of existence for one of the toughest men ever to grace the pages of a novel. You see him at rock bottom; you turn pages begging him to find the will and resolve to pick up the pieces. Scot Harvath is at his true breaking point, and you know why. For me, this book shows what a master storyteller is capable of when they want you to 'feel' the emotions of the protagonist. Without experiencing Harvath's trauma myself in the real world, I've never been so close to a fictional character's agony. I have no doubt you'll feel the emotion of this book like never before in a Brad Thor tale. Buy it.

I was a little disappointed in this book, judging from all the reviews and “best in the series” hype. A lot of time was spent retelling the details from the previous release, and it seemed like Near Dark could have been added as several chapters in the last book instead of a stand-alone. The ending felt extremely rushed and anti-climatic. That being said, there’s enough here to satisfy the series fans (like myself), but I think I was somewhat blinded by the advance reviews, and I was expecting more.

** spoiler alert ** I am a huge Brad Thor/Harvath fan! I will say that this is the first book that I didn’t care for. The first reason is that too much of the book was spent recapping the last books’ plot. The second reason is that I did not like that a love interest was introduced for Scot, knowing that his wife had just been killed. I know that Lara’s death was in a previous book, but when you think about the time line, this book is maybe two months since she was killed. When Scot started to have an inner monologue about Sølvi, or announced that he dreamt about her, I thought it was way too soon. Just my opinion.

In this latest entry in the Scot Harvath series, someone puts a $100 Million bounty of Harvath's head. Meanwhile, after the event of the last book, the quarry is drinking heavily, trying to get over his grief and guilt. After finding out he's Wanted: Dead, Harvath goes hunting for the man behind the reward. Along the way, he has what passes for a meet cute in these sorts of books with a beautiful Norwegian intelligence agent. The two combine their forces, and go after the assassins and the one who hired them. Pretty good. A little slower paced than many of the books in this series.
Near Dark is another good addition to the Scot Harvath series. It is as formulaic as some of the previous entries but still manages to be entertaining as ever. Brad Thor fans must read this.

So who put a 100 million dollar bounty and a pool of assassins after Harvath? I have heard that the Scot Harvath books are excellent international spy thrillers. Unfortunately Near Dark is #19 in the series and while usually these types of books can be read as standalones, this one just didn’t work. It is based very heavily on the events of the past few books, with TONS of recap. I think if I had read the prior books, the recap would be boring, and since I hadn’t, I had no clue what they were talking about. Also since I don’t know the characters that had died, all the grief and past recollections didn’t affect me. Having read a few other reviews from long time series readers, I’m not too far off the mark there. Either way there was tons of intrigue and I think it would be worth trying prior novels in the series. It also took a long time for Harvath to do anything exciting since he spent much of the book reeling from prior events and in hiding. Once the action got going it does seem like Thor can write a good spy thriller. I liked Harvath and Sorvi, the Norwegian spy. These characters just kick ass and have some Bond-like qualities and sometimes that’s what books need. I liked that he went there with the torture and murders too. My favorite side character was Nicholas the dwarf. A real dwarf isn’t something I see often in books and he was hilarious plus a brilliant hacker. Would love to go back and read the history there. In short … I would start back at the beginning and try the first book in the series before judging too harshly. The recapped action sounded awesome but I can’t recommend these as standalones based off Near Dark.

I am A huge Brad Thor fan and look forward to him every year. So it pains me to write this review that I hated this book. It was awful. At one point I had to look at the cover to make sure I had downloaded the right book/author. Most of the book was spent discussing the last book which I thought was one of the best books I've ever read. I found the action barely there and thought Nicholas wasnt used efficiently. I skimmed the last third as I just couldnt do it. I'll be back next year and the ones after that but this was a huge disappointment.
Pretty much a vengeful rehash of the previous 18 books. Lots of it was just blah blah blah.

Another hit it out of the park. Brad Thor keeps providing he is at the top of his game. Such an amazing tale full of suspense, drama and a simple love story. Scot Havarth is still someone you do not want to mess with. Liked how Brad showed this side of Scot and how he dealt with some of his ghost. I also enjoyed how Brad gives that quick back brief on some of the characters he uses to keep new read and returning readers up on his characters and how they fit into the storyline. Not a dull moment in the story. It’s a must read for everyone.

After a few weeks of “experimental” reading excursions, meaning “new to me writers”, I returned to one of my tried and true authors, BRAD THOR. Book number 20 in his Scot Harvath series is NEAR DARK. What a terrific writer of spy thrillers! Thanks for the great entertainment. In this story, which picks up right after book 19 (BACKLASH), Scot is suffering from a horrific personal loss. He has retreated to a luxury resort near Key West in southern Florida in the United States. He is drinking alcoholic beverages like there is no tomorrow. That is no exaggeration. If you read BACKLASH, you can understand his mental state. If you have not read the previous story, you probably should do so before you start this one. Harvath works for a private intelligence gathering company after many years of government employment including the U.S. Navy SEALS, the U.S. Secret Service and the C.I.A. As the story unfolds, Scot is drinking in a dive bar in Key West when two bums start to harass the female bartender. That action upsets Scot and he invites them “to step outside” with him. They do. A fight breaks out. A third man shows up with a gun and is about to shoot Harvath. A shot rings out. The would be gunman collapses. Dead. Scot’s team of Haney, Staelin, Palmer and Ashby have come to the rescue. They are there because it has come to his company’s attention that a contract for $100 million has been issued for Harvath’s death. His team also informs Scot that his good friend Carl Pedersen of the Norwegian Intelligence Service (NIS) has been tortured and killed. Carl had worked with Scot on a couple of cases. This is another blow to his collapsing psyche. Scot flies to Norway on a company jet where he meets Solvi Kostad an N.I.S. officer who was also close to Pedersen. The two team up together to find out who tortured/killed Carl and to find out who is trying to kill Scot. There are plenty of suspects including Filip Landsbergis, a high-ranking member of Lithuania’s State Security Department (VSI), who has also worked with Scot. Nikolai Nekrasov is a billionaire Russian oligarch who lives in southern France near Nice who has a grudge against Harvath. Andriejus Simulik head of VIS is another suspect. Paul Aubertin, born Michael Collins McElhone in Ireland, is a former French Foreign Legion operative, and is now a paid assassin. As mentioned earlier Harvath’s journey takes him to Key West and then to Boston, Oslo, Lake Garda (Italy), Lithuania and Mont St. Michel near Normandy (France). As typical of Brad Thor stories, there is plenty of action with a hint of romance. The book is fast paced and should be a quick read for most readers. This a perfect read for those people who have quarantined themselves during COVID 19 Pandemic. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED! GO! BUY! READ!

What a disappointment. This is probably the worst Harvath book in the series, and a shame that it came after what was maybe the best in Backlash. I put off reading this because I heard that was the case and that was correct. This is supposed to be a thriller, but I kept waiting for said thrills and there were none. Harvath is a bad ass character and the reason to read this series. However Thor decided to not put him into an action sequence until over 90 percent in the book. Instead he drinks, rehashes details from previous books that we already know,talks to people trying to solve a mystery we already know the answer to, falls for a hot Norwegian chick even though his wife was just murdered, and then everything wraps up really quick and in a way that's anticlimactic. , I'm not sure what Thor was trying to accomplish. If he wanted to reset the series after Backlash he could have. This book seems unnecessary because the character work falls flat. That's not the reason to read this series. It could have really been a kick ass action packed book full of pursuits and Harvath avoiding contract killers. Instead it was a phoned in placeholder. I might be done with this series.

Scot Harvath has a problem. Someone wants him dead; badly enough to put a 100 million bounty out on him. The book follows this main storyline, with a couple diversions. Harvath develops a drinking problem and this takes up a good portion of the narrative. He gets to work side by side with a Norwegian operative named Solvi. They end up good friends and maybe a bit more than friends. If you want the details, you'll have to pick up the book and discover what a great thriller writer Brad Thor actually is. Overall, a very good book.
I loved his last book so much that this book disappointed me.

Wow, just Wow!! How in the world could Brad Thor out do himself again. I thought he was at the top of his game when he wrote, Backlash, but i was wrong. Near Dark is even better and keeps the thriller genre on the edge of the seat waiting to see how Thor can out do himself again. Near Dark almost read as a Swan Song for Scot Harveth but I believe it is a new beginning and even better things to come. With a huge cast of characters from Harvaths past it really brought all 20 books together! With some Younger members of the team getting more action and a great new "partner" for Scot. The future and the sky is the limit.!!!

Really a 3-star, but it is a Brad Thor "Scot Harvath," so 4-stars it is..."Near Dark" extends from last Summer's Harvath, "Backlash" as a Russian Oligarch seeks revenge by putting a $100 million bounty on him...Much of the story deals with Harvath and company peeling back the layers of the Byzantine maze of the intelligence world to find the source of the bounty...Okay Summer read!

Near Dark was a very impactful follow up to Backlash. After the events of the previous book we start with Harvath at rock bottom trying to drink away all of his devastating losses. Little does he know that there is a massive bounty taken out on him by someone and put to a pool of assassins to whichever can get to him first. Once he gets caught up with all he has missed since going off on his own and with what they’ve been able to find out about the bounty nothing will stop him from getting to the bottom of it before someone else gets him before he can get payback. He eventually goes to work at dismantling who is involved one by one, all the while making sure his remaining family is well taken care of. Soon after he starts on his mission he meets NIS operative Sølvi Kolstad. They realize very quickly that they are after the same certain person and team up to get him and answers. While getting to him is only part of Harvath’s goal, it is all Sølvi is after for personal reasons. Sølvi is a very lethal and and focused on getting what she needs to done. She is also very to the point and doesn’t play games with anyone. She made a very worthy ally to Harvath, and it was fun to read the banter between the two. They had a fantastic chemistry that really made the story. I was really glad to see how healing their partnership was for Harvath after all the trauma he has recently been through. I really enjoyed the fast paced storyline, brutal action sequences, and characters that feel completely real. While the ending was wrapped up a bit quickly, I am looking forward to reading what is coming next for Harvath and his team and hopefully getting more into that ending! Overall it turned out to be one of my favorite Brad Thor novels and I enjoyed every moment.

Scot Harvath is a broken man. Brad Thor's masterful story telling takes you into the mind of a man that has lost all hope after the devastating loss of the most important people in his life. Once at the top of his game, Scot has lost his will to keep going. Only after nearly being assassinated himself and discovering that the largest bounty ever has been placed on his head does Scot snap out of his stupor and take his life back, or does he? Only after teaming up with Sølvi Kolstad, a Norwegian operative, with a history every bit as dark and haunting as Scot's, does he finally start to regain a sense of purpose. Scot and Sølvi have a shared interest in finding the man that killed their friend and mentor. Along the way they each develop a respect and understanding of each other and quickly become an unstoppable team. Brad Thor's uncanny ability to make you feel the raw emotions of the characters, brings to life another expertly written, emotionally draining, pulse pounding and suspenseful Scot Harvath thriller. Near Dark is a departure from the tried and true formula that Brad Thor has used to remain one of the best Authors in the thriller genre, however, it is a testament to Brad Thor's evolution as an Author, along with Scot Harvath's evolution as a man that has too long kept his emotions bottled up. The ending however, was too rushed and lacking the great detail that makes Scot Harvath stories a staple in the thriller genre. I highly recommend Near Dark to anyone looking for another great Brad Thor thriller and anxiously await the next installment in the life of Scot Harvath (and hopefully more Sølvi Kolstad).

Almost gave up a quarter of the way through - soooo much exposition and filler and repetition of the history of Scot's angst and why he's now a boozer and giving up on life... A lot of talk talk talk and review review review of previous ops, characters, and situations from earlier books. If you're a huge fan, I'm sure it's a nice romp down (previous novels') memory lane. Thin plot: Scot is the target of a bunch of assassins loosed by someone offering a huge bounty. I thought there were subplots to this story, which kept me reading, but really it was just find one assassin, torture him to get to the next guy, find that guy, torture him to get to the next guy, then torture him to get to the next guy. The last three links weren't even shown, just explained. Very weak ending when Scot goes into the final confrontation. Miracle, all is solved. Also, a lot of deus ex machina saves sprinkled throughout. Not a lot of action (except the fight and torture scenes - solution to all problems is shoot the guy in the knee). If you insist on reading it, skim! If you are into listening on audio, it doesn't merit close attention. 2.5 stars.
I felt the ending was rushed.
The most boring installment yet in the Scot Harvath series. This was a huge disappointment for me and felt more clip a greatest hits rehash than a new stand alone.

This is another great installment in the series about Scot Harvath by Brad Thor. I'm glad to see that he seems to pull himself together after everything that has happened but what happens in the end of this book, is it smart? I sometimes wonder when I reed these books about top tier agents and assassins. They live in the same time and place right? Should their paths not ever cross? Victor should have been a deadly foe but he could always call 1-855-2-NOWHERE. It would actually be rather fun to see some of my favorite characters appear in the same story. If someone out there has missed this series I recommend that you remedy that.
An excellent read, as always keeps you on your toes.
Very well done. Brad Thor did not disappoint. Lots of intrigue and twists as well as taking you to interesting places that I now want to visit!
4.5*. Scot is the character that I remember from the earlier books and I’m glad that he is back.

I enjoyed the story of Scott Harvath on the rocks. Brad Thor sketched a good portrait of a man struggling with his grief ready to destroy himself. I’m glad that despite the loss of Lara, we still have Nicholas. He has always been a fascinating character. The main villain (no spoilers) is also quite interesting. I think Thor did a good job of writing a thriller and the story of a man struggling to move on after a terrible tragedy.

We were looking so forward to this book after the high-action ending of the last book. There was a lot of backstory telling and not much action here. It was fine and mostly a setup for future books but not what we expected.

My one word to describe this book would have to be “retribution”. In Near Dark, we have the continuation of a, thus far, three book story arc. In the first of this arc, we have the mission that leads to the pandemonium to come; the second, we have the hunt, and the beginning of the spiral; and in this book, Harvath has the backing of his team, and is out for retribution. We get the introduction of a kickass character in this installment! With a very similar flawed background as Harvath, hopefully this could be a teaming of the ages. I can’t recommend this book enough!
Scott Harvath is one of my favorite characters. If you enjoy reading the espionage thrillers then this book is for you. First page to last it’s non stop adventure

Scot Harvath, the hero of Brad Thor's terrific long-running series, has had a really tough go of it lately. He has lost his wife; his mentor, Reed Carlton, of the Carlton Group, which employed him; and a trusted colleague, Carl Pedersen. He has elected to drop off the grid and drink himself into oblivion in Key West, Florida. But after being asked to leave his regular resort following an altercation, he drives to the far end of the island, checking into a lowbrow hotel for two weeks. The action in NEAR DARK takes off when he visits a seedy local bar. The prologue features a conversation between Andre Weber, a Westerner, and Lieu Van Trang, an elderly Vietnamese gentleman. Both are extremely wealthy and powerful. Their discussion quickly shifts to the amount of money they need to hire the best assassins in the world to take out someone permanently. That target is the one and only Scot Harvath. As he is fighting two bikers outside the Key West bar in which he had been drinking bourbon, a stealthy gunman takes aim at him. A shot is fired, but it is not Harvath who goes down --- it is the shooter himself. Harvath is rescued by a small team that he had become acquainted with during his top-secret government work. He is whisked away to Washington, D.C. for a meeting with an old friend. Nicholas, the diminutive dwarf and his one-time foe, has stepped up in the absence of Carlton. He is an expert at many things, not the least of which are hacking and scanning the dark web, where he finds chatter about a hit put out on Harvath. Now they need to determine who wants him dead to the point where money is no object and all the top assassins are invited to claim the bounty on him. One of these hitmen is a former Irish citizen now living in France under an assumed name. Michael McElhone is now Paul Aubertin and is one of the best in the business at what he does. He has a special love for the French national landmark Mont-Saint-Michel, which not only will play a role in the story but also is keenly depicted on the book’s cover. Against the wishes of his superiors and peers, Harvath decides to throw himself back into the most recent places in which he had stirred up trouble to see if he can pick up the scent of who is paying to have him killed. Everyone at the Carlton Group wants Pedersen's killer dead, but they are not confident that Harvath is going to figure it out. We also are introduced to a Norwegian version of our protagonist, a tall and striking female operative named Sølvi Kolstad. She has experienced a tragedy of her own involving personal loss and drug addiction, and finds an almost instant kinship with Harvath. Having an ally is a good thing at this point, but he still has no intel on how, when or where the attempt on his life will come. In true Brad Thor style, the book continues to globe-trot across the planet as Harvath and Kolstad fight, torture and go clue-tracing until they get a jump on the assassin. A final breathtaking showdown will take place, like something out of a James Bond novel or film. NEAR DARK is everything you would expect from a Brad Thor book. A staunch conservative who has shown his disillusion for the current political landscape through his recent work, Thor gets an opportunity to step away from these trappings --- and the result is an outstanding chase novel. He knows his stuff, as evidenced by his work in many secret government think tanks throughout his career, his depictions of “spook life” and his knowledge of great international locales. He dedicates the book “To all those we lost. And to all those who bravely served so that the rest might live.” I am looking forward to the next installment (the 20th!) of this series, which hopefully will be set amidst our current global pandemic. If there is anyone who could get to the bottom of this mess and come up with a solution, it would be Scot Harvath. Reviewed by Ray Palen

Brad Thor’s NEAR DARK is viewed by many as the third book of a trilogy written by Thor, placing Scot Harvath in the position of weighing his future, both personal and professional. It began with SPYMASTER, where a mature, seasoned, professional intelligence operative, Scot Harvath, looks to his future and decisions he has side stepped over the last couple of years. His body is showing the wear and tear of someone pushing into several decades of espionage work. How much more can his body take is the question that sits in the back of his mind. What of Lara and her son Marco that Harvath has come to love deeply? Then there is his mentor, boss, friend, Reed Carleton,slipping into dementia’s abyss, a man who groomed Harvath to take up the reins of running his company along with Lydia Ryan. Harvath, never one for indecision, finds himself traveling to New England to marry Lara at the secluded haven of Reed with dearest friend and colleague Lydia Ryan as witness. SPYMASTER leaves us with a cliff hanger of dead bodies and a missing Harvath. BACKLASH, the second book of the trilogy finds a kidnapped, physically injured, mentally and emotionally traumatized Scot Harvath being hauled off to Siberia as so much Russian freight to be tortured and pried loose of all his secrets, both of US intelligence agencies and that of Allies overseas who have always stood at Harvath’s back. A freak blizzard by Mother Nature crashes the plane in Arctic regions leaving Harvath in a visceral struggle to survive against nature’s viciousness, attacks by enraged Russian special ops military, and holding the slim sliver of hope that his trusted posse of Chase, Mike,Tyler,Sloane, and Nicholas could find him in the backwaters of the Finland-Russian Border. NEAR DARK, the third of the trilogy opens with a numb, traumatized, despairing Scot Harvath seeking ANYTHING to stop the pain of loss, the loss of those dearest to him, personally and professionally and an uncertain future. It opens with Scot seeking solace and pain relief in the bottom of a bottle. After all, alcohol has been man’s coping remedy for pain for thousands of years. But alcohol makes one careless and arrogant. And Harvath almost gets his wish to see and hold Lara again. It’s so good to have trusted friends at your back. But a stuporous Harvath is not a risk that the Intell community can ignore, especially with a massive price on his head. Scot’s rescue from the jaws of death comes at a price. He learns of another death laid at his feet. A Norwegian intell peer, friend and colleague who is found tortured to death and authorities ascertain the death of Carl Pedersen is tied to a large reward for the death of Harvath. The scramble is on to locate,secure,and haul him back to Washington,DC. Once there, a semi-sobered Harvath meets with the one man who has had his back over the years, knows him like family, has shared his joy and his pain - Nicholas. The man who stepped into the breach, ran Carleton Group in the absence of its destroyed and missing leadership and who has a personal share in the future of the world’s leading intelligence security agency. Nicholas is family, so he doesn’t mince words. He lays all the cards on the table. Harvath needs to get his act together or go to ground as there is a $100Million reward on his head. The two of them must decide the future of Carleton Group here and now,and how to proceed comes into question. Harvath has a choice, climb out of the alcohol soaked abyss and resolve the issue of the murder and who is behind the massive reward of the assassination plot or look at permanent seclusion. So many people rely on Scot Harvath at the moment for their livelihood, his decision making,and leadership. He feels guilt over the deaths and his refusal to take over the helm of the company, but with Nicholas’s pending fatherhood, the guilt intensifies, he accepts fate and acquiesces to the return into the world of espionage. The question remains is he mentally, emotionally, and physically functioning well enough to handle this latest challenge. Where does he begin? Who is behind it all? Those answers lie overseas with the investigation of the death of Carl Pedersen and a commonality, the introduction of possibly new partner-Solvi Kolstad. Like other thriller authors, Brad Thor has turned to examining the inner thoughts, feelings, and beliefs of this hardened, seasoned professional. What makes him tick. What is his limit for mental and emotional torture and added physical abuse. What parts of his psyche and belief system enable him to survive in Nature’s Hell. He indirectly examines nuances of leadership and how they drive a person onward, forward, to resolve a conflict or problem. What is the role of family, loyalty, and country in decision making. The reader finishes the book with a much better defined persona of Scot Harvath. You leave with a clear image of this new female, the mirrored image of Harvath and exciting new possibilities for the future. There are plenty of the fistfights and weaponry that everyone loves in a Harvath novel. But in this one, and this trilogy, Thor does the stretch and embraces the character fully, he delivers a more robust knowledge of the man, what drives him and what could lie in the future. This is the path that Thor has created. The one that leads to a split in the trail. The question of where Brad Thor takes the Scot Harvath series. What new journey awaits? Is it a merging of Nicholas’s brilliant management and IT,logistical skills,coupled with Scot’s intelligence and on the ground operational knowledge and operator skills? Do they work together as partners,a team in the Carleton Group? Is a third party introduced to actually handle the CEO responsibilities and day to day operations? What happens to the company? Will it continue to hold the prestige of one of the world’s best intelligence operations? Meanwhile, Harvath sets out on a quest to exact revenge and track his suspected assassins. The body count starts as he joins forces with Solvi Kolstad to avenge the death of their mutual friend Carl Pedersen in tracking down the bounty hunter and the money behind the hit in some of the most noteworthy tourist spots in the world. Key West, Washington DC, Oslo, Norway, France’s Mont-Saint-Michel and Normandy, Basel,Switzerland. And one by one Harvath and his posse track down the ultimate money source. A slight quirk, but indeed the Russians will rue the day they decided to take on Scot Harvath. Our story wraps with our man contemplating a summer in Norway with his stepson Marco. And he leaves the door open to explore new possibilities with his mirror image. Thor has explored in this trilogy what the deepest, darkest thoughts of man are in a slide into the abyss. It also examined how a strong, focused intelligence operator faces the most traumatic events in anyone’s lifetime, and how Scot Harvath survived. That survival of the worst made him mentally, emotionally stronger and opens a myriad of directions for Harvath in the intelligence field of Carleton Group. NEAR DARK concludes with a look toward the future, a future that only the author’s creative mind can determine,in the direction of Scot Harvath’s next role and the series future. We look forward to that next adventure. It’s been one hell of a ride so far! Hope there are 20 years more! NEAR DARK is a superb finish to this trilogy! KUDOS!!

This was my 19th novel in the Scot Harvath series by Brad Thor, and the 20th overall. I have now read all 20 Brad Thor books. I wonder how many more in India have done that? For those who have not read Scot Harvath novels, his chronological career bio is: ● U.S. national ski team member ● U.S. Navy SEAL (Team 2 and then Team 6) ● Senior White House Secret Service Agent ● Covert government-sponsored operative working in a fictional off-books unit created by a former fictional U.S. President himself, whose mission is to save America and Americans from the most deadly terrorists, and to do 'whatever is necessary' in order to achieve his mission. In other words, a covert government-sponsored assassin who does not exist on paper. ● A new President who is 'soft' on terror disbands the unit and Scot Harvath now basically does the same job, but as an employee of "The Carlton Group" (TCC), a private intelligence/security government contractor set up by former senior CIA officer Carlton Reed. TCC takes up the most dangerous missions from the U.S. President, the Department of Defense, the CIA, and for private clients. And Scot Harvath is TCC's main operative. In the previous novel "Backlash", Carlton Reed, TCC's CEO Lydia Ryan, and Scot's wife Lara are killed by Russian Spetsnaz (special ops) operatives. Scot had gone inside Russia and killed many people, including the Russian President's son. In "Near Dark", Scot receded into coastal South Florida in his grief and had become a drunk. Then suddenly an armed assassin tried to kill him and he was rescued by his teammates who flew in from the Washington D.C. metro area based on intelligence from Norwegian Intelligence. Someone had put out a $100 million (one hundred million dollars) bounty on Scot's head. The 'contract' was given to several skilled assassins and the money would go to the first one who killed him. Who wanted to kill Scot that desperately? Against the wishes of Scot's new boss (the new CEO of TCC), Scot flies to Europe... he wants to find and kill his hunter/s before they kill him... An excellent book, like most Scot Harvath novels by Brad Thor. Deserves the full 5 stars I have given.

Scot Harvath suffered loss, including his bride, and exacted revenge in the previous book. In Near Dark, we find him in an isolated part of southern Florida, filled with rage, drinking to forget. In a favorite bar, two brawny men pick on the female bartender, and it is just the excuse Harvath was looking for to release tension. After besting the two in the parking lot, he turns to face a gun aimed at his head. Sure that he is going to die, and not too sad about it, he is surprised when a gun shot fells the shooter, not himself. His team rushes in, whisks Harvath away to Camp David, and he discovers someone wants him dead - a hundred million dollars worth of dead. ISIS? Russia? Irish? French? All these countries are possibilities as Harvath and his team track (with the fantastic computer help of Nicholas-the Troll) and a Norwegian agent, Solvi, and ultimately discover the source of the threat. Amazing story.

Let's be honest. It is very difficult to follow up a book like Backlash, Brad Thor's 2019 thriller featuring Scot Harvath. That being said, NearDark was a terrific read. After suffering the loss of many very close to him, Harvath finds himself the assassination target of an unknown enemy. As he faces his demons, he pursues to find out who is behind the hit with the help of a sexy Norwegian Operative, who adds an amazing dimension to the story. This more introspective look at the psych of Thor's hero sets the stage for many interesting future adventures. Thor fully develops his characters and provides significant detail to have a clear picture of his fictional world. While there is some criticism over his reflections and recap of his prior books, I personally found it helpful and provided a better understanding of the evil behind the past events. Overall, I highly recommend and look forward to more terrific thrillers from Brad Thor.

This is a bit of a different look at Scot Harvath. It is not the usual action that you would expect. That being said it is still a good book and gives a glimpse into the character's life. Which makes sense since in the last book his life took a big hit and he lost people dear to him. It makes sense that he would need a bit of a chance to re-assess life and see where to go from there. He takes on a new mission to track down the killers that killed his wife. But who can he trust? The situation is made more complicated by he fact that there is the world's biggest bounty on his head. Will he be able to outrun the assassins and still be able to complete his mission? Well written but a bit different than you would be used to-still worth reading.

I thought this was good, but I didn’t quite feel it lives up to my expectations. In many ways, it was a continuation of the previous book which I didn’t mind, but it felt like a lot of time had to be spent retelling what happened vs. advancing the story. I found some the character development lacking as well, and some of the issues the characters were dealing with just seemed to end at the flip of a hat with little consequences. I found the ending extremely rushed and anti-climatic too. All of that is to say I do enjoy the Harvath series quite a bit especially the last few, but this one fell a bit flat for me.

** spoiler alert ** Fantastic follow-up to Backlash. Scot Harvath may be down and out, wallowing in heartache and pain, but at least finds purpose to give him some direction and revenge. By the time things are all said and done, his heart may just be bouncing back too. Again, for me, it's a tribute to Brad Thor's writing and character development that I can care so much for and be invested in the characters in an action/thriller series. That's not often the case. There is plenty of action, intrigue and suspense too. Another highly recommended read.

(3). like a dependable restaurant, a go to place for coffee, a bartender who knows your name, you mostly know what you are going to get in a Scot Harvath book. This one has more planning, more figuring out and a little less action than some of the previous offerings, but the feel is still there. This isn't the best one in the series, but it isn't bad. There are a couple of fast turnarounds here, and the ending wraps up so quickly it is almost hard to believe, but the overall product is still solid. always a fun ride. Good stuff.

Excellent story. Great action and plot. Thor brought into characters from earlier books that made this book even more intriguing. Fantastic setting. Brad Thor could write city tour guides for as a side gig if he wanted to. His research on his settings is great. Makes me want to visit Norway. Love how he humanizes Harvarh and makes him relatable to those who have experienced personal tragedy. Already have the next one and ready to go.

Another amazing book! This story started very differently and it took me off guard. The spycraft thriller stuff was up front and was exciting to follow along. I could feel the tension build and I just knew Harvath was about to go do Harvath things. And like everything done by Thor, it ended with a fun twist. Each book gets better and better.

This has everything you will want in a spy/thriller novel: Dramatic action scenes, exotic locations, badass main protagonist, cool technology/devices, and an epic team up! Very easy to read and enjoy!
Another solid effort in a fun series Read this in basically two sittings. Could not put it down. Story moves fast and develops quickly. Looking forward to the next one.
Liked this book a lot.
This was good, but not Thor's best.
Meh. It wasn’t bad but it wasn’t anything spectacular.

Scot harvath is back with 100 million dollars bounty on his head. And he finds the person who has put the contract and claims it for himself. Plenty of action and thrilling episodes of who done it to create a dossier on him.

Not my favorite by Brad Thor. Maybe is was just me, but I couldn't get into it. It turned into one of those books that I had to finish. I kept reading hoping it would grab me. That it would interest me. But it never did.
It was a thriller for sure. No complicated language and an easy read, it was about what I was expecting. It is indeed a page-turner though.

While Brad Thor never fails to deliver, he has outdone himself this time! A year ago if you would have told me that Brad Thor could top Backlash I would have thought you crazy, yet here we are. Near Dark finds Scot Harvath a broken man slowly drinking himself to death. Having lost his wife and mentor Harvath has nothing left. Then after a failed assassination attempt Harvath learns of a 100 million dollar bounty on his head. His only chance of survival is to find who placed the bounty and end their life before an assassin's bullet catches up with him. Thor has written a tense thriller that is impossible to put down and leaves you begging for the next book.

Scot Harvath has a bounty on his head. Who is after him? The Russian? Islamic Terrorists? Someone else. The chase goes through Norway, Lithuania, and France, and if you know France, you may recognize the structure on the cover of the book. Reminds me of James Bond going after Spectre. Cons: Long way to get to the one person that helped the bounty, but once they talked, the puzzle pieces fell too quickly and the ending was rushed.

Usually Thor's books are home runs but this one fell on the warning track. Sure, when Scot and Nicolas could do their magic the story picked up but before that it was such a rehash of the other books that it became a bit boring. Still, well worth the read.
