High concept, structurally complex literary fiction is so tricky. It tends to send readers in drastically different directions in response. And this will be one of those for sure. It's a book that deliberately makes the narrative more obscure, more confusing rather than offering the gradual increase in clarity we expect from a novel. I loved it. At one point, near the end of a novel, is a scene so baffling that I could have responded with anger and frustration. At this moment, as a reader, you simply must surrender to the book. You can no longer fight it, no longer try to impose your own expectations on it. You have to give up and say, "I have no idea what you are actually doing here, Katie Kitamura, and I think that is the point." Or at least, I did. Does that sound terrible? I suppose it does. I admit that I often enjoy novels that work as puzzles to be solved, and the idea of one that refuses any kind of clear solution can be a real frustration. But one of the things about my brain that works so hard and loves sussing things out is that it also loves to just stop and give up and let go for a little while. By refusing to be solved, this book just let me have an experience. And that is, ultimately, the thing I want most from a novel. At the heart of all of this is so much about art, about performance, about perception. Secrets and long relationships. The choices we make and the paths we never took. It is not that I think Kitamura wants to give us any particular theme or insight around these topics, instead she teases them out, lets us consider them, lets us see just how much we know and then takes it all away from you. Her prose, as always, is beautiful, spare, propulsive. It made me want to go back and reread INTIMACIES, which I enjoyed very much. And honestly I would not be surprised if I sit down with this one again to see what experience I have next time.

(3.5) Audition opens in a restaurant, where our narrator – a successful, well-established actress – is having dinner with a younger man. The nature of their relationship is ambiguous, but she’s convinced onlookers assume she’s paid him to be there (although in true Kitamura style, it’s not at all clear whether anyone is really thinking this. The line between perception and projection is smudged beyond recognition – something that’s spelled out when the narrator pulls up the memory of a time, years ago, when she was mistaken for an escort while dining with her father). We soon learn that the young man, Xavier, initially approached the actress with a misunderstanding about their connection to each other. This is (seemingly) quickly dispensed with; still, she doesn’t dismiss him outright, and he becomes a sort of avatar for existing anxieties around her career and life choices. The narrator is in the middle of rehearsals for a play, and much of her energy is focused on her inability to grasp a transformative scene. Then there’s a break in the novel in which she seems to nail it; she goes from frustration to enlightenment without us seeing anything of how she achieves that. Except that isn’t all that’s changed. Her family is mysteriously transformed. If Kitamura’s work might already be described as a fiction of overthinking, Audition takes her characters’ trademark maladaptive daydreaming to its not-so-logical conclusion. Lines blur between performance and reality, art and truth – between one’s real life and a what-could-have-been version of it spun out from a fleeting thought. So thick are the layers of meaning, so stark the gaps in any explanation offered, that it’s difficult to discern whether we are being presented with an elaborate roleplaying exercise, a deep-rooted delusion, a thought experiment or an alternate reality. No answer is forthcoming. The gaps are part of the architecture. And yet, for all its conceptual ambition, Audition fell a little flat for me. Maybe that was inevitable – I’ve been really impressed by the two Kitamura books I’ve read so far, and this one has been hyped as a breakthrough moment, a new peak. Expectations were, possibly, too high. I still think she’s a phenomenal stylist, and no one writes obsessive rumination quite like her, but the high concept here works against her usual strengths. Compared to A Separation and, especially, Intimacies, Audition feels thinner. Kitamura thrives on the friction between people, the way perception warps in relation to others; here, that interplay is transposed onto big, splashy themes rather than playing out a hundred little times in minor interactions. There’s plenty to chew on, as always with this author, but Audition left me hungry for something more substantial. Kitamura’s best work burrows deep into psychological ambiguity while still maintaining a strong sense of narrative momentum; here, the ambiguity feels untethered, the story fragmented to the point of weightlessness. That’s the point of course, and I did find it interesting to read something more postmodern from Kitamura – this makes a lot of sense as a direction for her work, and framing the story within a performance theme is really clever. I just found the core questions of the novel less appealing than the broader-ranging, yet more intimate, concerns of A Separation and Intimacies, both of which I’d recommend above this. I received an advance review copy of Audition from the publisher through Edelweiss.

All the world's a stage... The tension pulled me in to this a lot more than I was expecting. Audition is about the roles we play in relationships. We follow the perspective of the wife. She is an actress in a play, but she is also accepting the role of mother at home. Her husband becomes an actor and the line between performance and reality gets intertwined and blurred. What stands out to me the most is Katie Kitamura's clinical precision in crafting relationships, specifically the spaces between people which create the oddest and most lasting impressions. I think these subtle or nuanced clues in body-language often get overlooked in day-to-day life, or at least, they do not get analyzed to the level Kitamura achieves. I love how the author grabs details from the space that might normally be overlooked but is able to capture so much emotion and intrigue in small moments. I don't have much knowledge of theatre, but this novel screams theatre performance! . The characters take on precise movement as if they are on a stage. And there are brief moments that somehow get drawn out through relational tension. The writing at times did remind of some work by Susan Choi, who I adore, and I think is also very gifted at drawing out relational experiences in the space between characters. This litfic may not be for everyone but I recommend if you like Susan Choi, theatre, or really off-beat suspense. 4/5⭐️ tw: child loss

I really can't find one redeeming thing to say about this book. Kitamura was perhaps trying to capture the inherent deceit and performance of existence, but unfortunately the approach was not executed well. The two parts never connected in any meaningful way for me, and I felt like I knew absolutely nothing substantial about the narrator despite having read nearly two hundred pages from her pov by the end. This book was definitely trying to be clever but it just wasn't

Having finished reading this novel, I was thinking of a totally different writer I have admired, Naiyer Masud. Though he is not widely known and writes in Urdu, he is incomparable stylist and his elliptic stories have totally ‘invaded’ my imagination. His way of writing is composing the whole story with intricate plot and the level of details and then taking out a big chunk of the whole before finishing it. The effect of these 'holes' in the narrative is disorienting, seducing and almost etherial. He was explaining how it works through the following parable: There was this woman who was an accomplished cook. A certain dish that required only four ounces of ghee she’d cook with two-and-a-half pounds of ghee, removing the extra when it was done. But the dish tasted very special and retained the flavour, the essence of the finest dish from the table of the nobility. In this novel, i think Kitamura has tried something similar: to deliberately keep out the essential parts of her story in order to enhance the atmosphere and disorientate her reader, take him out of the comfort zone and create a memorable experience. But in my view she has ‘overcooked’. And it is not the problem that she has taken too much out. The problem that whatever has stayed did not add up into 'a noble dish’ for me in spite of a lot of sophisticated tricks and signposting. The main character who is also a narrator is an actor by profession based in New York. The novel consists of two parts. In fact they are two very distinctive narratives involving the same characters. And intentionally so. I’ve enjoyed the first part. It probed the psychology of acting and of an actress: what does it mean to successfully impersonate someone else for the sake of art? How does it feel to be an actor? She comes up with some profound insights: Although every beat of the scene was tightly scripted, I felt as if I had an infinite amount of time, I moved at my leisure. And while I hit my marks and cues, never deviating from the script, I was not in control of what took place, there was an alchemical process by which the scene unfolded, mysterious even to me and Max. In those moments, I was in communion with something, some force that was larger than myself and the scope of my ordinary life.. The question has lead me towards more universal query: how often a human being ‘performs’ in real life rather than presenting her true self into the world. Is there even such thing as a true self. I also caught myself thinking of the english phrase ‘acting naturally’. If one think of it properly she would realised that it is an oxymoron. I tried to translate it into the other languages i know. And it simply does not translate. Maybe one might trace. this to a character trait of an English speaking person... But i am digressing. Let’s come back to the novel. In fact, this part is digressive in style. It seems Kitamura is inspired by Javier Marias style with his focus on minute gesture, perceived physiology of his characters and lengthy digressions into his narrator’s thoughts. I think Marias in his turn was inspired by Henry James. And there are shades of of both of them Kitamura’s writing in this part (not in terms of the elegancy of the sentences though. Her best sentences are sparse.) She also tends to ‘tell not show’ instead of the opposite ‘show not to tell’, the way of writing any english speaking child should pick up at school aged five. That is why I always find ‘telling’ in fiction more refreshing, almost to the point of being ‘experimental’. Another subject matter that is dealt in this part is perceived ambivalence of the main characters to the whole issue of having children. I thought the sense of baby’s anticipation by a male partner and the aftermath of miscarriage both were dealt rather poignantly. So i was settled into a contemplative novel. But rather abruptly i was thrown out of it with the second part. The style has changed and the plot quickly turned into itself into something akin to a thriller. The psychology of acting was shelved (apart from the very beginning). It seemed the narrative has become overloaded with the tropes of a genre fiction. I won’t list them not to spoil ‘the plot’, but many of them are painfully familiar. The characters have become very different people in all but their names. It was of course a very deliberate decision by the author. I was dreading how she would connect those two parts as they were so disparate. And she did go by the easiest way possible: a production of play within the play and ‘a woman who can no longer distinguish between what is real and what is not real.’ A snake biting his tale so to speak. It has been done so many times before with so much more elegance (Poe, Cortazar, Borges etc, etc. etc.) At least she had a mercy just to hint, not explicitly say what her characters were really up to in the second part. So all her readers including me can indulge themselves in “interpreting” her text. In the first part there is a scene where our actor is having a conversation with her playwright. Max (the play writer) was looking at me but when I stared back her face closed down a little, as if she had been confronted, and I knew then that she had no idea what she had written, no idea of how it would work in the play, how it would bridge the two versions of the character, the scene she had written was nothing more than a placeholder. She had grown bored of the character in the midst of writing, I realized, and wanted to write a different character, and so had created this impossible scene to segue between not two versions of the same character, but two different characters altogether. I could see it now, I could see it all over the writing. It has exactly described my impression of Kitamura and her characters. And i was thinking: was it ironic or was it meta-fictional? In fact there was even more succinct diagnoses imbedded in the text: Weakness of interpretation which were in fact weakness in the writing. Let’s interpret this generously and say it was a conceit. Then in my view, it was a a little too clever for its own good and instead of introducing ‘a lacuna’ into the coherent text, it has created a ‘placeholder’. The overall result seems a little too pretentious. So after finishing the book, initially anger was percolating through me, a series of small internal eruptions. (using Kitamura’s interesting turn of the phrase). But then i was just thinking of a waisted opportunity to go dipper in the actor’s craft. Having said all of that, I can see that this author tries to experiment with both style and themes much more than many others. I feel guilty as I might come across of discouraging her of doing so. That is not my intention. I might try her earlier novels one day as they received a positive feedback from people whose taste I admire. Ps Trigger warning for people who find a bohemian life style in modern New York insufferable. I am sure it was the part of the character’s credibility. Still, I found quite a bit irritating the repetitive references to procuring pastries from the nearest cafe for breakfast with a spouse, bringing it home and considering this as an acumen of intimacy aged forty nine. PS2 This has been nominated on the Booker. I've read just three out of this year list. I was amazed how easy was to read them. It did not require any effort whatsoever. In one word they were "readable". I guess that is the purpose of the prize to make people read fiction. And all three of them venture into the territory bordering thrillers in a way how they are written: (pacy plot, noting what it seems, cutbacks and cinematic tricks). I am not sure whether it is a theme of the long-list or a theme of the modern novels that moved away from auto-fictional interiority. It is just an observation as I do not plan to pursue booker novels further.

⋆˙⟡ 1.5 ⭐️ audition was soulless. hollow. joyless. i went in excited and ready to be impressed, but that excitement didn’t survive the first chapter. it quickly became obvious that our leading lady reads less like a character and more like an outline. cold, emotionally vacant, and impossible to connect with. if this book was meant to provoke thought, it succeeded only in producing detachment and boredom. part one is monotonous. part two drifts into the bizarre without coherence or clarity. i continued in the hope that the ending would unify the narrative and justify the praise and multiple award nominations. surely there had to be something here... there wasn’t. perhaps i don’t get it. perhaps this is the kind of book that confuses emotional vacancy with depth and minimalism with meaning, asking the reader to do all the work while pretending that’s the point. perhaps i haven’t marinated long enough in pretentiousness and emotional detachment to appreciate this level of “brilliance”. perhaps i’m simply too stupid to understand the genius at work here. whatever the issue is, i don’t care. i read for enjoyment. this offered none.

I had absolutely NO idea what to expect from this book. It was recommended by my aunty who loved it, so I was curious to see if it lived up to her hype… I found the reading of ‘Audition’ a rather curious experience 🧐 I felt like I was playing connect the dots; always a little confused by what was going on. That’s not to say I didn’t enjoy it. I very much appreciated the beautiful prose. It was quite a unique piece of work and for that I commend Kitamura 👏🏽 2 people meet for lunch in a Manhattan restaurant. 1 middle-aged woman 1 young man Who is he to her, and who is she to him? The nature of their relationship is ambiguous. Over the course of this short novel, the narrative slowly unravels yet no sure answer is forthcoming. In that way it is somewhat frustrating at times. However, there is a deliberate destruction of the storyline into two parts: Part 1 - we learn that the young man’s name is Xavier. He initially approached the woman due to a misunderstanding about their connection to one another. Then there is a shift, focusing on the actresses role in rehearsals. However, she never totally dismisses him; their relationship goes unspoken. The silence is what gets you thinking… Part 2 - from confusion to clarity. This part of the novel was much clearer. The same elements remain, yet completely reconfigured. The shift is mysterious, but welcome. I personally found part 2 much more enjoyable due to the emotional depth and sharpness of the narrative. The parts pull in completely different directions however, there is an ongoing theme throughout: questioning what these two people are to each other and our understanding of the different roles we play in each others lives - partner, parent, creator… And it was with this knowledge that I FINALLY began to understand the book as a whole: One woman. Two different lifetimes 🙌🏽 Overall, this was a rather fascinating story. By the end, we are still offered no clear or definitive explanation. Yet, despite the uncertainty there is a strong emotional tie to the protagonist throughout. Kitamura leaves us with 2 very different scenarios for the same set of characters. Unusual in structure and style but interesting nonetheless. ‘Here, it is possible to be two things at once. Not a splitting of personality or psyche, but the natural superimposition of one mind on top of another mind. In the space between them, a performance becomes possible.’ 🎭 3.5 🌟🌟🌟💫 (rounded up)
I like to think I like unconventional fiction, and then this type of abstract litfic rolls along. I have nothing good to say.

Audition is full of ambition held hostage by one very bad idea of how to convey it. The novel is really a diptych of two novellas. In the first, the narrator has lunch with a young man who's shown up to work on a play she's in, after some previous conflict is vaguely alluded to. The young man, Xavier, later tells her that he believes he's her son. The narrator's husband, Tomas, seems threatened and upset by seeing the two together. In the second half, Xavier is the narrator's son. She behaves as if this has always been the case and recalls memories of his childhood. Her husband is still Tomas. Xavier moves in with her and her husband. Audition asks us to be intrigued by these two arrangements of the same characters in different roles. The narrator is an actress-- are they all actors, then, a group of people who aren't related but pretend to be in two different plays? These would be interesting questions if we saw anything but cliche, superficial interactions between them. It's as if Kitamura is afraid to dig too deeply into any one dynamic or idea and, when you realize what the novel's gimmick is, you see why. One thing I did love: when the narrator is thinking about an actor's performance in a film she liked, which he was bewildered and earnest. She believes he brought his entire, authentic self to this performance after decades of phoning it in. It turns out that he was genuinely bewildered because he can't remember his lines, so the production crew wrote his lines all over the set for him to read off of. I thought this idea was going to be explored but it's just sort of hung on the novel's wall for you to look at while the colorless interactions continue rolling. Sure, okay, maybe the narrator is performing real life, then? Maybe the first novella is the play and the second novella is real (Xavier is, after all, writing a play in the second novella and the narrator is a working on a play in the first novella), or vise versa? Maybe both novellas are plays? In order to keep all these questions unanswered, Kitamura has to strip out everything that makes a novel interesting to me. We can't learn about the environment because Kitamura wants to leave us with the possibility that everything is a prop. We can't learn about the other characters' day-to-day lives because Kitamura wants to preserve the possibility that they're all actors. The only thing left is the narrator's inner dialogue, from which we don't get much more than confused impressions, leaving us with only one explanation for how sparse and disparate Audition's world is, and it's a trope as annoying as it is inauthentic, one that gives Audition freedom while removing the potential for character depth and any vivid or meaningful environment: the narrator losing her grip on reality. Even this is uninteresting, because the flavorless prose and the narrator's affectless, incomplete interactions with the characters offer no substance and no consequences for such a drastic condition. The idea has been explored in much better ways by David Lynch, John Fowles, and John Cassavetes. When the narrator thinks about how Xavier living with them "is not exactly like having our child back home again, it was like having some ideal version of him returned," you could wonder at the similarities between cohabitating with your son after a few years apart and being in a play with a young man you've worked with years ago. It doesn't matter whether the feelings associated with these situations--good, bad, confusing, complex, whatever they might be--are comparable. It doesn't matter that if you commit more than a few seconds to thinking about it, you understand the emotional and intellectual landscape of the two circumstances would be totally different. Audition's solution is to simply not include any emotional or intellectual pallet at all. Audition is content to merely suggest the comparison and hope you don't think about it too hard. Everyone seems to agree, whether they liked the novel or not, that the writing is beautiful. Personally, I find the sentences in this book homely, vapid, and clumsy. Publishers and reviewers these days all seem to praise "crisp, clear" prose and for me it usually means simple, uncomplicated sentences that carefully avoid the contemporary writer's lack of any unique or deep knowledge about the world. Sentences that hyper-focus on a single moment while somehow saying absolutely nothing interesting or insightful about it. Audition's Quotes page is full of such examples; here are a few of what I think are the worst offenders: People always talked about having children as an event, as a thing that took place, they forgot that not having children was also something that took place, that is to say it wasn’t a question of absence, a question of lack, it had its own presence in the world, it was its own event. I had given in to his story, his narrative, because it had been easier, and because of his persuasiveness—persuasion, which is only one step removed from coercion. But although Xavier was so evidently at home, he did not behave as if he were actually in his own home, he never inhabited the space as someone who had previously inhabited the space might do. I also noticed that the line spacing and margin width in my hardcover copy are abnormally large, I'm guessing to pad out the pages and make it seem longer than it is. Less a serious critique than a peeve, I guess, but one that would've been easier to ignore for a less pretentious, more thoughtful piece of work. It just puts publishing marketing in the forefront of my mind, with its attempt to sell this as something more profound and clever than it is. Kitamura's dedication to keeping all the relationships here ambiguous leaves almost no room for depth. She wants us to question what it means to be a "mother," "wife," "actress," or "woman," or so the summaries say, but there are zero insights on any of these things. Is that the point? If you're an actor who spends a significant part of your life portraying shallow, poorly written and undeveloped relationships, do you lose curiosity about the people around you and live a shallow, undeveloped life? It's not an uninteresting idea, but it's executed with cardboard. You can write about shallow people without writing a shallow book. You can write a book about the mysterious distances between people without writing around giant, arbitrary holes in your story and characters. Audition does neither.

The writing was incredible - beautifully written and so taut with tension it felt like a thriller. But even as a reader who likes a challenge and ambiguity, I still struggled to really “get” this. I understood bits and pieces of the commentary, but untangling the events of the story is still escaping me. The exploration into motherhood and performance were thought provoking, but the commentary about race never went anywhere deep for me. I’m still scratching my head trying to understand the ending - I feel like you could offer me a dozen interpretations and all would seem equally reasonable. On one hand, I like that Kitamura makes the reader reflect and work a little, but on the other - it feels a bit meaningless to speculate when so much is left unknown. I’ll read her backlist eventually, but I need to process this for the next 6-12 business days.

i’ll probably always be confused by this one but i didn’t hate it. it had some pretty great writing at times, and a lot of super symbolic writing, im just a little dumb for it lol. this is written in a way that really leaves you guessing where it was going with the plot

Audition is a beautifully written and thought-provoking story with moments of tension and cerebral tautness. The story is centered around identity and focuses on who we are to family members. Audition is a fast and entertaining read that overall I enjoyed. I'll have to admit that I found myself A bit confused at several points but its one of those books where you have to keep reading to understand where the author is going. I think a lot of literary fiction readers will love this one however, Audition is very much a postmodern, metafiction, style of writing so if abstract storytelling is not for you, then I would pass on this one. Audition by Katie Kitamura was published on April 8 so it's available now. Many thanks to Riverhead books for the gifted copy!

Kitamura continues to write the same female narrator over and over again, but each book becomes increasingly mannered and pointless. There are only so many times you can read a woman’s over analysis of the constant “ambiguity” she sees in every situation and relationship. Some good sentences and observations but to what end?

Two scripts, one life. In "Audition", Katie Kitamura crafts a spare yet mesmerizing novel about performance - on stage, in love, and in life itself. The publisher's synopsis perfectly describes the book as "a mesmerizing Mobius strip of a novel that asks who we are to the people we love" - referring to a single, endless surface with no distinct inside or outside, challenging concepts of duality and boundaries. The story begins simply: an accomplished actress meets a younger man for lunch in a Manhattan restaurant. But nothing in Kitamura's world stays simple for long. Despite the book's short length, there are two dual realities in this novel - across two mirrored narrative strands, the book offers distinct versions of the same relationship, each refracting questions of identity, desire, and the fluid roles we inhabit. The unnamed narrator, a middle-aged actress in rehearsals for her next play, feels both exposed and elusive. True to her career, her life seems like a constant act, the lines between her stage performances and private self dissolving until we can no longer tell where one ends and the other begins. The novel blurs the line between her stage roles and the roles she plays in life, especially as a wife, mother, and self. It's not a Sliding Doors scenario so much as a meditation on possibility, perception, and the masks we wear even with those who think they know us best - on how two people could know each other in two different versions of reality. I listened to the audiobook, which was skillfully narrated by Traci Kato-Kiriyama. A short but taut, beautifully written exploration of art, intimacy, and the slippery nature of truth, "Audition" is less a novel you devour than one that stays with you, echoing long after the final curtain falls.

Audition is a thinking reader’s book and at the core of it are questions: what happens when the self’s illusory nature is exposed, and one is no longer left with a reliable script or props? What if a family is if not a shared delusion, a mutual construction? Our narrator is a middle-age stage actress who has achieved fame and renown. As the book opens, she is in a restaurant with a young actor, Xavier, who looks erringly like her, right down to some of his tics and gestures. He, too, is an actor and believes he is her son, which is physically impossible. The actress is in the throes of a professional crisis: it is up to her to bridge the two halves of the play with a particularly challenging monologue that, she believes, is a failing of the playwright. To make matters more daunting, her husband, Tomas, is suspicious of Xavier because of his wife’s earlier affairs. Then we are plunged into Part II and everything is topsy turvy. The play has been successful. Xavier, it turns out, is their son, and he is now living with them, causing discord among the three “actors”, or family members. As a metaphor for the art of acting, the narrator ponders how it is possible to be two things at once – a natural superimposition of one mind on top of another mind. Maybe, she reflects, in the space between them, a performance becomes possible. As an admirer of Kitamura’s work, I have thrilled to her former books, A Separation, and Intimacies, both of which were also narrated by an unnamed woman. This one did not pull me in quite as much as the others. Perhaps it’s because the character, due the analytical structure and themes of the novel, becomes unknowable. The narrator reflects, “…the actual story, the reality of what was happening between us in that moment, was much less easily imagined.” Audition is a clever book, constructed with acrobatic prose, that focuses on the performances we relentlessly give on the stage of life. I very much admired what Kitamura was accomplishing. I just wish I loved it a little more.

going in completely blind was frankly hilarious because this was not at ALL what i expected it to be lmfaooo definitely the type of story where you have to surrender to the madness (which in this case i guess was surrendering to the structure). i honestly really enjoyed both parts, the writing is fantastic and while disorienting and jarring at points... idk the effect it had on me was refreshing! i can understand why people wouldnt jive with it though. opened up a new perspective on relationships to me and i love when authors can spur stuff like that but leave you without a clear ending. feels like i get to play around with it in my head for a while, very cool.
I didn’t get it. My IQ is too low. Couldn’t wait for it to be over.

Longlisted for the 2025 Booker Prize. Wowsa, what in the world did I just read. There have been enough reviews explaining the narrative I feel I don’t even have to write about it at all. I think this is the first time I have not given any stars to a book and that is because I truly feel that I do not understand it at all. I feel like I have paddled into the iceberg that sank the titanic with the foreknowledge that I can only see the tip. The iceberg is the story, and my understanding does not break the surface to the depths below. I watched in an interview with Kitamura as she explained that she likes the reading experience to be a collaborative effort between the writer and the reader and that this novel can be interrupted many ways. That may just be the understatement of the year. Did I enjoy this novel, I don’t know. Am I still thinking about this novel, yes indeed. Will it win the Booker, probably! This was a buddy read with Nat K and I am very happy to report that she is as flummoxed as I am. Spoiler alert. My current take on the book at this moment is that the novel is about a play that the woman’s son has written about her slow decline and memory loss to dementia. The success of the play is because the protagonist is not really acting, she is actually struggling with her lines, her confusion making the performance and play a critical success. There is an anecdote in the first half of the book in which a famous actor with dementia did exactly the same thing. Her damaged mind may explain how she interprets her husband and son’s behaviour and relationship to Xavier’s girlfriend. But like I said to Nat I really have no idea. And here I am still thinking about this book three days after I finished it. :-)

An accomplished actress meets with a young man, a theater worker and actor in his own right, in a Manhattan restaurant. There’s obviously something going on between them, even though she’s old enough to be his mother. The relationship is murky, and gets murkier when he gets a job at the off-Broadway production on which she’s featured. Her husband suspects things, and after a few days it’s hard to tell what she is to him and vice versa. Mother and son? Former lovers? Mentor and mentee? Kitamura has a dreamy, stream-of-consciousness style that takes concentration. I don’t normally go for it, but there’s something about her narrative that’s deep, intelligent, and honest. She writes this one in the first person, and the thought processes are direct and clear, very unlike other authors’ attempts. I felt the narrator’s confusion and anxiety and followed her strange trip through a bizarre situation. Perhaps it was the short length, the knowledge that I wouldn’t be stuck for hundreds of pages, that helped. But I really wanted to know what would happen. There’s a wild perspective shift, sorta, right in the middle. Agh! I can’t do spoilers but let me try to explain: something happens between the narrator, her husband, and Xavier (the young man) that forces us to question their relationship. I wonder if it was in her mind, if she’s just imagining it. Maybe it was a dream. Or maybe she’s engaging in some cognitive dissonance: going along with some behavior that doesn’t make sense, that might even be maladaptive, because her mind drifts that way. She wants this to happen, or at least doesn’t mind following a different path, so she acts it out. It was weird. I felt like I had to go back a few pages to understand what was happening. But I decided to go with it, and I’m glad I did. Maybe all the symbolism didn’t penetrate my thick skull, but it was thought-provoking and artful. Also, I loved the inside look into her craft as an actress. Speaking of art, I suggest you get ready for some artistic license. Not only for the wild narrative to which I refer above, but also for the looseness with grammar. That was true of Intimacies, and it’s true here. No quotation marks, and dialogue between characters shows up often within the same paragraph. Lots of run-on sentences, too. Again, I can’t explain it: as a captain of the Grammar Police, I find it hard not to shut off my spidey-sense. But it was beautifully written, smart, intricate, and sharp. One of the cleverest works of the year! Thanks to Riverhead Books and Goodreads for the advance giveaway copy, for which a review was requested. Audition will be published on April 8, 2025.

AUDITION Katie Kitamura I bought this book with my own money!! If this book can be exactly both of the things it is, then I can have two minds about it, too. On one hand, I wondered if it relies so much on this overt intuition of the main character and flirts so much with cliche throughout while it offers only enough to create a hint at a story. Or, is it not that? Does it eventually coalesce into something I have to think is profound and maybe actually pretty freaking fresh? About performance, family, womanhood, manhood, humanhood, intuition, speech, conversation… UGH! Every time I felt like I had the book figured out (AHA!! There it is! The cheesy corny on the nose thing I knew was coming!!) it pulled itself through and steadied itself out on the water. HOW. The novel touches on a central performance, a scene that’s a black hole at the very center of a play that unites it all, and while this works on so many literary layers it starts to feel uncanny, it kind of also felt like the scene may have said “oh, honey, you wouldn’t get it if you don’t live in New York…” Is the black hole at the center a decision point the main character made—a choice about keeping a child or giving it up? Is that what this is? A swirling unfolding around the two universes that unfold from the decision to have a child or not? Is that the unifier? Oh we could go on here for days interpreting, theorizing, I’m sure, but did the book say enough to be worth all that? The end cascades back into itself and fleshes out this very hard-won, WROUGHT piece of work I imagine must have been fathomlessly difficult to get right. Part of me wanted to say: “there is hope for all of you!! If you have an unfinished manuscript, fear not! Just submit! Say the rest is up to the reader OUT LOUD! Make it about that!” But, considering the character work, the dialogue, the hiding and revealing…DAMMET was it good? Was it????? Really??? No… no. I grappled here. Update after a while. Nevermind. I hated this dang book so much.

4.5 Incredibly compelling, and clever in so many ways that won't even hit you until you've reached the end and given it some thought. Audition is the story of an accomplished older actress meeting a young man for lunch in a Manhattan restaurant. You do not know what their relationship is to each other, or why they are meeting. This is really all I can tell you about the story without spoiling it... ***SPOILERS*** This is a novel of two parts, and whilst in the first part you think you have a grasp on what their relationship appears to be, the second half presents another reality. Which one is true? The novel clearly plays with the idea of us all having different parts to play in life, whether it be a mother, a parent, an actress, a writer, a father, a lover, a friend and so on... what happens if we become estranged from one of these parts of ourselves? Do we remember things differently from whatever really transpired in our lives? Do we forget our lines, and how to play the role handed to us? It's hard to know for sure exactly what Kitamura is doing, and whether the above is all that's at play. I often wondered if the protagonist had dementia (there is a section where she alludes to another actor needing his lines written everywhere around him due to dementia) and this is what caused her endless frustrations and somewhat brash behaviour. Then the final scene ends with her son Xavier giving her a play that he has written based on her. Is this what we've just read? Her monologue? It is one of those novels where more questions are raised than answers given, and I'm sure this will prove to make it a marmite book for the majority of readers. Was I completely satisfied? No. But I did hugely admire it, and I really couldn't put it down. It is in many ways a genius little book. It's my first time reading Kitamura, and although I did find her style quite cold, I think I'd be far too intrigued not to read more from her. Audition was one I was excited to read and keep going back to. And I'm dying to talk to anyone who has read it to compare thoughts!
Ha! Ha! I’m acting!

Booker Prize Longlist 2025 - BOOK 1 This was my first novel on my Booker Prize Longlist TBR and, oh boy, was it disappointing. This book had a promising start but quickly went off the rails. Where is the plot? Character development? A reason to read this book? It's nonexistent. The characters in Audition make decisions that will make you go "WTF???" Additionally, I have no idea what the author was trying to explore in this novel. Infidelity? Aging? Parenthood? I guess I'm not intelligent enough for this book. Finally, the climax of this novel is simply meaningless. Luckily, the book is only about 200 pages long, so I only wasted two evenings reading this nonsense. If I could describe this novel in one word, it would be "pretentious." This was my first and most likely last book by Katie Kitamura. DO NOT RECOMMEND.
*sighs, yawns, goes on to read Jane Austen*
i think i get it? but maybe i was never meant to?

Hmmm I’m not sure where to begin with this one. First and foremost the storytelling and writing is absolutely fantastic. The basic idea is that two people meet in a restaurant. One is our unnamed narrator who is old enough to be the young man’s mother. They both work together at the theater producing a play. Things begin to progress as we delve further into their relationship. This is one of those that I think is made more for readers way more smarter than me. The entire time I was wondering what was going on and the unease was palpable. Then it ended and I have no idea what happened. After it ended, I still felt unsettled after reading it. So obviously the writing was fabulous. As for a rating, I’m actually gonna give this 3.5 rounded up. There’s something to be said for a book that still has you thinking about it even though you have no idea why or what the heck happened. If you do by chance read it and understand what was going on please let me know

Audition by Katie Kitamura is a book for those who appreciate form over substance. 2.5 stars. An unnamed actress walks into a busy NYC restaurant to meet a young man named Xavier. The conversation she’s sharing with him is cut short by her husband Tomas randomly walking in and out of the restaurant - does he think she’s cheating? What is going on? What is he doing here? That scene jumpstarts the book that follows. The unnamed actress goes about her life and the story slowly unravels how she sees and interacts with the people around her after Xavier walked into her life like a wrecking ball. The book is told in two parts that can be sort of summarized as ‘Xavier walks into MC’s mundane uninteresting life’ and ‘Xavier is part of MC’s life,’ I guess? The last 50 pages of the second part were too much. At no point did I understand what I was reading, but the ending just really had me… frustrated? A lot was happening and I didn’t get why or what was the point. There was an important conversation left out between Part 1 and Part 2 that I wish had been in the book. And, I do have to ask: (view spoiler) The writing was beautiful, but the story made me angry and frustrated. It had nonsensical and confusing stuff that bothered me. So, yep: no effing idea what the point of this was. It’s plotless with nice writing. The only thing that kept me interested was my own theory-making about why the book is titled ‘audition.’ PS. Question for those who have read Kitamura before - this is my first time reading her, are all her books plotless-y/similar? *ARC received for free, this hasn’t impacted my rating.

This is one of Book Riot’s Best Books of 2025: Kitamura starts us out with a tight and masterful portrayal of people playing roles, and thinking about playing roles. Then, at about the halfway point, the stakes are changed, not in terms of register but in terms of what stories are and can do. Like many novels that contest and break expectations, Audition is not a general-purpose recommendation. (I would expect it to have the lowest Goodreads star rating of any book on this list, for example). But for readers who are interested in what else is possible in a book, or hell, what else is possible in a life, Audition is something other than satisfying—it is confounding, provocative, and new. - Jeff O'Neal
This elegantly written book kept me captivated until the end.

Audition is a tough book to talk about, because I truly believe the less you know the better, going in. Here is what I can divulge : a woman meets a younger man at a restaurant. She is an actress. We don’t know who he is, or the relationship between them— or, more importantly, why they are meeting. The book is split into two parts. I raced through the first part, due to the impressive writing, which kept my heart in my throat the whole time. In the second part, my jaw just unhinged and fell to the floor. Nobody could have pulled off this novel like Kitamura. Expertly written, insightful, and ultimately a very human story. Out next month—brace yourselves. Thank you, as always, to @riverheadbooks , for the review copy!

“What was a family if not a shared delusion, a mutual construction?” I’m a sucker for narratives that play around with form and structure, so I couldn’t wait to pick this up. This is one of those super cerebral novels that I don’t entirely get, that is smarter than I am. And there’s something so alluring about that. I didn’t love it. I wouldn’t recommend it to most people. But I also couldn’t put it down. I appreciated the challenge and ended up finishing it basically in one sitting. What’s it about? The roles we perform in our everyday lives—in the most literal sense—and the inevitable distances that exist in even the closest relationships.

Slowly and unsurely I make my way through the Booker Prize Longlist... will I finish them all? Highly doubtful. But at least I add Audition to my 2-book repertoire! So far, Audition's my winner. 50p. in, a coworker asked what I was reading, and I said I didn't know. At that point, my knowledge comprised only of a one-sentence blurb on Booker Prize's Instagram (how literate of me), with author Kitamura describing, "a desire to write about the long process through which children must unnecessarily grow up to become strangers to their own parents." That was enough to catch my attention. But I couldn't remember when someone asked about it. The book follows an unnamed female actress, aged past an evolutionary prime some male podcaster would assume is scientifically viable. I bring that up only because main character did so herself, in a roundabout way. A small ingredient to this book is age, and as it goes with all parents, the years on your life influence how you interact with the world around you. As does it influence others' perceptions. Take the simple scene of a woman at dinner with a young man. It means something different when the woman is 20 versus 40. This young man posits that he is our narrator's son. Narrator entertains this relationship although she tells us (and him) it is impossible. What we encounter is a strange, even surreal, narrative shift between parts 1 and 2, where—and I'd rather not spoil those of you interested—the truth may not be too far from fiction. And guys. I found this particularly satisfying as the transition mirrored one in the fictional play our narrator starred in... a parallel! Ohhh. It's not wrong to say we got a bit meta there. But not too much! Just enough so the book didn't collapse in on itself. A healthy spoonful of meta. While I admire Kitamura's imagination, I kept wishing for this "son" perspective. Maybe it's because I'm a child, not a parent, that I feel this way. I'm sure the foggy mystery would be lost on all readership if she chose to follow a clearer character, clear like this "son," so here's where subjectivity comes in: the "mother" (our narrator's) perspective annoyed me. Just as Booker Prize's Instagram hinted, the child can become to a parent some unknown creature, but personal biases make me feel that this unknown state of the child is the fault of the parent. Why is the parent, the mom, our narrator, what have you, so abrasive to the possibility of a child's change? Maybe that it why you find him unknowable? I rolled my eyes. Is that a critique? No. But where else do I put these feelings? A bit that did intrigue me was the relationship between parents. Again, I'm trying hard not to spoil, so apologies if this seems convoluted. And another apology, but in advance, for bringing Instagram up again: a reel I saw ages ago suggested that parents must take opposing perspectives when raising their child, so as to represent all viewpoints, whether or not the two are convicted in one side or other. What an interesting dynamic... two opposing forces representing two opposing truths out of necessity, rather than belief. This exact dynamic I was lucky enough to see spring out of Audition, as well. But I will not put it in context. No spoilers, I'm so good. I keep trying to revert to authorial technique/style writing this review, but my mind is swept by theme! I think that's a good sign as any. To me, that means a book has done its job. Kitamura accomplished a foggy, unreliable narrative questioning parent/child roles in relation to our personhood. Solid. I can't put a finger down on why I'm rating this 4 rather than 5 stars... maybe it is the (very intentional) detatched tone that I find off-putting. I guess we can't all be purveyors of objectivity.

Could ‘Audition’ actually claim to be a work of existential philosophy? I kept asking myself this as I worked through its 197 pages - surely the author is not Katie Kitamura, but Simone de Beauvoir. Has anyone else noticed the similarities, or is it just me? That said, it’s a strong and intriguing piece of writing with just enough unreliable narration to eventually become irritating. No creative writerly fluff, just cool, detached observations that command attentiveness to a breathtaking sleight of hand. But it’s the parallels with the Beaver that I find the strongest and most fascinating.

listen, there's something about writing a negative review of a book that really icks me out these days. especially on goodreads, which is by and large a platform that does not protect authors whatsoever and, in fact, often actively disadvantages them. it's a fact that publishers take goodreads data overseriously, and a book with a lower than 4 star average can literally tank a debut author's career. it's a shame, because i do believe vehemently in the value of negative reviews. literary criticism is a dying art, and readers still deserve to be able to write and engage with negative reviews of a book without feeling like the responsibility to protect an author rests on their heads. anyway. you may have guessed that i did not like this book. another thing that makes this difficult is the fact that i really liked katie kitamura's last book, INTIMACIES. i honestly am now gaslighting myself and feel like i need to go back and reread that one to verify my opinion lol. the two thoughts that were at the forefront of my mind while i was reading this were as follows: this book was not properly edited. and katie kitamura needed to have taken one less creative writing class (i found out afterwards that she's actually a professor of creative writing at nyu, which is very amusing). i really should get in the habit of marking pages so that i can include lines as evidence, but i haven't so you'll need to take my word for it that the writing in this book was fluffy, self-congratulatory, and full of run-on sentences and redundancies. it read like KK drank a glass or two of wine every night before she sat down to work on this. cloudy brain writing fluffy things. the thing is, INTIMACIES, despite a similar (albeit tighter) writing style, managed to overcome stylistic flaws by crafting a really immersive and magnetic atmosphere. i remember feeling so riveted by the setting especially as it was so influential on the mood of the story. here, you can feel the author grasping at conventions of creative writing in an attempt to develop a sense of creepiness and uncanny in a wannabe gothic way. i haven't given a plot summary because i cannot be bothered, but for some context this book has a part 1 and part 2 and essentially the idea is that a number of the plot/character points that are laid out in p1 are reversed in p2 (obviously without any warning or explanation, for sHoCk fAcToR!! a very high brow technique, of course) ((sorry i told myself i was gonna take this seriously and not be mean or sarcastic)). i digress. my point is: the attempt to manufacture tension and suspense is desperately transparent and ultimately just becomes frustrating to read. that's perhaps a good segue to talking about the characters here, all of whom feel so vacuous, slippery, and obscure. you can tell, again, that KK is trying to give them a sort of dreamy quality, probably both to make the novel feel ambiguous and also to coax the reader into imagining that they actually are the protagonist. but her main tactic for achieving this is to subtract detail, the effect of which is, naturally, characters that feel intangible and empty. another icky thing is that it seems like the author felt that she needed to include some Serious Bad Stuff to give the plot gravity. in essence what she decides on is a good old abortion, an affair, and a miscarriage. but again, these are tossed into a mix of already emotionally distant and disconnected sentences and plotlines and they just end up feeling like cheap, tokenized plotpoints with no real in depth exploration of their emotional consequences. as a final note. why did these characters spend so much time in restaurants or getting coffee? fr honestly the volume of pastries that were consumed in this book makes me worry for their blood sugar. you may notice i have not formally star-rated this book and that i've mostly fallen out of the habit of doing this. this is in large part because i'm morally against the goodreads industrial complex. im sure you can intuit what star rating i would probably give based on this review. if anyone important reads this, i believe katie kitamura should be given the money and resources to write more books, ok!! just get girlie a better editor. *edit (30/08): i have changed my mind and decided to star rate this as part of my attempt to read through the whole Booker longlist this year. kitamura has enough industry fame/support not to suffer from it, and in this case i think it's more useful to include it.

Reviews by friends @bookwormbecks and @books_with_taylor had me eager to read Intimacies by Katie Kitamura. I added it to my #25ishin25 shelf and read it last month in a day or two. Intimacies is described as, “…a taut and electrifying story about a woman caught between many truths.” Taut perfectly describes the writing and electrifying accounts for the compelling pacing. Set in The Hague, which made for a fascinating backdrop, I was intrigued with every aspect of this story. When I sat down with Audition, I felt that same immediate pull. “One woman, the performance of a lifetime. Or two. A mesmerizing Mobius strip of a novel that asks who we are to the people we love.” The story starts out straight forward, or so you think, and then things shift. The main character is an actor who meets a man for lunch. They have a strong connection and even favor each other. Could he be her son? He thinks so. But that’s impossible. Or is it? The second half of the story switches to that alternative narrative. It’s about performance masks. And performance itself. Who knows us really? The roles we play within families. What’s real and true and what is created by these roles we slip into every day. I could keep going. If you read this one, DM me so we can chat. I absolutely loved this novel, and the way it made me think. Its openness and its brilliance. Katie Kitamura is cornering the market on the slim, razor-sharp novel. I can’t wait for more. I received a free copy of Audition from the publisher. Many of my reviews can also be found on my blog: www.jennifertarheelreader.com and instagram: www.instagram.com/tarheelreader

I adored this novel. Katie Kitamura has tapped into a thrilling kind of ambiguity that is both the subject and the form of this novel. She cultivates a tense atmosphere through silences and elisions, and constant subtle shifts in her characters’ behavior and the textures of their environment. Focusing on the idea of performance as something inherent to how we interact with one another and inhabit our daily lives, the novel is narrated by an actress whose profession begins to bleed over into her real life. This establishes an incredible tension between her roles onstage and the increasingly blurred and precarious boundaries of her “roles” offstage. The language of performance forms the core grammar of the novel. From scene to scene, the characters’ identities feel provisional and contingent, and the structural choices embody the idea that life is built on “mutual constructions” and fragile performances sustained moment by moment. It’s a perfectly executed novel that finds Kitamura in stellar form, and, most impressively, lives up to its intellectual ambitions through its depth of insight, the precision of the writing, and its trust in the reader’s intelligence.

Patterson continues his Jane Smith series with another exciting novel. And the same suspect, Rob Jacobson, is again accused of murdering yet another family. Action is abundant, This is a nice, quick read with just enough suspense to keep the reader’s attention. Well written with an atomic ending.

Global best-selling author James Patterson teams up with legendary NYC Sportswriter and author Mike Lupica for the third novel in the unique and highly suspenseful Jane Smith thriller series entitled THE HAMPTONS LAWYER. The title may be quite matter of fact, but the circumstances are not. Defense Attorney Jane Smith, resident of Long Island’s famous East End, has been fighting a mostly losing battle against cancer as she continues to deal with a large tumor in her neck and head. She realizes that she could very well die at any moment, yet she continues to throw herself into her cases. No case has confounded and challenged her more than her defense of Long Island rich bad boy, Rob Jacobsen. Jacobsen had already been acquitted before with Jane’s help and now throughout this new novel is on trail once again for the murder of a family on Long Island. He swears he is being set up and the fact that he is in the pocket of infamous mob boss Sonny Blum, in much the same way that his father once was, does not make this an easy task for Jane. However, Jacobsen claims that Blum and his influential colleagues were setting him up to be the fall guy in this triple homicide of an innocent father, mother, and teen daughter. It is for this reason only that Jane Smith is continuing on as Jacobsen’s counsel, to see that justice is done for this family and that the actual killer or killers go down for it, even if it ends up being her own client. Assisting Jane, as always, is Hamptons bar owner and ex-NYPD Detective Jimmy Cunniff. He has direct experience with Sonny Blum and his entire racketeering organization and provides much needed backup, security, and detecting aid to Jane. While she is mentally zoned into this case and also dealing with her losing battle against cancer, her boyfriend and veterinarian to her beloved dog Rip, Ben Kalinsky, proposes to her. Jane does not need to think too long about an answer as she gives him a firm no, indicating that a wedding needs to be a happy event not a sad one where everyone knows the bride has a short expiration date. Her doctor has put her on a new level of chemo treatment partnered with new meds. This and the fact that her once terminal friend, Fiona, had just beaten the dreaded disease provide Jane with some reason for hope. Unfortunately, she cannot feel the same way about the Jacobsen case, which was just complicated by the unexpected surprise that he hired a second chair for his defense in the form of Thomas McGoey --- a shady attorney whom Jane is sure is in the pocket of organized crime. Another plot line adding more suspense and dread is the fact that a deadly hitman for the Blum family by the name of Roddy Sassoon is out there and waiting for the green light to take out both Jane and Jimmy. We get to witness a trail of bodies that have been left behind from his various hits and Sassoon indeed means business. One of the individuals who is in deep gambling debt to Sonny Blum ironically is Jane’s ex-husband who owns a popular East End restaurant. He reaches out to Jane for help after a visit from Mr. Sassoon, but she cuts him off, claiming the last time she paid his debts was the final time. As the case begins to ramp up in intensity, with several verbal battles between Jane and her opponent from the prosecution, events outside of the courthouse continue to provide more reason for Jane to worry. This comes in the form of the unexpected deaths of several individuals either directly tied to the case or potential witnesses. Add to this fire the fact that Jimmy personally serves Sonny Blum a subpoena to also appear at this trail. This is a dangerous ploy which may very well come back to bite Jane and her defense strategy. THE HAMPTONS LAWYER is a great summer beach read that is never predictable and hard to put down. On top of that, and in spite of the fact that Jane is gambling with the Grim Reaper, the novel ends with a terrific cliffhanger which will hopefully open the door to a fourth installment in this engaging series. Reviewed by Ray Palen for Book Reporter

“The Hampton’s Laywer” is the third book in the James Patterson -Mike Lupica “Jane Smith Thriller” series featuring their anti-establishment hero, defense attorney, Jane Smith. And yes, that appears to be her real name. “The Hampton’s Lawyer’ continues Jane’s story and starts up right where the last book – “Hard to Kill” left off, and continues what is basically one large ongoing legal thriller and overly dramatic soap opera. These are not separate books, just one story that is being published in individual 400-page increments. Each book ends with a shocking murder that just leads into the next one. I was thinking that this would be a 4-book series, but now my guess is it could be somewhere between 4 – 6 books in length. I googled it, but there is no clear available or available answer. When “The Hampton’s Lawyer” begins, Jane is preparing to defend her lying and cheating client, Rob Jacobson, who is charged with killing a family of three for the second time. This time his DNA is found at the scene and his situation is worse than the first time Jane helped him avoid a long-term prison sentence. At the same time, Jane continues battling her own problems. Serious medical problems involving her own fight with stage 4 cancer that’s currently winning. She’s 8 months into an estimated life expectancy of approximately 12 months. Even with support from her best friend and personal doctor, Samantha Wylie, her boyfriend and love of her life, Ben Kalinsky, and Jimmy Cunniff, her investigation partner, ex-NYPD police detective, and local bar owner, she is not doing well. Things are so bad that her doctors want her to try an experimental drug that may very likely be her last chance at survival… Jane is facing the biggest challenges in her life – trying to stay alive long enough to figure out who is trying so hard to frame her client and put him away for the rest of his life. A client who keeps making things worse for her defense and has even involved the local mafia leader who is warning Jane to keep him out of things, or he will eliminate her. And the new drugs are wreaking havoc on her body, keeping her from doing what she needs to do to be effective. Jane’s biggest fear is that this will be here her last time in court… After finishing this book, I felt a lot of the same things that I did after the last one in this ongoing, never-ending story. First, the good stuff. Thie strength of this series comes from its heavy character driven story. Other than his big three series – Alex Cross, Michael Bennett, and the Women’s Murder Club – I don’t usually think of James Patterson as a strong writer of character. In this one, he has created another strong, yet empathetic lead that grabs my heart and pulls on it with a tight grip. Jane Smith takes center stage and is in almost every scene that takes place. Although there are selected chapters told from Jimmy’s point-of-view (and I really enjoyed them), Jane carries the weight of the overall story, pacing, and ambience. Don’t get me wrong. For the most part, it works. It works very well. I found myself fully immersed emotionally in these books as Jane dealt with her professional challenges and personal medical issues. Jane is what makes this work. She is an unfiltered, stimulating character. Unfiltered. Outspoken. Flawed. Emotional. Stubborn. Underdog. Brilliant. And someone you cheer for. There were even moments in this one when Jane was struggling, I was really starting to feel the reality of her illness hit me. Hopefully, Patterson and Lupica will not take any cheap ways out in dealing with the outcomes when dealing with her serious medical issues. They have a chance of delivering on the promise of her being one of Patterson’s greatest characters. For me, the secret sauce is Jane’s personal life and professional relationships. How she relates to others. Protects them and at the same time keeps secrets. Goes out of her way to anger others by her flippant and disrespectful attitude yet sacrifices for others in ways they’ll never know and understand. She’s selfish, yet serving, but mostly on her terms. These facets of her character, her strengths balanced by her weaknesses are compelling to us. We all want to be like Jane and say whatever we want, regardless of social expectations, but her facing death allows her the unique freedom to let her inside voice out. Shout it out loud. As for the things I didn’t like, the primary one was the overall storylines involving Jane’s scum bucket client, Rob Jacobson. Although this was an enjoyable, escapist read, it was heavy on style and delivery, and repeated plot development of a second triple homicide (as if one triple homicide wasn’t enough). We continue with the storylines of bad cops, mobsters, and people with political and financial power (the usual in Patterson books). For me, it got fairly convoluted. Lots of characters. Several cops. A few mobsters and an interesting hit man. It wasn’t terribly too hard to follow, but it didn’t really propel the overall storylines forward as much as it felt repetitive. As a matter of fact, Jane’s personal battle with cancer was more compelling than the courtroom drama in this one (at least it was for me). And of course, right at the end, when it looked like you were going to get some closure on outstanding issues, nope, you get another shocking murder that will involve Jane again in the next book… For me, that was a bit of contrived overkill. Overall, compelling characters, especially Jane, made this a fast-paced entertaining read. However, what started out as potential plot development kind of whimpered out in the end and will carry on repetitive plotting into the next entry in the Jane Smith series. I can’t help being left with the feeling that Patterson (and Lupica) are going to milk this as long as they can. To be honest, part of me appreciates that, but the other part is still struggling with the pacing and dying creativity of the legal plotlines. The good news is that isn’t stopping me from reading Jane Smith, but the rope is definitely getting shorter. You can make your own call... 3.5 out of 5 stars (and yes, Goodreads doesn't round off).

Stale Series I rated the first Jane Smith thriller a 5-star, the second a 3-star, and this latest installment a 3-star. The only thing keeping my rating from being a 2-star is that it's an easy read. The same scumbag client for all 3 books and over 1000 pages became very monotonous. It is just not believable that someone who has been targeted for assassination as many times as our protagonist would enter a murder house without protection or escorts - a real person just wouldn't do that but a novel looking for cheap thrills can. Found myself not really caring about Jane's plight or whether she gets the total scumbag off to continue her perfect streak of murder cases.
Just a so-so story.
Could have been a 4 had Lupica not made such a constant effort to offend people of faith.

3.5 / 5.0 I like the gritty sheer determination of Jane Smith, I love the character how she shines through in the pages but what I don’t like is when loose leads solve themselves so convincingly it’s too good and they tie up too soon then expected. It’s giving cliche with this book. I was annoyed that I’ve read the third book in this series with the same guy on trial again after the first two. But what I am happy about is reading and following the journey of Jane Effing smith. This time we truly see Jane fight through everything in this book quite literally, it’s heart wrenching at time. I do like how each character in this book has their own personality shine through. No one is boring and everyone has a story to share. But what I don’t like is reading the same guy on trial 3 times and its the same unlikeable corny misogynistic dude. It’s getting a tad boring, but I am hoping that we don’t see this dude again because this time round it was borderline unbearable. Again we see Jane smith in court defending this same dude, and pulling out all the stops to prove his innocence. It has you questioning your morals at points and respect the role of barristers even more. I’m only in this series for Jane smith, her cute dog Rip and her relationship with Dr Ben Kalinsky!

Rated 2.97 This series keeps getting more boring. I like #1 and it kept moving along with new characters and twists and turns. This book is #2 revisited. Same characters.....very predictable. Cancer continues for Jane and Bridget. Attempted killings, again. Too much the same. Not worth it until the last 100 pages. Probably will not read #4. The Hamptons on Long Island is known for its beautiful beaches, its luxury lifestyle—and its exclusive legal advice. When Jane Smith takes on a famous celebrity client, she’s armed and with brilliant arguments, hard evidence—and two Glocks. Yet she’s chased down, shot at, and risks contempt of court. That’s when mounting a legal defense turns into self-defense. Knowing every day in court could be her last, she’s a survivor. For now.

Patterson is now calling it in. This book read like it was written by an AI bot! No Hamptons authenticity at all. It could have been anywhere USA. The plot was confused and stupid. I am sorry I wasted my time.

Book 3 in the Jane Smith series. Jane is once again defending Ron Jacobson for the murders of three people. Did he actually do it or was he set up. In addition, Jane is undergoing treatment for cancer and she is having a difficult time time staying focused.
