This is, to date, the longest book I’ve ever written. - Preface, Wind and Truth TL;DR: An absolute storming gorgeous read, a treat for the fandom, and a unique and radical take on the epic fantasy genre itself. A highly recommended series, if you can stomach books over a thousand pages, and a backlist of at least five other required reads to understand the ending. I recommend starting at Mistborn :D Sanderlanche (noun): A fast-paced finale sequence with rapidly changing POVs, oft found in all Sanderson books, that culminates the plot threads set up in the majority of the book. Wind and Truth, the final segment of the first half of an epic fantasy series, the Stormlight Archive, spanning decades of work is a sanderlanche for the whole series. While that makes it wonderful for the fandom, who have been waiting for this book for years, it also contains an arduously slow plot in the middle of the book, which could irk some readers (me). I am a victim of the reduced attention spans that plague my generation (I tend to read multiple books at a time, rapidly switching between them), but perhaps this book could have fixed me. I suppose it did, because I forced myself to slow down and savor it. Clearly, the intent of this series is volume. Big, meaty books (this one itself weighs over a kilo) with subplots, subtexts, wandering philosophical discussions, and warring action sequences, which reward the reader with significant reveals at the end. The number of characters seems to surge (hehe) in every subsequent book, and I fear I will need copious notes to read the next books in this series. As much detail as possible is meticulously stuffed into these pages, and I’m going to choose to be appreciative of an author who cares enough about the fantasy community to keep building a fantastic universe rather than even mentioning the word bloated. Damnation, the words escape me. In the true spirit of Sanderson, this review will probably ramble, have insightful quotes, and be humongous. Should a book review be proportionate to the length of the book? Probably. “Life breaks us,” Dalinar said. “Then we fill the cracks with something stronger.” The Cosmere of it all: The Way of Kings could have been read as an introduction to this (wonderful, beautiful) series with almost zero insight into what a Cosmere was a decade ago (I asked myself this so many times over the course of the year), but no more. The Cosmere, a fictional universe where the bulk of Sanderson’s fantasy novels are based, is the underlying character of this book. There are so many interconnected threads to the Cosmere (incredibly, upon reading this book I realized that they had been there since the beginning) that are quite explicitly included and explored in this one. It’s brilliant, but it would be a big impediment to folks who would pick this series up with no other information. Please be warned, there are reading orders to get to before this book and crossovers and easter eggs galore. Even the storming interludes need to be deciphered, and the epigraphs remain an elaborate jigsaw puzzle. The Conflict of it all: My biggest gripe with Rhythm of War (the penultimate book) was that the political and religious conflict in the world was almost forgotten to move the series forward. Granted, there was conflict in that one, but not enough. No more! Sanderson delivers on that front, and how. Mythology, history, war, and magic systems are easier to write than politics I feel, since it requires multiple moving pieces. Sanderson rounds everything out well here. No wonder the book is hefty. The Gender roles+Romance of it all: Sanderson is an ally?!? Love that. He also dials up the romance in this one and executes it very well. It’s like he saw all the online discourse about him being terrible at it and took it to heart. I mean, it isn’t romantasy, but it’s a notch above his usual deal. I’m incredibly happy that some of my favorite characters get some much-needed respite from the pain Sanderson rains down on them XD The Growth of it all: Sanderson’s debut novel, Elantris, was published in 2005, and kickstarted the Cosmere. Since then he’s published multiple books creating new fantasy worlds and advancing the Cosmere piece by piece. I’ve read most of them by now, and they range from mind-blowingly amazing to lackluster duds (I said what I said). What is important is the fact that every single gripe I’ve ever had with any of the books (some dated, vaguely sexist/racist undertones) disappears in this series. Why? As I understand from the subtext of this book (and the series as a whole), and his numerous interviews, Sanderson is a writer who has earnestly grown over the decades and intends to not only include diverse characters but also critically question the world rather than blindly accept beliefs. "Feeling real is enough. The things in our heads can be some of the most important things in our lives. Love is in our heads. Confidence. Integrity. All things we make up, but they’re still very important." The Epic Fantasy of it all: There are tropes in every genre, as there are in fantasy (and they get more dramatic as it gets more epic). Admittedly, I have not read a lot of the staples, but enough to understand why this book is so incredible at paying homage to the tropes (The Chosen One, Good vs Evil, Magic Powerups, Tests and Trials), and turning them on their heads. This makes the series incredibly satisfying. If you want likable main characters, cool scenes, a payoff after a long ordeal, conflicts and clashes, archetype and nuanced villains, archetype and nuanced heroes, multiple magic systems, and slowly unfolding backstories, best believe you’ll find it all in this book. It is definitively, incredibly epic, and in retrospect, it does make sense why it is so long. Sanderson has influenced this genre to a great extent already, and I’m sure this book will end up igniting a new wave of inspired takes. “We’re on a journey,” she said. “Between who we were, and who we want to be. Both of us.” I’ve gotten to this point of the review freely writing without mentioning my favorite characters. Maybe I shouldn’t be so hard on Sanderson for writing tomes. I think I won’t do so, to not include spoilers, but suffice it to say that list will likely have more than 20 names, which is why this book is so incredibly readable—you don’t want to leave the characters and this universe. Before I conclude, a minor mention of the bad: Firstly, the fact that there are more new spren in this one? I can’t understand if these are easter eggs or foreshadowing for something big in the future books. My money’s still on depressionspren appearing someday and becoming a major inconsistency. Secondly, open plot threads or ones brushed under the carpet—a lot of the reveals are given one paragraph of explanation, and trauma is dealt with over the course of *checks notes* ten days. But what’s the alternative? More chapters? Storms, am I advocating for this book to be longer?! Thirdly, there was some weirdly cringe prose in places, which didn’t match the tone of the book, kind of like weirdly timed MCU jokes, or a trite insight. Then again, The thing is, the deepest truths always sound a little trite. Because we all know them, and feel foolish being reminded. So I will always have a lovingly annoyed feeling towards this book series because there is so much cool stuff here but it takes so long to get to the storming point sometimes that that my eyes glaze over. Still, the worldbuilding is so unique and majestic, the characters are so interesting, fascinating, and endearing, and their trajectories are so unexpected, that I can’t not herald (hehe) this book series as one of the best fantasy series ever. Call me the Knight of Tears because that’s what this series does to me. Love the hype, will keep contributing to the hype, will need a TV adaptation of this series in my life pronto.

the very end makes for an interesting set up for the future arc of the series but this book is entirely too long, full of filler, the most important characters are either shadows of their past selves or barely glossed over while the book tries to emotionally manipulate u into caring about up-until-now irrelevant povs or storylines. cartoonish at times too. just overall not a good time and proof that even well-established authors with editors and beta readers need to be slapped back into reality every once in a while. mutual enabling just lulls us all into mediocrity.

This is the most divided I have ever felt about a Stormlight Archive book. As I read through the beginning, I grew increasingly worried. For some reason, it just wasn't hitting. Why? Was something off? Why was I, despite my best efforts, just NOT able to immerse myself in the story? Was it me, or the book? Luckily, by around the 70% mark the plot started to build, and I was safely hooked. Everything after that crashed toward the finish line with all the momentum and intensity expected from this massive "Avengers: Endgame" level fantasy event. Overall, I think this book does stick the landing, resolving most of the countless threads of plot and character in a satisfying way, and setting up the future of the Cosmere. Some standout details in no particular order: • My boy Szeth-son-son-Vallano, Truthless of Shinovar. I have always loved him <3 and continue to love him <3 and I loved finally getting his backstory! It was a fascinating backstory, and explained a lot about both him and the worldbuilding. The way his family determined to go with him when he was first taken away by the military as a boy TRULY got me in the heart. • Adolin continues to carry at least half this series on his back in my opinion. Every time I got to one of his chapters, it felt like a relief. His Azish siege was some of the best action and one of the most compelling storylines in the book, especially during the first half when it felt like almost nobody was doing anything elsewhere. I love his relationship with the Azish Prime, and the way the deadeye spren plot thread was resolved. Wholesome. Heartwarming. Inspiring. • Gavinor :( :( :( :( :( No amount of sad face emojis will adequately express how I feel about this. • Taln................................................. His is such a horrible, horrible story. When he stood up during the Azish siege, I was shook. That scene had serious resonance. • I don't really like visions. I never really like them, in any medium and in any story. Dalinar and Navani's field trip through the Spiritual Realm was made bearable by the tension behind the worldbuilding mysteries they were unraveling. It was better than the extended time in Shadesmar in some of the other books, but not by much. • TANAVAST IS ABSOLUTELY INTOLERABLE. I HATE HIM AND HIS STUPID ALL CAPS CHAPTERS. • The ending... I was okay with. Dalinar's ending. Kaladin's ending. Despite not resolving everything, enough was resolved that I'm walking away from this book not feeling jilted. • I understand The Sunlit Man a lot better now. Might need to reread. • I still don't care that much about the singers, but I kind of like how the battle at the Shattered Plains was resolved. Feels good, feels right. • "Honor is dead... but I'll see what I can do." ALRIGHT, KALADIN. WHY DID THIS HIT SO HARD AGAIN? For some reason this worked super well, even though I almost don't understand why. This whole time Kaladin was kind of just a hype man and helper on Szeth's journey, but for everything to end the way it did still somehow made perfect sense. • Shallan, in this book, was possibly the least annoying she has ever been. I'll admit, I thought we had no more buried secrets to unearth from her incredibly avoidant psyche, but I was proven wrong. • I don't care about any of the Heralds except Taln. I wish I did. It would have made the visions and Szeth storylines much more impactful. • Did I mention how much I enjoyed the Azish siege? Adolin being a brilliant tactician AND social engineer... Adolin mentoring Yanagawan... Some very cool action scenes... An absolutely rip-roaring finale sequence... All right. Now, let's talk about the concerning part: The Cringe I have always been a delighted cosmerenaut. I have cringed in the past at Sanderson things, but only the deliberately cringe and annoying things like Wayne, The Reckoners and Frugal Wizard's Guide. I have never been a huge fan of the quintessential Sanderson corny humor but, again except for in the aforementioned works, it has never really gotten in the way of my enjoyment. Certainly it has never been a real issue for me in the Stormlight Archive, with the possible exception of how annoying early Shallan was. I read almost SEVENTY PERCENT of this book before I really got into it. That is CRAZY and extremely alarming, given that this is book five of the Stormlight Archive. You have to ask yourself, what on earth is going on?!? 1. The first issue was the corny humor. It seemed really overwhelming and in-your-face at the beginning of the book, and kind of tonally dissonant. This book starts up RIGHT after the end of RoW, which was a massive, high-stakes battle and it takes place over the course of only ten days. In those ten days, everyone is staring down the potential end of the world as they know it. That is an absolutely breathless pace, and I'm therefore pretty surprised at how slow the beginning of the book felt. Why did everyone seem to have infinite time to crack awkward puns and genital/potty humor jokes at each other? Thankfully, this slowed WAY down as the plot actually picked up in the second half. 2. Second issue was the odd fakeness/shallowness of the characters. I have traveled with these people for five (LONG) books now, and I know and love all of them. I'm deeply invested in them and their inward journeys. So why, at the beginning of this book, could I NOT seem to connect with anyone? Shallan's relief over finally coming to a place of stability with her multiple personality issues. Kaladin's relief at his own stability, and beginning journey to focus on himself as well as helping everyone else. Adolin's continuing sense of inferiority and anger at Dalinar. Szeth grappling with his longstanding moral injury. For some reason, all of this seemed very very shallow and extremely repetitive. These introspective passages came up so frequently and seemed so exactly the same that I was repeatedly thrown out of my immersion in the story during the first half of the book. I'm sitting there wondering why the heck I'm almost bored by hearing about these characters I have LOVED in the past? With how slow all of this felt in a book that takes place over only ten days, it seems like perhaps some tighter editing could have helped us out here. 3. Third issue was The Cringe. Some things just seemed... off. Some things just didn't hit the way I would have expected them to. Kaladin's therapy shtick with Szeth, for one. I liked the beginning of this in RoW! But the way it was implemented over the course of their Life Changing Road Trip just seemed unrealistic and very cringe. If someone had tried that on Kaladin when he was at his worst, it would NOT have worked. So why are these hamfisted attempts at "Talk about it! You'll feel better! You deserve to be happy! This stuff wasn't your fault!" working on Szeth, who is probably worse off than Kaladin was? Again, he had TEN DAYS to make a total breakthrough and heal Szeth's broken psyche. This is magnified with Nale, whom they had what, only two days with? It just doesn't seem real, and the way this was written was almost as maladroit and awkward as Kaladin's actual therapeutic attempts. The rapidly increasing usage of the word "therapy" just didn't work for me, either. You can handwave your way out of that by using Wit's offworld vocabulary as an explanation, but that doesn't make Kaladin's "No, I'm his therapist" quip any less embarrassing. Kaladin's speech to the librarian after she was mean to Syl was cringe. Definitely something Cliopher Mdang would have said, and then everybody nearby would have clapped. Jasnah's debate with Odium was cringe. Not going to lie, I did skip most of the last chapter of that because I was just going "eugh, eegh, agh," all the way through it. Shallan's tension with Mraize was cringe. I cannot convey how much I do not care about Mraize or his relationship with Shallan, and frankly I'm surprised that SHE cares this much. I don't know how many near-miss encounters they had in the Spiritual Realm, but it felt like way too many. Even some of the actual formatting made me raise an eyebrow, particularly, "It was all he could do to stand there. But stand. Kaladin. DID." It's hard to miss what this ostentatious punctuation and italics is trying to convey: the rousing crescendo of a Hans Zimmer orchestral theme in the background as the wind whips Kaladin's hair and the light dramatically streams down upon him. This kind of scene happens semi-frequently in the Stormlight Archive, and most of the time I love it! But this particular prose was done so awkwardly and in-your-face that it punched me straight out of my immersion in the story at one of the most climactic moments. What about just writing words normally? I promise the reader can supply the suitable amount of drama for themselves based on the actual tone and content of the scene. Lastly, some of the portrayal of the characters' issues seemed oddly wooden. This was present in Kaladin and Syl's development as they traveled with Szeth. I understand what they were talking about in establishing their identities separate from their need to help others/each other, but why did it just feel empty and repetitive when they were talking about it? I've never before had an issue caring and empathizing with Kaladin, of all people. Renarin was another victim of this. His autism just seemed so very "here let me read a checklist of symptoms straight from the DSM-5." It didn't seem real to him, and I for some reason wasn't able to inhabit his perspective. This series has always gone out of its way to highlight things the characters were struggling with (most notably Kaladin's depression and Shallan's DID) but this time instead of feeling like a genuine expansion on a person's complex experience, it felt like ostentatious, unnecessary window dressing. This is my first time writing anything seriously negative in a Cosmere review. I enjoyed the book! After I got 60-70% through it felt like old times, like I was back on the solid ground of what I expect from this series. As I said, I thought it overall worked well as a colossal finale for a colossal story. I definitely want to know what happens next. But for some reason the writing quality, especially in the first half, was just kicking me in the teeth. This is genuinely upsetting and unsettling to me. I hope that this is just a wobbly step caused by Sanderson's extremely fast writing pace and his change in editors, and not my worst fear coming true. PLEASE don't tell me that I'm outgrowing his writing. The experience of reading an awesome book is so rare and precious that I would hate to lose that. There's only one way to know for sure. I need to do a Cosmere reread.

This book was a massive disappointment. I have read everything Brando Sando has ever written, most of it multiple times and loved almost all of it, but this was just awful. Obviously, spoiler warning. Part 1, problems with the plot: 1. If you remove every POV from Shallan/Rlain/Renarin does the plot change at all? Nope, nothing they did contributed to the ending in any way. The entire ghostbloods/mishram storyline was basically pointless, not to mention boring. Oh no! Emotional issues that should have been resolved last book! You’re back! Should I free the openly genocidal demigod? Yes, because… oh I actually can’t think of a good reason, but there is one, I promise. Will there be any consequences from freeing the genocidal demigod? Nope! Everything works out just fine! Tbh if we had just not seen anything from them until the end, when Shallan gets trapped in the cognitive realm, then they show all of this stuff as flashbacks in book six, while mishram is causing problems, these scenes would be much better. Because you would actually care about what happened, because it would provide information about what’s currently happening. 2. The Adolin storyline was the only genuinely good storyline, but the ending of it was horrible. The “un-oathed” twist seemed like such deux ex machina. Brandon broke all three of his rules of magic with this one, but especially #1: “An author’s ability to solve conflict with magic is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to how well the reader understands said magic.” Adolin should have become a radiant. That would have been a better more satisfying ending, that actually fits in with the current magic system. Adolin’s headspace was also really frustrating during the ending. His obsession with there being a difference between promises and oaths seemed ridiculous when an apocalypse is going on, and I thought it would have been much more satisfying for him to forgive his father, then swear some oaths and become a radiant. I was waiting for it the whole book, only to have it stolen away so some random characters I don’t really care about can get plates and blades. One last criticism on this topic: All due respect to Adolin as a duelist, but a guy with one leg, who just fought for hours and hours on a battlefield, somehow beats a full shard bearing fused with a candlestick? Nah. 3. We didn’t need all of those flashbacks in the spiritual realm. Leaving aside the fact that the spiritual realm feels way less impressive and way more gimmicky than it’s been hyped up as this entire time, we could have gotten the exact same information if all of the flashbacks had been eliminated and we just got the tanavast POV scenes. It was also really frustrating on every battlefield for them to be losing so badly when dalinar’s presence and Stormlight could have helped them win literally every battle. Not to mention that the Stormfather could have just told Dalinar all of this stuff from the beginning, without them needing to waste the entire book getting exposition that they DONT EVEN USE. 4. Losing Thaylena(hope that’s spelled right, I’m an audiobook person) should be important, but it doesn’t feel that way. The important thing is that Jasnah lost an argument and now she feels bad about it. 5. Moash. I’m annoyed that Navani finally punished him, and he finally had to feel bad about what he had done, just for neither of those things to matter whatsoever. The man was broken, blinded, overwhelmed by guilt and suffering because he had murdered his friend, then less than a week later he’s just out there doing it again, no consequences except now he can see spren! 5.5 Sigzil got done dirty in this book just to force him to into the sunlit man. 6. The big one, Kaladin. This man tried to end his own life literally 1 day ago, at the end of RoW. It feels pretty absurd for him to be Therapist(Tm) one day later, not to mention that there is an apocalypse and a war going on, like bro, all due respect, but what exactly do you think your character was developing toward? “I will protect” *leaves everyone to protect themselves* I did like that he became a herald, but I didn’t like how it happened. Especially after Szeth was built up towards it, I always knew it would be Kaladin instead, but it was literally just because Szeth was knocked out? And soup and music over ~a week is supposed to cure Szeth? What was the point of going to each monastery in turn? Just to drag the plot out so it takes enough time? Kaladin’s sections have always been my favorite, but this time it just dragged. I have more criticism but it will go in the writing section. 7. Finally the ending. A main question of the books has been is it okay to kill to protect? That’s been a mainstream theme of the entire book, and is the focal question of Kaladin’s entire character. But then when the time comes to answer it definitively and let the consequences fall where they may, Brandon cops out, dodges the question, and refuses to commit. Dalinar, the blackthorn, legendary warrior, refuses to kill one person to protect millions, if not billions. And his sacrifice is for naught, because taravangian resurrects his ghost anyway. 8. Oh and some older wiser super god pauses time to chat with Dalinar before he makes his final decision?? What is that guy doing, and if hes so old and wise and smart, why doesn't he come and solve some of the problems. It felt implied that Nohadon is adonalsium, so why is he just letting the bad guys win all the time bro? Its not as big a problem for this book, but its going to be a massive problem for future books. Part 2, the writing: Two of the three most interesting characters in the entire series on a quest to find and recruit a mad demigod, accompanied by another mad demigod, fighting duels with superpowered immortal beings mind controlling an entire nation is somehow boring???? How do you mess this one up that bad? 1. Modernisms: Nothing destroys immersion faster or harder than modern day ideas, words, phrases, or messaging. It is impossible to stay immersed in the story when words like therapy, racist, shit, genetics, dating “back in fifteen”(like everyone has clocks that measure minutes???) etc. are being thrown around constantly. Therapy as a concept is basically a post ww2 invention. So having completely modern therapy techniques and ideas pumped into everything is utterly ludicrous. It absolutely destroys any sense of antiquity, immersion, or gravitas in the world when all the characters seem to be worried about are modern problems and themes. I’m reading this book to get away from modern political and social themes, not to wallow in them. 2. I don’t need to know how every character is feeling at every single moment for the entire book. Show me what they do and say, and let me draw my own conclusions. I don’t need 3 paragraphs of explanation of their every feeling every time they do something. It’s exhausting, boring and makes the book lose flow. Let me make some inferences about the character! If you explain every single thought, it actually makes the character feel less deep, less real. The more dimensions of a character you tell me about, instead of showing me actions and letting me guess, the less there seem to be. My imagination about their motives will always let me relate to the character more than you telling me about every single motivation they have ever had. Less is more, and in this case, more was way way less. This is why Shallan drags so much as a character, we have had too much insight into her inner thoughts for way too many pages/hours across too many books. 3. Just straight up bad prose: Go read the intro to ch 24. It’s a very prosey section where Szeth is dancing, then for no reason at all we have this line: “Five feet across and three feet high—at least the part that emerged from the soil—“. Bro what? Why include that? It wrecks the flow of the scene completely! I was listening, and I remember being jarringly brought right back into the real world by that one line, disrupting the story, breaking the immersion. 4. Too many POVs, too frequent POV changes. I don’t think I need to say anymore about this. 5. Sexualization characters. Why did we feel the need to mention that Syl has human anatomy? Are her and Kaladin going to have a physical relationship? Like whats the point here? It feels very fanservicey. The same with the Adolin Shallan shower scene. This is not a romance novel, don't make it one. I don't mind when characters are obviously in a physical relationship, I'm a huge fan of the wheel of time, but the way it is done is just not it. Part 3, Vibes: 1. Preachy: Lots of scenes where Brandon has a goal of a message he wants to get across, and instead of showing, tells us exactly what message he wants us to understand. Eg. Kaladin roasts librarian lady for being mean to Syl. 2. Not hard hitting: I don’t spend much time on reddit or reading theories or anything like that, until recently I havent spent much time on sanderson related YouTube, so I didn’t get any spoilers about stuff like Shallan’s mom, or Gav as Odium's champion etc. But even though I had no idea, they still did not make a big impact. I remember being surprised, but instead of that surprise sticking with me, it felt hollow. Maybe its because I didn’t actually care who the champion would be, or who Shallan’s mom was? But I don’t think there were any surprises in the whole book that actually hit hard. 3. Too much explanation: I want to know stuff, but he gave us too much stuff. This book felt like he had a prequel written about the heralds (which sounds totally dope), and he just cut random chapters out and gave it to us, but it didn’t actually give us any deeper understanding of HOW they did stuff. We got more about what they did, but not really how or why. 4. Boring. I could not care less about huge sections of this book, the plot, the writing, the character development, all just fall flat. 5. Felt very YA. I came here for an adult epic fantasy, not a YA romance stormlight fanfic. 6. Too long, and I like long books, but not when they are full of this crap. Part 4, politics: What makes great stories great is that they are relevant in any time period. Lord of the Rings was written almost a century ago, and it is so enduring that people are still making movies and TV shows about it. Eternal concepts like good vs evil, order vs chaos, duty, honor, suffering, and self sacrifice, will always be mainstays of good storytelling. Themes like these are what made the first 2 books so good. What will not be a mainstay of great storytelling is hypermodern gender, queer, and therapy themes. People will still be reading books like the wheel of time(which has progressive themes, just not at the expense of the plot) and the lord of the rings in 50-100 years. Up until this book I was sure that the SA would join them, and some of the books still might. However I fear WaT will join the likes of other politically active stories from hugely popular storylines that quickly become irrelevant and forgotten because the focus shifted away from good writing in favor of political messaging. Its the same reason that Christian entertainment has done so poorly for so many years, because the message comes at the expense of the story. One last point about the political messaging is that once again it breaks the immersion. In the Wheel of Time, progressive themed characters felt natural and organic, part of the world, the same way they are part of historical events in our world. In WaT, they felt like a lecture from a gender studies major at a private university. Whether or not you are in favor of it, it breaks the immersion. Conclusion: I love the Stormlight Archive, up until WaT it was my favorite series, and I would recommend Sanderson to everyone I knew. I cannot do that anymore. The first two books are phenomenal, the third is kind of boring early on but sticks the landing, I really like RoW and everything that we learn and the character arcs. WaT is an unmitigated disaster. It's depressing for me to have to write this, because I love Sanderson as a storyteller, but this isn't it. His editors and pre-readers did a horrible job, and I can't help but feel that political messaging was put above storytelling. I highly doubt that the story I just read was the one he imagined when he wrote TWoK 15 years ago.

This book was so good! It took me a little while to become immersed in this book but once I did I was hooked in awesome world building and story. The pacing was slow in the beginning and middle, then picked up near the end. Sanderson is such an excellent writer, his writing is descriptive while also engaging and cinematic. The characters in this series are some of my favorite characters of all time. They are well rounded, relatable, complex and all go through challenges. I love Shallan, Syl, Kaladin, Adolin, and Dalinar so much! I also really like Rlain, Renarin and Navani. I wished that there were more interactions between Shallan, Adolin and Kaladin. Szeth’s character development was excellent, I enjoyed learning more about him and realizing how his past shaped him in many ways. The world building continues to amaze me, there is so much detail and complexity to the world. I greatly enjoyed that there was a focus on the past and the history of the world, but I was hoping the plot would move along more in the present. The build up to the end was so well done, there were so many surprises and interesting plot details. The ending was so great, there plot was action-packed and I was on the edge of the my seat the last 200 pages. These characters will stay in my heart for a long time. I can’t wait to read the next book!

If you prefer watching videos, I have a BookTube Channel! The only good thing I feel after reading this book is validation for choosing Adolin as my favorite character very early on in the series. I took a lot of good natured ribbing from friends about loving him so much, so it feels good to know I made a great choice. (In my opinion) That validation was not worth reading this book for though. Characters acted...well, out of character. 98% of the book was spent in the past or in visions of the past which gleaned nothing of use and way too much repetition to slog through. I had intended to reread the first 4 books prior to starting this one and now I'm really glad that I didn't since it all got recapped in great detail. (I would have been even more mad had I reread those though.) I only finished because I expected a Sanderlanche and I wanted to see if it could redeem 1,000 pages and boy was that a waste. ELANTRIS got a better Sanderlanche than this one! Immersion kept getting cracked due to modern day word usage that was not prevalent in prior books and not only that, Sanderson described these things differently previously, so why not continue the trend? Why are we all of a sudden using these words? It didn't fit the mold, so that's likely another reason why they were so disruptive. The "humor" was terrible. Some of the plot points that were added to be more inclusive to all felt forced and in my opinion, because of the way other characters reacted to these or their inner monologue, it felt more like an insult that inclusive. For the love of your fellow human - please if you are going to write these things, write them in as though these are the norm. If you're just going to have your characters question them or point them out as "odd" then just don't do it. Normalize it. Have your world show a good example by displaying acceptance. FFS This is only the second time I've read a last book in a series (or arc of a series in this case), where the final book destroyed the whole series for me. This is the end of the first arc in Stormlight Archives, the midway point for the series. By now you know what to expect, and on every front you expect Stormlight to deliver, this book does in spades. Not only that, Sanderson experiments with structure here in a way that breaks the series mold and feels extremely fresh and earned. There are some issues I have with the book that are minor and personal, and largely have to do more with my expectations than the book itself. So I will not hold that against it. I can’t say anything else about the book that isn’t a spoiler, so I will just say I devoured this book in two days. That’s how good it is. There are however two main issues that stood out to me that I feel are worth addressing. The first is the community around these books. Not that the community is bad, on the contrary it is really quite amazing. It feels akin to the Fromsoftware community in the way that engaging with it seems like the intended design. The Cosmere is so vast and detailed that you almost have to consult a wiki or forum. The issue lies with this: due to Brandon’s meticulous plotting and attention to detail, and nerds inability to do anything but agonize over those details for the greater part of a decade, many major plot points of this book were already guessed and considered all but canon by the community. Many of the heavy hitting moments fell flat for me, as I already expected them just so. So take that with a grain of salt - but for me it hampered my enjoyment of the book. And that is no one’s fault but my own. The second, and larger issue, is Sanderson’s attempt at addressing mental health. I realize this is the golden cow of Stormlight - a cast of fundamentally broken characters who progress through each book as they battle and conquer and fail against their past traumas and mental anguish. It really is riveting, and some of the greatest intersections of character and plot development happen in SA for this very reason. But the issue arises mostly in the last few books Sanderson has published. And that is that his approach is becoming more and more shoe horned, and less natural. The word here is anachronistic. You have a group of characters fighting for the fabric of their very world, and I am not exaggerating, they often openly discuss their mental health, identity issues, or what have you as greater trials then the end of the world. And the cast accepts these conversations with more openness and ‘awareness’ than ANY group of real people I have met. And I live in the modern west, not antiquated Roshar. Now I am not saying these aren’t important conversations to have or even that Sanderson’s point is lost on me (it isn’t), but rather his attempt at making these moments land feel tone deaf in light of the world and its events. And they take me out of the magic, almost every time. To quote another reviewer, it feels often like many of the times dialogue was written with an HR rep standing in the room. And I see this pattern developing and growing with each new entry. All in all I love this book, but these things stood out to me too strongly to ignore. I’ll see all you lads in six years.

1.75/5🌟 Spoiler Free First of all, I want to start off by saying if you loved this book, I am so happy for you. Keep loving it! Unfortunately, I did not and had to fight for my life not to dnf it. I’m going to break this down into categories to give y’all an idea of why, for me, W&T is far more than a bad Stormlight book, it’s one of the worst fantasy books I’ve read in recent memory. Prose - Sanderson has never been known for having strong prose but my god, has the quality dropped significantly. It felt like the book was constantly talking down to me. Repeating the same info from 6 different povs, 20 chapters in a row. The use of modern language took me right out of the story, and the dialogue was nearly unreadable at times with a strong YA vibe that had no business being in an adult fantasy epic. For me, W&T read like the fanfiction of a 14yr old SA fan with a DSM-5. Pacing - The amount of nothing. This word count is absurd. If you cut out the middle, slammed the beginning and end together, you’d be able to figure out what’s happening. This book is almost entirely filler, with nothing of value to add to the arcs or the plot. World building - Is it cool? I guess, but it doesn’t matter. What you learn has no bearing on the story. For a series that prides itself on “Journey before destination” there is a severe lack of actual journey. Sanderson breaks his own magic rules for plot, and sacrifices logic for moving the story along. Everything about the Spiritual Realm fills me with rage. How does it work? When the author wants it to. Arcs - The kumbaya of it all. Why is everyone suddenly so unrealistically self aware? I should be punching my fist into the air. I should be inconsolable with grief, yet I feel absolutely nothing. Adolin was the only pov I actively enjoyed. The snap of this man’s back carrying W&T echos. These characters felt nothing like the people I’ve grown to know and love. There were fundamental technical writing skills, outside of storytelling, that I had issue with here. I’m glad Sanderson isn’t writing another SA book for some years, I need that long a distance to decide whether I’ll pick up book 6 or not.

This is a frustrating review for me to write. For a long time Brandon Sanderson has been my favorite modern fantasy author, and the Stormlight Archives my favorite unfinished series, but after reading this book that has changed for me. While parts of this book are absolutely incredible, and it doesn't change how much I love the first three books, there are several issues I have with Wind and Truth that I just can't overlook, and they ruined the reading experience for me overall. The first issue, and by far the most detrimental to how I view Wind and Truth, is the same-sex romance agenda that Sanderson places front and center. While he's included passing references at homosexuality in some of his past books, in Wind and Truth, these same-sex relationships are championed by some of the main characters, and it is heavily glorified. Due to my convictions, and my conscience, I started to skip each section where these characters would show up once I realized what was going on, but I'm incredibly disappointed that Sanderson chose to include this. It was completely unnecessary, and makes it so I can't recommend this book. Other issues I had include the way that Sanderson tries to write humor. A lot of the jokes sound like they're coming straight from a group of middle school boys, which quickly loses its charm and feels jarring to read in this kind of epic series. Likewise, Sanderson's attempt to address "mental illness" in a fantasy book where people wear super suits and kill stuff with magical swords comes off as shallow at best and preachy at worst. It seriously feels like he took a psychology textbook and copy pasted some sections into this book. Taken together, these issues compile to make one very frustrating read. Were there some awesome parts? Yes. Does the ending absolutely blow your mind? Yes. Will I ever read it again? Nope.

Ever since The Way of Kings, I regarded Brandon as, perhaps, the brightest modern fantasy writer. Yes, he's not Martin with his encyclopedic knowledge of history and impeccable talent for writing smart characters, and not Rothfuss either, since Brandon's writing doesn't come near enough to his poetic charm, and definitely not as fresh and almost revolutionary to the genre as Abercrombie. Still, the scope of Sanderson's body of work is so ambitious that it hides his flaws behind the sheer scale of enormity and, the most important of all, sincerity. The first two Stormlight books were brilliant. I instantly adored Roshar, appreciated how unfamiliar and alien it was, and enjoyed slowly understanding the rules and principles behind this land and its societies. The Way of Kings was much more ambitious than Mistborn and all of its derivatives, and it made so many promises of mystery and novelty that I was instantly hooked. Words of Radiance expanded upon it, adding even more of what made the first book great. Oathbringer was good but not as great, though still, it was only a middle point! RoW was where everything started to fall apart. As the penultimate parts often are, it was tense and right on the edge of giving all the answers Wind and Truth should've provided. Still, I feel like Brandon got too excited about writing and explaining a "complex magic system"®, which got in the way of the story itself. The book turned out to be half misery and suffering and another half a weird combination of natural philosophy with fantasy mumbo-jumbo. The final book is underwhelming. Maybe it's my fault, as I had too many expectations. Journey before the destination and all that. And yet, I can't shake off the feeling that Stormlight started as the most fresh, original, and exciting fantasy book series of the 21st century and ended like a season 5 of a mediocre TV show from the CW - on a really annoying cliffhanger, full of too-modern-to-be-immersive jokes, and, worst of all, confusing mental disorders with personality traits. But these would be forgivable if not for the book's biggest problem: it's oversaturation. There's too much of EVERYTHING - from the number of characters to their overflowing emotion, from forced romance plots to connections with other Cosmere books - what once was a fun nod to other stories, connecting them into one universe, now became an annoying reminder about how much the Cosmere changed in recent years, as to follow the plot of this book one needs to read about 10 to 15 other ones from Sanderson, and this is just too much commitment to a single author, in my opinion. And don't get me started on an overabundance of everything magical - light, voidlight, anti-light, anti-voidlight, but wait, there's more! The lowest point of the book comes right near the end, where a particular character gets asked who they are, and they respond, "Well, I guess I'm a therapist." It was the single most immersion-breaking thing I ever expected to read, almost akin to screaming, "Hey, it's a JOKE! In my HIT BOOK SERIES, THE STORMLIGHT ARCHIVE! THERAPIST, LIKE IN THE REAL WORLD, Y'KNOW?" It just came off as... cheap. I felt the same after The Lost Metal. Like the Cosmere is collapsing on itself. And Wind and Truth, unfortunately, confirmed this. There's too much and too many - worlds, interconnected and overarching plots, characters, and magic systems, and I feel like because of that overabundance, because of interconnectivity, the present, here and now, isn't getting enough time, energy, and story relevance to pull off a satisfying conclusion, everything should always be about one more mystery, one more story, about references and implication, and it just became... boring. At one point, I figured that if anyone could pull this gargantuan project of dozens of books connecting into one story off, it would be Brandon, but it seems the ambition was too much for one man, sorry. I think after Wind and Truth, the series (and the universe) is only at half-point, but I'm done.

DNF. When I first discovered BS the first two books of SA were out. The WOK and WOR quickly became the best fantasy books I had ever read. Since then I’ve read all his works. Since then release after release I started to not enjoy his works as much as the last. While during that time I’ve read other authors like Hobb and Abercrombie which had shown me that while Sanderson is a master of world building and magic systems, his writing leaves you wanting a lot more. When I read the last SA book ROW, I found it unnecessarily long and a bit boring other than the typical Sanderlanche at the end of his books. But for me that one was a 6/10. I wasn’t really looking forwards to this one based on his last entry in the series and my opinions were validated. 350 pages in and I’m bored to death. None stop world building and people talking about other people and other systems on and on and on. Not to mention the modern “humour” and dialogue really stuck out and a negative way making it feel like a YA novel or a CW show. I find Sandersons cosmere has become too complex with too many characters and too many turning pieces. I know there’s a lot of people that absolutely love the “marvelization” of Sandersons works, but it’s starting to feel way over bloated and too complex for my enjoyment. Lightly skimmed the middle of the book with not a lot grabbing my attention and read the last 300 pages to find myself equally unimpressed with the last 300 pages as I was with the first 300 pages. Also I really really dislike shallan and it’s been obvious since the last book that she’s the main character. Sanderson writes characters too on the nose. Kaladin is dark and brooding so Sanderson makes him say dark and brooding things. Shallan is smart and whitty so Sanderson makes her say and do smart and whitty things. It all just makes me feel like I’m reading forced dialogue to tell the reader again and again “hey these are how my characters are supposed to be”. I’m a character first reader and I want them to feel organic and have their words and actions speak for themselves, so that I can be shown who the character is. Not told who the character is. I’m glad Sanderson exists, but it’s time for me to move on.

And so the end is here. The first thing to say is that I admire a lot of the choices Sanderson made in this book, choices that I don't think he could be sure fans would like. They were the choices of a brave author with a vision. This is also the best paced Stormlight book outside of Words of Radiance. This book also has some of the worst writing Sanderson has put out for a longgg time. Sanderson and his editors need to do better moving forward because I personally will not be able to endure with writing that stunts his storytelling like in Wind and Truth. The concept that you can read Cosmere series by themselves is now proven to be but a myth. Handled much more deftly than The Lost Metal, Wind and Truth deals with the grand concept of the Cosmere directly throughout. Despite being so well-paced, the book failed to produce many emotions from me. As opposed to other entries in the series, this book felt almost systematically assembled, like a brick house built without mortar, it was a construction missing the emotional veins that make me *feel* a story. I will be taking a long break from Sanderson following this book. We both need it.
