Ok I am back on track with the longlist! I really enjoyed reading All The Little Bird-Hearts by Viktoria Lloyd-Barlow, there was something just so wonderfully heartbreaking about it. This is one of two books on the longlist told from a neurodiverse character. This one though was written by an author who is herself autistic. In contrast to How to Build a Boat which had a more stereotypical voice of a teenager All The Little Bird-Hearts sang with an authenticity of voice that both warmed me and made my heart ache. Sunday lives with her 16 year old daughter Dolly in the English countryside. Her sister and parents died when she was young and she prefers to live a quiet and ordered life. It soon becomes clear that Sunday’s very specific life of routine, discomfort with social interactions and preferences for white foods is a result of neuro-divergence. The sad thing is that these traits are seen to be wilful disobedience or oddness and Sunday is often perplexed by the world around her. Their lives are changed though when a vibrant couple Vita and Rollo move in next door over the summer. As she is on the cusp of losing Dolly to the adult world this couple swoop in and bring excitement and glamour to their lives. The couple soon become more focussed on Dolly though as she practically moves in with them and becomes a part of their world as opposed to the safety of her mother’s small life. This change between Dolly and Sunday was hard to watch. Dolly seems impervious to her mother’s need for her to stay safely with her and Sunday is at a loss as she watches Dolly move farther and farther away. I loved the way Lloyd-Barlow’s writing so vividly described Sunday’s inner thoughts. This was not a fast paced novel and the ending is obvious to the reader well before it is obvious to Sunday which adds to its pathos. I felt so deeply for Sunday as I watched her experience rejection and insecurity. I really enjoyed the reading experience and found this to be less bleak book than many of the other longlisted books which was a welcome relief.
About a neurodivergent mother, her daughter and a rich entitled couple that step into their lives and change them forever.

"If loud noise and artificial light do not pain you, you cannot know the sublime relief of silence, of dullness. I intimately know both states; I have learned to live through the chaos and wait for the reward of stillness, knowing it will eventually come for me" Sunday Forrester, an autistic divorcee, lives with her 16-year-old daughter, Dolly, in a house that she inherited from her parents (we then learned that Sunday also had a sister, Dolores, who drowned when she was young and Sunday's mother blamed her for Dolores's death). Sunday has a fixed routine: She eats only white food, drinks only cold and fizzy drinks, is obsessed with Sicilian folklore and proverbs, and uses the Etiquette Guide for Ladies written in 1959 by Edith Ogilvy to guide her through confusing social situations. Despite this, she is willing to "work harder on the illusion of normalcy" for the love of Dolly, who seems to distance herself from Sunday and increasingly resent her fixed routine. When charming and eccentric Vita moved in next door together with her husband Rollo, a special friendship developed between Vita and Sunday. Vita is the opposite of Sunday: Vita is confident, a social butterfly, and unconventional. When Vita starts to befriend Dolly, Sunday notices that Vita's presence is slowly invading and changing her life, especially her relationship with Dolly. When Dolly decides to leave Sunday and move in with Vita in London, can Sunday rescue her relationship with Dolly by observing the usual social conventions, or adhering to the rules in her etiquette guide? As the author, Viktoria Lloyd-Barlow, is also autistic, she managed to beautifully construct a character who observes, and occasionally criticizes, social norms and conventions from a neurodivergent perspective. From Sunday's point of view, readers are able to understand the world and behavior of a person who suffers from autism. Sunday's critique of what we deem as "normalcy" and a performative societal convention/manipulation, often from her observations of Vita's eccentric behavior, is brilliant: "In a painting, the artist intends all the uncomfortable truth he has put there, somewhere within the beautiful image, to be read. In life, the opposite is more often true"; "I had not considered, before meeting Vita, that acquaintances could be more beneficial than injurious. I had not properly understood, then, that people could be played like instruments to produce whatever sound you demanded of them"; "At Vita's house, too, there were tricks. But they were not exposed over tantrums thrown at the table; they were played as a long game and could only be recognised some time afterwards"; "I would rather be a tiny person who wonders and trembles at their surroundings than rule over everything, manipulate it to my preference, and in doing so, come to despise it"; "I am unlike Vita and Rollo, unlike the Forresters, who believe love is a performance and something to be sold to an audience". The theme of motherhood flourished in Sunday's relationship and dynamics with Dolly, as well as Sunday's strained relationship with her mother, which somehow scarred her. She often considers herself "an unloved child" because of her peculiarities. As Dolores was deemed to be more "normal" than Sunday, Sunday's mother favored Dolores, and Dolores's death unleashed her cruel attitude toward Sunday: "Ever since her death, I have consoled myself with the thought that wanting your mother to find something worthwhile in you was probably the most normal condition I would ever find myself in"; "I had been a witness, at least, to her maternal love". Interestingly, the theme of motherhood somehow developed from Vita's relationship with Dolly, where it is implied that Dolly is a daughter that Vita never had and her ulterior motive in befriending Sunday, is to have Dolly all to herself. The recognition of this debut novel by the Booker Prize is commendable as I daresay that the writing here is impressive and the story definitely stuck on my mind for quite some time. All the Little Bird-Hearts is a dark, devastating, and distinctive examination of motherhood, love, and the standards of "normalcy" from an underrepresented voice. A strong 4.8/5 star rating!

BOOKER PRIZE 2023 LONGIST ALL THE LITTLE BIRD-HEARTS by Viktoria Lloyd-Barlow **** Another debut author longlisted, Lloyd-Barlow is autistic and has written a very emotional story of a high-functioning autistic protagonist, a single mother whose very regimented and predictable life gets turned around with the appearance of new neighbours. Sunday Forrester lives her life incredibly self-aware of her own mental processes and patterns, her need to repeat to herself the words spoken to her, their intonations, their accents. She has obsessions with decorum of social interactions and fascinated by the ways of Sicilian life. She has faced repeated loss, first of her sister, then her parents, then her marriage. She lives a schedule set largely by work and her teenage daughter, Dolly, who has grown frustrated with Sunday’s behaviours and limits. A well-to-do couple, Vita and Rollo, move next door and quickly become the central force in both Sunday’s and Dolly’s life, which brings joy to Sunday, but soon worry as Dolly becomes the centre of their attention. Told from Sunday’s perspective, this is a novel driven by voice and it is a voice often neglected in literary fiction, a very complicated and vulnerable view of a neurodiverse person. Sunday is filled with doubts, regrets, guilt but also enormous amounts of love and trust, traits that others take advantage of. Some reviews felt annoyed by the repetitive nature of her stimming behaviour, but I think that is the point to understand that this is the mental process that those with neurodiverse individuals require to function as best they can. The lack of patience some readers have expressed feels like the lack of patience those like Sunday experience every day with those who surround them. Although I flew through this book and found the writing filled with tension and empathy, it has problems. I found it bothersome that Sunday, although richly developed and with potential agency, mostly ends up accepting the fate others have deemed appropriate for her. She is angry and disappointed with the outcomes, but also lethargic and passive when she feels unable to alter the course of events she has accepted as inevitable. This may be a reality Lloyd-Barlow wanted to convey but also left me disappointed when Sunday’s anger could easily be discounted and ignored by those around her. Probably not a short-list for me but still a powerful read. #bookstareadsthebooker2023 #bookstagramreadsthebooker #bookerprize #bookprizes #literaryfiction #igbooks #neurodiversity

“Occasionally, and only in front of Dolly, I would showily eat something that did not adhere to my assigned list of foods. You can eat normally then; you can do what the rest of us do without a fuss. My mother said this, often. I answered her silently when she was alive and I continue to do so now she is dead: There is a cost, Mother, always a cost to such transgressions, and I am the one who pays. I am the one whose throat and body burn when I politely swallow down food of the wrong colour; it is my arm that itches when a neighbour greets me by lightly placing a hand on my skin. I wear the marks of these encounters, these painful sensory interruptions.” This novel affected me deeply. The character, Sunday, touched me deeply. The portrayal of the neurodivergent experience felt honest and authentic. As a parent of young adults who are, one by heart-wrenching one, fleeing my nest, I also identified with the unintentional cruelty inflicted on Sunday as her daughter excitedly looked to a future away from her mother and the perceived banality of life in her hometown. This novel keeps you on your toes with suspense while tugging at your heart with empathy and hope for a just and gratifying ending.

This was a surprise. I picked it up thinking it had a good chance of being shortlisted for the 2023 Booker, and after How to Build a Boat's utter failure to provide a convincing neuro-divergent narrative voice, I hoped this would be better. And it is. In fact, it is so much better at offering a rarely captured narrative that I was pleasantly taken aback. And although the book has a number of problems - the pacing, foremost among them - I found myself not caring about them and instead caring a great deal about Sunday, our protagonist. And the longer I read, the more I understood that the sometimes glacial pace, the repetitions, the overuse of the title metaphor, all made me understand the narrator so much more. Even when I got angry on her behalf because other people were horrible, I never felt it was going too far - and in many cases I had to withdrew my harsh judgement because I suddenly realised there was another way of interpreting the actions of some characters. And others were simply assholes (they exist!). I loved this book because even the annoying parts of it helped me understand Sunday and her daughter better. I struggled with rating All the little Bird-Hearts, because objectively it is not perfect; it could be tighter, it probably would have benefited from a stricter editor. But it still completely convinced and captivated me, and if that's not the mark of a great book, I don't know what is. So this book has flaws, and I can understand why people find it lacklustre. I even understand why it did not make the short list (though if we were going for composition, really, Pearl should be there instead of Western Lane). But for me it was an emotional revelation, and I will absolutely recommend it to a lot of people.

Most of us have our vulnerabilities, those things we love that make us fragile. But not those two. It is not a security I envy. All The Little Bird-Hearts was a pleasant heart warming read. The audiobook was really good and narration was spot on. The voice change for characters was good but I found at places that few characters sounded exactly the same and I had to listen very hard to understand who was actually speaking. Apart from this issue which bothered me towards end of the book more, everything else was really good. All The Little Bird-Hearts tells us a story of an autistic single mother Sunday who is well immersed in her daughter's life, her whole life actually surrounds around her daughter. She has got no luck in finding love at any place. It had been an assault of some years rather than a few moments, and the assailants were people I loved. Because of being autistic she is always misunderstood and is looked down upon for being "not normal". Her own parents did not like her. Her spouse and his parents could never understand her. But the worst part I felt was how her daughter treated her. I realise, now, that my mother could still have loved me, if she had chosen to. It is possible to know the oddities of people and to love them regardless. I want this to comfort me, but it does not. I had always thought that I was an unloved child purely because of my peculiarities. Normally we have read many books about struggles of an autistic child and his parents who are learning how to raise an autistic child. This book felt different because a neurodivergent is trying to raise a neurotypical kid. It took me back to an embarrassed parent elbowing the back of my school blazer as I silently organised perfect sentences in my head but struggled to bring them to the surface, like a deft swimmer trapped underwater. Enters Vita who is charming and beautiful. Vita is staying next door and even though it is not in the nature of Sunday to make friends fast, Vita and she strike a bond superfast. They become good friends. Sunday is actually mesmerized by Vita's charms and modernness. Where I am pale and insubstantial, Vita was dark and deliberately formed, as real as a piece of marble. And as cold under your hand. I am a stutter of a person, a glitch that flickers; I am the air blurred by the summer sun. But is Vita a really good sunday can ask for? Many might find it a simple story and it is a simple story but in my opinion, a very well written one with a powerful lesson. I loved the writing style very much and I found myself immersed in world of Vita and Sunday. It kept me engaged till the end. Thanks Netgalley and Hachette audio for this wonderful audiobook ARC in exchange of an honest review. Quotes that are worth mentioning : There is a cost, Mother, always a cost to such transgressions, and I am the one who pays. I am the one whose throat and body burn when I politely swallow down food of the wrong colour; it is my arm that itches when a neighbour greets me by lightly placing a hand on my skin. I wear the marks of these encounters, these painful sensory interruptions. I listen to dialogue intently; since childhood, this practice has protected me from eyes that are always seeking mine in greetings or conversation. Facial expressions typically tell me nothing more than what is being said. The manner of speaking – the tone, the points of hesitation, the emphases – these are what talk to me. What would it be to live without the laborious work of translation, to hear and instantly know what you have heard? I would have survived as a Sicilian wife, for I can follow rules as clear as these. But I was married to an English King, and so the wolf consumed me on my own doorstep. I had not known that protectiveness could be both furious and tender. That a first sighting could feel as familiar as a reunion. Possession is a form of love, after all. The warm weight of my daughter in my arms was all I had ever wanted, before I even knew I was wanting. Before Dolly, I had thought myself to be missing the basic components that would make me human. Her little body made me real and not only paper, like my own family; just as I had made her, she fleshed me out. The lack of visible social effort on my part was what she always criticised me for most harshly. I believed, even then, that if I could only convince her of my constant attempts at normalcy, she would forgive my resultant failure. She thought my difference was a deliberate pose; thought my remoteness was something I was consciously doing to her. As if, deep down, I had always known all the secrets of communication, just as my sister had, but I had wilfully turned away from that knowledge. ‘I try. I have always tried.’ In fact, I learned, all the questions could be satisfied only by my regular admissions of guilt. And of course, I knew Dolores’ death was my fault, had always known it, but it pained me to say out loud what I carried with a silent reverence. And it was not the condemnation of me that was painful, for I already knew this pronouncement of her feelings to be sincere; it was the public announcement and the flippancy in her voice that finished me. Ever since her death, I have consoled myself with the thought that wanting your mother to find something worthwhile in you was probably the most normal condition I would ever find myself in. It is not always possible to recognise an experience as the final of its kind – such things are often known only in retrospect – but I am grateful for what I did not know as I stood and shivered on the shore that evening. The secret was that an ending was approaching my family. We walked home afterwards in a silence that I did not question. I could not see, as we walked together in the darkness, that my sister was still submerged; was, in fact, a dead girl walking. I did not know, then, that she would struggle all night with an invisible and watery enemy; that she was being kept somewhere below the surface and unable to summon help. I still believed, then, that my way of not seeing only made me strange and unpopular; I did not know that it blinded me to all the fires that were not in the fields. Since Vita and Rollo and their cheerful celebration of my strangeness, I wonder if there was something else Ma witnessed in me, something that she found not simply different, but abhorrent. But, like Dolly and Rollo, she did not have to sacrifice very much of herself to be lovable, and this perhaps spoiled them for others. Should great love be attained without effort? I do not believe that anything so easily won can be prized at all. I am unlike Vita and Rollo, unlike the Forresters, who believe love is a performance and something to be sold to an audience.

All my reviews live at https://deedireads.com/. All the Little Bird-Hearts was longlisted for the 2023 Booker Prize, and I’m glad it was, because otherwise I probably would never have picked it up. But this was a book very much worth my time (and yours). The main character, Sunday, is a lovable but lonely autistic single mother whose world (and relationship with her teenage daughter) is shaken up when glamorous, electrifying new neighbors move into the house next door. Throughout the book, there’s a dark tension that grows more and more ominous as you read, making it both deeply engaging and tenderly heartbreaking. This is a refreshingly authentic portrayal of autism by an autistic author (amidst the “finest fiction” Booker-esque literary canon, anyway). I read an interview with the author where she talked about her intentional choice to set this in the ‘80s before our modern understanding of autism became prevalent, because Sunday was not in a privileged enough position to outwardly challenge biases. Setting it in the ‘80s allowed her to form a more autonomous understanding of herself. And I think this choice was extremely successful. If you were on the fence about this one because it was longlisted but not shortlisted, do yourself a favor and pick it up anyway. It’s worth it! CONTENT AND TRIGGER WARNINGS: Ableism; Gaslighting; Death of a child/sibling (in memories)

Well well I guess this is why you shouldn't judge a book by the first 50%..... A young man, Daniel Sutherland, has been found deceased on a houseboat. Leaving the scene of the crime is Laura, a young woman known to police. Fortunately for Daniel, there is a noisy neighbor Miriam who takes detailed records of all of the comings and goings. However, Daniel's mother, Angela, died just a few weeks before Daniel in an accident. Are these deaths connected? Was it Laura? What do we really know? This was one of my most anticipated reads of 2021 (this book as well as Survive The Night) so my hopes were HIGH. The first half of the book was extremely complicated and slow and going. There are quite a few characters to keep track of and how they are related and connected to each other. The first half of the book would have easily been rated a 2 or 3 stars, just average if not a bit overly complex. However, the last half of the book was extremely entertaining and had some twists that I was not quite expecting. At the last half of the book, it was revealed why the book was so complex. When I think back on this book, there was one character who said something that if it was not said might have changed quite a bit of the book. A Slow Fire Burning book reminds me of The Great Gatsby because it is so perfectly woven together, unexpected, but it also has characters trying to do the right thing and imperfectly loving other people. Overall, I am greatly looking forward to reading this book again. It has the complexity of The Great Gatsby - everything was set up perfectly and was surprising at the end. Nope! That bloody disappointment choo choo train sound started playing in my head! After being introduced to Ms. Hawkins with her psychological, twisty thriller “Girl on the train”, I was so drawn into her story about complex, broken, unreliable characters. I found her second work: “Into the water”a little disappointed me. Maybe I was expecting to read something similar to her debut : something riveting, more mysterious, exciting, character driven with smart twists and you didn’t see it coming revelations but it was full of crowded unlikable characters and suffering from lack of mystery. And her brand new work “A slow fire burning” has exactly the same problems! The author decided to create a slow burn mystery which could be helpful to build high tension and increase the expectations of the readers as the pace gets faster at the second half. But unfortunately this book couldn’t be defined as a mystery. It looks like a contemporary fiction about crowded and very unlikable characters’ connections with each other! It is slow and it is a little compelling to read because when you start one of the narrators’ chapter, you ask yourself who was this character and you get to turn back for reading his/ her story one more time to refresh your memory! You keep asking yourself why you’re doing it because you reread about a character you already disliked and you didn’t pay enough attention to remember why you really disliked him or her. After getting the full picture and understanding the characters’ back stories and connections, your reading journey gets less bumpy but it’s still struggling and requiring your extra efforts. Overall: maybe this book may have been promoted as contemporary fiction, I could have a chance to like it more. From the beginning of the novel, I expected something big, earth shattering, surprising will happen or something so smart will come out to fool me but none of them happened. That’s why I still hear the choo choo sound of disappointment train. Sorry but I have to admit this is not one of my favorite works of the author and not one of my favorite reads of this year!

NOW AVAILABLE!!! hawkins' debut thriller The Girl on the Train came out hot on the heels of the film-adaptation of Gone Girl, when the psych suspense market was craving MORE LIKE THIS, PLEASE, and it became a runaway bestseller that everyone either loved or loved to hate, but its success ushered in a WAVE of twisty suspense novels trying to hitch a ride aboard the gone girl on the (gravy) train, so many of which unabashedly featured the word "girl" or "woman" in their titles. her follow-up, Into the Water, was a much quieter release, and wasn't even a mystery, IMO; it was a character-driven investigation of a situation that happened to have a body count, in a similar vein to ivy pochoda's exquisite These Women. (i reviewed both of these books for l.a. review of books and i used plenty of capital letters. links to hawkins and pochoda, if you're interested) A Slow Fire Burning is a return to the twisty twisty murder myst'ry style that put hawkins on the map, with a large cast of unlikable, unreliable characters full of secrets and hidden agendas, carefully clipped clues and misdirection. there aren't any trains this time, but there are SEVERAL boats. it also features a mystery novelist character who gives a little meta-commentary on the genre as well as roadmap to the novel itself: It was a book that exposed the way the sympathies of the reader might be manipulated, laying bare how quickly we jump to conclusions about guilt and innocence, power and responsibility. there's even a novel-within-the-novel, giving the book an unusual shape hawkins seems to anticipate will invite criticism, which she cheekily addresses, using the novelist character: "I thought it was so interesting, the way you turned the whole thing around, you know, telling the story backward in some parts and forwards in others, letting us see inside the killer's head—that was so brilliant! At first you, like, you don't know what's going on, but then it's just like...woah. So cool. I loved the way you turned everything on its head, playing with our sympathies and empathies and all that business." "Really?" Theo laughed, faking incredulity. "I thought everybody thought that was a terrible idea." "Well, I didn't. I thought it was clever. A new way to tell a story like that, makes you think, doesn't it?" the title, however, does not describe the book—this fire burns fast—a highly engaging page-turner that whisks the reader to and fro—edging close to the truth before shifting the focus away each time in a delicious flurry of NOT YET, MY LOVELIES! unsympathetic characters, unintended consequences, unexpected connections...and murrrrderrrrrr. i dug it. come to my blog!!

It's London in the 2020s, it's the canals and the big houses around Islington and Clerkenwell. One, now old, woman suffered a horrific abduction when she was 15 years old. One middle aged divorced woman suffered a horrendous loss when she was a young mother. One woman in her 20s suffered a brutal hit-and-run as a child that resulted in brain damage causing behavioural issues. All three women have many secrets and tell some lies, and ideally would like some sort of justice... or even better, revenge! Daniel is found murdered on his canal boat. All three women knew him, did one of them kill him? I loved, loved, loved this whodunnit on so many levels. I love it! With some truly remarkably complex yet realistic characterisations of people across many generations; intriguing, beguiling and most of all interesting, even after finishing the book I want to know more about them. Yet, a big YET, despite the book being character led, Hawkins uses the characterisations to create a beautifully weighted read. I read a fair bit of crime fiction but only now and again do I find a non-Scandinavian writer that can compete with our Nordic Noir geniuses and this is one of them. This is the work of an assured writer in her peak. 100% deserves its existence as an INSTANT bestseller. 9.5 out of 12 masterclass Four Star read, where simmering pain, injustice and most of all revenge, is a slow fire burning. 2023 read

After a young man is found murdered in a houseboat in London, it brings to the forefront three women who have unique and complicated connections to him. A nosy neighbor, a one-night stand, and a resentful family member, all who are juggling their own secrets and hidden agendas. You won’t know whom to trust in this twisty murder mystery.

Paula Hawkins writes an ambitious thriller with multiple characters, all in one neighborhood in London. Her setting is in an area near a canal with moored houseboats. The title, “A Slow Fire Burning” reflects the emotional simmering of the female characters, all who have reasons for revenge. In an interview with NPR, Hawkins admits that while she was walking near her London home, which is near an area of moored houseboats, she often contemplated where would be a perfect spot to hide or dispose of a body. Hawkins liked this area because both wealthy and poor are living amongst each other in an unusual setting. And we know that Hawkins loves her unstable female characters whom the reader feels frustrated and sympathy with, in equal measure. The central character is Laura who is a hot mess. “It’s not my fault” is her motto. As the story opens, she is seen leaving a houseboat in the early hours of the day the man who occupies the houseboat is found dead. Laura is carrying more emotional baggage than is imaginable. She’s not the only distressed female in the story. Miriam finds the dead body of Daniel, and through the story, the reader learns of her horrid past. Carla is the aunt of Daniel, and she is a grieving mother whose young son died tragically. Theo is Carla’s ex-husband; he is an author and a bit of a slippery character. Hawkins provides a map of the neighborhood with the homes of the different characters. I referred to that map often. Who killed Daniel and why? I found it ambitious in that each character had reasons to be the murderer, depending upon the chapter. Each character endured tragedy and trauma; each has a suspicious pedigree. No one is an unreliable narrator, yet in reflecting their pasts, we wonder what the truth is. Each of us are a bit of unreliable narrators of our past, or, I should say we “color” our past to reflect what we want. What Hawkins is great at, is exposing the “shady” parts, or the “grey”. That said, I enjoyed the story once I got the characters fully formed in my mind. There’s a lot going on in this one. It’s not a straight-forward story.

There is a murder because of course there is. Tenuous connections, deception, and betrayal embroil members of a family, a pitiable young woman, and a meddlesome middle-aged spinster in the investigation that ensues. Moving back and forth in time, the characters’ backstories are slowly revealed as Hawkins turns you every which way but loose. There is even a book within in a book. I was held breathless.

I’d enjoyed the author’s hugely successful mystery thriller The Girl on the Train and so despite my normal aversion to fiction set in the UK (too close to home, not escapist enough, yadda yadda yadda) I was excited to get hold of this one. It kicks off with the discovery of a body on a houseboat in London. It’s clearly a case of murder, so for the police it’s now simply a case of identifying who had both the opportunity and the motive. We are soon to meet a small cast of characters who seem to have both – or do they? We have the nosy neighbour who had found the body, a young woman who’d had a recent one night stand on the victim's boat and an aunt who seems to be nursing a whole bag of resentment, for reasons we are to discover later. And there are other linked characters too who are perhaps worthy of consideration. Could one of these be the killer, or are we being sold a shoal of red herrings? Well, it’s a complicated tale, and readers will need to pay close attention if they’re to have a chance of successfully resolving this one. There are a number of separate storylines running in parallel as we step back and forth in time. I found it a little confusing, in truth, though I confess I am easily lost if too much information is put on the table. Each person the spotlight falls on seems to be hiding something and as additional information is progressively fed in I found that my perception of what was going on in the background was subtly (or sometime not so subtly) challenged. The characters – all of them – are a pretty dislikeable bunch, and I didn’t find myself becoming sympathetic to the cause of any of them. So this, added to the complicated way in which the story is told, had the effect of distracting me to the point I’d put the book down and not pick it up again for some time. There wasn’t a moment that I felt like giving up, but neither was I in a hurry to burn the midnight oil working through the outstanding text. I was expecting a big surprise, a major twist, and I suppose it is here. But the reason I framed it in this way is that it came and went before I’d realised that that's what it was. I can’t say it was an explosive moment for me, and that’s perhaps because there are many minor twists here, and this one sort of melded in with the crowd. In retrospect, it did explain things. It was the moment all should have become clear in my mind (as I’m sure it will be in the minds of more switched-on readers). One highlight is that the audio version I listened to was impeccably narrated by the brilliant actress Rosumund Pike. But in summary, I enjoyed this tale, but I didn’t love it. It didn’t do for me what The Girl on the Trian did. I’ll be interested to see what others think of it: I expect some will absolutely love it though others might feel as I do, that it rather passed them by. My thanks to Penguin Random House UK Audio, Transworld Digital, and NetGalley for providing a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

Oh yes, it was good. Hawkins, who finally came through and published her third novel after a three-year hiatus, proved why I found her debut so compulsively readable - this was very similar, and in my opinion just as good! I really think this would make a great movie as well. Bravo, Hawkins, and welcome back!!! When a young man is found brutally murdered in his houseboat, an investigation immediately ensues and we are introduced to three main suspects, all females who each seem to have plenty of motive, opportunity and means to commit the heinous crime! Was it the young, pretty, traumatized girl who just can't stay out of trouble? Or was it his nosy, lonely, middle-aged neighbor with a horrific past and plenty of built up anger? Or was it someone very close to him, perhaps a relative? This was a very dark story as a whole, and I don't even know that the murder mystery in itself was what I was most intrigued by; the characters however were another thing! Even though all of them were incredibly damaged to the point it was sad and depressing, I was intrigued with their stories and felt an incredible sense of empathy for them. That being said, I believe my favorite character in this one was 80-year-old widow, Irene. She seemed to be the most rational and least pessimistic of the group, and that was refreshing. With a limited cast, a whodunnit reveal it is rarely shocking anymore, but the reasoning behind the crime itself was something that actually made my jaw drop! Needless to say, Hawkins is a master in her portrayal of damaged people! The combination of intriguing mystery and fleshed out and equally intriguing characters was superbly executed and really elevated this rating for me. I recommend this one for anyone looking for in parts a character study, mystery, suspense/thriller - you won't regret it! I do believe Hawkins is back with a vengeance, and I cannot wait for her next novel. I'm hoping I won't have to wait another 3 years to read more work from her! :-)

3.5 Stars Told in multiple POV, 3rd person, it’s a standalone novel. This story has all the elements I like in my thrillers but I don’t know why I didn’t enjoy it as much as I expected to. It’s suspenseful; a young man is murdered and everyone here has their own reasons to be the killer. It is unpredictable with a satisfying ending, contains short chapters, and has too many flashbacks (albeit a bit annoying). Apart from “The Girl On The Train” (read it years ago and loved it), I haven’t read anything by this author so I wasn’t familiar with her writing. So maybe my problem was with the pacing; it was a bit too slow for my liking. Overall, I still enjoyed it and hope you like it as well!

A woman is witnessed leaving the scene of an unthinkable crime. A man has just been found murdered on a house boat and left for dead. Who killed Daniel? Sounds like a simple plot, right? Nope, not this one! A Slow Fire Burning is Paula Hawkins’ third thriller and truly a slow burn. I loved The Woman on the Train, but DNF’d Into the Water, so I was curious as to which direction I would land with this one. Unfortunately, this book felt overly complicated and contained way too many characters and sub plots. I found it very difficult to connect with any of the characters and even more challenging to follow all of the threads. If I wasn’t reviewing this book for the publisher, I am not sure that I would have finished it. I am starting to wonder if Paula Hawkins will be able to follow the success of The Girl on the Train with another stand out thriller. However, I am keeping my fingers crossed that her next book is a five star read! 2.5/5 stars rounded down Thank you to NetGalley and Penguin Group Riverhead for my gifted copy in exchange for an honest review.

3.5 stars Being that Into the Water is one of my most hated books I’ve ever read, I would say a three star rating for another book by the same author isn’t so bad. I never read Girl on the Train, but maybe I’ll give it a chance now. A Slow Fire Burning introduces a cast of characters in a somewhat confusing way. I listened to the audio, so I’m not sure if the switching perspectives was easier to tell in the written version, but for me I was a bit lost at the beginning of this book. I will say for sure, the second half of this book was so much better than the first half. But I wouldn’t reread this book or see myself recommending it, so three stars.

I'm a latecomer to the Paula Hawkins' party. I waited a few years after the author's popularity rose before I read her two earlier books, and now, I'm over a year delayed in reading her latest release, A Slow Fire Burning. Since her next book will release in April 2022, I wanted to get current this month... and I borrowed this one from the library as I am running out of space on my shelves (plus moving this month, so I can't buy anything for a while). Unfortunately, while much of this book was good, overall, the mystery had huge letdowns and failed to tie things together properly. I tend to like every red herring and side story pulled into a pretty package with a nice bow, but even I reduced my expectations here, and they still weren't met. Laura had an accident as a teenager, and it left her slightly disabled physically, but more importantly, with the lack of knowing when to keep her mouth shut. Instead, she's verbally abusive (because she doesn't quite know any better) and struggles to find the balance in trust with others. The cause of the accident is really much bigger than we know until mid-book. As a result, she's often taken advantage of by others, and in this case, she's the last one to see a man before he's found knifed to death. The victim's mother died recently too, and his aunt and uncle are in the middle of a divorce. There's an interesting backstory there too... plus a strange hermit of a woman who seems to be pulling strings behind the scenes in all these people's lives. What is really going on? So... sounds like a great tale, right? It could've been... except the ties binding them together were weak, amped up to seem bigger, and then when the ending comes, it's all so loose and not fully explained that readers are left thinking... wait... why did we need to know about that? It wasn't that the side story was a mere distraction, it was that the author actually purposefully tied them together with such intangible connections that served only to confuse us. All that said, the writing was good, and I kept turning the pages to get into the details. I liked the darkness of the characters, and the potential for how it all could've come together. I think this suffered from a case of "if you add too many coincidences, readers won't believe it." But at the same time, if you fake add things and don't give us some sort of wow factor in the end with it all, we also don't believe it. So... I'll still read the next book, but I'm not rushing out to get it in April when it releases. I'll add it to my TBR and when I find myself in need of a thriller and not having any in my immediate queue, I'll give Hawkins a chance. It wasn't bad, just not good enough for all the hype.

A Slow Fire Burning by Paula Hawkins, another thriller by the best-selling author of The Girl On The Train. Going on the same themes that author writes, we get another thrilling story of troubled main female characters. The pace of this book was quite slow as compared to her other novels I felt. The cast of characters are definitely unforgiving, unrelated and unreliable at the same time. I also did not like some of them at various points in the story. Daniel is brutally murder, who was a one night stand of Laura. Laura was the last suspect and person seen on site of murder. The book is very straightforward till three forth of the story, but the ending had me hooked. Theo, Miriam, Carla, Angela all the characters are to be liked and disliked at some point in time as well as given benefit of doubt for their actions. I would highly recommend you to not judge the book in the first 50%, because everything picks up at the end and it's worth it.

Another great read by author Paula Hawkins. A young man is found gruesomely murdered in a London houseboat and there are no shortages of suspects. Three women Laura, Carla and Miriam all knew him and all three are full of resentment. Laura is a fiery woman who had a brief relationship with the man. Miriam, the inquisitive neighbour who knows everyone’s business and is hiding something. And Carla his grieving aunt who is already trying to come to terms with the recent death of yet another family member. Was one of these women seeking revenge. Lots of twists and secrets that are all slowly unleashed as the reader learns the truth. Well written with interesting characters make fascinating reading.

Full disclaimer, I alternated between the audiobook and the physical book while reading A Slow Fire Burning . I really enjoyed Paula Hawkins' debut The Girl on the Train, but the alcoholc female protagonist troupe is sooooo 2018, so I am not sure that Paula Hawkins came grip readers on her books. She doesn’t use this troupe this time, but I feel that is probably a main selling point to why her debut did so well. I skipped Into The Water because I heard it wasn't a mystery. I was really excited to pick up A Slow Fire Burning because I heard that it is Paula Hawkins back at her mystery and suspense roots. I'm here to tell you that I think this author will be a one-hit wonder for me. I am toggling between 2 and 3 stars, but I bumped it to 3 as I didn't dislike the book, it was just a slow fire boring for me. It took almost two weeks to get through this one and that is probably the longest a book has ever taken me since I created my Goodreads / Bookstagram accounts. The story focuses on Laura (who we hear her name literally in almost every paragraph -_-) and two other women, Miriam and Carla, respectively. After a man is found dead, each of these women have motive to be the culprit. Throughout the book, we get a very deep and twisty whodunnit, which is probably why I bumped it to 3 stars. I did enjoy how Hawkins was able to humanize the characters in this story by diving deep into their psyche, but this will also provide somewhat of a lull period for readers as this book is very slow. During this time, we see how the three main protagonists relate to each other in some way (no spoilers). I think the issue that I had with the pacing was that it started off fast paced and wild, and then the fuse dimmed until the end. I've been reading a lot of books providing this storyline build up lately and it's really hit or miss so go into that preparing for a slowly drawn out story. Overall, it sounds like I'm a big complainer, but I did think the book had some great moments. It's definitely a darker type of story than I expected. We get some explicit mentions of the crimes at hand which I always appreciate. Overall this book is a character driven suspense novel and you need to go in with realistic expectations.

This is the perfect book for a plane ride, train ride, sit-by-the-pool diversion. It's face-paced, has well-drawn characters (especially Laura), and is filled with twists a turns that keep you guessing about who the murdered is. It takes place in northeast London along Regent's Canal and in a few other locations in the immediate area. It has a good sense of place and all along I felt I was in the hands of a writer who knows what she's doing when she constructs a thriller. I enjoyed it.

3.5 stars. Definitely different from GIRL ON THE TRAIN in style and pacing, this is a much slower burn and not so twisty. But quite similar in looking from multiple viewpoints and embracing unlikable protagonists. I found myself going back and forth on this one. I really liked the way Hawkins leans into the idea unlikable protagonist here, it makes you realize just how easily we throw that label around, since Hawkins is willing to go much farther with it than most. We jump between multiple characters, so you get to see them from each other's point of view to really nail it home how much one will not like another and how they come off. Most notable is Laura, who suffered a traumatic brain injury as a child and now has a lack of inhibition that ends up getting her constantly in trouble. Laura is, in a lot of ways, the best part of the book. Hawkins really digs into her, just like how she dug into a struggling alcoholic in her first novel, and even as you watch her make the same mistakes over and over again, you get to really understand her as an earnest chaos monster. On the other hand, this book does what I've experienced with a few crime novels recently. It starts off pretty much right away with the big crime and then about 25% of the way in the action mostly stops and we hold for a good long while. Hawkins has a lot of sleight of hand to make it feel like maybe there's more twists and questions but there aren't, really. I knew who had done it quite early and I knew why because, well, there was one very obvious motive. But really this isn't a whodunnit, it's more of getting to know these characters and how they're connected. That said, the first several chapters are disorienting. I couldn't remember who was who, a character would get a whole chapter and I wouldn't be able to remember if we'd met this person already or not. The ways they're interconnected eventually become clear and by halfway through the book I was comfortable. But I won't lie, it took a while to get there. I could have absolutely done without the book within a book, it did that thing that often happens in these situations where you can't figure out how this would be a whole book, not to mention one that people would want to read. If you are up for the slow burn then I think this is mostly pretty good, even if I didn't like the journey much more than the destination. I, for one, would have liked a lot more of some characters and a lot less of others (Theo and Carla, supposedly the most normal of the bunch, were to me the least likable, when it all comes down to it, so maybe that's more subjective than we'd think) and the end was overly fussy given how straightforward the book is at heart.

Thank you so much to Paula Hawkins, Riverhead Books, and Libro.fm for this twisted domestic thriller. It was such a joy to listen to on audio and I really loved the narrator. The book is about three women that are connected to the death of a man on a houseboat. The first is Laura, a woman with previous issues with the law, who’s one night stand with the victim leaves her suspicious. The second is Carla, the victim’s aunt who is surrounded by death and misfortune. Finally, there is Miriam, a nosey neighbor keeping secrets from everyone, including the police. They are all connected to the victim, all have a grudge, and all want revenge for something. Thoughts: I love how twisted Paula Hawkins books are. There are so many possibilities of what happened and who did what and I love that. I couldn’t help but feel for Laura in this book, and empathized with the situation she was in. I also felt bad for both Carla and Miriam for how lonely and unfortunate their lives are. None of the characters are necessarily likable, but they are interesting to read about. The book was so well written and only made better by hearing it on audio. This book is a slow burn, which is perfect because the story is about a slow build of anger, jealousy, resentment, hate, and fear. This story has a book within a book, which is one of my favorite literary devices. Even though you know the ending from the beginning, there are tons of twists and red herrings and the ending is still surprising. The web Hawkins weaves is intricate and I enjoyed the multiple viewpoints. It is not as fast-paced as Girl on the Train, but I really enjoyed it, and I can’t wait to see what she writes next. 4-stars for this book.

4.5 rounded up. This has been a disappointing year for thrillers, so it's nice to see one finally deliver. The first half of the book is a bit slow. There are five POV characters and there is a lot of back story to get thru, in addition to the current events. There are some time jumps between current day and past events, but it wasn't too confusing; it was pretty clear which events were "now" and what was "then." For having 5 POV characters in a 300 page book, I think Hawkins did a great job of developing the main three. The other two were less developed, but enough was done for them to serve their purpose. There were also non-POV characters with their own story, so a lot got packed into a smallish novel. My biggest complaint was probably the novel inserts for The One Who Got Away. They did what they were meant to do, but it just kind of throws off the consistency in the book and they felt out of place. Anything revealed in the inserts could have been handled the same as other characters' back stories. Some of the twists you see coming and others you suspect, but the knowing didn't feel like it took away from the story. Even when I was pretty sure I knew where it was going, there was a chance I might be wrong. All of the twists felt earned and nothing felt like it came out of left field. I liked this one a lot. It had some great characters and a good story. I'd say this is easily the best new thriller I've read this year.

The newest of Paula Hawkins creations truly is A Slow Fire Burning. While initially slow, Hawkins builds a web of unlikable characters that keep the plot twisting and turning until, like a runaway train, you crash into a fiery ending. A twisted tale of secrets, lies, resentments carried, revenge plotted, and culminating in murder... this thriller is sure to be a scorching end of summer treat. Though Hawkins always gets mixed reviews, I will tell you that she is one heck of a story teller, and you can’t go wrong reading A Slow Fire Burning! I’d go ahead and pre-order this slow roasting thriller now as Hawkins plans to fan the flames of this gem August 31, 2021. I am so grateful to #NetGalley, #PenguinGroup #RiverheadBooks ( @riverheadbooks ) and the bonfire building wordsmith herself Paula Hawkins for sending me an electronic ARC in exchange for my honest opinions. You can see a full review on http://oceansofbooks.com on August 31, 2021. I will definitely recommend this title as it’s sure to be a summer hit.

I am one who really enjoyed The Girl on the Train . (Even though that and Gone Girl started a whole thing of having the word Girl in every other domestic suspense/mystery title going forward. Or woman, wife, lady, dame…you get my point. I don’t think there’s really one with dame. Yet…) And I liked but didn’t love the author’s second book. One of the things I struggled with in that one happened again in this one and I found myself not as able to get past that this time. I’ll start with that. So here we go: ❌ Too many characters. In her second book, this was also the case but by the halfway point I had everyone straight in my head and was invested in them all enough to care. In this one, it took about the same amount of time for me to get up to speed. But unlike the second one, the halfway point is where my interest started waning and this multitude of characters I was supposed to care about didn’t help. ❌ With this huge cast of characters, came multiple POV. And within those POV, things would go from present to past. Then within this there was a novel within a novel that one of the characters wrote. That was also connected to another character’s backstory. Maybe it was my mood but it just felt like a lot of work and I got tired. Actually I’m tired just explaining it. 😂 ❌ The plot. I think this author writes really well. The first half I was confused but engaged. I thought it was all building up to something really big. But when I got to the end I kind of felt like, “That’s it? All this convoluted, tangled drama and this is the conclusion?” 🤷🏻‍♀️ ❌ There’s a good chance I will forget absolutely everything about this book in a day. So yeah. This wasn’t the book for me. I felt cranky at the end and a little bummed that I hadn’t just abandoned it. I can’t even make myself get on my computer and add gifs. Maybe later. I’ll try whatever she writes next but I won’t be afraid to DNF. Thank you and goodnight.

I had a good time with this one. While there were characters that I wasn't especially fond of, I didn't abhor them either. Paula Hawkins again visits the theme of blackout drinking in this one, which makes me wonder if she has been in this state and worried about what could have occurred with this theme that keeps coming back through her writing. Girl on the Train was an "experience with a psychopath" view that resonated with me strongly when I first read it. Even if you guessed it, the mystery had so many moving parts that it was well thought out and well executed. I like the ending contemplation and how all the tiny threads somehow came back together. Another well-done novel by Paula Hawkins. She takes her time to set the scene, but every detail is essential in some way or another. **Paula: I love the book entry sections the most, and you should go darker with a future novel and pick up on that thread. It read brilliantly! Solid 4-4.5 Stars for me.
How'd I just notice the faces on the cover?? Anyways, I absolutely LOVED this book
Twisty. Secrets. Hidden Agendas. Predictable. Murder. Revenge. Take it or leave it.

This is Paula Hawkins third novel. The first one – “The Girl on the Train” was a runaway bestseller and a suspenseful, tense, and mesmerizing read. The second one – “Into the Water” – was a lesser quality follow-up that had too many points-of-view, discombobulating the complex story. This one – “A Slow Fire is Burning” – unfortunately leans more towards the weaknesses of her second book rather than the simple strengths of her first one. “A Slow Fire Burning Fire” starts off with the murder of a young man, Daniel Sutherland, whose body is discovered in a London houseboat. When the investigation begins, there are several potential suspects, including: Laura Kilbride - a troubled young lady with social challenges, who had a questionable one-night-stand with Daniel and was last seen leaving his houseboat the night previous to his murder. Carla Myerson – Daniel’s aunt, dealing not only with Daniel’s death, she is still recovering from the recent death of Daniel’s own mother and her sister. Theo Myerson – Carla’s ex-husband, who still shares an on and off relationship with her, is struggling with his writing career and jealousies. Miriam Lewis - a nosy neighbor who has a houseboat close to Daniel’s and seems to know a lot about him, as well as Laura’s troubled past and Theo’s writing sources too. Each of these four had their own personal connections to the victim and the secrets that included. Could one of them been harboring thoughts of revenge? Could that person be capable of killing? As the title suggests, is it possible that one those fires slowly burning has exploded in an act of madness and murder? When I was reading this book, it didn’t take me long to realize that it really felt like I was reading a Shari Lapena suburban mystery rather than the Paul Hawkins untrustworthy narrator point-of-view style that she so creatively developed in his first outing. I realize that this avenue of thought will not sit well with some readers and I understand that. It is not my intent to criticize any author or their works. However, having read all of Lapena’s novels, as well as Hawkins, this was a Lapena book in all of the key elements. Characters that were weak, flawed, and detached from reality as they try to overcome the negative influence of prior traumas. Plotting that involved a current murder mystery while moving back and forth in time to fill in back stories and secrets that each primary character is carrying. And the kicker that really makes it a Lapena product is that none of the characters (except for maybe Irene) are likeable. Not at all. They are strange and full of dark idiosyncrasies that make them interesting, but not sympathetic. Almost the whole time I was reading this book, I kept thinking is this Lapena writing or Hawkins? Or is it Hawkins writing a tribute to Lapena? I am sorry, but I couldn’t help it. Now, the real question after that becomes, was it good? For me, the answer is a bit yes, but mostly no. Yes, in that I liked how Hawkins moved back and forth between the various characters, as well as mixing in their past to link everything together. Most of the time she pulled this off in a smooth and somewhat seamless manner that delivered an additional depth to the various plotlines and character behaviors. However, I found the inserts of Theo’s mystery novel between the chapters to be distracting and annoying. Maybe that’s me, but I didn’t find them helpful. It felt like they were included to increase the page count beyond the 300 -page mark. No, for the primary reasons that I already stated (making me feel like I was reading a Lapena book). I wasn’t as interested as I wanted to be in watching each of the characters suffer psychological self-breakdowns, mostly driven by their own weaknesses and stupidity. I also found myself conflicted in that Hawkins had a lot going on with each of her characters, and at times it made the novel strong and interesting. However, at other times, it came across as a bit messy and convoluted in the delivery. I almost needed a scorecard to keep up with the activities. I understand that the current trend of psychological mysteries focuses on untrusty character viewpoints and building up to big twists and surprises at the end. Those can be incredibly hard to conceive and deliver in an exceptional manner. It takes superb plotting in which the clues, red herrings, and critical information is doled out slowly at key moments throughout as the author builds to a big and shocking climax. Characters must be fleshed out enough to be interesting and captivating, carrying secrets and demonstrating dark behaviors. Anyone who can pull that off successfully has my full respect. Hawkins uses her title to create multiple storylines that examine people dealing with real and personal problems, creating a slow burning fire within them, building in fury throughout the book, and finally combusting at the end in tragic and revealing ways. However, as well as it may have been conceived and constructed, Hawkins falls short on the execution and delivery. The first 200 pages take a long time to get going, and then the last 100 pages didn’t really provide an emotional payoff. Again, maybe it’s me, but I not only figured out who the killer was early in the book, I also nailed the reason for him/her committing the murder. Even with all that Hawkins had going on, it still felt predictable. My primary struggles were the same that I have with Lapena; although the characters are interesting, they are not sympathetic or empathetic in almost every way. There is no one to cheer for, no one to really draw on and emotionally care about and invest my attention on. It’s like flipping through the channels and hitting on an old Jerry Springer episode where the guests are so unrelatable that you aren’t rally invested in their outcomes. That’s the same here. Interesting, obnoxious, and dysfunctional in a trashy way, but not necessarily memorable. Overall, this was not bad, but not as good as it could have been either. I wanted to like it. I truly did. But the truth is, it just didn’t provide the level of excitement that I was hoping for as I plodded through it, hoping it would get better. It just felt like it could have been better, as if Hawkins was trying to do too much and it showed at times, and not relying enough on what her own strengths really are. Here’s to hoping for a better outcome next time…

*https://www.instagram.com/mrsb_book_r... 🙏A very big thank you and shout to my fantastic buddy read partner @bmichie31 who was amazing. What a full discussion we had about this one, especially in regards to the mental health status of the cast! 🔥Slow Fire Burning is a 2021 release by international bestselling author Paula Hawkins, which I turned to fairly soon after finishing her latest novel, The Blue Hour. This marks the fourth book I’ve read by this author and once again, she’s delivered a story of intricate relationships, unreliable perspectives, a high level of uncertainty, hidden truths, psychological revenge and suspense. 🔥Hawkins presents us with a full cast in her 2021 release. These protagonists are truly a complex and messed up bunch. Hawkins gradually reveals why these figures are complicated, raising issues of childhood trauma, medical crisis, loss, family reflection, plagiarism, abduction and murder. I couldn’t help but feel a great deal of sympathy for certain cast members of this tale, while others I found myself wishing they would book a session with a psychiatrist asap! There are moments too of sheer heartlessness and other episodes where acts of benevolence warmed my soul. The book intricately explores themes of trauma, rejection, infidelity, murder, tragic accidents, cover-ups, death, betrayal and revenge. There was definitely no shortage of intense, thought-provoking topics to unpack with my fellow buddy reader. 🔥The setting was another highlight for me. The houseboat and boat canal backdrop added a unique atmosphere that felt atmospheric and isolating, perfectly fitting for the tense plot. While the story was filled with twists and turns, it’s the way Hawkins dives into the emotional and psychological impact of these events that stands out. I also enjoyed the book within a book format, where excerpts from the novel written by one of the key cast members incorporated within the narrative. It added an extra level of depth to the plot. 🔥Overall, Slow Fire Burning was a solid 🌟🌟🌟🌟4-star read for me.

An anticipated release, Hawkins has been a name on thriller readers lips ever since Girl On A Train. Now, I really enjoyed that book but didn't love it as much as some readers. But I was super excited to read Into The Water, which was just an ok read for me. And her latest, A SLOW FIRE BURNING, reminds me of Into the Water in terms of a very large cast and the apropos title as this is definitely a slow burn of a suspense read. One man found dead. Three women who have every reason to kill him. LET'S GO! It took me a bit to get into this story as it has a very slow start. The many characters are unreliable and very unlikeable, both of which I do not mind in the least, and which makes for a very character driven book. These types of books are usually very hit or miss for me and for this particular read, it ran a bit down the middle. I really did love the premise of this and Hawkins keeps you guessing through every chapter. I think the trouble I have is the pacing, which inevitably had me checking out a bit towards the middle. So, in a weird turn of events, there's no pin pointing of why I did or didn't enjoy this book. Hawkins, as usual, does an oustanding job of throwing a lot at you and bringing it all together at the end. I am once again impressed with how she keeps this all organized as she's writing. Maybe it's my mood that didn't allow for me to enjoy this as much as I could have. Maybe I have to come to terms with the fact that she may not be the author for me. 🤷

I liked Paula Hawkins previous novels in different ways. I quite liked this one too, having bought it off the back of several recommendations and some social media hype. It is a twisty psychological thriller for sure, will please fans of that genre and it is a good read that holds interest despite being pretty predictable due to the character depth and the fact that it is a clever character drama. The writing is beautiful and probably what I liked most about it, the plot itself is a bit popcorn, addictive in the moment but immediately forgettable. Which sounds like a negative but isn't really, I mean who doesn't love some moreish popcorn. A solid read which the quality of the writing elevates.

When a mother dies in a tragic accident, nobody thinks much of it. But when her adult son dies several weeks later due to foul play, things begin to look suspicious. This is a slow burn thriller with absolutely superb narration by Rosamund Pike. There are quite a few characters, multiple timelines and a book within a book, so the audio was difficult to follow at first. Once I got a grasp of who's who and the timeline, I was completely emersed.

4/5 I was super hyped for this — and WOW did it ever deliver. It threw me for a loop, keeping me invested and guessing from beginning to end. It centers on three women who are all known by the victim Daniel, who at twenty-three is found brutally murdered on a London houseboat. •Laura, his one-night-stand, who’d had a traumatic brain injury. •Carla, his grief-stricken Aunt. •Miriam, his nosy neighbor full of secrets, who found him. •And for more twisty fun we have a fourth possible suspect, Theo his Uncle, a writer, who’s also full of secrets. Dun Dun Dun… Told in multiple POV’s, there’s quite a number of damaged, sketchy and unreliable characters — sporting anger, jealousy, revenge and deceit, so many troubled souls that I had no idea who the culprit was. They all had a motive for murder… with the exception of the sweet eighty year old lady, Irene. After all, she is eighty, she wouldn’t be able to hurt anyone right? Figuring out WHO did it was a mystery in itself, especially finding the characters were all inadvertently connected to one another. This has a book within a book. It gets down and dirty exploring the destructive nature of past trauma’s that become the slow fire burning within each character. And let’s not forget the red herrings mixed throughout giving me something more to chew on. Bravo to Paula Hawkins who has written a clever, character driven story with murder, mayhem, and a handful of suspects putting me in mind of my favorite old-school Hallmark rerun — Murder, She Wrote. (one more thing — I absolutely loved the complicated family relationships 👍🏻) A Slow Fire Burning is a win-win for me. Recommend! *At the beginning I had a bit of trouble keeping the characters straight. It’s slower paced at first, but is well worth it so stick with it. (the title suits perfectly) ***Caution for death of a pet.

Hmm, this is a tough one to review. In the end, I liked what Jodi Picoult did with Wish You Were Here. I like that she took it in, let's say, unexpected directions, and explored a subject I knew very little about. I did not predict the way this story would unfold. Which is good. That being said, I found the first half of this book very slow. Diana finds herself alone in the Galápagos islands, her boyfriend thousands of miles away fighting to save people from COVID in the emergency room, when the island is put on lockdown. With no way to get home, Diana wanders around being a bit of an ignorant tourist, meeting the locals, and trying to find a way to feed herself. Diana becomes involved in the lives of local businessman, Gabriel, and his daughter, Beatriz. Through these new friendships and interactions, she begins to question what she had thought she wanted from her life, to question the path she is on and whether it is the right one. This goes on for more than half of the book (192 pages in the e-arc). I was not enamoured by it. As I said earlier, though, the book does go on to take some interesting turns. It's unfortunate that what I liked about the book would reveal too much, so I can only really talk about my complaints here. It's rewarding for the patient reader.

I get what the author was trying to do with this book… I guess.. but it was a no from me 🤷🏻‍♀️ I thought the main character was so obnoxious and frustrating and I really don’t understand the glowing reviews. Did I miss something? 😅 Part 2 of this book takes such a surprising turn, but like.. not in a good way. It just felt kind of ridiculous to me 😬

Waiting out COVID-19 from the Galapagos Diana O'Toole has always been a planner. She has serious life dreams, and she is steadily making progress. Her career is promising, and she has a hunky doctor boyfriend. She even has a travel list, and she is planning on visiting the Galapagos Islands. Timing isn't always ideal, and the pandemic breaks out just as she lands in the Galapagos. What will Diana learn about herself from this time? How much of life should be planned? The first half of this book was dynamite, definitely 5-stars. It was incredibly engaging, and it would cut from times in the Galapagos to back to certain time periods of Diana's life. I had a ball looking up the different animals from the Galapagos and all different pictures of the islands. The second half of the book was extremely slow paced and felt like running through sand. It was far too long. I would rate the last half of the book two or maybe three stars. There is a twist that I never saw coming which was pretty delightful.
