It did get better as the book got better and as I got used to it. But wasn't the most enjoyable. I'd still listen to it. What worked amazingly: - Character development for literally Every. Single. Character. They all took their space, without overstepping on others, and without feeling rushed or unrealistic. 10/10 💞 - Xaden, okay I'll elaborate. His journey was compelling and heartbreaking. He was intense. It was intense. And although we don't get his POV, we get his truth. Being on that trek with him... How dark can the world get before it taints our souls? 🖤 - Violet's focus and confidence are shining in this book. Her relational growth, emotional growth, and her behaving with the mind of a scribe and the heart of a rider are one of this book's highlights. 💜 - The potential. While I hope that books 4 and 5 don't have any fillers, I hope even more that the potentials that this book opened are really fulfilled. OS is a medium book, bridging the 1 story to the world story; it probably introduced all the elements that will help win this war, knowingly or otherwise. I can't wait to see what Rebecca does with this. 🚀 What wasn't working in the book: - The first part was so messy, that I felt stupid for not understanding half of what's written. Mind you, I just finished my re-read so I am very much in the world. 1️⃣ - ⛓️‍💥Rebecca was aiming for mysterious and foreshadowing hints, but they presented as her interrupting a conversation mid-way just to build anticipation. That left me frustrated. 🔇 - While it was only natural for politics to take up more place in this book, it was also a huge dump of names, locations, strategies, and battles that were not as mapped out as they should be. 🆘 - 🔮Too much was going on, and yet not enough. There was travelling, readings, and finding items/pieces of the story, but I ended up with more questions than answers, and many half-truths/facts. What ruined Onyx Storm? But I will not be condemning Rebecca over this, hence my rating, because I believe this happened for 2 reasons: If you'd rather hear me say it than read it: Instagram - TikTok 1) This is Rebecca's first fantasy endeavour, and at some point, she took on more than she was able to. However, she did realise her limits and I look forward to her taking her break before she can come back fresh to continue writing this series. 🔃 2) The fandom ruined this. It is incredulous that I and almost every single one of my friends decided to put ourselves on a self-imposed social media ban, and binge-read OS because WE DO NOT TRUST THE FANDOM! We don't trust each other not to spoil the book, or ruin it for each other. And In this craze, the fandom went out of its way to come up with crazy theories and read too much into things. It became a lab dissection instead of a journey, and I hate that this affected everyone's experience. 🕳️🕳️🕳️ ⚠️‼️SPOILERS SPOILERS SPOILERS SPOILERS‼️⚠️ Most emotional and favourite moments - Xaden channeling to save Sgaeyl, Tairn, and Violet... His entire chapter. I was sobbing. And Sgaeyl sticking by his side. "Do not do this to save me!" - How fucking dare they pull my dragon from the sky, snare and hurt the one who anchors my existence. - Andarna leaving, and Violet letting her go... I am upset that it was so short-lived because her comeback wasn't given proper attention. I would have preferred she come back in book 4. - Aaric stepping up. - Jealous Xaden and Protective Xaden - Violet bringing him back from the edge every time... - Xaden letting himself go and being with Violet. I could feel his struggle so clearly on the page, his yearning, and need for her. "My power, my body, my soul-it's all yours. Take whatever you need." "You are every fantasy I'll ever have." - Quinn's death, but mostly Imogen's POV. - Garrick-Imogen "I'm not leaving you!" - and "I'd better find some fucking way to do something"..... Not Garrick too!! Guess we know what Imogen will be doing in book 4 now.... - I am worried about Tairn's silence and withdrawal in this book. He's there but not as intensely as I am used to. I think he is hurting, for Violet and for Sgaeyl, but it's also emotional for him - "I will not lose her as I did the one who came before!" And. WTF was that ending??? Before the book was even published, I KNEW that OS will end with Xaden walking away. But all of that??? I guess we have a Duchess now who took her memory away so that she can't hurt the love of her life. -- Pre-read: We ride at midnight into the dark era, ready your flight leathers and reading goggles. 👓 Also, group therapy 🫂 spots are still open, for more information call 📞 2-107-WHY-00-WHY 📞 WE GOT an official PLAYLIST PEOPLE!

Legal suspense at its best! We have a corrupt judge that gets tangled in a game of cat and rat. Could he have been found out? After all this time? He is arrogant and worried (with good reason). "For the first time in his life, he felt like he was on the run". Murder here, murder there, seems like everywhere? What is the connection? Someone knows....... a lot! I really enjoyed this one and was reading it simultaneously with Bone Deep, the true crime novel that highlights massive corruption in the legal system which made it seem even more credible. The investigators are on his trail, trying to stay off his deadly list. There are some suspenseful moments and a few nail-biting scenes as they closed in, this made for a fantastic legal thriller! I read the first in this series, but this could be a standalone. If he writes a third, I'll be in line for it. If you enjoy strong female leads, brilliant characterization, twisty "gotcha" moments and the behind the scenes hunt for a creepy psychopath, you may enjoy it as much as I did. Own a copy/ Feb 2022

** spoiler alert ** 3.5 stars— I have always considered myself a John Grisham fan beginning with “A Time to Kill”. After going back and counting I believe this makes the 28th John Grisham book I have read. I have rated his books everything between 1 and 5 stars and this book ranks somewhere in the middle in my opinion. “The Judge’s List” starts strong with a cloak and dagger type opening where a mysterious, anonymous lady reports very serious allegations about a sitting judge to the Florida Judicial Inquiry Commission. The back and forth between the Investigator, Lacy Stoltz and Jeri Crosby, the complainant, is very entertaining for the first half of the book. The more you learn about the Judge the more you understand why Jeri would be terrified to report this and give her identity to traditional law enforcement. That is why when Lacy finally agrees to open an investigation into the judge’s actions, it seemed absolutely absurd that Jeri would tip the Judge off that he was exposed with taunting letters letting him know he was under investigation and the extent of his crimes. Once the Judge was tipped off, Grisham does an admirable job of keeping the suspense ramped up until the end but uses a few “shortcuts” that make the book a lot less believable. This includes a “super spyware” program that would make Julian Assange salivate and the Judge’s super deduction skills that allow him to easily guess the person who has figured out he is a serial killer. Even with the inconsistencies, I enjoyed the book and would give it a thumbs up.

** spoiler alert ** The latest release by Grisham is the second book with Lacy Stoltz, who was introduced to us in “The Whistler”. As like that book, the storyline is about an investigation. It’s a chase between cat and mouse. There is a serial killer and we know who he is, so there is no mystery. The thrill is the discovery, is how to proof. The development of the story is quite slow. The first 18% was very boring. The protagonist, who is very intelligent, is far from thrilling. We get to know the whistleblower, a woman who lives in fear and whose father was killed over or about 20 years ago, and who had a remarkable resource to investigate the case on her own, during all that time. She sounds crazy, is totally obsessed and is very persistent to the point of being annoying. She knows how to keep her identity unknown. She sounds so remarkable that I found hard to believe in this character. She hires a private detective. They both were able to connect all the dots but the police or even the FBI were totally clueless. Then we have the murderer. I confess that I found his POV the most thrilling part of the book. But for a great part, I was completely bored. But there are some exciting moments (or gruesome moments). I just couldn’t (and I can’t) believe that Grisham wrote this book. It’s so different from his style. The dialogues are very repetitive, very uninteresting. And that ending? Such an easy way out. Will I read another book with Lacy as the protagonist? Yes, as long as it is written by Grisham. Edited for correction on Nov 11, 2021.

What can I say about John Grisham that hasn't already been said a hundred times over. He really is the master of the legal thriller and The Judge's List is just more evidence of that. His books always draw me in from the first few pages and leave me needing to read more. I binged this book in one lazy Saturday at home during lockdown and I am not sorry about it. I will read anything this man writes and have been doing so for many many years now. The Judge's List sees us reunited with Lacey Stolz from The Whistler. It is 3 years later and she is almost 40 and trying to work out what she wants from life. Her job at the Florida Board on Judicial Conduct is not exciting her anymore and she is contemplating a change. That is until a mysterious phone call leads to case like no other she has ever worked on. The FBJC does not do murder cases, but there has never been an allegation that a sitting judge was a serial killer before. We know from early on who the killer is, a very clever and cunning judge who has a list of people who have wronged him in his life. He is patient and doesn't leave any evidence behind. But somebody has figured him out now. It is a page turner, and you will not see the ending coming. I certainly didn't. It was a WHAT moment at midnight that made me applaud the brain of John Grisham. Never a dull moment as we watch Lacey and her team try to get the evidence to take the judge down. Thank you to Hachette Australia for sending me an advanced copy of this book to read. Out on October 19th.
Do they pay for 5 star reviews?

The Judge’s List by John Grisham was a pleasant surprise. I listened to the audio CD that was performed very well by Mary-Louise Parker. There had been several positive reviews for this book and I hadn’t read a Grisham book in a very long time so I decided to take the plunge and listen to it. The Judge’s List was the second book in The Whistler series. I hadn’t read the first book in this series but it did not take away from my enjoyment of this one. It can definitely be read as a stand alone book. The Judge’s List was an intriguing, twisty and suspenseful legal thriller with a well developed plot and great character development. John Grisham’s talent as a masterful storyteller was evident throughout this book. Lacy Stoltz was known as the Whistler. She was employed by the Florida Board of Judicial Conduct where she investigated corrupt judges. Lacy was good at what she did but she might have overstayed her time in this position. She was getting bored and yearned to do something where she could earn recognition for herself. Then a woman named Jeri Crosby entered her life. She was secretive and appeared to be very nervous and frightened. Jeri believed that one of the sitting judges in Lacy’s jurisdiction was a serial killer. In the history of the Florida Board of Judicial Conduct there had never been a judge suspected of committing murder. Jeri believed her father had been murdered by this judge. Could Jeri convince Lacy to help her prove that this sitting judge committed several murders while acting as a judge in the state of Florida? The Judge’s List by John Grisham was fast paced and kept me guessing throughout the book. The characters were colorful and complex. I was quite satisfied with the ending as it pulled everything together. Overall, I really enjoyed listening to this book and recommend it highly if you enjoy legal thrillers.

More Lacy Stoltz. More Lacy Stoltz. More Lacy Stoltz. This second book in the Whistler series gives Lacy a tricky dilemma to untangle. A woman wants to remain anonymous while reporting a sitting judge guilty of multiple murders. A serial killer is on the loose and this sociopath has on-line skills that keep him ahead of law enforcement while highly capable of tracking down his victims. Who will be next? Jeri Crosby, the woman who has been tracking him since her father's death twenty years ago? Lacy Stoltz, the interim director for the Board on Judicial Conduct? This rises to the top of the pack for me in the field of Grisham's novels. I enjoy a woman protagonist and in this one we get two. There is plenty of cloak and dagger as well as a thrilling game of cat and mouse in multiple contexts. Finally, this is a legal thriller without any political strings attached. It is just downright entertaining. Mr. Grisham, please give us another Lacy Stoltz book soon. With the future she has planned, there would be many ways for her to stumble upon another legal dilemma to untangle. A big thank you to Doubleday and NetGalley for a DRC in exchange for an honest review.

This book is filled with all the things that I love from Grisham… A tight story, a page turning legal thriller, a desire to see justice prevail… Especially...When, well, I can’t say... Because...Then I would be spoiling it – But...Then again, maybe the title does in a way. No, don’t try and guess it – just read it! By the way, you need not have read The Whistler to read this one. Turnover was ridiculous and morale was somewhere between low and non-existent at Florida’s Board on Judicial Conduct. Well, you’ve got to admit that if Aileen Cannon is a real-life example of the judiciary shenanigans which the BJC would be required to examine, low morale ought not to come as a great shock! But I digress … kinda! THE JUDGE’S LIST is the story of Jeri Crosby’s obsessive hunt for a serial killer spanning more than twenty years. With intuition and detective skills that would rightfully embarrass the FBI and any number of municipal police departments, Crosby has accumulated a barrel full of circumstantial evidence suggesting that a well-respected, practicing Florida judge is a relentlessly patient, ruthless, sociopathic, and very skilled serial murderer with over 10 kill notches on his gavel. His knowledge of police procedure, forensics and, of course, the law has been a shield that kept even his existence as a serial killer off police radar. Knowing that her information would be summarily dismissed by police agencies as unfounded and meaningless, Crosby has lodged an official complaint against the erstwhile judge killer with the BJC. Lacy Stoltz, in her position as interim Executive Director of the board, has 45 days to assess the complaint and determine how to proceed. The clock is ticking and Stoltz and Crosby are only too aware that their names have been added to the killer’s target list of future victims. In past novels, John Grisham has had the ability to make his thrillers pertinent to the real world and to current affairs dealing with issues ranging from elections to racism or capital punishment, for example. THE JUDGE’S LIST does not achieve membership on that elite list. But, you can be assured that it is a high-speed, compelling and completely gripping legal and suspense thriller that will entertain you from first page to last. Like so many other thrillers of this nature, the story details aren’t likely to stick with you for very long but it will be an easy and assured pleasure to recall how much you enjoyed the reading while it lasted. Paul Weiss

This is a second book of a series but it can be read as a stand alone novel. In this one Lacy receives a complaint against a judge. This person is stating that the judge is a serial killer. The person is a family member of one of the victims. She has proof that the judge has committed these murders even though not one agency has put two and two together. I might be a little generous with my rating here but I did love the concept of the story. I also was invested in how it would all play out. That being said there are some major flaws with this book. Like I said I was invested in the story as I can get behind a story about a well respected person of authority being a killer. They would have opportunity and the knowledge to get away with it and who in their right mind would suspect a judge. I also enjoy the idea of following Lacy who works for an agency who keeps an eye on judges. I also liked the motive of the judge too. So where did this novel have flaws? There were some major plot holes in this book. Sometimes characters seemed to act differently to move the plot along so we can get to the thrill of it. I also thought Lacy was relegated to a role of intermediary in this book. She really did not do much to move the investigative plot forward. I would argue if we took her out of this book it would basically happen the same way. Lacy's role was to get the FBI involved. That was it. I believe Grisham is the king of courtroom dramas and really cannot do no wrong. This is a little out of his area of expertise even though it is in the same realm. It is more of a thriller about a serial killer. It shows that this is not Grisham's area. There are plot holes that made me think that does not seem right. One of them is Lacy and her involvement. I liked the book but these plot holes stopped me for loving it. It definitely needed some polishing. There are better Grisham books and better serial killer books out there.

I have read a few books by this author (The Firm, The Partner, The Broker, and The King of Torts) but that was way before I have a blog so I don’t have links to my reviews. I believe I loved them all including this one. I was hooked to this story. I haven’t read a book where a judge was accused of murder before. The characters were well developed and well liked. The main character somewhat worried about herself being unmarried with no kids approaching 40 but at the same time enjoyed her freedom and her own space. I have a friend in that situation and I know the struggle. The other character, Margie lead an exciting and lonely life of collecting information from her father’s killer. I liked that the killer’s view appeared as Lacy investigated Kronke, a victim. It explained how the event happened without speculation. This book followed Lacy, 39 years old lawyer as she received an anonymous phone call from a woman who referred to herself as Margie, 46. She wanted a private meeting with Lacy to ask for her professional opinions. Lacy, for 12 years, has been specializing in investigating judges who are accused of wrongdoing. Margie said an active judge killed her dad among many others and hoping if Lacy will take on her complaint. Lacy was bored with her current job and thought that this new accusation sounded intriguing. Accusing a judge of murder is rare. Lacy decided to hear her out. Lacy has an older brother Gunther and an FBI boyfriend named Allie. There’s a surprise view of the killer. There were many views after that including Margie, which was not her real name because she feared for her safety. She had been stalking her father’s killer for 20 years and knew that the killer had been killing up to 8 victims. She hoped that Lacy can send the killer to jail. The Judge’s List was well written and a fast paced read. A little too many point of views than I care for but I do liked the detailed view of the killer and the persons chasing the killer. I liked that the killer was created as a smart person, one who stayed a couple of steps ahead of the police. It was thrilling to read when the stalking was reversed, the killer knew he was being stalked. Definitely interesting also to see how technology was utilized for good and for bad. The ending was good and I didn’t guess the course of action. This book has good diversity. Although it’s a book 2 in a series, it can be read as a standalone. I haven’t read a legal thriller in awhile but sure won’t be my last. I recommend everyone to read this book! xoxo, Jasmine at www.howusefulitis.com for more details Many thanks to Doubleday Books for the opportunity to read and review. Please be assured that my opinions are honest.

I don’t believe for a minute that John Grisham wrote this book. It has none of the depth or character development of his other books. The plot is padded with unnecessary prattling and descriptions, and the plot is ponderous. ** spoiler alert ** Contrived, convenient and without care. This story needed a character to care for, whom I believe is Jeri & she is left with nothing and with no mention of her future. Are we supposed to be relieved, or angry, or what?” Lacy shrugged and said, “I’m afraid I can’t answer that.” Excerpt From A Novel Grisham, John This material may be protected by copyright. She SHRUGGED like she didn’t care. And that describes Lacy’s character for the entire book which, in turn, means she didn’t care which is felt throughout the book. This is completely devoid of her character developed in The Whistler. Lacy did nothing but complain and push off taking on the case. She was cold, burnt out & unkind. 4.5 rounded up to five as it’s the best Grisham I’ve read in a long time! Grisham writes like Grisham of old. This is the second book in ‘The Whistler’ series by author John Grisham. I really enjoy a good legal thriller and there is no one better than John Grisham when he gets it right. This is a very good read, excellent characters, good plot and expertly written. Three years ago Lacy Stoltz investigated a corrupt judge who was taking millions in bribes from a crime syndicate. She got the criminals locked away and suffered in the the proceeds by been attacked and having her life threatened. Now Lacy is looking for a change in life. Lacy meets a woman who goes under several aliases to protect herself. Jeri Crosby’s father was murdered 20 years ago, a case that remains unsolved and all potential leads have gone cold. Jeri has suspicions but needs proof, she believes the man responsible is a Florida judge who comes under Lacey’s jurisdiction. A man with a brilliant mind and always a step ahead of law enforcement. He has a list, with the names of his victims and targets, all unsuspecting people unlucky enough to have crossed his path and wronged him in some way. The problem Lacy faces is how does she pursue him without becoming the next name on his list? Fast paced entertaining legal thriller.
I loved this 2nd book in John Grisham's "The Whistler" series!

Lacy Stolz has been an investigator for 12 years for Florida’s Board on Judicial Conduct, which is responsible for investigating complaints filed against Florida judges. Jeri Crosby is convinced that a sitting judge murdered her father 22 years earlier. She has devoted her life to discovering the truth. The judge terrifies her, because it appears that he has kept a list of those who have wronged him and can take years to exact his revenge. “Eight murders, at least in her book, in seven states, over twenty-two years.” The evidence is scant but after years of research, Jeri is convinced that the motive and method are strong warranting Lacy’s attention. The judge needed to be stopped and to pay for his crimes. Grisham is a master storyteller, and in this book he weaves a tale of murder, cold cases, and revenge in the legal profession. I remember reading The Firm and loving it. At that time, Grisham had only written one other book, A Time to Kill, which I thought was even better. His books were typically entertaining legal thrillers with the underdog protagonists in extraordinary situations fighting against superior adversaries. I used to avidly read and enjoy all his books and then stopped. Why? Not sure. Maybe formulaic. Maybe I wanted something new and fresh to read. I just lost interest. However, I started reading him again and saw him at the Miami Book Fair. After I finished reading this book, the ending with the suspect bugged me and overall the story felt contrived and implausible. How could a 49-year-old judge with his background have such resources? How could the murders go years unsolved for such a prominent individual? (view spoiler) Also, I knew there was no such inquiring agency. Grisham did acknowledge at the end that the Judicial Qualifications Commission, not the Board on Judicial Conduct, investigates complaints filed against Florida’s judges.

For my first Grisham, it was entertaining! Love a good thriller with a female lead. Lacy investigates a claim made by a woman named Jeri that a sitting judge might be a serial killer, who Jeri suspects murdered her father twenty years ago. As you can image, it was a crazy twisty cat and mouse chase. The anticipation was definitely there, but portions of the story were slow. From what I’ve heard about Grisham, his recent books have been falling flat. He definitely knows how to write a legal thriller, but The Judge’s List wasn’t really a thriller or a mystery. We KNOW that the suspect is the sitting judge. That is made clear very quickly. We needed more mystery and suspense. Unfortunately, I think the ending was very unsatisfying and frustrating. Lacy is pretty one note and the real star here was Jeri. I really thought her character outshined everyone else in the book. I still think this book was worth the read, and I would suggest definitely reading it. I ended up doing the audiobook for most of it and although the narration was done by Mary-Louise Parker, her narration fell very flat. Every character sounded the same which made it feel like one big blobby narration. Review: ⭐️⭐️⭐️ Genre: legal thriller

Lacy Stoltz is an investigator for the Florida Board of Judicial Conduct. She meets a woman named Jeri who has been tracking her father’s suspected murderer for 2 decades. She suspects this man is also a serial killer and has killed again and again. He has never been charged with any crime. How is this possible? He must be highly intelligent, understands forensic evidence, and knows a lot about the law. That is because this man, Ross Bannick, is a Judge! Will Jeri ever get enough evidence to get this Judge off the bench and behind bars? You can add THE JUDGE’S LIST to the very long list of great John Grisham books. I am a big fan of legal thrillers and this one delivers. The writing was perfect as always and the story held my interest. The concept of a judge being a serial killer is crazy, but Grisham had me believing it! Many thanks to Doubleday Books and NetGalley for my ARC in exchange for my honest review. This review will be posted to my Instagram Blog (@coffee.break.book.reviews) in the near future.

A gripping continuation of John Grisham's The Whistler series.The Judge’s List by John Grisham is a chilling legal thriller that follows an investigation into a sitting judge who may be a serial killer. With a tense, slow-burn pace and sharp twists, it’s a dark and compelling read that keeps you guessing until the end. I loved the very unique and unsettling premise, a judge, sworn to uphold the law is suspected of being a calculating serial killer. The tension builds as investigator Lacy Stoltz gets closer to the truth, knowing her target is smart, powerful, and always one step ahead. This chilling cat-and-mouse dynamic keeps the suspense high and the reader hooked.

The Whistler's Lacy Stoltz returns, still working for the Florida Board on Judicial Conduct three years after she investigated--and put away--a corrupt judge who was taking millions in bribes. The investigation led to her being injured and nearly killed. Now she's tired of her work on the Board and looking for a change. Then she meets Jeri--a woman so scared of being discovered she'll only meet Lacy anonymously. Jeri's father was murdered over twenty years ago, and the case is long cold. But Jeri's convinced he was murdered by a serial killer. She's stalked this man for years, becoming more obsessed and sure that he's killed other victims. She's pretty sure she's right, but evidence is hard to come by, because he's a sitting judge. One who knows the law, police procedures, and more. This judge is cunning and evil, so how can Lacy investigate him without becoming his next target? "'Okay, you're making me nervous, so let's walk through this real slow. You believe a sitting judge murdered your father twenty-two years ago.'" This is a fairly interesting read and pretty typical Grisham fare, overall. It took me a moment to recall Lacy, but once I did, I liked her again. I even grew to care for Jeri, even though she's a fairly melodramatic character. She's spent most of her adult life tracking the supposed serial killer who killed her father, at the expense of everything else in her life, and let's just say, it shows. The idea of a sitting judge who is also a killer is a compelling one, though I must admit I was often expecting a bit more--one more twist or turn beyond what happened. Still, this was a creepy and dark story, and Jeri was a pretty impressive amateur sleuth. I enjoyed most of the book, but felt like the ending petered out a bit. Usually you can count on Grisham for a better dramatic ending than what was offered here. Overall, still a good mystery and worth a read. 3.5 stars. Blog ~ Twitter ~ Facebook ~ Smashbomb ~ Instagram

This one, IMHO, is the author at his best. Loved it, hated to put it down and was upset that keeping my husband fed and the need for sleep got in the way of polishing it off in one sitting. It's actually the second in a series featuring attorney Lacy Stoltz, but it stands alone quite well. I say that because although I read the first book, The Whistler, it was so long ago (2016) that I don't remember a thing except that I thoroughly enjoyed it as well. Here, Lacy is working for the Florida Board on Judicial Conduct, which investigates allegations against members of the judiciary, and has an FBI boyfriend named Allie Pacheco. Their relationship is serious, but so far it hasn't progressed to a ring-on-the-finger stage. One day, Lacy gets a call from a woman who calls herself Margie; she wants Lacy's agency to look into a judge she insists murdered her father years ago, when the judge wasn't even on the bench. But wait, there's more; Margie - real name Jeri Crosby - claims to have some evidence that her father isn't the judge's only victim (far from it, in fact). Even though Jeri says several other victims had unsatisfactory interactions with the judge, thereby providing him with motive, Lacy is skeptical (lawyers, after all, rely on actual evidence, which is noticeably missing in all these instances). Lacy also makes it clear that if evidence is found, her agency will have to turn the case over to the police and/or FBI - and Jeri's identity, which she's intent on keeping private for fear of her life - most likely would be revealed. As the story progresses, readers also get a glimpse into what the judge himself is up to, and one thing is clear: He's guilty as all get-out. Unfortunately, he's also smart, manipulative and has no intention of stopping until he makes his way through the list of people he believes have wronged him over the years. As circumstances in Lacy's agency open up new possibilities, she agrees to at least look into the case with help from her task force members Darren and Sadelle. Once they start delving into past murders (all with at least one common M.O.) and the victims' connections to the judge, it becomes clear they're dealing with a serial killer. Now, they must collect enough evidence to file a formal complaint on behalf of Jeri (under a fictitious name). But that also will mean the judge knows they're on to him, raising the question of how far he will go to avoid charges and protect his good name. In fact, it's a pretty sure bet it will be far enough that lives that aren't on the judge's original list find themselves on it now.

Having recently finished While Justice Sleeps this book showed up in the GR recommendation list. While Grisham narratives tend towards being formulaic, others I've enjoyed lacked the predictability of this one. And while the notion of a sitting judge being a serial murderer is unique, it stumbles through repetitive plot points in every chapter. Jeri is a late 40s, highly educated black woman who discovers her father was murdered by Russ Bannick, a Florida judge and seeks justice. In the process of research she finds he'd murdered others using the same technique, aka serial killer. Afraid of being discovered by Bannick, she approaches Lacy Stoltz at a FL Judiciary investigation bureau to tell her story, but meets resistance since the bureaus is not equipped to investigate murders, nor is it the type of cases they handle. Chapters toggle back and forth between Bannick's history and Jeri's research. As he makes his way through law school and joins a law firm, he takes unsavory events personally and over time, draws up a list of those who were the cause whether attorneys, clients or otherwise. When an opportunity arises to 'even the score', he takes pride in 'eliminating' the problem due to the precision and technique he's developed. Classic contradiction in terms which is the ONLY unique element in the story. Jeri and Lacy continue the dialog and eventually come to terms. You don't have to be Sherlock Holmes to figure out where the story is going and this is NOT what I expected from Grisham. While I've enjoyed many books by this author, this is far from what I'd hoped. And that's how the cookie crumbles

It has been one of my annual late Fall rituals. The leaves are falling. School is back in, College and Pro football are in high gear, and it’s time to open the new John Grisham novel, “The Judge’s List”, and re-visit the law in action through the eyes of a challenged do-gooder. This time out, Grisham changes it up a bit. Although this new book involves some aspects of the law and legal issues, it is more of a Michael Connelly or David Baldacci crime thriller, written with that unique Grisham storytelling touch. “The Judge’s List” re-introduces us to Lacy Stolz, an investigator for the Florida Board on Judicial Conduct (BJC). Her job is to respond to any complaints dealing with ethical or judicial misconduct by members of the court. Lacy was one of the protagonists in his previous 2016 legal Thriller, “The Whistler”, investigating a corrupt Florida judge who was taking bribes from a major crime syndicate. Although she helped catch the judge and members of the syndicate, her partner killed, and she barely survived being attacked herself. Now, three years later and closing in on the age of forty, she is still working for the BJC and waiting for her big legal claim against the syndicate to settle so she can move on to better things. Then things change when Lacy gets an anonymous call from an unknown woman. Not just any woman, but one who is so scared she is using burner phones, multiple aliases, and unbelievably paranoid. After agreeing to meet with her several times, Lacy learns that the woman’s name is Jeri Crosby and she has an incredible story, that if true, will rock the sanctity of the Florida legal system. Jeri has been stalking a man for twenty years that she passionately believes is a cold-blooded serial killer, who kills those that have angered him in some way. It doesn’t matter how serious or minor the reason. The killer is patient, willing to wait to more than a decade to seek revenge on those who angered him. His pattern of murder and weapons used is the same every time and Jeri has been obsessive in her research of his relationships to every victim, which adds up to at least seven or eight victims that she is aware of. But she knows there are probably more, because her father was the potential third victim, and that started on this journey that she cannot stop until he is stopped. And to make the situation more complicated… According to Jeri, the killer is a Florida judge, under the jurisdiction of Lacy’s own BJC. Because Jeri distrusts the police, and even the FBI, she files a complaint to the BJC through Lacy, thinking that will protect herself. The good news is that she has motive and intent, but the bad news is that she has no hard evidence or proof. Everything is circumstantial. And what Jeri and Lacy don’t know is that the killer is an expert not only in the law, but also in investigations, forensics, evidence, and not leaving a trail. He’s constantly one step ahead of law enforcement and now he is setting his deadly sights on Jeri and Lacy… Over the last several years, it seemed to me that Grisham was shifting his writing from pure legal thrillers to more plots addressing his personal feelings of injustice within the American legal system. His themes have been more aimed on exposing serious societal issues like the death penalty, wrongful convictions, race inequality, and how the law can be abused by those in positions of power. Grisham is definitely an advocate of the underprivileged and mistreated, and well, this book allows him a large soapbox to stand on and deliver both a legal drama combined together with resolving the inequalities of an imperfect legal system. However, this time he has chosen to branch out and try his hand at writing a crime thriller rather than a courtroom-centered legal drama. He doesn’t do too bad, primarily for two big reasons. One, his premise and set-up is enticing and good. The plot is interesting and pulls you in easily and fast like most of his books do. The second reason is that his writing style is just so dang good. Grisham is a master writer and his writing style just demands your attention is such a fluid and effortless manner. His descriptions are brief, focused, and vivid. His dialogs are sharp and flow like a Robert B. Parker Spenser novel at its best. More importantly. Like Stephen King, Grisham is a pure in heart storyteller, and his storytelling skills are pretty flawless – smooth and flowing prose with no wasted or unnecessary words, a constant focus on moving the conflict forward. Now, that doesn’t mean there was not some areas where the book could have been better. There were some weaknesses, most of which come from stepping into a different genre. For example, it took Lacy a long time to be drawn into Jeri’s situation and it never felt like she was really ever fully invested in the investigation. Also, you could see where Jeri was headed in the storyline pretty fast, and the way she acted at times made her less sympathetic. I wanted to like her more, but I struggled at times more than I wanted to because of her being so overly protective one moment and then so outrageously stupid the next moment. I know it was because Grisham needed her to interject twists and turns into the storyline, but sometimes I wanted to say, seriously dude! Stop it. I guess my biggest complaint (and it is not a major one) is that her silly behaviors were what provided the most conflict and suspense into the storyline. I also found myself conflicted by the ending. I need to be careful here and not give anything away for those who haven’t read it yet, so I will tread lightly. I know that Grisham was trying to surprise his readers with an unexpected outcome, but I am not sure he stuck the landing. I’ve been thinking pretty hard for the last 24 hours about how I felt about it and I am still feeling less than satisfied with the overall outcome. Enough to deduct a half star for it, even if it puts me in the minority of most readers. Sorry, but that’s my current state of mind. Overall, this was still a pretty enjoyable and entertaining book, another of his usual page-turners from beginning to almost the end. Although it wasn’t stretching too far from his home turf, it turned out to be a safe risk that turned out pretty well. Let’s face it. Grisham sets such a high bar that sometimes it’s hard to review his work with full objectively, since beauty is in the eyes of the beholder. I believe that that the key to Grisham’s continued success is his exemplary power to tell a captivating tale and this one was, although not one his absolute best novels, was still one that checked enough of the reader’s boxes (story, characters, and setting) for me. My rating – 3.5 out of 5 stars. See you again next year, John…

I think Grisham’s early work is really good and enjoyed reading stories like The Firm, The Runaway Jury, and The Client. Stories with an early hook to grab your attention and interested in how the story develops and unfolds. It’s too bad his latest work doesn’t measure up to those stories. This is less a story of the law but rather a murder mystery loosely connected because the murderer is a judge and the case is brought to a judicial investigative office. I’ll avoid any spoiler descriptions and just say the brilliant judge who leaves no clues or evidence turns out not to be so smart while new id, money, or properties are conveniently introduced when needed. I wish authors that wrote bad stories had to give the reader back the time lost reading the book. I knew this was a dud early and shame on me since I plowed on hoping it would revert to Grisham’s excellent early work. I'm done reading the Whistler series...

A waste of time I’ve been a Grisham fan for decades and I can hardly believe he wrote this book. Sociopathic serial killer judge who, of course, is so brilliant that he’s stayed out of trouble for over 20 years while he seeks revenge on people who have wronged him. And don’t even get me started on the ending. Give me a break. I couldn’t decide whether to give it one star or two. Don’t waste your time.

More fun from Grisham. He said in promotional materials that he wanted to write a thriller in which the villain is a sitting judge, and he has managed with his usual wit and style. Looking forward to more in this series.
4⭐💖 This was pretty good. We follow a judge that's a serial killer and the people tracking him down. The story was fast paced but I would have liked a different ending.

This is one of the worst books I’ve ever read. It was incredibly boring considering the promising synopsis. There was almost no connection to the murderer being a judge. We never got to see the judge really use his position as a judge to cover up murders. He didn’t even use his position as an authority figure to rope anyone into his scheme. There was very little suspense given that we already knew he was a murderer from the beginning, and half of the book was spent on one character trying to convince the others to take the case. The characters were so boring I could barely tell them apart. I wasn’t rooting for anyone. The two female leads of the novel ultimately both had to be saved by very minor characters. Nothing set this book apart from any other thriller except that it wasn’t very thrilling at all. Given that we already know the judge is the murderer, there could have at least been a twist or more interesting writing showing how the judge was able to use the law or his position to avoid being caught. Everything about this book was hollow and the plot took the path of least resistance the whole way through.

After reading The Whistler last year and enjoying it, actually right before the release of The Judge's List, I was counting down the days to this book's release, and it was just as good as The Whistler! 3 years after the events in The Whistler, Investigator Lacy Stoltz is ready to resign from the Florida Board on Judicial Conduct. That is until she meets Jeri Crosby, a mysterious woman with many aliases. Jeri's father was murdered 20 years ago, the killer was never caught, and has become nothing but a forgotten and cold case. But Jeri believes she knows who killed her Father all those years ago, a sitting Judge, in Florida under Lacy's jurisdiction. According to Jeri, this Judge has a blacklist of people who have wronged him, and has killed many of his victims, leaving no clues behind and disappearing without a trace. He knows the legal system, including forensics and Police procedure. Jeri comes to Lacy for assistance, not wanting to go to the Police in fear of being put on the Judge's List. Lacy is skeptical where she has never dealt with a matter such as this. But she reluctantly agrees to investigate, knowing that in doing so she is also endangering her own life. Another winner by Grisham!

This legal thriller centers around Lacy Stoltz, a veteran investigator for the Florida Board on Judicial Conduct. When she receives an anonymous tip about a respected judge who may be involved in a series of unsolved murders, Lacy is drawn into a complex web of revenge. The anonymous tip who introduces herself by the alias Margie believes presents circumstantial evidence that her father, a law professor, was murdered by the judge twenty years ago shortly after graduated from law school. She also attests that the judge possesses a list of individuals who has wronged him in the past often waiting years to plan his revenge, i.e., to murder them by strangulation. Margie is secretative because fears that the judge will identify her and kill her before she obtains her own revenge through the courts. Although the judge possesses resources that the ordinary citizen don't have, I did think the wealth of his nefarious tools was a bit unbelievable. Other than this flaw, the story moved quickly. Although I read several of Grisham's novel several years ago, I tired of this genre. However, I'm glad I picked up this one and, hopefully, a few additional ones in the future. Grisham does know how to keep you on the edge of your seat.

This book follows The Whistler and we find Lacy Stoltz being called to investigate a sitting judge for serial murders. No one has suspected this man of any wrong doing, but Jeri Crosby, one of the alleged victim's daughter, has meticulously researched this man for the past 20 years. But she is deathly afraid of him and doesn't want her name released. Lacy goes to her supervisor who states that the Florida Board of Judicial Review does not investigate murder and tells her to drop it. But Jeri is desperate and soon Lacy is drawn in. The idea of a judge being a serial killer is definitely a first but in Grisham's very capable hands, this was all very tense and believable. Definitely a great legal thriller!

This book was a gift from secret Santa. Thank you Santa! 🎅🎄🎁 I haven't read whistler #1, but this can be read as a stand - alone. This is NOT a legal thriller, though the title has a 'Judge' in it. So what is the Judge doing in the book? The plot is exactly what the title says- it is about a judge who has a long list of people he kills. There is no mystery here. It doesn't even have Grisham's usual heart-wrenching human stories. The plot is far-fetched, but Grisham's story telling hooked me from page 1. The first half of the book tells how the daughter of one of the victims found about the killer- Judge by stalking him relentlessly for 20 years and the next half is how the judge goes about finding who found his secret 'list'. It was just a game of cat and mouse. One of them is even called 'Jeri'. I am surprised that the Judge was not named Tom. The timeline is inconsistent, going back and forth, suddenly jumping into how one of them was killed, talking about the motive for another, not in any particular order. I had become a fan of Grisham's narration style in 'The Partner'. In that book it worked well, as it was uncovering new things as the story progressed. But in this book, we were not finding anything new. I enjoyed it, even though I have complaints (listed above). This book is strictly for Grisham fans. Just lock your brains in the freezer, sit back and enjoy !

I haven't read a John Grisham novel since I read The Firm in high school.
