This may be one of those 'it's me, not you' cases...or maybe I've read too many stories exploring a complex mother/daughter relationship. To be perfectly frank, I bloody hated this book. It was painfully intent on nauseating the reader. We get it, the human body is base (Julia Kristeva has been there and done that). Burnt Sugar is ripe with garish descriptions of the abject human body: we have bodily fluids and waste, failing bodies, changing bodies (pregnancies, puberty), body parts compared to food or objects (breasts like dough, buttocks like empty sacks). The narrator of this novel, someone who was so remarkable I can no longer recall her name, is the classic disaffected woman who is alienated from everyone and everything. A few days before listening to Burnt Sugar I read Luster, a novel that features a similar type of character except that there the author manages to make her protagonist into a nuanced human being, one who isn't nice or extremely likeable but is nevertheless realistic and capable of moving the read. But here, dio mio! The narrator comes across as petulant and myopic, understanding nothing about anything and no one. Readers are clearly not meant to like her but there are various scenes that try to elicit some sort of sympathy (the nuns mistreat her, her mother is mercurial, her 'silly' Indian-American husband is blind to her anguish) on her behalf. Except that I didn't. The MC goes and on about her mother, but we never gain insight into her actual feelings towards her. The MC is happy detailing all the wrongs she has endured, and seems to insinuate that she has become such a stronza because of her mother. The whole thing is incredibly superficial. Here we have another mother who is 'hysterical' just because 'hysterical' mothers can make for some dramatic scenes. Indian-Americans are portrayed as foolish and brainwashed. Everybody is nasty and disgusting. Ha-ha! Oh wait, that isn't quite 'caustic wit'. There were a few—and when I say a few, I mean two or three—phrases that under certain circumstances (if you are as high as a kite) may come across as slightly amusing, but for the most part the MC's cutting humour fell flat. Viewing everything as grotesque is hardly funny, and it gets tiring, fast. I also found the author's treatment and portrayal of postnatal depression and dementia to be highly insensitive. The mother in question becomes 'monstrous', the type of character that one may expect in Victorian literature. Who cares about realism when you can write explicit and 'subversive' things for the sake of shock value? I think this was an awful novel...and it seems that I'm in the minority. Who cares. If you want to read it or loved it, good for you. I'm glad I was able to return this audiobook and I sincerely doubt I will ever try reading anything by this author. Books with believably fraught mother/daughter relationships featuring alienated, disaffect, or challenging main characters : You Exist Too Much, The Far Field. Can a child ever really know their mother and can a mother ever really know her child? Though we're made to feel there should be a natural, inextricable bond here it's seldom ever so simple. It certainly isn't for Antara, the narrator of Avni Doshi's heart-aching and intensely thoughtful novel “Burnt Sugar”. As an adult she finds herself in the tricky situation of caring for her mother Tara who is showing signs of dementia. But Antara seldom felt cared for as a child when her mother abandoned her unhappy arranged marriage, joined a religious commune, had a passionate affair with an unpredictable artist and spent some time living as a beggar on the street. Given their turbulent history together, Antara naturally feels ambivalent about being her mother's carer and confesses in the novel's opening line “I would be lying if I said my mother's misery has never given me pleasure.” Painful emotions run deep throughout this narrative where Antara is haunted by her past and because of this burden struggles to negotiate her relationships with her husband Dilip, her often absent father and her mother in law. I felt intensely involved in this novel which asks poignant questions about the bonds of family and the nature of memory. Read my full review of Burnt Sugar by Avni Doshi on LonesomeReader

“Burnt Sugar” is a work of extraordinary insight, courage and sophistication. It is also the world’s worst Mother’s Day present. “I would be lying if I said my mother’s misery has never given me pleasure,” the narrator begins. “The sympathy she elicits in others gives rise to something acrid in me.” This is a family tragedy laced with equal parts wit and strychnine. It’s not that Doshi has written something no one has ever thought before; it’s that she’s written something no one has ever expressed so exquisitely — and so baldly. The narrator is an Indian artist named Antara, whose mother is presenting symptoms of Alzheimer’s. The doctors offer only a dose of vague hope; there is no concrete diagnosis and certainly no cure. Hovering in the dusk of competency, Antara’s mother still manages to live alone, but increasingly she wanders, forgets where she is and what she’s doing. This is the book i came across due to its inclusion into Booker 2020 longlist. I am very interested in all aspects of India and its culture. So i was very happy to see the author with South Asian heritage and the story set in India in the list. Overall, my initial impression of this year's list was more positive than the usual as I did not know more than a half of the names there. I've made a list of the books I was interested in. Since then, my enthusiasm has cooled down somewhat as I realised that quite a few of these books were the type of confessional writing often based on the author's life. I do not mind it general, but after reading Real Life, i think i have enough for a while of the the sub-genre. This book is confessional as well. It is also hyper-realistic and detailed. But the difference is that Avni has actually created a fictional story and fully developed a fictional character! That seems to be quite an achievement in the recent literary climate. Though the story is fictional, the style is totally modern auto-fiction. Antara, the main character and the voice of the novel is dealing with her past and her mum who seems to be succumbing to the early dementia. The novel set in Puna, India. Antara is an artist. But her childhood was tricky. Her mum has ran to an ashram from her husband and her family taking 3 year old Antara. It has resulted in a childhood trauma for a little girl multiplied by a year in a dreadful catholic convent later. My understanding is her mum has had her quite young as well. All in all, their relationship never was easy. It was in the past, and even in the present it is very competitive, critical and easily moving from love to hate. At present, it is exacerbated by her mum's state. The book jumps backwards and forwards from Antara's childhood to the present moment. There is a supportive cast of characters. But none of them are very strong, in my view. However, Antara's super-frank, unsentimental voice and her reflections, often angry, about herself or her mum have won me over. Her similes sometimes made me wince: occasionally too much physiology for the sake of it (salivas, periods, perspiration being described and more). But the social commentary was interesting. And the ideas were quite profound in a way. It made me think how many of us, daughters, are starting our lives thinking that we will be everything opposite to our mums. But then, somehow notwithstanding, ending up more similar to them than different. I did not think the last few chapters when Antara gave birth to her own daughter added much. It was very clearly inspired by Rachel Cask's Motherhood memories and they were not more insightful or new for that. Also it was one dark twist too many at the end for my liking. But overall, I enjoyed the energy of this.

Longlisted for 2021 Women's Prize for Fiction. Avni Doshi's Burnt Sugar, shortlisted for 2020 Booker Prize, has a distinctively bitter bite that my readerly palate has enjoyed. An unsettling, humorous and horrifying account of a mother-daughter relationship that binds them in a toxic love-hate codependency. The book starts with a killer first sentence that very much establishes the first-person voice of the daughter, Antara: "I would be lying if I said my mother's misery has never given me pleasure". What wonderfully delicious and dark wit. We quickly learn that the mother (Ma) is suffering cognitive degeneration and rapid memory loss. We get the following a few pages in: "Sometimes , I refer to Ma in the past tense even though she is still alive. This would hurt her if she could remember it long enough.... Sometimes I cry when no one else is around - I am grieving, but it's too early to burn the body". This really pulled me in. There is a quality of almost vicious, pained intelligence from the narrator as she peels back the layers of this relationship revealing what's led to this. At one point, further on in the book Antara reflects: "There was a breakdown somewhere about what we were to one another, as though one of us were not holding up her part of the bargain, her side of the bridge. Maybe the problem is that we are standing on the same side, looking out into the emptiness. Maybe we were hungry for the same things, the sum of us only doubled that feeling. And maybe this is it, the hole in the heart of it, a deformity from which we can never recover. If our conversations were itineraries, they would show us always returning to this vacant cul-de-sac, one we cannot escape from." As the mother loses her memory we rely on Antara's account of this painful relationship and there are questions raised about the reliability of her memories. Antara herself is very much aware of this, almost as a tragic self-realisation that her childhood has locked her into a particular even peculiar, constrained way of interacting with the world. This is also expressed in her artistic practice of drawing. The book also has a strangely claustrophobic feel, a sense that the reader is trapped with Antara inside the "cul-de-sac" of stories she keeps telling herself (and us) about this childhood she has lived and its suffocating impacts on her current life, including her marriage to Dilip. I will update this review soon, with some further thoughts as Burnt Sugar isn't without a few flaws. Fascinating book with such a distinctive voice that is both loving and cruel. Definitely worthy I think of its shortlisting for the Booker.

I’m always game for a mother-daughter story, and even though I’m fortunate to have a close relationship with my mom, I’m drawn to stories that reveal the complexities in that special bond. Burnt Sugar, nominated for the Booker Prize is about Tara and her daughter, Antara, living in India. Tara is losing her memory, and Antara has been through trauma and neglect throughout her childhood. The story is dark, intense, and raw, as these two navigate coming together even as the rifts of the past drive them apart. At times I was super uncomfortable while reading, and I felt a sharp want for something better, for healing and hope, for the characters in their lives. Even if it wasn’t an easy read because if its darkness, I was invested and along for the ride. I received a gifted copy. I’m really unsure what to make of this book. Whilst stylistically speaking, it’s quite beautifully written, its needlessly intense, borderline disturbing, unsettling and lacks focus. I was never quite sure if Doshi’s intent was to explore the lasting impact of child neglect & abandonment, a toxic imbalanced mother-daughter relationship, a woman’s search for her sense of self or just a deep dive into the unstable psyche of two very troubled women. Tara-Antara, mother-daughter exert almost this opposing yet undeniable pull for one another, each trying to escape the clutches of the other and yet in some twisted way always seeking the other out. Tara is suffering from Alzheimer’s and some form of dementia; people, identity and actions slowly slipping away as if stepping out of a snapshot. When pregnant with Antara, Tara had left her marriage seeking solace in an ashram as a mistress to a very questionable, self-proclaimed man of god. Antara spent her initial childhood years in the ashram, followed by a brief stint where she and her mother lived as homeless beggars, before finally being accepted into her grandparent’s home. The guilt of now, having to look after her mother, who hadn’t looked after her when she was vulnerable and a child hangs heavy in the air. In the present day Antara is an artist of sorts married to Dilip, a man who seems to hardly have any personality, yet with abundant patience and tolerance for his wilfully enigmatic, puzzling wife and mother in law. Antara’s turbulent childhood has obviously had an impact on her, but along side her unpleasant personality, Doshi presents Antara’s convoluted thoughts with such aloofness, such casual cruelty, it almost jolts you out of the book. So many sections felt really gratuitous and unnecessary, almost as if she was trying to shock the reader with her subversive darkness. Whilst there is an overall plot arc, it digresses much too often, spiralling into incidents that don’t add to the story but rather subtract from it. Doshi’s narrative style is also very matter of fact, clinical, detached and almost cold. The act of penning down my thoughts, however random, has made me realize I actually didn’t like this book very much. Aside from the writing, some sentences genuinely glittering in its finesse, there wasn’t much I could appreciate. Don’t let the abstract lavender cover with aloe vera mislead you into thinking this is some breezy read. It is deeply visceral, intense, unnerving and personally for me, one I could have done without.

A strong-headed and often selfish mother and divorcee—Tara—slowly being bogged down in dementia; a visual artist and former's daughter—Antara—who worries about her career, her marriage, and the tension-filled strings weaved in the relationship with her mother who is gradually losing her memory; a narration spilled through dual timelines—one painting the current events against the backdrop of a modern Indian city, and the other recounting years marking Antara's childhood. ➵ consider reading this review over on my blog! Like sugar that's caramelizing, this shortlisted title for Booker Prize 2020 is dangerously scalding while it entangles a mother-daughter relationship in unmet expectations, lost dreams, unhappiness, and years of neglecting sensitivity, love, and passion that every fulfilling relationship demands. And like caramelized sugar searing on the flames, Burnt Sugar can scorch with painful evocativeness around abuse, loneliness, and post-partum depression wrapped in the flawed characterization of a woman. Despite the very many invigorating and individualistic themes with potential to manifest empathy, understanding, and relatability, and equally important depictions of timely tensions like classism and religious strain, this debut fails to let a reader indulge in the absolutely realistic mess due to the lack of a compelling voice, an excessively floundering narration, and unnecessarily cliched portrayal of disturbing instances, nauseating descriptions, and the typically gross, pathetic, and filthy rendering of India—not to say there aren't issues in the country or stray dogs or pervert gurus, but the way Burnt Sugar paints the picture of this third-world country is wildly acclimatizing to the western audience and so-called intellectuals with awards to give. —if you wish to support: blog | ko-fi | twitter

I admired but didn’t particularly like this book. I’ve talked before about how I don’t really get on with books about motherhood, and sometimes the reverse is true too, I don’t always love books about daughterhood, especially when it’s the book’s main focus. (Something like Transcendent Kingdom is the exception, where the mother/daughter relationship is one thread among many.) I was finding something salvageable in the first half of Burnt Sugar, but the second half just lost me. While I tend to enjoy 'unlikable' protagonists, Antara was often too much for me--I found her to be deliberately belligerent toward the reader in a way that I didn't think was particularly interesting or well-executed. I think this book does have a lot going for it in terms of its chilly depiction of a strained mother/daughter relationship, but Antara herself staunchly refused to do any of the heavy lifting to earn my investment. I just didn't find her believable or her actions comprehensible; this book is written in the first person and still I struggled to discern some of Antara's motivations (this isn't helped by the book's awkward structure, flitting between the past and the present in a way that was occasionally challenging to follow and which I didn't think ultimately did it any favors). Avni Doshi's prose also failed to impress me, but, like most of my criticisms here, I feel that might just be a matter of personal taste. I do see why this book has been so critically well-received, it just really wasn't for me. Thank you to Netgalley and Abrams for the advanced copy provided in exchange for an honest review.

There is something irredeemably and irretrievably acrid and acidic about Doshi’s depiction of Pune, a Pune bathed in violet sunrises, a city which is home to the tempestuous relationship between Antara and her mother Tara. Doshi’s story stands out for its knack of defying conventions, from the unconventional nature of Antara’s relationship with her mother, which is as rooted in mutual antagonism as it is love, to Antara’s own musings, from the ambivalence with which she regards her own motherhood, to her mother’s past, from leaving her family, to homelessness, to her time in an ashram and her affair with an aloof artist. What gives ‘Burnt Sugar’ its power is its sense of honesty and rawness, as the narrator hides nothing about how she feels from the reader, from her relationship with her husband, to her tempestuous relationship with her mother, to the feelings of hatred and violence she sometimes experiences towards her newborn daughter, Doshi is able to circumvent the social conventions which women are expected to navigate. Many may come away from reading ‘Burnt Sugar’ with an intense dislike of Antara, viewing her as a selfish and self-absorbed person, but the point is that Doshi is attempting to portray a real person, warts and all, as opposed to a caricature, after all fiction is as much about depicting well realised characters as it is well like ones. ‘Burnt Sugar’ is an acerbic exploration of modern Indian, a brilliant portrayal of one woman’s struggles to overcome a childhood and upbringing rooted in a sense of rootlessness and a relationship with her mother which has been irrevocably shaped by her unconventional upbringing. Many may walk away from ‘Burnt Sugar’ with the feeling that they like neither the protagonist, the plot or any of the characters, but the reader should also walk away feeling that they have experienced a female voice which has hitherto been the sole domain of male writers and characters. 'Burnt Sugar' may be imperfect, but it is also indelible.

My 8th book from the 2020 Booker long list. I liked this one. I have read enough plotless sentence-level incisive devastating-secret devi novels to know it's a thing and not a thing I'm a big fan of. I like how the book addresses dementia, which I could relate to, and how it uses local culture in Pune and Mumbai, how it touches on life in an ashram, and how it addresses some of the characteristics of American-born Indians, and their relation to India. I enjoyed it. It's a mother-daughter story - Tara and Antara. Mom has progressing dementia and Antara is trying to deal with it, and is bitter about it. She still has hurts to respond to, and Tara is there, but there can no longer be a reckoning. It's too late. But also, Tara has less and less control over what she says. She starts hinting at dark secrets about to her son-in-law and Antara, our narrator, is getting a little anxious...and a little unstable. This is a debut novel by American born Doshi, and takes place in Pune, India. It's read beautifully by Sneha Mathan. (I think there is another version with a different narrator.) ‘I would be lying if I said my mother’s misery had never given me pleasure.’ Wow, what an opener. That sentence alone really just captures the essence of the novel perfectly. Written so carefully and with such power, I couldn’t help but consistently appreciate how talented Doshi is at writing stunning prose. Having said that, I’ve given this book a lower rating than I initially anticipated as I didn’t feel I connected with or understood it in its entirety - though I can still appreciate it for what it is. This narrative was beautiful, but with a constant melancholic undertone. Some of it confused me, I’m unsure how we as readers were supposed to perceive the narrator and how accurate the narrative was told. I think maybe that’s part of the beauty of it, but I don’t think I properly appreciated it as much as I could have because I wasn’t reading between the lines enough. Either that or there was nothing /to/ read between and I should’ve just taken it at face value. I’m not sure. It started off so strong but the more I read, it struggled to hold my attention quite as much. I found myself getting a bit distracted when I was reading and caring less the more I progressed through it. That being said, it’s very character focused and while I usually like these types of novels the characters here didn’t really compel me enough. I enjoyed the depiction of a taut mother/daughter relationship, but I didn’t feel connected to them as individuals at all. It just felt like something in the characters was missing for me.

I came across this book as Shortlisted for the Booker Prize of 2020 and the purple cover. "Never judge a book by its cover" they say. I just don't understand what I read. I thought about DNF-ing this book but I kept reading to see the point, the plot. It never came. This book read like a non-fiction autobiographical recap of the author. I had to keep reminding myself it was fiction because the storyline felt like real life, dull and drab. This is the story of a mother who was abhorrently absent in her daughters' life while defiantly pursuing a guru. The daughter is now an adult and her mother has Alzheimer's. She is now responsible to not only take care of her mother but overlook the wrongs that she may never make right. The daughter spends the rest of the book recanting all the mishaps of her childhood while simultaneously caring for her mother but hating her but kind of still liking her. It felt like a complicated mess to unpack. I don't think the author had a clear storyline established for the protagonist. Many parts felt intolerable to read like the obsession with her "ugly" body and her random sex life. I am disappointed in a book that I thought I would like, it just didn't sit well with me in any way.

“Sometimes I can feel that girl crowning at the back of my throat, trying to come out through any orifice she can. But I swallow her until the next she wants to be born again.” Antara is slowly losing her mother Tara to Alzheimer’s and in losing her she begins to remember for her. In remembering for her she begins to peel back at the years of her never truly having a safe home. Burnt Sugar has me sitting with a variety of questions. Mainly if women in novels are “allowed” to be irredeemable? Are they “allowed” to be throughly unlikeable specifically if they are mothers? I am use to reading about mother/daughter dynamics that attempt to explain, expand and seek understanding for the ways in which this relationship can go wrong or the ways in which is nourishes. But I’m not use to reading about the ways in which it can damage & crush like a tidal wave meant to break someone. The brutal toxicity that can exist in this link/bond and that we may be able to distance ourselves from but will remain with us and in us. I wasn’t ready for that. I also wasn’t ready for the tone of this book that felt fractured in the way that trauma can fracture a human. The dullness life can carry when the past weighs so heavy.
Very interesting novel looking a relationships love and interactions can see why was shortlisted for booker prize

I'll just preface this by saying that Doshi is a good writer. She understands her craft and how to navigate through themes and topics and involve things to evoke emotions. She is good. That's that. No arguing it, no denying her skill. This book FRUSTRATED me. I wanted everyone to die and the book to end much before it did. There were moments that I liked, but it was mostly an annoyance to get through this. I was even willing to take my review up to a flattering 3 star if someone could explain to me what I missed in my reading. But as you might notice, there are still 2 shiny yellow stars here. While reading it, I kept checking off a mental checklist of award-winning/ heavily lauded Indian books in English. ((This coming from a place of having to study such books in a class setting and the horror/distaste that comes from such an experience.)) ☑ parent-child love-hate relationship ☑ semi incestuous undertones ☑ psychopathic violence/ desire for violence ☑ sexual abuse ☑ the NRI or desire to escape ☑ India is dirty and gross but that is part of the charm ☑ drugs ☑ religion (more specifically babas fakirs phonies) ☑ pretentious art clique ☑ lesbian relationship but not quite ☑ in-laws being asses ☑ what is normal even ☑ narcissism and self-loathing in the same text ☑ marriage sucks and kids are a spiritual experience ☑ hostels are abusive ☑ food as a coping mechanism ☑ body issues ☑ adolescence and the realisation that your body is suddenly "desirable" as a shock ☑ partition ☑ babri masjid ☑ emergency ☑ loss/ death I guess this would be an English teacher's wet dream come to life. There's visibly so much to talk about here. Is it done well? ummm...well. The problem with tackling as many issues as these is that none of them get truly addressed. It is like trying to make a peanut butter sandwich but trying to add salads, mayo, and sauces because they normally make a pretty decent sandwich. Judging from reviews, I haven't misunderstood the book. It is a nuanced look at the very complex relationship between mother and child. it examines memory and experience and how reality is formed. It looks at identity and tries to create an immersive experience of that specific relationship and it kinda does it? I suppose? I JUST DIDN"T CARE FOR IT. I didn't give a shit about Kali Mata or Dilip or Whoever is that person. The watchman was about as interesting as the major characters in the book. When Reza Pine was introduced to me, I didn't want to give him a second glance! He kept assaulting me with his presence, nudging with his importance to the women, but I didn't care! I wanted him gone as far as possible. The Baba was a minor point of intrigue but what of it? There was a lack of commitment from Doshi for the rest of the characters and I acquiesced by not caring. I am still willing to listen to reason (or the lack of it) and try to understand why someone liked it while it felt like a chore to me. However, I might write an academic paper on this somehow because it is packed to the brim with content.

Just whaaaat was this?! Giving it a two stars because I don't want to be too mean. But I just didn't enjoy this book at all. Tara, the main protagonist has a weird exaggerated life and is not likable at all. Her daughter Antara is not without flaws either. The basic story is about how Antara becomes mother to her own mother Tara, who had been a neglectful mother to her, because she was busy running behind a baba and didn't have time to be a mother. Get it? I felt like Avni Doshi deliberately put in themes to shock the reader and grab eyeballs. The story didn't seem organic. And the Ashram storyline, which is the most enigmatic part of the book, is not explored properly. Why do the main characters keep thinking shit? And why does the author write about literal shit? Not like I have a problem with it. It just gets gross sometimes. The complex mother-daughter relationship is sometimes relatable and sometimes just "what the FFFFFFFF". I wanted to abandon the novel 2-3 times, but managed to finish it in the end. And wasn't very happy with it.

From the first line of this novel, I already knew I would love this book! “ I would be lying if I say my mother’s misery has never given me pleasure”. The story is about the relationship between Tara and her adult daughter, Antara. The story is told in Antara’s point of view and tells the story of the present as her mother is slowly losing her memory, and the past as Antara recounts the trauma of being raised by a mother who abandons her marriage and neglects her as she joins an ashram and devotes her life to the spiritual leader. The writing is raw, the language is at times shocking, but told in a voice that is courageous and fearless. I enjoyed this witty and dark exploration of the complex relationships not just between mother-daughter, but also the ambivalence of motherhood, being a wife, a woman in a patriarchal culture, and being seen as who you really are. Fantastic read I enjoyed! Thank you @booksparks and The Overlook Press for the gifted book. All opinions are my own.

The years of revision Avni Doshi is said to have spent on the manuscript for this book are apparent in this tightly formed book where every sentence counts. The story of a mother and daughter as the mother descends into dementia and their historically fraught relationship is utterly compelling as well as unsettling. Mother hood and madness, art and science are all part of a novel that makes you think and question all the way through. 0% in - Let's effing gooooooooooo. 0.5% in - Junior? We're going with JUNIOR??? Are we solid on the name or can we workshop it a bit...? 100% in - That was certainly...a book. And we really should have workshopped the whole Junior thing. That was a rough patch that didn't improve with time. The biggest impression I had upon closing this book was... that was a lot. Not of plot or character development. Just a lot of sex and I feel numb. Look, I like a spicy scene here and there but when nearly the whole book is a montage of sex (and rather explicit, kinky and...unusual scenes), I noticed that my brain actually started disassociating from the book. Objectively, it was an interesting phenomenon because I've read hundreds of audiobooks but I've never had to work so hard at keeping my attention focused on the book. But there was such an overwhelming number of explicit scenes that it ceased being fun or spicy, but something I had to slog through to get to the next plot point (which felt few and far between). The whole Junior/Lauren relationship felt bland to me despitethe frequency of their... scenes. Basically, he was her top subscriber, she was a top-earner on the OnlyFans equivalent of this world. But there wasn't much depth to their relationship. He's stalked her for years and she finds it charming. He's obsessed and willing to pay, she's a sex-positive online content creator who happily took all the money he offered. Something I did find interesting, is that junior says over and over that he is fine with her job and while we do see Lauren "at her job" quite frequently, she's never really shown sexting or filming specific videos for other clients. It's mentioned that she does and will continue to do that, but the author only focuses on her custom work for junior. So there's this weird dynamic where realistically, junior feels like he's getting this unique experience but he really isn't but the author chooses to only highlight relationship building moments from sexting and whatnot between the two MCs. Anyway, what's wild is that the first book (Lights Out) had a somewhat similar premise (obsession and being charmed) and yet that one worked so well for me. I thought the banter between the characters was hilarious, the scenes were spicy but exciting, and I liked the push-pull of the relationship. But Junior and Lauren felt like shadows compared to Josh and Ali. Honestly, the most interesting thing was Lauren's best friend getting a request to cover herself in food and when the friend was like, "hey, is this weird?" And Lauren's like, "oh he's a cannibal, just ignore it. " and I'm like, "What? WHAT!?" but nothing ever comes of that plot point! I'm not saying one of the characters should've been eaten but why throw that tidbit in there if you aren't going to use it? With book 1 being so good, and book 2 being rock bottom...I wonder where book 3 will land? P.s. I don't believe for a second that Junior actually has money. At the rate he was throwing it at Lauren - couple of hundred to thousands a week? Yeah right. He couldn't save up to save his life. I think the author had an "ohsht" moment where she realized she was making Junior poor cause he spent so much on custom photos and videos and retroactively wrote in that he was uber rich to compensate. That's my headcanon and you won't ever convince me otherwise.

A Crimson Waltz of Power, Pain, and Passion! Mafia romances used to thrill me. It’s been a while since I let a mafia dark romance crawl under my skin —less a love story, more a dissertation on inherited violence and the quiet, terrible cost of wanting to be good in a world that never taught you how. So Caught Up is a dark, erotic, and deeply contemporary romance that interrogates the intersections of trauma, power, and healing. Navessa Allen uses the conventions of the mafia romance and the sex work romcom to subvert expectations, centering consent, agency, and the messy work of forgiveness. The novel is unflinching in its portrayal of violence—both physical and emotional—but refuses to glamorize it, instead showing the cost of generational harm and the courage required to break free. At its heart, the story is about reclaiming narrative: Lauren reclaims her sexuality and her story from shame, while Junior reclaims his future from the grip of his father. Their love is not a panacea but a partnership, built on honesty, mutual respect, and the willingness to do the hard work of healing. The found family at Velvet, the celebration of kink and sex-positivity, and the ultimate triumph over cycles of abuse make Caught Up a powerful meditation on what it means to choose love, again and again, in a world determined to deny it. 🩸 The Premise What happens when the man you loved kills your father—and then becomes your most loyal subscriber? Nico “Junior” Trocci was born with a bullet between his teeth and guilt in his bloodstream. The heir to a mafia empire, Junior has done terrible things, but none worse than what he did to Lauren Marchetti. Years later, he worships her anonymously through a camgirl screen, a ghost in her inbox, craving penance through pixels. Lauren—saint, sinner, survivor—is not the same girl who fell for a boy with a gun. She owns her sexuality now. She sells it. But on her terms. With her girls. With her queerness. With her fire. They’re not just two people with history. They are an open wound with no stitches. And when they see each other again? It’s not a love story. It’s a slow-motion trainwreck dressed like a second chance. 🔖Junior Trocci (aka: Mafia Malfunction in Designer Shoes) Eldest son. Haunted heir. Certified emotional disaster. Has enemies in five countries and eyes only for you. PS:I have a thing for Hot Italian Mafia's!! Was raised to be a killer, fell in love with a girl who charges by the minute. Violent? Yes. Vulnerable? Unfortunately, also yes. Obsessed with Lauren in a way that's half Romeo, half "I’d burn down the city if you asked nicely." Redemption arc incoming, but not before he threatens a few dozen people and breaks your heart. Therapist recommendation: URGENTLY. “He's ruthless; a walking red flag. Good thing red is my favorite color.” 💄Lauren Marchetti(aka: Saint Camgirl of Don’t-Mess-With-Me) Sex work advocate with eyeliner sharper than her trust issues. Has been betrayed by everyone—including her own last name—but refuses to stay down.. A woman who has been slut-shamed, exiled, fetishized, and filmed—but who builds a family out of the ashes. Built an empire in fishnets and fury. Witty, wounded, and 100% done with your judgment. When Junior shows up with mafia daddy issues and sad eyes? She considers forgiving him… then makes him grovel (as she should). Boundaries? Set. Power? Reclaimed. Will stab you with consent and style. This was the problem with us. He could stalk me, interfere with my life, and put up more red flags than an entire circus, and I would still look at him and remember the boy I’d grown up with. "When someone shows you who they are, believe them the first time.” It had become my mantra because I had learned the hard way that if you give people second chances, they’ll only use them to hurt you more.” 🏷️Storyline recap: Mafia heir Nico “Junior” Trocci gets a dead body for his birthday. Classic. It's just another night of blood, rain, and guilt—until he realizes the man he helped kill was the father of the girl he’s been obsessing over since high school: Lauren Marchetti. Lauren? She’s not the same girl he left behind. She’s a camgirl now, loud about sex work rights, unashamed, and on fire. She’s got scars, rules, and a one-strike policy. And guess what? Her number-one sub online—the only one who really sees her? Yeah. It’s him. What follows is a head-on collision of past betrayals, mafia mess, kinky club nights, and way too much tracking (both emotional and literal). Junior wants a second chance. Lauren wants answers. But between groveling, stalking, church confrontations, mafia dinners, and literal blood on the floor… nothing’s clean here. This isn’t some soft redemption arc. It’s messy, feral, and laced with hurt. But maybe—just maybe—love can crawl out of all that darkness. In a world of mob violence, sex work stigma, and chosen family, Caught Up Into the Darkness asks: Can love survive when it was born from lies and built in blood? ╰┈➤ Now let’s give love to the side character goldmine: 📌Moira Trocci Italian mob mom with eyeliner sharp enough to kill Junior’s mama. Was probably born in heels and holding a switchblade. Quiet strength, ancient secrets, terrifying maternal energy. Has been through hell but still gets dinner on the table. Will smile sweetly as she slaps the patriarchy out of her husband. Matriarchal rebrand: activated.She’s got secrets. She’s got strategy. She’s got a knife in her purse and a prayer on her lips. Wears Chanel No. 5 while dismantling patriarchy from the inside. She sees everything, says little, and moves like a queen in a game full of pawns. And when she finally does speak? Everyone listens. 📌Taylor (aka: Bad B*tch with a Weapon and a Dildo) She’s Barbie if Barbie had anger issues and a switchblade in her bra. Will defend Lauren to the death (or until someone bleeds—same thing). Loud. Loyal. Lethal in heels. Would absolutely post bail for you, but will also roast you the entire way home. Her motto? “Slut-shaming is cancelled and so are YOU.” The human equivalent of glitter on a crime scene. Will throw hands, wigs, and insults in the same breath. Swears like it’s punctuation. Has a secret soft side for her friends, but only when the cameras are off. Will absolutely bring a flamethrower to a knife fight—and bedazzle it.. She fights with stilettos and dildos and I would trust her with my life (and my passwords). 📌 RYAN (nonbinary brilliance, here to save your life and your Wi-Fi) Emotionally intelligent. Gender-fluid excellence. Codes like a god and cries during Pixar movies. A literal unicorn in a house full of feral chaos gremlins. Brings peace, boundaries, and spreadsheets to the table. May be quiet, but you cross Ryan and your router will mysteriously combust.Could erase your digital footprint in 3 seconds—would only do it if you said please. 📌 Nico Trocci Sr. (aka: Toxic King No One Asked For) Walking manifestation of generational trauma and expensive cologne. Thinks love = control and parenting = trauma bonding. Wants Junior to be a clone of him. Secretly soft inside? Maybe. Probably not. Who cares. We're just waiting for him to catch a poetic and painful downfall. Also: Your daddy issues should NOT look like this. 📌 Aly (aka: Mafia Nurse, Soft But Deadly) Sweet? Yes. Soft? No. She’s kind, but don’t test her. Aly’s the kind of girl who knows how to bandage a bullet wound and deliver a brutal truth in the same breath. Could’ve gone no-contact with the Troccis, but chose to fight instead. Icon behavior. 📌 JOSH (the “hacker with a heart” trope perfected) Gives “I accidentally got caught up in a mafia scandal but I’m having fun now” energy. Madly in love with Aly and will absolutely risk prison to help her cousin’s mafia drama. Snarky. Scruffy. Lowkey brilliant. Has seen too much but still believes in love and snacks. Will blow up your firewall, then offer you soup. 📌 GREG, ALEC, STEFAN (aka: the bloodline of dysfunction) Greg: Will 100% die on the “loyal to the family” hill. Unwell, unhinged, unloved. Alec: Has read Nietzsche once and won’t shut up about it. Stefan: The type to casually stab someone and then ask “you okay?” like it’s small talk. Each one’s more emotionally suppressed than the last. Together, they are a therapy group waiting to happen. 📌 TYLER (finance bro with a felony past) Bookie. Manipulator. Probably knows your credit score. Wears designer suits and moral ambiguity. You’ll never know if he’s helping you or plotting your downfall. Smiles like a villain in a cologne ad. Too charming to trust, too useful to kill. Junior’s necessary evil. We stan (but also fear) the ambition. e ╰┈➤ Plot Devices- -Dual POV: Mafia prince & camgirl—two worlds, one collision. -Secrets: Lies unravel, past haunts, trust shatters. -Intimacy: Power, healing, truths... 3.5 ⭐️ I didn’t love this the way I loved Lights Out, but I still had a good time with it. 🖤 The Premise Nico “Junior” Trocci is a mob heir who wants out—of his father, the life, and most of all the damage he did to Lauren Marchetti, the girl whose heart he shattered ten years ago. Lauren is no longer the shy, bookish girl Junior walked away from. She’s a confident camgirl, sex-work advocate, part-owner of a local play club, and a woman with firm boundaries and zero tolerance for men who can’t handle her. What she doesn’t know? Her most devoted subscriber—the one who’s adored her through a screen for years and spent thousands—is Junior himself. 🐾 My Thoughts “I cared about her so much that I'd broken both our hearts to keep her safe.” This book is much heavier than the first. The dark-comedy chaos is mostly gone, replaced by guilt, fixation, and intensity. Junior’s obsession with Lauren is quiet and slow-burning. His stalking isn’t flashy or feral—it’s controlled and deliberate. “I don't want to clip your wings, Lo. I want to see you fly.” Even though I wanted more chaos, Junior’s emotional security made up for it. He supports Lauren without hesitation and never tries to dim her shine. Kneeling? On his knees? Yes. “Don't boss me around or I'll come.” Lauren is bold and fully in control of her sexuality. I loved the sex-positive rep, her confidence, and the way she takes the lead in introducing Junior to new kinks. That said, their history does a lot of the emotional heavy lifting. They had a brief teenage relationship that ended badly, followed by years of Junior watching from afar. While I enjoyed the devotion and protectiveness, I wasn’t always convinced by their connection in the present. The attraction was strong, but I wanted more grovel—and more payoff—to make their bond feel fully earned. For a mafia romance, the stakes were surprisingly low. The mob element stays mostly in the background, and whenever things could’ve gone darker or messier, the story played it safe. The found family moments were a highlight—Walter included. Nonna was hilarious, and seeing Aly, Josh, and Fred again made my heart happy. I also really liked the Trocci brothers, especially Alec. 🥀 Final Take “She was my match, my queen, and I would spend the rest of my life worshipping her like one if she let me.” A kink-heavy, obsessive second-chance romance with intense vibes and very little humor. It didn’t give me kick-my-feet excitement, but I still enjoyed the ride. The duet narration by Teddy Hamilton and Kasi Hollowell helped a lot, and I’m definitely excited for Tyler’s story. Josh and Aly were lightning in a bottle, a totally unique pairing both in this world and in dark romance as a whole. Junior and Lauren are entirely different. It does not have the same humor or emotional lightness as Lights Out, instead leaning into heat, tension, and intensity. I love Navessa’s writing and the way she explores themes of freedom, being seen, and what it means to choose your own path. Did I love it the way I loved Lights Out? Ten year obsession is crazy, but like… commitment 🎥💕 Caught Up delivers exactly what you’d expect from a dark romance built on obsession, messy power dynamics, and unresolved teenage history — and for the most part, it works. Lauren Marchetti is a camgirl and sex worker rights advocate who feels confident, sharp, and unapologetic in her choices. Nico “Junior” Trocci, meanwhile, is a reluctant mafia enforcer who has been quietly obsessed with her for a decade. When he reconnects with her online after pushing her away in high school, that obsession reignites in a way that’s equal parts swoony and slightly unhinged. The dynamic is intense. There’s tension, possessiveness, and that morally gray edge dark romance fans look for. Allen’s humor is still very much present — there were moments I genuinely laughed out loud, which I’ve come to expect since reading Lights Out. That balance of sharp banter and heavy themes is something she does really well. That said, I didn’t feel quite as emotionally immersed as I did with Lights Out. The chemistry is there, the spice is there, the obsession is definitely there — but I wasn’t as deeply invested in the emotional arc. Some of the power dynamics and redemption beats didn’t hit as hard for me as they could have. Still, it’s entertaining, funny in places you don’t expect, and unapologetically dark. If you like obsession, mafia tension, complicated history, and a heroine who owns her space, this absolutely delivers. Not my favorite of Allen’s, but still a solid, fun read. Final Verdict: Dark, funny, and intense — just not quite as emotionally gripping as I wanted it to be. A strong 3.5 stars.

The initial allure of the narrative, encapsulated in the assertion of desire from a man who typically achieves his wants, sets the stage for a potentially gripping dark romance. However, the execution disappointingly falters, relying excessively on clichéd archetypes such as the brooding, possessive anti-hero and the innocent heroine who undergoes a sultry transformation. Nico “Junior” Trocci is depicted as obsessively dangerous rather than intriguingly enigmatic, and his fixation on Lauren veers unsettlingly close to stalking rather than the passionate romance the story aims to portray. Rather than cultivating a nuanced and compelling relationship between the protagonists, the plot hastily propels them into lust-driven encounters that lack the emotional resonance and character development necessary to engage the reader fully. Lauren’s journey from a timid bookworm to a confident club-goer holds the potential for a powerful narrative arc, yet it is regrettably reduced to a mere backdrop for Junior’s objectification and possessive tendencies. Her internal struggles and emotional complexities are superficially addressed, rendering her more of a fantasy figure than a fully fleshed-out character. The club scenes, while undeniably steamy and explicit, overshadow any genuine attempts at plot progression or meaningful relationship dynamics. Ultimately, the novel resembles a collection of spicy fanfiction rather than a thoughtfully crafted romance, leaving readers yearning for depth and authenticity that remains tantalizingly out of reach. the only thing that I loved is the bike that Junior has...and it's such a waste..

I LIKED this one BUT didn't LOVE it like I did Lights Out. I didn't feel as connected with Junior and Lauren as I did with Ally and Josh. I wanted MORE- not sure what of but just MORE. I found myself at the edge of my seat wondering when Lauren was going to give in to her desire for Junior. I liked Junior's touch her and die vibes. I liked the mafia aspect but did want a little more of that. I felt like Lights Out was edgier if that makes sense. I did like the sensuality in this book - the tension at the club was STRUNG TIGHT. Very much a voyeuristic vibe that I enjoyed with the club and Lauren's job. I liked how supportive Junior was of all things Lauren did AND that he had been her literal number one supporter since day one. I liked how Lauren empowered Junior to go out on his own and get away from his father and all that toxicity. When these two did get together, it was electric. I love how committed Junior was to Lauren and even though there was bad blood from when they were younger there was a GOOD reason for the bad blood. Junior was such a morally grey GOOD man. Lauren is living her life. Her work is THRIVING to say the least. She feels like she is making headway for women and men in her industry to not have the stigma it has had for all these years. All is well until she runs into Junior Trocci. The boy (now man) that she was in love with all those years ago who ghosted her when things went south. And now he is here looking at her like she is a snack. Like he still wants her. Like nothing bad went down between them all those years ago. Well who does he think he is? And why is she still having this reaction to him? The way he acted led her to have YEARS of therapy. Yet for whatever reason he is making amends and wants to see her. He wants to support her. He wants to join her at her club. He wants to play and watch. He wants HER. But should she let her heart open again? Is he here with ulterior motives? Or is everything he is saying true? Either way she can't help it. She is falling for this man who shows her a side that no one else really gets to see. The side that has dreams outside of the mob. The side who can love and support and cherish. The side who makes her toes curl in the BEST way. The side who is willing to try almost anything once. But then a miscommunication comes between them. And Lauren has to decide how much she trusts Nico and his intentions. And if how she feels about him is worth fighting for. Nico has always had one woman on his mind, Lauren Marchetti. The one who got away. The one he let go to save her. The one who he was threatened to stay away from. But now there are no obstacles in his way. And he is determined to make things right between them and to show her what they could be. He doesn't expect a warm welcome when they see each other again. But he also doesn't expect to see the hurt still there. So now he really has to apologize and make things right. Which he does. He wants a chance. A REAL chance. So she offers him to come to her club with her. To see what she likes and they can go from there. And that night is an experience Nico didn't know he would like. But he realizes he likes it even more because Lauren is with him. He knows her walls are still up. He just has to prove to her what she means to him. So he opens up. Tells him all the things he has been doing behind the scenes for her. How much he supports her in everything that she does. And he wants her to succeed. Their connection is unmatched. He has never felt like this before. He just has to make it through a little bit longer to get on the other side of his dad. And when a misunderstanding comes between them Nico is that much more determined to show Lauren his love for her. Because he has ALWAYS loved her. Even when she didn't know it. Can I just say that the church confessional booth scene was ALMOST key word ALMOST as hot as the knife scene from book 1. IYKYK. Our girl Navessa can get creative with these *bedroom* scenes and I am here for it. I liked the cameos we got of Ally and Josh and how much they supported Nico and his quest to get away from his dad. And I liked Lauren and Nico. I liked their banter. I liked how they were real with each other. I liked how down bad Nico was for her from the jump. I also LOVE that Tyler was in this. Yes THAT Tyler. And that it seems like he is going to be the MC for the third book- hoping I am right on that one. Anyways even though this didn't blow my socks off like book 1, I still very much enjoyed it and found it entertaining. But seriously LISTEN to it- Teddy is just SO GOOD!

Dark Hours is quite possibly the best book Connelly has penned in recent years and yet I was uncomfortable reading it. He cut too close to the bone on this one. Dark hours referrers to the dark hours of graveyard shift, aka The Late Show a title from another Ballard novel. Connelly doesn’t pull any punches and describes the aftermath of societies the current upheaval; the defund the police campaign, and Covid. Usually I don’t finish a book if there are political messages or even undertones. I read to be entertained, to escape the world I live in, not to rehash it. But in this case—it’s Connelly for crying out loud. I read the whole thing. In the story there are two crimes being investigated but they take a backseat to the dark tone of the book. Both crimes are particularly heinous and double-down on that same noir mood. Connelly had to have done it on purpose and by my estimation it was masterfully done. Ballard is more cynical and callouses than before with little patience for fellow employees, no sympathy for what they are going through only judgement. Ballard’s dog is even killed off. Yikes. The absolute brilliant part of this book is the last two pages. Connelly hits us again and again with darkness then right at the end at the bleakest point he shows us a little light. Great read but not for the faint of heart. It will make you want to curl up on your couch with a half-gallon of cookies and cream ice cream. David Putnam the author of the Bruno Johnson series.

Review to be posted to blog: books-are-a-girls-best-friend.com Nowadays, times appear rougher than they used to be. Danger shows itself in different ways. Here and now, you can’t always see what’s right in front of your face simply because everyone is hiding behind a mask and Covid is ever-present. Never one to shy away from reality, Michael Connelly’s new novel, The Dark Hours brings it home. It’s in The Dark Hours that Detective Renee Ballard does her best work. She is a night owl and she loves flying solo. When a homicide occurs on her watch in the Late Shift, she wants it, even if the investigation should go to the detectives in the Hollywood Division. Once she dives into the case, what she finds, makes her want it even more. Her case links to an old unsolved crime, a cold case of retired Detective Harry Bosch’s, and wouldn’t you know it, the two decide to work together to solve them both. Ballard, of course, investigates other crimes as well, one of which involves several women assaulted in their homes, in the middle of the night, by a group called The Midnight Men, which brings about a different type of danger altogether. This was a nail-biter, to say the least! A very well-written, well-done police procedural, which took place during the pandemic. Something very few authors even attempt. I truly appreciated the care that Michael Connelly took, to center a police procedural in and around the pandemic and give major kudos to him for that. What I love most about this series is the camaraderie between Ballard and Bosch which warms my heart. If you know me, you know how much I love these characters, Harry Bosch specifically. I could, in fact, wax poetic about my love for Harry Bosch (and have, in many a book review in this series, lol). While I wish that Bosch took a more prominent role here, I still adored this novel and love the character of Renee Ballard. It's clear that there will be some changes in store for both of these characters and I look forward to seeing where life takes them. A huge thank you to Little Brown and Company and NetGalley for the arc. Thank you for always being so generous in feeding my Harry Bosch obsession (lol). I have been a fan of Michael Connelly for many, many years. I have enjoyed Harry Bosch and have read every single book in his series. I've also read all of the spin off series. We all knew that Harry was getting older and realistically there was going to be a limit to how much longer his character was going to be able to continue. So, I thought the teaming up with Renee Ballard was a smart idea. Unfortunately, this is another author who has made the decision to insert the woke politics of today and certain views on masks, the vaccine, defund the police and BLM into the story. I lost count of how many times "masks" were mentioned. Either being put on, taken off, describing the masks by color - even the people who chose not to wear one. It was so often and at times, so very not relevant to whatever was happening on the page. It does truly pull the reader out of the story. The inclusion of the "hate Trump" graffiti, the January "insurrection", the BLM "protestors” (rioters) and many, many other similar events just seemed superfluous and wasn't really necessary for the story. I'm not sure why it was needed- especially since this entire series has been a police procedural series that have centered on the actions and cases of a cop and the LAPD. Besides that, I have grown to really like Harry. Harry Bosch was a cop. He devoted his entire life to the LAPD and was already screwed enough by them. Now, we have the police department shown in an even more horrible light. Who knows, maybe the LAPD is completely corrupt, but it seems to take everything that Harry worked for and believed in and throw it back in our face. Anyway, that is neither here nor there. That was just an observation. I didn't find the plot and the story itself up to what we have come to expect from Mr. Connelly. I didn't finish the last page with a feeling of accomplishment on the part of the protagonists. I really felt just...sad. There is enough going on in the real world today that I don't want to come away from a book feeling even worse. I'm hoping this was just a one off and that we can get back to what made the series great in the first place. If not, it might be time to say goodbye to this series. But...I truly hope not.

3.5 stars This review was first posted on Mystery and Suspense. Check it out for features, interviews, and reviews. www.mysteryandsuspense.com/the-dark-h... In this 23rd book in the Bosch World series, Renee Ballard and Harry Bosch work together to solve two related homicides and Renee tries to track down a tag team of rapists. The book works fine as a standalone but knowledge of the characters is a bonus. ***** LAPD Detective Renee Ballard worked in the elite Robbery Homicide Division until she accused her boss of sexual harassment and got transferred to the night shift. On the graveyard shift Ballard gets to start investigations, but then has to pass them off to the day watch. Renee resents this and often finds a way to continue the investigations, to the chagrin of her superiors. On New Year's Eve 2020 Ballard and her temporary partner, Detective Lisa Moore of the Sex Crimes Unit, are sheltering beneath an underpass while Angelenos follow the tradition of firing guns into the air. Falling bullets often shatter windshields, so the detectives are staying out of the way while they anticipate a call about the Midnight Men, a team of two rapists known to strike on holiday eves. Shortly after midnight, Ballard and Moore are called to the scene of a death. Auto shop owner Javier Raffa, who hosts a neighborhood party every New Year's Eve, was shot in the head. Renee would normally turn the Raffa case over to West Bureau Homicide, but they're overtaxed so Renee gets to keep the case for the time being. As it turns out, a shell casing connects Raffa's homicide to the unsolved murder of rapper Albert Lee ten years ago, a case investigated by Detective Harry Bosch. Bosch worked for the LAPD for over thirty years, but was always a maverick, and was finally pushed out. Bosch now works independently, looking into cold cases. Ballard contacts Bosch - who's her mentor and friend - about the deaths of Raffa and Lee , and the duo decide to investigate the homicides together. Renee and Harry discover that Raffa had been a member of the Las Palmas gang, but borrowed $25,000 to buy himself out. As it happens, victim Albert Lee had also borrowed a large sum of money, and the detectives speculate that the debts connect the murdered men with their killer. Meanwhile, on New Year's Day, a woman named Cindy Carpenter reports that two men raped her the night before, and the modus operandi proves they're the Midnight Men. Ballard has to pursue the rapists on her own because Detective Lisa Moore has sneaked off for a vacation with her boyfriend. This lackadaisical attitude has become common in the LAPD due to the Covid pandemic, public vilification of the cops, violent protests, and the defund the police movement. The malaise hasn't spread to Renee though, who works day and night to capture criminals. Meticulous police work by Ballard and Bosch uncovers clues about the Raffa and Lee shootings, and a man walking his dog gives Renee a lead on the tag team rapists. Ballard's fervent pursuit of the perpetrators puts her life in danger, and flouting the rules gets her in trouble with her lieutenant. As the murder and rape cases head toward resolution Ballard considers leaving the LAPD and working with Bosch full-time. Will a visit from the chief of police change Renee's mind? On the light side, Ballard adopts a chihuahua mix from Wags and Walks. The rescue pooch, named Pinto, goes paddle-boarding with Renee on her days off and stays in 24-hour doggy daycare when Renee's working. Ballard also meets an attractive EMT called Garrett Single, who helps Renee out in a pinch and invites her to a firehouse dinner. Is there romance in Renee's future? This is an excellent thriller, and I look forward to seeing Ballard and Bosch work together again. You can follow my reviews at https://reviewsbybarbsaffer.blogspot.com

I've been a huge fan of Michael Connelly's Harry Bosh series since the first book, The Black Echo, appeared in 1992, and I've eagerly looked forward to each new installment in the series. Bosh was introduced as a veteran of the Vietnam war and was in his middle thirties when he first appeared, and Connelly made the decision to age the character in real time so that Harry is now in his late sixties. This decision has presented the author with some significant problems, principally in that Harry was forced to retire from the L.A.P.D. and is obviously not the man he used to be, physically at least. Connelly kept the character relevant by allowing him to investigate cold cases, by having him get his license and do some work as a P.I., and by temporarily detailing him to a small police department outside of the city. But several years ago, he introduced a new and younger detective, Renee Ballard, who is as much an outsider in the L.A.P.D. as Bosch was. This is now the fourth novel to feature Ballard and along the way, she has managed to team up with Harry who serves as a mentor to Ballard and who assists her off the books with her investigations. This book begins on New Year's Eve as 2020 turns into 2021. Ballard is soon working two cases and, like Bosch before her, is managing to antagonize her superior officers and a number of her fellow cops as well. One of the cases involves two men, known as the Midnight Men, who have committed a series of rapes. The other involves the murder on New Year's Eve of an auto shop owner. Ballard soon discovers that the gun that was used to kill the man ties back into an old, unsolved case that Bosch once worked. Naturally, she turns to Harry for the details of his case and in short order, the two are working together again with Bosch as Ballard's silent partner. The investigations play out against the backdrop of the Covid Pandemic, the Black Lives Matter movement and the Capitol insurrection. Much of the book moves pretty slowly, and it doesn't really pick up speed until the last quarter of the book. Part of my problem with the book is that I love the character of Harry Bosh but I still have not been able to warm up to Renee Ballard who seems to be a pale imitation of Bosch. And in my humble opinion, the author is having something of the same problem. Bosh has always been a riveting character and the stories Connelly created around him were always charged with tension and pulled the reader along at a breakneck pace. With Ballard, it often seems to me that Connelly is basically going through the motions, giving us a lot of police procedure without much spark. Back in the day, when I opened a typical Harry Bosch novel, I was basically out of circulation until I finished it. But I don't find Ballard or these stories to be nearly as compelling. I read this book over the space of four days and had no problem at all frequently putting it aside and going on to other things. In the end, this may simply come down to the fact that I hate the idea of an iconic character like Harry Bosch being reduced to the role of somebody's sidekick. I realize that Connelly basically painted himself into a corner by letting Bosch age in real time, but I wish he had come up with a better approach to keeping the character relevant. Perhaps at this stage of the game, he might have gone back in time to tell a story from earlier in Bosch's life when Harry was a younger and more vigorous man. Lawrence Block did this once with his series character, Matthew Scudder to very good effect. Ultimately, I don't know if I really care to read any more "Renee Ballard and Harry Bosch" novels, but I'm comforted by the fact that I have a shelf full of real Harry Bosch novels that I can return to whenever I need a great read.

As one of my favourite authors, a new Michael Connelly book is like Christmas come early for me. His books were some of the first police procedural books that I ever read, thanks to my dad who thought I would like them. And he was right. All these years later and Harry Bosch is my all time favourite fictional detective. There was a happy dance happening when I opened this bookmail in the middle of lockdown in Sydney 2021. A very big thank you to Allen and Unwin, who understand my obsession with all things Michael Connelly. This is the 4th Renee Ballard book and I am liking her more and more each book. She is one tough cookie, working the Late Show (or graveyard shift) for the LAPD in Hollywood. She sees the more hidden and darker side of the city and that is the way that she likes it. This book starts on new years eve 2020 during the pandemic. It has been a tough year with lockdowns, department politics, Black Lives Matter and the scrutiny of the police force as a whole. On the job is now more dangerous than it has ever been. As always with a Connelly book, there is alot going on. Renee is called to the scene of a homicide early on new years day. She wants to hold on to the case and gives it everything she has. When she finds a link to an old case that her friend and mentor, Harry Bosch worked on, the pair team up once again to hunt down the killer. While she is doing this, she is also working on the Midnight Men case where women are being in attacked in her own home. A serious page turner, The Dark Hours shows the lesser seen side of the law. Renee is not one to stick to the rules and probably why she gets on with Harry so well. They are a team that will never give up and really care about the victims of the crimes. They question the system and it is not always taken well by the higher ups. It will come as no suprise to anybody that this was a 5 star read for me and will be one of my favourite books of 2021. Do yourself a favour and pick up a Connelly book, sooner rather than later. The Dark Hours is released November 9th.

As a fan of the Harry Bosch series, I enjoyed Connelly's latest police procedural story. Renee Ballard is the main character, and she works The Dark Hours, meaning the midnight shift. She enlists retired cop, now private detective, Harry Bosch, to help her solve the two crimes she's investigating. Ballard is a loner, a surfer, and a good cop, but she doesn't always let department policy get in the way of finding the bad guys. She has a few narrow escapes, plus a new love interest. She also adopts a puppy, Pinto, a cute chihuahua mix. I didn't like a lot of the police jargon but it provided authenticity, a trademark of the Bosch series.

It's New Year's Eve, 2020. LAPD detective Renee Ballard is, along with about every active-duty officer in the Los Angeles area, out on the streets. New Years is apparently a holiday rife with violence and idiots committing crimes, so the police are always out in force. Right out of the gate, minutes after the ball drops, Ballard and her partner are called to a potential homicide. An auto shop owner is killed by a stray bullet during a raucous block party. It could just be an accident, but when the victim is discovered to have a background with one of LA's deadliest Latin gangs, the focus of the investigation changes. Ballard and her partner have also been investigating a string of rapes, committed by two men in ski masks. A new victim provides some new clues which could help. Ballard's plate being full, she asks Harry Bosch---now a private detective---for help. "The Dark Hours" is the fourth Ballard book and the 23rd Bosch book. Author Michael Connelly could spend the rest of his career writing nothing but Ballard-Bosch novels and I'd be happy.

3.5 stars. I struggled to rate this book because it's not a Harry Bosch novel and that's what I wanted it to be. Yeah, I get it. It's now the Harry Bosch Universe. He's retired. He's going to be a secondary character from now on, but I'm just not as intrigued or compelled by Ballard. She's a good cop. A bit of a hothead, but her heart's in the right place. I just don't feel like I can get close to her as a reader, and that disconnect impacts the whole story. It's well-written, as all of Connelly's books are, but it's missing the spark that Bosch or Haller provide.

This is the twenty-third book in the Harry Bosch series, however, in the last few, Renee Ballard, a young female detective, has been taking a greater role—this is the fourth book with her in a major role. In all but one of these she is partnered with Bosch. She was first introduced in the 2007 book The Overlook. In this book she is the lead and Bosch is only a minor supporting character. Ballard is a feminine clone of Bosch. She likes working alone and she is almost constantly in conflict with her superiors. This mystery involves a couple of serial rapists, but while tracking them Ballard is called to the scene of a murder. When the department heads try to hand off the murder case to another department Ballard continues her investigation hoping to solve the case before the handoff while simultaneously working the rapist case. This two case story line seems to be popular with the Bosch books of late. I don’t remember the earlier books having that type of story line. This story occurs at the beginning of 2021 and includes several references to some of the happenings of the time. There are several comments about these circumstances by Bosch, Ballard and others. The “Defund the Police” idea is described as having a detrimental effect on the police department. It is said that the police have become reactive instead of proactive. They want no unnecessary interaction with the public. When Ballard mentions that she is thinking of leaving the police force, Bosch points out that true reform must come from inside the police department and she should stay and become part of that reform. There is also mention of the importance of wearing a mask due to the Covid pandemic. But in another eery coincidence as I write this on the anniversary of the Jan. 6th insurrection, Bosch and others express their shock at the Capitol being invaded by Americans when that event occurs during the story. I doubt if many readers pick up a mystery like any of Michael Connelly’s books expecting some social commentary. The fact that I agree with many of these views does not negate the distractions they brought to the story. At the end of the book Ballard has resigned from the police department, but there are hints that she will return. She is an interesting addition to the mystery genre and I will look forward to the next book by Michael Connelly hoping he continues her story.

DNF. First Connelly book I could not (and DID NOT want to) finish. After dozens of great novels (Bosch, Haller, etc ...) without ZERO current political commentary, evidently Connelly had the same reaction to the Trump election as did Stephen King ....crazed mouth-frothing hatred! The most recent Haller novel had a gratuitous Trump slam while they were picking a jury, but it was a quick joke. But this is a total immersion into the alternate reality of the Regressive Democratic worldview. I certainly don't need to read CNN inspired virtue signaling prose like "mask up, badge out" every fourth page. Also don't need the rah-rah BLM instructions. Wow, what a total collapse of a once great writer ...

I don’t think you can beat a Connelly for the characters and detailed police procedural descriptions. Lucky to pick up 2 books at the local Charity shop. This one and the one that follows in hardback. A discerning reader must have moved into the area. Ballard is similar to Bosch. A loner, dog lover and entirely focussed on doing a great job. In the last book I read she was living on the beach. Surfing, walking her dog and working the midnight shift. In this story her dog has passed and she is living in a condo. But still working nights. Two stories in this book. One about a pair of rapists - ‘The Midnight Men’ and the other about the murder of an ex gang member. Set in Covid times so Ballard wearing her mask and dragging Harry off to get his jab. Thankful that I still have more Connelly’s to read👍

The pandemic is in full swing in Los Angeles and much of the force is burned out. But LAPD Detective Renée Ballard is not letting herself be one of those officers. In fact, she's picking up the slack of her fellow coworkers. Ballard is working a rapist case deemed the "Midnight Men," whose lead seems like she could care less about the case or the female victims. And New Year's brings Ballard the shooting of a former gang member. While she should pass the murder on to homicide, Ballard tries to work it as long as possible when she realizes the shooting is linked to a cold case of Harry Bosch's. As Bosch and Ballard team up again, they start to realize where their cases intersect. And as they do, they come on the radar of a killer who would much prefer to stay hidden. "She knew this could be the solve she needed to save herself." Harry Bosch will forever be my one true love. I love him dearly and always will. Ballard is definitely growing on me, and I really respected her in this book. This is a really timely read, as Connelly does not shy away from the pandemic, riots, anger toward the police, and police apathy and burnout. As always, we get his superb knowledge of police procedures, excellent research, and two wonderful investigators in Bosch and Ballard. I've never watched the Bosch show, but I feel like I can picture Bosch and Ballard so clearly due to Connelly's wonderful writing and world building. THE DARK HOURS finds Ballard in a tough place. She may love doing the actual police work, but she does have growing disillusion with her job, department, and the people. But, as she says, Bosch is her true constant. (I feel you, Renee, he's mine too!) She's going through a lot and always fighting an uphill battle against the jerks who seem against her at every turn. But Ballard is tough--much like a certain Harry Bosch--and watching the two of them solve cases is pure joy. Both cases presented in HOURS are complex and interesting, especially the New Year's shooting of Ballard's that links to Bosch's cold case. The two zig and zag around L.A., making connections and generally keeping us on our toes. It's wonderful having their two minds together. Overall, this is another great mystery, featuring two excellent characters, and since the ending leaves us hanging a bit, I look forward to another book. 4+ stars.
