DNF I’m always interested in an author’s inspiration for a novel. This one is based on a true story of how a young black prostitute was sexually abused by police officers . This is a debut novel written by a seventeen year old girl and there’s a lot to praise here , but reading about the abuse was just too much for me so I’m giving up at a third of the way through . Please read the other reviews because it’s an important story. I’m not going to rate it since I didn’t finish . I received a copy of this book from Knopf through Edelweiss.

based on a true case involving the oakland police force , nightcrawling is a searing debut novel which explores the dark underbelly of a city and justice system rife with exploitation, corruption, poverty, and structural abuses of power which have been allowed to fester for years. albeit difficult to read at times, the novel’s darkness is softened by its lyrical prose, which becomes even more impressive once you realise that the author was only 17 when it was written. the book's protagonist kiara is a force of a character, serving as a raw reflection of the violence enacted upon black women and girls, but also a celebration of their strength and courage. she’s one of those protagonists that you will continue to think about even after you’ve closed the book.

“A NEW YORK TIMES WRITER TO WATCH - A dazzling novel about a young Black woman who walks the streets of Oakland and stumbles headlong into the failure of its justice system--the debut of a blazingly original voice that "bursts at the seams of every page and swallows you whole" (Tommy Orange, best-selling author of There There).” Did you know Leila Mottley wrote Nightcrawling when she was seventeen years old? In this powerful tribute to her city and inspired by true events involving corruption, Nightcrawling is the story of teenager, Kiara Johnson. Her father has passed away, her mother is in a halfway house, and her brother, who promised to protect her, is pursuing his music dreams; this leaves Kiara alone with rent coming due. Finding a job at seventeen is not easy. Kiara lands in a very dark place trying to survive. Not only is she taking care of herself, but she’s also caring for an often alone, too, nine-year-old Trevor. Nightcrawling is penned flawlessly with emotion in its every precise word. In the author’s note, Leila Mottley shares that while Kiara is fictional, the true story is not, and in turn, it’s not just the story of one young girl exploited, but many, many times over. An urgent story addressing the adultification of Black girls and the failures of the justice system. Let us listen to this powerful voice and be inspired for what is next. I received a gifted copy. Many of my reviews can also be found on my blog: www.jennifertarheelreader.com and instagram: www.instagram.com/tarheelreader

DNF on page 100. The abuse is just too hard to read right now. I took a long break from reading it, but still can’t digest it. It is amazing that this was written by a seventeen-year-old. I would definitely try something else by the author. There are several other positive reviews, so be sure to give those a read before being swayed by my thoughts. Thank you to Penguin Random House Canada for providing an arc via Netgalley.

I have to say that I’m very thankful for Ophra’s Book Club. Because of this club, I have read some terrific books such as A Fine Balance (my very favourite book of all times), The Pillars of the Earth, I Know This Much is True, House of Sand and Fog, Fall On Your Knees, An American Marriage, The Invention of Wings (just to name a few). There was a time that I truly believed that I couldn’t go wrong with her choices. But unfortunately some did not impress me. Some I couldn’t even finish. This one is one that I almost quit reading. I do (must) give a credit to the author, after all she was only 17 when she started writing this book. My main problem was the lack of passion (or emotion). I thought that for a story being told in first person was too dry. I didn’t feel a thing. Not even anger (where I should have). Also, I thought that the writing style, although not bad, was not very consistent (I’m not sure who to blame, the author or editor). The storyline is sad, no doubt about it. Some readers found it disturbing or depressing, but because I was not emotionally involved, I did not feel it. It does not matter to me if this is a fiction, a true story or based on a true story. I needed it to be told with the heart. I needed to feel that heartbeat. I needed to feel that there was some authenticity. To give you an idea of what I’m talking about, I once knew this singer who had a terrific voice, but unfortunately, instead of singing with his heart, he would sing with his brain, worrying about being perfect and trying to impress the public with his high notes. If I had felt at least engaged, I would have given this book a higher rating. I’m quite sure that this author will have a terrific success in her career, and I’m truly looking forward to reading her next work, just to witness her growth.

3.5 Longlisted for the 2022 Booker Prize Longlisted for Center for Fiction First Novel Prize "In 2016 in the Bay area, a case broke where a young girl was sexually exploited by many Bay area officers… I was wondering about this girl and this particular iteration of police violence that I think a lot of us don't talk about. " Leila Mottley to Trevor Noah on the Dailey show Nightcrawling, Leila Mottley's much-lauded debut novel, has earned her the reputation of "wonder kid." Written when Mottley graduated high school at 17, Nightcrawling has been a New York Times bestseller, selected by Ophrah Winfrey's Book Club, and longlisted for prestigious literary prizes. After finishing the novel, I found myself intrigued by three stories: the author's tale, the novel itself, and the 2016 case that inspired the book. The Author: Who is Leila Mottley? Leila Mottley was born in 2002 and, at 20, is considered a rising star on the literary scene. She grew up in Oakland and is the youngest of three children of a biracial couple Ann Bauer, the Director of a local pre-school, and Norris Mottley, a fundraising consultant, and playwright. Leila learned her love of writing from her father and began writing poetry at an early age. Her interest in the writing led Leila to enroll at Oakland School for the Arts, a 6-12 charter school emphasizing arts education. Here Leila's poetic talents were recognized by her teachers, who encouraged her to apply to the competition for the poet laureate of the city of Oakland, a title she won in 2018. As a result, Leila began to give poetry readings and participate in poetry slams throughout the city. When Leila was fourteen, in 2016, the story of the teenage sex worker exploited by the local police broke in the news. The story moved her, and she followed it with great interest. Then, in her senior year, Leila began to write a novel about a young black woman who became trapped in this situation. When Leila entered Smith College in the fall of 2019, she showed the story to her creative writing instructor, Ruth Ozeki. She recognized the book's potential and referred Leila to her literary agent. After a bidding war, the novel was picked up by Knopf publishing. The Novel: Nightcrawling Nightcrawling is the story of Kiara Johnson, a 17-year-old African- American Oakland teenager whose options have run out. Both of her parents are out of the picture. Her father, a former Black Panther, died of prostrate cancer upon release from prison. Her mother is in a halfway house for drowning her infant daughter. Oakland is gentrifying, and the rent on the apartment Kiara shares with her older brother has just been doubled. To make matters worse, her brother has decided to pursue a career as a rap star and refuses to work. In addition, Kiara cares for and provides a semblance of stability for her next-door neighbor Trevor, the 9-year-old son of an unreliable drug addict. As Kiara is a high school dropout, she has difficulty finding work and decides to turn a few tricks to make rent and food for the month. Unfortunately, Kiara is caught by two unscrupulous cops who threaten her with arrest unless she provides sex at police parties. She complies, and the abuse is brutal. Then, one of the officers involved commits suicide and names her in a tell-all suicide note. Internal affairs get involved, and Kiara's life spirals further out of control as she becomes the key witness in a massive police scandal. When Nightcrawling was longlisted for the Booker, I decided to read it or rather listen to it on audible. I was interested in finding out what had inspired a group of critics to select the work of a 17- year- old for such a prestigious award. I finished the book two days ago, and I think that what makes the book work or what made it work for me was the authenticity of the protagonist's voice. What Leila Mottley understands is what it is like to be an adolescent. This book could have easily become a work of sordid sensationalism, but it doesn't. Sad, abusive scenes are followed by segments demonstrating friendship and resilience. There are happy and tender moments with the nine-year-old Trevor and with her best friend. I didn't feel that Nightcrawling was a great work of literary fiction. It doesn't compare to a book like Shuggie Bain, which won the Booker two years ago. However, it is quite an accomplishment for a 17-year-old, and I look forward to reading her future work. The Case that Inspired the Novel or Truth is Stranger than Fiction (Forgive the Cliché) When I finished the novel, I googled the 2016 Oakland police scandal. I found the story of Celeste Guap ((pseudonym). Celeste's family is originally from Nicaragua. Her mother worked as a police dispatcher for the Oakland Police, earning over $100,000. Celeste's mother was involved with a police officer who was like a father to Celeste. Unfortunately, he was killed in the line of duty when she was 12. After his death, she began to occasionally exchange sex for money. In a newspaper interview, Celeste said that she did it because it was "all around her." She made connections via social media and slept with three police officers as a minor. Celeste believes that none of what happened to her would have occurred if her mother's boyfriend had been alive. She claims he would never have allowed it. However, she was coerced into providing sex to multiple partners at police parties. Unbeknown to her mother, several of the officers involved were her " friends." When one of the officers committed suicide and named her in his confession. Like her fictional counterpart, Celeste became the center of a police scandal. A few officers lost their jobs, and others just received reprimands. Celeste sued the Department and received a million dollars in compensation with no liability. She is now 23, lives with her two-year-old son, and works as a Sex Workers' Rights Activist. On her Facebook page, Celeste was asked about the book Nightcrawling. She said, "It's pure fiction." NPR News Account: https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-w...

Rating: ⭐⭐⭐ Genre: Literary Fiction Kiara is a seventeen-year-old girl living with her brother Marcus in an apartment in Oakland, California. All Marcus is thinking about is launching his music career, leaving all the hard work of money earning to Kiara. The girl has to do something so they won’t be evicted from their apartment. Being a high school dropout with no resume makes it even more difficult for her to get a job. One night, something happens to Kiara, which leads her to become a prostitute as a last resort. We follow her story, her struggle, and all the hardships this black girl endures. This is a good debut novel for a 19-year-old author (her age when she wrote it). I think Leila Mottley will have a strong career if she continues writing on hard-hitting subjects like this. Being picked by Oprah's book club is a big recognition in itself. Then the book successfully made it to the longlist for the Booker Prize. So there is a lot going on for this author. The story is gripping and deals with dark subjects. The characters are quite strong too. The writing was sometimes poetic and, at other times, it felt too descriptive and different. I am not sure how to explain it, but it is apparent that the author has written this at different stages of her life. There is a polarity between the chapters when it comes to the writing. At times, this novel might disturb you because what you are reading about are things that actually happen in our world. So beware of the trigger warnings because they are many.

3.5 As many others had stated before me, this is an impressive debut novel, written by a teenager no less, when she was seventeen-eighteen. The fact that it is based on a real life case makes this novel more powerful. Of course, it's horrific that the police, who are supposed to protect and respect the law, disregard it, not to mention the ick and moral considerations - using a seventeen-year-old for sex parties. The narrator of this novel is seventeen year old, Kiara Johnson, who had been dealt bad cards in life - her father passed away, her mother is in jail, and her guardian, her older brother is a lost, head-in-the-sky dreamer, who can't help to pay the rent. The rent is put up yet again, there are no jobs to come by, so what's one to do? Start night crawling. I appreciate Mottley's intentions and writing, to be honest, I wasn't quite as affected by the novel as I should have been. Something was missing. Grittiness (is that a word?)? Throughout the novel, I felt distanced from what was happening to the characters - I could always sense the author's hand and viewpoints when writing beautiful, impressive sentences, which I didn't quite believe as they were supposed to come from a teen who hadn't finished high school. While I'm not one to care about endings, I don't expect books to have nicely wrapped endings, in this case, the last part of the novel and the ending felt rushed, unbaked and left me unsatisfied. Regardless of the fact that I wanted a bit more from this novel, Mottley showcased her talent in this novel, so I'm looking forward to reading more from her.

Oof this book is difficult to read in the sense that it deals with some darker topics but man is it gripping. This book is a slow burn book with a slight mystery to it, but the mystery is really not the focus of the book. It is really about following Kiara day to day, seeing what she is forced to do in order to survive and how she is constantly used, abused, and exploited. There are so many reveals and twists that will break your heart. Watch me discuss it more in my June wrap up: https://youtu.be/7_AW_bJl1LU

4.5* stars, but I rounded this one up to 5 because I HIGHLY recommend! My God this book was engrossing. I couldn't put it down. This story felt so authentically captured. It never felt far-fetched, hyperbolic, or ingenuine. You can tell that Leila Mottley is telling this story having grown up in Oakland and seeing this life in real time. Her writing is excellent overall. I only took off half of a star because I personally wasn't looooving that sometimes her writing style sounds like spoken word poetry to me hahahah. A lot of times it did work for me, but sometimes it grated on me a little.

Letting the streets have you is like planning your own funeral. I wanted the streetlight brights, the money in the morning, not the back alleys. Not the sirens. But, here we are. Streets always find you in the daylight, when you least expect them to. Night crawling up to me when the sun’s out. Nightcrawling is fine: Teenaged debut novelist Lelia Mottley stuffed this gritty urban tale with just about every inner city social issue imaginable, and with the writing style dialled up to eleven, there are many fine lines, many fine scenes, but also an unrestrained exuberance that made me a bit impatient. Nightcrawling has been longlisted for the 2022 Man Booker Prize — meaning people whose opinion counts more than mine does found this novel to be among the best released in English, worldwide, this year — but it didn’t really engage me on a literary level. The nomination may have led me to expect more from this novel, and I have to admit that the writing does not betray the author’s young age, but overall, this was just fine. Slight spoilers (not much beyond the publisher’s blurb) from here. (Note: I read an ARC through NetGalley and passages quoted may not be in their final forms.) There’s not a thing Daddy could’ve done that would’ve made me hate him. When he died, I thought maybe it was a consequence of not resenting him more, not playing into karma like Marcus had so the world wouldn’t have had to kill him to keep the good-evil balance in check. That was before I learned that life won’t give you reasons for none of it, that sometimes fathers disappear and little girls don’t make it to another birthday and mothers forget to be mothers. Nearly eighteen-year old Kiara and her older brother, Marcus, live alone in a seedy East Oakland apartment complex — their father is dead and their mother is in prison — and when their rent is doubled, Kiara doesn’t know what to do: She is about to lose the few under-the-table shifts she works at a liquor store and Marcus is refusing to get a job beyond recording the rap album that he’s convinced is their ticket out. When Kiara gets drunk and a man mistakes her for a sex worker, Kiara accepts as inevitable that she’s going to need to start walking the streets to keep her brother and herself safe. And when the mentally unstable, drug-addicted woman downstairs abandons the ten-year-old son that Kiara has always felt affection and responsibility towards, the stakes are raised even higher. I did appreciate the agency that Mottley gave to Kiara in this decision (beyond that first encounter) — she never feels sorry for herself or loses respect for herself for doing what she feels she has to do for her family — but Kiara loses that agency when she is picked up by the police and forced to work private parties for them, for which she isn’t even always paid. (The police angle is based on actual events and it was this news story that first prompted Mottley to write Nightcrawling.) How Kiara deals with this exploitation, and her efforts to support her brother and the boy from downstairs, are the bulk of the plot. “We still family, Ki.” And I think he means it, beyond words, beyond this moment, beyond the things our parents did to leave us broken. I nod and, for the first time, I think about what I did, about the panic that sets in when anyone else touches me the way Marcus just did, how many guns have been pressed to my skull, fingers scraping my skin, fists in my hair. In this room, with these golden boys, all the things I’ve done feel vulgar, devastating, like I do not deserve to be loved good again. There are plenty of shocking events in Nightcrawling — the sex work, drug abuse and trafficking, police brutality, suicide, guns, child neglect, roadblocks to justice for the powerless — and colourful details from the Black commmunity — the Black Panthers, basketball, rap, braids — but shocking events and colourful details, on their own, don’t add up to a deep dive into a community to me; this all felt so surface, even with the exuberant sentences. Mottley obviously has big ideas: in the afterword, she writes, “Like many black girls, I was often told growing up to tend to and shield my brother, my dad, the black men around me: their safety, their bodies, their dreams. In this, I learned that my own safety, body, and dreams were secondary, that there was no one and nothing that could or would protect me.” And I found that very provocative — not something I had heard before — and while I can see that this is an idea that Mottley was exploring through Kiara’s story, I would love a deeper, while more subtle, literary exploration. Again: More important voices than mine have singled Nightcrawling out for praise; this is naught but my small contribution to the conversation.

Feces, dung, poop, excrement, egesta, shit, no matter how it is stated, the courteous thing to do is to pick up the doo-doo. At the Regal-Hi, located in a project of Oakland this common courtesy is not extended. Thus, this novel the debut from Leila Mottley lets you know from the start that this is not going to be a Cinderella story. The world in which the characters inhabit this story is a cold one, filled with woe and pain. The glimmers of hope are few and far between found in places like a funeral, in which the protagonist, Kiara and her friend Ale go to get their grub on or the basketball court where Trevor hustles a few dollars off of kids. Almost everyone in this world is trying to exploit their neighbor and more often than not, Kiara is the one whose pound of flesh they are taking. With a jailed mother, a deceased father and a delusional brother, Kiara has been on the precipice for a while. Too young to be an exotic dancer and not interested in earning nickels on the dollar as a petty drug dealer or fast food worker, her options are limited. School, never much an option for furthering her plans is completely off the table as she has dropped out. She is faced with all of this turmoil and to top it off rent is about to double due to gentrification. With dwindling funds, she decides the only acceptable solution is to ply her trade in the oldest profession. While plying her trade, Kiara is befriended by a transgender prostitute by the name of Camila. Camila acts as a bit of an older sister to Kiara, giving her tips on how to dress, present herself and where best to make her living. Alas, Camila is not just doing this out of the kindness of her heart. By acting as a conduit, she is trying to persuade Kiara to join with her pimp. After a raucous party, Kiara is forced into the arms of an adversary much more vicious than any pimp: the Oakland Police Department. Under the guise of protection and having limited recourse, Kiara is forced; essentially being a sex slave to a number of Oakland’s finest. Not only do they have her profession to blackmail her but her brother, Marcus has been picked up for intent to distribute drugs on a trumped up charge. On the throes of degradation she is passed along like the proverbial dobbie where she encounters one particular harrowing scene, in which a cop is brandishing his firearm in a pseudo-sexual manner. She is so used to the dehumanizing behavior that when a cop gives her the girlfriend treatment she is more taken aback than the pump and dumps. During a police function, a detective described as wearing a “purple suit” tries to get some information from Kiara about the rumors of a police sex ring. Not trusting her, she is reluctant to part any information to the lady in the purple suit, Sandra. Sandra gives her card and tells her to call if she can be of assistance. Leveraging the situation with Marcus’s impending incarceration, Sandra coaxes Kiara by giving her the number of a good attorney, Marsha. Marsha takes the case pro-bono and seems to be the legal eagle that Kiara needs. She is meticulous in appearance and craft. She has a fearlessness that gives hope to Kiara. Despite her best efforts in coaching Kiara and doggedly going through the proper channels an indictment never came. Kiara is left further broken. Risking life and limb, a pariah as a snitch, she has been exploited further. Her shitty situation has somehow even gotten worse. Even with all of this turbulence, Kiara has somehow still found perspective. No doubt life is hard, hers especially so but she has continued to survive. She has formed a tightknit community with her best friend Alejandra who has become her partner and her next door neighbor Tyler whose home situation is even more fraught than her own. With a past that she would like to forget and a future that is at best cloudy, she must live in the present. This means she has to savor what she can and hang on to the ones she loves and those that reciprocate back. As a debut novel at the young age of 17, Leila Mottley has written a novel with a strong protagonist and weaker secondary characters. The laser focus on Kiara for the part is necessary, as it shows the exploitation and negligence of those surrounding her. Not only has the system failed her but the apparatus in place is used by the authorities to gain clout while pushing her down. Whether it is the detective using Kiara to advance her career in the police department, her lawyer gaining publicity for her firm during the trial or the police blackmailing her, no one in positions of power comes out looking good. This is a dog-eat-dog world in which Kiara is merely a pawn.

Oddly, this felt like a very long 288 pages for a book where quite a lot happens. It did grab me initially with its graphic, gritty opening. The authorial voice also worked for me - - managing to be both poetic and street-wise. But for all the unrelenting misery that was the plot, I didn't feel much. There was one scene toward the end that should have been completely heart rending, and I just felt nothing. I'm not sure if I just became inured to the horrors because there were so many of them, or if it was a problem with the character development. Personally, I lean toward the latter. On some level, none of the characters felt fully realized to me. Maybe that's because it was written strictly from the narrator's point of view, but I'm not sure that should matter? At any rate, I was bored after the first third and had to push myself through. I know I was skimming by the end, because I had to go back and re-read certain sections that were referenced later on. Apparently, this author is quite young, and I was impressed by the expressiveness of her writing, but unfortunately the storytelling didn't really work for me.
CW: police violence, statutory rape, death of a loved one, self harm, drowning

Life is hard for 17-year-old Kiara Johnson. She lives in a studio apartment with her older brother Marcus and they can't afford to pay the rent. Neither of them are employed - Kiara left school early and no supermarket or restaurant is willing to give her a start, while Marcus is focusing his efforts on a rap career. No parents are on the scene - their father died years ago and their mother is in a halfway house after committing an unforgivable act. And if that wasn't enough, Kiara has taken on the responsibility of looking after Trevor, a young neighbour whose mother is a crack addict. Kiara visits a strip club one evening to see if a friend who works in the bar can get her hired. There is no luck on that front but she drowns her sorrows in some free drinks. Feeling buzzed, she walks outside where a man takes advantage and has sex with her. He pays her $200 and she can't believe how easy it is. Suddenly she has a solution to her money worries. She decides to try this line of work full time, but she has no idea of the kind of trouble she's getting herself into. For a first novel from a 20-year-old writer, I have to say that Nightcrawling is a pretty impressive debut. Leila Mottley grew up in Oakland where the story is based, and she displays a keen eye for documenting the city's problems. Poverty and police corruption are two of the main issues that are addressed, and they are so oppressive that it feels like there is no hope for these characters. But Kiara is brave and resilient, the kind of girl that is easy to root for. The writing did get a little florid for my liking at times but I reminded myself that this is a young author still honing her craft. I'm glad that the Booker committee decided to longlist Nightcrawling as this kind of talent deserves a leg-up. Her best work may still lie ahead of her - I predict a bright future for Mottley.
I’ll write a review at some point but I know it won’t do this book justice. Highly recommend.
2022 Best Books of the Year [#03 of 11]

** spoiler alert ** This is really bad guys, I’m sorry. There’s a few reasons I dnf’d it at 60 pages: there are really important plot beats that are glazed over, unconvincingly, while paragraphs talking about what every single space she enters looks like take up more word count, just for starters. She’s having a drink then she’s having some pretty iffy sex and gets handed some bills, no idea how she feels about that really, and then suddenly right after meets a hooker with a heart of gold who just knows she’s going go be a sex worker too, but she was just walking home, no? And then sets up a friend to watch out for her with her first appointment and you have no idea what happens in that car, pretty much. Her physicality is not convincing at all, and it is again, really important just in so far as to be able to know what the heck is actually happening in the scene, which should have a lot of gravity, but doesn’t. Or even how she feels about it. Or if she’s on the pill. Or if they even had sex in the car. Like what the heck is going on. Aforementioned friend wants to “take care of her” and she’s all, all I got is blood, my good for nothing brother and all so no, and then when he leaves she’s all like hope my brother will be “my shadow”. It’s really unconvincing and melodramatic, has terrible, terrible similes All. The. Time. A weird always-on prose work that just smooths out absolutely everything happening, even when it’s better prose than you’d expect. It robs its own style of any punch. The character dynamics and issues are convincing, but foregrounded in a way that feels really awkward for people living in the area to talk about, fairly often. Then it’s granular about the innocuous, making it really, really boring. Until something interesting happens, only to be treated like it’s less than the description of her brother in a booth trying to rhyme. It’s not good. I’d recommend trying it on audio, it has to be better than on the page, If it’s got a good narrator.

it's very difficult for me to describe why this book lost a star. This book is missing a punch that it so deeply needs and I believe that is because of the writing. The book towards the middle seems to go from event to event without any real context to ground the scene. We get so much great detail in the beginning which makes it feel like we are setting up one type of story but it seems like that gets abandoned half way through for a lot of introspection and to hurry the book along. Things are happening to our protagonist but we are not fully feeling the impact (although I believe that could be intentional in order to convey its message) but what that does is makes you feel left out of the story. With that all being said this was written by a teenager and is such a remarkable feat and this is overall a very good story. but I can't help but feel like someone 10 years older than author should have written this book. You feel so disconnected from the main character at so many times. the "true crime" element falls short and is the worst plot in this because we are never truly faced with the way our protagonist is hurt outside of the obvious. our protagonist never feels vulnerable because the scenes where she is being abused are not written to the best of their abilities.

From reading the blurb, I thought I was going into a fast-paced page turner with an explosive plot line and unforgettable characters. But nope, no explosions here. Inspired by real events, this is the story of a Black teenage girl sexual assaulted by police officers. I'm so disappointed in this book. It's been a real flop for me. I've eaten pancakes with more dimensions than the characters here. Entirely flat. No personality, no development. All these pages read, and I don't know these characters. What there is of a plot is slow. Everything happens in two pages, then two hundred with nothing and repeat. The pacing is massively off. Plus, so much happens off page and is only referred to in a past tense that you can't see what's happening in real time or form any feelings on it. I do understand that the author may want to protect the reader, but this is a book about sexual assault and this level of protection resulted in me not connecting at all. This book clearly wants to tackle some big issues, but you've got to come out from behind the sofa to do that, and for me, the author didn't do that. Great idea but an emotionless execution. Two stars.

Wow!! This book!! The writing was so vivid that I felt like I was there up close watching it happen. It’s fiction based on a real investigation of a police ring in Oakland, CA that exploited underage sexworkers. It was told from the POV of Kia a 17 year old girl who by circumstance was forced to sell herself to make money. It is just so well written I eagerly await more writing from Leila Mottley.

As soon as I found out how old this author was when she commenced writing this book I was astounded, her maturity beyond her years to tackle such a delicate and difficult subject matter made this book even more outstanding. I wish Leila all the success in the world for her bravery in exposing the unspoken crimes that go unpunished towards the often forgotten and misrepresented sector of society. Her voice is an important addition to the contemporary world of fiction. A star is born.

** spoiler alert ** P.S.: note how in the Oscar award candidate film “American Fiction”, the fictional book “WE’S LIVES IN DA GHETTO” about black people has a made-up cover that looks very similar to the cover of this book… same exact colors, similar effect… maybe someone thought about the link here, and not in a positive way. ——- Kiara and her brother, Marcus, live in a squalid Oakland apartment complex. Both have dropped out of high school. Marcus clings to his dream of rap stardom while being unemployed, Kiara looks for work to pay their rent (in a job hunt that is not nearly as determined as it could be, but we can discuss that) and to keep the little boy next door, abandoned by his mother, safe and fed, which is a subplot that gives her an additional 1,000 points in moral superiority. One night, Kiara sells her body "without realizing what is happening" because she is very drunk. By the way, not even "being drunk" was her fault, because an older woman gave her several cocktails, and she drank them all, because she is 17 and that's what 17-year-old kids do when you give them drinks, they go all the way and it's not their fault. Not in the least. Her world breaks open even further when her name surfaces in an investigation that exposes her as a key witness in a scandal within the Oakland Police Department. In short, the author picked up a story from the news and, based on that story, she wrote the imaginary story of a prostitute, a victim of abuse. As many readers and critics have said, the writing is really impressive for the author’s age (19). Leila Mottley writes with the lyricism of an angel, sometimes excessive, sure, but I cannot imagine how high she can take her craft if she keeps working on it in the coming decades. Mottley went to an arts school where she had the chance to write creatively for at least 3 hours each day. That opportunity (and privilege) + her amazing skills generated an incredible voice. She writes with the heart and the instinct of an accomplished poet. The final paragraphs of every chapter are such diamonds. And I LOVED the ending. However, wonderful and lyrical writing, in itself, is not enough to make a book good. As you could understand from the way I summarized the plot, I didn't like the content of this novel. Having read a few interviews with the author, and having watched her videos, this seems to me the fantasy of a smart, well-off girl based on the elements of a news story. It doesn't sound like she has enough real-life knowledge and experience to write a book like this and make it sound real. A reviewer wrote: " I worked with so many homeless, poor, drug addicted, struggling women of color in my life and I never met anyone as clueless as the character the author created. The falseness began to grate on me, and as one reviewer put it, it exploits and takes away from the truth so many women live." Another reviewer wrote: "I was also baffled that despite growing up very poor Kiara didn't know how to access food banks and other emergency services" . It's not hard to guess why the author did not include food stamps and any other social services in Kiara's life: it would have ruined her "living in poverty" fantasy. It wouldn't have allowed her line about how Kiara was "counting the crackers", and it would have made it clearer that Kiara didn't go into prostitution for "survival". There are many social services for low- or no-income families in the US, especially in California, but they wouldn’t have made the victim narrative as satisfying to the author. Kiara doesn't even have a smartphone, that she could and should use to find a job. More than 80% of Americans living below the poverty line own a smartphone, and I imagine this percentage grows to 120% in Oakland (I live in L.A. and I’m not kidding, the majority of the homeless who live around my house have a smartphone). But again, that would not sit well with the author’s SJW vision. Of course, an author CAN create stories and characters that do not reflect her own ideas. But Mottley was raised in far-left Oakland, and she attended a school where leftist propaganda was served daily, even more than in the other schools in California. So her choice to tell this story, in this way, is not a coincidence. She is also an “abolish the police” campaigner, and that clearly transpires from her pages. That should not surprise anyone. Just like, in the eyes of some, a minority of perverted priests make the entire Church a criminal and rotten organization, and every priest in the world an abuser, in this hagiography every cop is a mean, depraved, abusing bastard (“I’m scared of being saved”, complains Ki in her mind when the police catch her selling sex). The concept of "abolishing the police" might be very satisfying from the emotional standpoint, especially if you've been fed a certain narrative by your teachers, but it's also nonsense. So many African Americans are, in fact, advocating for more funding to the police, in the interest and benefit of black communities. Since when does a minority of corrupt cops - no matter how unethical they are - mean that you have to burn down the entire building? In any case, I’m not saying the protagonist is painted as a saint. I’m saying that her idealized poverty and personality give her the moral high ground every time. I found it impossible to buy this as a real-life story, because the fictional reality is too heavily massaged by the author's ideology. The problem is that, in the novel, all the “greys” of real life are noticeably missing. Which, not coincidentally, is how every political narrative works: strip reality of nuance, and you’ll have “good guys” vs. “bad guys”. A reality that is very easy to digest. So you can go straight to the feelings, the "candy", instead of doing the boring work of researching deeply and fully engaging your mind. Now, let’s get to the worst thing about this book: p.235: "Why you start fucking with the cops, especially after...[...]?" "I don't know, I didn't really have no choice. I just kind of ended up in it and then there wasn't no way out, you know?" No choice? This is the answer given by the protagonist to her mother. Everything suggests that the author likes this answer: Ki is the main character of her first big novel. You really want to tell me that Ki has “a life of her own”, and that the police-hating author is this objective, detached scientist about it? Consciously or unconsciously, she is not. This approach is the same that led the director / maker of the movie "Fruitvale" (a film based on another Oakland-based episode, very similar in tone to this book because it sanctifies a petty criminal, in order to elicit a strong emotional response) to make his protagonist save a dog, only to see it run over shortly thereafter, as a plot device intended to manipulate the emotions of the audience. When confronted about it, the director admitted that he made that episode up. If we didn’t live in a time when virtue-signaling has been elevated to the level of an Olympic discipline, I wouldn’t feel as strongly about this way to look at reality, but that's the world we live in today — and Ki, the prostitute, wins the gold medal. It’s a worldview that, moving from an injustice, can easily bring to another injustice: a heightened hostility towards an entire category of people (example: police) including the good and very good ones, who do not deserve that hostility. Someone who works with the LAPD told me that the “defund the police” campaigns have been deleterious to the LAPD, not because the politicians decided to defund the LAPD (they didn't do anything), but because the morale of the good cops is at a historic low, with a big chunk of the public drinking the media narrative that all cops are racist and abusive. For a certain modern ideology (that's largely coming out of California) the finger of blame is always pointed OUT. Never towards yourself, where it should be, for any human being to experience any real growth, including yourself, including myself. Change must start from myself. This is ancient wisdom, but it’s almost been lost. "Dear sir, I am!", wrote G.K. Chesterton to a newspaper, in answer to the question: "What's wrong with the world?”. How many would have that same wisdom and courage, today? It’s so crucial and urgent to bring the role of black women to the forefront, after the endless history of abuse and injustice (and of neglect) that they have suffered. I feel like we shouldn't even say this, as obvious of a statement this is. But this book has little to do with that, and a lot to do with the far-left woke ideology that is ruining our kids. (I’m not even considering the possibility that Mottley might have written this just to ride the current zeitgeist, because that would make her one of the most dishonest people alive). If you think these comments are excessive, ask yourself this: do you think that, when it comes to voting, the people with these fantasies in their heads are able to differentiate between lazy fantasy and complex reality? Do you think they start to reason and discern, all of a sudden? Right. That’s why she wants to abolish the police. The end is, again, beautifully written, but it leaves things open. The $1 million payout that the real-life Ki received as a result of the investigation is, obviously, not mentioned.

Phew. Finally, I can let out the breath I’ve been holding since I started reading this nightmare. Mottley started writing this book when she was 17, and she is truly a woman wise beyond her years. We follow Kiara, a young girl struggling to make rent. When she stumbles upon the sad, unfortunate fact that she can trade her body for cash, she lands herself in a ring of sorts involving members of the Oakland Police Department. Parts of the book were a bit slow for me, but there were other times where I was racing through the pages and hoping that at some point, I would find Kiara free. Based on a true story that broke out in 2016, Nightcrawling exposes sexual exploitation and trafficking in a way that I’m not confident has been done before. While I wish it stayed a bit more accurate to the real events, I would recommend this read—just know there are differences and don’t neglect researching the case.

This is a novel to look forward to. Incredible writing for a debut. Those poetic lines sprinkled through the prose made this book shine even though the story is super heartbreaking. Leila Mottley is a new voice that I’m excited to follow. Can’t wait to see what she writes next because there’s no denying the talent that she has.

3.5 Longlisted Booker Prize 2022 This debut novel (written when she was just 17-19) by Leila Mottley sears with its ferocious intensity and anger. It burns and seathes with the injustice for how too many black women are mistreated in the USA. In this respect it's an important book and an unsettling read. Nightcrawling tells the story in first person of Kiara Johnson, a 17 year-old young black woman struggling to keep her life together on the streets of Oakland. Her father has died and her mother is in detention. Kiara's life is a daily struggle to make ends meet, trying to pay the rent and put food on the table for both herself and her older brother, Marcus. Marcus has checked out somewhat on his responsibilities pursuing a dream of making it big as a rapper. Kiara also finds herself the defacto carer for a young boy, Trevor, who has been essentially abandoned by his mother . This relationship between Kiara and Trevor is a highlight and the loving humanity of it provides some hope in this otherwise gritty and dark work. Kiara finds herself resorting to prostitution to make the long over-due rent payments. She ends up exploited and abused by a group of police officers and much of the novel concerns the implications of this. The description of this abuse and its impact on Kiara is brutal and crushing. There are though moments of tenderness, including in her relationship with close friend Ale. This account of police abuse and corruption is grounded in events surrounding the Oakland Police Department in 2015 involving police participation in the sexual exploitation of a young woman and the cover-ups surrounding this. The voice in this work is powerful, a scream at the socio-economic reality in which such abuse lives and thrives. "Mama hooks her fingers in my mouth and spreads my jaw open like a door with hniges, until I make an oval with my lips, keeping her hands on my cheeks and telling me to scream. The screech comes out in bursts, spasms of sound morphing their way from an eruption of rage to an infant's cries, moans and whines and all the in-betweens of woman and child. The sky takes each flurry and sends it right back with just a hint of music lingering in the echo, a belt from some invisible trombone, the lowest note on an organ drawn out. Sound after sound flooding from my body like war-zone fire on a cold day. Here you get a sense of the poetic sensibility threaded through this scream of a work. So why the 3.5; partly because as I read this book I had a strong sense of still developing potential, not yet quite fully aware of the imagery, voice and strcutures she's working with. The writing is uneven, with paragraph after paragraph trying to wring out too much affect, at least for me. Mottley is an emerging author that I'm very much looking forward to seeing what she does with future books.

OMG this book.... Be warned, this is not a happily ever after story, this is not a happy ending story, there is very little happiness between these covers. It is raw and real in a way that makes my skin crawl. After their father's death and their mother being committed 15 year old Kiara and her 18 year old brother Marcus were on their own. Two years later and they have both had to drop out of school, but working together they've managed to scrape by so far. When Marcus quits his job to pursue fame as a rapper things begin to crumble. Rent has increased, there is a 9 year old boy in their complex who's mother abandoned him and with no help from Marcus, Kiara desperately seeks work to keep them from getting evicted. While searching and being turned down for every job she asks about, Kiara ends up at a strip club that would love to hire her but not until she turns 18 (which doesn't help at all right now). Unable to help, a kind bartender offers her free drinks so she stays to have a few. Before long she is drunk and being led away by a strange man who has his way with her on the roof, hands her $500 and leaves. Prostitution becomes the job Kiara needed, and she was able to make it work for awhile, (it's just skin after all). It isn't too long until she is picked up by the police, but not arrested, instead taken to a party and used by half of the police force. They keep calling her back but start paying in "protection" instead of the cash she so desperately needed; she's too broke and scared to say no. Her world breaks open even further when her name surfaces in an investigation that exposes her as a key witness in a massive scandal within the Oakland Police Department. Forced to tell her story, exposing the police officers involved Kiara is eventually convinced by her attorney that speaking the truth will set her free and protect other young girls in the future. But, what will be the outcome when one young girl stands up against many men of power?

2022 Booker Prize Longlist Challenge NIGHTCRAWLING by Leila Mottley I rarely get emotional when reading novels. Movies and TV open the taps quite easily, but with books I tend to be quite tight lipped even when caught up in the emotional waves of a compelling novel. A LITTLE LIFE is one of my favourite novels and although I was moved and upset, my eyes remained dry. Leila Mottley’s NIGHTCRAWLING managed to break the seal, the anger and frustration overwhelming me. NIGHTCRAWLING is a remarkable work, one that is amazing not only because of who the author is but what she has managed to create, a novel that is expertly plotted, beautifully written and one that manages to expresses the deep anger of a generation of Black youth constantly victimized by the police and criminal justice systems and speaks to the specific experiences of Black and Brown women, whose vulnerability and experiences of state violence is often muted and not centred in the stories and accounts we do read about. In the mid 2010s, Bay Area police are accused of sexually exploiting an underage girl, causing uproar in the community. But while officialdom worry about the negative impact the disgusting acts toward the girl may impact police relations with Black communities, Mottley wondered about the experience of the young sex worker, her story, her struggles, and how she would have navigated the circumstances so beyond her control. So emerges Kiera, a fictionalized version of this girl, living in an Oakland that still has echoes of radical Black politics and culture but is being overrun by increased gentrification and housing costs designed to push out working class communities from their homes. Effectively orphaned, Kiera turns to sex work to survive and becomes entangled in a police ring that uses her and threatens her if she doesn’t cooperate. When the story of police abuse becomes public, Kiera becomes the centre of attention and doesn’t know how she will keep herself and the ones she loves safe. While NIGHTCRAWLING does not delve into experiments in form and language that often defines Booker-type books, the novel is perfectly plotted and written in a prose that is both gripping and beautiful, conveying Kiera’s circumstances and emotional tension in a way I found believable and maddening. Beyond that, what felt most impressive is how the novel manages to capture a rage and frustration of a generation of Black youth whose formative years have been marked by Black Lives Matter and the George Floyd killing. Although Mottley’s youth has left many in awe that she has managed to create such a formidable piece of literature, her youth I think also brings with it an experience and a voice that an older writer would not be able to capture. An extraordinary novel. A great audiobook. The book of the year for me so far.

Nightcrawling is a novel based on a 2015 court case in which the Oakland Police Department was accused of sexually exploiting a teenager and trying to cover it up. In the book Kiara, a 17-year-old high school dropout is desperately trying to keep herself and Trevor, the 9-year-old son of her crack-addicted neighbor from losing their flat. Feeling she has no other options; she turns to prostitution. The writing is what elevates this story to something special. The author has a gorgeous, lush style, which at times almost feels like poetry, and sometimes she even manages to create so much rhythm that you can hear the music it’s set to. She contrasts this beautiful writing with all the ugly things described. And yes, Nightcrawling isn’t perfect. Sometimes the writing became superfluous and I also would have liked to see more character development from the secondary characters. But read the scene where Kiara and Trevor gets separated and tell me that this is not one of the most heart-breaking scenes ever written.The 20-year-old author is the youngest ever to make it to the Booker longlist, and I can’t wait to see what she’ll be publishing next. I listened to the audio version, narrated by Joniece Abbott-Pratt, and if possible I recommend that you too listen to this as Joniece does an outstanding job in infusing every sentence with emotion.

Very, very tough read but an absolutely amazing book! The writing is so extremely well done and I cannot believe that the writer started writing this book when she was only 17!! This is one of those books that will change you as a person. Definitely heartbreaking and unforgettable. This book itself is fiction, but is inspired by true events; I feel sick knowing that things like this happen. I just cannot understand how!?! The story deals with some very difficult topics such as poverty, sex work, police brutality, sexual abuse, racial and gender inequities and so much more. The main character, Kia, is such a strong and determined person who still does not allow all of the injustices she faces cause her to give up or lose her ability to love. I have no idea how that would even be possible. You can't help but root for her even when you know the hand she was dealt in life leaves her so completely and utterly powerless. It really gives you an inside view of the day to day struggle to survive that results from poverty and how you really can't understand any decisions made until you are actually in that position and able to feel what they are feeling in that moment. I am so angry at both society and the justice system for letting things like this happen. It is really just so hard to comprehend. I 100% recommend this book, but please keep in mind that it deals with some very heavy but important topics. I think Leila did an amazing job and can't wait to see what else she comes out with; will definitely be following her future work. I received a copy of this book through Netgalley in exchange for an honest review.

Leila Mottley has taken a story that blazed on local news several years ago, and with an amazing flash of brilliance, turned it into this incredible novel. There are several layers of Oakland, but Mottley has Ki, her main character, doing what she can and using what she has to survive on the East side. As I live in Oakland, I feel it's important to read of the city through the eyes of Ms. Mottley and of Tommy Orange as well in order to fully realize this place. Astonishingly, Ms. Mottley has just had her 20th birthday, wrote this in her late teens. The debut of a truly original artist.

A disturbing but entirely relevant novel that is based on a real case of police corruption and exploitation. Nightcrawling examines the bleak truths of poverty, the disproportionate incarceration of black men in America, and the drug epidemic. Though harsh and candid, it is also a story of experiencing joy and love in times of hardship, and of finding the courage to stand up against abuse and intimidation, no matter the result. A powerful debut that packs a punch of truth and emotion.

Motley is definitely a gifted writer and I think she will go far as she progresses with her writing. That being said, I couldn’t connect with this through out the whole book. Some parts were great and absolutely heart wrenching and other times I was just bored. Definitely an important and real topic that should be discussed but I can imagine it to be triggering for some. Thank you to Netgalley for an advanced copy of this book!

I'm setting this aside for now. I'm struggling to connect with realist literature - just not a headspace I have open at the present time. I also struggle with writing that forces a style on characters that doesn't fit them. The protagonist is a seventeen-year-old high school dropout, and yet her interiority reads like an MFA graduate. Kiara Johnson is a 17-year old girl from Oakland whose father has died, whose mother is in jail and whose brother only cares about becoming a famous rapper. It falls on unemployed Kiara to pay the rent and take care of 10-year old Trevor. It doesn't come as a surprise then that she makes a wrong choice for which she pays dearly. It was refreshing to read something from the perspective of the poor Californian suburbs and very interesting to hear the voice of a new generation. For much of the book I thought the story was autobiographical, admittedly because the author is so young but also because it is quite straightforward and chronological. The fact that it's not and still felt realistic is a compliment.

Being an imaginative adolescent poet does not unfortunately give an author enough lived experience and control over language to leap into being a novelist. This book is overly ambitious and presents a fantasy in the guise of real life.it inadvertently exploits the actual people involved. And it's full of caricatures, not characters. And it fails the credibility test when Kia remarks that her lawyer's office design is "straight from Pinterest. " Really. This is an impoverished girl with no smart phone or device and she's talking about a middle class hobby site? And her lawyer is just like " most white women default to thinking they own every room they walk into." Really? And then later, this pro bono lawyer who is helping her is "Just another white woman who's never gonna understand d what I been through, who can't find anyone besides Harriet Tubman or Gloria Steinem to compare me to." So, Kia is a ghetto girl who knows who Gloria Steinem is, but doesn't know how to get food from any food banks, and takes up sex work without once mentioning birth control or a fear of sexually transmitted diseases. Did the author ( a college student now at the noted private school Smith) talk to any sex workers or genuinely poor people, because after 40 years of working with street people,I can tell you they have the survival skills to find food banks, soup kitchens, to get on medical assistance and get birth control. She makes her heroine both savant and stupid at the same time. I gave this 2 stars only because some of the prose was lyrical, as befits a poet, but this is a threadbare Booker choice nominee. In another 10 years out in the world, perhaps Mottley will acquire the depth to write of the serious issues she cares about.

Nightcrawling is a visceral, unflinching debut that refuses to look away from the intersections of systemic failure, survival and girlhood. at its center is Kiara, a teenage girl navigating the harsh realities of poverty, abandonment and exploitation in Oakland, California. Mottley constructs her world with unrelenting realism, never romanticizing the violence or reducing Kiara’s experience to victimhood. Kiara is the beating heart of the novel. her voice is direct, lyrical and sharp and what makes this story unforgettable. she’s not written as an archetype of resilience or strength, but as someone constantly pulled under by circumstances far beyond her control. Mottley resists the temptation to offer tidy arcs or moral clarity and instead lets Kiara’s choices, sometimes desperate, sometimes defiant, speak for themselves. what stood out most to me was Mottley’s prose: poetic without being precious, urgent without losing control. her background as a poet is evident in the rhythm and cadence of the narration. there’s a rawness in her writing that suits the story perfectly and even when the subject matter is at its heaviest, the language carries moments of unexpected grace. the one element that held this back from a full five stars was the pacing. certain sections, particularly in the middle third, lose some momentum as the narrative loops through similar emotional beats. while this might reflect Kiara’s stasis and helplessness, it occasionally undercut the tension the story builds so effectively elsewhere. still, it is a remarkable first novel. it is not just a story about one girl’s nightmarish reality, but rather an indictment of the systems that fail people like Kiara over and over again. Mottley has written a debut that demands attention, one that balances lyrical beauty with political urgency.

** spoiler alert ** If we stand on the backs of Black women, who will carry them? Who will water us as we are constantly planting seeds and watering others? Nightcrawling by Leila Mottley was created due to police departments in the Bay Area like the Oakland police department who sexually exploited young women only to cover it up and leave these young women broken, abused, used, and silenced. Nightcrawling tells a story just like this. Where there is no happy ending, Leila gives meaning to the main character Kiara. You get to see her, hear her, understand her sacrifices, and ache because this young girl had to become a woman and diminish her childhood to survive not only for herself but for others around her. At just 17, Kiara has lived many times over. Set in East Oakland at the Regal-Hi apartments, Kiara introduces us to poverty, rent increase, and Oakland’s gentrification. Kiara lost her father to the system multiple times only to have him released to his death. A mother whose need for her father causes an aching that results in sudden death, a suicide attempt, and her mother in prison. All that Kiara has left is her older brother Marcus, her 10-year-old neighbor Trevor, and her best friend Ale’. Kiara’s mother instinct kicks in as she becomes a high school dropout with no resume, rent due, and her neighbor Trevor is hungry and without food because his mother has been consumed by drugs. Kiara goes as far as having a funeral day with her best friend. A way to attend services to get free food and clothing left behind while others are mourning. Being unable to find work due to age and lack of a resume, Kiara is now facing her eviction and Trevor’s. Her older brother no longer holding her hand because he wants to live a false dream, but Kiara just wants to ease the hardship. A frustrating day turned into Kiara being drunk and losing her virginity to a white man who thinks she a prostitute. After payment, Kiara calculates how to make a living by becoming a streetwalker. 17 and dressed up, Kiara walking the streets for money leads her on a twisty slope filled with men and police officers degrading her body, her spirit, and mind, but her bills are paid. These same cops start to bring fear through pointing guns at her during sex, threatening to arrest her, and often ignoring paying her because their payment is in protection. As the underground corruption of the police force starts to leak, Kiara not only struggles with the decision of coming forward but must also deal with her everyday life and facing her broken mother. Balancing friendship and love, Kiara is stuck between being a mother and a child. Nightcrawling is not a book to ease your thoughts. Nightcrawling is the means to survive in a world that makes you feel smaller by the second. The shift in structure, accountability, and access. Kiara has 17 years of life but has been aged in mere months. The mental strength it took to tell herself it is just a body. It is just sex. To face the crooked police system with the odds already against her, Kiara finds a way to survive and be loved.

Whew, this was so intense. Some mostly scattered thoughts below. I'll start by saying that my experience with this book is very much coloured by my own ignorance of the term 'nightcrawl' and how it is used in this book. So, I was not really prepared for the content - which was much heavier, darker and more graphic than I anticipated. This book follows Kiara, who turns to sex work as a desperate teenager trying her best to make ends meet. Kiara is trying to make rent, keep herself and her older brother fed and cared for, and also trying her best to parent another young boy whose own mother has abandoned him. Unable to find other work, she begins sex work and soon gets caught up providing sex for money to Oakland police officers, many of whom are brutal. This book is...intense. Every word, every sentence, it rocked me and upset me and devastated me all at once. The content of the book is hard to read, and quite jarring in many places. But, in all of that, there is a beautifully written story here. Leila Mottley's writing is poetic, haunting, visceral. She is an incredible talent. And there is so much to be said about Kiara and the characters of this novel. They are written with such tenderness and love. They are facing the hardest circumstances of their lives, but they are human and we see and feel all of their humanity throughout. They will stay with me a long time - I feel like I knew them and I am rooting for them to all be okay, wherever they are. The sense of place in this book is incredible. The city of Oakland almost functions as a character in the book too. Every place we follow Kiara features prominently in her story, it was really something special. That being said, this is not a book for the weak. It was probably not the right time for me to read it - the world is awful and there is so much dark shit to contend with every day. I'm not sure if I had known how much this book was that I would have read it in my current mental state. But, I am glad I did, even though it was really emotional and really difficult. That's all I got for now. No star rating because it feels weird to do that with this kind of book.

🚫 Not Picking Up Another Emily McIntire I think after this, I am not picking up another Emily McIntire book again. It just doesn’t cut it for me. The plot is underwhelming, the twists obvious, and the downfalls handmade by the MCs’ idiotic decisions. This series had so much potential, especially with the “villain gets an HEA” concept, but it fell flat. Same problems in book 1 and 6. Which tells me: not much improvement has been made. 1️⃣ Flat Origins & Missed Potential While the plot tries to give the “villain” their HEA, and I actually liked that the villain remains a villain but more nuanced, the execution just isn’t there. Instead of truly delving into origin stories, we only get a couple of mentions and that one convenient story that somehow ties everything together. But even then, those elements aren’t used to their full emotional potential. And listen: this is not a short book. It had the space. It just didn’t use it.🤷🏻‍♀️ Enzo’s background? Explored, but too lightly. Aside from one tiny mention near the climax, it barely mattered. 2️⃣ Smut for “Fuck’s” Sake I’m a smut girlie. I love spice. But I like it to make sense. Here? It was mostly cringe. • Enzo having sex with Aria while thinking of Venesa. • V having a sex dream. • The brewing tension between them wasted except for one scene. There was substance to build on. But instead we got five (?) sex scenes back-to-back, which was just exhausting. And don’t even get me started on the male narrator in the audiobook. 😬 He made the cringe ten times worse. 3️⃣ Dumb Decisions on Repeat The MCs constantly act like fools. Venesa does the exact same reckless thing multiple times, gets in trouble each time, and still repeats it, until the final pinnacle moment where, honestly, she deserved what happened. Enzo wasn’t much better. For a mafia world, these characters had zero street smarts. Yes, you can be trusting, but not blind. Yes, you can be relaxed, but not when your life literally depends on anticipating threats. The lack of basic logic? Maddening.🤡 4️⃣ Rushed & Box-Checking I do appreciate the attempt at authenticity by pulling in as many elements from the original fairytales as possible. But here, it felt rushed, like a checklist being ticked off rather than integrated meaningfully. Some resolutions happened way too fast, losing all their impact. 🎧 Audiobook Ick Factor I’m no expert on US accents, but the drift was so obvious. Whatever tilt the narrator started with, it quickly faded, only popping back on certain words like “sugar” and “sweetheart.” And again: the male narrator gave me the absolute biggest icks, especially in the smut scenes. Trust me, even at 2x speed, it wasn’t fast enough to escape the cringe. 😒 Goodbye Flat. Underwhelming. Predictable. Not actually fun. This series could’ve been so much more… but it wasn’t. Thank you Makayla for choosing this for my 25 books from 25 friends for 2025. -- Pre-read: I might as well throw myself to the sharks and see if I survive this...🧜‍♀️

This one is my favorite book in the Never After series so far. McIntire truly outdid herself with this dark, twisted Little Mermaid retelling. Venesa is one of the strongest, most compelling FMCs in the entire series, cold, intelligent, morally grey, and shaped by trauma in a way that feels raw and believable. I loved watching her step into her power instead of softening for love. Enzo was the perfect match for her: dangerous, loyal, and emotionally layered. Their chemistry was intense, forbidden, and slow-burning in the best way. The romance felt earned, not rushed, and I appreciated that neither character had to lose their darkness to be together. The mafia setting worked incredibly well, adding high stakes, tension, and violence that enhanced the story rather than overshadowing the romance. The Little Mermaid parallels, especially the symbolism surrounding voice, sacrifice, and control, were subtle but clever. At the beginning, I actually felt sympathy for Aria. — 4 stars 🐚🪸 ”you have changed me. irrevocably. i don’t want you in a different life. i need you in this one and all the ones we’ll have after.” enzo and venesa’s soundtrack ₊˚⊹🧪 hexed is the sixth installment in emily mcintire’s never after series, and my personal third read of the series. though it wasn’t quite a five star read for me, it still delivered an enjoyable, gripping story. this book was one of the more plot driven entries, offering a refreshing take with a female villain lead and weaving a compelling dynamic between forbidden love, loyalty, and betrayal. while not my favorite of the series, it sits comfortably between my thoughts on hooked and twisted, bringing both strengths and weaknesses from each. — plot: unlike the more atmospheric twisted, hexed was very much plot driven, and for the most part, it worked. the story was fleshed out, characters outside the main couple were given meaningful roles, and the forbidden aspect of their relationship tied in nicely with the larger narrative. i appreciated how mcIntire took her time building the world and weaving the subplots into the main storyline. — venesa was easily the highlight of hexed. she’s dynamic, complex, and the perfect embodiment of a morally grey female villain. what stood out was how round her character felt; she had depth, clear motivations, and genuine development throughout the story. venesa wasn’t just a flat “bad girl” trope; she was layered, powerful, and driven by her own sense of justice and revenge. watching her navigate her ambitions while being forced to confront vulnerability gave her a strong arc that i genuinely appreciated. her character alone was enough to keep me invested. “you can't ever count on a man, but you can always count on the poison that will kill him... or whatever that saying is.” — enzo’s character development was enjoyable as well, especially in how his loyalties shifted over time. his internal struggle between duty and desire added much needed tension to the story. that said, while i liked him, i didn’t love him. compared to the soulmates level chemistry i felt with julian and yasmin in twisted, enzo and venesa’s dynamic didn’t hit quite as hard. their connection was compelling in a forbidden love, can’t have you way, but it lacked the slow burn build up and tension that really makes a romance hit emotionally. (even if the first smut scene was 300 pages in, they had feelings for each other very early on.) from the very start, they were drawn to each other, which worked for the plot, but didn’t leave much room for that slow burn angst. ”she's poise and grace in the face of adversity. polished on the outside. and it gives me a thrill to know she's capable of being so bad at the flip of a switch.” — romance and chemistry: this brings me to the romance: good, but not great. their chemistry was there, but it didn’t scream power couple energy. they felt more like two very broken people who found comfort and desire in each other rather than a destined, soulmate level match. and while that worked for the story, it didn’t give me the same level of emotional payoff as other couples in the series. think more “we understand each other’s darkness” than “fated lovers”. as a bridgerton season 2 lover, i appreciated the “i want you but i can’t have you” dynamic, and hexed definitely scratched that itch, but it still missed that extra spark that would’ve pushed it to a five star for me. — the pacing faltered at the climax. the final twists, especially the reveal of who killed who, felt brushed over too quickly. after so much build up, those pivotal moments lacked the weight and drama they deserved. the deaths toward the end, particularly in the first epilogue, felt anticlimactic. with characters who were hyped up to be so dangerous and untouchable, seeing them taken down in just a few pages was underwhelming. for a book that invested so much in creating tension, the payoff didn’t quite match the setup. -1 ★… i deducted one star because the romance lacked the emotional build up and tension i wanted, making venesa and enzo feel less like a power couple and more like two broken people who happened to fit. the final twists and character deaths felt rushed and anticlimactic, especially after so much build up. plus, the long break in my reading hurt my connection to the story, which dulled the overall impact. (i started this book in december, got 400 pages in, then never picked it up again until may bc school started back 😭.) ₊⊹⁀➴ in conclusion, hexed was an enjoyable read that kept my interest and made me want to continue the series. venesa’s character alone was worth the read, and the forbidden romance trope was done well enough to satisfy, even if it didn’t fully deliver that all consuming chemistry i love. the plot was engaging, even if the climax stumbled a bit, and the book’s sheer size allowed for more layered storytelling compared to earlier installments. it didn’t dethrone twisted as my favorite, but it absolutely sits above hooked. if you’re a fan of morally grey female leads, forbidden romance, and plot driven dark romance with a dash of bridgerton season two tension, you’ll enjoy this one. as for me, i’m cautiously eyeing scarred next, even if the fantasy element makes me a little nervous. and i’m STILL manifesting that princess and the frog inspired book from mcintire. give me new orleans and my tiana and dr. facilier dark romance PLEASEEEE. ➸ never after book 1 review ➸ never after book 4 review
