I went into Heart Lamp with a lot of expectations even though I am not a fan of Booker Prize winners. But this was an anthology and I love them. So I picked this up. Heart Lamp was... not exactly disappointing, but I don't know why it won the Booker Prize. There are 12 stories that offer a glimpse into low to higher class Muslim women in South India. However, the general understanding is that they can be transformed into any other woman of any other religion and the outcome would be the same. We often see comments on social media by religious Muslims about how Islam teaches equality to women. But what was said 1400 years ago hasn't remained the same. Women covering their head and body as a submission to God is now a tool for oppression. Sisters asking for equal rights in property is seen as a rebellion against men. These changes may or may not be seen in other societies but in South East Asia, the cultural influences of different peoples and religions have massively reshaped the Muslim society. In fact, it can be said the every person from every religion has been influenced in some way or the other. The underlying thread of patriarchy, however, remains unchanged and has, in fact, grown stronger over the years, even with the various feminist movements. Where once the Prophet praised the birth of daughters - indeed, he had only daughters and, out of them, Fathima is one of the most highly regarded in Islam - now, the birth of a daughter is seen as a burden. The Prophet also preached multiple marriages for a man but also stipulated that he must do so only if he is able to provide equally for all his wives. Over the years, only the first part of his preachings - the multiple marriages part - has remained, while the equal provision part has somehow mysteriously been overlooked. Of course, there is nothing really mysterious about it. Heart Lamp does manage to convey the message but I felt some stories were too preachy. Stone Slabs for Shaista Mahal was one such. When Iftikhar declares unending love for his wife yet sees her as a vessel to carry his children, we know what is going to happen next. Other stories like The Shroud, A Taste of Heaven, and High-Heeled Shoe didn't seem to have a direction. They started somewhere and ended somewhere else. Same with The Arabic Teacher and Gobi Manchuri. Maybe it was I who couldn't understand them - I don't pretend to be a scholar but I believe that if you start with a person's high blood pressure complaints and then insert a Haj trip and a shroud into the narrative without a satisfactory ending, that does not make a good short story. Some characters in the stories also behaved in some ways that felt totally weird to me. Why would a man be so enamored with a high-heeled shoe, make his wife wear it, and then just walk away? Why would a son arrange a marriage for his widowed mother, seeking grooms and even fixing the date, but not even talk with her about it at all until the eve of her marriage? Another point that annoyed me to no end was the translation. Whenever I read a translated work, I give a lot of leeway for language. There are some emotions and some words that simply cannot be translated into English. But when you write stuff like "the auto went away making a barrrrr sound" or "she began to sniff loudly making sarraa-harraa noises," I begin to lose faith in your translation. Yet another thing is that most Indian languages (at least the ones I know) have the tendency to repeat certain words, especially numbers, for emphasis. For example, we might say, "naan rendu-rendu tharavai ponen" in Tamil or "chaar-chaar roti khaayi usne" in Hindi. But when we say two-two or four-four in English, it seems very childish. The translator's note has included a word in the end for her choice but by the time I reached there, I was fed up with the usage. That said, I liked some stories. Fire Rain and Black Cobras were both memorable but the best of the lot was Be a Woman Once, Oh Lord! However, I am not sure I will remember them after a few days because the stories began to run together with each other after a while. This review has reached the length of a short story itself so I will stop here. I wish to say at last that yes, women are oppressed in every religion but there was a much better way to say it. I think I will keep to my resolve of not reading award-winning books again. I don't seem to understand them. 3 stars.

Even before I started reading Banu Mustaq's Heart Lamp, I knew I was going to love it. A collection of short stories written in Kannada, later translated into English by Deepa Bhasthi, reached the global stage when it was longlisted for International Booker Prize 2025. I was filled with pride and I knew I had to read it lest somebody 'spoils' the book for me. Guess what? I spoiled it myself! I should have waited longer so that ultimately, like countless books in my TBR, I would have forgotten the existence of this one. That way, I would not have to wrench my heart for writing this review. I have strong opinions on many books which I have read and did not like; I never actually thought twice before writing about it. What is so special with this one? In the translator's note, Deepa Bhasthi sums up Banu Mustaq's career with one Kannada word: bandaya. Bandaya is "dissent, rebellion, protest, resistance to authority, revolution and its adjacent ideas". As a woman and a citizen of this world, I understand the importance of bandaya in our lives. And I deeply acknowledge the sheer strength it takes to resist. I have not still reached to my thoughts on this collection of short stories because I feel very guilty for 'criticising' the voice behind Heart Lamp. The collection started pretty well, the story was readable, I wanted to know what happens next, I was capable of understanding the women and what they were going through. I did not realise it in the beginning, but that is where all the good aspects of this collection stops. One story after another, I was left wanting for more and not in a good way. It was supposed to capture the hardships of Muslim women living in southern India. But, in trying to be a universal story for women, the stories belong nowhere. I reached my tipping point while reading pages upon pages about an 'adult' man's obsession with high-heeled shoe that seemed to be going nowhere. It was not just boring, but downright torturous. The stories lacked an intention: was it written to show women's small acts of defiance, or was it for depicting that they were nothing but "the husband's most obedient servant, his bonded labourer"? All this is not to say that Heart Lamp is a bad book. As a reader, I was not able to make much sense of it. I can point out a lot of arguments to everything I have said, but somehow, they are not just strong enough for me to agree on. Is this a good book? Yes. But did it deserve to win the International Booker Prize? I cannot, in good conscience, say yes. Heart Lamp stirred me a little, but it failed to leave an impact.

Imagine my delight when I saw a book that was originally written in my mother tongue get shortlisted for the 2025 International Booker Prize. Reading this collection of short stories featuring Muslim women was an interesting experience. It could have been my familiarity with the original language or my experience of witnessing similar characters as the women in the stories, that made this book feel very real. I can see why this anthology made it to the shortlist. The stories and its characters featured important social issues but what made it all possible was the exceptional translation. No two stories written by Banu Mushtaq are the same. The characters and their plights vary from each other, but there’s an undeniable sense of helplessness and unjust that attaches itself to these women who want to just live as per their rights. The sharia law is different from the normal law, giving the husbands or men in general an upper hand and this detail has been highlighted time and again in her stories. She covers the lives of the rich and the poor, of women of different temperaments, fighting or pushing for their needs and wants. What makes this collection impressive is also the worrying aspect that these stories feel extremely real. When fiction collides with real life, it sometimes blurs the line between the two worlds. Deepa Bhasthi has made it possible for people across the world to access this incredible piece of literature through her clever and thoughtful translation. By selecting such simple yet profound stories, and by carefully translating them, she has made it all the more remarkable. These stories aren’t just about the Muslim women but somehow encapsulates the collective feeling of what it takes to live as a woman in this patriarchal world. I highly recommend this. @penguinindia I can’t thank you enough for sending this copy.

I would recommend reading the translator's note, "Against Italics", found after the collection of stories, first, to both aid in the process of reading this book and for contextual comprehension. There is work to be done for readers outside the religion and community of the author, even though the themes are universal. These stories delve into the everyday lives of women and girls in Muslim communities in southern India. Clearly, the focus of these narratives is on women facing societal, religious and familial challenges imposed by class, patriarchy, dogma and even misogyny. This collection is both a feminist critique of the oppressive constraints placed on women in these circumstances and a tribute to their loves, losses and resilience. The collection shed light on a world largely unknown to me on this granular level, yet it appeared familiar in the ways women lacking agency struggle everywhere. You shouldn't put a Western feminist perspective lens on these stories, however, as that would diminish their unique cultural setting. These settings and circumstances are communicated to us with an interesting conversational storytelling style, and the translator has left many words untranslated for you to investigate and learn, so the text doesn't lose touch with its community. There is little dialogue, making this dense collection a slower read for me, but I appreciated being transported to that world so effectively.

₊˚ ✧ ━━━━⊱ international booker prize shortlist 2025⊰━━━━ ✧ ₊˚ book 1 : ‘heart lamp’ by banu mushtaq ☆ ☆ ☆ ☆ 1/2 I really enjoyed this book! Even as an Urdu reader, I was able to track how English diction is being affected by the Kannada original in this translation. I also admire how the English itself is an "Indian" or an Anglophone South Asian English, as opposed to translation into British or American English diction. I otherwise got to think about the importance of reading Banu Mushtaq's stories for Pakistani readers here: https://dunyadigital.co/books/banu-mu...

A Muslim woman’s plea to God (“When you so leisurely created the animal kingdom, the delicate threadlike parts inside flowers with gold coating, these marvellous ponds and lakes, rivers and streams, did you not have the time to peep into my heart and see my fears, my wishes, dreams and disappointments?”) addresses him as ‘Prabhu’—divided by land, religion, class but united by misogyny. A very nuanced translation overall.

It doesn’t try to impress the reader with grand language or dramatic twists. Instead, it unsettles you with how real and uncomfortably familiar it feels. What I appreciated most is Mushtaq’s restraint. The stories are sharp, observant, and emotionally honest without ever becoming preachy. She writes about women, faith, family, and power in a way that feels deeply rooted in lived experience. The pain her characters carry isn’t exaggerated, it’s everyday, normalized pain. The kind society often teaches people to accept without question. That’s what makes it hit harder. Some stories are stronger than others, which is why this lands at four stars instead of five for me. A few narratives feel a little abrupt, almost like they end just when you want them to go deeper. But even then, the emotional core is strong enough to make you pause and think. This isn’t a comforting read, but it is an important one. Heart Lamp asks you to sit with discomfort, to notice the quiet injustices we overlook, and to listen to voices that are too often sidelined. If you enjoy short stories that are socially grounded, morally complex, and written with quiet confidence, this book is absolutely worth your time. Rightfully the winner of the 2025 international Booker Prize 🏆.

While it won the International Booker, the reviews here and on SM were pretty underwhelming, which kind of kept my expectations low. But right from the get go, Mushtaq's stories, translated brilliantly by Deepa Bhasthi take you by the scruff of the neck and give you pauses only between the stories. The stories themselves are rooted in the everyday, people dealing with just living their lives. And in a way you could say the common theme is the plight of Muslim women, where they have few rights. With a lesser writer they could have easily become one story after the other detailing the same horrors. But Mushtaq doesn't let them, or rather Bhasthi chooses her stories to translate keeping that in mind. One thing to remember, short stories are written over a long time, the curator, the translator in this case, needs to have an idea of how they'll read together in a collection. Bhasthi's translation makes the Kannada leap out and dance in English. There are the 'it seems', things are black-black. I especially loved the work in Black Cobras which is also by far the best story in the set. But despite all that it is a dark book, holding little in the form of hope. The last story and its last line captures it perfectly. "Come to earth as a woman, Prabhu! Be a woman once, O Lord!"

I'm someone who is historically sensitive to having a lot of characters - particularly a lot of main characters - and this did not bother me. I also did not find the stories repetitive; sure, certain themes were repeated - abused women, men taking on younger second wives and abandoning their first wife and children, etc. - but I felt that each story was fresh with something new and different to say. The fact that this seems to have been the least popular of the shortlisted books has me very curious about the rest of the shortlist. I love Bob Mortimer. Not in a creepy way. Just in the way you love someone who can make you laugh about a pie, a squirrel and existential despair in the same breath. “The Satsuma Complex” charmed the pants off me. “The Hotel Avocado” did it again. So, I came to “The Long Shoe” already half smiling. Matt, poor bugger, has lost the lot. Job gone. He can't afford his flat. Girlfriend vanished into thin air. Then, he’s offered a job that comes with a swanky apartment, which feels less like good fortune and more like someone upstairs fiddling with the dials. He thinks it might win her back. Instead, he starts to suspect she didn’t leave at all. On paper, it’s a caper. A noir-ish muddle involving missing women, dodgy employers and the usual creeping sense that something isn’t right. In practice, the caper is a kind of camouflage. What drives “The Long Shoe” is loneliness. Thick, persistent, slightly shame-faced loneliness. The kind Mortimer wrote about in his autobiography. The jokes are there, of course. Talking animals, odd metaphors, bits of sideways logic that make you blink. But underneath it all is that familiar ache. Ordinary blokes who don’t quite know how to be alone, or together. Harriet’s disappearance isn’t just plot fuel. It’s an enforced audit of her relationship. What does she miss. What does she feel oddly lighter without. Mortimer lets both lists sit there without judgement. The quiet realisation that love and relief can share the same kitchen table. The tone is still Mortimer through and through. He can move from mild peril to an off-kilter metaphor about a feature measured in small rodents without breaking stride. There’s danger, introspection and feather-light humour all jostling in the same corridor. It never tips into syrup. That’s the trick. He keeps the decency intact even when the situation gets murky. That said, the template is starting to show. The sharp-tongued neighbour. The slightly passive, bewildered man. The missing girlfriend who may not be as missing as she seems. If you’ve read “The Satsuma Complex” and “The Hotel Avocado”, you’ll clock the pattern early. The surreal flourishes still land. The talking cat earns its keep. But the novelty feels less freshly caught, more reheated with care. The premise itself is a bit over-engineered. It has the air of an Athletico Parsnips episode that’s wandered off into the weeds for a smoke and come back insisting it’s a thriller. Things click into place a shade too neatly. The peril is low voltage. The mystery zips along so briskly there’s barely time to feel genuine tension. Events happen, then more events happen, loosely strung together like mildly chaotic beads. And yet. The prose is still the reason you’re here. Mortimer’s sentences have that pub-story cadence. Slightly rambling, oddly specific, then suddenly bang on target. He notices launderette-scented vape smoke, cheap suits that sit like damp cardboard, luxury flats that feel like borrowed skin. His metaphors are homespun and peculiar, but they stick. Even when the structure wobbles, the voice carries you. There’s also that sweetness to his worldview. Loyalty matters. Small acts of courage matter. Even shithouse blokes can step up when it counts. He’s not writing Dostoyevsky and thank Christ for that. He’s writing about ordinary people who’d never headline anything, trying not to make a complete mess of their lives. So yes, there’s repetition. Yes, the formula is visible. Yes, I’d quite like him to tear it up next time and surprise us properly. But I was fond of this. I laughed. I winced a bit. I felt that quiet thrum of loneliness beneath the nonsense. Four stars. I’ll keep turning up for whatever fruit or footwear he throws at us next. I just hope one day he smacks his own arse with a fish slice and swerves somewhere completely new.

4.5 ⭐️ I absolutely loved this. It’s full of laughs, suspense, unreliable characters and a Goodmonson WHO TALKS. You’ll meet Matt, a man who makes me want to crawl up my own arse, a wet lettuce if you will. Harriet, who needs to go travelling and find herself, specifically away from the lettuce man. A yoga instructor with uncharacteristically tight butt cheeks. A cockney gangster who likes darts, beer and boobs yet has an affinity with abnormally (some would say quirkily) long shoes. Lawrence, a sketchy man who owns Sastuma Heights. And how could I forget, fucking Carol. The woman, the myth, the legend. A book you won’t want to put down because you’ll be so confused, intrigued, hooked by the way Bob writes. Will definitely be reading more from him.

I've been hugely fond of Bob Mortimer's endearing whimsy since he and Vic Reeves burst on to our TV screens in 1990 in an updated, more arch and knowing version of childhood favourites Morecambe & Wise. I'm not a huge fan of celebrity novelists and actively avoid them, but between fond sentimental remembrance of the tv of my 20s, and being the owner of a Patterdale terrier just like Ted in Mortimer's show Gone Fishing (same age, same attitude, less pronounced underbite), I saw this book was available on Libby and decided to try it out. I'm very glad I did, it gives very strong Nick Hornby High Fidelity-era vibes, and is beautifully written and expertly narrated by Bob Mortimer, Diane Morgan and Arabella Weir. For a few hours, I too was back in my 30s like the protagonists here, and it was great fun. It's not 5⭐️ because it's a little derivative, but it's pretty darned close. I'm going to read his other books now

Bob Mortimer has such a unique style of writing, with quirky protagonists who always come across as entirely unassuming and just normal. I like how the crime element is almost in the background of this book, and instead it’s the story of an ordinary guy who’s lost his way in life and is just trying to get his girlfriend back. I really liked Hot Dog Man and most of the characters in this book. Nothing dramatic happens, and even the twists just feel like a normal part of life, but there’s something compelling about Mortimer’s stories.

Like all of Bob Mortimer’s novels it’s at its best within his comfort zone of human observation and mild surrealism and he again crafts a collection of enjoyably oddball characters with real human emotional arcs that keep them anchored. The premise is fun, nicely structured and just realistic enough to make its flights of whimsy stick, even as the contrivances starts snowballing. It’s a bit shakier when the pace ramps up right towards the end and it has to draw to a conclusion that feels a bit half-baked. It’s more fun just spending time in this world than it is having an intricately plotted narrative.

At first I thought the book was a rehash of Bob’s previous books, and maybe they are but I wouldn’t level a comment like that at Agatha Christie. It’s certainly written in the same style and I couldn’t help but read it with Bob’s voice. The narrative was well put together, and I liked the range of characters. It has that absurdity in the text, which I enjoy. The humour is reincorporated which keeps the smile on my face. The question now is will there be further instalments of Matt and Harriet? I do hope so.

Bob Mortimer’s most recent novel, "The Long Shoe", is another charming addition to his bibliography, but for me, it doesn't quite match the magic of his Gary Thorn books. While it's a delightful read, the characters feel eerily familiar - Matt reminds me of Gary, and Carol has a similar personality to Grace. Even the themes, like the longing for differences within relationships, seem like they've been explored before in the Gary Thorn series. To be honest, I felt like I was reading a Gary Thorn book with different character names. The writing style, humor, and even the voices Mortimer uses in the audiobook are all so similar to his previous works. It's not a bad thing, but it does make "The Long Shoe" feel like a variation on a theme rather than something entirely new. One thing that does stand out is Mortimer's love for satsumas, which makes an appearance in this book as well. And, as always, his narration is top-notch, bringing the characters to life with his signature wit and charm. I didn’t really like Carol because she was a bit vain. Overall, I'm giving "The Long Shoe" 3 stars. My favourite Mortimer book is still "The Satsuma Complex", and while this is a solid effort, it doesn't quite match up to that standout title. Still, fans of his previous books will likely enjoy it, and it's a great way to spend time with his unique brand of humor and characters.

The long shoe - Bob Mortimer Bob Mortimer is a master at placing deeply whimsical characters into bizarre, often outright hilarious situations. The Long Shoe certainly continues that tradition, and like The Hotel Avocado, it contains several genuine laugh-out-loud moments. There were more than a few occasions where I caught myself laughing manically, earning some very concerned looks from Louisa and raising legitimate questions about my sanity. That said, while the humour is unmistakably Mortimer, The Long Shoe ultimately felt far more hollow than his previous work. The comedy often seemed to act as a crutch for what I found to be a rather lacklustre story. Unlike The Hotel Avocado, where the mystery played a central role and worked in harmony with the humour, here the narrative never fully grabbed me. The plot felt thin, and the double-bluff ending landed with little impact, largely because I never felt particularly invested in how the story resolved. While Mortimer’s voice remains charming and his comic instincts are as sharp as ever, The Long Shoe didn’t quite balance its humour with substance in the way I’d hoped. Fans of his surreal comedy will still find plenty to enjoy, but for me, it lacked the emotional or narrative depth that made The Hotel Avocado a much more memorable read. Overall, if you love bob you’ll love this book from him but in terms of story power it doesn’t have much. It’s just a good bit of bob, and we all love a bit of bob.
