In case it’s not clear, this book is painfully, excruciatingly, obnoxiously, agonizingly, boring. Every time I put it down I dreaded picking it back up. I really shouldn’t have bothered finishing but I am always holding out hope that it’s going to get better. That it must be nominated for a reason. Baffling. Anyway. I think that’s probably where I’ll end my attempt to read the Longlist. There are a few others I will be checking out: Creation Lake which actually sounds interesting and unique, so long as it isn’t a fucking astronaut poem I think I’ll be okay. James which has been gathering buzz all year and I’m excited to read. Playground with a concept I love. The Safekeep which I was interested in independently of the prize. Possibly Wandering Stars, someday after I read There There. Maaayyybbeeee…. Enlightenment and This Strange Eventful History… but I’m not in a rush.
Solid, had a cinematic quality to but make it indie, wonderful character work
This felt like an episode of Fair City

The characters are why you may want to read this. The plot is unremarkable but serves well to exhibit the characters in stressful situations. Its a modest crime story, in a modest town with relatively modest criminals. The writing was easy to read and descriptive. I enjoyed this modest family drama and look forward to reading more from Colin Barrett but I'm hoping she provides more depth than this one did. Recommended to those wanting an episode of a small town family crime drama and don't mind if its shallow and feels kind of pointless.

As much I admire Barrett's style, this story is way to s l o w. At 60% we are still at the same point as in the beginning. Too much description, e.g. when the author explains the plastic stoma bags Dev produced: seriously? I quit at the dream description, something no novelist seems to be able to do without nowadays, but in most cases are just page fillers.

Gritty and bleak, the characters elicited my interest at first but held little sympathy or compassion. Lots of Irish slang that apparently lower class or drug trade folks use. It’s not a long book and the story moves quickly. Lots of adjectives and descriptions of common things made it feel like more elevated writing. The female character is the smart gal among the not as smart hoods. Since many descriptions tout the novel as humorous - I found there to be almost none - with the possible exception of the dog who behaved like a little dog.

** spoiler alert ** Not the greatest written book. I felt it went all over the place like having ADD. It was very hard to read. There was a few interesting parts but I felt like there was a lot of things in it that didn’t need to be, and I felt it was put in as fluff to make the book longer. Should have been made a shorter story.

Wild Houses is the debut novel of Colin Barrett, a prize-winning short story writer. It is novel about drugs, violence, alienation, and a kidnapping in rural western Ireland. I found it enormously sad. The novel is told from alternating POVs. There is Dev, a veritable giant of a man, who is weak, introspective and afflicted with anxiety and depression. He has a good heart but has trouble standing up to people. And there is Nicky, the 17-year-old girlfriend of Doll, the boy who was kidnapped. She is smart and intelligent and probably won’t be staying in Ballina, the small Irish town where much of the story takes place. Though Dev and Nicky don’t know each other, they are two outsiders in Ballina. One is probably stuck there; one will probably leave. I thought this novel was very, very well written. Individual sentences say exactly what they need to say, and nothing more. There is some dialect in the novel, but it is easily understood. But I had trouble getting into the story and identifying with the characters. However, by about half-way through the book, I was hooked and didn’t want to put it down. By the end of the novel, I was emotionally connected to the characters, but the novel ends without any hint of what the future holds for Dev, Nicky, and Doll. I wish we could see their lives in five years’ time. I hope they are happy and settled wherever they might be. Easy 4 stars. When I reread it, I might rate it higher.
Not a terrible book, not a great book, just kinda meh.
irish lit fic 🤝 me

I found this to be an immersive read, even though I couldn't quite tell you what Colin Barrett would like his readers to take away from it. The novel follows two characters on the periphery of drug dealing gone wrong. I found Dev in particular to be hugely compelling. The geography of the small Irish town of Ballina, from the countryside to the local pub, is depicted in believable, gritty depth.

This was a joy to read - the plot (around a kidnapping in County Mayo) not really providing the main energy here, but the poetic concision of his style that allows us to see into the interior world of his characters. One example: "...He was touching forty but looked ten years older again, with a face on him like a vandalised church, long and angular and pitted, eyes glinting deep in their sockets like smashed-out windows." The dialogue too is spot on, as characters navigate the violent pitfalls of their situation,often with dark humour. Great debut novel, from an acclaimed short story writer.

Love Colin Barrett as a story writer and now can confirm I love him as a novelist too. He just paints such a picture, such an Irish picture, and really takes the time to lay the groundwork to have you so completely invested in his characters. He scratches the same itch for me as Thomas Savage but in a completely different world. Just really lovely writing with some real gut punch moments, especially with dear Dev, whom I love.

3⭐️ While this was a quick and enjoyable read, I wonder what the point of this book is. There‘s a kidnapping, but it‘s so laidback and uneventful that it‘s kind of underwhelming. I suppose its main focus are the characters though, and especially Dev and Nicky were so well written. Their loneliness if very different but palpable. After Sappho is a story of women and womanhood, a story of creativity, freedom, and excellence. This is scholar Selby Wynn Schwartz’s debut work of fiction, published by the excellent Galley Beggar Press. Schwartz traces the lives of European women in the Sapphic tradition who pushed against boundaries and laid the groundwork for liberation on their own terms. Many of these women are unsung, at least in our male-dominated society, although they are hardly obscure. Schwartz’s focus is unapologetically Euro-centric and covers the roughly 50-year period from the 1870s to the 1920s. Others have noted where writers of color seem to have been excised from the record, with Schwartz focusing instead on white woman who are already part of the canon. Despite that limited focus, I appreciate Schwartz's willingness to play with form and sit at the intersection of genres.

I wanted to like this one a lot. It won a prize. The cover is beautiful. The premise had me. What went wrong? Not that this is exactly that, but I have issues with short stories. The hopping back and forth between POVs gets confusing. 🎧 Thank you to NetGalley and HighBridge Audio

This novel drives home for me that my reviews here on goodreads aren't in any way recommendations to read, or not to read a given book. They are just my thoughts about what a book has meant to me. Here is a novel where I can see the merit on every page. The novel is thoughtful and full of surprises and new revelations, and it even has a thesis or two about women and creativity, and how creative women survive, or not, in a repressive patriarchal world. But here's what happened to me when I read it. I felt no connection, as I read, with the mind and works of the women I was reading about. Late in the book I realized that there is almost no attempt in the book to enter the interior mind of any of these women--the story trots along from one exterior fact to the next. It feels like a missed opportunity. It leaves each woman a cypher on the page. I think, in this way, that Schwartz's nonfiction roots for the novel show through--she doesn't allow herself to speculate beyond what can be observed from the outside of each historical figure she surveys. Surely any novel with Virginia Woolf as a character would venture inside her mind and give her passages a rhythm not unlike what Michael Cunningham imagined for his modern Mrs. Dalloway? In some passages the women's voices join in a sort of greek chorus, or to answer one another wittily, but I was more interested in the solitary interior truth of each of these women. Fiction allows you to speculate about what someone was like on the inside, and to take the most intimate and audacious liberties about what people think and how they feel. Another reader will love the novel for exactly what it does so well and be glad it doesn't do what I'm craving for it to do.

After Sappho is a sapphic historical fiction, which involves many women and is told in cascading vignettes. The book begins with three women: Lina Poletti (Italian poet), Rina Faccio (Italian writer), and Anna Kuliscioff, who was born in Ukraine, but studied medicine in Italy and became one of the first doctors in Italy, and strong voice for women across Europe. It’s a story of women who fought for human treatment of women. They didn’t want lives that led to asylums. They also demanded freedom to grow intellectually, to be able to read and discuss it with other women. They argued that voting for men only is not democracy, but tyranny. The story involves many fascinating women and this is what I appreciate, shedding light on them. As the story is told in brief pieces and keeps introducing new women, it hardly feels as a novel. After the introduction of the three women, they in a way connect, but I thought there would be more to their stories. Instead, the book progresses with introduction of more women. The short vignettes give it a feel of brisk introduction of different women, but I wanted to connect with those women on a deeper level. That was the missing part for me. Overall, it is a fascinating story of women who were brought to light. Source: ARC was provided by the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review.

I loved the overarching concept of this book, but really didn't enjoy the experience of reading it. After Sappho shares the lives of a number of women who were feminist, lesbian, and living in Europe over a span covering the late 1800's until just after WWI. Most of the women were also involved in the arts (writing, theater, painting, etc.). The book is broken into paragraphs, each with a heading, and each paragraph tells a snippet (not even a vignette) about one of the characters before moving on to the next snippet. The idea of focusing on the intertwining lives of women striving for visibility and recognition in a man's world is such a good idea. But, When We Cease to Understand the World did something similar, except with scientific discovery, and it was so much more engaging. I wanted to like this book, or at least appreciate it, but it was pretentious and overwritten and really didn't bring these women to life in any way. Plus it was nearly impossible to discern the biographical from the fictional, and I didn't really care enough to even try. I can so see this book being taught in an English lit class somewhere, and there were some gorgeous turns of phrase . . .but at the end of the day, I want a novel to move me emotionally and engage me with some semblance of a story, and this book just didn't do that for me at all. There was one paragraph that really encapsulated this book for me. . . .we might open a seemingly ordinary biography, its chapters neatly partitioned, and find that it was webbed throughout with the most extraordinary filaments of a life. A life after all did not happen by itself, in discrete units. Thus this biography would be bound together with all of our lives, twined through from preface to index: curling, animate, verdant. I think this is what the author was trying to do, intertwine the biographies of these women, and I love the concept of that! But the reality just didn't live up to the promise.

Rating: ⭐⭐⭐ Genre: Historical Fiction + LGBTQ+ After Sappho is a fictional reimagining of the lives of a few famous and influential female figures in the literary, poetry, and other artistic fields. The author takes the readers to experience the imaginary stories of these feminists in different time frames to see how they fight for their own rights and equality. They seek full liberation from societies that tend to treat females in a stereotypical approach. The book is both important and informative at the same time. The reformative approach that the author has taken makes the stories intriguing. However, the continuous jumps from one character to another and from one period to another have hindered the impact that this book should have made on me. I enjoyed the parts about Virginia Woolf the most because I’m already fascinated by her as an author and by her life story in general. Another problem that I feel this kind of narration will cause is the inability of the readers to connect with the characters. The narration gave me the impression that I was reading a magazine article about these women rather than a story. You need to have a suitable scene and setting, as well as other story components like a build-up to a conflict and a satisfying conclusion, in order to qualify something as a story. All this was lacking here, hence the feeling of reading an article instead. Despite its flaws, I nevertheless believe that this was a good read on such a crucial topic.

Shortlisted for the James Tait Black Prize for Fiction The manuscript of Una donna had initially been rejected by a set of editors in Milano because it was too boring. It was only the story of a woman, they said. It was a story that they already knew, there was only one story. It had no dramatic tension. A fascinating novel in “cascading vignettes” and a welcome diversion from the character and plot driven novels that tend to feature on the Booker. A novel I finished, appropriately, on the day that England’s Women’s team, one where players are open about their diverse sexuality, erased 56 years of hurt caused by the men (men’s football still chronically inflicted by homophobia). And yet the big question hanging over the representative nature of the England women’s team is the lack of racial diversity, a fact often attributed to the lack of ground-level opportunities for women to access football. And another brilliant discovery by the UK’s finest publisher of Anglophone literature, Galley Beggar Press, twice winner of the Goldsmiths Prize for innovative fiction. It is always wonderful to have a book featured on a prize like the Booker when one’s name is in the back of the book as one of the Galley Buddies who helped fund it. The novel intersperses snippets of lightly fictionalised biographies with a narration driven by a Greek chorus of women’s voices. It focuses largely on women (men are largely and consciously written out) from the first three decades of the 20th century, notably Lina Poletti and Sibilla Aleramo, Virginia Woolf and Vita Sackville-West and the Paris salon gathered around Natalie Barnay, with Sappho’s inspiration a key link, alongside (as the years are marked by both WW1 and the rise of fascism in Italy) Cassandra (whose inclusion is also a nod to Christa Wolf’s work). Some quotes from the book and related works: But which books should we read? asked one girl very seriously, twisting the ends of her plaits. Virginia Woolf replied, If a novel bores you, leave it. Try something else. Poetry is too like fiction to be a change. But biography is a very different thing. Go to the bookcase & take out a life of anybody. From the author’s afterword: Moreover, men like Gabriele d'Annunzio — who swaggers pre-potently through every account ever written of Eleonora Duse and Romaine Brooks — do not merit here even a footnote about who they married or how they died. It has been surprisingly easy to leave out these sorts of men: a simple swift cut, and history is sutured without them. I think of Vita Sackville-West, who said in a letter in 1919 that the only revenge one could take on certain men was to brazenly rewrite them. At that time, all she had at hand was an unfinished chapter of her novel Challenge. Therefore, Vita recounted, 'last night I went to Aphros and imprisoned all the Greek officials, which gave me a certain ferocious satisfaction'. The fact that my claim here about gender and fiction rests upon a quote from a real letter -which I have gleaned from a reputable scholarly source, Georgia Johnston's The Formation of 20th-Century Queer Autobiography: Reading Vita Sackville-West, Virginia Woolf; Hilda Doolittle, and Gertrude Stein — in which the author explains that she has, in some fictional yet satisfying sense, gone to Greece for a night, in order to exact narrative retribution for the wrongs done to her protagonist (under whose name she sometimes went around in the world): this, I think, illustrates the genre of the present work. Review by Virginia Woolf of The Feminine Note in Fiction by W.L. Courtney (Chapman & Hall, 1904), from the Guardian, Jan 25th 1905 Women, we gather, are seldom artists, because they have a passion for detail which conflicts with the proper artistic proportion of their work. We would cite Sappho and Jane Austen as examples of two great women who combine exquisite detail with a supreme sense of artistic proportion. Quote from Lote by Shola von Reinhold, winner of the Republic of Consciousness Prize 2020 ‘Indeed, I would venture to guess that Anon, who wrote so many poems without signing them, was often a woman,’ Virginia Woolf said. ‘And/or Black,’ Malachi said. This last highlights one obvious criticism of the book - that the women featured are almost exclusively white and privileged. The author has acknowledged this in an interview: DO YOU SEE THIS – THE KIND OF QUEST AND RIGHT TO ONE’S OWN IDENTITY AND LIFE – AS ONE OF THE CENTRAL THEMES OF THE NOVEL?) Yes! And I believe that this should also hold true for people who are not mostly well-educated white women with comfortable incomes in Western European cities. 4.5 stars

“After Sappho” combines everything I love in fiction: seductive prose, fictionalized history, experimentation in form, and the invitation to go on a parallel multimedia adventure. The book focuses on female trailblazers around the turn of the 20th century, from Virginia Woolf, to Romaine Brooks, to Natalie Barney, Sarah Bernhardt, Lina Poletti and many others. These are all women who don’t belong. They are deemed too interior, too volatile, too alchemical for their times. They defy their circumstances, take on new identities, find comfort in the arms of one another. They burn with a dry rage against the long tyranny of men, then transmute that rage into art. They are writers, actresses, poets, painters, dancers, prophetesses. Guilty of the crimes of sapphism, of insubordination, of harbouring outlandish desires. Schwartz tells their stories in glimpses and in shards. Reading “After Sappho” requires the reader to suspend expectations of plot, of narrative, of dramatic tension. Instead, it invites the reader to kick off her shoes, to venture out barefoot, to find refuge in the work of those who have come before, to reclaim literature, to reclaim language, even if only one word at a time. For women cannot create art by relying on the tools and frameworks designed to oppress them. Or, as Cusk asserts in Coventry, “The women writer might have to break everything — the sentence, the sequence, the novel itself — to create her own literature.” Yes. “After Sappho” is fragmentary in nature, but intentionally so. It is abrupt and full of interruptions, for “interruptions there will always be” (Virginia Woolf). It invites the reader to fill in the gaps, to consult historical texts for missing context. To read Orlando, to connect the dots of Romaine Brooks’ paintings, to pick up The Well of Loneliness, to consult the fragments of Sappho’s surviving poetry. To me, reading “After Sappho” is like the striking of a match. It sparks in me some distant memory, some primal notion of how things could be, even though I don’t quite have the language to explain exactly what, or how, or why. Mood: Defiant, experimental, alchemical Rating: 9/10 Also on Instagram.

An intertwined biography of fact and myth which highlights the legacy of liberation, defiance, and creativity left by Sappho, one of history’s most beloved and speculative queer icons. This is a chorus of several artists, writers, and feminists of 19th and 20th century Europe, pushing back against oppression, conventional gender roles, and the male gaze of the arts. After Sappho is an academic thesis of feminine expression and freedom, using bulletins of early western feminism to support the spirit of Sappho as she continues to inspire and defend creative minds.

We had begun so long ago with our poems after Sappho, carefully styled in fragments, our paintings and blushes all done in likeness. Perhaps at last the future of Sappho would be delivered into our hands like a packet of books knotted up with string. For example we might open a seemingly ordinary biography, its chapters neatly partitioned, and find that it was webbed throughout with the most extraordinary filaments of a life. A life after all did not happen by itself, in discrete units. Thus this biography would be bound together with all of our lives, twined through from preface to index: curling, animate, verdant. In the end we might become the readers of our own afterwords. When I started After Sappho I got that same kind of breathless feeling that I had when I read Naomi Alderman’s The Power or Emma Cline’s The Girls — that deep-gut reaction to having feminist truths named that had formerly only been experienced — and I luxuriated in author Selby Wynn Schwartz’s lyrical prose; was intrigued by her episodic biographies of women who dared to break the patriarchal molds they had been born into. But as the book proceeded, it began to feel less like a novel and more like a textbook or a series of Wikipedia entries: it read as all surface, no depth; all sizzle, no steak. It became a bit of a slog — despite frequent yummy prose — and while I admire the effort, and appreciate what I learned, this, unfortunately, did not satisfy me novelistically. (Note: I read an ARC through NetGalley and passages quoted may not be in their final form.) We longed for writing tables that were not in the kitchen, stained with onions; we wanted to read the novels kept from us because they were decadent and suggestive; we wanted to exchange the finger-pricked linens of our trousseaus for travel guides and foreign grammars; we wanted to meet each other in rooms and discuss the rights of women, we wanted to close the doors to the rooms and lie in each other’s arms, the light pouring in the window, the curtains drawn back, the view over the bay running in cerulean and azure swaths into the open sea. We dreamed of islands where we could write poems that kept our lovers up all night. In our letters, we murmured the fragments of our desires to each other, breaking the lines in our impatience. We were going to be Sappho, but how did Sappho begin to become herself? Covering a period between the 1880s and the 1920s (and mostly centering on queer white women from Western Europe), Schwartz sketches the lives of women artists familiar to me (Sarah Bernhardt, Isadora Duncan, Gertrude Stein, or Virginia Woolf among others), and many more names unfamiliar. And while I was moved by Sibilla Aleramo’s early experiences of watching her mother dive out the window, and being married off to her rapist (as per Italian law at the time), or learning of Radclyffe Hall and her efforts to convince the British House of Lords that she was as fine a gentleman as any of them, there were so many unfamiliar names, criss-crossing each others’ paths over the years, that the storyline became both confusing and tedious to me. And because these lives are treated at a surface-level, with no effort made at exploring these women’s interiority, the lyrical Greek chorus/fragments from Sappho bits just added to the confusion instead of elevating the material. Readers according to Colette were like lovers. The best were attentive, intelligent, exigent, and promiscuous. She urged us to read widely and well, to seek out precisely the novels prohibited to us and lie down for hours in bed with them. We should read to gorge and sate ourselves, Colette enjoined us; after a good book we should lick our fingers. I wish that this book had impelled me to lick my fingers in its aftermath, but despite its initial promise, I lost engagement with this material pretty quickly. Certainly not a waste of my time, but simply not to my taste.

'But life itself was in constant variance, Virginia Woolf protested, a novel ought to run alongside it the way the shadow of a railway carriage travels over the landscape. Now rising fleetingly along a low wall, now falling away into a riverbed, passing its silhouette unevenly over grass and gravel: that was a novel, that was the spirit of a life moving on a page. Is it not the task of the novelist, Virginia Woolf demanded, to convey this varying, this unknown and uncircumscribed spirit, whatever aberration or complexity it may display?' After Sappho is many things. It is the story feminism, sapphism and the artistic (and otherwise) emancipation of women, it is the story of Modernism as seen through the lens of myriad (female)artists, it is the story of how language can help define relationships, it is the story of the rise fascism and how the background informs the foreground; It is a history of great women producing great works of art; it is, itself, a Great Work of Art. Written in sharp, vivid and often sumptuous poetic prose (birds are everywhere), After Sappho plots the lives of multiple women (Amongst whom; Virginia Woolf, Gertrude Stein, Natalie Barney, Colette), each inspired by Sappho (or inspired by people inspired by the words of Sappho) to be the writer of their own lives. The lives interweave -in a way most redolent of Sebald- over a period of thirty or so years, ending with the publication of what one must assume is the biggest inspiration behind After Sappho itself. I found myself regularly looking into the lives of the artists referred to, not because I required context, but because there was so much I didn’t know, and wanted to. Its confidence in itself is astonishing- I didn’t know I wanted to know so much about these people (hadn’t heard of plenty) and now I want nothing more than to read everything by them all. A fantastic, educational and often very funny debut novel by a staggeringly talented writer.

2022 BOOKER PRIZE LONGLIST CHALLENGE AFTER SAPPHO by Selby Wynn Schwartz *** After the surprise hit DUCKS, NEWBURYPORT was shortlisted for the Booker Prize a few years ago, Galley Beggar Press wrote a long essay about how difficult the process was for tiny presses (required to provide tons of free copies, being able to keep up with the demand shortlisting involves). It was nice to see Galley Beggar keep its foot in the water though, submitting the experimental, blazing, feminist AFTER SAPPHO for consideration. Told through short vignettes, Schwartz delves into the lives of several women artists at the end of the nineteenth and beginning of the twentieth centuries. Novelists, poets, painters, performers, all inspired in some way by the radical and separatist traditions of the Greek poet Sappho, we get into their minds, hear their artistic justifications, all eager to create space for art focused on women, outside the male gaze, even when that gaze insists on scrutinizing and vilifying. It is filled with intellect and history, Schwartz placing the art into the middle of women’s political struggles for autonomy and citizenship. At times AFTER SAPPHO is riveting, especially when the women’s art begins to intertwine with tumultuous and revolutionary era that was throwing into question institutions that once felt indominable, including the most patriarchal ones. But there wasn’t enough of this and it felt like Schwartz skirted and avoided some of the more interesting developments in women’s struggle in the period after the First World War because her interest felt more situated in a space devoid of men, even when those spaces were occupied with common struggle of women and men. That’s a fair artistic and thematic choice but it also felt something was lost. It didn’t help that the feminism of AFTER SAPPHO felt narrow, especially for something written in 2022. It felt white, Western and very privileged and again this takes away from the punch the novel could have had. AFTER SAPPHO is ambitious in form and style, the most so of the ones I have read, but the structure (quickly changing perspectives, the very short vignettes) brings with it a loss of momentum for a reader and unfortunately for me that only furthered my issues with the themes and how they were explored. I wouldn’t be shocked if this was shortlisted but I doubt it at this time.

Haunting, hypnotic, delightful and remarkably well written and researched, this hybrid novel will stay with you for an incredibly long time. Part biography, part slice of life, part novel, After Sappho is first and foremost a reflection on queer womanhood and literature, an ode to language and its cathartic power. Through the lives of extraordinary women, Selby Wynn Schwartz weaves together biography and social commentary, gender studies and the classics to illuminate the spaces that queer women have carved for themselves throughout history. The prose is dense and poetic, the material extraordinarily well researched, and the characters fascinating and tormented by then flame of literature, a spark that survived then erasure of some of them and connect their writing to Sappho and History itself.

Overall I thought it was boring even though the idea behind it was really intriguing.

This is one flighty book. One which defies classification too, as even it admits, in the afterward. And the purpose is the main point of the book, so revealing it would be a spoiler and ruin the fun. But it is a series of vignettes, fictional mixed with non-fiction, through various characters. It charts around 150 years of history. It’s form and function is paired to Sappho’s fragmentary work. This, to be honest, made it simultaneously fast to read and difficult to actually pay attention to. You are constantly getting resituated in space and time and a new character. It’s a bit of a puzzle, and one that can be really frustrating sometimes. Things do come together with enough patience. And I do typically gravitate towards stuff that is unconventional, so I’m somewhat predisposed to extending a fair amount of good faith to even new-to-me authors. I doubt this is actually a novel, though comprised technically of a lot of short snippets of stories. I am also not sure what else it is, though it goes into that after the end, if you’re curious, and you can figure where you’re at with it yourself. Prose wise, I liked it. The format makes it so it’s quite poetic but it is also grounded in what is concretely happening in the life of the character, typically. It gets in, gets out. It’s unabashedly angry, rightly so, when charting the path of men oppressing women. Probably put some people off but it didn’t bother me even slightly. And a special note: I highly recommend you get this in the hardcover binding from the US coming, because the paperback UK has really crap binding. The gutter is terrible and so tight, it’s actually annoying to keep the pages apart, almost like a mass market paperback, but oversized.

My favourite books take biography, existing literary material, and smash it together into something completely new. After Sappho takes this to a dizzying extreme, a whirlwind of lesbians and sapphists from the cultural past who intersect, find their own paths, and communicate in the most beautiful ways. The result is an extraordinary novel which has forced me to pick up the pen once more on my own.

"An invert is not exactly someone thought backwards. An invert is someone thought in a different order. A part that others display on the outside, like a bronze breastplate, is instead chambered in the heart. Or inverts may have their warmest parts turned outwards, like orchids or octopuses". This book is a collection of voices of some trailblazing inverts. A scrapbook of vignettes flaunting tales of empowerment and resilience of some queer women from history in late 19th century and early 20th century and the connections they brewed over love and art. Challenging the chains of civil codes and artistic restrictions imposed on them, "these little vines" documents the disruptive creative energies of women like Virginia Woolf, Natalie Barney, Romaine Brooks, Vita Sackville- West, Lina Poletti, Isadora Duncan, Sara Bernhadt, Gertrude Stein and Radclyff Hall. Spread across domains of fiction, art, essays, music and dance, these women, identifying as daughters of Sappho, sketched themselves vehemently into a tradition which viewed them as misfits and preferred their silence. "It was time for women to write into being what they want to." Like its women, the book transcends generic boundaries. There is biography, imagination, poetry all in one. Like its women united by the strengths of their identity, the narrative moves ahead in the voice of 'we'. An ode to Sappho's Greek chorus and solidarity binding women across the history. I had some of Sappho's fragments in my MA syllabus and I am overwhelmed by how much Schwartz's poetic language exudes the elegance and lyrical finesse of Sappho's fragments.

'As long as we stayed in the rooms of Natalie Barney, we felt, we would be lit from within by the images of what we could be. On Fridays at Natalie’s we thought of Sappho: Evening/you gather back/all that dazzling dawn has put asunder. But Romaine Brooks, exasperated by our poetic and overheated rooms, demurred. Amazons, not nymphs, Romaine said brusquely. And no one is going back to those islands.’

“Aurel hoped that women writers would disobey the laws that bound men’s books. It was time for women to take language for themselves, Aurel said, even one word at a time, to take their own names and become. To become even one word.” The most honest review I could write about this book is that I finished it. I could wax eloquently about the writing style, the poetic nature of words deployed and the reimagination of lives lived - but it does not explain the helplessness I felt in placing real people whom I did not know about, whose lives the author seemed to infiltrate. The women, mostly artists and authors, had to break the societal expectation of women in favor of choice in their personal lives brandishing their love for Sappho and lesbian love. The voice is a collective "we" that bucket characters across time. They have to resort to convention to express themselves in art forms - a male character who is actually a woman in the author's mind. The problem for me is the writing style which did not account for readers who may lack context. Who may need to know the writing is a lot more than poetic brilliance. Quoting Sappho from time to time throws you off and the social commentary, though intriguing in parts becomes nothing more than an instant emotion that has no bearing on the rest of the story. Not for me.

This was a lovely homage to Sappho and her words. Schwartz really shows how she has made an impact through history, in different ways for different generations. What I liked the most was how it showed the connections between authors and their context, and the femininity that coarses through it. I don't like poetry and "highbrow" literature very much, so I didn't care about the extracts and how she inspired literature that much, more about women and their lives in general.
Probably the slowest book for my Booker Prize list. The message is there but…maybe just not for me.

Everything about this novel is fragmentary. The structure, in small broken sections, the inspiration being the broken pieces of Sappho’s verses, even the observations of some of the characters: ‘Some art can only be written in fragments’, says Sibilla Aleramo. One of the things that I love about the ancient Greek poet Sappho is that her scholarship can never be static. By that I mean new verses and fragments are constantly being added to her known works. No doubt scholars argue back and forth in learned journals about whether the latest fragment is really by Sappho or just some pale imitator. Given the brevity of some of the pieces, how would they ever know? Anne Carson translated her in ‘If not, Winter’ in 2003, but a whole new poem of Sappho’s came to light in 2014, rendering all previous translations incomplete. It must be a challenge to any classical scholar that an archaeological discovery could overthrow years of scholarship at any moment. One of the observations made by one of the characters in After Sappho is ‘Our lives are the missing lines from the fragments.’ This is what the whole book does, adds to the little we know with a sprinkle of something else. One of my favourite quotes from the book reads: We imagined Sappho watching us, expectant or even impatient, waiting for her future to arrive in the form of us. We thought of Virginia Woolf: short pieces from life now. Yes, said Romaine Brooks, enough lyric poetry. Not another still life with flowers. More portraits of us. What the book so eloquently does is to chart the lives of a group of feminists, Sapphists, artists, writers and actors through the late 1800s to the 1920s. I love the way we follow the fortunes of various women who rebel against the outdated order of society, against the suppression of women, their treatment as property and their marriages to unsuitable men. I love that there are women who change, who are fluid, even their names are not set in stone. When the novelist asks her name, Rina said it was Sibilla, like the Sybil of Delphi. A new name was like a blank notebook; Rina could write herself into it with a folio of fresh pages she could write herself into becoming Sibilla, enigmatic and sibilant. We move back and forth across a wide cast of characters, until it is only by frequent repetition of one or two that we begin to discern out central figures. Throughout the weaving stories there are wonderful flashes of brilliance, take for example this description: Anna Kuliscioff had sung for her supper in the parks of northeastern Ukraine, she had survived tuberculosis and childbirth and exile: the only thing she feared was compromise, the soothing voice that licks down rage until it is nothing but a small smooth lump in your hand. We constantly bounce around characters and years. I can see that this might put some readers off, disrupting the flow of the narrative, but what it does allow is the constant forging of new connections, for example where characters come back into the story. The book is all about women, so that when a man does turn up, in the form of London cabman William Seymour, it is quite a shock. Until we learn that his real name was Margaret Honeywell. We never learn the name of his wife. Themes of feminine creativity constantly circle fluid identity. Names and sexes will change throughout. Words and language are other themes we frequently return to. A particular word or case are often highlighted. The vocative occurs in one place to give us the poet talking about herself, ‘Sappho, why?’ I had never heard of the optative before, but listen to the beauty of this description: In ancient Greek, to utter a wish or a hope, there is the optative. The optative is a mood, almost a feeling. It hovers in the air just outside of time or subject, wistful in colour, its edges slightly tinged with foreboding. A new word that I learnt was ‘lucubrare’ which is a verb that means to think by lamplight. I never knew how much I needed such a word. Schwartz is a scholar of French and Italian comparative literature, and her feminist selections are drawn heavily from this milieu, although more familiar names gradually enter the stage; Colette, Sarah Bernhardt, Gertrude Stein, Virginia Woolf and Vita Sackville-West. As we progress, there is more and more from Virginia Woolf and her lover Vita Sackville-West. We watch Virginia developing the inspiration for a novel, until at last she fixes upon the idea of Orlando. The pair write each other, making each other up. ‘Bit by bit they laid out their lives for each other as if they were swaths of coloured fabric on the table.’ Woolf’s love-letter-novel was, in 1928, a landmark in the writing of sexually fluid characters. At one point we see Virginia working at the Hogarth Press: At first Virginia Woolf has set up each letter in the place herself; added the flourish of titles and frontpieces; blown the ink dry with her own breath, for the first book she had also stitched the spine in red yarn, so that when the pages lay open it was like a bright day in winter: the snowy margins, the black stick-legs of birds hopping towards the red berries in the rowan tree. It reminded me of Jeanette Winterson’s fine collection of essays, Art Objects, in which she talks about the joy of owning early editions from the Hogarth Press, just for the knowledge that they were once handled by Virginia herself. The end of the book arrives very suddenly in the form of a three-page afterword which attempts to wrap up the biography of Lina Poletti, the person with whom we began the book: We wrote the lives of Lina Poletti, but did not always understand them. In some way Lina was always beyond us. She would crest a wave that left us thrashing for breath. These lives are beautifully captured at points throughout the book, and I especially liked the way Schwartz describes Lina’s love letters: …when Lina desired someone she would often change her name. Ardent, mysterious letters would arrive to you from whoever Lina was, Sibilla said, and you simply had to know. Or you guessed, because it could not have been anyone else. The letters were like hushed breaths on the back of your neck: you wanted to turn around and embrace them, but you also wanted to wait, feeling them arrive one after the other, steady and thrilling. What impressed me most about the book is that although the fragments are set at least a century, if not many centuries, ago, the novel manages to feel modern and contemporary. This year the Booker Prize has three debutant novelists on the longlist of thirteen, but After Sappho must rank as the most experimental. And one of the most pleasing.

Early on there is a line about how many people die in childbirth and there are far less that die in shipwrecks. That line sums up the drive of the restless characters from this book perfectly. This is a book about women who long for adventure. Who don't fear the unknown or the dangerous precisely because they are crushingly aware of the certainty of their deaths merely from staying where they are. Death finds you wherever you are, wouldn't you rather be a challenge for him? To have him find you in a hot air balloon, instead of on a toilet? All it would take is a revolution. A rejection of society's demands. How hard could that be? This is a book about a collection of defiant and resourceful women that really lived and rejected the lives expected of them. Who charted a new course for their lives; often encountering enormous obstacles and not always making it through unscathed. People who held a torch to light the way for countless others. Literary fiction at its finest. It isn't an easy read, but it is infinitely rewarding. It makes use of condensed snapshots of their lives. Moving quickly, it never drops pace. Spectacular staccato blasts of insight into the lives of fascinating women from history. You've got to marvel at a narrative that uses small fragments to build a stepping stone pathway connecting multiple lives. It takes skill for a writer to pull at all, let alone this well. This is definitely a book to be read multiple times, so there is no shame in the first reading bringing nothing more than scrumptious descriptions and emotive quotes. It is a perfect book to underline things in. And it presents plenty of sharp humour to temper the hardships laid out. From the publisher of Ducks, Newburyport I'd expect nothing less. A novel that challenges convention as powerfully as the women it faithfully conjures into being.

Oh, this was wonderful! After Sappho is a novelization of the lives of various historical women, from Vita and Virginia to Colette and Josephine Baker, who all came, well, after Sappho. Artists, sapphics, writers, feminists. Not necessarily non-fiction, we get to glimpse into their lives and work in short vignettes, going back and forth in time to see how they fight for a better future for women, while also seeing how their lives might occasionally intertwine. Another reviewer called this hopeful and a novel of movement, and that's exactly what it is. The way it's written, in this unique, poetic, nearly short story-like way, works perfectly for what it's trying to do. It truly caught me by surprise because I don't think it's necessarily what I thought it would be when I bought it on a semi-sunny day back last autumn while going home after defending my MA thesis, but it managed to be so much more, so much better than I imagined. I highly recommend it!

Elliptical and fragmentary, After Sappho takes a form that reminds me Maggie Nelson's Argonauts or Sarah Baume's Seven Steeples, but is not as successful as either of these. Schwartz focuses on the development of a lesbian or sapphist identity in early 20th century Europe, and the group of sapphists that grew up around Natalie Barney's opulent salon in Paris. Schwartz draws on a range of figures from this time, including well-known writers such as Virginia Woolf and Gertrude Stein, and figures who are less well-known to me, often from Italian or French backgrounds. These women are all brought together by their identification with Sappho, and the way in which they use Sappho to explain their own attraction for women, and to develop a culture around female desire. It's an uneven book: I found its premise interesting, but its fragmentary style can feel disjointed or meandering, and I got very bogged down in the middle, while other sections are very moving or exciting. Schwartz chooses to use the first-person plural (we) to write from the perspective of all lesbians -- or maybe all queer women who are in Barney's circle -- echoing the choral we from Greek plays. For me, this was not successful: the choral sections are clunky and frustrating, and I found the idea that the "we" spoke for all queer women troubling. There is a lot that is interesting here, and I find it works better for me if I think of the book as being in conversation with other queer histories. I also think that this would have absolutely blown me away if I'd read it ten years ago: ageing makes some stories seem obvious when they would have once felt new, and I can't blame Schwartz for that!

Well, let me kick this off with a little confession: I didn’t exactly fall in love with Phantasma. In fact, I struggled with it and found myself hesitating to dive into the second book of the Wicked Games series. I kept wondering—does this sequel really deserve all the hype? But then, one of my guilty pleasures came to mind: Ready or Not—especially that iconic line: “– Jesus Christ, what happened to you? – In-laws!” That movie is pure gold, and the pitch “Ready or Not meets Throne of the Fallen” felt like a siren song I simply couldn’t resist. Add in the fact that purple is my absolute favorite color (and that cover? Drop-dead gorgeous!), I thought: “What have you got to lose?” And wow—was I glad I gave it a chance! This book completely exceeded my expectations. It delivered all my favorite tropes in one go: enemies-to-lovers, forced proximity, a marriage of inconvenience, and yes—my beloved locked room mystery vibes. Oh, and let’s talk about the chemistry. Rowin and Genevieve brought the heat—so much steam, the pages practically fogged up! I’m a sucker for spice, and this one had enough to make you sweat, gasp, and maybe fan yourself a little. 🔥 Beyond the romance, the twisted family dynamics of the Silver siblings were absolutely delicious. Dysfunctional? For sure—especially when your family tradition involves hunting each other down every equinox due to a devil’s curse. But they’re also fascinating. Sevin, with his irresistible charm and sweet tooth, completely stole my heart. I need a whole book about him! But I’d also happily dive into stories centered on the darkly magnetic Grave, the mysterious and chaotic Covin, the softer, more shadowed Remi, and the enigmatic Wells (who I hope we get to know better soon). And Ellin—the only sister in the clan—was such a standout: sharp-tongued, fiercely independent, and a powerful healer. She’s begging for her own story too! The plot kicks off with Genevieve Grimm trying to find peace on an Italian vacation, still reeling from her mother’s death, the trauma of the Phantasma competition, and the emotional wreckage left by a lover who shattered her trust in relationships. Following a trail of crows and a series of letters between her mother and the mysterious Barrington Silver, Genevieve winds up at the Silver family’s imposing estate. But instead of meeting Barrington, she’s greeted—rudely, might I add—by his son, Rowin, who promptly slams the door in her face. Challenge accepted. Little does Genevieve know, she’s arrived at the worst possible time—Equinox. Thanks to Barrington’s deal with a demon named Knox, the entire Silver family is now immortal and cursed to play a deadly game of hide-and-seek every equinox. To survive, she must become one of them… which means marrying into the family. Cue a spontaneous wedding with none other than Rowin—the grumpy guy who tried to kick her out just moments ago. Suddenly, Genevieve’s stuck in a blood-soaked, high-stakes game where trust is scarce and danger lurks around every corner. She doesn’t trust Rowin—or anyone, really—but the more they face together, the harder it becomes to deny the electric tension between them. As her feelings shift and their connection deepens, she has to face the terrifying truth: survival might cost her more than she expected—especially her heart. And let’s be honest… she’s definitely not ready. Overall: This was a wildly addictive, adrenaline-fueled rollercoaster of a read! A perfect blend of fantasy, high-stakes suspense, irresistible romance, and jaw-dropping twists. I devoured it and now I’m begging for more! Sequels, spin-offs, bonus scenes—I’ll take it all. I loved everything there is to love in this book: world, magic system, side characters, location, vibes, premise, and MCs. What I did not feel fully satisfied with however, is: Rowin’s character elaboration and th romance. Also, I can never forget about Laura Horowitz's narration 🤌🏻🤌🏻🤌🏻👌🏻👌🏻 Rowin, your shadow sin from Hell 😈 This man has literally EVERYTHING: Backstory ✅ personality ✅ depth ✅ magic ✅ sinful mouth ✅ haunted gaze ✅ trauma and sadness ✅ protective ✅ possessive ✅ capacity to love deeply and unconditionally ✅ Unfortunately for us, not all of this was explored fully on page. We knew it was there, but we rarely got to see him wield his magic, open up about his guilt, or dive deep into his relationship with his family. It felt like all these layers existed, but we weren’t allowed to savour them. The Romance 💔➡️❤️ Because the story is mainly from Genevive’s POV, we saw her emotions so clearly, but not enough of Rowin’s. We got glimpses of tension and attraction, but I craved a few more pages of his side: his thoughts, his feelings, his growth. The pacing was perfect and proportionate for the book’s length, but I wanted to feel the depth of their bond, not just know it’s there. Moments We Were Robbed Of 🥲 • Genevive has haunting nightmares that relate to her love life and her self-worth and image, but we got no intimate scene of vulnerability there nor Rowin soothing her. • Rowin’s magic requires deep sleep to recharge, but we got no moment where he was vulnerable and needed care and Genevive was able to show her protective and caring nature. These two scenes alone would’ve enriched the romance massively, and it’s a shame they weren’t there. Could’ve Been Longer 📖 This book could’ve been 100 pages longer, and I’d eat it up. Nothing was unnecessary. But more POV from Rowin, more family dynamics (Rowin & his family, Genevive & Ophelia), and more world-plot development would’ve only made it stronger. Family clearly plays a huge role in this series, and it deserved more space here. The Bigger Picture 🌌 This instalment is clearly bridging toward book 3 and setting up the overarching plot. And while I have a lot of burning questions, I also have predictions 👀: • Book 3 = dual POV (likely Sevin). • Book 4 = multi-POV, connecting all the MCs for the final resolution (calling it now it will be named: Nocturnia). The Ending 🤨 No spoilers, but I wasn’t fully sold on the last 10%. Some choices felt forced, like props to push the romance or open doors for future books, when there were other, more natural options available given the powers in play. This was an incredible ride with a rich world and characters I adore, but I needed more from Rowin, more vulnerability, and a bit more care with the resolution. Still, I’m absolutely hooked and already desperate for the next book. -- Pre-read: 🪄 Entering Enchantra like: hex me, wreck me, and maybe resurrect me if you’re feeling kind. 4 stars! ☆ ⤿ major spoilers ﹒⟢ i didn’t expect to like this. i thought it’d be the same as the last one—cool concept, flat execution, characters i didn’t care about. but this was actually fun. like genuinely fun. i liked the plot. i liked the romance. i even liked the characters. especially rowin. was i still annoyed sometimes? obviously. but i had a good time. i remembered nothing from the first book. didn’t even realize this was ophelia’s sister until someone said it. and that didn’t matter at all. this felt completely separate. i was interested immediately—creepy invitation, gothic italian estate, weird family with secrets. it basically gave ready or not but with magic, and it worked. the crows, the train ride, the gate—it was already more interesting than anything in phantasma. and then she gets there and immediately gets the door slammed in her face. i was sold. genevieve made some of the dumbest decisions i’ve ever seen. she eats random berries off a gate. she trespasses into someone’s house after being told to leave. she expects strangers to want to help her. she expects a man she’s never met to talk about her trauma with her. like. what are you doing. and she doesn’t stop. she just keeps pushing back against everything like she has a choice. she argues with everyone who’s actually trying to help her and makes it harder for them—like they clearly know more than she does, but she refuses to listen. you walk into a magical murder house and think you’re gonna reason your way out? she does get better eventually, but for a while i wanted to shake her. honestly, the plot was one of the best parts. the whole magical loophole marriage thing was just fun. it made everything feel more tense, and i liked that there was an actual goal instead of everyone just running around. the game itself was chaotic in a good way, and something was always happening. i did freak out at the memory loss part—i hate that trope—but it didn’t end up bothering me. the ring, the letters, all of it actually worked. it was cute. i’ll allow it. rowin was easily the best part. from the second he told her to leave and slammed the door in her face, i knew. he was blunt, dramatic, and so over everything. and the romance? it worked. it really did. the fake dating turned into actual trust, and it didn’t really feel rushed. their banter was fun. their dynamic made sense. i liked seeing them go from reluctantly working together to something real. and his siblings were unhinged but entertaining. the names were ridiculous but also kinda cool—i weirdly liked them. definitely better characters this time around. some of the dialogue was weird. genevieve said a lot of insane shit. and the logic? not always there. but i was having fun, so i didn’t care. this gave me everything i wanted the first book to have. and now i’m actually excited for the third one. didn’t think i’d be saying that. ━━━━ ⊱⋆⊰ ━━━━ ☆ 🖇️ pre-read 𖥻 ＜꒱ wasn't a huge fan of the first book, but this setup sounds way more promising. trying not to get my hopes up too much. wicked games ⌗﹒ 01 phantasma — 3.25 ☆ ⌗﹒ 02 enchantra — 4 ☆

I am in love with the way that Kaylie writes. Her pacing. Her prose. Her characters. This world and this setting. It is just fabulous!! I was intrigued to learn this book was about Genevieve and knew that the bar had been set VERY high with how much I enjoyed Phantasma. But yall this book meets the HYPE!! Kaylie created a whole new world in this world. One with delicious depravity and NEW wonderful characters. I found myself saying I want there to be a book for each one of Rowin's siblings. Can we all talk about the endings of their names are all ington IYKYK! My heart broke a little for WHY Genevieve was taking this journey. She had seen her sister find her person and felt a little untethered. She did not have the relationship with her mom that Ophelia did. She had her heart broken by a man who she thought was her forever. She just wasn't in a good head space. And her entering Enchantra was just fate I think. Rowin was beyond a grump borderline jerk. BUT we learned his behavior was a protection layer. This family was stuck in a terrible curse and each of the siblings had learned to cope with it in their own ways. Rowin and Genevieve were the definition of enemies to lovers. There was an INSTANT connection but he was so rude and vague to Genevieve and kept pulling the rug out from under her that she didn't know how to trust him. She actually kind of hated him. Kaylie did a great job of letting their relationship morph. As we all know there is a fine line between love and hate. And watching them cross that line was pretty delicious. I loved that Rowin was a shadow daddy! I feel like I need to start ranking those LOL. Anyways these two were bonded and in a short period of time realized that their relationship though *fake* meant something to them both. Genevieve feels a little lost. All she wants is to find out more about her family. She doesn't want to bother her sister since she is in bliss with her love. So she does what she does best- she finds trouble. She ends up at a mansion after being summoned. She meets Rowin almost immediately and dislikes him just as quickly. Why is he being so rude and trying to make her leave? He won't get rid of her that quickly. And now that plan backfired because Genevieve is to be included in their annual rite. The one where Knox, a powerful demon, has all of the siblings (all 7 of them) fight to the death to entertain his people. The one caveat to being able to leave this place is if one of them gets married. Which is how Genevieve finds herself kissing and wedding Rowin before the ceremony begins. Now she is supposed to trust him to protect her throughout this whole thing. She doesn't trust him one bit. She KNOWS there is more going on that he isn't telling her. But then he slowly starts to show her his cards. About how his mother is involved and this ceremony prolongs her life. How he has been searching for a cure during his year away after he has won the ceremony. How he actually really loves his siblings so much and how it is beyond hard to have to kill them over and over again. Should she trust him with all of this? Because he starts to tell her more. About how he feels for her. And how much he is attracted to her. But this can't go anywhere right? She is either going to die or leave after they win. But she can't help the attraction and what they share goes beyond anything she has experienced. And now she is imagining a future. She is plotting along side him and his family to help them get out of this horrible situation. Because even though she didn't think she would she has learned more about her family and she has FOUND her partner and LOVES his family. They just have to figure out how to do all of this and plot twist a demon without giving anything away. I think the only thing I didn't like about this book was that I wanted MORE! I wanted more of the siblings and their banter. More spice between Genevieve and Rowin (since it happened so late in the book). More shenanigans in the house with the familiars. I like that we don't know EVERYTHING because that leaves SO much that Kaylie can still teach us. I loved that we had new species (?) in this? We got introduced to wraiths- blood, shadow and void I believe. This series and book have everything I love in a fantasy. I also like the added bonus that it is set in a city that we are familiar with but in a different time. If you haven't picked this series or book up- do it! I can't recommend it enough!! Now I have to find the chapter in Rowin's POV LOL. I am guessing book 3 is going to involve Sevin and his ex (pretty please because that sounded so intriguing!!).

3.7 Stars One Liner: Dark and entertaining Genevieve Grimm has been adrift since her sister became the head of her family after their mother’s death. So, when she got an invitation to attend an event in a grand palace in Italy, she jumped at the chance. Rowin Silver doesn’t want complications or outsiders in his home. No point in risking more lives in a game where none can win. He shuts the door on Genevieve’s face only to realize she snuck in without his notice. Now, the two form an alliance to compete as lovers, hoping to increase their chances of survival. But with Rowin keeping many secrets, Genevieve wonders about her chances. The story comes in Genevieve’s third-person POV. My Thoughts: The book works as a standalone, but there are references to the previous one and a spoiler. This cannot be helped. If you are particular about spoilers, you may want to read that first. While Phantasma was no masterpiece, it was a fluffy read with a good dose of spice; something to grab when you want to stay entertained (and not use your brain cells). This is pretty much the same. Both books are huge (464 pages) and paced on the slower side, so pick them up accordingly. Genevieve is Ophelia’s (heroine of Phantasma) young sister, someone who spends her time fluttering around like a butterfly to avoid her feelings of abandonment. In this, she thinks an entry into Enchantra would help her find others like her, but little did she know she’d be fighting for her life. She is quirky, curious (worse than a cat), mouthy, and messy. She is entertaining too, what with her penchant for getting into trouble often. Rowin is your dark, grumpy, brooding, alpha guy with a soft heart, which is revealed over time. He has tattoos and piercings (some of those must have really, really hurt), which add to the vibe. Also, those shadows he controls! Given the genre, we have to accept that things will get gruesome and bloody in The Hunt, as well as result in some spicy scenes. I felt this was a bit less extensive in spice than the previous one, which is a good thing. Not that there isn’t attraction or the other stuff, but on a slightly smaller scale, say 3.5 to 4. The setting is great, of course. It’s creepy, atmospheric, and suffocating. What with the devil and other dangers, this is not a house you’d want to visit. Oh, those mirrors! Be warned if you have eisoptrophobia or spectrophobia. The side characters are the siblings (and fellow participants) in the Hunt. I felt they were done well. Each of them has a definite personality and is easy to track. Though we don’t get a lot of detail about everyone, we know enough to form a picture. The climax felt relatively bland (compared to book one). It seemed a bit too easy. Still, after reading 400+ pages by then, I was ready for the ending. There’s quite a bit of gore, but it’s written in a matter-of-fact manner. I didn’t feel put off by it (nor did it frighten me in the least). However, this may vary based on your reading preferences. Maybe gore level 3.5 on the scale of 5? The ending is HFN and partly open, providing a lead to the next book. Though we don’t have the details yet, there has to be book three. Someone needs to answer the remaining questions! To summarize, Enchantra is a dark horror romance with devils, immortals, hunting games, and a dose of spice. The best way to enjoy the book is not to think much. Forget logic and go where it takes you! Thank you, NetGalley and Second Sky/ Forever, for eARC. This review is voluntary and contains my honest opinion about the book. #NetGalley #Enchantra

Updated Review: OBSESSED is an UNDERSTATEMENT! A cursed palace in the Italian countryside, an arrogant shadow daddy with tattoos and piercings galore, who happens to be a wraith, a competition run by an evil devil, a marriage of convenience, baroque ballrooms, masquerades a trip into hell, sisterhood and more, may I present, one of my most anticipated releases of this year, Enchantra by Kaylie Smith. Both Phantamsa & Enchantra have done something to the inner workings of my soul where I feel a physical pull towards the books that make them impossible to put down. I legitimately feel like a teen fangirl swooning and screaming over like One Direction. That is how obsessed I am with this world, these books and these characters. Enchantra follows our new FMC, Genevieve, who has fled her hometown of New Orleans and gone to Italy in search of something more, a purpose, and some answers regarding all of the secrets her family has kept from her. If you don't know, Genevieve is the younger sister of the FMC from Phantasma. While in Rome, Genevieve receives a mysterious seemingly magical invitation that brings her to a stunning hidden palace in the countryside where she is greeted by the very handsome, rude and mysterious Rowington AKA Rowin. He demands that she leave the premises, but driven by curiosity and a desire to find out more about her mother, Genevieve slips inside and instantly regrets it as she finds herself in the midst of a very deadly game between Rowin and his family. As it turns out, Rowin and his siblings are wraiths, and they are locked in an eternal yearly game run by a devil and watched and celebrated by the citizens of Hell, and the catch is there can only be one winner and all of the losers are killed and dragged back to Hell. For Rowin and his siblings, they are immortal, so they don't actually get killed, but for Genevieve, if she does not win, she will actually lose her life. Her only way to survive this game is a fake romantic alliance with Rowin, where the pair must put on the show of their lifetimes for the devil in charge and the citizens of hell. The duo begin this book absolutely detesting each other but as the stakes of the game get higher, their feelings for each other seem to sway as well, which is not ideal since Rowin taught Genevieve that the first rule of Enchantra is to never, ever trust your heart. Enchantra has the same addictive qualities as Phantasma, but the story still felt so fresh and unique especially because of the characters. Genevieve is a PHENOMENAL FMC with a huge louder than life personality. She is hilarious, witty, outspoken, brave, vulnerable and sensitive and I adored her character. She made me laugh so much while also pulling at all of my heartstrings. Vivi's story was really beautiful, because although we love the romance, we also follow her along on her quest to find herself, find her purpose and realize that she is enough and that she matters. We find out that Genevieve is dealing with the aftermath of a traumatic heartbreak, as well as trying to cope with her mother's recent passing, and dealing with the negligence she experienced from her mother her entire life. And trust me when I say you girls are going to adore Rowin, he is swoon worthy, he is drool worthy, he is a morally grey moody shadow wraith with tattoos, a lip piercing, other piercings and his romance with Vivi is exceptional. They definitely give grumpy sunshine in the best way possible. Also, if you were wondering, yes, yes we do get a Blackwell cameo, and I did in fact screech because if you did not know he is my favorite book boyfriend. Finally, I do want to give a shoutout to Kaylie Smith's writing, Addictive does not cover it like I need this series like I need air. Although obviously this is a dark gothic world, Kaylie's writing style is almost light hearted and whimsical in a way that makes it feel like a gothic rom com and I mean that as the highest compliment. The chemistry in the romance is palpable on every page and I found myself laughing SO much throughout this book because Kaylie infused so much humor into this story and I loved every moment. The Wicked Games series is already one of my favorite series ever, like I want to live in this world so badly I don't even care.

I hope the next book comes out quickly, because the last chapter made me gasp out loud. Talk about a cliffhanger!
