Brandon's review: I read this since it is our August book club pick, and would give this book a 3.5 to a 4 star rating. I don't think I need to summarize the events of the book, since Cora did it so eloquently below! I will keep my review brief. I read the The Guest List by the author a while ago, so I had mixed feelings about starting this book. I really disliked almost every character in that book, where they felt cartoonish at times with how bad of people they were. Compared to this book where they were portrayed more realistically (I actually liked Jess as a main character). I enjoyed the relationships between characters and contrast in behaviors with Ben and Jess with their upbringing and interactions with the rest of the cast. The constant POV changes in this book contributed more to the story in this book versus the multitude in the previous book that felt unnecessary. I liked the storyline and the mystery in this book more as well. The one thing in my opinion that the previous book had over this one is that the atmosphere and the setting were better. I ended up liking this book more than I expected. Foley's writing was easy to get absorbed into. I wasn’t really surprised by any of the mysteries and twists revealed, but they weren’t as obvious as other books in the genre I’ve read recently. Overall, this was a nice quick read. I have to admit that it got tiresome when all the introductory chapters of each individual ended with pretty much “everything was fine until that man, Ben, got here.” Cora's review: Somewhere between 3 to 3.5 stars The Paris Apartment was an entertaining mystery/thriller taking place in a posh Paris apartment. My rating is based on my being spoiled by The Silent Patient by Alex Michaelides and that some of the twists were a bit easier to guess. All that notwithstanding, I found myself absorbed by the story. Everything was sketchy as soon as the story opens. Our protagonist, Jess, has come to Paris to visit her half-brother, Ben. (view spoiler) Jess is no angel, scrappy and reckless, yet readers will find themselves rooting for her to solve the mystery of this story. Jess arrives at her brother's address, but he's not answering. Of course, Ben is not there to buzz her in. He seems to have vanished into thin air. She has nowhere else to stay, so ends up getting herself into the apartment building with the help of one hostile resident and her own ability to pick-lock doors. Every apartment resident she meets over the course of a tense couple of days treat her as if she's dangerous, and tend to start at her questions of where her brother, Ben, is. Let's just say they all gave off airs of hiding something. It definitely kept me guessing. Let's take inventory. There's the reclusive Mimi, with serious psychological issues. (Serial killer in waiting?) She lives in one of the apartments with her more outgoing, party-girl roommate, Camille. Then there's Antoine, an abusive drunkard, whose wife, Dominique, is leaving during the time this story is set. Antoine's seeming opposite, the Cambridge-educated Nick, seems to be the most normal of them, although he is clearly troubled. Finally, living in the top-floor penthouse, there is Sophie, and her frequently absent husband, (and raging, misogynistic) Jacques. Me @ Jacques: Jess enlists the help of a few people to help her untangle the mystery: Nick, who'd been friends with Ben in their Cambridge days and seems to want to help, and Ben's journalistic contact, Theo. (Although, I was screaming at Jess not to trust Nick, because he was clearly hiding something, like everyone else in the cursed apartment building, even if he was a "nice guy." If there's anything I've learned from the few mystery/thrillers I have read, is to trust no one. Even Theo, I had questions about.) Turns out Ben was working on some sort of investigative piece that he had pitched to Theo before his mysterious disappearance. This is where some things started to click for me in the story. Rich people don't like people like Ben digging into their business. This premise made the story all the more realistic, notwithstanding that in the background, the Yellow Vest protests were happening in other parts of Paris. The whole atmosphere becoming sinister and almost echoing each other. There was the obvious violence of the loud street protests and the more silent, but no less violent happenings in the shadows. This is proven by Jess's various excursions into both the rich and poor sections of Paris in search of clues. Although, I gotta say, the author clearly set up that Ben had been hurt or worse by someone in the apartment building. I was saying to myself, "Ah yes, one of you silenced Ben and the rest of you are covering." But when what ultimately had happened was explained, I was not expecting the twists (in retrospect, I should have) involved. Ultimately, The Paris Apartment was a decent enough story to keep me occupied, a good literary escape into a city I have not had the opportunity to visit yet. 3.5⭐ I finished this last night and I have some thoughts. I adored some of this book and some of it was just okay for me. Firstly what I loved - Being back with these characters felt like catching up with old friends. Richard Osman's humour - I laughed out loud many times reading this. The reference to David Tennant which made me squeal and THEN a reference to Pierce Brosnan with Ron saying Pierce Brosnan was his favourite Bond! (Both David Tennant and Pierce Brosnan were in the Thursday Murder Club movie and Pierce Brosnan plays Ron so this just made my little heart very happy). The exploration of grief. I'm so glad he didn't just sweep Elizabeth's grief under the rug. Now, what I didn't love - I guess the main thing was that the story and the mystery just didn't capture my attention at all. In fact the mystery was very basic, and we've been conditioned by the previous books to expect a very complicated but tight story. This just wasn't it. I saw the "reveal" coming a mile off and even when it happened it was just so anticlimactic. The "heart of the story" was missing. Let me explain - what I love most about these books is that there is always a deeper story underneath the mystery, that delves into love and grief and compassion and morality. This always adds the heart. Without spoiling it, in this book that story was supposed to be about Ron's daughter. But she was barely in it. The book explicitly tells you that this story wasn't about the mystery, it was about that story but I felt no connection to it because we never got to really get to know Ron's daughter. If she was in it more and we maybe had her POV this could have been really impactful - imagine writing an anti domestic violence plot whilst never actually looking at the perspective of the abused person. It made no sense to me that we got so much from Joyce's daughter's POV but not Ron's daughter. The side characters weren't very interesting either. I love how Richard Osman writes his suspects and villains and their characterisation seemed lacking in this book. Not enough Bogdan and Joyce - seriously my two favourite characters didn't even need to be in this book for all they contributed. There is at least some self awareness here with Joyce noting that she hasn't been much help but I thought she would turn it around at the end, and she didn't. Bogdan was wasted in this book. He was basically just Donna's boyfriend and I just missed him. I guess in summary this felt rushed, not well thought out and perhaps a little bit short for what Richard was trying to say, but I still love these characters and his writing so I still had a good time reading it.

It has been a relatively quiet year at Cooper's Chase for the Thursday Murder Club... Elizabeth has been grieving. Ron has been sifting through family matters. Ibrahim has continued to help his special client. Joyce has been busy planning a special event. At the reception, the troubled best man approaches Elizabeth, desperate for help. Without delay, the Thursday Murder Club starts investigating a case involving kidnapping, cracking a code, murder, and more... The Impossible Fortune was worth the two year wait. The author's humorous writing style felt familiar, the short chapters kept the pages flipping quickly, and each character's subplot added texture to the story without feeling too busy or overwhelming. It was nearly perfect! I wanted to hug Elizabeth, but she would have hated that. I loved Joyce's journal entries, which are always a highlight for me. I'm slightly worried about Ron, but seeing him with his grandson warmed my heart. That leaves Ibrahim, whom I adore—enough said. This was an immersive reading experience; the audiobook is narrated by Fiona Shaw, who does it again. I've missed Fiona as much as Elizabeth, Joyce, Ron, and Ibrahim. I can't just read the book. Listening to the audiobook, too, is a must for this series. The Impossible Fortune has themes of friendship, family dynamics, grief, and aging. I'm looking forward to Book #6, and I hope the wait won't be as long! 4.25⭐

There are some mystery series that are fun to follow, just because. Either we grow to love the continuing characters, or value the storytelling of the author, or the creative premise. Which would leave readers with one specific question… Where will the adventure take us in this book? With the Thursday Murder Club (TMC) mystery series, readers follow Elizabeth, Joyce, Ibrahim and Ron. Elizabeth, an ex-spy and TMC club leader; Joyce, a former nurse; Ibrahim, a retired psychiatrist; and, Ron a former union activist all happen to live at the Coopers Chase Retirement Village. Which leads readers to the next question… Who will ask for their help and what rabbit hole will they end up traversing to provide it? For anyone who hasn’t read the series, it is always best to start at the beginning. But even after saying that, this can still be read as a stand-alone with its own mystery to solve. Still, when you start at the beginning of a series, you have a better sense of the characters and their journey from book to book. Another way to ‘meet’ and enjoy these characters is through the recent Netflix movie just released this summer. “The Thursday Murder Club” Official Trailer is here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50DYg... So, why am I reading this one, after recently making the decision to only follow a few mystery series? And, the fact that this particular series was eliminated from my ‘continued reading’ list that would have me choose to pursue it? Well…what do you think happened to this Little Free Library (LFL) Steward? The book was donated to my Little Free Library Shed. A sign I should reconsider? Or just an opportunity to read this particular book? This is the 5th book in the series. It still carries the same wily wittiness we have come to expect of our characters, especially as they navigate their daily lives. Along with their commitment to amateur sleuthing when a ‘situation’ is before them. Yet, it also includes a few more ‘family’ characters brought in to the story who play a stronger role in what happens throughout and with the TMC members. Which makes the heart of this story seemingly less about solving the crime, and more about the characters – where readers can revel in their quirkiness and relationships and reflections. Especially as it relates to aging. And, with aging, this is where the author also does a good job of being realistic, by showcasing the common issues that befall one that is aging – including challenges of family dynamics, issues of grief or loss and friendship. Still, we can’t ignore that this is also a twisted, cozy, engaging, fast-paced, intergenerational mystery that makes us readers question who to trust. Which leads me to… That ending. Hmmm…what shall we make of that? 🤨 (No spoilers from me.) And, finally, in answer to my two questions above about this series, ‘a sign I should reconsider? – or just an opportunity to read this particular book?’, what do you think?

__________________________ Not all that glitters is cryptocurrency. Dear Ms. Publisher: You are probably asking yourself: Self, how many Murder Club series do we need? You may think the Murder Club market is saturated. After all, we already have two series about old codgers, James Patterson’s Women’s Murder Club, a London Ladies Murder Club, and—astonishingly—a Hot Girl Murder Club, a Very Merry Murder Club, and a Murder Club for witches like my ex boss. It is true, you can look it up. And yet, despite this embarrassment of Murder social organizations, one demographic remains tragically underserved: primary school pupils. Here is my book pitch. I will write a series of mysteries called The Recess Murder Club. There are 4 girls, in the club. There’s Jane the science geek, Sally who can spell real good, Luna the de facto leader of the Recess Murder Club, and Red Herring the grumpy ginger kid. Luna’s "San Trope Suzi" doll has been beheaded, her head popped off by some sicko. Is the murderer Luna’s little sister Puff, who is jealous of Luna’s pristine doll collection. Is it Spot, the twice convicted, doll-munching pooch who was recently released from the big doghouse on parole? Is it Sergeant Dick, a handsome, former Navy Seal action figure who believes San Trope Suzi was spreading rumors about him. Or is it Red Herring, the founder of The Recess Murder Club who hates how Luna had taken over the group? I am proposing a 64-book series. I will write them this weekend if there is nothing on TV and I have received a large advance. I have not yet decided who the murderer is, but Red Herring has not once been convicted of murder in any of the hundreds of mystery books I have read, so the readers will never suspect her. Thank you in advance for my humongous advance. Pseudonymous d’Elder 🔍🔍🔍🔍🔍🔍🔍🔍 Gentle Reader: 🌟🌟🌟🌟 Stars. Since my gigantic advance hasn’t arrived yet, I shall use this space to remark on the latest Thursday Murder Club book I have read. The Impossible Fortune is the 5th book in the series, and I have given it 4 stars. Well, it’s no Recess Murder Club: Death of a Stupid Doodle Head is it. The plot is a complex one. Elizabeth is approached by Nick Silver, the best man at Joyce’s daughter’s wedding. He knows about the reputation of the Murder Club and tells her that someone had tried to kill him just before he came to the wedding. A bomb under his car. Why? He and his business partner had decided to accept $20,000 in cryptocurrency years ago as a payment on a debt and locked it away someplace safe. The value of the crypto has gone up, up, up, and now, to their surprise, it is worth a quarter of a billion dollars. Some greedy crook wants the moola but needs the crypto code needed to retrieve it. Nick has memorized half of the code. His partner has memorized the other half. Neither of them knows the entire code. Why then would someone want to kill Nick? The mystery is intriguing, but the members of Murder Club and their kin seem more ruthless and less human than in previous books, and not nearly as likeable. It was also good to see Elizabeth come back to herself a little here, but not without a lot of introspection and careful study of grief. It's such a complicated emotion, and one that's often so hard to portray in fiction, but I think Osman has managed to do so with a lot of grace and understanding. The plot is just as silly and outlandish as I've come to expect, but with all the heart and good humour I want. However, the focus in this book is on Ron, the strong man of the team who is feeling vulnerable and with plenty to worry about. It is interesting to see how he copes with his situation and whether or not he can stick to his principles when the heat is truly on. The plot revolves around a request for help from a friend of Joyce's new son-in-law who has approached Elizabeth to help find out who is trying to kill him after he finds a bomb under his car. What follows is a fast-paced search for answers taking in a couple of quirky experts, some possible bad boys and the complex world of cryptocurrency and 'cold storage'. Some fabulous new characters emerge. There are some side plots too. As well as Ron's story, Joyce's daughter is getting married and she and her fiance take on strong roles in this book. As in Osman's other books, there are some poignant moments to remind the reader of the ages of the key protagonists, for example, Joyce's daughter suddenly realising how much she loves her Mum after being constantly exasperated with her until that moment, and Ron becoming aware of his increasing vulnerability. Fortune favors the old. "Sometimes the most dangerous weapon in a room is a pensioner with a plan." But peace never lasts long in Coopers Chase. When Elizabeth crosses paths with a wedding guest in trouble, the gang is once again pulled into a case involving an uncrackable code, a missing fortune, and a villain who will stop at nothing to get it. Cue another whirlwind of kidnappings, corpses, and chaotic pensioner heroics - all wrapped up in Richard Osmans trademark blend of humor, heart, and humanity. "The Impossible Fortune", the fifth installment in the series, proves once again why the Thursday Murder Club remains unbeatable: there is crime, sleuthing, laughs, and lots of heart. Osman balances mystery and emotion beautifully, giving each of our beloved retirees a moment to shine (and yes, Joyce's daughter Joanna finally gets her own storyline!). The dialogue sparkles, the clues keep coming, and spending time with this crew always feels like coming home. The Netflix adaptation could never. Witty, warm, and worth the two-year wait. Long live the Thursday Murder Club.

The Impossible Fortune by Richard Osman I have become a bit of a gawping fan of Richard Osman’s Thursday Murder Club series. What is not to love in a murder series about a bunch of cheerful septuagenarians at an England old age home who solve murders to keep themselves busy? The lightness of tone, the sparkles of humour and the canny observations about life in general make for a spritzy weekend reading. Having read all of his books so far and watched the lovely movie based on the debut novel, I was only eager for more. So when I came to know that his latest was in store, I queued up to procure it. As I sank my teeth into the latest escapades of the jolly geriatrics that comprise the Thursday Murder Club however, I found the whole business moving along at the pace of an elderly aunt describing her knitting, with the occasional knitting needle pokes to the listener to keep one from nodding off entirely. It has its moments of charm, wit and wisdom. However, one gets the distinct feeling that the author is getting tired of his own characters. Or perhaps he was under severe time pressure to churn out yet another episode so as to not leave the loyal reader frothing in the mouth for their next fix? The murder spirals into a bit of a misunderstanding than a blood-curdler and the impossible fortune turns out to be a damp squib. I couldn’t shake the feeling that the plot had gone off like a lukewarm soufflé - rising valiantly at first, then collapsing into a sort of amiable mush best left for the dog. Avoid. Now to find some Listerine and look for something tastier to read to get rid of the filthy after taste of the pig’s breakfast that is The Impossible Fortune

I genuinely didn’t think I could love these characters any more than I already did… and yet here we are. THE IMPOSSIBLE FORTUNE just reinforced how much I adore the The Thursday Murder Club — and also reminded me that this series is eventually going to end, which I am choosing not to think about for my own emotional well-being. At this point, these characters feel like old friends. Over the last couple of books, Richard Osman has started weaving in these quieter, more intimate moments - little insights into their lives, their grief, their relationships - that just hit so hard. There were a couple moments in this one that absolutely got me, and yes… I cried. Again. Rude. Of course, we still have a murder to solve, and I had a great time with this mystery. I actually thought I had it figured out pretty early on… and, as usual, I was completely wrong. I love that this author can still fool me every single time and then somehow make the final reveal feel so obvious in hindsight. But what continues to stand out to me most about this series is how it portrays aging. There’s something really special about the way these books show both sides of it - the joy of staying engaged, connected, and involved in life, alongside the very real loneliness and loss that can come with it. It feels honest, but also hopeful in a way that I don’t see very often. And I have to say… this series is low-key making me look forward to getting older, which is not something I ever expected a murder mystery to accomplish. If you love character-driven mysteries with humor, heart, and just enough emotional damage to sneak up on you, this series continues to deliver in the best possible way.

This is a terrific book of course, like the whole series, and I can’t think of any more superlatives. Joyce is at her best (or worst if you’re her daughter), and this time we get a good deal of Johanna. The mother and daughter arguments are awesome, and the way the son-in-law tackles them is admirable. Ron gets a lot of space in this book, which is fine by me; he’s pretty good for a West Ham fan. I always give Richard Osman’s books a solid five, and I see no reason to change.

Ugh This one really jumped the shark for me. I think maybe I'm done with this book series, I found this one super annoying to read.

Another great addition to this series. I considered rating this a 4 star only because it isn’t as good as some of the others in the series, but compared to most other mystery books it’s a 5. Without giving away plot of previous books, readers will enjoy this elderly group of retirees as they investigate unsolved murders and crimes. Be sure to read them in order as events can be spoiled if you read out of order. The addition of Kendrick, who is Ron’s grandson, is my favorite part of this book and I hope he continues to be a featured side character similar to Bogdan. I think he’s been included in previous books but his character is much more fleshed out in this one.

Potential Spoilers Ahead! This novel totally shows off Richard Powers’s signature style - mixing deep emotional moments with sharp takes on current events and a really cool look at how humans and nature connect. Honestly, it deserves a spot on the shortlist for the 2024 Booker Prize. At its core, the book is all about protecting the environment, with a big focus on the ocean. But unlike his earlier works, which were all about the battle between destruction and preservation, Playground follows Evie, a marine scientist, as she endlessly explores the ocean and marvels at its wonders. Powers paints the underwater world so beautifully - every creature comes off as innocent, charming, and mysteriously wise. Once you’ve seen the magic of the deep, it’s hard to forget. Then there’s Todd, another main character who dives into today’s hot topics like AI and social networks. His story - and his connection with Rafi - brings out a bittersweet vibe about loneliness, friendship, and where things ultimately lead. Todd’s crew of tech geniuses have whipped up AI and social platforms that seem to have taken on a life of their own, maybe even in a bid to create a never-ending, perfect game. The book’s “playground” is this multi-layered world: Todd’s social platform, the ocean seen through Evie’s eyes with its countless swimming creatures, the evolving friendship between Todd and Rafi, and even Ina’s artistic universe. But bit by bit, everything starts to fall apart. The ocean suffers from human actions taken in the name of progress, and though we don’t know exactly what price we’ll pay, it’s clear that true harmony between humans and nature is slipping away. That leads to a radical new path, one where AI starts pushing boundaries. Still, the roles of who’s in control and who isn’t remain up in the air. Powers’a storytelling pulls you right into these heavy themes. With multiple narrative perspectives bouncing between different times and places, you quickly get a feel for each character and their intertwined stories. After just a few chapters, you’re pretty confident you’ve got the plot figured out. But then, I was totally caught off guard. I’d assumed the “I” narration was just talking to us, the readers, and that the third-person sections were simply there to tell different characters’ stories. So when an important twist hit in the second-to-last chapter, I was nearly floored. Turns out, Powers had set up this entire playground where readers are actually cast as a super-evolved, all-knowing AI—one that’s picked up on every story and has the power to rebuild a world where the lost can come back. All those third-person bits? They were stories the AI was feeding Todd, drawing him into a new game of reunions and farewells. Everything is reset in an instant, and it’s never too late to change course. It’s a brilliant twist that pulls you deep into this ocean of fiction, stirring up both sadness and awe. At that moment, Powers nails it - showing off the wild possibilities and potential terrors of AI. Whether it’s a trick or a miracle, it all depends on how you look at it. A fun little detail is in the dedication where Powers writes to Rayray: “750,000 thanks to you, better yet, let's make it a million.” I was stumped until I noticed those same numbers popping up throughout the book. Yeah, that’s the playground. 4.6 / 5 stars

It didn’t take a supercomputer to figure out we’d get another remarkable novel about artificial intelligence from Richard Powers. In 1995, Powers published “Galatea 2.2,” his Pygmalion tale about training a neural network called Helen to take a graduate exam on Western literature. At one point in that haunting story, after Helen has finished “reading” fiction and poetry, she’s given a CD-ROM containing recent news, human rights reports, political exposés and police bulletins. Overwhelmed by the horrors of human behavior, Helen announces, “I don’t want to play anymore.” Well, almost three decades later — a millennium in computer time — Helen’s got her mojo back. Powers’s new novel, “Playground,” leaps across the circuits that enable large language models and delivers a mind-blowing reflection on what it means to live on a dying planet reconceived by artificial intelligence. The book won’t be officially released until Sept. 24, but it’s already been named a finalist for the Kirkus Prize and longlisted for the Booker Prize. Although “Playground” is nowhere near as mammoth as the author’s Pulitzer-winning opus, “The Overstory,” it follows a similarly fragmented structure. But trust me, any disorientation will eventually melt into wonderment. The main narrator, Todd Keane, was once “a soldier for the digital revolution” and is now its king. He’s a world-famous tech genius who created an app called Playground. Part Facebook, part Reddit, Playground has hooked billions of daily users by gamifying engagement in a self-contained economy that runs on Playbucks. Closely shadowing the influence of social media, Playground affords Powers the opportunity to satirize and mourn the platforms that have colonized our lives. When we meet Todd, he’s been diagnosed with. . . To read the rest of this review, go to The Washington Post: https://www.washingtonpost.com/books/...

Perfectly correct. Too many themes. Unequal multiple perspectives. Bad ending. An environmental novel shouldn’t try to show the problems of the entire planet and resolve them just for 100 people. The best part was Evie's story. I rarely encounter stories like hers, where dreams become reality and turn out exactly as imagined.

I read Playground for a family book club. Two people who I greatly admire recommended the book to me. I tried reading it and felt lost after the first 60 pages and set it aside. When I picked it up again, it was like reading a completely different book. I started on page 60 and fell in love with one of the four protagonists, Rafi. Rafi has a challenging childhood, some of it due to Moody Stepdad. Rafi LOVES to read books and hides himself at the local library. Rafi states, "I get free when reading." (Oh, be still my heart!) Evie is a strong, independent woman who loves diving and spending her time underwater. She has over 900 hours of diving time but gets turned down for living long-term underwater because decision makers feel that men and women cannot live together for months at a time and not cause chaos. Evie's love of the ocean impacts her marriage. Her husband, Bart, is "responsible for keeping their small craft of a marriage from being lost at sea." Todd is a master game player and creates games with AI. He and Rafi become good friends. Todd is described as a soldier for the digital revolution. The setting of the book is the island of Makatea in French Polynesia. Americans are arriving on the island to rebuild Makatea as a floating city on the ocean. The locals living on Makatea have to agree to the rebuilding plan. Floating cities are the dreams of tech billionaires because there won't be any regulatory requirements. Richard Powers does an incredible job weaving together the lives of multiple protagonists. His prose captured my heart. Some of the memorable passages include: * A fabulous truth had her by the brain stem. * The great game of Destiny after decades of dormancy. * Moving the goal posts is our best trick. * My father was busy breaking all the accumulated nest eggs. * Death by live burial is what occurs when you throw your dreams away.

Longlisted for the Booker Prize 2024 Since The Overstory, which won him a Pulitzer in 2019, Powers has become a sort of Jonathan Franzen for ecofiction, and "Playground" is another attempt at the Great American Anthropocene Novel. Build as a sweeping epic, we get narrative strands that move and intertwine: There's Evie, the daughter of one of the inventors of the aqualung and herself a maritime explorer; Todd, a wealthy tech genius and the inventor of a parallel digital world called "Playground", who becomes fascinated by one of Evie's books; Todd's friend/rival Rafi, a Black writer; and Hawaiian-Tahitian sculptor Ina. Rafi and Ina get married, Rafi falls out with Todd, and the wedded couple moves to a small atoll threatened by investors trying to build floating cities around its perimeter, which is, you know, NOT good for oceanic life. See, I'm torn when it comes to Powers' novel Bewilderment, because it's spectacularly written, the character depiction is just fantastic, the sense of urgency is palpable, but it's also partly simplistic, manipulative and overly moralistic - and that's also the case with "Playground": I loved every minute of it, because damn, Powers can write and make me care about his characters, but the the depiction of KI and digital communication in general is just so undercomplex, and the messages (save the oceans, people are highly questionable animals, eat the rich, KI bad, etc.) are hammered home in a sometimes obnoxious way. The level of complexity added towards the end also seems a little over the top. But have I mentioned that damn, Richard Powers can fucking write?! Interestingly, writer/activist Powers wanted to be an oceanographer as a child, then worked as a computer programmer, so he both knows his themes and gets the fascination, and it shows in his writing. He's driven to show that humans and the natural world are interconnected, and I applaud him for it, but I still think his masterpiece remains The Overstory. But to critique "Playground" is complaining on the highest level of literary talent, and this dude deserves all the praise. You can watch Richard Powers being a wonderful human in this recent interview: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PiIoG... You can listen to the podcast crew discuss the German translation Das große Spiel in our Booker special: https://papierstaupodcast.de/podcast/...

Brilliant. The book I've been waiting for someone to write. Bravo Richard Powers. In Playground, Powers explores the oceans. They cover nearly three quarters of the planet and we know less about them than we do about space. And yet we are still managing to pollute them to such an extent that plastic has been found in the Mariana Trench - 6.7 miles down at Earth's lowest point. The book revolves around the tiny island of Makatea, an atoll in French Polynesia in the middle of the Pacific ocean. It has a fascinating history that Powers delves into suffice to say it has been ravaged before by outsiders. The main characters are Rafi, a young brilliant black guy from the wrong side of the tracks; Todd, the son of wealthy parents; Ina, an artist who becomes Rafi's girlfriend; and Evelyne, a deep sea diver. Todd narrates the present, explaining how he and Rafi came to create Playground, an all encompassing "game" that has made its creator billions of dollars. Juxtaposed with this technology is life in Makatea where people live a natural life that depends on the ocean that surrounds it. The clash of cultures comes when a new project to create floating living spaces off the coast is mooted to the islanders. Should they accept the offer to create more jobs and wealth or should they preserve their way of life and save the ocean. I thought Overstory lost its way and Bewildered just a rehash of Flowers for Algernon. This book, however, did not disappoint in any way. The writing is superb. The characters are engaging. The situations believable yet horrifying and all I could think when I'd finished was "if only". The narrative talks a lot about the oceans and AI and many other issues that affect every one of us on this planet. I'll be honest, it took me a little while to get into this book but once I saw where it was going I was hooked. I loved it. I've always been fascinated by the deep oceans and so I fell hook, line and sinker for this incredible novel. Powers must have done some heavy duty research for this novel. It was worth it. Stunning. (And if you struggle imagining these creatures and the amazing lives they lead then watch Sir David Attenborough's Blue Planet and Blue Planet II). Thankyou so much to Netgalley and Random House for the advance review copy. Most appreciated.

The Earth is a playground for living things. Whether we physically labor, work with the intellect, or help in social services, we all engage in play in some form. Writing book reviews and working in my garden are ways that I play. As I would expect from a Richard Powers book, Playground is full of ecological wonder. We meet Todd who escapes his toxic and wealthy family by walking under water and honoring the sea creatures. Todd develops a deeply intimate friendship with Rafi in college. Rafi pursues poetry while Todd is committed to starting up an AI gaming platform. In a way, capitalism is presented as a type of game where people can work in exchange for goods and climb the ladder for success, presenting a never ending dilemma which could go in a dangerous direction. As a mixed race friendship, Powers captures the complexity of the bond, and the deep hurt that swells between them. Soon, Rafi falls in love with Ina, a native of French Polynesia. Todd has feelings for her too, and the bond I would have thought could never be broken ends painfully. Rafi and Todd have different ideas of what is fun in play and when the game is over. These different perspectives are catalysts at examining the current world state. Todd's AI network eventually finds its way to French Polynesia where the question is for the future of wildlife and native species there. I found the conversation amongst the islanders about the pros and cons of using this new technology very interesting. This book is lingering on the precipice of what is happening presently in our reality and presents ideas for ways to move forward so we can all play together on our playground cooperatively.

Powers continues to be as subtle as a sledgehammer. His dialogue and characterizations are always so on-the-nose, it drives me nuts. But I guess his nerdy passion for his environmental and social activism is commendable and inspiring. Whereas with THE OVERSTORY, he introduced us to a new way of thinking of trees. This time, he zeroes in on the ocean and its kingdom. With characters and locations ranging from Montreal (yayyy), Chicago, and French Polynesia, which always keeps the narrative pulsating. However, Powers’ depiction and/or exploration of race and women needs work. At times, this book felt so dated and out of touch. There are times when I seriously wonder if Powers has ever interacted with other humans. Maybe he’s more about writing allegories and metaphors, instead of characters. But ironically, what tries to be progressive comes off as reductive. But I’ll digress. Am I being generous or not generous enough? PLAYGROUND is an exhilarating ride, sometimes tedious but mostly the former. Overall, I did enjoy my time with it, in comparison to my muted or incredulous reaction to THE OVERSTORY. The oceanic scenes are wondrous. And there’s also a clear-eyed innocence in the way Powers decided to write this. Even though you can always see Powers peeking in on every page, you can also pick up on his child-like innocence and fascination. Maybe I like my literature to have a bit more acidity and cynicism, but I gotta admit this gave me a nice feeling

Powers really knows how to write a deep dive about the intersection of humanity and nature that is still a banging good story. This is the third of his books I’ve read and loved, and surely not the last. In Playground, Powers turns his attentions to the magnificent, mysterious, absorbing world that are our oceans. Through this medium, he tells a story about big issues and ideas like technological development, AI, capitalism and its environmental impact, and the tentacles of colonialism. Where it could be didactic, it never feels it, because it’s a story with a living, breathing heart. A world where characters, and the planet are alive. It’s the best book I’ve read this year. Exquisite. A travesty this wasn’t even shortlisted for the Booker, it should have won.
Stunning. It leaves me speechless.

So fuckin' awesome. Awkward family dynamics in childhood, friendship, love, vocation, gaming (chess, Go, and some video), the rise of information systems and artificial intelligence, and most deeply, that source of all life on the planet, mother ocean. Deep, insightful, wonderful, filled with awe of where we are and who we are. Another big win from Powers, whose Overstory I also loved.

Time for another ‘Blind Library-pic’ 📚 First up I have to say this book was a MASSIVE undertaking and a HUGE accomplishment! It is my first Richard Powers’ book and I have been totally blown away by his writing ability. 👏🏼 This story is essentially a love letter to the Ocean 💙 …but the scary thing is, whilst reading this book, I couldn’t tell if it was real or dystopian 🤨 Quick summary: Richard Powers draws together the lives of 4 individuals in this far-reaching novel. Evie Beaulieu. Ina Aroita. Rafi Young. Todd Keane. They all meet on the tiny island of Makatea in French Polynesia. This special little corner of the world has been chosen for humanity's next experiment: a floating, independent city out into the open sea. But first, the island's residents must vote to greenlight the project or turn the seasteaders away. This magnificent story is set in the world’s largest ocean, exploring topics from colonisation, AI, destruction and preservation of our environment and deep, complex human connections. Personally, I found the first 50 pages a bit hard to wrap my head around. I wasn’t sure who’s POV I was looking at; It seemed to be a random collection of different lives mashed together…then it got GOOD! The thing was, it was a collection of different lives, weaving in and out through time and place. I just had to get my head around where I was and who was narrating. The characters in this book are what really and truly made this a very special read. Evie - WOW, was she a powerhouse. At the age of only 12, she was first person in the world to use Aqualungs; allowing her to dive deep into the ocean. To breathe underwater. A whole new grace came over her. She had never felt at home on land, above the surface, with its noise and politics. She was made for the water. 80 years later, at the age of 92, Evie had secretly nursed the wish to die diving. But first, she had one last task to accomplish: to compile another book - ‘to try one more time to make the land dwellers love the wild, unfathomable God of waters.’ Evie was adventurous, fearless, naive, and crazy passionate, but only about the sea. ‘She swam at night, in waters full off bioluminescent plankton. The sea sparkled like silent fireworks….’ ‘With luck, Evelyn might live to see the stunning ritual one more time: the great mating courtship train of two dozen or more mantas swimming head to tail, twisting and weaving and corkscrewing through the reef like a high-speed, crazed conga line.’ Then, we have Ina Aroita who was born in Hawaii before moving to the tiny island of Makatea to garden and fish and weave and knit a little and raise two children, all the while trying to remember why she was alive. In her youth, she was liquid confidence. She grew up on naval bases across the Pacific. Art was, and still is her only home. And then, we have the boys. They were total opposites, yet they created a deep bond over a 3 thousand year old board game. Rafi Young, a man after my own heart - he was a book man: “I can get free. Sometimes. But only when reading. When I read… the other place is more real than this one.” He totally lost, and found, himself in literature. Todd Keane was probably my least favourite character. He was a computer man. AI was his thing. His startling ability to create computer codes was slightly concerning to me, as he created crossed the line into controversial computerised territory. The story follows the lives of these four individuals, going back and forth in time and changing POV frequently. These characters were so complex and unique. I wanted them to be real; they certainly felt real. The story was told in such a unique fashion, and very much character driven. However, the way Powers’ intricately described the underwater world was phenomenal. The core of this book was about protecting the environment, largely focused on the ocean; yet it felt so much greater. The way Powers’ created a deep connection between nature and humanity was brilliant and beautiful. I can’t put into words how expansive and powerful this book was. All I can do is highly recommend it, to one and all. “How inappropriate to call this planet Earth, when clearly it is Ocean.” 🌎 🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟

Book Club Best book club quote: “I didn’t think I’d get it from the library (since it won awards/has popularity) but I did.” “That’s because everyone hated it and returned it immediately!” Yet another literary fiction piece describing how AI will ruin the world, this time in a marine environment setting. You know, some of the best sci-fi books/movies were so good because they created fear of the future. The best ones were where the fear was completely new or unexpected. Others were good where there was a real threat, but still distant. I seem to notice a new wave of books on this topic. Is it really that creative/new/speculative/exploratory? It’s already here. It doesn’t take much imagination to think of what computers can do. It was interesting when The Terminator came out, but now…I see AI novels as following a trend now, and I am already bored with it. Rant over. Here's what the others thought: The pace: “a slog,” “felt like a long book.” The characters: none grabbed us. “Not a character I liked,” “The ruined friendship seemed unjustified.” The plot: about as heavy as taking a guided tour in an underground aquarium. Lots of talking about animals, not much else. Oh, and AI is coming, we’re doomed I tells ya. Doomed! The themes/messages: “preachy”, “research, copy, paste,” “so you read a magazine, novel, poetry, can you please stop.” Any feminism: yes, women choosing career over family. Comparisons: an offer to make an illustrated book on coral reefs. “Crawdads anyone?” “And like Bruny by Heather Rose, but heavy-handed and not explorative.” Overarching feelings: “lost interest,” “hated it,” “the descriptions of the ocean were beautiful,” “liked the playful cuttlefish.” Ratings: 2, 2, 2, 1 and my 1. Average = 1.6. Higher than what the discussion suggested.

Written from multiple narrative perspectives and moving back and forth in time gives this novel a somewhat disorientating feel. At times, I felt a little 'at sea'. At no point did I find this an easy read but like Powers' novels 'The Overstory' and 'Bewilderment', 'Playground' is thought-provoking and leaves the reader willing to invest in it: changed. Powers is clearly a literary genius. The theme of exploration is considered through our exploration of the oceans as well as exploration of AI as we enter the fourth industrial revolution. The theme of 'play' overlays both these ideas. This novel encapsulates what it means to be alive in 2024 - with concerns over climate change and the accelerating speed that AI is taking off and is inevitably going to change how we live and die and live. This is a remarkable read. I would be shocked not to see this make the Booker lists in 2025. Thank you to NetGalley for providing me with an ARC.

Rating: Pulitzer material Richard Powers has demonstrated his mastery of theme, plot, characters and premise for years and with this story, he ups the ante. Evocative, enlightening and engaging, the reader is immersed in a story world that toggles character back story to the present as 'building blocks' for whats to come. Driven by themes of friendship, family and advancing technology, we're introduced to Todd Keane, Rafi Young, Ina Aroita and Evie Beauleau whose lives will impact one another's on the island of Makatea. As the narrative progresses, contrast plays a role as do ecology vs technology that illuminate critical issues facing humanity and Mother Earth. Powers' lyrical prose and research engage the reader as does the emotional context. The title can be interpreted a variety of ways due to Evie's experiences with giant mantas rays, Keane's billion dollar company or Rafi and Todd's friendship. Regardless, this is a remarkable work and for those who prefer inspired storytelling as I do, it can't be recommended enough! I feel its a disservice to expose details, plots, back story and specifics especially for narratives of this quality, however if you feel a need to know, read reviews from others :) Do yourselves a favor and add it to your list and immerse yourselves in a remarkable journey.

I already hated AI, and this book didn't move my needle on the subject in either direction. Playground starts off clunky, and it takes ~80 pages for it to find its flow. We've got 3 concurrent narratives here, two in plaintext, one in italics. I've never minded disjointed timelines/multiple perspectives before. The problem here is that Powers doesn't give us enough time/space/characterization before switching viewpoints, so you feel adrift for dozens of pages going "wait, who even?" and "where/when are we again?" We don't even get character names from the jump, so we're left floundering until enough foundation has been built. There's ultimately a narrative reason for this, but I don't agree with it. Who do we meet in these narratives? An aged marine biologist who fought through rampant sexism to achieve success in her field, an ailing billionaire, and an American couple living quiet lives on a tiny French Polynesian island. Playground feels like Richard Powers thought up the ending first, then worked backwards. Reviews and blurbs herald the book as "awe-filled" and a love letter to the ocean. I didn't get that. There's good information about the oceans in here, sure, and, like The Overstory, there's a plea to give a damn about the world around us. That said, those moments are merely that: moments. The bulk of the book focuses on human ambition and disappointment. What's more: none of the characters are particularly sympathetic. Now, a story doesn't need likeable players to be successful, but they need to at least be compelling. I didn't find anyone compelling in Playground, save for the giant mantas, and we got precious little of them. The climax of the book, which hits ~20 pages before the story is finished, deflated me. Richard Powers writes beautifully, and there are a couple of wonderful passages within these pages (hence the 3 stars). Nevertheless, I turned the final page feeling very much like flotsam: churning in the sea, never getting where I wanted to go.

Definitely my favourite of the five Booker nominees I read this year. One of my best-loved themes is when a character turns their deep passion for something into their profession - think The Amazing Adventures of Cavalier & Clay, Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow and The Animators. In Playground I hit the mother-load as all four the characters - tech whiz, poet, artist and deep-sea diver does exactly this. I love getting to experience their devotion for their callings vicariously. But there so much more to this easy-reading, engaging novel with it's multiples story lines and divergent themes. I especially enjoyed the focus on play and how the author interweaves it through all the narratives. I wasn't a 100% sure what happened at the end and had to google it. And yes, this final "play" by the author was a fun idea and an extension on the main theme, but for me it didn't really add anything to this panoramic story.
Loved the story!
Review To Follow...

[3.5 rounded down] Playground refers to the Domain created by the narrator, Todd Keane. Todd got into coding and computers in the early days, like Gates, Dell, Jobs. He’s now wealthy AF and struggling with a new diagnosis of Lewy Body Dementia, and he’s recounting an estranged friendship that was painful and most impacted his life. Subsequently, Todd redirects his wrecked friendship and becomes obsessed with the future of technology and the revolutionary, “Deep Learning,” otherwise known as AI. Rafi, Todd’s old friend, is passionate about literature, worships words in concert with each other. What kept Todd and Rafi together is their love of the game Go. The competition and the infinite moves of the game, they have concluded, could never be usurped by a computer’s “skill.” Rafi is Black and poor, Todd is white and wealthy. Powers failed to make much out of it except plot device. For all its supposed drama and tragedy through the years, the execution was dry and artificial. Rafi falls in love with an artist, Ina, a military brat who lived all over the world. The relationship between these three felt stilted and flat, despite all the (melo)drama. Makatea, a French Polynesian atoll in the South Pacific, was stripped and exploited for its phosphate many years ago. Currently, in the story, it’s a quasi-primitive civilization of eighty-two souls, including the now elderly Evelyne and an older Rafi with his wife and small adopted children. They have been approached by outsiders to modernize and get with capitalism, turn Makatea into a prototype floating city and attract even more investors. They promise more jobs, better health care, nicer housing, recreation, and a growing population. Is it improvement or another form of colonialism? It’s up for a vote on whether to let this happen. The best and definitely wondrous story was Evelyne Beaulieu, a “Canadienne” ginger-haired, six-feet tall prolific diver of coral reefs who was also a breakthrough oceanographer that worked twice as hard to be recognized as a woman scientist (and serious diver). Her quirky story was brilliant—that was the narrative that pulsed. Evie’s descriptions of life underwater were like fireworks from the deep. Most of land is underwater, so the masses are sheltered from our own planet. Going down to the reefs reminded me of my brief but poignant period of scuba diving at coral reefs. Day, and night dives, too. I saw the moon from 40 feet below and so did Evie, many times. Her love of all species under the sea is like an aria. The sea is an opera. Unfortunately, the three narratives did not hang together organically, despite the author earnestly trying to make it so. It was like, “He loves her,” and so he loved her. I don’t know why, but the Todd/Rafi and Ina story was low energy. Evie and her family story vibrated and was three-dimensional. For me, she was the main story and it was what kept me reading, Powers had his characters channel his own precious maxims, so it was unsubtle and heavy-handed. When Todd talked about race and class, for example, it was preachy and flat. It was written like a sermon. Aesthetically, the less italics, the better, imho. Todd’s present-day troubles and his struggle with Lewy Body Dementia are all italicized. I understand it, now that the book has ended, but it felt like he tried too hard to tell a story via expounding, but it lacked spirit and perfusion. He got stuck in the telling. Playground was the Domain that Todd originated. He coded the zeroes and ones and chose the topics of discussion that would invite more users to participate. It made him obscenely wealthy and Playground spread globally. I get what he was aiming to achieve, and it could have been a masterpiece with more edits and maturity. As it stands, it was mostly predictable, and, as I keep saying (in probably so many, too many words), it lacked oomph. The author touched down on some provocative themes of climate and environmental changes, the wealth divide, race, class, art humanity-- but he didn’t let them grow and expand organically. Still, there were pearls of wisdom and warning. “We were creating wealth and novelty out of sunlight and thin air almost like trees.” And my favorite: “We were all about finding the moves that the rules forgot to outlaw.”

First off, a big thanks to Penguin and Cam Waller for hooking me up with an ARC of Richard Powers’ latest novel in exchange for a fair review! Powers, who I’ve read since The Overstory, has become a sort of middleman between the worlds of science, nature, and literature. With Playground, Powers turns his eye toward the world’s oceans in an effort to do for the sea what The Overstory did for trees. Along the way there’s a heaping helping of software development and the looming spectre of AI. To be frank, this seems like two big ideas smashed into one. I know that Powers has an older AI novel, but I found myself longing for the longer dives into the abyssal depths as the novel wore on. This is to say that the effort to centre the ocean often clashes with the AI subplot that becomes the centrepiece by novel’s end. There’s multiple POVs here too that varied in their ability to keep my attention. I liked a great deal of the stories at play, but I’d be lying if I said the French Polynesian plot did anything for me until the last 100 pages or so. By contrast, there’s a beautiful tale of ocean obsession from an aging diver, and the story of two friends who have drifted apart with time that kept my attention and the pages turning. The weakest moments in Playground will be familiar to anyone who has read Powers’ work before. The personal and human aspects of the story can come off as stilted and stiff compared to the beautiful writing about climate and the natural world. This is especially true when the reader is juggling so many characters, relationships, and POVs. This wasn’t an issue with the emotionally arresting Bewilderment, but that novel also benefitted from a more straightforward structure and smaller cast. Of the Powers novels I’ve read, this is my least favourite. With that said, the novel is in many ways thought provoking and the reveal at the end feels earned even as it pulled the rug from under me. Would I recommend it? I think that depends on what you’re after. If it is the ocean version of The Overstory, I think you’ll come away slightly disappointed. If you are looking for Powers’ intellect and experimentation on full display, I think you’ll leave satisfied! [3.5 Stars]
Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war. Review to follow.

"Once people witnessed the abundance of underwater life, once they lived there, they would ache to take care of the place like it was their home." "As Arthur C.Clarke has observed:'How inappropriate to call this planet Earth, when clearly it is Ocean'." Talk about the most relevant book of 2024! This book takes on some of the most radical ideas that are in circulation and builds a tale in parts fascinating, in parts scary and for most parts entertaining. Richard Powers flexes his research capabilities and writes a book that does to Oceans what Overstory did to trees. 70% of the world is made up of oceans and is it any wonder that the humans would soon want to colonise this? Makatea is an Island of 82 people which is chosen for seasteading pilot - a concept very much in vogue and being toyed around the world by billionaires as tax havens. The residents of the island, including children, get a vote to decide if they are to choose growth over the ocean. Among the residents is an artist and teacher couple who once upon a time made a trio with an AI pioneer. Rafi is a philosopher poet (black) who wanted to raise the dead in words. His wife Ina is an islander and artist who is building a sculpture from plastic that gets washed onto the shores. We see the writing of Toddy Keane, the son of a billionaire, whose friendship with Rafi defines him and he goes onto become the pioneer of AI who creates the virtual world of Playground. Watch out for the chapters on Deep learning and machine learning that gives a layman gist of what the potential of the technology is - even if it over simplifies it. Evelyn the nonagenarian marine biologist has some of the best parts describing the world under the ocean. Chapters written to inspire awe in the reader with playful Mantas, symbiotic shrimp and gobi fishes and a whole new world. Her book and her life inspires the world to understand the ocean better and she finds herself on the island as well. With Mr.Powers, it is not the story but the ideas. Like how the children should get a vote in any decision that impacts the future. Or how an AI system left to figure out the best strategy for living on earth, would probably choose not to do the mistakes we did. I probably highlighted more passages than I have done in quite some time. This book has the power to change. And hence I wish it gets the recognition it deserves. Thank you Netgalley for the ARC copy of this book.

I am a complete fan of Richard Powers. I have read all except his first two books and he has never disappointed me. He is so smart, he is so good at integrating the science of our days with the lives we live, and so full of heart. Playground is about many things: the ocean, the creatures and living entities in it, the divers who explore it and the islanders in French Polynesia who have seen exploitation come and go. It is about men and women who have dreams for themselves and other creatures. It is also a unique viewpoint concerning AI and how this growing technology impacts all aspects of our planet from writers to coral reefs to pretty much any part of life you can imagine. I loved Playground. I was not always sure what Richard Powers was trying to tell us, and I will at some point reread it. The story works on many levels and I want to make sure I comprehend all of those levels. I reread the ending three times, I have discussed the book with my reading group, I have watched every interview I could find with the author. In recent years I have discovered the riches that come with rereading. Have you read Playground? If so, what surprises did you find in it? If not, I recommend this novel to every serious reader. Reread: I reread this before the second reading group of mine who read it, to make sure I understood the ending and to clear up some confusions I had. I read it like an assignment, keeping a list of characters, following the story line, the jumps between times and places. It took me many days. I got to the end and understood quite a few things that had mystified me the first time, especially all those sections in italics. I did all this work because I wanted more understanding but also because I had recommended the book to that group and wanted to be able to defend myself in case no one liked it. Happily, the majority did love it and some even seemed to get it better than I did! The only thing that still nags at my mind is what was Richard Powers trying to tell us? I got it that the ocean is adept at repurposing much of the garbage we throw into it, that sea creatures can adapt to almost anything, that people are amazing in both good and bad ways. I am still not sure what he was trying to tell us about AI. Perhaps he just wanted to ponder this new technology, just as most of us are doing.

I didn't like Overstory and I didn't like this. Once again, it feels like an extended exercise in virtue signaling, a white-centric world and women existing only under male gaze. I'm sure Powers' boyfriends* appreciated it (and apparently his fans did too,) but for me, from the moment an island child finds plastic inside a fish ('bad food') and stares adoringly at pictures in a book written by a beautiful redhead it was difficult to give it the benefit of the doubt. Did Powers' get criticism for being too white or something previously? It seems like Rafi is a reaction to that because he's a series of clichés that drew attention to Powers' inability to write anyone other than a white man convincingly. Better to write nothing than such an awkward caricature. If the whole thing was written in first person it could have been excused as a flaw in the narrator but instead it was consistent throughout the mixed first and third person descriptions. Towards the end there was an interesting segment with Rafi reaching out to Todd to put a price on his contribution to Playground but that was the only part of the plot that didn't feel overworked and inauthentic. Why is this two stars not one? I don't know. I guess because I think Powers could have done a waaaaaayyyy worse job. *Is gendering 'friends' annoying and confusing and reading as slightly homophobic? Good. It felt exactly like that when female friends were constantly referred to as 'girlfriends'. Also not helped when you have the cliche beautiful, loyal wife who is (shallowly) grappling with whether or not she's straight (does she have a girlfriend all of a sudden? Oh, no, it's just Powers letting us know we need a gendered qualifier when a woman is doing anything that doesn't directly involve her beauty or gendered anatomy).

If you have read any of Powers' previous novels, you don't need to know more than this: this is another masterpiece which you will absolutely adore. If you are new to Powers, I have this to say: read this, but also read his previous two novels, for though they are not connected they form a triptych of sorts. The themes that run through this have echoes in his other works, and reveal an intellect, curiosity and empathy for the human world missing in most other novelists works. Powers is indeed writing at the top of his game here. This novel has multiple stories and narrators, and reading it does require concentration from its reader. However you are soon swept up in the literary swell that you won't feel adrift. Powers takes you on a journey under the ocean, into the cyber world, and to a very human love story. It is gripping, powerful stuff and makes me very grateful that writers like Powers are still writing and being published. I fully expect to see this on awards shortlists in the coming literary year. This is a superb novel, epic in scope yet intimately told. Just read it. It is already my favourite novel of 2024, and I cannot see how it can be beaten! Thank you to Netgalley and the publishers for the ARC.

Sheer genius and I am not exaggerating. Just how Richard Powers managed to pull this off increases my admiration for this author’s talents. Told in three narratives: one about two friends creating AI, another about a marine biologist and the third about a Polynesian island that will undergo heavy development. They are all tied up but in a way that will raise the reader’s eyebrows. Infusing themes such as artificial intelligence, art, underwater life and conservation Richard Powers has written a novel that not only reflects contemporary society’s problems but in a way that will dazzle. Then there’s the writing! So many descriptions about sea life - I just loved reading about manta rays and shrimps and sharks.Plus there are heartbreaking moments as well. It’s 100 % accessible (as opposed to the more pynchonian writing of his works pre Overstory) This is not highly recommended but mandatory reading.
Oh I Am Going Absolutely Nuts

This was pretty much everything I expected and wanted ... and more. Sure, I preordered it. And, yes, much as I enjoyed The Overstory (and agree that it was a deserved Pulitzer Prize awardee), I actually preferred Bewilderment, which, as I was reading (and savoring it), felt as if it were written specifically for me. (Ah, hubris!) And, OK, laying my cards on the table, it didn't hurt that, thrilled as I was that Powers spoke at one of my kid's college graduations, it was icing on the cake that his speech was one of the best I've witnessed (and, alas, I've been to more than my share of graduations). Fortunately, the book didn't disappoint. Rather, it not only frequently defied description, but it exceeded expectations. I concede that, at numerous points, I thought of this work as a nice, almost elegant, companion to Zevin's well-crafted Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, ... and, frankly, I'm glad I read Zevin's offering first. In terms of Powers' prior work, I wasn't surprised to see, in the acknowledgements, a reference that brought me back to the thread from the non-fiction Finding the Mother Tree (which I can't recommend enough) to The Overstory. But none of that diminishes the creativity in play here (sorry about the pun), or quality of the construction and effectiveness of the delivery. At some level, I wonder whether the number of themes in play here - from programming, gaming, and artificial intelligence (or machine learning), to scuba diving and oceanic exploration and climate change, with more than a dollop of broken families and the refuge (or sanctuary) of libraries and the transformative, life-altering privilege of higher education, to friendship and parenting and language and, oh my, aging, memory loss, and the quandaries posed by navigating one's end-of-life - might turn off some readers. But, at least from my perspective, I found all of the threads compelling, and Powers wove them together into a cohesive, integral, poignant, and ultimately satisfying, whole. Part of me is curious to hear what a true newcomer - to Powers or the book itself (picking it up and reading it with no preconceived notions or biases) - would make of it. But I can't walk in those shoes. It worked incredibly well for me, and I strongly recommend it.

The first half of the book is good but not great. I thought 'Bewilderment', his previous novel, was fantastic primarily because of the relationship of father and son. In 'Playground', the characters seemed a little more cliche. Keane and Rafi's relationship is interesting but the racial stigmas seemed too apparent and forced. I agree with another commenter that Powers' writing was maybe too earnest at times. The twist towards the end of this novel is what makes it great. It is thought provoking and moving. Some reviewers have shared that they felt it was a cop-out ending. But they've missed the entire point. I also like the idea of ghosts of people past still having a stake in the fight. The title of the book is perfect too. We are all children at play, and Earth serves as our playground. But we have arrived at a new dawn. This is the birth of a new age in which the stakes for humanity and our beautiful playground are higher than ever. High four stars.

My expectations going into this book were on the low side as I wasn't a huge fan of Bewilderment, but I ended up liking it very much and totally see why it was nominated for the Booker longlist. As a young child, Todd, is totally mesmerized by a book written by an elderly oceanographer, Evelyn, which he wins when he beats his father at chess. Todd is arguably both the protagonist and antagonist of this book which slowly reveals Todd through different lenses. His love for Evelyn's book. His relationship with a young black man, Rafi, with whom he is constantly competing - - to both his benefit and detriment. His unbridled ambition and need to win. His struggles with Lewy body dementia. It's hard to know where this book is going with these disparate storylines, but each one is engaging in its own right. From beautiful descriptions of the ocean, its creatures, and man's relationship with the sea to insights on the double edged sword that is technology and artificial intelligence, Powers writes a sweeping novel that at the end of the day is more plot driven than anticipated. From my perspective, the entertainment value was more in the 4 star realm, but after I finished the book, I literally went right back to the beginning and started re-reading huge swathes of it. And lo and behold, there's some really great foreshadowing and big picture storytelling going on here, and I find books like this endlessly interesting to pick apart and discuss. So 5 stars it is! Kudos Mr. Powers for changing my opinion of your work. I'll definitely be revisiting more of it.
