** spoiler alert ** I put PLAYGROUND on hold at my local library months in advance of its publication because I consider myself a big fan of its author, Richard Powers. This is the eighth of his books that I’ve read. This is something I’ve said before in other reviews of his books, but even though I think of Powers as a favorite author I haven’t been uniformly impressed by his work. I’ve liked them all—and the same is true here—but not all of them strike me as five-star material. In fact, the book of his that I read most recently before this one, PLOWING THE DARK, did not keep my attention; as a result, it took me an inordinately long time to finish. I had sort of a similar problem with PLAYGROUND. I was not drawn to read this book in any free moment the way the best books tend to do, so it took a longer time to read than I would have liked. I unfortunately started to think of the book as a hurdle to cross to move on to another book instead of something to savor. I did get more into the story as it neared its conclusion and the various individual threads started converging, but for so much of the book I was… not especially engaged with it. The format of the story is somewhat reminiscent of THE OVERSTORY, in that it follows a handful of people whose narratives get entwined especially as the book nears its conclusion. The primary players are Todd Keane, a tech billionaire experiencing symptoms of dementia and reminiscing about his younger days; Rafi Young, Todd’s friend in youth and at-times bitter rival; Ina Aroita, Rafi’s girlfriend and a native of Makatea in the Pacific Islands; Evelyne Beaulieu, a 90-some-year-old diver who in her younger days broke the glass ceiling for female marine biologists; and various residents of Makatea as they wrestle with whether to let American venture capitalists exploit their island for mutual profit (and some unknown but inevitable cost to the island). I knew going into the book that it was about the ocean. The cover image, an illustration of a manta ray from below with stabs of sunlight breaking through the water around it, makes that much clear. In fact, though, the book is also about artificial intelligence and game-playing in general. Todd and Rafi’s relationship is largely centered around their playing chess and then, later, Go. I read some reviews that complained that threading the friendship of Todd and Rafi (one white, one black) through these games (where one plays as “white” and one plays as “black”) is a little discomfiting; to that end, I also saw some objecting to Powers’ portrayal of Rafi and of the various residents of Makatea as cringey or inauthentic. I don’t know that I personally held those feelings reading the book, but I can understand why one would raise those concerns. Additionally, there’s a secret fourth theme about the stories we tell ourselves and how they “create” our realities. I did appreciate the ideas about “play” and “playgrounds” appearing in various contexts throughout the book. Part of the idea of a playground is the ocean itself, teeming with alien creatures of the wildest design. Part of it is about the animals in the water, who Evelyne sees chasing each other for fun and spinning through bubbles. Rather than trying to rationalize this behavior away through the lens of hunting or evading predators, Evelyne recognizes the animals are playing. She “had spent too many decades of close observation to be cowed any longer by the prohibition against anthropomorphism. What began, centuries ago, as a safeguard against projection had become an insidious contributor to human exceptionalism, the belief that nothing else on Earth was like us in any way.” Powers goes on to assert: “Play was evolution’s way of building brains, an any creature with a brain as developed as a giant oceanic manta sure used it. If you want to make something smarter, teach it to play.” In fact, though, there were only a handful of quotes I saved, all clustered closer to the front of the book. There wasn’t a lot that sang to me the way that Powers’ writing often does—that very intricate poetry and, dare I say, playfulness in his language just didn’t seem as on display here as in earlier outings. One I did save, though, came when Todd as a child discovers a book about the ocean written by Evelyne (though her authorship of the book isn’t explicitly revealed until much later). He marvels at the truths it conveys: “[T]he book insisted even the oddest fish was still my first cousin, compared to the other beings down there. The ocean teemed with primordial life—monsters left behind from evolution’s oldest back alleys—ring-shaped, tube-shaped, shapeless, impossible plant-animal mash-ups with no right to exist, beasts so unlikely I wondered if my beloved author invented them. Evanston was nothing. Chicago was nothing. Illinois and even the U.S. were a joke. There were insanely different ways of being alive, behaviors from another galaxy dreamed up by an alien God. The world was bigger, stranger, richer, and wilder than I had a right to ask for.” Beautiful language and a beautiful meditation on the odd world of the ocean. Despite this, though, I maintain that the poetic vision espoused here is not maintained throughout the book. PLAYGROUND largely splits between words in normal text regarding the lead-up to the vote on Makatea about whether to submit to the American usurpers or to keep their independence and, as a result, their relative indigence, and text set in italics which is Todd’s present-day ruminations on his life, especially during that period that he, Rafi, and Ina spent together. This threesome called to mind TOMORROW AND TOMORROW AND TOMORROW for me, especially as they share what is important to them and as Todd creates a social media website which Rafi recommends he “gamify” by awarding points for popular posts and making users “spend” their allotted points. Having made the connection with TOMORROW AND TOMORROW AND TOMORROW, I considered whether this one matched the strength of the other. I’m not sure it does, frankly; the creation of new games in Garbielle Zevin’s book wowed me each time and I didn’t feel that way here. The other work that PLAYGROUND calls to mind—and this is quite spoilery, so I’m putting this under a spoiler tag—is Ian McEwan’s ATONEMENT. I suppose this is a spoiler for ATONEMENT, too, if you haven’t read/seen it, so be forewarned. As this book nears its end, billionaire Todd Keane sends an advanced AI machine to answer questions for the Makateans about the specifics of the planned sea-steading venture. The twist is revealed not long afterward: in the italicized sections of the book, Todd is speaking to that same AI, or a later generation of it. Accordingly, the non-italicized sections of the book are the AI program telling Todd a story about his friends (and also Evelyne Beaulieu, I guess). That is, it is not entirely clear that there ever really was any sea-steading project near Makatea, nor any vote there. Allegedly Rafi and Ina and Evelyne all lived on the island and participated in the vote, but in actuality Evelyne died 20 years earlier and Rafi had died in Chicago more recently. I appreciate this twist ending for the way it pays off an obsession Rafi had throughout the book of defeating death, though the idea of defeating death through storytelling is, at root, not terribly original. On the other hand, even if it’s not especially original, I do find the thesis about life existing through language, in storytelling, a compelling thought regardless. So this is where I am. Ultimately, as with all of Powers’ books, I would say I liked PLAYGROUND overall. If I had to give it a pure thumbs-up or thumbs-down vote, I’d come down more on a positive side than a negative one. There’s not even much that I felt was poor about this book; so much of my issues with it are ineffable… found in my lack of connection with it, rather than any specific failure I can point to as evidence. I wished I felt more strongly about this book. I don’t have any advice to offer the author on how to better impress me, one random reader. I’m still intent on reading all of Powers’ output to date, this isn’t such a misstep that it would cause me to rethink that but it is a bit concerning that the last two books I’ve read by him have felt at times during the read like more of a chore than a pleasure. I’m hopeful I’ll feel differently about the next one.

** spoiler alert ** When I say spoilers I mean SPOILERS. Don’t read until you have finished the novel. 6 stars Absolutely stunning. I tried ‘Overstory’ before and stopped so I need to go back. This book is incredible. It’s annoying me that so many people in their reviews and comments are giving the ending away. Luckily I didn’t read any too closely as I was reading but it could have ruined it for me. It’s really important to not know the meta narrative version of the story. The writing is incredible. I dive and it truly is one of the most wonderful things to do but to write about the world underneath in the way that Powers does blew my mind. There are multiple narrators who as you can imagine connect in various different forms by the ending. Which is INCREDIBLE. The ending I mean. Utterly. People have seemed confused about the ending. Or irritated. I thought it was perfect. We begin to get clues about half way through that there are two versions of Todd’s story. I listened to it so can’t quote or be exact, annoyingly (yet another book I need to get a hard copy of). And my spellings might be wrong. Soon after Ina and Rafi are introduced on the island in one chapter, Todd, elsewhere in his own narrative, says that this moment was where things began to go wrong between Ina and Rafi. There are many indications from the start that Rafi will break and be unable live up to his potential. It was clear too that Rafi had the idea to gamify Playground and that Todd would take this idea and not credit Rafi. So from the start it is clear that the two of them fall out. And gradually the two Rafis in the novel begin to be different people. So I began to understand that one of these narratives was a fantasy narrative that Todd was creating. Or having created for him. It was only towards the end that I began to work it out. Todd was dying. He had made a mess of his life despite being so wealthy. He was lonely and a voluntary ‘incel’ as he describes himself. His brain was slowing down so that he couldn’t remember things and he was disorientated in his movements. He gives his third generation AI ‘being’ all the correspondance he had with Ina and Rafi - and we are told this several times (‘You read the emails,’ he tells the ‘reader’) and the grandchild of his first AI creation is able to generate believable and positive stories about all the various people in his life who had had an impact. Evie, Ina and Rafi Evie - I did wonder when that book he read as a child would come back. I don’t remember if we ever learnt its name but I should have realised when Evie tells us about the amazing book she wrote (I want that book - what a chapter that was when she explained what she wrote. And of course in a way we have that book in the form of ‘Playground’. I am definitely getting a hardcopy!) So in Todd’s fantastical world Evie lives beyond 70 and gets to resolve a few things. But not all. She still has terrible relationships with her children and now it seems her grandchildren. (But of course Bart’s death which is so beautiful in the novel is - we realised at the end - all AI generated.) And here is the thing. When we read a novel we enter into a contract with the author - if you create a believable world for me, I will indeed believe it until the book ends it. It’s about trust. That’s why bad writing can be so jarring - we are reminded that there is a Writer behind the text. When a writer shakes the foundation of the contract (to mix my metaphors) it is very uncertain. And we can question the role of the narrator. The role of creators. The role of truth. There are plenty of writers who do this brilliantly elsewhere. I am not going to cite too many cos of spoilers but Kate Atkinson’s ‘Life After Life’ is an example of this which doesn’t involve ruining the story. Powers is showing us through AI the way that we construct our own various alternative narratives. Our own day dreams. If this hadn’t happened, maybe this would have done. We can have everyone living happily on an island. Interestingly based on Todd’s character that the AI model has understood, he still has to sabotage things and have control. He still wants to ‘gamify’ the island. It’s like he still hasn’t learnt where he went wrong all along. Just so he can have a nice death and be forgiven by his friend. And of course it is a commentary on AI too but not so much I think. It’s more about the narratives we create for ourselves. Sadly in no version of this story does the sea not get trashed. Back to Rafi. Rafi is a damaged boy whose ‘success’ was always going to be associated with the death of his sister and the absence of his father. He has too much to prove. He was always going to implode. So when he goes off the rails I was sure that he wasn’t ever going to be living in harmony with Ina on a Polynesian island. His true final contact with Todd is to ask for $750,000. Which we learn later he saved and gave to Ina. In Todd’s fantasy version, it is Todd who leaves Ina everything because Todd still wants to win over Rafi. Oh my goodness I loved this novel. So much more to write but my fingers are now going numb!

A well-written sentence can hide a weak voice… …to encapsulate this book. First, Powers’ bombastic words do not center around a reverence for the ocean - nor for the environment. The Pacific is merely a decorative background while attempting to portray an image of cultural competence. And to that, Powers ought to be called in. A white male author writing a BIPOC’s experience? Because here’s the what of the what of it: it’s not that he speaks to it, he speaks for it. Can one string together another question beyond, “Are you f*cking for real?” The only thing Powers succeeded in is White empathy making racist ideology. He consumes the Black and Pacific Islander identities for his own needs. He uses stereotypical language which denigrates anyONE other than the person who looks like him. And he crafts a false narrative which promotes commonality and assuages White guilt. Shall we move on to how he has “included” the queer experience? Except to say that he has disparaged Lesbians by perpetuating the patriarchal viewpoint that you “stick with your man”? How a woman can realize she loves women - sure, sure - but the White-picket fence vision of love and family is what matters? Or do we tackle the incompetence of the potentialities of AI? You want to include a last page flip? At least have the technological substance to hold it. Overall, this book was absolutely atrocious. And I sincerely hope that critical thinking folx speak to that.
