I have been reading Susan Choi for a couple of decades now. She is always good, but for me her last two novels were spectacular. Flashlight, to me, felt like a return to her older subjects and style. It's a story inspired by real events, it's an exploration of identity and secrets, family and race and nationality. There is so much in it that you can sink your teeth into, but it never came together to me as a novel. We focus mostly on a small nuclear family: Louisa, Anne, and Serk. Serk is Korean, but who lived his whole life in postwar Japan and has little connection to that identity. Anne is a white American woman who left a traditional life only to end up back in something very traditional married to Serk. And Louisa, their biracial child, starts out as simply precocious but gradually defines herself in opposition to her mother. All three of these characters keep so much of their lives secret. It is hard to talk about because learning what those secrets are is part of the novel's greatest pleasures. But I noted over and over again how much each of these characters was defined by what they do not say, what they do not share, about themselves. How much these decisions to hold back parts of themselves define their lives. This isn't a novel that moves in a straight line. Not in its structure and not in its plot. By the time you get to the last third of the novel you realize that it's something very different than what you thought it was. Choi has made this kind of move in her books before, but here this turn did not pull me in further. The problem, though, was not really about the story. It was the telling of it. Somehow the prose here had long stretches--especially for Serk--where the story feels flat, where there is so much that has to be explained, so much time that has to pass, that it feels like page after page of exposition. Compare that to some of Anne and Louisa's chapters--Anne with the strawberry picking trip and Louisa going to Europe--are riveting, masterfully done and incredibly affecting. To read one of those deeply impactful chapters and then to feel like I was reading through a rather dull text was jarring. I recognize that this was likely purposeful, that there is something about the telling of Serk's story that Choi wants to do. But for me as a reader, it felt like I was trying to walk through mud. Still a lot to admire, some really rich themes. Choi is certainly still a force.

“Love is, perhaps, the sensation of expertise that erupts out of nowhere, and as time goes on accumulates enough soil at its feet to be standing on something.” I had the unique experience of finishing Flashlight the day that it was announced it had made the Booker Longlist ! The book starts with a memory—Louisa is ten and walking with her father along the breakshore in Japan. Hours later she is discovered soaking wet and alone. Her father is nowhere to be found. It’s clear that Louisa’s memory is distorted, but the damage is equally obvious. From there, the novel steps back. We examine the family from the beginning: who they were as individuals, who they were together, and who they are, after this event. Though the mystery of what happened to Louisa’s father (Serk) is at the core of this novel, it is not the central takeaway. It isn’t a thriller, you don’t burn through the pages, and it is, in fact, quite dense. I was often challenged by this entirely impressive novel. The scope of it blew me away. I don’t even know how one begins to craft a story like this! If you are hoping to sneak in one last really, truly great novel this summer… Might I suggest starting with this one?

5⭐️ I could not put down this big beautiful expansive story! Filled with emotion, love, grief, and family drama, the gorgeous prose grabbed me from the first pages. Told from alternating POV chapters of Louisa, her Korean Japanese father, Serk, and her American mother Anne. Multi timelines add to the dramatic telling of a tragic and engrossing tale that leads to the tearful ending. The main characters of Louisa, Serk, and Anne are flawed and unlikable at times but I fell in love with each of them in the telling of their stories. Anne’s older son Tobias is also equally flawed but has a quirky likeability. Lots of post WWII history in Korea and Japan adds the backdrop to an intriguing, mysterious, tale that is gripping as well as satisfying. Issues of immigration, ethnicity, culture, belonging, parenting, and forgiveness are prominent in the unfolding drama. There is a big twist well into the story that surprised me and kept me on the edge of my seat. I highly recommend this book! Thanks to NetGalley and Farrar, Straus, & Giroux publishing for the ARC In exchange for my honest review.

What happened just now is because of the way flashlights work. This book grabbed me and devoured me. I could not walk away. It called to me. When a book devours me like this, I give in completely and allow it. Gorgeous prose highlights the intimate moments of a family in grief. I loved diving in deeply with the characters. Flashlight never teeters on the surface, but it goes to all those places that are left forgotten or neglected. Flashlight does not blind you but illuminates small and very intimate moments. Even 'ugly' moments are made beautiful. Susan Choi captivated me on a journey through mixed cultures and utter emotional devastation. “Death is the only sure thing, but we never expect it.” Every sentence is a craft that deserves a framed case in a museum. "Love is, perhaps, the sensation of expertise that erupts out of nowhere, and as time goes on accumulates enough soil at its feet to be standing on something." "Electricity is part of nature. And the supernatural, whatever different people want to believe, is part of nature, too." "She felt included in the workings of the world, and in its movements among other worlds, and in whatever the great gyre was that encompassed them all. She felt, not quite that she could see beyond where she was sitting, but at least that she didn't fell blinkered, as she had by their window frame in the apartment, which was always crammed full of the ginkgo..." Towards the end there were a few chapters I could have done without, and I would have preferred a little more open of an ending. This was a beautiful read!

“Flashlight” is a kind of quiet twin to “The Orphan Master's Son.” It deals with the triangle of America, Japan, and North Korea and with fates that are determined by their respective national backgrounds. At the center of the story is the investigation into the disappearance of a father and husband, which is conducted in a strangely emotionless manner. This is because the social relationships within the family are highly dysfunctional and there was no real “family atmosphere” even before his disappearance. As a result, the silent struggles of the family members with themselves and each other are viewed with a great deal of detachment. Only rarely does one feel connected to them. This may be because none of the characters are really likable. No sooner has one become attached to one of them than the perspective changes and one is served further negative traits about the others. This may be realistic, but it fails to inspire identification. There are jumps in time and resulting gaps, which of course makes sense when taking stock of several lives. But sometimes the jumps in time are so big that you also distance yourself from the characters here. Suddenly, one of them reappears decades older, and you have to rethink the changed character. Added to this is Choi's extremely detailed storytelling. Some authors manage to draw the reader into the story in this way, but Choi only succeeds in doing so in a few places. Fatigue sets in instead of insight. Nevertheless, there are passages that remain in the memory. In particular, Louisa's journey from Paris to London by bus and Serk's story stick in the mind. They illustrate how far we are—from a global perspective—from a humane, just society. The mechanisms of power are questioned by showing them in an unvarnished light, and that is the great merit of the novel.

3.5 Flashlight gives us the story of Anne, Serk and Louisa Kang and is narrated by all three. Anne is an American who was forced to give up her first child, Tobias. Her husband, Serk, is a Japanese born Korean whose family split when his parents decided to go back to North Korea while Serk stayed in Japan. When their child, Louisa, is still young Serk is persuaded to return to Japan for work. While there Anne falls ill and Serk and Louisa form a bond which leaves Anne alone a lot of the time. During a family holiday to the coast Serk and Louisa go missing. Louisa is found almost drowned but Serk never returns. The story that follows describes Louisa and Anne's fractious relationship in America, along with the occasional visit from Tobias, which Louisa resents. We do not find out Serk's fate until the end of the novel. I have to say that while this novel is clearly extremely well researched and well written it did become, for me, incredibly tedious. Every part of the three's lives is described in endless detail and I got very bored in the second half. I did enjoy parts of the story including Louisa's travels in Europe and Tobias' story, such as it is. These seemed to flow beautifully but just as I was getting interested we switch back to Anne's troubles. The characters are also quite irritating. Anne seems to find everything dull and not worth her time, Serk is an obsessive father who drives a wedge between mother and child and Louisa begins as a spoiled child and turns into a permanently irritated adult. I have no clue why she is angry with her mother- and its not occasional, its everything her mother does or says. I'd like to say Louisa is the least sympathetic character but, to be honest, none of them are particularly pleasant people and I found it very hard to care about any problems they encountered - and they encounter huge, life changing/threatening changes. Thankyou to Netgalley and Farrar, Strauss & Giroux for the advance review copy.

Susan Choi is an elegant writer. In My Education, she considers the thin and blurring lines between lightning-bolt love, emotional intimacy, friendship, and sexual ardor. In her brilliant novel Trust Exercise, she dives right into how much we can trust each other’s exercise, and ultimately, how much the reader can trust the author in her narrative. Suffice to say that this is an incredibly ambitious author, who takes her readers in unexpected directions. I was pretty sure I would love Flashlight, which promised to balance personal and historical narratives. And I did…sorta…until the love turned primarily to admiration. The novel begins with a short story that made its debut in The New Yorker and has since been fleshed out. Louisa, a 10-year-old, went walking on a Japanese beach with her father one night. Her memory is murky: she is found half-dead on the beach and her father is missing, presumed dead. A mystery is set up, but we only get to it through a lengthy, circuitous, and sometimes overwhelmingly detailed journey. The author spends considerable time crafting the characters and getting readers up to speed on the Korean diaspora. Serk, Louisa’s father, was born to Korean migrants – he spoke Korean at home and Japanese at school. In 1952, as an ethnic Korean he was made an alien registrant in the nation of his birth. Eventually he married Anne, an American, whose fling with a married man led to her son, Tobias, who will re-enter their lives. And then there’s Louisa, who grows up the troubled daughter of a remote father and a mysteriously ill mother, who lives with a huge hole in the midst of her life. She does not possess any events to fill the space between stepping with her father onto the damp sand and waking up in a hospital bed; the stories of her father’s death by drowning is one she somehow both authors and received passively. As a result, she wonders: what shapes does a life take when a change takes away all the points representing events and all the lines forming stories. Certainly, Susan Choi is an expert at a balancing act of exploring a complex history with a personal narrative that weaves its way through decades, continents, and memories. Like a flashlight, it shines its light on certain events and emotions while obscuring others and eventually widens the illumination. The role of identity remains central: who are we when we don’t really know all the details of who we are? I am so grateful to Farrar, Straus, and Giroux for giving me the privilege of being an early reader in exchange for an honest review. I do believe that lovers of luscious prose and historical complexities will devour this book. Although it didn’t capture me as much as previous books by this author, I applaud her for spreading her creative wings and admire its scope.

I decided to quit this book at 56%. It was not holding my interest. I may give it a try another time, after all I did purchase a copy. For now I will not rate it. But when I started reading I was very impressed with the writing and storytelling, so I was absolutely sure that this was going to be a 5 stars read. Unfortunately the development of the story became extremely slow and uninteresting.
a legitimate masterpiece. i want to read it all over again.

Book 3 of my Booker Prize longlist challenge, each year I dedicate my time to reading all the books on the booker longlist/shortlist so I can attempt to predict the winner. (Key word here is attempt) This has led me to read some incredible books, pushing me out of my comfort zone & expanding my taste. My first DNF! I swear every year there is one DNF from the booker, this year Flashlight was the lucky winner. Incredibly long, arduous & honestly, dull. We start out with the story of Louisa, she is 10 years old and her father goes missing whilst they are on a walk on the beach. We jump perspectives and timelines throughout this story, seemingly never getting any closer to a resolution or even a plot? So many pages of nothing, NOTHING. The plot moves forward at a painstaking pace. I just couldn't give myself any more time for this. I felt a book slump incoming hard and fast. I had to save myself. Onto the next!

"Light shows us only what it touches. The rest of the world remains invisible." 🔦 Ambitious. Interesting. Intriguing. But very drawn out… 10-year-old Louisa and her father, Serk, go walking on a Japanese beach one evening. Hours later, she is found washed up on the beach, half-dead, her father missing, presumably drowned. From this brief mysterious introduction, Susan Choi whisks us back in time creating a generational saga interwoven with intrigue that sweeps across decades and countries… My intrigue was sparked immediately by this devastating prologue. A mystery is set up, a thrilling tale expected. However, we must take a longggg, sometimes frustrating journey to get to the disappearance of father Serk. As Louisa and her mother return to the US, the mystery of what really happened that night slowly unfolds… Choi spends the first 30% of the book backtracking, delving into details of the family’s past. Then, following the disappearance of Serk, she spends a large proportion of the book tracing four generations of a Korean-Japanese-American family through time and space, weaving together the personal and the political. Exploring themes of family, loss, immigration, and culture. I fully appreciate what Choi was trying to achieve with this novel. It was quite fascinating and the premise was both highly original and thought-provoking. However, I think the scope was a little too wide, and the context a little too dense. There were parts of the book that really captured my attention, whilst other sections had me questioning what on earth they had to do with the mystery. Overall, this was a very creative and complex piece of work. It was both a sensitive family portrait and an investigative read. While it didn’t fully capture my mind and heart, I was compelled to keep reading, and as I did the shocking horrors of the world unfolded. The plot builds layer upon layer, concluding with a beautiful crescendo, full of emotion and wonder. 3.5 🌟🌟🌟✨

Flashlight relates the story of a man, Serk, who returns to the country of the his origin, Japan, with his American daughter and wife. Serk's parents are Korean, so Serk in some ways is a man of three countries (Japan, Korea, US) and in other ways a man with no country. The story of this family is meticulously detailed, and when Serk's parents return to North Korea, without him, there are ramifications both large and small. I want to give this book 4 stars. I really do. But I just can't. It's so overwritten. There's like ZERO space for the reader, and I don't care if you are writing romance or historical fiction, please leave something for my own brain to fill in. That all being said, Choi sure can craft a beautiful SENTENCE. This book is filled with very specific details, each evoked with perfect words. I admire that immensely. It cannot be easy to write 450 plus pages and have each sentence be like artwork. So hats off to her talents. But storytelling requires more suspense, and even though there were some quite harrowing scenes, I never really felt the suspense viscerally. By the end, I really wanted to skim. I resisted the urge, but I just wanted to be done. (view spoiler) Another thing I really did enjoy about the book was the historical aspects. I didn't know much about the history of post WWII Korea, and Choi helpfully lists ten books in her acknowledgements, and I am super interested in delving into the non-fiction that she references. I am always appreciative if I learn something new from fiction - - whether it's about history or the human condition or something else. This book was a winner from that aspect, but I probably won't be running to read more from this author.

One star seems harsh considering the writing itself is decent, but I can’t in good conscience rate a book that I spend the whole time wanting to quit reading a higher rating than this. I think this novel could’ve benefitted from a lot more editing, as it commits a lot of what I generally consider to be writing sins - things that bothers me: - Long passages for the sake of being long. I’m all for meandering, descriptive prose but it has to contribute to the atmosphere, characterization, or plot in some way or make you feel something. This books feels like the words are just languishing on the pages. It also doesn’t help that the subject matter is rather depressing, with the main character grieving the loss of her father. Maybe this could be the right read for someone in a specific mindset, but in general, I thought that it was a little too indulgent. This is the type of book in which I’m afraid a casual reader would pick up and then conclude that reading is boring. It’s really evident that the author put a lot of thought into this work, but it just didn’t work for me as a reader. - Lots of exposition right off the bat to explore the different characters’ backgrounds. Most of the book is written in past tense, so it feels like the events already happened and the characters don’t have any agency in the story’s events. It’s also composed of a lot of flashbacks and non-linear events, which doesn’t help with the story’s progression. - A lot of contemporary novels have alternating characters’ perspectives. However, for this one, it’s written in third person and the writing style does not vary from character to character. I think any story with multiple perspectives is similar to an actor playing multiple parts in a show/movie - it takes an incredible amount of skill to showcase the different characters’ importance and perspectives and to give them an equal (or equitable) weight to the story. - The plot doesn’t really go anywhere. I think this is meant to be more of a character study, but it doesn’t bring a lot of new ideas to the table. Special thanks to Farrar, Straus and Giroux and NetGalley for providing an eARC in exchange for an honest, independent review.

4.5 stars. Booker Book 5 of 13: 8.5 out of 10. I loved the first 75% of this book wholeheartedly. I loved the sweep, the digressions, the richly drawn characters: Anne, Soek, Louisa. It's been a long time since I have read a great American novel that goes so unabashedly in deep on character and relationships rather than ideas and artistry (compare Audition, which I read at the same time). It's very different than the other Choi that I've read, and is largely a rich layered old-fashioned family saga that also chillingly relates some dreadful episodes in Japanese and Korean history (interesting that the book begins in the same world as Pachinko - Min Jin Lee and Choi were the same year (a year behind me) at Yale (I have loads of mutual friends with both, but don't really know either), and my first (ignoble) thought was that Choi was trying to cash in on the success of Pachinko). Anyway, I just loved this book and found it entirely propulsive, even (sometimes especially) the episodes that I've seen criticized as digressions, such as the beautiful episode of Anne and Walter or Louisa's trip to Paris (which perfectly recreated so many things about student travel in that era). The North Korean chapters were chilling and riveting. The book slightly lost its way for me towards the end. Choi has a trick of having the gutpunch moments (except the very end) happen off screen, and I was OK with this, until some of the end material (a very long chapter in China and an overly long flashback on Anne's part) seem to be overly dilatory when I (the reader) was longing for revelation and resolution. I had never been frustrated with the pace or the doubling back before but then in the penultimate chapters, I suddenly wanted a tighter editorial hand. Choi does stick the landing though. The end is just as it should be. Highly recommended for anyone who loves long immersive reads that sweep through the 20th century - a departure from anything else I've read so far on the Booker list.

My first Susan Choi and it didn't disappoint. It reminded me a bit of Elif Shafak: she takes a topic of interest and then weaves an intricate plot with around it, criss-crossing continents, spanning decades, and at its heart an intriguing mystery. 'Flashlight' revolves around a dramatic event where little Luisa's father, an American immigrant of mixed Korean-Japanese descent, disappears on a beach in Japan. It is assumed he drowned but his body is never found. All kinds of subplots keep the reader guessing what on earth has happened, and in the process we learn more about Japanese-Korean post-war relations. It works well on audio too as it is plot-based.

A favorite of this year, it's easy to see why this is on so many awards lists. Although it starts as a slow burn, it picks up and gathers speed as it continues. Spanning decades, the story spools out unrelentingly, with complicated characters and twists in plot unforeseen.

You’re gonna have to work for this one. But the work is worth it if not for that exquisite ending. The family relationships are so real that they leave you feeling neither crummy about your own family nor puffed with pride. These characters are human with their likeable qualities and the ones that make them horrific pains in the butt. The brutality of daughters to their mothers. The meanness of husbands to wives. The superiority of wives to husbands. Daddy and daughter love. Step children trying to find their place in the pecking order. Sons loving their mothers hard. All of these relationships forging the river of living through these lenses: Aging Death with acceptance. Growing up and forging a real relationship with a parent. Taking care of parents in their last days. To me these interspersed themes far outweigh the plot of the story. The plot was complicated. The relationships were real. In sum it’s one of those books that left me marveling at the gift that an author has to written words.

4.5 stars rounded down. I found this novel uneven and I didn’t massively like the audible narrator which didn’t help. She was a bit breathy! There was stunning writing and very interesting questions posed. It made me do some research about Korean history and its relationship with Japan - I knew none of it. The characters were not likeable but that didn’t matter. At times I thought the novel was outstanding and I couldn’t listen to the last 30 minutes for a while cos it had got under my skin. It was definitely an uncomfortable novel and it is by no means an easy read in any sense but that’s no bad thing.

Flashlight was so many things, a complex story of a multi cultural family, of the relinquishment of a child, of 4 people whose lives came together then split apart and who we continue to observe, often decades later. Not everything that happens forms part of the plot. We fill that in ourselves, creating connections as the narrative leap frogs forward from one character to the next. It explores the effect on each person in the family of their cultural past, their birth circumstance, the moves they make that shift perceptions of who they are. It exposes the cruelities of nations, abuses of humankind, the determination of those who seek the truth, the perseverance of those who want to bring justice and the importance of closure, of being present even when someone seems beyond comprehension. Wow, what an effort to bring all that together and create a novel that traverses so many elements of the cross cultural family, the immigrant life, the (false) allure of the return, lost family members and the dangers of trying to find them. This was such an eye opening, thought provoking read that almost felt like two novels, The first half relatively straight forward, the second half mysterious, disconcerting and dangerous.

I know I’m contrary to much of the opinion on Flashlight, but it is a lengthy and dense read that was static in character development. Susan Choi is talented, but my take is that Flashlight is not compelling or dynamic. It is average. See the review linked below. https://youtu.be/hJYPrZFvVmg?si=TWaAu...

‘Flashlight’ by Susan Choi is an unusual book in that the main characters are unlikeable yet the novel itself is an operatic masterpiece of writing, research and history. The title is apt in following the lives of the members of a mixed-race family, each sharply illuminated in a narrow cone of bright light whenever the narration switches from one family member’s point of view to another’s. However, the timeline as lived by each family member is a chaotic one, moving from the present of the late 1940’s to the present of 2011, from Japan to the United States back to Japan and North Korea. The timeline is one which is tumbling around in each chapter, illuminating the present, then the past, then the parallel paths of each family member, none knowing what the other is doing due to intentional avoidance of the others except when necessary to get in touch. I wouldn’t say they communicate much, either. None of them appear to have much curiosity about anything. Trying to fit in without looking as if they are panicking about not fitting in appears to be the main motivation of all of the main characters, except one. There are four main family members. Hiroshi (Japanese name)/Seok (Korean and given name at birth)/Serk (American name) Kang, a college academic born in Japan but ethnically Korean, and Anne, once a secretary and later a housewife, born in America, marry and become the parents of Louisa, American-born. Tobias is Louisa’s half-brother, whom Anne had given up to be raised by Tobias’s American father and wife before she met Serk. Except for cheerful Tobias, who is a wannabe Japanese Buddhist monk with a heavy focus on self-effacement and abasement, Serk, Anne and Louisa are spiky characters, never satisfied with each other, expressing very little empathy, especially Louisa, who absolutely hates her mother for many reasons. All of Louisa’s hatreds for her mother Anne, as far as I can see, are from a lack of empathy and maybe some racial jealousy of her mother’s white race and beauty. Anne is blond and blue-eyed, unlike the mixed race Louisa. Serk is a person with much anxieties. None have what anyone would call a sense of humor or fun. As children all felt they were in the wrong body, either living in families at odds culturally with the countries they grow up in, unaccepted by the dominant culture if they looked different, or in families that didn’t particularly notice or care for them, leaving the child to feel unaccepted, even unwanted, which can happen in American families and other cultures. The book, through flashbacks, follows the childhoods of each character. Readers can soon see there are some good reasons for each member of the family to be unable to bond to each other. (view spoiler) When Louisa was nine years old, Serk moved the three of them to Japan for a temporary teaching position at a Japanese college. At first Louisa was frustrated by her lack of knowledge of the Japanese language, but she was soon speaking Japanese well after a year. Louisa had hoped her darker skin and hair, a lot darker than Anne’s, would allow her to fit in, but she discovered her hair was not as dark as that of the Japanese people. She did not look Japanese or Korean enough. Serk, of course, spoke flawless Japanese. Anne spoke no Japanese, and she soon became afflicted with some sort of physical disability. Japanese doctors, as well as her husband and child, thought it was mental illness. Louisa scorned Anne for her lack of any knowledge of Japanese culture, but especially hated her for seemingly faking a physical illness. Things were very unsettled for all three of them, but they had hopes of fitting in eventually. Except a mysterious disaster occurred which upended their already shaky foundations. I have copied the book blurb: ”A novel tracing a father’s disappearance across time, nations, and memory, from the author of Trust Exercise. One summer night, Louisa and her father take a walk on the breakwater. Her father is carrying a flashlight. He cannot swim. Later, Louisa is found on the beach, soaked to the skin, barely alive. Her father is gone. She is ten years old. Louisa is an only child of parents who have severed themselves from the past. Her father, Serk, is Korean, but was born and raised in Japan; he lost touch with his family when they bought into the promises of postwar Pyongyang and relocated to North Korea. Her American mother, Anne, is estranged from her Midwestern family after a reckless adventure in her youth. And then there is Tobias, Anne’s illegitimate son, whose reappearance in their lives will have astonishing consequences. But now it is just Anne and Louisa, Louisa and Anne, adrift and facing the challenges of ordinary life in the wake of great loss. United, separated, and also repelled by their mutual grief, they attempt to move on. But they cannot escape the echoes of that night. What really happened to Louisa’s father? Shifting perspectives across time and character and turning back again and again to that night by the sea, Flashlight chases the shock waves of one family’s catastrophe, even as they are swept up in the invisible currents of history. A monumental new novel from the National Book Award winner Susan Choi, Flashlight spans decades and continents in a spellbinding, heartgripping investigation of family, loss, memory, and the ways in which we are shaped by what we cannot see.” The book blurb is right on! The novel is astonishingly multi-layered, shining a fascinating light on a family of individualistic travelers, unable to settle down in their own skins much less a culture. Each in their own ways are stateless residents in their countries of birth. Each of them live a life of quiet inner desperation (except Tobias, a fool in any culture) in their attempts to find and fit into an identity, yet each of them so damn prickly and judgemental of others, it is obvious they could only fail at connecting. They are not broken people, though. They are people who can’t find acceptance in the being of themselves for themselves, full stop, and they are looking at everybody else with an unhealthy outlook of suspicion, paranoia and criticism. But, similar to what happened to the American Native children in the 19th and 20th centuries, the children of Japanese Koreans in Japan, for instance, were told they needed to fit in with the dominant culture, but if in having made an effort to do so, were estranged from their families and were still not at all accepted in the dominant culture. This situation is currently happening in China with Uyghur Muslims. I’ve read it happened to people from India who moved to England and raised several generations of culturally English children born in England. And on and on. However, there certainly are even more terrible governments who are intent on forcing what is an impossible and insane monoculture on others of different cultures and beliefs….(read the novel 1984 for how terrible a government can get. Or read up on the Soviet Union government of the past. Or of the current North Korean government.) I think these are some of the themes, gentler reader. Please post alternative opinions in the comments below. This is not just a well-written novel, it is a grand opera of national histories, culture and politics affecting personal relationships and personalities. Although the social characteristics and expectations of the three governing nations involved in the book are seemingly only backdrops of the stages on which the family performs, society and governance policies have devastating affects on the four ordinary, basically non-political, people. I could not put the book down for three days, reading every chance I could get. Despite that I couldn’t like any of these characters, I really had to know what was going to happen next. The writing has the driving energy of a thriller, even though the story is often only about a family becoming dysfunctional and drifting apart. The mystery of the disappearance of Serk is one I solved right away, though, having read of the real-life and truly bizarre situation in newspapers some decades ago. (view spoiler) Although the novel is a high-end literary read, and on the shortlist for the Booker Prize, I highly recommend this thought-provoking novel about family, identity and generational dysfunction from what I believe to be primarily external governance causes.

what a ride, a sometimes uneven reading experience. one thing is for sure despite my mixed feelings: susan choi knows how to weave together a complex story full of history and multifaceted characters. i had a difficult time getting into the beginning of this book. i remember particularly around page 20 i found myself stuck rereading the same page because i just couldn’t get into that flow state. once i got through each character’s introductory sections, i found it a lot easier to progress. i think my main hurdle was that i found the metaphors and sentence structure to be clunky at times. i am, however, truly impressed with the novel’s plot, following a family torn apart by korean and japanese conflict. while i’m no expert in the subject, this felt very well-researched and enough context is incorporated to explain the history that runs so deeply throughout this book. i’m glad i took my time reading and getting to know the characters - seeing how they reflect each other despite their differences and distance between them was really touching. choi doesn’t hold the reader’s hand. there were a few instances where situations felt important but were glossed over, and it got longwinded talking about things that were less relevant to the plot. despite my struggles with parts of the book, i think the themes it presents are very impactful and i can see why it was longlisted for the booker prize. kind of curious to pick up trust exercise to see what else choi has to offer. 3.5 stars

This is one of Book Riot’s Best Books of 2025: Susan Choi's sixth novel is a masterpiece, a family saga wrapped in a mystery that haunts its characters. Young Louisa and her father are walking along a beach at night, carrying flashlights. Hours later, Louisa is found alone, barely alive, and her father is never seen again. As Louisa grows up with her mother, the loss of her father hovering over their lives, parts of their pasts are revealed, including a long-held secret. Flashlight is a sharp examination of not only the physical loss of someone, but loss of place, estrangement, and loss of self, as Louisa and her mother carry around a grief with no end. It's a stunning heart-puncher. - Liberty Hardy

Blown away by this one. Shortlisted for the 2025 Bookers and Pulitzer buzz is well deserved. Multi-layered, incredibly and impeccably researched, and character driven. I can appreciate that many reviewers didn’t love the characters, however, I became more sympathetic towards them while reading about their traumas and it rationalized (to me) their respective responses. Very interesting and ambitious book and the vast geographical references made this so much more enjoyable. History of North Korea was interesting to me and Choi has really honed in on the politics. I’m short on time and won’t do this review justice, but an impressive piece of work!
The Booker Prize FOMO is hitting hard (I've only read two of the longlist) and everyone is raving about Flashlight so here I am... nothing more than an impressionable sheep just trying to fit in

This book was a slow burn. At times I was a bit bored and it felt very long despite being just 466 pages. I felt I’d heard enough about this odd little family of misfits. And then suddenly things shifted when Louisa - the daughter of an expatriated Korean born in Japan who moves to the US and an American mother - heads to London. Things get a bit dark and the action speeds up. Then a mystery from Louisa’s childhood also begins to emerge under new light. It’s hard to say much more without spoilers. I’ve liked a number of books that feature the complicated relationship between Korea and Japan… This book exceeds all the others. I always learn something new that I didn’t know - well my history knowledge is generally weak, admittedly, so it’s easy for me to learn things about this part of the world. This is the second book I’ve read with a reference to the Korean island Jeju. I think I’m meant to travel there. It intrigues me.

Susan Choi’s latest novel is an extraordinary work that artfully blends themes from family to the brutality of North Korea. At its core, it is the story of a family: Serk is a Japanese born Korean, who stays in Japan after his family is lured back to North Korea after WWII, receives an education and becomes a professor in the United States; Anne, his wife, is a tough, lonely Midwesterner, who is plagued by disease and choices made in her youth; Louisa, their child, is precocious, but suffers from having to bounce between her parents’ quite different personalities. When Louisa is 9, the family moves to Japan so that Serk can complete a one year academic position there. Serk and Louisa go for an evening walk on the beach. Serk disappears and is presumed dead by drowning, while Louisa survives. That sets the stage for the rest of the novel, which follows Serk through brutal imprisonment in North Korea; Anne through illness, the reappearance of the child she gave up for adoption, and life as Louisa’s mother without Serk; and Louisa through high school, college and life into adulthood. I feel that I am just touching the surface in trying to review this complex novel. Families, family interactions (or lack thereof), acknowledgement of family (or lack thereof), loneliness within a family, mother/daughter relationships and marriage are among the many themes deeply explored in this book. Just as powerfully, the treatment of Koreans in Japan during and after WWII, the brutality of the North Korean prison system, the rampant starvation in North Korea, and the position of North Korean refugees in China are themes as well. With beautiful language, Choi leads us to examine who we really are - - from our life in our family and our relationship with our other family members, to our life as a member of an ethnic group, and to our life as a citizen of a country. I likely originally chose this novel just because of its connection to North Korea, and at times I felt that some parts of it could be shortened. But upon finishing it, I know that this complete, multi-faceted, wonderfully written novel spoke deeply to me and merits its selection as a nominee for the prizes for which it has been nominated.

4.5 rounded up although I understand some of the criticism that Choi overwrites at times I did not find that this occurred too often. for the most part. I found this an incredibly compelling and engrossing family saga, mystery, beautifully written literary fiction. one of the best novels of the year.

I love a chunky saga, and Flashlight delivered on this front. It’s a big beast of a novel, a family tragedy and a study of its ripple effects, an examination of the weaknesses of human memory, and a historical novel all swept into one. There’s lots of interesting storytelling here about connection and isolation, and lovely extended metaphor about the flashlight. It is a story that reminds us that in any moment or experience we only part of what is happening is ever illuminated for us. Having struggled to get on with Choi’s previous novel I found this an absolute treat, and think in circumstances where I could have given more of my attention to this, it could easily have been a five star read.

A well written tale, but just wayyyyy too long and slow. It’s tragic, and explores so many themes that intrigue me: complex grief, trauma responses, identity exploration/loss, etc. If you have the time and willpower, pick this one up!

Thank you fsgbooks for the gifted arc I kept holding off on reading Flashlight after seeing some call it dense or slow. After not being able to put it down this weekend I can say it was anything but. I won't go over too much plot since I feel that gives some things away and also you'll hear about it multiple times now that it was, deservedly, Booker longlisted. All I’ll say is that Choi shows us how the geopolitical and personal are intrinsically linked through the lives of one family over three countries. At first this book is disorienting as Choi throws you into the aftermath of the ‘mystery’. We have a limited perspective (definitely a theme) and don’t know why certain things are being said or thought or what’s real or not. Then Choi abruptly takes us back decades, maybe not to THE beginning but a beginning, and through the decades after. Choi will literally time jump years in the middle of a sentence! This is the kind of novel where we are sometimes ahead of the characters, or at least are able to see what they can’t, and at other times things are kept from us completely. It's frustratingly lifelike - how often do you have a complete picture of someone you know, or I would argue even yourself? We all censor ourselves in a way. Sometimes you don't know what you remember or the meaning of a moment until someone else brings it up or there are moments in time you just skip while obsessing over others to the minutest detail. This is not confined to just memory, but language and in turn the history we are taught, or not. The feeling of not belonging is experienced by every character but they are blind to each other’s plights. Sure language barriers and ethnicity play a role here, but I thought the concepts of what ties you to a ‘homeland’ and what it’s like to essentially be stateless were pretty current in today’s news. I thought this was reflected through the unknown half-brother, what do you owe someone that you only have a blood-tie too? It’s fascinating how most of these characters are quite frankly annoying at the best of times, straight up terrible at worst of times. Louisa is going to frustrate the hell out of you BUT I will say that Choi gives us enough about each character to, mostly, understand them. My heart really went out for Anne and Louisa- as a child Louisa doesn’t understand what’s happening with her mom’s body and loses a sense of stability or safety. Add to that a move to another country, one where you may just fit in if it wasn’t for you mom, well I can see how that would warp your love and relationship. Louisa unfortunately holds on to this for most of her life. Girl, LET IT GO!

A flashlight illuminates something invisible in the darkness. While there is a literal flashlight in this book, and while it bears relevance to the story, it is a metaphor, as well, for secrets kept, things unseen, and things understood only when the cloak of darkness has been vanquished. I found this book quite interesting, and I applaud the character, cultural, and historical development, but everything was painfully dragged out, making it a challenge to always remain engaged. I am glad I saw it through, though, as the ending made those sluggish moments worth enduring. I am immensely grateful to Macmillan Audio and NetGalley for my copy. All opinions are my own.

This certainly dealt an emotional blow and while I’m not always a fan of overly long novels I feel it was justified for this story. You really had to feel the progression of time and the events that transpired in the 30 years + to understand the impact of Serk’s disappearance on each of his family members. The writing was beautiful and immersive with character depth and development. It left me wanting to know more about these “taken” people, and I guess that’s the point.
Basically I liked the story, but in the end it's getting too sentimental.
For what it's worth, this book had the rare effect of making me gasp out loud in the middle. Beautifully done.

A flashlight illuminates one specific area while leaving the remaining space in darkness and that is exactly what Choi does in this complex novel. A fractured family saga, told by alternating characters that sometimes moves in a very slow meandering way and then it will jump to another timeframe. But I think that is exactly the author's intention; to focus intently on one scene while purposely just giving us glimpses in another area. Overall, a heartfelt story that brings awareness to a dark part of history and Choi gives an impressive list of books about North Korea that she used during research.

A heart-wrenching beautiful story about grief, loss, and family dynamics. The book explains dynamics between families and nations with various family secrets slowly being revealed throughout the novel. This book has multiple POVs allowing us to see and hear information from all of the main characters. I absolutely loved this book, while it carries some deeper material it is such an incredibly written novel. A great character-driven book that really allows you to dive in and think.
4.5 dare I say my favorite book of the year??? 🥲🥲🥲🥲🥲🥲🥲🥲🥲

3.5/5 Flashlight is my first Susan Choi, and while I liked it, I was also frustrated by how close it came to being a great book without ever quite getting there. At its center is a harrowing story about North Korean totalitarianism and its impact on those suffering through it, but that story often felt obscured by an excess of writing that, though engaging and well-crafted, came across as a bit quaint and jarring in comparison. Because this part of the narrative does not come into focus until the latter half of the novel, I felt that the most vital and urgent material was kept at arm’s length for way too long. The richly detailed construction of the characters serves as the novel’s primary narrative engine. The writing style effectively captures their rhythms of thought and intense emotional expression, and I appreciated the effort to create such vivid characters, because this is where the book most succeeds. The novel examines how trauma and grief shape identity and life in both subtle and overt ways, and how those emotions are often permanently embedded within the mind and body. It explores what it means to be separated from one’s family, homeland, and cultural roots, and what happens when those experiences are left to fester in silence. Choi shows how the past refuses to stay buried no matter how hard the characters try, and how family secrets can warp relationships from the inside out. The structure of each chapter being told from a different character’s perspective is my least favorite kind of scaffolding because it often results in awkward pacing and tonal shifts, with the author working to establish a distinct voice for each character. That is one of my biggest issues with Flashlight. I think the structure worked against the book’s ambition and made the novel feel too slippery and unfocused. Still, there was much to admire, and Choi’s strong writing offered enough depth and emotion to make the reading experience worthwhile.

I’m not sure what to make of this fascinating but enigmatic novel, with its equally fascinating and enigmatic characters, who are so deeply flawed but still improbably sympathetic. Yes, the novel is marked by unexplained gaps and leaps in time and place, but there is an underlying coherence—you just need to be patient to see it revealed (even then, however, not all questions are fully answered). What I do know is that the writing is jaw-droppingly brilliant…these long, complex sentences that, in their descriptive and emotional weight, take your breath away. And the many embedded stories…almost set pieces in character and length…never fail to break your heart. I do recommend it…as one reviewer wrote, however, you’ll feel like it’s taken you hostage once you pick it up (which is both good and bad).

2025 Booker Prize Longlist 12/13 2026 Women's Prize for Fiction Shortlist 2/6 A unique family saga that I wasn't expecting to like as much as I do. The only reason I picked this up was because of it's inclusion in the Booker Longlist, and reports of it's being too long and overly circuitous are absolutely right, but whatever mood I find myself in these days, probably because I have eliminated the conveyor belt of ARCs from my life, this turns out to be the type of book I used to love, pre GR, pre podcasts, when it was only me and my own devices that selected my reading matter. With it's over and back between the US and Japan (and Korea), it constantly reminded me of Ruth Ozeki's "A Tale for the Time being", but parts of it also recalled the things I learned about North Korea in "The Girl with Seven Names" and Korean/Japanese relations in "Pachinko". I think that busy me of the netgalley deadlines that faced off with the library book stacks would have resented the seemingly unnecessary places the author brought me to, but I feel richly rewarded for having experienced the random sprawl of the various trajectories of this complex family. There are very difficult passages in this book. There are acts of violence and war crimes and references to normalisation of dehumanisation, not only in the obvious places, but also in more familiar settings too, and every single character has something to despise about them, be it grumpiness, selfishness, brattiness or just plain annoying, and that's not even counting the "baddies", and yet despite their shortcomings, despite the author's refusal to manipulate the reader's emotional response, it's impossible to ignore the humanity of these characters and to feel deeply for them. It also highlights the difficulties of negotiating diplomacy between cultures and nations whose histories are so layered in complexities that any move will invariably be the wrong move.

My my my. This is a saga of a book that’s structure is also its title: Choi gives us a family saga and historical fiction and generational trauma in from multiple perspectives, but she only gives us what’s immediately in front of the “light” in the moment. There is SO much that we don’t get in this story, much like what we can’t see in the dark beyond a flashlight bulb. This is also a hefty novel, with lots of moving pieces covering decades in the US, Japan, Korea, China and Europe. There are a wide range of characters, all of whom have deep and secretive histories: Anne, a white woman from the Midwest who has a baby who was given up for “adoption” to the father of the child who then marries Serk, a Korean born in Japan who has come to the US to teach, cutting off all ties and connections to his family. They have Louisa, a bright but seemingly troubled kid who worships her dad and seems to have little time for her mom. The book opens with us learning that Serk and Louisa went for a walk on the shore of a small Japanese town where they were living as Serk was teaching at a local university, and Louisa is found nearly drowned with a flashlight but Serk is never found. We learn of their lives before the incident, as well as the many decades of the aftermath. Choi writes in such an accessible yet visceral way, that I was compelled to keep going in this book despite not loving all the characters. It felt like the longer we spent with each person, and the more we learned, the more we were able to piece together enough of the picture to understand and empathize with the characters in a way that I would not have guessed I could at the beginning of the book. Really fantastic book I’ll be thinking about for a while.

[Copy provided by publisher] READ IF YOU LIKE... • Dense and demanding prose • Struggling to find your place in the world • Little known aspects of East Asian history I THOUGHT IT WAS... A formidable piece of literary fiction that's beautifully rewarding for those who stick with it. In Japan, ten-year-old Louisa goes for walk at dusk along the beach with her father. Later, Louisa is found washed up on shore. Her father is nowhere to be seen. This pivotal event frames the lives of this sundered family as we attempt to piece together what happened. This is peak Literary Fiction. Long, complex, meandering sentences convey almost every thought, forcing you to read slowly and methodically. But if you don't mind this type of prose, or you persevere through it, you'll discover that Choi has artfully spun a solemn and human story about the search for belonging, wrapped within the political turmoil of Japan, North Korea, South Korea, and China. Louisa's father, Serk, is a Korean born in Japan, who took pride in his supposed Japanese identity before Korea was liberated from Japan. This sudden rift in racial identity creates a dissonance jarring enough to affect all the members of his future family. Indeed, almost every character is ill at ease with themselves, and Choi masterfully depicts this in a variety of ways. Though Choi's writing is anything but straightforward, its richness rewards you with a story that uncovers a lesser known corner of East Asian history, the soul of which lies with a broken family where a mother and father try to do everything possible to protect their only daughter.

Reviewing Ken Follett at this point is difficult because I feel like I've said it all before. This is another lovely pastoral historical that follows the everyday lives of characters in Neolithic Britain. The formula works: we've got love stories, historical/technological developments (in this case, early carpentry and stonework), and shitty villains. Follett writes the best scumbags who you love to hate and here Troon was such a petty little tyrant that I enjoyed hating him so much. Don't be put off by the blurb telling you this is about the building of Stonehenge. As with The Pillars of the Earth, you don't have to have any great interest in architecture to enjoy the stories about all the characters surrounding the central building project. There's plenty of human drama, betrayal and heartache. In this time, there are three main groups of people: the herders who herd cattle, the farmers who grow crops, and the woodlanders who forage for nuts and berries. Each has their own ways and beliefs, and oftentimes they come into conflict with one another. When the land is hit by a devastating drought, some of them are willing to risk upsetting the others and clashes between the tribes become inevitable. I love how Follett makes everyday life engaging. There are the bigger political struggles always in the periphery but the focus is on the people, their families, and how they can survive and feed themselves for another winter. His depiction of societies where sexuality is fluid and sexual revels are the norm are a fun blend of archaeological theory and imagination. I'll read whatever he writes next.

Follett can always deliver an epic story in mammoth form. This one isn’t about 🦣 mammoths- it is a little later, beginning in 2500 BC. The cultures of these different tribes - their traditions & values. Peace among them until one murders another and war breaks out because the gods demand a balance. Violence where there was peace; the fight for land; the near extinction of a tribe and the means with which they survive. The once harmonious tribes now face a fallen civilization with the only hope of Stonehenge becoming the centre to reunite these people. I did struggle with the some of the engineering details for which these rocks were moved. I also didn't have that character connection which I have not encountered when reading Follett. Yet, despite its shortfalls, it was still a riveting, rolling rock, kind of read. 4⭐️

Set around 2500 BCE, Circle of Days explores the mysterious story of Stonehenge. Seft comes from a family of flint miners. The work is grueling and his father is harsh. When Seft meets Neen, a girl from a family of herders, he notices something different within her family - love and kindness. When the farmers secretly take over land traditionally used for herding animals, Neen’s mother fears the outrage could spark a war between the two communities. Though she has never experienced war herself, she remembers the stories her parents told about a past conflict between the herders and the woodlanders. Joia, Neen’s younger sister, is fascinated by the priestesses who guard the secrets of the sky. When the High Priestess teaches her a new way of counting - using discs instead of body parts - Joia becomes deeply intrigued and begins to understand her true calling. At this time, the Great Plain is divided among three tribes: herders, farmers, and woodlanders. Mistrust among them is growing and acts of savage violence threaten to escalate the conflict. A devastating drought forces even the most generous to reconsider their willingness to share. Survival becomes the driving force. When a wooden monument dedicated to the priestesses is destroyed, the High Priestess orders it rebuilt in stone. The necessary heavy stones lie far away, and fifteen of them are needed. Transporting them could take years. Yet, as heavy and impossible as the task may seem, one person is driven by greater force – a vision of the stone monument rising. The bloodshed, the loss, the arguments, and the violence all fuel the determination to bring it to life and to bring peace. The story of Pia and Han – two young people from different tribes – unfolds during a time when inter-tribal relationships are forbidden. Despite the rules, they find a way to be together. The forbidden love and the suspenseful search that follows add twists that keep readers on edge. The detailed depiction of how the stones are transported, and how the monument is built stone by stone, makes Circle of Days a captivating read. With its intriguing elements of ancient history, the story feels remarkably authentic to its time period. It’s an absorbing novel that turns pages quickly. Ken Follett is a master storyteller; with fascinating characters he weaves a mesmerizing tale rooted in the mysteries of the past - authentic, engaging, and utterly captivating. “Circle of Days”, by Ken Follett 4 stars ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ Set in prehistoric Britain, specifically during the Neolithic period around 2500 BCE, and centers on the construction of the monument we know as Stonehenge. The story unfolds on the Great Plain, a landscape divided by the tribal groups. This one was the most anticipated book of the year, for me (along with “My Friends”, by Fredrik Backman and “The Ekements”, by John Boyne). I pre-ordered a copy and even purchased the audiobook narrated by Richard Armitage, which I paired with the ebook. Listening and reading at the same time is quite an experience, especially with Armitage’s narration. I was captivated from the beginning by the storytelling and I could have read this book in one sitting, if I had started reading it on a Saturday morning or Sunday. As for the writing, I do not believe this was written by Follett, as the writing was too simplistic and even juvenile in some parts (but it wasn’t painful as in “Never” - the lowest rating I have ever given to Follett). There were some similarities to “The Pillars of the Earth”, so I believe that this book was conceived by Follett, but perhaps written by a ghost writer. Thanks to Armitage, I loved all the characters that I was supposed to love, and despised the ones I should. The interactions and dynamics between the characters were well displayed. I found the storyline to be very entertaining and interesting. His narration brought everyone to life and I couldn’t have enough. There are plenty of drama between the characters and tribes (woodlanders, herders, miners and farmers). There are plenty moments of brutality and gory scenes, that perhaps is a bit too much for some readers. As this is a work of fiction, I was not expecting any historical accuracy or evidence, but the creativity and speculation of the facts were quite interesting, although I thought that the language and even the attitude or way of thinking of some characters were way too modern. The development of the story has a perfect pace, but the building of the Stonehenge happens very late in the book. Yes, this book is not flawless, but I was completely enthralled, hence my ratings. Hardcover (Grand Central Publishing): 704 pages E-book (Kobo): 697 pages (default) Audiobook narrated by Richard Armitage: 19.2 hours (unabridged) at normal speed

3.5 stars This novel is set on the Great Plain of England in the Neolithic period, around 2500 BCE. The story focuses on three tribes: herders - who raise cattle, sheep, goats; etc; farmers - who grow crops; and woodlanders - who hunt deer and eat nuts and berries. Other inhabitants of the Great Plain, like flint miners, carpenters, and craftsmen, travel around to trade their goods and services for food, baskets, animal skins, shoes, and other necessities. The story leads up to the building of Stonehenge, but is really about the tribes and their interactions. Though the tale, necessarily, springs from author Ken Follett's imagination, it would appear Follett believes greed, self-interest, male entitlement, thirst for power, dishonesty, and other bad behavior was firmly entrenched by this time, at least in some groups. The novel comes in at 700+ pages, so I'll just give a brief overview of the story. The tribes of the Great Plain are generally insular, but meet four times a year, at the Spring Rite, Midsummer Rite, Autumn Rite, and Winter Rite. The Rite celebrations take place in Riverbend, at a sacred circle made of a ring of bluestones surrounding a ring of tree trunks. During the Rites, priestesses sing and dance, and traders set up outside to barter for goods. A major attraction of every Rite is the evening revel, when celebrants - single or married, from teenagers on up - go off to have sex with people from other tribes and places. This is done to avoid inbreeding, which is dangerous for both humans and animals. The book contains a wealth of characters, but for brevity I'll focus on a few important members of each tribe. ❖❖ Herders - In the herder tribe, widow Ani is an elder with two daughters named Neen and Joia, and a son called Han. Ani tans hides to barter for other goods, and she's a peacemaker who tries to avoid conflict with neighboring tribes. Ani's chief adversary amongst the herder elders is Scagga, a loudmouth who's always spoiling for a fight. Scagga would like to arm every male herder with a bow and arrow, to be ready for battle. ❖❖ Farmers - Troon, the dictatorial leader of the farmers, relishes and flaunts his power. In farmer society, women are the property of men, and may not leave the tribe for marriage or any other reason. In addition, Troon can force women to marry, even if the men are VERY unsuitable. Troon's wife Katch fears him and his bullyboy son Stam adores him. Troon's right hand man is Shen, a skinny creep who spies on everyone and reports back to Troon. Troon is constantly scheming to enlarge the farmers' domain, and hopes to become the 'Big Man' of the entire Great Plain. ❖❖ Woodlanders - Bez, the leader of the woodlanders, has a woman named Gida and a daughter named Lali. The woodlanders are generally peaceable, and Bez likes to walk in the woods with Lali and teach her about nature. Bez doesn't usually seek clashes but has a strong sense of justice. In woodlander society, when a wrong is committed the gods demand a balance: what's stolen must be replaced; a lie demands a truth; and a murder requires a death. This differs from other tribes, who use shunning and expulsion to deal with crimes. The three tribes are compelled to interact with each other, as well as outsiders, who come to the Rites to barter their goods and services. Communication can be sketchy since each tribe has its own language, but some inhabitants of the Great Plain are (at least somewhat) multilingual, which is necessary for commerce and negotiations. To get on with the story: Some of the most valuable possessions in the Neolithic period are flints, because everything that has a cutting edge is made of flint - from axes, to arrowheads, to knives. Everybody needs flints. Seft is a teenager in a family of flint miners. Seft's mother is dead, his father is cruel and abusive, and his two brothers are mean, stupid oafs. Flint mining is hard, dirty, exhausting work, but worth the effort because flints can be traded for food, clothing, livestock, etc. During a Midsummer Rite, Seft meets Ani's herder daughter Neen. Seft and Neen fall in love and want to marry and live with the herders. However Seft's horrible father would kill the boy before letting him go. There are beatings, an escape, and a lot of clashes, but in the end Seft and Neen wed and have a family. In the meantime, Neen's younger sister Joia becomes an apprentice priestess. Most Neolithic people can't count above twenty, but the priestesses have songs and rituals that allow them to count all the days of the year, and to pass on the knowledge acquired by their forebears. Thus priestesses are invaluable, because they know when the seasons will change, when the deer will migrate, when the crops should be planted, and so on. In exchange for their knowledge, the priestesses are provided with food and supplies. A major conflict arises between farmers and herders when farm leader Troon plows up the Break, a swatch of land between the herder and farmer communities. The herders used the Break for grazing, as well as a pathway to the river, so their cattle could drink. Troon's land grab, to grow more crops, could lead to war. But herder elder Ani advises against violence, despite the hardship of taking the cattle 'the long way round' to get water. In the long run, the herders' forbearance just encourages Troon to become more and more grasping and avaricious. Unwisely, Troon even has designs on a piece of the woodlander's environment, and the woodlanders are a vengeful tribe. The rivalry for space and resources on the Great Plain is always tense, but it becomes overwhelming during a years-long drought, when the cattle die, the crops don't grow, and food in the forest becomes scarce. All the inhabitants of the Great Plain are starving, and even the priestesses fear they'll be cast aside. The dire situation leads to selfish deeds and a GIGANTIC disaster. The subsequent act of revenge destroys the sacred circle in Riverbend, which is so important for the Rites. Joia, who's become Second High Priestess by now, wants to rebuild the circle with large indestructible stones, which are far away in Stony Valley. An old craftsman points out, 'We're talking about moving a giant stone a distance that takes all day to walk, up and down hills and over uneven fields. How many days, or weeks, or perhaps even years would that take?' Even more daunting, the sacred circle requires 80 stones. Regardless, once the drought ends, Joia is determined to rebuild the sacred circle with stones. Luckily, Joia's brother-in-law Seft (the former flint miner) is a brilliant carpenter and craftsman. Seft devises a plan to relocate the stones, which requires sophisticated engineering and the assistance of hundreds of people. Many herders oppose the plan to rebuild the sacred circle with stones, and there are endless arguments and setbacks. Moreover, farm leader Troon is determined to stop the project, which would make Joia the 'Big Woman' of the Great Plain and derail his plan to be the 'Big Man.' Thus Troon plans for disruption, sabotage, and eventually an all-out war. Still, as we know, Stonehenge got built (but probably not as described in this book.) 😊 My brief synopsis is the bare bones of this very long novel, which follows the lives of many characters as they work, attend Rites, fall in love, marry (or are forced to marry), have children, lose loved ones, experience grief, make friends, sow dissension, devise schemes, cook meals, build weapons, hunt food, and so on. There are slice-of-life scenes for each tribe, which demonstrates the diversity of their lives and ambitions. There's plenty of action and adventure in the novel as well. For example, when a farm woman runs off to be with her lover, she's hunted down by Troon's 'Young Dogs', who commit murder to get her back. Revenge for the heinous killing results in a perpetrator being tortured, then burned alive. The book has plenty more violence, as well as other misbehavior, and it's a lot to take in. To me, this book feels a lot like a Young Adult novel, though I don't think author Ken Follett aimed for this audience with the orgy scenes. Overall, the novel presents an interesting picture of Neolithic times, and the descriptions of transporting the stones to Riverbend, and putting them in place, are enlightening. Readers curious about prehistoric days and Stonehenge would probably enjoy this book. Thanks to Netgalley, Ken Follett, and Grand Central Publishing for a copy of the book. You can follow my reviews at https://reviewsbybarbsaffer.blogspot.com

"From a bestselling author of epic fiction comes the deeply human story of one of the world’s greatest mysteries: the building of Stonehenge. A FLINT MINER WITH A GIFT A PRIESTESS WHO BELIEVES THE IMPOSSIBLE A MONUMENT THAT WILL DEFINE A CIVILIZATION" It is 2500 BCE, and the tribes of the Great Plain are divided. Seth is a flint miner who is in love with Neen, a herder. Joia is Neen's sister, who becomes a priestess and has an extraordinary ability to lead and unite people. There are woodlanders, herders, miners, and farmers. We are introduced to characters from each tribe and follow them throughout the story. Seft and Joia are central to the story as Joia has the vision of what it is, and Seft has the talent to execute and plan this massive project. Ken Follett is a masterful storyteller, scholar, and historian. This project is massive in scope, and the ability to make something ancient come to life with relatable characters is remarkable. It does get somewhat bogged down in the minutiae of repetitive detail. The story would have benefitted from an edit as there were many similar situations repeated with characters. An author's note including Folett's resources and inspiration would have been appreciated after reading a 700-page saga. I really enjoyed the second half of the novel, where antagonists are stirring the pot to prevent unity and progress and encourage war among the tribes. The building of Stonehenge is absolutely spellbinding. There are many parallels to the present day regarding leadership, group dynamics, and women's rights. For historical fiction fans that enjoy detail and length, this one is for you. Many thanks to NetGalley, Grand Central Publishing, and Ken Follett for an advance reader's copy in exchange for my honest review.

Speculation on how people with primitive tools and nearly no math or engineering skills could create the astronomically significant circle of megaliths on the great plain (of Salisbury) from stones weighing 25 tons each a day's walk away. It appears they did not even have the wheel, though the brilliant engineer within the story, Seft, seems to have spontaneously developed two or three simple machines (the lever, the pulley, and the ramp) to address needs at the moment. The names England and Salisbury did not exist at the time of the building (2500 BC or so), and so Follett does not use them. Nor is there a name for the religion the people follow, and this was interesting to me. There is no priest in sight, but priestesses lead the people in their devotions and drive the effort to create their Monument to the Sun God. We get social and cultural speculation as well, including the clash of social groups based on herding, farming, and the hunting/gathering of the people of the woodlands. The relations of men and women, leadership, and sexual license (beware of inbreeding!) are also brought into the story in interesting and plausible ways. Follett gives us a good story with a large cast, but gives it something of a Hollywood feel when he compresses the duration of construction to about 20 years so that the priestess Joia and her engineer brother-in-law Seft get the satisfaction of seeing their idea come to completion. Anthropologists speculate the creation of what we know as Stonehenge actually took 200 years. That's okay. It's a good story that kept me reading. The title comes from how the priestesses use each standing stone (originally built of wood) to count the days of the year. Their devotions and songs are numerical and calendrical and help keep the society organized over its annual course of seasons and festivals. In his theory, Follett supposes that numbers and true counting ability were the somewhat secret purview of the priestesses. Everyone else was limited to numbers that could be calculated from fingers and toes. We've come a long way, haven't we, baby? Entertaining and thought provoking. Another good one from a good storyteller. 3 1/2 stars

No one makes me want to read 700 pages in one sitting quite like Ken Follett. When I found out this book was about Stonehenge I was even MORE excited. I have always loved imagining the lives of people throughout history and the challenges they likely faced. With Follett’s rich cast of characters and vivid historical setting we can find comfort in knowing that while technology may have changed, the tenacity and indomitability of the human spirit likely has not. I laughed, I cried, I celebrated with these characters. And while they are fictional, I feel the author has captured the truth in the strength of character that has echoed through time, and is evidenced in Stonehenge itself. As always, thank you Ken Follett for writing this book, and thank you Grand Central Publishing and NetGalley for sending me a copy of this ARC. It was a treat to be able to read this early.
