Background – “Never Flinch” was originally published in May 2025 as a Scribner crime fiction hardcover. Length-wise - my original hardcover lists it as 439 pages. Plotline – This continues the story of Holly Gibney, one of King’s most unique and empathetic characters ever. Holly is currently the owner and lead investigator of Finders Keepers Investigations Agency, along with supporting help from the brother and sister team of Jerome (published author) and Barbara Robinson (award winning poet), and her close friend and confidante, experienced detective Izzy Jaynes. When it the book begins, Izzy’s boss, Lieutenant Louis Warwick has received a letter. A dangerous and disturbing, letter from someone named Bill Wilson, promising to “kill 13 innocents and 1 guilty” in what he calls “an act of atonement” for the death of an unnamed innocent man. The City Police Department is not sure whether to take the letter serious or consider it the work of a crackpot. Warwick asks Izzy to investigate it quietly in case something actually comes of it. But things move quicker than expected. Before Izzy can even share her concerns with Holly, random murder victims start showing up with notes of names placed in their hands. The man calling himself Bill Wilson is deadly serious, killing individuals of different ages, in different locations, and no visible patterns. And what is the list of names found on the victims for? While Holly tries to assist Izzy, she has her own client to deal with. And not just any client. Kate McKay, an outspoken and extremely controversial women’s rights activist, is in the middle of North American lecture tour promoting her new book. She’s drawing packed venues filled with diehard fans and supporters, as well opponents who disagree with her brand of female empowerment. To make matters worse, a stalker has targeted Kate, sending her threatening messages of violence to come. Then Kate’s assistant, Corrie, is attacked by the stalker, mistaking her identity. Kate’s had enough and decides she needs protection, but on her own terms. No police, and it must be a woman, which leads Corrie to research and find Holly. Even though Holly’s never done bodyguard work and has concerns about her ability to protect Kate, she thinks of it as learning opportunity, and accepts the job. However, what Holly doesn’t know, is that the stalker not only has financial support from a wealthy and powerful source, this brother/sister team is driven by their own religious mantra to eliminate Kate completely, and will sacrifice their own lives to accomplish it. Holly will need help this time to not only protect Kate, but also to keep her friends from being killed by a serial killer that is becoming quickly addicted to murder. Before the end, both of these narratives will come together in an explosive climax where no one is safe, and for any lucky survivors, their lives will never be the same again… Thoughts and Reflections – Let me say right up front, I a bit conflicted in my thoughts for this book. I enjoyed it, but at the same time have some constructive comments. Let’s start with the good stuff first. The plotting, pacing, and tension throughout worked well for me. There just didn’t seem to be many (if any) slow spots, although there was some wandering off on some unnecessary paths that I will address further. For me, King did a pretty good job of mapping out the frame work and structure – two major mysteries (serial killer and stalker) and several supporting sub-plots that involving Holly, Jerome, Barbara, Izzy, and gospel singer, Sista Bessie, that all intertwined together in a well delivered reading experience. It started slow, laying the groundwork and setting up the storylines, then heating up the temperature in the middle section, and delivering a strong King-esque climactic ending over the last 100 pages that left me a mostly satisfied and pleased reader. King’s last two “Holly” novels – this one and the prior one – are pretty much hardcore mysteries, in a similar style of John Sandford’s popular “Prey” series featuring Lucas Davenport, a politically oriented, hardcore detective and serial killer hunter. The dark tone, sarcasm, and political slants feel very relative to one another, especially the later “Prey” novels. Maybe even with a hint of William Kent Kreuger thrown in too. I don’t say that to be critical, but more so to provide a reference point for readers, and maybe some compliments. Either way, King has temporarily put aside his supernatural elements (for the most part at least) and focused on his writing on the traditional mystery genre, which let’s be honest, is no easy task. It requires strong plotting, peeling the onion on the killer through legitimate clues and red herrings, and staying disciplined in delivering a climax that makes sense and payoffs for the reader (which is one of King’s strengths, especially in this one). For me, what really makes King’s entry into the mystery genre work as well as it does (at least for me), is his character of “Holly”; she is the quintessential complex detective/private investigator character. She is a dysfunctional character (on the spectrum) that has a unique ability to deduce clues and analyze crimes. She is conflicted much like Benedict Cumberbatch’s present-day version of Sherlock Holmes in the BBC television series, and Tony Shalhoub’s private detective, Adrian Monk, on USA network. Much like those characters, Holly is able to synthesize complex clues and evidence, while at the same time struggle with emotional intelligence and almost any social situations. I love how King delivers situations and moments that challenge and stretch Holly, forcing her to become stronger and heroic in her own ways. For example, Holly makes a deduction in this novel during the investigation of the serial killer; half of which is correct, and half of which she is off on. It was cool to see how she is not perfect, but headed in the right direction. Holly is most successful when she follows her intuition, develops personal indomitable spirit, and refuses to surrender to the bad things in life. For me, King takes the Shakespeare and Monk premises, and then builds on them to create a uniqueness and quirkiness that only belong to Holly. I also enjoyed the Izzy Jaynes storylines – her investigation and pursuit of the serial killer, as well as her being pulled into the baseball charity game as the pitcher. It felt like King elevated her role to the main stage in this one, along with Jerome and Barbara. I thoroughly enjoyed Izzy’s handling of the opposing team’s number one jerk, George Pill. I really wanted her to punch him out on more than one occasion. I also appreciated Barbara’s developing friendship with Sista Bessie. It was special and a joy to read about. Now let me deal with the unnecessary paths that wasn’t always fun to go down. King doesn’t dance around political and religious overtones in any subtle manner. Instead, he deals religious and political themes in a head-on collision that may be hard for some. Too hard for others. I saw enough negative feedback regarding the abundant use of these emotional, enflaming topics in social media. It seems that there are those who were turned off by his overly direct style. I am not going to take any sides on that and just respect that everyone has their own opinion. I will just speak for myself and say that I get what King was trying to do in using strong political and religious conflicts as integral elements of his story. The challenge is that using a very polarizing situation and divisive time in our country also unfortunately makes us relive conflicting issues and deep emotions that we really want to have moved on from. Painful issues that we would prefer to see in the review mirror and not have to live through again. For some readers, this may cause a less than enjoyable reading experience, and even potentially border on bad memories. Do I think King used some of his political and religious references too much? Maybe… Probably… And I can see others being sensitive to that. Again, each person has their own opinion and I respect that. I won’t argue or disagree, even though this is a real-world battle being fought in front of us in pretty much all forms of media. For me personally, I didn’t let the references or comments take away from the story being told and will wisely I will leave it at that. Other Notes – “Never Flinch” is the seventh book or novella that features the character of Holly Gibney, and King has mentioned in a podcast that his early inspiration for this novel was the Lady Gaga dognapping case in February 2021. Overall – As mentioned fairly extensively above, I enjoyed this book and give it a 4-star read. I would also not be surprised if King decides to write another “Holly” novel. I think that he just cannot let go of her. And truth be told, politics and religion aside, neither can I. Here’s to more Holly!

In the afterword to this new novel, author Stephen King comments that it was difficult to write and that he's "happy enough" with the final version. That's largely how I feel as a reader, too. This is pretty far from the writer at his best, and in fact, a lot of it plays out as him repeating some of his previous work -- not only the earlier Holly Gibney and Bill Hodges detective stories, but also shades of Insomnia with its extremist attack on a feminist rally. The most original element here is an alcoholic serial killer's comparison of his two compulsions, a sharp characterization that's presumably rooted in King's own admitted struggles with addiction. Structurally, the book is all over the place. We're following two murderers whose paths eventually happen to cross, but that entanglement occurs so late in the text that their separate plots seem fairly coincidental. One is a religious zealot stalking a liberal activist, although her politics are so vaguely defined that it's hard to understand the bigot's anger at her as a specific target, while the other is embarking on a somewhat goofy mission to kill twelve random people in protest of a jury who convicted an innocent man. (He leaves names of the jurors in his victims' hands, apparently to try guilting them into suicide.) The latter takes a ton of risks in his opportunistic murders, which fits with his nature as an addict but makes it frustrating that the various investigators aren't able to capitalize on his missteps to easily track him down. They don't even look into how he knew the identities of the anonymous jury, which should be an obvious first step! Holly Gibney and her friends Jerome, Barbara, and Izzy are back as those protagonists, although the piece is basically standalone and probably works fine if you haven't read their prior adventures. It's also an entirely mundane crime thriller up until a stinger in the epilogue, which I continue to think is an odd approach for a series, alternating between the existence of the supernatural or not. Finally, I'd be remiss if I didn't complain about the treatment of gender in this tale. King is pro-choice and an outspoken Trump critic, but he's also a 77-year-old with some rather regressive attitudes and knowledge gaps. Thus he has his political mouthpiece here repeatedly crow about how no men have ever had an abortion -- ignoring the reality of transgender men, some of whom have indeed undergone that procedure -- and his secondary villain turns out to have Dissociative Identity Disorder and a genderfluid presentation, sometimes manifesting and dressing as his late twin sister. It's problematic to say the least, especially in a work with no other meaningful queer themes or characters, and it strikes me as the sort of unwelcome throwback a competent editor should have vetoed. Still, King is compulsively readable as usual, and I'd say the title is his typical page-turner overall. But I've never loved Holly Gibney myself, and I'd personally be okay if he retired the heroine and her world at this point. Stephen King, master of suspense, horror, and humanity, returns with Never Flinch, the fourth book in the Holly Gibney series. Readers familiar with Holly—first introduced in The Outsider and later featured in If It Bleeds and Holly—will find her sharper, more determined, yet achingly human in her latest outing. Never Flinch delivers a twisted narrative with two interwoven stories: a calculated killer on a mission for "atonement" and a feminist activist’s life under siege. Both paths collide in a crescendo only King could orchestrate. King combines psychological horror, crime fiction, and a dose of societal critique to keep readers on edge. But even with its brilliance, there are aspects deserving critique—a testament to how high the bar is set for Stephen King. The Plot: Twisted Threads of Revenge and Justice At its core, Never Flinch by Stephen King follows two gripping narratives: - The Killing Mission: A cryptic letter delivered to the Buckeye City Police Department chillingly promises to kill "thirteen innocents and one guilty". Detective Izzy Jaynes, a seasoned investigator still haunted by past cases, recruits the reluctant yet brilliant Holly Gibney. What starts as cryptic threats quickly escalates into calculated murders—each a horrifying reflection of justice twisted into revenge. - Kate McKay’s Tour Under Siege: Kate McKay, a controversial women’s rights advocate, embarks on a multi-state tour. Her message of empowerment provokes a stalker whose righteous wrath turns violent. Holly is pulled in as Kate’s bodyguard, and what begins as routine protection spirals into a life-or-death cat-and-mouse chase. King balances these plots deftly, juxtaposing a meticulous killer’s methodical descent into madness against Kate McKay’s palpable defiance. It’s in the slow, chilling unraveling of these two threads that King strikes gold. Strengths in Plot Execution: - The dual narratives allow for seamless tension-building, keeping the reader engrossed. - King’s decision to intersect Izzy, Holly, and Kate’s stories elevates the stakes, leading to a thunderous, satisfying climax. - King’s trademark horror infuses the everyday—parks, auditoriums, and even quiet homes—transforming normalcy into terror. However, at moments, the pacing falters. The sections detailing the killer's thought process become repetitive, offering less intrigue than expected from a master of suspense. Readers may find themselves yearning for tighter storytelling as the middle stretches longer than necessary. Characterization: Holly Gibney’s Continuing Evolution If you’ve followed Holly Gibney’s journey, Never Flinch solidifies her as one of Stephen King’s most compelling characters. Introduced as a socially awkward but brilliant investigator in The Outsider and evolving through If It Bleeds and Holly, she reaches new emotional depths here. King explores her cautious bonds with Izzy Jaynes and her reluctance to assume the role of protector in Kate’s volatile world. Holly Gibney’s Growth: - Holly remains sharp, resourceful, and resilient, yet King masterfully allows her humanity to shine—her vulnerabilities, fears, and insecurities are palpable. - King deepens Holly’s emotional layers as she faces ethical dilemmas and ghosts of past failures. Alongside Holly, the supporting cast shines: - Izzy Jaynes: As a foil to Holly, Izzy’s hardened demeanor contrasts Holly’s softness. Izzy’s moments of vulnerability resonate, especially as her past tragedies resurface. - Kate McKay: Fierce, headstrong, and at times difficult to sympathize with, Kate embodies modern-day heroism and its costs. - The Villain: The killer—motivated by justice warped into vengeance—stands among King’s most terrifying antagonists. Their righteousness, coupled with chilling precision, evokes dread on every page. King’s nuanced portrayal of good and evil underscores the novel’s power. Both heroes and villains feel real, flawed, and frighteningly human. Themes: Justice, Empowerment, and the Human Psyche Stephen King’s Never Flinch transcends the crime thriller genre by tackling themes that cut deep into modern society: - Justice and Atonement: The killer’s belief in retributive justice challenges societal norms. King forces readers to confront uncomfortable questions about guilt, innocence, and who gets to decide either. - Empowerment vs. Resistance: Kate McKay’s character highlights the enduring struggle for women’s rights and the backlash such empowerment often faces. Her stalker’s fury symbolizes the darker side of societal resistance to change. - Addiction and Recovery: Subtle nods to addiction—as seen in characters attending recovery meetings—tie back to King’s own battles and reflect themes of redemption. - The Fragility of Innocence: Whether it’s victims of calculated killings or the collateral damage in acts of vengeance, King explores how quickly innocence can shatter. Writing Style: Stephen King at His Best (and Almost Too Much) Stephen King’s writing in Never Flinch is quintessentially his—sharp, evocative, and rich in detail. The vivid imagery of parks, empty auditoriums, and suffocating hotel rooms immerses readers in his world. His ability to turn the mundane into the macabre is unparalleled. Strengths: - King’s prose is immersive, with razor-sharp dialogue that crackles with authenticity. - He captures horror in subtle details: the chilling tap of a killer’s footsteps or a phone call that freezes time. - His pacing in the final third accelerates, delivering a conclusion that leaves readers breathless. Critiques: - At times, King’s characteristic verbosity slows the momentum. Descriptions of minor actions—walking, driving, or waiting—can become redundant. - Certain subplots (like the recovery meeting attendees) feel underdeveloped, leaving readers wanting more clarity. The Climax: A Collision of Chaos and Catharsis The final act of Never Flinch is where Stephen King excels. The killer’s motives, Kate’s vulnerability, and Holly’s ingenuity converge in a violent, cathartic crescendo. King’s skill in tying loose ends while maintaining unpredictability is a testament to his mastery of the genre. The conclusion leaves readers rattled yet satisfied, lingering on the novel’s haunting message: monsters can be made from anyone, and the line between justice and vengeance is perilously thin. Critiques and Praise: A Balanced Perspective What Works: - King’s ability to craft a compelling, character-driven thriller with horror undertones. - Holly Gibney’s growth and the layered dynamics with supporting characters. - A terrifying, all-too-real villain who challenges moral boundaries. What Could Be Better: - The pacing drags in the middle, testing reader patience. - Certain subplots feel unresolved, particularly those involving minor characters. Conclusion: Should You Read Never Flinch? For fans of Stephen King and the Holly Gibney series, Never Flinch is an essential read. It delivers a twisted, thought-provoking thriller that balances horror with humanity. While not without flaws—namely pacing and minor redundancies—it showcases King’s storytelling prowess and leaves readers reflecting long after the final page. King doesn’t just tell stories; he builds worlds, populates them with unforgettable characters, and forces readers to face truths about human nature. In Never Flinch, Stephen King reminds us to question our sense of justice, trust our instincts, and, most importantly, to never flinch in the face of evil.

A few months ago, I read and really enjoyed King's novel Holly which featured one of my favorite King characters, Holly Gibney. Holly is the singular woman turned detective who was featured in the Mr. Mercedes trilogy as well as The Outsider and If It Bleeds which were all very suspenseful and enjoyable King stories. Never Flinch is King's new novel which also features Gibney. In it, Holly is hired by an outspoken women's rights activist named Kate McKay as a bodyguard while she is on her lecture tour. Her assistant had been assaulted by a young woman who threw bleach in her face and who is warned that McKay is a target because of her pro-choice stance on abortion. Holly takes the job while meanwhile back home in Buckeye City, a person is threatening to kill innocent people as proxies for a jury who wrongly convicted a supposed pedophile. The case has been assigned to Holly's friend Detective Izzy Jaynes and when the killer makes good on his threat by killing some innocents, Izzy turns to Holly to try and identify him. Holly uses her friends Barbara and Jerome to help in the identification but can she stop both threats before her loved ones are the ones being targeted? This was another thriller from King that did not disappoint. Although Holly was the main protagonist of the novel, the focus was really more on the antagonist, Trig, the deranged killer who is trying to put guilt on the jurors who convicted an innocent man; or is he? He is really more of a psychotic killer in the vein of Norman Bates. Overall, this was an enjoyable read but I felt it fell a little below King's best. I do, however, hope King writes more Holly Gibney stories.

As a young avid reader of classic literature in the 1970s, I decided to give popular fiction a shot. I loved horror, so I latched on to a new author named Stephen King. After reading CARRIE, THE SHINING and ’SALEM’S LOT, I was forever sold and realized there was serious modern horror beyond what I had seen in the works of Poe and Dickens. Now, 50 years later, I am still just as excited to pick up a Stephen King book --- and happy to say that he has not lost a single literary step. NEVER FLINCH does not have any supernatural elements. The horrors depicted here are entirely human in nature, which makes them that much more frighteningly real. I have enjoyed seeing the progression of King’s career over the past five decades and how he has evolved from being "merely" a horror author to one of the finest writers working today. The book continues the adventures of characters who originated in the Bill Hodges trilogy, specifically Holly Gibney, who runs the Finders Keepers private investigation firm just outside of Cleveland. In HOLLY, she had to face pure evil with a supernatural bent. This time, she gets involved in two separate cases that will converge in the cleverest of ways to create a finale that will have readers gripping their chairs in fear and delight. The first of the very earthbound evil characters here is Trig, who attends an AA meeting in Buckeye City, Ohio, where Holly and Finders Keepers reside. We will soon learn that Trig has an agenda that presents him as a serial killer seeking to right a wrong done to someone who lost his life in prison. It turns out that this prisoner was wrongly convicted, and Trig is making it his business to symbolically kill 13 people to represent the jury and attorney responsible for the tragic fate of this man, who was beaten to death behind bars. The homicides are eerie, brutal and shocking, and I will keep the particulars secret in this review because it makes for such intense reading. Meanwhile, Kate McKay, a fiery and outspoken women’s rights activist, is in need of a bodyguard. Her rhetoric has angered some unhinged conservative religious types, particularly when it comes to her views on abortion. Someone in an obvious disguise attacks her with what appears to be acid to the face. It is actually bleach, and the victim is Kate’s assistant. Nevertheless, Kate insists that she has additional help to keep an eye on the throngs of haters and the villain behind this assault. Holly agrees to take on the role of protector and goes on tour with Kate while trying to zero in on the individual who appears to be acting on behalf of a much larger religious syndicate that wants nothing more than to see Kate’s head on a stake. While not as horrific as Trig’s murderous rampage, this situation is still extremely intense and dangerous, and Holly may be in over her head. What makes these unrelated narratives that much better is when the brilliantly fertile imagination of Stephen King finds a way to bring them together in a final act that will endanger everyone involved as these two villains cross paths to unexpected and violent results. Despite the book’s title, I found myself flinching several times at the well-placed plot twists and suspenseful turns the narrative takes. It is further confirmation that Stephen King is the “king” of fiction, and he is never better than when he is scaring us with supernatural or human monsters. Reviewed by Ray Palen

Today is a sad day. It's the day that I revoke the "read anything King writes" card. And it's not that this is one of his worst. There are several books of his that are outright misery (pun intended). There are some of his books that are not particularly good or bad but are too long for the idea. So for this book to break me, it's not some Tommyknockers level tragedy that deserves scorn. What Never Flinch is, is a book that is dull and did not need to be written. It feels phoned in, which is made sadder by the afterword in which he talked about how much he had to rework it and how much effort he put into it. It doesn't show, Stevie. This should have been abandoned, but King is transfixed by Holly, a character who has not progressed enough in the last 4 installments of her appearances to warrant this focus. Jerome remains one of his worst characters ever written, it just boggles my mind that this character has appeared in 6ish novels and nobody has pulled King aside to be like, "you gotta stop with this or take a workshop or something". Nearly every line Jerome has is cringy in some way. Even a benign one like showing up and asking Holly "did you get my vid?". What 20 something person talks like this out loud to another human being? Just gives me a headache whenever he shows up. A headache caused by the days of forgotten past when King was great with character voices. None of the other characters are worth talking about because theyre all boring and I've forgotten them. Theres a sassy pop star whose sassy and THE SHIT and you don't mess with her. There's a killer who is perplexing only insofar as King claimed he had to plot out this novel ahead of time for the first time because he wanted to do a traditional mystery novel, and yet we get the villains POV (who feels exactly like every crazy villain King has ever written but worse, sometimes I would just think I was reading The Outsider or Holly again) and we get his entire motivation so I am truly gobsmacked, completely bamboozled in every direction at what on earth he could have possibly needed to plot out ahead of time to keep the "mystery". what mystery. where. This seems like a lot of vitrol for a book I didn't hate. But this book committed the sin of boring me to tears and wondering why I still consider this man one of my top favorite authors. Need to go reread one of his great books again and forget this one ever existed. 5/10

As always, enjoyed the heck out of reading this latest Holly Gibney book. It had all the features I have come to love in a King book, the writing style, interesting characters, and clever twists and turns that take me places I don't expect go. I would suggest new readers read the Holly Books in order to really appreciate the character's development and how the recurring storylines weave through out all the books she is present in. But if you are just seeking a good thriller, this fits the bill as well. Now for a bit of a rant: I don't care if other readers are tired of Jerome and his sister Barbara, or if they felt the storyline with Barbara and Bessie might have seemed over-the-top, or their interpreting Mr. King's comments in the afterword that he struggled with the book meaning it isn't up to his usual snuff. Nope, nope, nope. I love the Jerome and Barbara characters, not as much as I love Holly's character, but I want them in the story. And citing any plot-line in a King novel as over-the-top? That's bananas given most of his stories include over-the-top elements and supernatural components. And struggling with a book doesn't equate with less-than. End rant.

Stephen King's reoccurring character in Holly Gibney was initially only to be a minor "walk-on" character in his novel Mr. Mercedes. However, King became so enthalled with the "meek as a mouse" character with a neurodivergent condition that she came back again and again in six novels and one novella. I have enjoyed observing her growth as a character in each subsequent books. I hope that King isn't through with her as a protagonist. This suspense/thriller involves two coexisting plots, one involving a vigilante serial killer and another involving a stalker of a pro-choice advocate. Early in the book, Holly and her detective agency, Finders Keepers, is contracted by her friend, Detective Izzy Jaynes, to assitst in finding a vigilante serial killer aiming to kill 13 "innocent" people to avenge a wrongfully killed prisoner. If this assignement wasn't enough, she has also agreed to protect a controversial feminist author and firebrand, Kate McKay, from a stalker. In Stephen King's usual style, these two storylines will eventually converge in an explosive, high-stakes finale. One of this author's major strengths is his character development. Both Holly as the protagonist and the villians are complex with nuanced personalities. The novel is well-paced and fast-moving. The author builds tension through the use of short, alternating plot lines that begin with date headings transferring to titles with one times by the end of the book. If you have avoided Stephen King because of his horror and supernatural themes, don't worry with this book. If you are a fan of gritty, realistic crime stories, you will enjoy this book. The story is dark, but without the horrifc elements.
