Not bad but it’s been a while since I really enjoyed a Reacher novel.

The 26th book in the Jack Reacher thriller series starts right off with a shocking scene which leaves the reader asking, Wait? How can this be?? Then when more is revealed, we can sigh with relief and think, Well, that was certainly well done! Our hero, Reacher, is a 6'5", 250 pound ex-MP, drifting across the USA, heading slowly towards the Pacific Ocean, but in no particular hurry. He is currently in Arizona, close to the Mexican border, when he comes across a woman whom he thinks needs his help: she appears to have crashed her car into the only tree in sight. Reacher is soon set straight about what is going on here--it seems there's an evil man who may be holding the woman's twin brother captive and/or may be forcing him to take part in a dastardly plot. This is the second book in Lee Child's series now co-written with his younger brother Andrew Child (aka the writer Andrew Grant). I didn't care much for the first book Andrew helped write, The Sentinel, which I found overly violent. This one has its share of violence of course but it is not wholesale. There is a difference in Reacher's persona now that is hard to put one's fingers on. Less humor perhaps?? Less heart? A lot of the story involves Reacher thinking through each move he and his opponent(s) make in every fight scene. As a long-time reader, I could do with less detail there. I did enjoy how he thinks things through and figures out what is really going on and what needs to be done to thwart the evil doer and his minions. There you go! That's the kind of hero we need. I received an arc of this new thriller from the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for my honest review. Many thanks for the opportunity.

Overall I would not recommend this book. It isn't realistic, Reacher a drifter that prides himself for not taking a bath or changing clothes very often, doesn't carry a cell phone, doesn't know computers, whose background is an MP, suddenly is very knowledgeable about the intricacies of advanced electronics, bombs and detonating systems. He gets free rides in military jets, copters, and can drive anything, he knows people who knows things. Yet he is off of the grid. He explains things to experienced military personal that do know electronics, bombs and detonating systems, but aren't smart enough to understand what this wandering ex MP is relaying to them. Seriously? Give me the old Reacher, that knew guns, tactics, people, motivations, greed and stupidity. The defender of one or two or a cause. Not someone defending the world from bad guys, I have Bond, James Bond, to do that. Actually, this story should have been a one star, but I am a sensitive kind of guy so I gave it 2. If you are like me, you will read the book regardless of the reviews, if I read this review I would still read the book, after all it is Reacher. As a Reacher fan you must read it, but as a Reacher fan you will be disappointed. I have decided I am not that sensitive, I am giving it a one star.

Jack Reacher is back and he’s as good as ever. Other authors have aged their characters, giving them wisdom but adding in creaky bones and grey hair. The Childs, brothers, have kept their protagonist intact, as wily and capable in book #26 as he was in the beginning. With his large size and hands like catcher’s mitts, much of Reacher’s success is based on his physical prowess coupled with his opponents’ poor planning. Much of the series’ charm comes from the narration of the fight scenes that always result in Reacher outwitting a gang of bad guys. BETTER OFF DEAD is no different in that respect although there are some very nice twist and turns in the story that I did not expect. This is a fast read and a welcome diversion. I received my copy from the publisher through NetGalley.
Following the exploits of Jack Reacher is always fun. I just got through seeing the new Jack Reacher series on TV. Much easier to see the character that portrays Reacher in my mind now.
It was...fine. But I'm done buying these. It's best to just remember the older, better books.

Our lonesome paladin is back with a so-so 3-star story, but because its a "Reacher," I've got to give it 4-stars...All the usual Hemingwayesque sentence structure, overly descriptive settings and human observations and the science of street fighting, but what was missing, was a wonderful plot...What have here is very thin gruel...observing a woman setting up an ambush draws Reacher into a weapons smuggling and bomb making operation that may have international terrorism implications...Just Okay!

If you have read previous Jack Reacher novels, Lee Child has a definite style and when that style changes, the character also changes. These changes and the style difference is what leads me to believe Andrew Child was fully in control of the the writing. Change is good. Change leads to growth. Change is needed to grow a brand. Change is also hard for people to deal with. Most people fight change. No matter what, some people will never agree with change. Reacher has changed, slightly. Andrew Child's Reacher seems more brash, more aggressive but also more caring(?). It is these small changes, I believe, that will open up new avenues to grow the brand of Reacher and why Andrew Child will be a successful successor. I would like to thank NetGalley and Random House for the opportunity to read an advance copy of Better Off Dead.

This was the usual Jack Reacher book as in the Story is fast moving and keeps you turning those pages although after about twenty odd books he must be getting too an age were he will have to start getting a working over occasionally I really enjoyed reading this and recommend this for fans of Jack Reacher

Last year I read the first collaborative effort from Lee and Andrew Child, two years ago I read the 24 previous Jack Reacher novels, and also the Jack Reacher short stories, novellas and crossovers. In fact, I had to make sure I read other books in between. So it was a long wait of almost a year for this volume to be released. When it came out I was very busy with work and some other books on the go. But once I started I devoured this book in less than 24 hours. I just could not put it down! It is one of my favourites! And how the story ties in some pieces of previous stories, just masterful. That is how I would describe this book a masterfully written suspense thriller! I read this the weekend after binge watching the new Amazon Prime Series, and I could just picture the action in a whole new way. But let us get back to this specific story. Reacher has a soft spot for fellow veterans, as we have seen before and as we see in this story. And in this case it is a female veteran, Michaela Fenton, who is trying to rescue her brother Michael, also a vet. But things go sideways right from the start. And Reacher as intrigued as he is a couple of times has thoughts about walking away. But that is now his way. When Reacher is hiking towards the coast, specifically the Pacific Ocean, he comes across a scene that is odd, and it is not what it appears to be. Just outside Los Gemelos, a tiny Arizona town near the border. Soon Reacher is vested in figuring out what is really going on, and to do that he will need to crack some heads. And the game is one. Once Reacher gathers some of the intel he knows he needs more, so he reaches out to Jefferson Wallwork of the FBI, who owes Reacher. And as Reacher and Wallwork both work the case they soon realize this is much bigger than either of them expected, and could have major national and international repercussions. And Reacher cannot leave a man behind, or in this case a women. In this story many things are not what they appear. But Reacher has a knack for finding the truth, and for finding people who do not want to be found. And in this case his Lizard mind keeps getting pinged and the question is can he catch what it is trying to warn him about before it is too late? Once Reacher discovers a large cache of ordinances, and starts to realize the scape of the work. He cannot back down. In this volume Reacher does not end up in a relationship. The story takes place over just a few days. We have no incidents of Reacher getting new clothes. Cleaning up, or pressing his clothes between the mattresses. But we do have some decent fights, a mystery to be solved, and some big risks taken. It is another great volume from the Child brothers. And will leave readers desperate for the next instalment ‘No Plan B’. After I read the last one Lee and Andrew wrote together I planned on starting to read some of Andres works published as Andrew Grant, I started the first as soon as I finished this one. A good book in an always entertaining series!

Edit 2: I did want to give Jack credit where credit is due, and mention that over the last few novels I have enjoyed the inclusion of cyberspace as a field of battle. Did he need to take shots at hackers for being dweebs? No. Did he get much of how the technology works right? No. But, as someone working on defending cyber space, it was nice for it to be acknowledged as an important component of modern warfare. Edit 1 because I am triggering a lot of folks: The book just isn't well thought out, and the prose is poor. I have read all of Jack Carr's books, and they have only gotten weaker in their plot over the last few years. He leans too heavily on grandstanding about his own political beliefs instead of focusing on what makes James Reece an awesome character. Some reviews will cite the violence as a turnoff; that doesn't bother me. I don't quite care for in-depth descriptions of internal organs—I passed college A&P over a decade ago—but it doesn't bother me. The constant product placement doesn't bother me. The poor storytelling does. I am on pace to read 100 books this year, and this is one of three that I have marked as forgettable. In addition to the above, Jack Carr demonstrates a new skill in this novel: self-fellatio. There’s a whole chapter describing a “liberal soy latte-drinking snowflake journalist.” It goes on and on about vaccinations, love for EVs, inability to find a girlfriend, etc. I couldn’t figure out what the point was until we got to the part where this character had negatively reviewed an ex-SEAL’s thriller novel. I literally started laughing my ass off at this point. World’s biggest self-insert. Carr goes on to explain how the negative review had backlash and then spends a page listing every author who ever served in the military. He takes his revenge fantasy further by explaining how this character tried to write their own thriller but failed due to a lack of detail around the firearms. Defending your incessant description of gun parts much, Jack? Anyway, I’m done with Carr. The books used to be about a badass character taking on the world. Now they’re just a way for Carr to jerk himself off and make us pay for it. I can only hope that this review triggers Jack Carr to kill me in his next novel.

I find myself conflicted over my feelings towards Jack Carr in general, and the last two books (Only the Dead and Red Sky Mourning) in particular. On the one hand, Carr (real name George Petersen) crafts intricate thrillers that are taut with tension and high stakes. The characters (rather lead or bit players) that inhabit his world are fully realized and fleshed out in such a way that you can feel the weight of their history through their actions and words. The action is brutal and realistic-ish in a way that runs contrary to modern action stories. However, by the start of the third book in the series (Savage Son) the pattern and formula for these novels becomes painfully evident. In each of his novels you will meet: a corrupt politician (usually an American, but sometimes not), a person with ties to main character James Reece (or his father) who purposefully withholds information or harbors resentment towards him, a car chase of some kind, a grandiose end of second act gunfight, a grandiose climactic gunfight, a Hostelesque torture porn scene (Red Sky Mourning gives us two), and a massive exposition dump (Red Sky Mourning also gives us two). Of course all of these failings pales in comparison to the massive over explanation of the numerous brands that Carr chooses to highlight in excruciating detail. Whenever a character first appears, you are guaranteed to learn not only the brand of clothing they are wearing (Reece wears a Sitka pullover, Origin jeans, and Salomon running shoes) but what type of firearm they carry in what caliber with what optic with what type of ammunition in what type of holster attached to what brand belt. That's just the main character. Each of those grueling details is attributed to nearly each speaking character you meet in the book. To further compound the endless name dropping, each workout is given it's just due with origin and exacting information. Each vehicle, be it automobile, boat, or plane, is explained down its most granular detail. All of this brings me to book seven in The Terminal List series, Red Sky Mourning. (Also, fun fact, the series was not formally known as The Terminal List series until the production of the eponymous tv series starring Chris Pratt was released. A fact that Jack Carr is fond of repeating in every piece of published advertisement for himself and his books.) Red Sky Mourning starts off with a tremendous bang that sets in motion the whole series. But, from there, it all devolves into the formula that Carr is oft to use. The variables and details change, but by and large, if you can recognize the pattern then you will not be surprised by any of what transpires throughout the book. The action remains top notch. The setting remains taut. But everything else is an exercise in paint-by-numbers thriller writing. If you choose to dive into the pages of The Terminal List series, do so expecting each of the pros and cons listed above. If you are a gear head, then maybe the aforementioned gear dump won't bother you so much. If you enjoy quick reads without any surprise to it's conclusion, then maybe it won't bother you so much. But be warned, all these things become grating to the reader over time.

The most mediocre of the series so far. I can’t quite tell whether or not Carr is paid by the companies mentioned in these books or if he’s simply friendly with them, but giving brand name and model number for every accessory gets repetitive. A shame. The clear self insert in the chapter that mentions a character “writing a negative review of an Ex Seals novel” was, at best, corny. In general, the book was “fine”. The ending was unfortunately too fast paced and.. somehow eerily similar to the last book, while also being a borderline carbon copy of the ending of the first book/beginning of the second book. Hopefully a second read will change my score…

This book, like the others before it in the series is heavy on the tech. It's well researched and well written. Carr is cognizant that a lot of readers won't necessarily know the technical info or jargon - in reference to both the technological aspects of the book, as well as the military and combat portions. A lot of authors fumble the ball in such circumstances by making it really obvious that they are explaining something technical to the readers. It often comes off patronizing. Carr does a good job of making it part of the story by describing the actions rather than through dialogue. I like James Reece a lot as a character. I've followed him through all the other six books. Not sure I love the ending on this one, but it sure does promise a book 8. And that's what's important! Rounding up to 4.

4.5 stars. Fans of political thrillers and Tom Clancy will love this timely novel involving government corruption, artificial intelligence, and competition with China. Chilling and very plausible. Jack Carr’s meticulous research and writing prowess shine throughout.

To say I'm disappointed would be an understatement. I have enjoyed the Terminal List series to this point, but this one book may change what I am reading this time next year. Will TL #7 get a chance? Yes, probably. But I won't be afraid to set it back down and never finish it either. The overall story is a good one. It's pretty typical in this genre where the hero wins, with a certain amount of loss sprinkled in just to keep it from being totally unrealistic. However, the way the story is told (writing style) is where this book fails miserably. If this were Jack's first book, I would send an email and make the suggestion that maybe having an exhaustive list of South African authors isn't necessary to the movement of the plot. Maybe I would make the suggest that the reader doesn't need to know, or particularly care about every feature and catalog descriptor for every firearm listed. You know, unless the character actually uses one of them and it's something special, or experimental. However, all too often, the flow of reading gets bogged down by details that just don't matter. In business, I describe this as the "why?" factor. Why am I doing this? Does this make sense from a monetary return factor? Or am I doing this because I don't know any better and this is how I think everyone else does it? The same holds true with writing. Do I need to copy/paste the Wikipedia listing for South African writers through the years in its entirety? Or can I just put two or three and get my point across without having my reader skip ahead 2 paragraphs. Do I need a 3-4 page description of China's foreign policy without a word of dialog that pertains to the current event of the book? Will they play a factor in the overall outcome of the story? If the answer is no, then leave them out. Just plain disappointing for a book I was looking forward to.

I want to like this book. I want to like the adventures of James Reese but it’s just flat, emotionally void and 1 dimensional. Jack Carr is no longer a novelist, he is a staff writer for an infomercial. There is so much more detail and emotion behind the full load out of a rifle with names of products and add-ons to weapon attachments, coffee, honey and zero emphasis on character or story building. This a book, not a story, not a novel, it is far is less than that. This is a written description of what articles of clothing, what firearm with caliber & name branded attachments used, what coffee, what book to read for the “dress like a warrior” type person. It has the bones to be a good book but it’s not but it’s lost in the loadout; instead it was written for the person whose entire persona revolves around their 2A stance and dressing tactically. If you are not sure who? It’s the guy in the mall parking lot with a punisher tire cover on his suv. The accountant with the tattoo sleeve. The day dreamer of action and nothing more. This book is the sears catalogue of novels for those who feel it’s better to look a certain way than to be a certain way. For clarity, people who love camouflage but are not military vets or hunters. Punisher emblems but aren’t comic book fans. Cross-fitters all day long.

I'm rather surprised this is my first Jack Carr book, though I did stream The Terminal List. Does that count? :) There was a lot to like about this book, and it did remind me of many of the authors Jack Carr recommends at the end--Clancy, Le Carre, Fleming, etc. This was a high tech, government conspiracy, reluctant hero book, high octane book, and Carr does all of those things well. I especially enjoyed the subplot of AI and its influence on the military complex. That said, this is what I would term a "Guy's guy's book." So much detail about cars, planes, boats, even cigars! Seriously. It's a lot. It goes on for pages. And the torture scene? Don't get me started. I don't need every detail of a torture scene. So, depends on what kind of action flick you enjoy. Definitely well written. Recommend, with some caveats.

Another complaint is with (view spoiler) This is a bit of a minor complaint, but if you are going to kill off people or a person. Make the reader sympathetic to the person who is killed off. Great book

This review has me very conflicted. I like Jack Carr. On one hand, The Terminal List is one of my favorite books. Despite borrowing heavily from Brad Thor, Carr has the real world experience to make the details of a life in the shadows come alive. He knows violence and revenge, and as a reader you can tell. His follow-on books continued a good mix of spy thriller and modern day political/operational analysis/commentary that worked and kept me reading. On the other hand, this particular novel is just as much a work of contemporary threat inflation as it is a work of fiction. For a moment indulge me… following the political and international security trend, Carr makes his newest enemy the West’s Modern Cold War adversary - China. While I am quite sure he read (at least what he thought) was the requisite literature on the topic (see Rush Doshi’s The Long Game, Pillsbury’s The Hundred-Year Marathon, Dollar’s China 2049, etc), he is simply furthering a new “Red Scare”. In truth, most of Carr’s references and analysis in this novel read like a first semester international security studies curriculum. All that being said, I read and enjoyed it (minus the repeated deep sighs during discussions of Chinese nefarious activity and inclusion of pop culture conspiracy theories). He creates good pace and the details of “working in the grey” are enticing. Lastly, for those complaining about the references to companies and products, Carr name-drops for three reasons: 1. As a shameless plug for businesses owned by his special operator buddies and generate support/sales. So sue him for helping out friends. 2. As a literary technique to give the story validity and anchor it to modern day. “Oh he knows what he’s talking about, listen to the detail.” “He has Netflix? I have Netflix.” 3. As a trail of breadcrumbs for the reader to learn more about topics for themselves. If he lists books, authors, businesses, historical programs, etc. the reader can educate themselves and further understand the characters (and authors) point of view. This is also a military style of education “here’s a bunch of stuff, go figure it out for yourself.” All in all, if you like this genre of book or his previous books - well, you’ll like this one too. I couldn’t get past the over generalization of the current international security climate, hopefully this is just a hook for audiences. 3 stars.

Oh my. This book had me on my toes. I had to stop reading a few times to calm myself. It is amazing how disenfranchisement and greed can make people do diabolical things. And Alice? She takes the cake!! I appreciate the ending. Is it what I wanted? Not completely. Is it what was needed? Possibly.

Solid 5-star in my opinion! If you haven't been following along, I started reading the Terminal List series by Jack Carr in June of 2023 based on a recommendation from a coworker who is a rather large fan of the books. I've been hooked on them from the start and though it took me almost a year exactly, I got caught up right in time for the 7th book Red Sky Mourning to come out in June of 2024 here. I wasn't sure if I was going to be able to get to it this month with a rather full monthly TBR but due to also squeezing in a vacation which allowed me to get a lot of extra reading in, I was able to enjoy this one only a few days after release. The pacing was exactly what I come to expect from this series. I don't know how I'd feel if that changed with book seven in a series. This is still fast paced intense action. There are amazing fight scenes which I'll get to shortly, though even when there isn't action going on like that even the dialogue and story just seem to have me sitting on the edge of my seating wondering what is going to happen next. If I had to make a film comparison to this book and series, I'd have to go with the Jason Bourne series. They give me that similar edge of my seat feeling when watching them. Even though I do own physical copies of these books, I continue to opt for the audiobook versions narrated by Ray Porter who just does an excellent job in bringing these fantastic stories to life. If you have been enjoying this series with visual reads and don't mind or enjoy audiobooks, you've got to give Ray's performance a try. The world building continues to surprise me. I've always been drawn to more science fiction and fantasy worlds to give me that feeling of escapism. I never really thought I'd enjoy fictional reads based in the real world. This is even more so with The Terminal List series as Jack Carr continues to weave in current events into his stories. These stories always seem to stretch across the globe in each book and this one is no different. I also love the fact that the author continues to pull the current back a bit and let us know there are some parts of the story based on real life events, some that are twisted a bit to make them their own and others just a bit of pure speculation for enjoyment purposes of the story. I want to touch on the level of detail that Jack Carr writes in this book and really in the series. I know this can actually be a polarizing subject at times. I had this discussion with my friend whom was also reading Red Sky Mourning upon release and I talked about a scene that I just loved. Carr gets very detailed in explaining what goes through Reece's mind thinking step by step what he is doing and then performing it. It makes me feel like I am right there. It also gives me the vibes of the scene entering slow motion or bullet-time from video games. This just works very well for me in this series. I can see if not being for everyone though. The character development was great in Red Sky Mourning. We see some of our biggest growth moments for James Reece to date in this one. I can't help to also love so many of the supporting characters in this book and series as well. The Hastings family is amazing! Ox might have become one of my favorite characters in this book. And the ending was spot on! I won't share any spoiler speculation here but I'm happy the way this book ended for sure. As I begin to wrap this review up, I want to say that the timing for this one couldn't have been better for me. As I mentioned I wasn't sure if I'd get this one in by the end of the month or not. I actually started it on the last day of my vacation. A complete coincidence was, we woke up early to get our last hike and visit to Presque Isle State Park and when we arrived, there was actually a red sun rising over Lake Erie. I thought I'd share a picture of the view with my trail buddy and side-kick Indy. I started up the audiobook for this hike as well as the drive home as well and Jack Carr had me hooked once again. I really only had one small bit of confusion as this book wrapped up which I ended up discussing with a friend who was also reading it at the same time. Once he finished he reminded me of something that happened in the previous book which then made that entire chapter make much more sense. I had completely forgotten about that moment. It's always good to have friends reading books that can share thoughts or shed light on things like this. All in all I am still new to Jack Carr spending just the last year getting through this series and I don't know what the future holds. I'd love to see more books released in this series but if not, I have enjoyed this ride! I also know the author has his first non-fiction writing releasing later this year and since I do enjoy military history and try to sprinkle those reads in each year, I will keep my eyes out for this. If you've already started your journey through The Terminal List series, keep going with this one, you will not be disappointed. If you haven't checked the series out but enjoy Thrillers with a heavy dose of action, espionage and military aspects, you deserve to give this a chance.

I could have given this a 4, compared to his other books though, this was tough to get through at times. Starting with Terminal List, Jack Carr writes way too many details on weapons. Now he’s writing every little detail on vehicles and every little movement of characters and it’s just exhausting to get through. We don’t need that much detail. It took like the first third of the book to set up the story, just way too long to get to the plot.
Jack Carr is the absolute master of this genre. Wow!!!!!! Fantastic as always! 10⭐️
I have loved this series but this one didn’t flow as well as past ones for me. When it was pure storyline it was great.
Out of respect for Mr. Carr, I will not go in depth into this review. It’s a far fetched plot, recycled from the lest few novels, predictable, and I do not recommend this one sadly.
My least favorite book so far in the series. I felt like it was great book the last 1/3 of the book. Just had to get through the history lessons in the first 2/3 of book.

Every book in the series I’ve given five Stars, because of the way the books are written with extreme detail and articulation and explanation of the plot. James Reece is a complicated character, and that’s what readers want to read about. I was thinking that going into this book, and just thinking how is this hero going to find some peace? This book provides IN MY OPINION a logical way to find the character some peace. Not conclusive, and it’s an open ended. What I enjoy most of this series is Jack Carr’s ability to have current global dynamics and geopolitics, fast paced plot that draws you in, and a simple sentence “thesis” to each book. You know what the book will be about with military proficiency and bloody violence. Red Sky Mourning or the “007” book is great and definitely has ties to James Bond with comparisons of Bond and James Reece. The villain is meticulous and calculating, and Jack Carr’s writing shows his frustrations with politicians and senior leaders. There were similarities with Terminal List, and I enjoyed them. PERSONAL RANKING OF JACK CARR’S TERMINAL LIST 1. Terminal List 2. Savage Son 3. The Devil’s Hand 4. Red Sky Mourning 5. True Believer 6. In The Blood 7. Only The Dead

Jack Carr is not in the same league as Tom Clancy, Nelson DeMille, and Lee Child. But if you are a fan of Clive Cussler, Vince Flynn, Brad Thor, or James Patterson, this book is for you. The book could have filled 300 pages was bloated to over 500 pages. Much of that calling attention to name brands, exotic restaurants, and their foods and constantly repeating what the Chinese were up to every 50 pages. The protagonist, Jack Reece is very unlikeable by being too stuck on himself and being a cruel person, probably a sadist. It seemed like in every chapter he was whining about how he had culpability for the death of his wife and daughter. He has a new fiance who he also continually chants about putting her in a situation to die. Reece has the ability to identify the make of every pistol at a glance or by sound and feel if he is in the dark. I did not think it was very believable that he killed six armed assassins using only a pen and a champagne bottle. Carr goes to great lengths to indicate a qunatum will only communicate with Reese but that turns out not to be true since the computer also interacted with the president. Reese sounds like Trump in that only he can save the US from a horrible disaster.

Jack Carr did it again for the 7th time with the James Reece series. Jack is my favorite author because his attention to detail with weapons, places, food, and scenes in books makes you really feel like you’re there. Jack also does a phenomenal job of describing the history for weapons, places, vehicles, and many other things in his books. Throughout the James Reece series, Jack has made it to where you see Reece grow as a character due to his struggles, failures, and accomplishments like you’re right by his side and Red Sky Mourning did not disappoint. This book puts a spotlight on how technology is a double-edged sword and it made the read that much better. Fantastic book!

Jack Carr is a phenomenal thriller author who constantly pushes the boundaries of what is fiction and non-fiction. He taps in so well what is happening in the real world with smatterings of potential technological weapons coming on the horizon. He’s done such a great job of interconnecting all these books and that goes for this one so well. Hearing him on a podcast talk about how he loves writing these books makes me hope this series goes on for many more years to come!
Fast action, great fun.

I started the Terminal List series a few years back. I think what I like most about these books is that they are written in mostly the post Iraq/Afghan War world by a guy who actually fought in those wars. You can go back and read any number of thriller/spy books from the Cold War era and you would probably find some better books than these, but they are also dated. This can be a good and a bad thing. Eventually, I will go back and read more classic spy novels, but for now, one Jack Carr book a year is great for me. Red Sky Mourning is the seventh book in the Terminal List series and honestly it probably was my least favorite book in the series so far. I always hated that spies didn't have families in books and movies. Seemed a bit unrealistic that every single spy never had a family. But now I get it. If you are writing a story about a spy, you don't have a ton of good options. Either you have to acknowledge that the spy has a family and completely ignore it which makes the inclusion of the family superfluous or might make you dislike the character for ignoring their family. Or you have to acknowledge the fact that this guy has a family and make that a central theme to the story which can be very boring. It is much easier to say this guy has no attachments and center the plot around the spy action. My main problem with this book is the inclusion of Reece's fiance, Katie. I just think she is boring and is getting in the way of the story. I hope she has fewer pages dedicated to her in future books. I also think Reece's reminiscing of his dead wife and daughter slow the story down as well. Thankfully, near the end of the book, it kind of seemed like Jack Carr might have been setting up the story to move on from so much of Reece's inner monologue being dedicated to them. That said, this book was still fun for me. Carr's little details and anecdotes about real life events, people, and places always keeps me interested. I especially enjoyed the part of the book that took place in Sausalito, California. He really brought the area to life with his description of the buildings. I also love that he brought back the AI character. Moving forward, it might be difficult to balance out that character's abilities while keeping the story realistic and compelling (she's just a tad too powerful). But it still worked for this book, in my opinion. I would recommend this series to anyone who wants to read a modern spy book. Jack Carr is great at what he does. I also think he has a good grasp of geopolitics. There is a reason a lot of the themes in his book have kind of "predicted" current events. I give this book four stars. If you love the series, there's no reason not to read it.

** spoiler alert ** 4.4! At its core, this is a story about loyalty. Does James do this for love of country? Is it for love of fellow man? For love of his family? Does he even owe anything to this government who has betrayed him. Do any of us? I was a little concerned going into the book seeing that the AI super computer Alice was part of the story. Alice wasn’t my favorite part of earlier books. That changed this book though. Alice’s evolution and affection and respect for James made it enjoyable. Especially taking on James humor and at the end when she took on his revenge. It was also cool her voice was like Lauren’s. I thought this was Jack Carr's best work in some ways. Specifically how he tells the story of James' thoughts as he talks himself through the best tactical approach as he is in the fight. Chapter 34 had a really long fight scene between James and 4 enemy combatants and James telling himself the tactical approach to take real time was classic Jack Carr. Basically, how fast he processes actions around him for his tactical approach and skills, narrating as he goes. Badassery. A couple books back James started hearing his dad's voice more, coming back to abstract lessons he learned from his dad as a kid. Realizing when he needed it most these were not abstract at all. It was his dad giving him wisdom and lessons he would need for life. Lessons that James was already providing to Lucy before she was gone. These stood out for me in this book, especially when he is remembering sharing his dad's lessons with Lucy. James was also seeing and taking to Lauren and Lucy a lot in this one, which I loved. The book was also about forgiveness, something James learned from Caroline in a prior book and Jonathan in this one. Lauren and Lucy also play a part with this book. Powerful. I do not know if there will be a book 8 in the series. I am told there will be by someone, but I do not see that anywhere online, and the story in this one does end with some closure that would make this a reasonable stopping point. There were times in this one I legit thought it was over. We will see and I will be there if there is more. If not, I have loved this series. "You are familiar with his file. He has a history of solving problems through the direct application of violence." "Reece was in the dark with 4 armed assailants. Surprise. Speed. Violence of action. He had now given up the element of surprise. He had capitalized on speed. Now it was time to double up on the violence." "Being suddenly submerged in water in the dark, is an uncomfortable place to be for most people. Foe Reece, it was home." 🪓🪓

When I started this series, I never thought I'd see James Reece eventually become a James Bond-esque character. Sure, the man doesn't enjoy being in a suit, but I still very much enjoyed those chapters of the book. Knowing there was going to be a bunch of Bond easter eggs throughout, I wasn't sure if they would work, but you know what, they only went and did. From Navy Seal, to Super Spy, it all just kind of works. Then you add the not-too-distant future of Ai as Alice returns, and that all goes to make Red Sky Mourning a winner. It's is obvious Jack Carr has done a shit ton of research, that or he has some friends in high places. Probably a mix of the two. Everything you'd want from a James Reece adventure/thrilling mission is here - his reluctance to get involved, thrilling action, horrible torture sequences and I learn a lot along the way. And a bunch of slight jabs at the idiots of today, in that very specific Carr manner. At this point, it is almost impossible to guess where the series might go next - what with James Reece having a bounty of options out there for him. And as these books surely continue, I can see this fictional Seal taking on the next big global threat, just a few years before it arises in the mainstream news. I'm finally caught up, and can't wait for book 8.

Jack Carr’s latest installment delivers everything fans have come to expect: gripping intrigue, action, and political mayhem. Centered around James Reece, a beloved character who embodies the classic Navy SEAL badassery, the narrative is both timely and politically charged, reflecting current global tensions. The audiobook, narrated by Ray Porter, enhances the experience, bringing the high-octane scenes to life. Carr weaves in elements of foreign locales, cutting-edge AI, and the looming threats posed by China, keeping the stakes high throughout. At times, sections feel weighed down by excessive dialogue and overly detailed explanations, which disrupt the pacing. Also, the product placement is constant and detracts from the overall momentum. This latest in the beloved series is very similar to 007, and has its moments of drag, while still providing the thrilling ride that Carr’s readers crave. If you’re a fan of military thrillers, this series is worth the read—or listen! Still waiting on the bookstore/whiskey bar. To ponder: Who was the man with the Rhodesian accent in the end who owned the bar? Jonathan mentioned earlier in the book one of his buddies from the Selous Scouts moved to Malta and opened a bar, is it safe to assume it's the same guy? 3.5/5

This one started incredibly slow for me. I am a big Carr fan, and have read all the TL books within the last six months. In the first 75% of the book it felt phoned in. Seemed like Carr had turned the corner into writing books to keep a character alive and cranking out title after title without as much effort as was put in in the early volumes when you’re still trying to make a name for yourself. It didn’t end that way but that’s just how it started. Other reviewers noted Carr’s lack of subtlety in his worldview propositions. That is a valid complaint. I agree with almost all of Carr’s positions politically and otherwise, but he was trying too hard in this one to let us know how he felt about things. I also found comical and somewhat distracting the fact that Carr, rather explicitly, parodies real life politicians (or at least their caricatures) here with characters clearly playing off Gavin Newsom and Kamala Harris. Pacing was also a problem here, as it was in the first book. Carr spends a lot of time with laborious exposition of niche topics that’s simply not necessary to the progression of the story. All that being said, I’m willing to put all of that aside because the last 20% of this book is some of the best thriller writing I’ve ever read. A fitting and satisfying ending to this chapter for Carr’s writing career.

This book was solid, but I didn't enjoy it as much as the rest of the series. It took a while to get to the real action, which is not necessarily bad, but it felt slow in this case. There seemed to be even more recitations of brand names in this book; they all have these highly detailed descriptions of everyone's gear, but it seemed to be a bit much in this book. There was also some exposition dialogue that was too clunky. It sounded like podcast talking points. And the lack of contractions in the dialogue drove me nuts. People just don't talk that way, military or not. Still, it's another popcorn novel that is a fun, easy read. This may be the end of the series based on how it ends. Apparently, Carr's next book is coming out now and it's a prequel featuring Reece's father during Vietnam. I think that time period with less tech may be more fertile ground for a story. Hope so.

This book is a solid thriller, published so recently that it can incorporate references to the Ukraine War and the Hamas attacks on Israel. The plot winds its way from the United States to China to the Philippines, Indonesia, and even to Austria and Malta. For weaponry enthusiasts, there are plenty of technical details, and the story offers some dark warnings about dangers of Artificial Intelligence in the competition between China and the United States. The author's wry observations on recent American politics are also entertaining. Although some readers may want to skim through the rather graphic descriptions of torture in Chapter 39, the rest of the book is enjoyable and offers a series of plot twists that make it a page-turner. The novel is enhanced by more than 25 pages of technical glossary, which is very helpful for readers who have limited background in weapons and military intelligence. On the whole, this seventh novel in the James Reece Terminal List series is a solid success.

I didn’t realize this was part 7 of a series of thrillers about former Navy Seal James Reece. Carr does a good job of referencing the other books without overplaying the canon card. I was able to enjoy a solid summer thriller even without having read the other books. I didn’t love the first part of the novel—I gave it about 50 pages and was tempted to hang it up, but I’m glad I finished it. The last half—and particularly the last third is fast-paced and thrilling. If you are interested in the proper names of weapons or watches this book is definitely for you—and make no mistake James Reece is an ass kicker.

This book was amazing! Such a good addition to the Terminal List series. If you aren’t familiar with the Terminal List you should definitely check it out, but be prepared for violence. This book was intriguing because the use of electronic devices and AI were prevalent. It made for some interesting situations and opportunities to save lives. The ending was great and I’m glad things were resolved for the characters. Jack Carr really pulled out all the stops for this book and made me wonder how he researches some of the things he writes.

Pretty Good I thought the story was pretty good and had a classic Tom Clancy feel to it. My knock and this has been something I see more and more from this author and others is the “over marketing” of products and it just feels like a cheap marketing stunt. Also, the amount of indulgent food descriptions felt unnecessary. Make it one scene but I don’t care about the different wines and various alcohol and felt it would’ve tightened the story up without the description

Much like others that have read the series, I felt like Carr’s characterization of James Reece has declined. The plot in the later books has not been nearly as good as earlier entries. Chapter 10 served no real good emphasis to progressing the story, and as others pointed out felt like a caricature of a personal review Carr has received. The long lists of authors listed in several chapters just seemed to run on, 5 would have been sufficient but 15+ was overkill.

James Reese is a bad ass. Though Mitch Rapp is probably a bigger badass, lol Jack Carr is one of my favorite writers. I really hope that he finally lets Reese find peace. I really loved the first part of True Believer. I loved how at peace Reese was in Africa. I almost wished he would have stayed in Africa and not went with Freddie. But I'm not the Author lol.

This was good but it did have a heavier dose of product placement to me. It got to be too much at times and I found myself scanning over these spots just to get past it. Reece does it all and barely gets hurt just like the other books. This one I felt was drug out a bit too much. I’m kind of glad the series is over (or is it?) but part of me will miss Reece. On to the next book…

Quite competent military action work: hero is fighting Chinese and American traitor forces to prevent Taiwan being invaded and the next nuclear war. Lots of action sequences, shooting, fighting, exhaustive listing of military equipment. The motivations of the characters are simplified,except for the hero. A beefy book, like the Seal team members, about 560 pages in normal print.

Jack Carr gets it done again. This book will be accused of being science fiction by some but with todays technologies (known and unknown), I agree with Jack when he says it’s not. I will say you want to read this book on a full stomach. The authors ability to describe food in such delicious detail will make you hungry! Cheers Mr. Carr. Well done on the 007th book!

I saw a lot of people saying no more James Reece and too political. I feel like I read a different book. Maybe I wasn’t paying attention or it went right over my head. I do hope he gets paid for all the merch he mentions.

A book of two halves. The first one is a somewhat slow setup for the story with people talking to each other through cliched quotes from classic thinkers and the now customary (but completely unnecessary) pushing of products and brands. The second part is quite enjoyable action (if you don't count the 12% of glossary in the end - even less needed). As a positive, I was happy to see that the series is moving away from the Cold War legacy and to more relevant issues - China (finally), AI, space security.

Wasn’t expecting much but this book really tried it all. It felt a little ridiculous. Overly technical military jargon, US vs china, one man to stop world war 3 with the help of his AI super computer friend…

When are the bad guys gonna learn? You don’t mess with James Reece and you especially don’t mess with his family and friends. That said, this book met expectations… which were not high. I’m cooling off on my Jack Carr enthusiasm.

I grew up in the 80’s when the action movie reigned supreme! Jack Carr’s James Reece takes me back. This series is awesome and Red Sky Morning did not disappoint. The nods to Ian Flemming’s James Bond are great Easter egg moments. Read this book if you need a little action in your life.

The best thing about these books is that they feel so real. The action is awesome and I loved the 007-esque feel to this one. This latest addition to The Terminal List solidifies that this is still my favorite series!

** spoiler alert ** Well now what am I supposed to do? Wait for the next one?? Glad to see Alice used a lot more in this book and happy to see a seemingly happy ending to the entire series/please write another one!
** spoiler alert ** Love Love Love! Hope this is not the end!

Anyone who gave this 5 stars is sipping the Jack Carr Kool-Aid. The first few books in this series are some of my favorite ever. The past two have been a mix of absurdity, product promotion and just enough Reece to get us coming back.
Fabulous! James Reece is the modern day John Galt. Love this series. 📖

Like all the other useless reviews I saw, I haven't read this book. Unlike the others I saw, I'm not going to review something I haven't read. No one cares if you're excited to read it or have prejudged it. This is about reviewing a book on the merits of the book. Well, I've now read the book and thoroughly enjoyed it! I'm a fan of Louise Penny and, although it is unlike her other books, it was still a great read.

3.5 stars, rounded up I'm not much for political thrillers, but this one was pretty good. Probably won't go over very well with people who are fans of/loyal to 45, but seeing Clinton's name as author should make those people steer clear. I'm not a Clinton supporter myself, but she is a decent writer and I love Louise Penny, and loved the inclusion of Three Pines, Gamache, and others from her series. Overall, this is a fast paced, globe-trotting whirlwind of a story, chasing terrorists, bombers, and high level informants. I listened to this as an audiobook and Joan Allen is a stellar narrator, she is a great voice of Secretary of State Ellen Adams, the right amount of brains and snark to propel the story forward. At first I didn't think I'd be able to follow the story as there are a LARGE number of characters and the relationships are zig-zagged all around and intertwined. Yet the writing is clear and concise and I was able to keep everyone and everything straight and never got lost. The ending is definitely a set up for further installments in the series. Bottom line: If you enjoy a good political thriller, this is an excellent choice. Even if you don't, you might be surprised, especially if you're a Penny fan. I voluntarily reviewed a complimentary copy of this book, all opinions are my own.

PLEASE READ THIS BOOK! UPDATE: On February 21, 2024, I invited some wonderful, dynamic women friends to my home to discuss this book. I was surrounded by brilliant, accomplished conversationalists. The discussion was engaging, captivating, serious and thoughtful. The perfect book to discuss at this time. Why? Well…let us consider the following… Is this political action thriller really political action fact? Is there an undertone of something we should be paying attention to that could be coming? Is our democracy at risk because of what the previous administration put into play? What are the current extremist elected and appointed officials within our government (appointed by the previous president) planning that will upend our government as we know it? And what of the previous presidents need for reelection and the powerplays he made prior to his term ending? Yes, I am reading a fiction book – but, I feel like I am reading the pages of something much richer than fiction, because it feels too real to what is happening now – what has been happening before us. We cannot ignore it. And...Clinton’s rich background as a once First Lady, US Senator and Secretary of State gives her insights into the White House. Certainly her experience, our experience of the last administration, and what has since occurred, is still occurring, cannot be ignored. This book has me turning pages quicker than I can read them…I want to know what is going on – I want to hope for a good outcome. I want the bad guys to be beaten. I want our government to overcome all the hate and racism and misinformation spreading. I want civility back. I want the world to get along. I want neighbors to like one another again. And I don’t want terrorism across the borders to be terrorism within. Because it sure feels like it more and more. Besides, how could a patriot define themselves as such when their acts of violence and hatred tell a different story? This book makes readers think and want to protect our democracy, and look more closely at all those rights we have and what we are losing each and every day. Even a letter to the editor in one of our local papers made note of the following which can’t be ignored… “Numerous state houses across the country that are passing laws to limit and control access to voting ensuring that the politicians choose their voters rather than the voters choosing their politicians. And… state houses limiting woman’s right to access to reproductive health care and personal choice. And… laws making it easier to roam the streets with automatic weapons and taking the lives of unarmed civilians as well as laws limiting rights protected under the First Amendment. And local government gerrymandering boundaries so that they can cheat their way to a majority that isn’t theirs to have.” We are being assaulted from every angle here – and this book makes you wonder – should we be paying better attention? This is state of terror. And it is telling us to look within. And reading the last two lines of the authors acknowledgements, well…that in itself, is message enough. I don’t need to tell you the plot. I just need to tell you to read this book. And then…please, please, please, pay attention.

3.5 stars Authors Hillary Rodham Clinton (left) and Louise Penny For this thriller, Hillary Rodham Clinton drew on her experience as U.S. Secretary of State and Louise Penny on her talent as a mystery writer to craft a tale about a Secretary of State trying to stop nuclear terrorists from exploding bombs in American cities. The twist - a traitor in the upper echelons of the U.S. government is helping the terrorists. ***** Newly elected President Douglas Williams isn't Ellen Adams' favorite person. When Williams was a powerful senator and Ellen was in charge of a global media empire.... .....Ellen's journalist son Gil Bahar was kidnapped by Middle Eastern terrorists. Senator Williams wouldn't allow the government to negotiate for Gil's release and Ellen expected her son to be beheaded momentarily.....but Gil miraculously escaped. Gil has now converted to Islam and has friends and contacts in the Middle East. After Williams failed to help Gil, Ellen used her media conglomerate to lobby HARD against the senator being nominated for president, but Williams got the nomination and won. Now - to everyone's shock - Williams has made Ellen Secretary of State, but he plans to sabotage and disgrace her. The new administration has to repair the damage done by the previous president, Eric Dunn - called Eric the Dunce by his critics - who cozied up to dictators, allowed Iran to pursue nuclear weapons, damaged America's relations with its allies, and more. As if that's not bad enough, three bus bombs explode in a single day - first in London, then in Paris, and finally in Frankfurt. Just before the last bomb explodes a Pakistani-American foreign service officer called Anahita Dahir realizes a gibberish email she received, which her boss thought was spam, was a warning about the bombs. Secretary of State Adams gets the news just moments before the last bomb explodes, and is able to warn her son Gil, who's on the Frankfurt bus following a Pakistani nuclear physicist. Gil escapes the bus in time, but is injured and taken to the hospital. It turns out the bombs were detonated for the express purpose of killing three Pakistani scientists on their way to build nuclear weapons for other Middle Eastern factions. The theory is that Iran planted the bombs to stop its enemies in the region from acquiring weapons of mass destruction. The situation in the Middle East is always complicated, but the U.S. suspects the Russian Mafia - under the supervision of Russian President Ivanov - is selling nuclear components to Middle Eastern terrorists, and a Pakistani nuclear physicist called Dr. Bashir Shah is providing scientists to those same terrorists, all to help the zealots build nuclear bombs. Ellen and her trusted counselor Betsy Jameson..... ....along with foreign service officer Anahita Dahir and members of Ellen's staff - rush to the Middle East. Ellen plans to consult with the leaders of Iran, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, hoping to get information about the terrorists' identity and location. Along the way Ellen learns that three nuclear weapons have been placed in American cities, and are set to be detonated at any moment. Meanwhile Ellen's son Gil leaves the hospital and makes his way to his secret source in Afghanistan, who tells him a 'High Level Informant' in America is in league with Russia and the terrorists. When Ellen learns about the traitor she sends Betsy back to America to investigate the miscreant's identity. Betsy gets assistance from a disgruntled member of former President Dunn's administration, and their prying leads to murder. Meanwhile Ellen - with the blessings of President Williams (who's come to appreciate her intelligence and capabilities) - is in a race against time to stop the explosions on American soil. Ellen even confronts Russian President Ivanov, and gives him a taste of his own medicine. As with all thrillers, the plot requires some suspension of disbelief, but it mirrors several real world worries, like the Russian mafia arming the world, and Americans trying to undermine their own government. Fans of Louise Penny's Detective Inspector Armand Gamache series, set in the Canadian village of Three Pines, will be happy to see some favorite characters. Moreover, Secretary of State Ellen Adams' favorite poet is Ruth Zardo. 🙂 I enjoyed this fast-paced thriller, and got a kick out of Ellen Adams and her ally Betsy Jameson going face to face with some tough guys. Thriller fans (except for supporters of former President Trump) would probably enjoy this book. You can follow my reviews at https://reviewsbybarbsaffer.blogspot.com
I look forward to reading it because the inside knowledge Hillary Clinton offers. I am rating it five stars to try to counterbalance the preemptive one-star reviews by people who hate HRC.

I wasn’t sure what to expect when I first saw that Louise Penny and Hillary Rodham Clinton had teamed up to write State of Terror. At first, I felt skeptical about wanting to read this book but my curiosity won out. I actually listened the audio CD that was read by Joan Allen. State of Terror was most definitely a plot driven novel. It was fast paced, gripping and even suspenseful at times. Louise Penny used her writing talents to set the stage for a good mystery/thriller and combined them with the first hand knowledge Hillary Rodham Clinton brought to the table about international affairs and protocols to write State of Terror. Together they succeeded in writing a book that was compelling and hard to put down. Even Gamache found a role in State of Terror. It was pretty obvious who some of the political characters were in the book. Without giving too much away, State of Terror found newly appointed, yet a very questionable choice by the new President of the United States, Secretary of State, Ellen Adams, in a race against time. Only weeks after being appointed to her position, the Secretary of State was forced to navigate her way through Europe, the Middle East and Russia to diffuse a terrorist plot that included nuclear bombs. More problematic, Secretary Adams discovered that there were domestic traitors within the White House. Time was not on her side. Could she stop the nuclear bombs from going off, expose the traitors in the White House and win the respect of the President of the United States? I enjoyed listening to the audio CD of State of Terror by Louise Penny and Hillary Rodham Clinton. The ending led me to believe that this duo will be collaborating in the future to write other books together. I look forward to reading them. I highly recommend this book.

4.5 stars State of Terror turned out to be the savvy political thriller I didn't know I either needed or wanted. For me, this book covered almost the entire gamut of possible emotions or reactions. I laughed out loud, I shed a tear or two, I smirked, I scoffed. I was on the edge of my seat, I was bored, I was impressed, I was discontented. The scope of the narrative quite easily is reflected in the span of my reactions to it throughout. While Penny's influence and style are recognizable, this is not what you'd typically find from her offerings. Normally she borders on quaint and clement in her Three Pines mysteries, but with State of Terror the stakes are higher than ever and this is where the Clinton contribution comes in. Smart and fast-paced, this geopolitical thriller had my complete attention during the book's climax. The build towards to this peak was an increasingly intense rollercoaster ride that paid off in spades. There is a connection to Three Pines, as that village plays an important role in the plot near the end, but that injection, more than any other tongue-in-cheek reference, made me realize just how much fun these two authors had when writing this book together. There's such a balance to this novel — between the humor, the real-life allusions (the Trumpian former president, the Russian president who has ridden a horse while shirtless, etc.), but mostly it's the wonderful female friendship at the core. Even my reactions to it felt balanced. There was a constant ebb and flow to this one, stops and starts that elicited nothing but realism. If these two authors collaborate again . . . I'm in. Audiobook, as narrated by Joan Allen: Joan Allen was a slam-dunk for this audiobook performance. She has a fantastic, calm voice that reverberates with an undercurrent of strength. And the choice to have a woman in her sixties voice other women [characters] in their sixties is always the right move. In general, I'm finding that actors performing audiobook narration brings a more understated level of naturalistic performance than those of yore. They do so much more than reading out loud, and I am here for this transition.

In the Acknowledgments for State of Terror, Louise Penny, reminiscing about the writing process with fellow author Hillary Clinton, recalls at times having “literally lost the plot.” Though this comment is an aside expressed with humor, the sentiment describes the novel for me. The bombing episode that opens State of Terror is taut, dramatic, compelling, a page-turner. I cared about the characters and was anxious to know the outcome of the three bombs that had been planted. The book’s beginning is well done, and the authors are fully in control of their tale. Portions of the rest of the novel are a sharp contrast. The authors lose control of the story with multiple characters, multiple motivations, and multiple storylines, all vying for attention. At times, the story lines tend to compete, not integrate. At the book’s conclusion, the tying together of loose ends, a coda of sorts, has a lot to explain with twist reversal after twist reversal as the authors finally sort the bad characters from the good. With all this back and forth, I no longer cared. I found myself saying, “Hey, whatever!” As the book progresses from orderly at the beginning to wandering at the end, it feels like the authors just put something on paper, then punted on the necessary work of editing, consolidating, and focusing their story. I’m just guessing what happened during the writing process, but I do know what impression the book gave me. The novel feels unfinished, a collection of competing ideas, a story beyond the authors’ control. What about the credibility of the plot? Some political thrillers are vividly realistic and believable. Some are so absurd, they are good fun; the authors are enjoying themselves, and the reader willingly goes along for the ride. State of Terror fits neither of these categories. The novel is both wildly unbelievable and serious, a combination that led me to be distracted, even annoyed. You might conclude I didn’t care for State of Terror, but that’s an incomplete judgment. As noted, I appreciated and enjoyed the beginning. Maybe the authors should have quit there before they lost control of the plot and wandered into the absurd. Maybe I should have stopped reading. By continuing, I discovered there’s a good novella here, but not a satisfying novel.

Secretary of State Ellen Adams loathes her boss, and the feeling is mutual. She’s convinced he had named her to the post only to find a way to destroy her reputation. And when he torpedoes a vital diplomatic mission to Korea that is intensely embarrassing to her, she knows she’s right. The fractured relationship poses immense complications for her when all hell breaks loose in Europe, and she is forced to swing into action. Massive terrorist bombs have exploded in London, Paris, and Frankfurt. No one has taken credit. Thus begins the new Hillary Clinton novel, State of Terror, coauthored with Louise Penny. Now, the Secretary and her advisor, Betsy Jameson, must use all the resources at their disposal to unravel the meager clues that will help her identify the terrorists. This starts a cascading series of events that subjects leaders throughout the West into a “state of terror.” And they will find that the reality behind the bombings is even more terrifying than they’d imagined. A SURPRISE TO THE LAST Like reviewers for the New York Times, NPR, and the Washington Post, I approached this book with trepidation. Books by celebrities always flash red danger signals for me. But this novel, the first Hillary Clinton has written, surprised me. It proves to be suspenseful to the last. And it would hardly be uncharitable to credit veteran mystery novelist Louise Penny for much of the book’s success. After all, writing a suspenseful novel requires a set of skills that a politician is unlikely to acquire in decades at the pinnacle of public attention. A COMPLEX STORY THAT UNFOLDS AROUND THE WORLD State of Terror tells a complex story that takes readers around much of the world. Secretary Adams alone visits major cities from London to Tehran to Islamabad to Moscow. And we learn of other action taking place in Iran, Pakistan, Germany, and Afghanistan. The cast of characters is also large, including not just Ellen Adams and Betsy Jameson but Ellen’s adult son and daughter, her chief of staff, the President and his chief of staff, the Director of National Intelligence, and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. And those are just the most prominent Americans in the story. We also meet Iranians, Pakistanis, Russians, Canadians, and several other world leaders. Yet it all hangs together nicely. REAL-WORLD MODELS FOR THE CHARACTERS Every character in State of Terror is fictional. But many are based on real-life personalities. The two leading characters, Secretary of State Ellen Adams and her best friend and counselor, Betsy Jameson, are modeled on two of Hillary Clinton’s closest friends. Former California Congresswoman Ellen Tauscher, who served under Clinton as Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security, was the model for Ellen Adams. And Betsy Jameson was based on Clinton’s life-long best friend, Betsy Eberling. Both women died in 2019, as did Clinton’s younger brother, Tony. “The combination was devastating” to Clinton and helped motivate her to collaborate with Penny on this novel. The world leaders portrayed in State of Terror also have their real-world counterparts. Former US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, and Ayatollah Ali Khamenei of Iran all appear in speaking roles on the novel’s pages. And the authors eviscerate both Trump and Putin. Trump’s depiction is unsparing as “an arrogant fool, a useful idiot for the far right” whose policies had subjected the United States to great danger. Putin, in turn, is portrayed as not just vicious, conniving, and corrupt but as the head of the Russian mafia. A FUN AND ENTERTAINING BOOK It’s clear that Clinton and Penny had fun writing this novel. For the former Secretary of State, the exercise offered a juicy opportunity to take revenge on the man who was elected President in her stead. Her depiction of “former President Eric Dunn” is devastating. But Louise Penny had her fun, too. In the book’s closing chapters, some of the pivotal action takes place in the Quebecois village of Three Pines, the setting for the long-running series of detective novels she set there. And some of her familiar characters appear in the story as well. It’s all fun not just for the authors but for readers as well. ABOUT THE AUTHORS Hillary Rodham Clinton (1947-) was the sixty-seventh US Secretary of State. She served in office from 2009 to 2013 after eight years as a United States Senator from New York and eight years as the First Lady of the United States. She wrote or coauthored eight nonfiction books before State of Terror, her first novel. Canadian author Louise Penny (1958-) has built a successful career with her detective novels—eighteen strong as I write—featuring Inspector Armand Gamache of the Sûreté du Québec. They’re cozy mysteries set in the tiny fictional village of Three Pines in Quebec. The novels have won her the Agatha Award for best mystery novel of the year five times.

Hang on a sec while I smooth down the hair standing on end and ask my hands to stop shaking. This book kept me up most of the night and its scenarios and ideas are worms eating themselves into my brains, leaving me jumpy. In other words, a satisfying thriller! I have long been a fan of Louise Penny’s books and an admirer of Hillary Clinton’s body of work, so a political suspense novel written by the two of them together was irresistible. I love Penny’s humanism and her quirky characters but have sometimes felt the gritty edges of her plots were less than convincing, so my hope was that Clinton’s (or as I like to say, Rodham’s) intimate knowledge of the White House and the Secretary of State’s office would save us from naïveté. That was mostly true, even though this book in the end is as much about love and friendship as it is about international affairs. Ellen Adams is the U.S. Secretary of State in this tale, a former media mogul chosen for her post by a president who loathes her and wants to undercut her and destroy her career, the consequences to the nation be damned. I’ve known bosses like that. The story opens as she returns from a disastrous diplomatic mission to South Korea—disastrous, she suspects, because her boss has deliberately set her up to fail. It doesn’t help that the previous president was a useful idiot (yes, that portrait is all too recognizable) who has hollowed out the State Department and strewn celestial poo patties throughout America’s global relationships. The pit of vipers that is Washington, D.C., is evoked in all-too-heartfelt terms, and Secretary Adams has her hands full sussing out the hidden agendas and avoiding pitfalls, all the while trying to earn the respect that is so much harder for female leaders to come by. She does it with zest and a refreshing lack of self-pity. Very quickly, stuff starts happening—a series of terrorist bombs strike European cities, one (view spoiler). We get a credible view of the investigative tools available to the U.S. government, cranked up to maximum speed because, of course, time is of the essence. Equally of course, the bombs are the least of the problem, and soon Secretary Adams is careening all over the world, always one step behind the malefactors. This kind of fast-paced material can be tough to write and it’s done very well in this story, without losing sight of character development and the arcs of vital personal relationships. It’s a very polished work that kept me engaged from start to finish, and I don’t want to say much more for fear of spoilers. Louise Penny has a few quirks to her writing that I noticed here, but for the most part they worked to provide the occasional breathing space any thriller needs. Fans of her books will be happy to learn that the Canadian village of Three Pines has a cameo role in the story; it might have felt gratuitous except that what that village stands for is integral to reinforcing the humanity of the characters in this tale. And ultimately, retaining humanity in a vicious world, hanging on to love and trust and principles are what the good guys are fighting for. I tried to imagine how a conservative might read this book. The bits (and they are only bits) about the previous president might stick in the craw, but I like to think that the underlying patriotism, the love for democracy and family, would translate well across the divide. So many thrillers seem to be written by people of a rightward persuasion that it was interesting and occasionally jarring to read a hard-edged thriller that was imbued with a tinge of the softness we associate with liberalism. Also one in which the action heroes were mainly female. I found I quite liked these variations on what can be a stale theme. And I deeply enjoyed what happened to the president of Russia.

My Thoughts: It's been one week since I finished Iron Flame and I am still unwell. No matter how hard I try, I cannot get this book out of my head, all because of those last 25 pages . . . ⁠How dare Rebecca do this to us, knowing we have to wait god knows how long for book 3. 😭 ⁠ Did I enjoy it? Yes. ⁠ Was it better than Fourth Wing? No. ⁠ But will I continue the series? Abso-f*cking-lutely! ⁠ This book is really hard for me to rate because while I enjoyed the story and the ending, there were a lot of technical (plot/character) issues that definitely hindered my overall enjoyment. *SPOILERS AHEAD* ⁠ What I liked: ⁠The story is action-packed from start to finish, so you'll never want to put this book down. Iron Flame is divided into two parts. Part one takes place at Basgiath War College and part two focuses on the Revolution. There's 623 pages total, and I genuinely felt like I read two books because so much happens. I'm glad I took detailed notes because I've already forgotten a lot and I know I'll need to refer to them before starting book 3. The continued world-building is fascinating. Like I said, this story is non-stop and that includes uncovering new information about the history and politics of this world. We now have a solid idea on what's really happening on the continent, however, there's still so many unanswered questions about the past (before the unification), the venin, and the Empyrean. I love this phase of a long series because there's still so much we don't know or understand, and I can't wait to see everything unfold and come together in the next few books. ⁠ These characters are some of my favorites and need to be protected at all costs. Violet is still a badass. Xaden is still daddy. Tairn is fucking hilarious. And Andarna is the sassiest bitch in the realm. I do wish she wasn't away for half the story though. I'm glad that by part two she starts to lean on her friends more, but I'm worried how she's going to manage after the events at the end of book 2. PS: Violet during the torture scenes and and final battle when she saves Sawyer was impressive as hell! I respect her so much and strive to be just as badass.
