Atlas is a character you LOVE to LOVE. This is the story of Atlas and Lily. What could have been, what is happening, and what will be. The best part of It Starts with Us is Colleen Hoover's gift of Atlas' perspective. We get to see how he feels, where he is in his life, and what he wants for his future. We are introduced to a new character that plays a significant part in Atlas' life--but we’re not very interesting, unfortunately. Lily is a single mother, raising Emerson. Ryle and her are trying to co-parent. It's complicated. Ryle still has feelings for Lilly, what will she do? I liked Hoover's emphasis on Atlas and his journey. Lily lets Atlas read some of her old journals and in return, Atlas starts writing letters to Lily. However, Atlas’ POV sounded like Hoover was the writer, and didn’t get into HIS head enough. I wasn’t feeling the whole “Dory” the fish story line. I liked this book, but it didn’t have the punch of ‘It Ends with Us’. I think it is clear that Hoover's storytelling, more than her writing reels you in. An interesting plot, and multi-layered characters are part of Hoover's strength. ‘It Starts with Us’ is a very simplified version of real life. I don't believe things come easy in complicated relationships. Some of the more dynamic plots ended too quickly, in a less real world format. If Hoover would have dug a little deeper, showing the reader how dynamic single motherhood, the relationships we keep post divorce, and the hardship, it would have been more realistic. Overall, I loved Atlas and Lily's growth—but I don’t think it ties together on such a neat boy in real life This was a well done ending to the story. I hope we get a show/movie soon! 3.8/5 stars. “You're going to drive five miles just to give me a hug?" "I'd run five miles just to give you a hug.” Contrary to all my expectations, this book was absolutely beautiful. buddy read with the wonderful shell! ❤️ warning: spoilers ahead for It Ends With Us PREMISE. This sequel begins a few hours after the epilogue of It Ends With Us. Lily and Ryle have been divorced for a year and a half, and Lily and Atlas have just met up again. Both want to try dating, but Lily is terrified of how Ryle will react to Atlas in her and her daughter’s life. Ryle blames Atlas for their divorce, and he’s been grounds for several fights between Lily and Ryle. PLOT. As reviews were initially coming in for this book, I saw that a lot of people were very frustrated with the way Lily let Ryle stay in her life after the divorce. To that, I’d argue that while both we the readers and Lily know how horrible and abusive Ryle is, there's only so much Lily can change about her situation. Emerson is his daughter (and he still has the legal right to see her), Lily’s best friend Alyssa is his sister, and she doesn't want to abandon her whole floral business and dream of living in Boston out of fear of her ex-husband. Leaving an abusive relationship is extremely difficult, and with so many emotional and situational ropes tying you to your abuser, it’s nearly impossible to cut every rope. It’s an unrealistic expectation to place on anyone, and I’m glad Colleen showed just how messy and emotionally painful that split truly is. The other thing I saw many people saying was that this book was the quintessential “sequel that shouldn’t have been made.” I would disagree. Every action has consequences, and yet in many books, we don’t see those consequences. We see the happily-ever-after ending of Cinderella, skipping the part where the nobles reject and rebel against a commoner as queen. In many romance novels, we see nothing after the main couple get together. We skip the part where they get into fights over who picks up the kid and why one of them is working far too late. We see only the good and none of the hard. This book, on the other hand, showed those consequences. The consequences of abuse don't go away when you get out of an abusive situation. The consequences of divorce don’t end with signing a paper. Maybe the ending of It Ends With Us felt more final, more perfect, but It Starts With Us showed that even the best endings are messy too. CHARACTERS. Ryle Kincaid. I imagine that Ryle Kincaid is what happens if a classic male romance hero existed in real life. Ridiculously attractive, over six feet, very well-educated, possessive, slightly narcissistic, and has a tragic backstory. In any other novel, I don’t think very many people would think twice. Yet in these two books, Colleen examines the dark side of that archetype. In fiction, characters like him don’t have the abusive streak that often runs alongside possessiveness, narcissism, and a difficult past. Reality, however, is much closer to Ryle. I hate him for what he did to Lily, yet it’s worth noting how disturbingly similar he is to heroes that we love. Atlas Corrigan. I adore Atlas with every fiber of my being. In this book, we see more of his own journey with abuse and abandonment, one that was merely hinted at in the first book. If Ryle is the classic male romance hero, Atlas is the secondary love interest. He didn’t end up with Lily the first time around, but he gets a second chance. Like Ryle, Atlas worked his way out of a difficult past, yet unlike Ryle, Atlas overcame it. He didn’t turn possessive and narcissistic and vengeful. He sought to understand, to apologize, to forgive. He is the antithesis of Ryle, and the lover that Lily truly deserves. Lily Bloom. Lily, Lily, Lily. I am so proud of you. All the pain and deliberation you went through and the consideration of your daughter and the standing up against Ryle was beyond difficult, but you did it regardless. Lily truly broke the cycle of abuse. She began breaking it in the first book when she walked away from Ryle, and she ended it in the second book by not making the same mistakes. She changed a multigenerational cycle of abuse, and for that, I am so proud of her. “I can draw a seedling with two tiny branches. Yours and mine. We’ll be on our own brand-new, tiny family tree—one that starts with us.” Ratings: Star Rating: ★★★★★ If This Book Was a Movie Rating: PG-13 Recommendations If You Liked This Book: Beach Read by Emily Henry

writing a book that blows me away and then not publishing anything else for a million years is cruel and unusual. high expectations can be a curse. assembly, the author's debut novella, came out 4 years ago, and my anticipation for its follow-up have only grown since. that book is compelling and clever, vague as a means of rendering complete a story that feels sharp and specific. it's been years since i read it, but i think of it often. this book is very dissimilar. it crams a lot of details into its 176 pages: many washed-up and amoral journalists, several wannabe hippies, one or two half-formed aspiring movements, a quasi-mystery, a viral article. it's mixed media and multi-perspective, but its extreme level of specificity barred me from learning a lot from it. we all know about political "perspective" in the news, the rising voice of the malcontent white middle class the world over, the suffocating tide of income inequality. this book felt like it didn't give me more to consider, but fictional examples of the same. there were moments i really enjoyed, but the biggest pro and the biggest con of this for me were how realistic it felt! it didn't come together in the way fiction can, but all of it felt astonishingly real. maybe it's because i'm not british. bottom line: feeling slightly disappointed by things you're excited for builds character. Longlisted for the 2025 Booker Prize Finalist for the 2025 Orwell Prize 'We're open to everyone,' Indiya agrees. That said, the Universalists are a noticeably homogeneous group: young, middle class and white. 'This lifestyle takes a leap of faith,' she explains. Intentional living requires a step away from the 'activism myopia' that can ('Understandably!' she stresses) afflict marginalised groups. Natasha Brown’s Assembly was a brilliant debut and one of the finest novels of 2021, shortlisted for the Goldsmiths Prize and a finalist for the Orwell Prize for Political Fiction. Her sophomore novel, Universality, due out in 2025, is also destined to be a contender for major prizes. While it ostensibly is more conventional stylistically, in its impact it is even more challenging to the literary and political status quo. It’s a novel about the power of words and stories – the stories we tell about others, the stories we tell ourselves and want to be told about us – and about privilege and about diversity, and the assumption that it’s others who benefit from both. The first quarter of the novel is , an extended article, originally published in Alazon Magazine in June 2021, a New Journalism style investigative piece entitled “A Fool’s Gold”, based on an odd incident during lockdown when an illegal rave ended with one person being rendered unconscious, struck by a 400 ounce gold bar (current bullion price, close to £800,000). As the article’s author explains: Unravelling the events leading to this strange and unsettling night is well worth the trouble; a modern parable lies beneath, exposing the fraying fabric of British society, worn thin by late capitalism's relentless abrasion. The missing gold bar is a connecting node between an amoral banker, an iconoclastic columnist and a radical anarchist movement. The novel then moves on to the author of the piece, Hannah, a previously struggling journalist, who is hosting a dinner party with her friends to celebrate the news that the story is being turned into a TV story, although a fictionalised version with details changed to make it even more resonant (e.g. a key character becomes black) The truth, more often than not, benefited from the techniques of fiction. Every hack knew that. Although as we learn how Hannah came to write the article, we realise this adage applies as much to her original piece. The next section takes us to the story of the aforementioned “amoral banker”, Richard, original owner of the gold bar, whose life, to him entirely unfairly, has been ruined by the story. And the final section is an interview at a leading Literature Festival of the “iconoclastic columnist” Lenny Leonard who by contrast, is a beneficiary, parlaying her notoriety into a new career as a crusader against woke capitalism and a move from the right-wing press to the Observer [as she mentions more than once, appearing alongside ‘Cohen’, an intriguing reference]. During that interview she explains her modus operandi and that of the paper, including quotes such as We tell you want you want to hear, while convincing you that it’s the truth, told as close to objectively as possible and Your readers come away believing they are aggrieved on someone else’s behalf. And this is where the novel’s power lies. Whereas Assembly gave us the single narrator’s searing perspective on everything she saw around her (including, to an extent, checking her own privilege as an Oxbridge-educator city worker), here, with the multiple perspectives, everyone sees themselves, and those like them, as the victim. And the reader’s sympathy is then naturally drawn to those with who they identify – for me, far from being amoral, that would be banker Richard, at least for his professional (if not personal) life. I found myself nodding along with his lament when even an attempt, in GQ Magazine, to tell his side of the story turns into a hatchet job: Richard couldn't quite understand what it was about him that rankled these people so much. Hadn't he simply done what he was supposed to do? He'd taken the eleven-plus, made it into the grammar school, and simply followed that life path to its inevitable conclusion. He didn't hurt anyone, he didn't exploit anyone. He tried, as much as was possible, to work hard and fair. After the crash, he'd moved into regulatory risk ... working to prevent another crisis. And, as the divisional head, he'd ensured that there were women in senior roles, along with a broadly diverse management team. Indeed, he now had a network of colleagues who credited him as a friend and a mentor. He was proud of that legacy. His was not the monoculture of commoditised socialism, with its vague, moralistic promise to end discrimination. He was actually doing his part by hiring qualified candidates and giving them the same chance at success that he himself had received. All these 'writers' did, as far as Richard could tell, was spread gossip for fun and profit, stoking outrage and discontent without actually fixing anything. Inspiring stuff, at least to this reader. But that’s because as a white male (ex) banker from a working-class background, that’s not dissimilar to the story I tell myself as well – or indeed, of course, the story that Lou in Assembly told himself. And at the novel’s other end, are the “radical anarchists”who, as per my opening quote, have moved, in their view, beyond the ‘activism myopia’ of more marginalised groups, to an oddly exclusive worldview for self-proclaimed Universalists. So perhaps it is Lenny who is actually the one character who is most self-aware If anything, I’m a misanthrope. An equal-opportunity hater. Or is Lenny the least self-aware character of all? A novel which will provoke some fascinating and challenging discussions next year, and another brilliant novel from an author who, rightly, was named as one of the 2023 class of Granta Best of Young British Novelists, part of the 'A Fool’s Gold' piece featuring in the magazine. A resounding 5 stars. Thanks to the author, via my twin, aka Gumble's Yard - Golden Reviewer, for the ARC. A taster here of further content.

Now Longlisted for the Booker Prize 2025 Frankly, this starts out rather lame, as the first chapter is a mock-journalistic piece about an activist group illegally holding a rave in the country house of a finance bro, until one of the organizers, Jake, strikes down radical activist Pegasus with a gold bar stored on the premises. The language is an imitation of mediocre magazine writing, the story plays on cheap "eat the rich" impulses, white middle class Che Guevaras, and of course an ideologically flexible rage bait queen feeding on the digital attention economy. But then the story unravels: We learn how the article's author, freelance journalist Hannah, struggles since COVID hit and how social class and a changing media landscape impact her social and professional life - and what she does in order to survive, and we see disgraced banker Richard pressured between the expectations of his upper-class (ex-)wife, the relentless dynamics of the market, and the moral superiority of the media (which at the moment makes you think of the CEO who was caught cheating at the Coldplay concert - is the way he is getting humiliated all over the world a sign of the moral integrity of those who turn his family's misery into content?). We meet Lenny, who plays the attention economy like a fiddle, cynically thriving on the audience's impulses, because it's us who make people like Milo Yiannopoulos, and her whacky son Jake, you know: the one who attacks people with gold bars. And then there are the activists, wrapped up in their self-righteousness, far from reality. Brown refuses to give easy answers, to show a marketable good vs. bad dichotomy that appeals to the sense of righteousness on the side of the readers: Who doesn't want to feel like they are standing on the correct side of the cultural wars? But maybe the mediatized war is in large parts a scam to sell rage and fear, to keep us from talking about issues like class disparity and financial injustice, hence: to cement the status quo? In "Universality", there is no sense of coherence and solidarity anymore. People are leaving their jobs in the public service sector because they are disillusioned (understandably) and join well-paying genetics start-ups instead (less understandable), they lie about their heritage while claiming to reveal publicly relevant truths to secure their survival, they try to control a system that isn't even affected by any of their actions, they have stopped seeing how their perspectives are connected. This is a challenging read that defies easy interpretation, and it points way beyond post-Brexit Britain. Should be on the Booker list to get people talking.

Natasha Brown’s debut novel “Assembly” was a scathing critique of race, class and society. It was delivered through the voice of an upwardly mobile twenty something black woman on the cusp of heretofore unimagined success. Brown’s follow-up novel “Universality” considers the same themes through a different lens asking how language creates cultural myths and influences perceptions. The novel’s first section is an investigative magazine article exposing the consequences of a rave on a Yorkshire farm during the COVID lockdown. A young man has used a gold bar to assault the leader of the Universalists, a youthful political group intent on fostering an alternative lifestyle on the farm. The article, entitled “A Fool’s Gold,”is a thinly veiled amalgam of investigative journalism laced with sociopolitical overtones and inferences. In subsequent sections of the novel, the story is retold from the perspectives of the article’s author as well as the views of the disgraced banker who owned the gold bar and the thoughts of a controversial columnist.Each telling casts doubt upon the reliability of the other accounts. Gradually, the novel challenges the reader to sift through conflicting versions of “ truth.” There are no reliable narrative voices and the novel becomes an exercise in detection and evaluation of society and politics. The role of language as a driver of questionable facts is pivotal for understanding how political metaphors influence social narratives and sway group perceptions. “ Despite her cavalier talk, Lenny’s views are often nuanced and well considered; she doesn’t adhere to a single side for every debate…” “ Still, Lenny retains her characteristic style: heavy on aphorisms without wasting time on citations or justifications..” Lenny in the above passages is Miriam” Lenny” Leonard,a well known columnist and social influencer.This description of her style appears in the investigative article and reflects Lenny’s flexible relationship to facts and accuracy. Her jaundiced style is shared by many as Lenny herself notes saying,” The truth, more often than not, benefited from the techniques of fiction. Every hack knew that.” “Universality” is a subtle and sophisticated novel that merits close reading.As each section unfolds, more complexities arise regarding the role of language, deception and political realities.Years ago, one of my political theory professors constantly emphasized that words are fists.Throughout this novel, competing individuals and groups are subtly assaulting each other through the media , attempting to create narratives that will lead to influence and profit. The gold bar used in the assault is a symbol of the glitter and avarice prevalent in our political structures. Ultimately “Universality “ examines the ways that media controls perceptions and fosters either alliances or enmities among disparate social groups. Although the novel’s political milieu is set in Britain, the concerns resonate worldwide.In the United States, for example, we are witnessing segments of the population becoming marginalized and dispossessed as political narratives of questionable accuracy gain traction. This well conceived novel combines provocative observations with uncomfortable truths about the direction of our social and governmental institutions…Outstanding.

Is a book written like a New Yorker article good literature? Yes. I was unsure at first, wondering if everything was only on the surface. But with every new chapter and shift in perspective - revealing who wrote the article, who commissioned it, and who is actually the villain - I saw a strong novel taking shape. The theme of economic wokism is not as striking as the more familiar identity-based wokism (see Rejection by Tony Tulathimutte), but the message is important. The world becomes unsalvageable if we create villains based solely on race and gender. Instead of solving real problems, we end up feeding a destructive game of perception - one with dehumanizing consequences.

Another sharp and slim read from Brown. Very different from ASSEMBLY, though it also considers questions of class and success. The beginning is a longform piece of journalism, and the remaining parts show us the writer and her subjects through a different lens. It lets us ask questions about the state of media, about criticism and commentary, about how politics can infuse the way stories are told even when it doesn't seem like it on the surface. I don't know British media well enough to know if there are specific figures Brown is basing these characters on or how much it resembles the larger picture, but there is enough that is familiar for it to really hit. There are questions here of messaging, of who is using who, of what the message behind a story actually is, and which stories get told. It strikes me as a little strange that we haven't had more novels about media given the upheaval its had in the last twenty years and the now-constant question of bias. Would love to see more if they can be as smart and savvy as Brown can.

The rest of the book follows a number of different characters in the story but the entire thing felt really disjointed. I missed the shocking feel of the first part of the book and although it was all centred around the one event it felt completely plotless and like it wasn’t moving forward at all. The ‘reveal’ at the end just wasn’t as shocking as it should have been, and the book seemed to be slathered too heavily with social commentary for it to feel like it was in any way entertaining. If it wasn’t for how much I liked the first part I would have given this a lower rating, but it was certainly an experiment and a type of novella I’ve never come across before.

I loved the structure of this. Exploring race, privilege, and class in a candid way. Asking the question: who are we really, and how do we want the world to see us? Told through five chapters, each one revealing a little more dimensionality to what we initially thought we were reading. A social critique and a political satire intended to provoke. Although it’s a short read, it packs more of a punch than books twice its size. Characters who are either misguided, misinformed or deliciously monstrous. I blew through this thing because it had an addictive quality to it. Also, it made me tense because it embodies a world that I sadly recognize. I loved Brown’s debut ASSEMBLY, but I loved this one even more. This was all-consuming. Literary rage-bait.

After really enjoying the power and resonance of Brown’s debut novel Assembly, I was looking forward to a similar experience with her second book, but I am still feeling rather ambivalent about this. The core of the novel is about truth: our relationship with truth and how we can manipulate language to create versions of the truth, particularly in our current ‘post-truth’ era. I liked that it remained very British: it touches on class and race relations in modern Britain, and the journalistic culture wars we read every day, but unfortunately these themes weren’t explored in as much depth as I would’ve liked. Maybe that’s because the book is so short, maybe it’s because as someone who attended journalism school, a lot of the discussions in this book are ideas which I’ve written essays about and attended lectures on to the saturation point. Natasha Brown is a brilliant writer, but this one just sadly missed the mark for me!

Immediately after finishing this book, I didn't think I'd enjoyed it very much. I open my notes & highlights, I've highlighted paragraphs on paragraphs on paragraphs - all of which still make sense to me, without complete context. That tells me I did, in fact, enjoy this. The first section, A Fool's Gold, was the standout to me; no surprise if you read my reviews often, as dissection of the 'mother' role is my kryptonite. Across all sections of this book, Natasha Brown gives readers numerous opportunities to identify with the characters she creates. Written from a perspective of victimization, you navigate topics like sexism, classism, racism - a lot of the '-isms. Admittedly, comprehension took a lot more effort than I'd anticipated. This wasn't a book I could coast through or give only partial attention to. That being said, I'm going to wait until I have a little more mental bandwidth before I dig into her debut, Assembly, Assembly. {Thank you bunches to NetGalley, Natasha Brown and Random House for the eARC in exchange for my honest review!}

2.5 rounded to 3. Natasha brown is an incredible writer and knows how to fit a lot of content in a short book. Maybe I just need to think about it some more before I post my true thoughts! More detailed review to come. Thanks very much to the publisher for an advanced copy!

I really didn’t enjoy this one sadly, which came as such a surprise to me after adoring Assembly by the same author a few years ago. There was just something about this that didn’t feel like a cohesive novel at all. We started with a journalist investigating an assault and theft, and then meandered into the most random and uninteresting avenues. What started out with a lot of promise soon dwindled away. It ended up being all over the place and extremely messy and unfocused, almost like it couldn't really decide what it wanted to do. From the tone, it felt like an opinion piece essay rather than a story, or like a sort of documentary transcript. There was something off about the storytelling. It was detached and weird, and the length really hindered it. It almost felt like it was never supposed to be its one novel, but ended up having to be padded out to fit some sort of word count and qualify. It probably could’ve worked better as a short story. We also have so many characters and ideas and small sideplots going on in such a small space, that none of it was given sufficient development. Changing character and perspectives every few pages was so disorientating, and they were all so similar in my head they meshed into a single bland entity. The commentary and the themes it tried to address are really interesting, but it felt like a waste. Nothing that is said in the book is a new or exciting idea, and anything it did say is never built upon. It just felt half soaked and lazy, we start and end in what feels like the same place. It felt like the approach to everything was too blase and casual for the intended effect, so it never landed. The only positive really is that the pacing was pretty decent so I ended up being able to read it in a day. Such a shame because Brown is such an exciting and intelligent writer, but she missed the mark massively.

part news article and part novel, universality was a thought-provoking look at the language of the political vs. the personal and the way we talk about class, race, and privilege. we begin with an article about a man who was bludgeoned with a gold bar at an abandoned farm that was being used as an anarchist communal living space. we then follow the author of the article, the banker that owned the farm, and another writer who was involved. a lot of the characters were unlikable, but i think it worked to the book’s advantage and made its commentary feel even more poignant. i enjoyed the combination of forms and the fact that we got so many different characters’ POVs. the writing style was sharp and snappy, and i appreciate how much natasha brown was able to do in so few pages - i’d love to pick up her other novel assembly! thank you to random house for sending me a copy of this book - out now!

I was a big fan of Assembly, which was fresh, smart and surprising in all the good ways. This one was a bit less convincing. It somehow manages to be simultaneously topical and outdated. It cares about all the right things people in London should care about, but in a somewhat predictable way. It also creates an expectation at the start that it subsequently refuses to fulfill. It starts out as a plot-based novel, with a journalist investigating the disappearance of a solid gold bar after an illegal rave, but then does not follow up and morphs into something more like a pamphlet. I wanted a good story, but this is a book you should read when you are in the mood for caring about the right things. That being said, writing a second novel that is very different from a first, makes Natasha Brown an even more interesting writer and I will certainly read whatever comes next.

I’ve never been so excited in my life to give a book back to the library. You wouldn’t think a book about squatter hippies bludgeoning each other with a gold bar could be so excruciatingly boring, but I guess there really is a first time for everything.
Terribly smart book. These people drove me INSANE and that usually means the book is hard won if not great. Not just super enjoyable to read but i found it brilliant. The ending was perfect.

Natasha Brown went to the Claire Keegan school of not wasting my time... A man is bludgeoned with a gold bar and a journalist is handed the story on a silver platter. Through her article a web unravels that encompasses a new age commune, a politically-confusing reactionist public figure and her drug-addled son, and a circle of former uni friends who find themselves pulled apart by the perceived moral precarity facing England. Assembly was my favourite read of 2021, and the pivot here was quite a jolt—until it wasn't. Viewing Universality as a companion to Assembly heightens both. Where her debut was focused, a singular perspective that became universal in its specificity, Universality is concerned with the multiple perspectives. If the Assembly dealt in why, then this is an exploration of the how. Because every character sees themselves as a victim, their failures can be chalked up to how society has failed them; their triumphs, of course, are entirely self-made. This is a scathing dissection of British class systems and meritocracy through an entirely different lens. I am absolutely obsessed with the final chapter, in which events come to a head at a writer's festival. Brown's powers of observation are genuinely insane, the level of satire, the accuracy of the ridiculousness. I think this will definitely appeal more to those with knowledge of the publishing industry and the identity politics of arts organisations. The more I've taken time to consider this, the better it becomes. Rich characterisations and a remarkable lack of bullshit. You know I liked a book when I only wish it had been longer, which I felt this could have been. So, so clever.

Book 5 of my Booker Prize longlist challenge, each year I dedicate my time to reading all the books on the booker longlist/shortlist so I can attempt to predict the winner. (Key word here is attempt) This has led me to read some incredible books, pushing me out of my comfort zone & expanding my taste. Another let down, what I thought would be a sharp crime fiction circling around a man getting bludgeoned by a gold bar, turned into a commentary on activism, journalism, English politics & much more. This would of been interesting, if not for the small page count. There was not enough pages to flesh anything out. The crime gets solved immediately, the entire plot gets solved within the first chapter or so & we are left asking not much else. I struggled to even want to continue... nevertheless I did, disappointing. Just not my thing. A lot is thrown at the reader with no time to process and digest before moving onto another social commentary.

Universality is a big zeitgeist novella. It's satirical, a little bit wanky, very pointed, and has a lot to say about hot button issues like political tribalism, the modern media landscape, and truth (and its many versions). It's a novella that is very obvious about what it is doing, and also is very current, which I can see might be grating for some readers. I found it extremely captivating, and was engaged to read something as energetic, tight, and focused. It's very different to a lot of the other Booker longlisted novels this year, and I am interested to see how it fares. Feeling like the only person that hasn't read Assembly, I'll be adding that to the top of my post-Booker reading list.

Great writing! Some thought provoking ideas. There are phenomenal reviews out there that may explain or even provide full analysis of this work that perhaps should be read before. I went in completely blind. This small book shows views on class, race, sex, politics, the economy and the iniquity of diversity, equity and inclusion programmes. But unfortunately this one did not work for me. To me it went nowhere. It wasn’t even entertaining. At least it was very short. If you are looking for a book with a clear plot and likeable characters, this is not the book for. Hardcover (Random House): 152 pages

Where to begin? Universality is a deliciously brutal little book. It's centered around both an event, and an object. The object in question is a gold bar, and the event is a person using the bar to harm someone else. When the book opens, we follow a journalistic account of an illegal rave, during which someone was bludgeoned with a gold bar. The scope widens, panning out until we can see it in its entirety. Everyone involved, and how their actions and beliefs affect everyone around them, until the first smash of the bar into the skull. And then the story shifts. And shifts. And keeps shifting. It's addictive and effective- I found myself pulled in a million directions. Ultimately, it's an examination of classism, racism, sexism (to name a few) and how these topics affect us all. I loved it.

While this book might be a little bit "on the nose", I loved it. Which is really saying something because I'm not usually a fan of satire. But if there was ever a group that deserved skewering it's the media, and Universality does not hold back. More subtly, Brown also reflects our human nature and how much we actually like to be incensed and how the media leverages that enjoyment for their own financial gain. Right now, I think this book is almost too of the moment, but I think it's Animal Farm, a book that future generations will dissect with interest in literature classes. Unfortunately, I don't think this one makes the short list. It's a little too close for comfort. But wow, Natasha Brown, I can't wait to go back and read Assembly.

Booker Book 7/13: 3 out of 10. I feel like I didn’t read the same book that so many other people are praising. I read a very tired collection of characters speechifying about various hobby horses of contemporary discourse (wokeness, diversity, the disappearing middle class, the rapacity of “late capitalism”, the perfidious ways that media and the internet have cynically ruined us etc etc). If I wanted this type of thing, I’d listen to more podcasts or read more Substacks. Although there’s a bit of playfulness in the structure (switching viewpoints and briefly, form), there are no characters (other than cliched mouthpieces), literally zero plot (but a bunch of odd loose ends), and not much craft. The “discourse” this book offers already seems dated and very boring. Well the first bad apple in what’s otherwise been a stellar Booker crop. It was bound to happen.
Didn't really like it.

2.5/5 Universality is the second book I’ve read by Natasha Brown, after Assembly, which I enjoyed when it came out. I was glad to see her return with something new, and it makes sense to me that this novel was longlisted for the Booker Prize. Brown is deeply interested in how people perform their politics, especially online and in print. Though I don’t consider myself especially political, I recognized so many of the arguments and talking points that dominate our social media and news feeds today. The voices in this book sound exactly like what we’ve been hearing and living with over the past few years. It’s the noise of the times, captured very accurately on the page. That said, I didn’t love this book. There is too much emphasis on political commentary and not enough on character or story. The people in the novel often feel like mouthpieces rather than complex, fully realized humans. Maybe that’s intentional. Maybe Brown is trying to show how people lose themselves inside of ideological echo chambers. But whatever the intention, the book felt flat. The ideas didn’t feel fresh, and because I already live with this reality every day, I ultimately found myself bored. I admire Brown’s precise ear and polished prose, as well as her clear-eyed perception of the sociopolitical zeitgeist. But as a novel, it didn’t work for me. I felt it was too short to allow the characters to really come to life, and too wrapped up in our present moment to offer any new perspectives. Brown perfectly captures the spirit of our times, but I couldn’t help feeling like I’d read all this before while simply scrolling online.

Here’s what I think: - this book is essentially a novella critiquing modern society from a variety of angles through a variety of characters - there is some warnings (understatement) against media conglomeration, and the people who are now in charge of the news we receive (the general public, Zuck, Tom as Craigslist somehow makes a cameo, the Google gaggle, etc.). - the antiestablishment, “woke” crew is definitely a primary force, but I couldn’t tell what the hell the takeaway was supposed to be Here’s what I know: - I didn’t understand this book very well and all the above could be wrong - I don’t care if it is because that’s how I read the book and it’s left me frustrated - That is probably my own fault, despite being up to date and savvy on the current political climate - Gold bars could = prison yards y’all - This was a very quick and easy read, but I feel depressed and like I want to erase most of that reading experience Who could I compare this to? What readers would like this book?? Maybe authors like Katie Kitamura, Colum McCann, Garth Greenwell, Catherine Lacey and books like Audition, The Hypocrite, Small Boat, Hunchback, and The Coin. Again I apologize if those aren’t “right”, but I’m trying here folks. This book was odd. Pssst come closer (whisper voice): probably actually 2.5 ⭐️ rounded up and that’s being generous. Over and out!

Natasha Brown has hit her stride. She is a master at saying a lot and using a little. This, her second novel, while not as slim as her first, packs more dynamite on each page that other books that work at the same subjects and take at least twice the length to do so.

Stylish and very much of the times, Universality packs a lot in its 150 pages. I’m a sucker for shifting POVs, stylistically different chapters, and reinterpretation of previously assumed plot points. Books like Lisa Haliday’s Asymmetry and Susan Choi’s Trust Exercise are well within the range of acceptable comparators. I thought that Brown’s observations were sharp and her prose very true to life and the current moment. So many hot button issues are touched on and it’s impressive how each argument is able to sit alongside the rest of the novel in tension with what has come before. There’s a little bit of this novel that’s too smart for me, but I felt drawn in by my inability to grasp the entirety of the story rather than off put. I’d seen a few community reviews noting that it is occasionally like fancy nonfiction. Fair! For me, it worked quite well. Thanks to Jon for putting me on to this one!

An anarchist group takes up residence on an unoccupied farm that was purchased by a wealthy man as a retreat for when society breaks down. The police arrived to break up their party only to discover a body and a missing bar of gold. The group preached Universality, a place where all were welcome. A young journalist writes an article about the incident, bringing momentary fame. Another woman writes a book preaching ‘no mo’ woke’, reflecting the zeitgeist of the times, believing that white men ae the victims of ‘woke capitalism.’ This British novel captures the shift from the activism of Occupy Wall Street and Black Lives Matter to the veering away from race as an issue, with another movement calling itself universality. The writer of No Mo Woke says she only writes “what we’re all thinking,” claiming her ideas universally relatable. Our world was chaotic. Even the so-called experts and their supercomputers couldn’t predict the trajectory of a bouncing pinball. from Universality by Natasha Brown The characters discuss big issues. Are we “sleepwalking into idiocy”? Should job applicant’s DNA be tested to determine their suitability for jobs? Is “class the new race”? Is it immoral to be a billionaire? Original, a short read dense with ideas, and a universally relatable commentary on contemporary society. Thanks to the publisher for a free book through NetGalley.

I'm not usually a big fan of literary fiction; I tend to stick more to "old white guy" genres like sci-fi and thrillers/spy stories, with a little fantasy and foreign detectives thrown in. But friend reviews made this look interesting — especially that of Cardi C — and hey, it's short...so thought I'd give it a shot. And darn it if wasn't a solid 4+ stars...right up until the (for me) disappointing end. I know a lot of readers note that there's no real plot per se, but I thought I sensed at least a direction here. As explained everywhere, the first section of the book is a long and well-done magazine article, and then the next two sections dive in and deconstruct that article; the earnest writer may not be quite that earnest, the nominal bad guy may not be quite that bad, and the master manipulator behind the whole thing...just talks politics, and race, and class, and DEI and just "Britain" in general... I need to think about this one a bit, and read more other reviews. But I thought/hoped the various and slowly-revealing threads tying the characters together would weave a more revealing picture. FINAL NOTE: A number of readers commented that the book is "very British," which didn't bother me. But I realized that what DOES set me off "classes;" I hate classes. People are people and should rise or sink on their own merits and actions. The whole British idea of "class" is just one step above the Indian caste system — and at least they have a religion to blame that on.

Thanks to Random House for the gifted copy If Perfection is a historical artifact about a generation and about a city*, then Universality is a snapshot of our current sociopolitical climate i.e. the hell we're living through. In sharp concise writing Brown picks apart class, race, privilege, and identity. And that's the key to the whole thing- language. How words are used to manipulate, shape, and control. We learn of an assault involving a solid gold bar, an anarchist collective, an illegal rave during covid lockdowns through an article that reads like something that would go viral. As the narrative changes, layers are peeled back to show us the fallout of the event and the voices affected by it. The journalist who wrote the article - how, and more importantly why, they may have gotten access to some key players. She's gotten a taste of the limelight (but it's really the money that's come along) and craves more. The banker, and owner of the gold bar, who has become a pariah in his world. The columnist, I would actually call a grifter, who stokes the right and who is rebranding in a way thanks to the article, promoting her stance against woke capitalism. You eventually start to realize how everyone sees themselves as the victim, how fiction is used to twist fact, how this book is having a laugh. I loved every second of this novel. I will freely admit that this is very much preaching to the choir at times, but Brown directs her eye, or more like her scalpel, to both the left and right to get at the truth. While this is definitely a social-critique on Britain specifically, it's sadly universal, especially with how the media attempts to control certain narratives or uses certain words to engage or appease. *I'm totally quoting myself here 🤣

“Words are your weapons, they’re your tools, your currency”. That aphorism echoes through every page of “Universality” by Natasha Brown, a novel that treats language not as something neutral but as a form of power; a book that shows how stories can be weaponised and how narrative exceeds the needs of a reportage and becomes capital. Set in modern Britain, late one night at a Covid lockdown rave in Yorkshire, a young man called Jake wields a solid gold bar, nearly killing an anarchist activist, Pegasus. At this point we meet Hannah, a burnt-out freelance book reviewer/journalist, whose life is transformed overnight when she investigates the assault. From this surreal moment begins a viral exposé that rocks British media. The novel unfolds in interlocking sections each shifting the perspective and reframing the truth. Part of the narrative kaleidoscope is Richard Spencer, a banker that owned the gold bar and the farm where the rave took place, and Miriam “Lenny” Leonard, an opportunist journalist/writer that happens to be Jake’s mom. This deliberately fractured structure is really inventive and subverts narrative reliability, inviting you, the reader, to question whose version of truths hold up. The story is extremely interesting and managed to keep me alert until the last page. Brown’s novel is a savage satire that reads as an intellectual puzzle keeping the experience immersive and exciting. Her prose is sharp, but it is the aspect of the book that I enjoyed the least; her language unfortunately does not vibe with me and in some occasions sounds pretentiously smart for no reason at all. Her characters though are beautifully crafted and instead of presenting heroes and villains, the author builds protagonists that are all morally compromised and multidimensional. Definitely an original read that for me is far better than her first book and I did enjoy a lot. This is a book about the power of language and the use of words as weapons or as capital. About marketable thoughts, luck and opportunism. The immense power of money, relentless capitalism and consumerism. The difficulty of opposing the current status. A story about the media scene and spectacles. Click bait culture and woke culture. About political activism, protests, the power of people and the fight for a better world. The need to build solutions. About communal life, anarchism and the idea of opting out of the system. It is also a book about narrative control and reliability. Objective articles and subjective storytelling layered with motive and bias. The need of rationality in journalism and libels written on the pursuit of a good story. A story about race and racism, class and classism. Privilege, equality and inclusion. People that make it and others that fade away. How class, race and outrage perform for the audience. The idea of “privileged minorities”. Mostly though, this is a book about social fragmentation and the illusion of universality. Polarised identity politics and cheap populism. The idea that the show must go on and the ridiculous truth that everyone is trying to manipulate everyone. This is a 4-4.5/5 for me! Why should you read “Universality”? Because, in the era of viral journalism, it will make you question how stories are constructed and how truth and misinformation is spread. Because it will make you wonder whether moral values and journalism can ever go hand in hand. Because it will make you reflect on the idea of using our genetic imprint to predict the likelihood of various life outcomes. Because it will make you realise how immoral can be possessing extreme wealth while other people live under poverty. Because it will make you understand that money can ruin your life, literally and metaphorically. Because it will make you think about the possibility that high paid jobs might be given to people not based on qualifications but on the basis of woke politics. Favorite quotes: “Class is the new race”.
Like Trust by Hernan Diaz, but colder, sharper, and British. Each version of the truth neatly sliced by class, privilege, and self-interest.

Quite disjointed, as someone who’s grown up working class in south east england I’m a little confused. I feel like it throws so many ideas at the reader and fails to connect them in any meaningful way, rather shoves them down your throat and expects you to find a way to digest them on your own. Perhaps a longer book and a lighter hand would have improved it.
british ppl write about class in such a characteristic way…. i liked the various forms and perspective shifts but wish it was a bit longer!

This book is an excellent conversation starter and a compelling read. I did feel that a lot of problematic ideas were left unchallenged (which is fine if you are aware of the counterarguments already, but not if you aren't) and that it could have done with a bit more meat. That being said, this is a provocative and shape shifting narrative that spirals out in an exploration of the zeitgeist and capitalist system. Well worth reading if you like social commentary in your contemporary fiction.
Entertaining and clever. Punching in all directions! I really enjoyed it.

Having enjoyed Natasha Brown’s debut , Assembly, I was eager to read her second novel, Universality. The book opens as a long form article about a man who murders someone with a bar of gold. It’s written as an investigative piece with interviews, profiles etc. Then the novel evolves into a criticism on the manipulative properties of media: whether a journalist should seek the truth or create readership sales or the damaging effects media can cause, especially when half truths are told. This is achieved by the novel focusing on the journalist and various people who were mentioned in the article. For its brevity, Universality is a literary onion - full of layers that reveal a core. As satires go, it’s a great one. Also as experimental literature, it’s pretty accessible so highest recommendations here.

Honesty is about to happen, right here; get ready for it. Sometimes you don't know what to say about a book. I mean, what DO you say when you slam the book closed and there's no "that was amazing" exclaimed? Do you shout, "That was mediocre!" I doubt most of us do such a thing. The writing in Universality was well-crafted, decent, clever, and witty. The author has a gift for stringing words together into cohesive sentences that are pleasing to read. But the story didn't resonate with me. For me personally, I'm not one to discuss politics and capitalism. Never have been. In reading more world literature this year, my horizons have broadened significantly, but I still don't think I will ever enjoy politics. There are three reasons for which my disdain for the topic can probably be attributed. One, my parents showed no interest in what went on in the world outside of their tiny bubble—other than to voice their disdain when someone who was not a conservative Christian Republican was in office (thankfully my apple fell far from the tree in regard to this viewpoint). It's extremely difficult growing up in a family knowing that what you believe and what you SHOULD have been taught is completely different from everyone who is supposed to love you. I'm not just talking about politics here. I know many of us have to face this, but it doesn't make it any less challenging. Two, I witnessed my ex-husband and his older brother come to blows over politics during a NYE gathering when I was in my mid-twenties. I literally had to physically position myself between two GIANT MEN (6'7" and 6'4", respectively). I'm only 5'2". It was quite the sight. Visualize it if you are so inclined. And three, I don't like conflict. I really just want everyone to get along, and I know that this is not how the world works, but one can hope, no? Comedic anecdotes aside, I could appreciate the cleverness of the experimental structure of the novel. I wouldn't read this again, but I still would recommend it to anyone who enjoys such books, as the talent of the author is unmistakable. I'm going to go relax now; talking about politics gives me anxiety, and I really don't have anything else to say about this book. The end. 10/5/25 8/22/25 I think I'm at a 3.5 star on this. I enjoyed the experimental nature of the narrative. I am really not very big into politics, so I will admit some of this went over my head. I did learn some things and I could appreciate the concepts and ideas presented. Lenny is a bad-ass b*tch and I didn't know whether to love her, hate her, strangle her, or hug her. I guess that makes for one appealing character and a down to earth driving force that propelled this narrative forward. "I'm fighting for you."

𝘐 𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘶𝘨𝘭𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘢 𝘭𝘰𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘢𝘨𝘰.” I regret to report that I did this book injustice with my poor reading. I failed to see that the book is a clear look at rhetoric. What are we actually saying? What do we actually mean to each other? Through multiple points of view that front language based on different social class, I am reminded of the great uncomfortable dinner scene in the book, but also all the ones I went through myself. Having been asked and judged by my schooling, my major, my upbringing it was always difficult to code-switch, vague navigations to assume positions where I kept my place at tables, but went home with so much shame and embarrassment with how little net worth I had to my name. And so it happened again. This book, outside of further themes on identity politics and the rhetoric used around social issues, I am once again at the uncomfortable dinner table. I am left with little to say because I examined the book as a mirror, seeing too much of my uncomfortable self. I failed to look at the book as a window. I am left to say that I do no have the vocabulary or maturity to talk about this novella that packs a punch in its economy and form. It’s a timely novella, lively with the complications of the current cultural climate. Buzz words are played, holding meaning and then without as the points of view change, as the social classes are observed, and, ultimately, how we present ourselves at the face of language.

I can’t think of much to say about this book which generally means it wasn’t great nor was it bad. It was fine. It explores a lot of the same themes as Lambert’s May Our Joy Endure (one of my favorites of the year)—wealth, woke/cancel culture, victimhood, politics, capitalism, etc.—but whereas Lambert’s story soared, thrilling me with its innovative prose and the depths of its nuance, Universality felt a bit unsubstantial, unexciting, and could have benefitted from more multidimensional characters. While it doesn’t feel completely fair to judge this by comparing it to another novel, reading doesn’t exist in a vacuum. It is what it is. I’ve heard good things about Assembly, so I’ll still probably pick that up at some point. As for this one, I’m neutral. Unless more people start calling it the book of 2025, in which case, I may have to turn into a hater because—as the kids say—BFFR :-)

Ok first off, that last scene. Holy shit. One of the most claustrophobic, fascinating, and outright thrilling passages I’ve read in quite a while. This is a great little novel that delivers on an equally great and ambitious conceit. It’s full of complex, unlikeable, frustrating characters (which is the best sort of cast, in my opinion) whom Brown uses to act out the uneasy political and social sphere of contemporary Britain. Scene for scene, it’s an incredibly entertaining work, with plenty of biting commentary to return to once the initial shock of Brown’s taut narratives and character studies recedes. A book that encapsulates a sociopolitical moment as electrifyingly as works like Such A Fun Age, Luster, and Brown’s own novella from a few years ago, Assembly.
Brilliant!

Wow! I haven't been this excited by a recent release since I can remember. I'll try and put some coherent immediate thoughts down but realistically this review will likely need some space because I loved this book so much it will need to settle in. Without discussing plot, which is part of the joy of the book, this is really about VOICE. Narrative voice, messaging, target demographics, communication strategy, the real craft of writing. Writing is not just the structure of a piece and the choice of words, but the intuition of when to place it and where. And how to manipulate. Wow what an incredible book. This ticks all the boxes: it's a pandemic novel, it's a Brexit novel, it's an immigration novel, it's about the commodification of race and class and communication. Oh and it's a novel of 2025. Absolutely. I've only read 3 of the Booker longlist so far but far away this is my pick to win. It needs to get shortlisted at the very least. WOW.
