Longlisted for the 2022 International Booker Prize . Norman Erickson Pasaribu, a queer Indonesian writer, introduces the reader to a refreshing contemporary voice with ‘Happy Stories, Mostly’. A collection of short stories varied in length, these are cerebral depictions of being queer and young in Indonesia - the awkwardness, sense of dissociation, and questioning of identity and self preservation are laid bare in sharp prose. As a younger reader, I thoroughly enjoyed ‘Happy Stories, Mostly’, Pasaribu writes candidly and shows his skill as a poet turned fiction writer in their 20s, who will likely make the shortlist for the International Booker Prize this year.

Fantastic book of short stories from a queer Indonesian poet and author. “This world is the closed door. It is a barrier. And at the same time it is the way through. Two prisoners whose cells adjoin communicate with each other by knocking on the wall. The wall is the thing which separates them but it is also their means of communication. It is the same with us and God. Every separation is a link.” -Simone Weil Absolutely stunning quote ^^^ & I loved the call back later on in the story. “The high, thick wall surrounding this city wasn’t built to protect its residents – it was built to separate. Just try knocking on it, you won’t hear anything on the other side. “When a wall is too thick, Uncle, it ceases to become a means of communication.”

I rarely read short stories but this book made me do it. I don't know how to describe this book, but it feels surreal and real at the same time. This is the first Norman's book that I read, but I'm already in love with how he wrote the narrations: smart, beautiful, and enticing. The intersections between Bataknese, Catholic, and Queer identities made up the characters and impacted the stories here. One thing I noticed is that (almost?) all the main character is cis-hetero. I don't know what the author intended to convey here (does he try to re-create the reality faced by queer people here?), but damn it gave so much tragedy and sadness to the story. the way that those queer people too are also our friends, family, and even stranger, and they can leave an impact on our life. My favorite stories are: Siapa Namamu, Sandra?, Divisi Doa Tak Berjawab, dan Keturunan Kita Akan Sebanyak Awan di Angkasa (honorable mention: Pupil Matanya Cokelat Gelap Hampir Hitam, wow this one made me gasp at the end of the story)

A collection of short stories about life and relationships rooted in Queer, Batak, and Christian culture. The stories were heartfelt, poignant, and very true to the title of the book. My absolute favorite story was A Young Poet's Guide to Surviving a Broken Heart, the storytelling, the pacing, the rhythm was just perfection. But, I also really enjoyed Enkidu Comes Knocking on New Year's Eve, The True Story of the Story of the Giant, Welcome to the Department of Unanswered Prayers, Ad maiorem de gloriam, and Her Story.

"Hampir, the Indonesian for almost, only a letter away from 'vampir' - the bloodsucking demon. what does it mean to be happy? Also, what does it mean to be almost happy? To almost get in, to be almost accepted, to be almost there, but, at the same time, to be not there/accepted/in" Happy Stories, Mostly (now longlisted for the 2022 International Booker Prize and the Republic of Consciousness Prize) is a collection of 12 short stories (translated from Indonesian to English by Tiffany Tsao) blending different genres ranging from science fiction, experimental, dystopian, folklore, and metafiction. The main theme for these stories centered around LGBTQ issues, in particular, heteronormativity, in which Pasaribu seeks to explore the counterbalance between heterosexuality as the preferred norm and homosexuality as the "outcast", the "almost" (or the "hampir"), from the Asian perspective (or rather, the Indonesian perspective). Hovering around this main theme, Pasaribu inculcated various side themes such as the aftermaths of post-colonialism, the clash between religious dogmas in Indonesia (in particular Christianity vs Islam) as well as certain satirical comments on Indonesia's state and governance: "Indonesians - by which I mean, we - don't have time to make such lists or become such people. Too many problems. Too many news headlines: forced evictions, fake vaccines, anti-communist riots"; "If you ask me, is any nation - especially a postcolonial one - ever not at a crossroads? Even more so if you're poor". My favourite story would definitely be "The True Story of the Story of the Giant" and I believe this story is the longest one in this collection. The narrator of this story, a heterosexual, met Tunggul (a homosexual who suppressed his own sexuality) at university and the link between these 2 would be the folklore involving Parulian (a giant during the Dutch colonial times). After confronting his love for the narrator and being rejected by the narrator, there is a change in Tunggul's mannerisms and Tunggul eventually committed suicide. Aiming to complete Tunggul's thesis, the narrator took up the quest to research about Parulian and the Batak War and due to the lack of materials, the narrator decided to write a fictional story about Parulian as "in this version, we lived beyond the reach of Europe's long wooden arm". My other favourites would be "Metaxu: Jakarta 2038" (set in the near future where human labor is hardly needed and the characters are recounting the pasts of the old Jakarta), "So What’s Your Name, Sandra" (a mother's visit to Mỹ Sơn after her son committed suicide due to the mother's rejection of his sexuality), "Welcome to the department of unanswered prayers" (a satirical piece of work set in a bureaucratic afterlife). Pasaribu's writing is charming, emotional, and poetic. These stories, taken as a whole, portrayed a beautiful quest for love and acceptance for LGBTQs in this cruel world. It is a calling or a challenge against conformity, heteronormativity, and discrimination. I quote Pasaribu's interview with Tiffany: "We queer are always thrown to the hampir, to the almost, and there the idea of happiness turns into the vampir". A strong 4.5/5 star rating from me. Another worthy longlistee for the 2022 International Booker Prize.
so sad & gay, i loved it so much i really enjoyed the conversation between the author & translator at the end !!

Translated from Indonesian, Happy Stories, Mostly consists of 12 short stories that are centred around the queer community, particularly the topic of heteronormativity. Where the hetero is chosen as the normal ones, while the queer has to live in the ‘mostly’, hanging on to whatever they have. The stories range from 1 page to over 20+ pages. I found the longer stories are more impactful than shorter ones. The stories also incorporate the climate of political changes in Indonesia, folklores and traditions of the Bataks (an ethnic group living in North Sumatra). Some are set in modern contemporary, the others are set in a surreal world. The stories also touch deeply on Christianity, where people who are drunk on traditional customs neglect the aspect of humanity. At times, it felt like an autobiography where Norman pours out his internal struggles living as a gay with his faith. While I appreciate the themes and topics discussed, some stories are simply plain, or too brief. Rating: 3.5 stars

"Queer stories with a happy narrative? that's new (at least to me)," was my initial thought before reading. Only later did we find out that Norman had stated clearly in the title that most of them were "Hampir Seluruhnya". Despite having limited understanding of Batak, Catholicism, or various queer references (thanks Google) nor having ever lived in Bekasi, this book still speaks very clearly to me. Its cruel and saddening yet hopeful and dreamy characters are layered meticulously. I am laughing at the character laughing about their own miseries, but later on I remembered that some other days I encountered relatively the same scenario. This being Norman's first work that I read only makes me long for Norman's other writings.

I don't think this is technically perfect, no short story collection ever is, but I have to give this five stars because so many stories worked so well for me thematically, and I just loved Pasaribu's writing style, brilliantly translated by Tiffany Tsao. This was my first peek into Indonesian culture through literature, and to have it be a queer-centric one was fascinating. Happy Stories, Mostly is often very dark, sometimes quite sad and emotional, and where it really hit home for me was where queer identities and dynamics within families and relationships were at a crossroads with religion and society, and I loved the nods and critiques to Dutch colonization throughout as well. Just a very well done, well written little book that I absolutely adored.

Me on Nov 6, 2020: A Stacey Abrams novel? It could be the word “vote” for 80,000 words and it gets five stars from me. Me in March 2021 when I read the book: It turns out Stacey Abrams can write a DAMN good legal/medical thriller. This is a story about a supreme court with a swing vote, a judge in a coma, and a law clerk-turned legal guardian who is left to solve a mystery that will change the country’s future. This is a brilliant and brainy thriller that involves genetic bioengineering, political prowess, and a lot of chess. But it’s got a story that won’t quit and some awesome characters. Abrams can be a bit verbose at times, but once you get into the groove it’s hard to stop. Thank you to Doubleday books for my advance copy!

First and foremost, we should appreciate how talented this woman is. In the midst of helping to sway a national election and two senator races, Stacey Abrams wrote and edited a nearly 400-page thriller. And not just a boilerplate thriller, either, but one replete with genetics, chess theories, Supreme Court operating procedures, company mergers, political hierarchies, and a bunch of other moments of textured research I am surely forgetting. Some people are too talented-- can't she share some of her skillset with others? We start out with a rollicking first chapter, laying the ground for a complex thriller, posing several juicy questions to chomp into. The irascible Justice Howard Wynn leaves Avery Keene as his power of attorney, a controversial decision that leads Avery on a John Grisham-esque legal goose chase. Luckily for us, Abrams is a much better writer than Grisham. Unfortunately, the supposed strengths of this book are also, to me, what is holding it back. Every character speaks in an erudite, polished manner, indistinguishable from one another. No character has the quirks, complexities, and contradictions that would make them memorable. This novel feels like it has been through 1,000 drafts, every rough edge sanded down, every unique phrase stricken and replaced with academic verbiage. Avery Keene, the protagonist, is likeable enough, a young woman in the mold of "people keep underestimating me, I'll show them!" However, she had little personality, and is the type of character I’m liable to completely forget as soon as I put the book down. The best character, Justice Wynn, spends almost the entire book in a coma. We fall into a series of hurried, whispered conversations in the middle of the novel, exchanging information in a repetitive manner. This continues towards the end of the book, as the convoluted plot is explained by various characters stepping into the scene and explaining it for us, like a Scooby Doo ending, over and over again. I had largely lost interest by then because I didn’t care about the characters, although like any reader I wanted to grasp the mystery. The complex web of dark forces that conspired ultimately felt stilted, Abrams jamming every element together in a last-ditch effort to impress us. Abrams is very smart and painstaking in her research, but those two attributes alone do not make a great novel. Stop making fertilizer bombs in your basement and listen to full pods here.

I wanted to like this more than I did, but it's just not very exciting. There are a million characters to keep track of, and the third person omniscient POV makes for some jarring narration (there are occasionally passages where we jump into a character's POV for one paragraph or a few sentences before switching again). That, in conjunction with an abundance of unnecessary detail and some truly bizarre syntax and diction that read like Abrams wrote with a thesaurus tab open on her browser, make for a not-entirely-enjoyable reading experience. There are some really fun elements, like the chess theme, but not enough for this to rise above "pretty good, I guess?"
An engaging and well written political conspiracy thriller with a President who is rotten to the core. Hard to believe really.

Stacie, Stacie, what have you done? I love you, love all the work you do to make my country better, and to make my country honest. But this book is a dump. Abrams has written many romance novels under a pseudonym, and she has proven she can write. However, she needed to hire a professional editor for this novel. It is long, it drags, it has extraneous information, it has too many people of which to keep track, and too many law enforcement people of which to keep track. The average person does not know the difference between the FBI, the CIA and the President's personal staff. The idea was good - have legal aide to a Supreme Court Justice step in to have his power of attorney while he is unconscious. But the whole story was just convoluted. I was bored, often considered dropping the book but I love her so much, I kept going. It was not worth it - and we had to tag on a little romance at the end. Also, there is a lot of chess knowledge here - I don't know a John Doe move from an Albert White move; neither do I know the famous games in the past so I just skipped over the pages and pages of chess stuff. It did not matter except for finding clues, of which there were too many. I will only read another Abrams novel if I know there has been a real editor. This book is a mess and not worth the time I spent with it. Love you, Stacey and I will keep sending you money when you ask. peace, janz

Stacey Abrams is a force to contend with. Brilliant, visionary and dedicated to justice, she shines like a brilliant star. This being her debut novel, I assumed her intelligence and political background would play roles, but never fathomed she'd craft a high velocity political crime mystery such as this. Avery Keene is a young, dedicated law clerk to Supreme Court Justice Howard Wynn, the swing vote on countless cases for decades. When he's rushed to the hospital in a coma, the reader is immersed into a labyrinth akin to a Sherlock Holmes plot, filled with ciphers, oddball clues and 'chess moves'. As the judge lies in a coma, Avery learns he's authorized her to be his legal guardian complete with Power of Attorney. Her suitability for this position is questioned by Chief Justice Roseborough as well as the President, though Avery is steadfast. The subplot is focused on an East Indian genetics research firm seeking to merge with an American pharma company with the goal of bringing life changing cures to the world. Behind the scenes President Stokes, a power hungry, deceitful type carries out a plan to block the merger using Avery as one of the pawns. As the reader immerses into the storyworld, Avery partners with Jared, Wynn's estranged son and Noah, Wynn's estate attorney who battle underhanded FBI and DHS agents who are part of President's plot. Littered with crime, deception and chess references, the jigsaw puzzle gains complexity with each chapter. The combination of the author's research and ability to engage the reader bears similarity to Dan Brown, John Grisham and Conan Doyle due to pacing, character depth and plot twists. In addition she demonstrates mastery of momentum which continually builds toward the end. In the Acknowledgements section, she pays tribute to a jurist and two of her sisters of which one is a judge, the other an epidemiologist. Being a progressive politician who's fight for democracy is without compare, its easy to see a comparison of President Stokes to Donald Trump since they both manipulate, cajole and deceive. Put simply, this is well crafted story that will appeal to anyone who appreciates characters, plot and pacing. As someone who rarely hands out 5 star ratings, I'm eager to read her latest.

3.5 stars - This was a really fun and effective political thriller. Things went a little off the rails in the last third, but as a whole, this is a thought provoking and entertaining take on a political mystery thriller with a splash of medical ethics thrown in

I wrote this review a year ago on my Facebook page (2022). And I want it known I am forever grateful to this woman for all she has done for her state of Georgia. My review: First and foremost, we should appreciate how talented this woman is. In the midst of helping to sway a national election and two senator races, Stacey Abrams wrote a nearly 400-page thriller. And not just a boilerplate thriller, either, but one replete with genetics, chess theories, Supreme Court operating procedures, company mergers, political hierarchies, and a bunch of other moments of textured research I am surely forgetting. This after all, is a big book. Unfortunately, the supposed strengths of this book are also, to me, what is holding it back. There is so much the reader can appreciate, but it was tough (for me) to get through. It is dense with unnecessary knowledge, which I guess showcases how smart Stacey Abrams is but does not necessarily make for a good read. She included every detail but a compelling story in this one. We fall into a series of hurried, whispered conversations in the middle of the novel, exchanging information in a repetitive manner. This continues towards the end of the book, as the convoluted plot is explained by various characters stepping into the scene to tell us what happened and why. Okay, mystery explained. I had largely lost interest by then because I didn’t care about the characters, although like any reader I wanted to grasp the mystery. The complex web of dark forces that conspired ultimately felt stilted. Was Abrams jamming every element together in a last-ditch effort to impress us readers? Abrams is very smart and painstaking in her research, but those two attributes alone, to me, do not make a great novel. I really, really wanted to like this one.

I expected a lot from this, and I struggled. It was a slow start, which usually doesn't seem to draw me in, and the political jargon lost me pretty quickly after that. I read a lot of legal thrillers so was able to follow most of the Supreme Court scenes, but by then I was pretty sure I had no idea what was going on! As this was the audiobook, I would like to try the ebook as I think the quality of the audio also affected my experience.

While Justice Sleeps is filled with political machinations and intrigue that kept me turning pages and finishing the book faster than I wanted. Unsurprisingly, Abrams created a strong female character that smartly navigates the dangers of political ambitions and decisions that are made in the background by people who aren't as out front, but are arguably more dangerous than the political figureheads that they aim to influence and control. I won't go into plot details since the book's summary is more than enough information, but I will add that Abrams' atmospheric writing makes Washington D.C. feel real and tangible even to readers like myself that aren't intimately familiar with its streets, places, and people. Her ability to make me vividly imagine what the places look and feel like kept me happily engaged for the entire story. All in all While Justice Sleeps is a political thriller authentically written by an author with impeccable political chops. I am thrilled that I was able to read an ARC and I look forward to whatever Abrams gives us next. I received an ARC from the publisher in exchange for an honest review. While Justice Sleeps is a gripping, complexly plotted novel set within the halls of the U.S. Supreme Court and was penned by Stacey Abrams, former member of the Georgia House of Representatives and fervent voting activist; this is her new legal thriller. Avery Keene, a brilliant young law clerk for the legendary Justice Howard Wynn, is doing her best to hold her life together--excelling in an arduous job with the court while also dealing with a troubled family. When the shocking news breaks that Justice Wynn--the cantankerous swing vote on many current high-profile cases coming before the Supreme Court in Washington--has slipped into a coma, Avery's life turns upside down. She is immediately notified that Justice Wynn has left instructions for her to serve as his legal guardian and she will have power of attorney over all of his affairs; naturally, this both antagonises and upsets Wynn’s wife and son. Plunged into an explosive role she never anticipated, Avery finds that Justice Wynn had been secretly researching one of the most controversial cases before the court--a contentious proposed merger between an American biotech company known as American GenWorks and an Indian genetics firm, Avtar, which promises to unleash breathtaking results in the medical field. She also discovers that Wynn suspected a dangerously related conspiracy that infiltrates the highest power corridors of Washington. As political wrangling ensues in Washington to potentially replace the ailing judge, who is apparently suffering from Boursin’s Syndrome and whose life and survival Avery controls, she begins to unravel a carefully constructed, chesslike sequence of clues left behind by the wily Wynn. She comes to see that Wynn had a much more personal stake in the controversial case and realises his complex puzzle will lead her directly into harm's way in order to find the truth. This is a riveting and completely enthralling legal thriller with taut plotting and corrupt politicians and lawyers at the centre of it all. Abrams is a lawyer who studied at Yale hence this is full of gritty realism and authentic depictions of the courts. It moves at a rapid-fire pace, gets the heart-thumping and twisty surprises are in abundance as Abrams cleverly and devilishly pulls you this way then that. Palpable suspense, fluid prose and exhilarating excitement are enough to keep you feverishly turning the pages. A high-octane thriller jammed with legal intrigue, While Justice Sleeps is multilayered and occasionally convoluted, ending in a terrific set-piece legal showdown between Keene and those ranged against her. A cunningly crafted, sophisticated novel, layered with myriad twists and a vibrant cast of characters, and drawing on her astute inside knowledge of the court and political landscape, Abrams shows herself to be not only a force for good in politics and voter fairness but also a major new talent in suspense fiction. Highly recommended.

I'm not the biggest fan of political thrillers but my goodness, Stacey Abrams is an incredible writer (along with being an incredible human being and activist) and to my surprise, I ended up loving this book. The plot: While Justice Sleeps tells the story of Avery Keene, a brilliant clerk to larger-than-life Judge Howard Wynn. Judge Wynn is both loathed and admired in the political world because he's usually the deciding vote in important Supreme Court Cases. When he slips into a coma, to the surprise of everyone, he appoints Avery as his legal guardian and power of attorney. As the media, the FBI, and even the White House are breathing down her neck, she uncovers a series of clues that the judge left behind and what she discovers will change the country forever. I really want someone to adapt the Avery Keene series; maybe AppleTV since they've really been in their political thriller bag. Avery was a fabulous heroine: intelligent, determined yet still vulnerable and loyal (almost to a fault). As a reader, I felt terrible for her when the world was against her and breathed a sigh of relief when she was able to find people who were truly in her corner. Additionally, as a romance reader, I rarely get invested in romantic subplots in other genres, but you can tell that Abrams is a romance reader/writer because the relationship between Avery and Judge Wynn's son Jared was natural, subtle and more importantly, it didn't take away from the rest of the story. It also made sense for the characters. There's nothing more annoying than when an author who clearly doesn't like or respect romance just sticks a random romantic subplot for "reasons." EVERYBODY SAY THANK YOU STACEY ABRAMS, FOR A LOT OF THINGS, BUT ALSO FOR WRITING A GOOD ROMANTIC SUPLOT IN A POLITICAL THRILLER.

As if the last week wasn’t amazing enough, I received an advanced copy of Stacey Abram’s upcoming release on Inauguration Day. To say that I was SCREAMING would be an understatement. This is a book that I have been anticipating from a woman that can literally do anything. Stacey Abrams is the kind of inspiration I will carry with me for a lifetime. From celebrated national leader to best-selling author — she makes us all believe we really can do anything. Thank you, for all that you’ve done and now for this book. In While Justice Sleeps, Abrams brings us an intricately weaved thriller set within the walls of the U.S. Supreme Court. A plot rich, tangled story that literally had me on the edge of my seat. The story centers around legendary Supreme Court Justice Howard Wynn and a sudden turn of events which leaves his law clerk, Avery Keene, in the center of it all. This was a fast-paced book that gave me a lot more than what was expected, and I mean this in the best way possible. As a protagonist, Avery is intriguing and also relatable. Abrams has an innate ability to draw a reader into a character’s feelings even if the they are a relatively private. I found this style of writing to be extremely organic and engrossing. With each twist and turn, Avery’s feelings were palpable and also realistic. There were moments that I had to remind myself that this was fiction. When I say there was a little bit of everything - I mean it. Whether it be the intricacies of a child-parent relationship, loyalties to colleagues, attraction, court room drama, murder, attraction, even chess references...it was ALL there. The same kind of style flowed with the setting as well. A true D.C. experience with every page turned. I found myself delighted while imagining the inside of the Oval Office, as well as the genuine familiarity of a late night meet-up at Kramer’s. In addition, there was a big connection to India which I was NOT expecting. As a Desi myself, I was elated about this surprise that wasn’t mentioned in any synopsis or press release that I had read. Oh Stacey Abrams, you knew exactly what this reader was looking for! This book was absolutely PERFECT for the moment. It gives you an ultimate thriller with a plethora of dimensions and human emotion at the center of it all. I guarantee you will be thinking about it long after you read the last page. Thank you @doubledaybooks, @penguinrandomhouse, @netgalley, and @staceyabrams for the opportunity to read and review this title to be released on May 11th, 2021 ⚖️🇺🇸

A literary roller coaster with social insight With all the talk about landmark Supreme Court decisions in jeopardy, retirements, nominations and their consequences, Stacey Abrams’ new legal thriller While Justice Sleeps is not so much ripped from the headlines as it is the stuff of our most vivid nightmares. When cantankerous Supreme Court justice Howard Wynn slips into a coma, it propels the court into limbo, causing a constitutional crisis with his law clerk at the center of a political storm. Abrams knows this terrain—legal, social, and political—inside and out. With that expertise, the issues at the center of the story are drawn with precision and insight, but her characters are the book’s greatest strength ... The story is anchored by two indelible outsiders who have little in common save the institution for which both work and their prickly personas. Stacey Abrams’s thriller is an intricate one with a diverse supporting cast of allies and adversaries and a Russian nesting doll of legal maneuvering, politics and technological intrigue. Much of it is riveting. There are also subplots and clever details strewn like Easter eggs throughout. Somewhere in the middle, the plot starts to feel overstuffed, and the myriad of moving parts slow forward momentum. But...there’s something deliciously rewarding about a thriller that realistically and unflinchingly reckons with how a young Black woman like Avery Keene gets treated when she answers the call to serve. If you are a political junkie like myself, the name Stacey Abrams may sound familiar. Serving in the Georgia House of Representatives from 2007 to 2017, Abrams ran for governor of that state in 2018, losing to Republican Brian Kemp, who has since been accused of blatant voter suppression in that election. She would have been the first African-American female governor, ever. She’s not hurting, though. Abrams has made a name for herself as a vocal advocate of voting rights, having published two nonfiction books about voting and life in politics in general. Under a pseudonym, Abrams is also a well-known author of eight historical romances. Her latest novel “While Justice Sleeps” is her first novel published under her own name. “WJS” is a taut, fast-paced legal thriller in the same vein as the works of John Grisham or Brad Meltzer. She touches on some hot-button political issues throughout: genetic engineering, corruption within the pharmaceutical industry, presidential abuse of power. Her protagonist is Avery Keene, a feisty young law clerk who works for Supreme Court Justice Howard Wynn, a man known as much for his grumpiness as he is for his legal brilliance. He is the swing vote on a recent case involving a merger between an American biotech company and an Indian genetics company. While the merger could mean jobs and wealth for both countries, as well as promising leaps in the medical field, U.S. President Brandon Stokes is dead-set against it, ostensibly on moral grounds. Before he is able to make any ruling, however, Wynn inexplicably goes into a coma. Keene, like everyone in her office, is shocked. On top of the tragic news, Keene is immediately notified that Wynn, at the last minute, made Keene his power of attorney, to the chagrin of Wynn’s current trophy wife and his son from his first marriage. The news quickly attracts the attention of President Stokes, Homeland Security, the FBI, and the worldwide media. Keene—-a workaholic with no social life, a crackhead mother, and bills to pay—-is suddenly put in the national spotlight in the middle of one of the most important political issues of the day. It is, apparently, the Cuban Missile Crisis of business mergers. Thankfully, Keene is blessed with an indomitable spirit and an eidetic memory, two things that Justice Wynn saw in her that led to his decision making her his POA. When a toxicology report suggests that Wynn was purposefully put into a coma, Keene is forced to play detective. It’s a race against time as someone way above her pay grade is killing anyone who might know something, and it’s only a matter of time before they go after her. Abrams’s experience in politics and the law definitely elevates this book from what could have been a mere dime store potboiler. It is an edge-of-the-seat thriller that takes the reader on an exciting, and terrifying, journey through the deepest, darkest levels of government and the dark money backers that runs it.

The premise was intriguing and the characters well drawn. Unfortunately, for me, the pace for the first 160 pages was extremely slow. There was too much description without enough action. Still, the reader needed to pay attention and plod through because the information in those pages set the stage for the rapid escalation of the plot in the following pages. Despite the rapid escalation, though, there was still too much extraneous information that was frustrating to wade through. Many times I just read the leading few sentences of the paragraph. While Jared’s estranged relationship with his father was given a thorough context, the complicated relationship between Avery and her mother was not. It led me to question that, given the many years Rita’s drug addiction weighed so heavily on Avery’s life, the many lapses breaking Avery’s heart and putting her in debt to finance Rita’s number of rehabs and the jeopardy to Avery’s career if her mother’s sordid life were to be known in Supreme Court circles - what was the basis of Avery’s enduring strong bond with her mother ? There was so much other narrative but this crucial relationship was not given depth. I suppose we were to assume that Rita was an exemplary mother before the death of Avery’s father. But given the immense sacrifices Avery made for her mother, the reader needed some concrete examples in order to believe Avery’s devotion. This book had such promise with its unique plot and strong characters. It could easily have been 5 stars with more adept editing. Even so, there’s enough compelling material, in the hands of a top notch screenwriter and discerning director, to make a blockbuster movie.
Very entertaining for a legal thriller.

“Tell her…tell her to look to the East for answers. Look to the river. In between. Look in the square. Lask. Bauer. Forgive me.” (p. 12) Not much to work from – especially as the speaker, a Supreme Court justice, often appeared paranoid and erratic and was probably experiencing early dementia. Nonetheless, Avery Court, Justice Wynn's law clerk, valiantly and rapidly worked to save him, the US government, and the world. (I may be speaking in hyperbole, but not too much so.) Legal thrillers are not my favorite genre, as they dip their toes too deeply into paranoia. In While Justice Sleeps, for example, the bad guys manufacture a virus to kill an ethnic group with research illegally funded by the US government – while other bad guys were killing people left and right for giving them slant eye (more hyperbole, but legal thrillers tend toward the hyper-dramatic. I hope this is overly dramatic rather true.). Still, Stacey Abrams is a favorite of many of us in the US: a politician in Georgia, lawyer, and voting rights activist. She is someone to watch, both on the political front and in her writing. Although her story does not entirely make sense (her newfound friends can drop everything to help her???), logic is not necessary in some genres. I do like Abram's comments about the law. Some quotes: “Knowing the law isn’t about the school. It’s about the mind. The heart. About understanding what the law intends as much as reading beneath what it says. Knowing how to find one’s way to the truth.” (p. 10) "Chief, I haven’t done anything wrong,” she repeated shakily. Yet she—as much as the others in the room—understood the tenuous connection between crime and punishment. The allegation was often more than sufficient. Innocent until proven guilty was an urban myth. (p. 133) Under Stokes, the common touch had supplanted common sense in droves, driven by a mellifluous gift of charm. (p. 308). Abrams clearly indicates that this is Ms. Keene's "debut," especially good news for those of you who enjoy legal thrillers. (Good news for me, too.)

Stacey Abrams is someone I really admire, and when I saw she had written a thriller, I had to read it. I was not disappointed at all, and would highly recommend it – whatever your politics. I had sort of expected it to be anti-Republican, but it was not overtly so. President Stokes was definitely not modelled on Trump – and indeed, it took me a lot of the book to work out whether he was a bad guy or not. There was obviously something suspect going on – but whether or not it was a matter of genuine national security, whether the FBI, CIA, Homeland Security …. were involved, trying to stop terrorists (if so, which terrorists?), playing party politics – or something altogether more sinister – remained to be seen. In the tradition of all top-class thrillers, I was kept guessing. The hero, Avery Keene, was a young female legal clerk, who was thrown into an unholy mess when the Supreme Court judge she worked for fell into a coma, and named her as holding his power of attorney – not his son, not his estranged wife, not another judge. Why? There is a very important (again why?) ruling coming up for the Supreme Court, where Justice Howard Wynn is expected to cast the deciding vote. If he dies – another judge can be appointed. But so long he is in a coma, nothing can be done. By the way, he has an incurable disease, which makes it likely he will not come out of the coma. Avery does not only have the ethical (turn off life-support or not) and politics of the situation to deal with, but family issues too. Her mother is a junkie, always looking for money to feed her habit. And then people connected to Avery and Justice Wynn go missing and/or die. Like Avery, the reader is left floundering in the dark. Justice Wynn is not a sympathetic character. He expects everyone to dance to his tune, regardless of how much his machinations destroy their lives. He could have made things a lot more clear – but instead chose to hide obscure clues in chess games and other esoteric places. Thankfully, Avery finds two people she can trust, to help her. Apart from a very good plot that kept my avid interest throughout, the book was really well written. A couple of the lovely phrases that appealed to me were: ““Such a shame about poor Howard,” offered an eggplant-attired matron of impeccable breeding and questionable chromatic theory.” “Aware that her family ties to the White House faded with each president, she had made ingratiation her blood sport.” The book also raised important questions about the way the USA is governed. I like to think that anyone on the Supreme Court has earned their place there, and will make judgements based on the law and not personal desires or politics. But what should happen if a justice is no longer capable of doing their job. As one character points out, the founding fathers did not know how much or how quickly medicine could advance. Two hundred years ago, a job for life would have had a much more limited term. They also did not know how science could change, or the media – did anyone? “Despite knowing how vulnerable technology can be, bureaucrats placed their faith in the myth of privacy. Their job relied on the fairy tales Americans told themselves about their government, despite ample proof to the contrary. Surveillance. Covert research. Targeted retribution. All disguised by pleasing stories told by men like Vance and President Stokes.” Medical ethics and scientific discoveries play a big part in this story – making for a very thought-provoking – as well as compelling and fascinating – read. “I am suggesting that scientific curiosity may get the better of humanity yet again. As it always has. Oppenheimer wasn’t a pioneer. He was just another scientist afraid to stop thinking.” I received this copy from the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. All opinions are my own and not influenced by either the author or publisher.
Fast-paced and well-plotted. The ending was a bit 'meh', though. 3.5*

** spoiler alert ** Oh my goodness. I loved this book! Avery is such a badass, and now I really want to read more books from Abrams. I really loved the pace of the book. I didn’t have to agonizingly wait to understand what was actually going on. Everything was revealed at a great time, and it just continued to get interesting and interesting. I know this was fiction, but damn, the U.S. government is really shitty, isn’t it? Anyways, Avery better start a career as a detective because the way she kept figuring out the clues got me so hyped up. The court hearing scene was definitely a favorite. She really showed them who's boss. This book even added some biology in there. I mean, okayyy Abrams, showing off your brain I see. I like how subtle Jared and Avery’s growing love for each other was developed. I’m a sucker for romance but I definitely don’t mind when a book doesn’t have a lot of romance. Besides, this book was about how smart Avery is and it’s so crazy that Justice Wynn saw how smart she was way before she did. The title with its double meaning was perfect. Overall, such a great story! 5 stars.
This is a good story. However it tends to get a bit technical in the storyline. I did enjoy reading it. Stacey Abrams is a remarkable woman.

“Knowing the law isn’t about the school. It’s about the mind. The heart. About understanding what the law intends as much as reading beneath what it says. Knowing how to find one’s way to the truth.” (p. 10) Wow I love Stacey but this is my second book by her and we just do not click. I probably should have known based on the lack of reviews from certain people whose opinion I normally seek out but I initially brushed it off as them maybe not being into thrillers (or romance as the previous book by her I read). But the writing was truly not great here. The dialogue is theatrical and stiff. It's told from third person which when written well isn't an issue but here it just emphasizes how one dimensional the four central characters are and makes them feel distant. But don't worry each of those four characters has a very useful skill (another lawyer, a doctor, ex military dude and Avery with the excellent memory) which defines their role in the book, there's zero personality to any of them. We don't even get a backstory on how Avery and Ling met and became roommates which could have been a fun story to showcase their personality. This book made me understand the term "commercial fiction", it's meant to be endlessly entertaining and unbothered by nuance. There were so many painful sentences. It's particularly clear that Abrams is trying to come off as somewhat nonpartisan, or at least as someone who doesn't want to make this book only about Democrats. One wince-inducing sentence features another law clerk described as a "brunette with a piquant face and the soul of an archconservative" who extends Avery a brief moment of kindness. *Insert massive eye roll* This nonpartisan blandness is most apparent in Avery herself. It's interesting because in a NYT profile Abrams says "Avery's Blackness is evident" I would respectfully disagree. We spend far more time hearing about Avery's "naturally corkscrew hair" and "green eyes" (she's biracial spoiler alert and her eyes are remarked upon by almost EVERY character) than we do her relationship to her Blackness or how she navigates the world of SCOTUS as a Black female law clerk. She went to Spelman but somehow there's very little time spent on that or having her interact with the Spelhouse world. What was the point of even including that detail?? And of course there's no Black friend or living parent, I don't even think she encountered another Black person in the novel besides the security guard. It was truly bizarre and I know it's unfair but I didn't expect Stacey to write such a stereotypically light skinned and bland main character. Avery felt like a serious concession to white readers especially with Abrams' choice to have her mother be the living parent, a white woman who struggles with opiod addiction. Furthermore Avery is in her twenties in the 200s (we can assume because smartphones and Internet) but has an ANSWERING MACHINE?! Honestly that's when I should have closed the book but I was determined to carry on. We also did not need the chaste burgeoning romance, the male love interest was too humdrum to be interesting or sexy. There's also no chemistry between the two so it's a wholly unconvincing romance which is surprising given Abrams' romance writer background. Similarly there's some cringe-worthy moments where characters go out of their way to shame or sneer at sex workers which was really disappointing. The book isn't about sex work but they also don't move the narrative along and those details and rude comments could have been left out instead of revealing a weird mindset (and if it was just one character I wouldn't say it's the authors but the fact that SEVERAL characters feel the need to say something...makes me wonder). WHILE JUSTICE SLEEPS is an intense, high stakes (a surprising amount of violence combined with democracy being at risk) legal thriller but suffers from loquacious writing and underdeveloped characters, most notably with the main character Avery. Abrams' intelligence is on display in the plot, it's complex and juggling many many threads that allow her to show off her knowledge of bioethics, chess, espionage, medicine, international politics (somewhat), technology and of course the Supreme Court (I loved her author's note about how each of her genius siblings fact checked certain parts of the book based on their expertise). It's absolutely a page turner, I wanted to know how it ended but it took me forever to finish because it was overly long (there are some bizarrely short chapters and lots of unnecessary and meaningless chatter that feels like filler) and the writing frustrated me. At this point I could potentially be persuaded to read another Selena Montgomery book to give it another chance but I'm done with Stacey Abrams thrillers. This was entirely too long and wordy for me to enjoy trying to unravel the complicated plot. And as much as I wanted to root for the brilliant young Black woman at the heart of the novel she's so boring that I didn't care anything about her.

I'll be honest, I 100% requested this book simply because Stacey Abrams wrote it. I didn't even care what the synopsis said. That being said, Abrams delivered an incredible political thriller that had me fully engaged from start to finish. This is not one of those heart pumping, hanging on to the edge of your seat thrillers. Instead, this is one of those books that asks the question of what if and plunges into a dark and insidious possibility. Abrams poses the question of "what happens if a court justice slips into a coma and what repercussions would follow?". And what follows is an intricately woven tale that walks the fine line of potential reality versus conspiracy theory. I was thoroughly engrossed, and I can honestly say that I hope something like this NEVER happens. Bravo Abrams. I can't wait for her next book! Thank you to Penguin Random House Audio for providing a review copy. This did not influence my review. All opinions are my own.

This just wasn’t the book for me. I feel like Ms. Abrams used vocabulary that isn’t typical of the average reader. While I knew the meaning of the words, I felt like I had to think about individual words and that lessened my ability to engage with the plot. At the end of the Kindle free sample, I deleted the book. I am disappointed because the premise is interesting and this is my preferred genre.
OH HECK YES! Avery, you just took on the entire judicial system!!!

Avery Keene slaves away as a clerk for the controversial, though brilliant but possibly slipping?, Justice Howard Wynn on the SCOTUS. Avery's dark secret is that her mom is a drug addict, who only contacts Avery when she runs out of money to feed her addictions. Avery is as shocked as the rest of the country when she finds out that Justice Wynn has suffered a medical episode and now lies in a coma in the hospital. Her shock deepens when she finds out that she has been appointed his guardian! Not his wife from whom he is separated, nor his estranged son, but his clerk!! Avery is surprised to find out that the Justice had/has an incurable neurological syndrome -- and that a SCOTUS case regarding the merger of two pharmaceutical companies might have a direct bearing upon the treatment of his syndrome. Avery's first visit, after the hospital, would be w/ Ms. Lewis, Justice Wynn's nurse, after a barely-intelligible phone call from Ms. Lewis. However, nurse Lewis is dead, shot in the head, when Avery arrives at her house. Of course, Avery becomes an immediate suspect in Ms. Lewis' death. Noah, the Justice's personal Attorney, gives her the guardianship papers and helps fend off Celeste, the harridan wife. She also meets Jared, the Justice's estranged son, and instead of being enemies, they cooperate to try to find out WHY Avery was chosen as guardian. The Justice has left Avery a few very cryptic clues. They appear to be moves on a chess board in a very particular pattern, called Lasker-Bauer. First, Avery had to figure out that that was what the Justice was even saying to nurse Lewis as he slipped into the coma! This is certainly a thriller that keeps one on the edige of one's seat the whole way through, as the Homeland Security liaison to the POTUS - who is an enemy of Justice Wynn's, harries Avery, along w/ the FBI who might be protecting her -- or bugging her? And key witnesses have a nasty habit of turning up dead. But the core group of Avery; her roommate, Ling; Jared; and Noah work hard to solve the incomprehensible clues while saving all their lives, especially Jared's, and possibly Justice Wynn's. The denouement involves Avery presenting her case before the remaining members of SCOTUS -- pretty unlikely for a lowly law clerk, but a thrilling scene nonetheless. This novel had SUCH potential. There is no doubt that Ms. Abrams -- whom I admire greatly for her voting rights work in Georgia -- knows her law forwards and backwards, and that she can write some good scenes. However, I often felt like I was reading an old Dime novel from the nineteenth century -- very sensationalistic w/ overblown prose. I was often left cold by some her overreaches in alliteration and similes. Avery's leaps of imagination and understanding of chess moves definitely left me behind. So, 3.6ish stars, reluctantly rounded up.

A literary roller coaster with social insight With all the talk about landmark Supreme Court decisions in jeopardy, retirements, nominations and their consequences, Stacey Abrams’ new legal thriller While Justice Sleeps is not so much ripped from the headlines as it is the stuff of our most vivid nightmares. When cantankerous Supreme Court justice Howard Wynn slips into a coma, it propels the court into limbo, causing a constitutional crisis with his law clerk at the center of a political storm. Abrams knows this terrain—legal, social, and political—inside and out. With that expertise, the issues at the center of the story are drawn with precision and insight, but her characters are the book’s greatest strength ... The story is anchored by two indelible outsiders who have little in common save the institution for which both work and their prickly personas. Stacey Abrams’s thriller is an intricate one with a diverse supporting cast of allies and adversaries and a Russian nesting doll of legal maneuvering, politics and technological intrigue. Much of it is riveting. There are also subplots and clever details strewn like Easter eggs throughout. Somewhere in the middle, the plot starts to feel overstuffed, and the myriad of moving parts slow forward momentum. But...there’s something deliciously rewarding about a thriller that realistically and unflinchingly reckons with how a young Black woman like Avery Keene gets treated when she answers the call to serve.
