I heard that Karen Joy Fowler had written a novel called Booth and thought to myself: "Great! I'd like to learn more about this John Wilkes Booth fella." But that's not what this book is about at all. It's more concerned with the wider Booth family and their circumstances in the lead-up to the murder of Abraham Lincoln. We learn far more about the siblings of the infamous assassin than we do about the man himself. Rosalia is the eldest daughter, affected by scoliosis, single all her life. Edwin intends to become an actor, just like his father Junius, and he has plenty of ability, though the family addiction to alcohol has been passed to him. Younger sister Asia is beautiful but prickly. All of the Booths become anxious about the schemings of John. He's also an actor, a person who constantly strives for attention. And his opinions on the topic of slavery alarm his brothers and sisters. He makes bold claims and his sympathies with the South go against the liberal leanings of his family. But none of them ever truly believe that he is willing to act upon them. This is a long, slow-moving tale, bogged down in lots of unnecessary information. John is a peripheral figure in the book, and we never really get underneath his wild exterior to see what makes him tick. Of course his unstable home life must have had a profound effect on him, not helped by the malign influence of his troubled father. But as for what his going through his mind in the lead up to the assassination, it is not explored by this story in a satisfactory way. I didn't find his siblings all that interesting, apart from Edwin, who led quite a colourful life. And the crime itself happens so late in the book - we only get a glimpse of the shock and dismay that it thrusts upon the Booths. I found this a frustrating read overall. It's understandable that the author does not want to glorify the ideals and motivations of a murderer. But we end up with far more information about his family than we need, and learn precious little about of the personality of this historical figure, who is notable for all the wrong reasons. It's an unbalanced novel, and though it's rich in certain detail, it left me discontented.

In an author's note at the end of this novel Karen Joy Fowler expresses her feelings of ambiguity about fictionally recreating the life of John Wilkes Booth, one of the most notorious figures in US history. He was famed for being a handsome and talented actor until the age of 26 when he became infamous for assassinating President Abraham Lincoln in Ford's Theatre on April 15, 1865. Why give more attention to a fanatic and egotist? This was a defining moment in American history which forever reshaped the country so it's only natural to wonder how it came about. Fowler was interested in the way it affected the rest of Booth's family. She's also haunted by Lincoln's warnings about tyrants and mobs in this country and how this still resonates today. The impetus for this novel which recreates the story of the Booth family also presents a conundrum for the reader who will most likely only know of John Wilkes Booth for a single defining action. Therefore, following the story of his life from birth we're naturally attentive to any action which indicates a propensity for mental instability, extreme views or violence. Fowler peppers the text with such signs and we can only warily witness an emboldened John who states at one point: “It's a wonderful thing... to be right in the middle of something so momentous. To feel that you've touched history and history has touched you.” Unlike the author's previous novel “We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves” which contains a famous twist, there's never any doubt about how “Booth” will end but that makes this story no less gripping. The thing about significant historical events is that they can come to feel inevitable, but obviously in the present moment we're faced with an infinite number of possibilities. We also cannot know the many repercussions of our actions. Though Fowler describes John as having certain propensities, his family definitely didn't view him as having the potential to be a monster. This novel primarily focuses on the point of view of John's surviving siblings and the dramatic story of their challenging family life leading up to John's murderous action. Their father Junius was a famous Shakespearean actor and a complicated tyrannical larger-than-life figure. On one hand, he was an intelligent artist who respected all life as sacred. On the other, he was bigamist who abandoned his first wife, frequently neglected his family and occasionally drunkenly terrorized his mistress and children. Naturally living under his shadow his children grew to both revere and hate him. It's fascinating reading how they change over time and wrestle with their identities as the offspring of Booth. Crucially, their interactions with John feel like any complicated sibling relationship. There's closeness and distance as well as moments of tenderness and frustration. Read my full review of Booth by Karen Joy Fowler at LonesomeReader

Rating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Genre: Historical Fiction Booth is a historical fiction that tells the story of Booth's family, that is the infamous John Wilkes Booth, the American stage actor who assassinated President Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C. This follows the lives of his parents, Junius Booth and Mary Ann Holmes, as well as his siblings, Rosalie, Asia, Edwin, June, and Joe. The story is set in 1822 with the major part of the book being about the family itself, all the problems and hardships they face. There is also the social and political background of the country in that period that keep affecting the lives of the members of the family and the society. This was a very intriguing read for me. I have never read anything about John Booth before and was truly interested to know more about him. This book doesn’t just focus on him but on his whole family, which pleases me even more. I’m always in for dysfunctional families. Maybe not all the readers would agree if this family can be termed as dysfunctional but at least we can agree that it was a family with lots of issues and problems. The fascinating thing is that the author was concentrating on each one of the members, especially the siblings. And she did a fabulous job with that. Rosalie is my favorite character in the book. As for the issues, there is slavery, racism, alcoholism, and bigamy to mention a few. Another thing I appreciate the author doing is keeping the timeline linear which helped me to understand these characters’ situations. I’m glad about it. Towards the middle, the pace did slow down a bit but I wouldn’t call that a major issue as the beautiful writing style kept me engaged. How much of this book is true and how much of it is fiction is a questionable thing. But regardless of that, the author must’ve done an extensive research to come up with this story. It always impresses me when a book ends up being entertaining and educational at the same time. This is where Booth shines for me. Many thanks to the publisher Penguin Group Putnam, G.P. Putnam's Sons, and NetGalley for providing me with an advance reader copy of this book.

Full disclosure: Karen Joy Fowler is a dear friend. But here's the truth of the matter. If I didn't like her book, I would simply not offer a review of it. In "Booth" --probably the most infamous surname in the history of the US --Karen Joy Fowler has made an interesting and fascinating artistic decision. Instead of writing about John Wilkes Booth, she has chosen to create a historical novel based upon the family of the notorious assassin. And what a family it is! With a truly remarkable attention to detail, KJ puts her reader right into the middle of the Booth family, a group of people plagued by alcoholism and ruled by the king of alcoholics Junius Booth, who also is the foremost Shakespearean actor of his time. Capable of carrying off any and all of Shakespeare's great tragic heroes while sober, drunk, or in between, Junius Booth looms large to his children among whom are four living brothers, three of whom follow him onto the stage. Of these three, John Wilkes is the heartthrob but Edwin is the more famous and better actor. The reader gets to know all of the Booth children who survived to adulthood -- four did not --through viewpoint shifts throughout the novel. As a result, no one of them gets precedence over the other. All of them are equally fascinating. And of course, John Wilkes is fascinating, too. But the spotlight doesn't stay on him. Instead, KJ gives each of the siblings an importance that has been long lost to time. In this way, the reader sees the influences that shaped each of the children, allowing them to grow, develop, and--ultimately--cope with a horrific crime perpetrated by one of them as best they could.

The Booth family is gratified by the depth and breadth of national mourning for Junius Brutus Booth. Every American paper reports Booth’s death and most include long eulogies. But one response is memorable for its brevity. Rufus Choate, a storied trial lawyer turned Whig congressman, a man famous for his soaring and sustained bouts of oratory, says simply, “There are no more actors.” In an Author’s Note at the end of Booth, Karen Joy Fowler explains that “during one of our American spates of horrific mass shootings”, she began to wonder about the families of shooters — what it must be like to love someone who becomes universally despised — and then she began thinking of the Booth family, and started working on a novel about the family of John Wilkes Booth; pointedly not focussing on John himself as he was a man who had sought notoriety and was not deserving of Fowler’s attention. Then when Trump was elected president, Fowler recognised that “Lincoln’s warnings concerning the tyrant and the mob” were still true in the modern day, and she realised that the story she was writing about the radicalisation of the man who would become Lincoln’s assassin could be seen as a warning for the present: it is still true that a house divided against itself cannot stand and growing partisanship imperils the Union. So, on the one hand, Booth is stuffed full of interesting historical information about the Booth family (I had no idea how famous the Booth father and older brother, Edwin [the nineteenth century’s “greatest Hamlet”], were), and on the other, Fowler never lets us forget that she’s drawing a line between the past and the present; the parallels are obvious and underlined. As a work of historical fiction, this was well done (with the caveat that, as a longish book, too much detail can feel tedious to me), and as a work of political commentary, an essay expanding on the Author’s Note would have sufficed for me. This felt a bit of a slog; just okay to my taste. They were wrapped together in a single blanket, John’s little body hot against Mother’s breasts. She was looking down into his flushed and fretful face, when on sudden impulse she’d said a prayer asking to know what his fate would be. Instantly a flame rose from the ashes and, shaping itself into an arm, stretched toward the baby as if to knight him. In that flame, Mother said, she could read the word Country, followed by Johnny’s name. And then the arm fell back and faded away. This strange, unfirelike behavior taking place on their own little hearth has the whole family excited. It may be an ambiguous fate, but it’s clearly a glorious one, a narrative of such power that Asia will write a poem about it one day, forgetting how angry she once was not to have been given a glorious fate of her own. She was less upset by her own lack of a destiny than by the fact that nobody had ever even bothered to ask the fire if she had one. Junius Brutus Booth — celebrated Shakespearean actor of the London stage — wooed the beautiful Mary Ann Holmes, and in 1821, moved her to the United States, eventually settling her in a “secret cabin” in the woods northeast of Baltimore. Over the course of twenty years, Mary Ann will give birth to ten children, six of whom will survive to adulthood, and as Junius (equal parts genius, madman, and hopeless alcoholic) spends around nine months of every year touring with acting troupes, Mary Ann (and the enslaved people the family “leases”), work the farm and raise the children and try to stay above the poverty line. The family will move into Baltimore and back to the countryside again; eldest son June will leave to make a name for himself on the stage; Edwin will be taken out of school to travel with his father; the two youngest boys — John and Joe — will be sent to a boarding school; and the two daughters — Rosalie and Asia — will be left to take care of Mother, their brothers, and watch for marriage prospects. Throughout all the years, John Wilkes will be the pet; the scamp, the matinee idol, his mother’s and sisters’ favourite who can do no wrong. Fowler tells this story from three perspectives: From Edwin’s (the most celebrated actor in the family, his biography is well documented); from Asia’s (she wrote several [some would say apologetic] memoirs of herself and her more famous family members); and Rosalie’s (of whom very little is known, so Fowler was free to have Rosalie’s sections fill in the historical bits from the newspapers and the typical family life of the time). This rotating POV gave a satisfying backdrop for John Wilkes’ formative years, while never presuming to imagine what the future assassin was thinking or feeling. And by giving us the whole Booth story (ending not long after the assassination), Fowler is able to pinpoint a few transformative moments: John was present at “the battle of Christiana” — in which free Blacks repelled a Marshal’s attempts to capture escaped slaves — which some historians point to as the beginning of the beginning of the Civil War; he joined the Richmond Grays militia unit to march on Charles Town to ensure John Brown’s hanging (the battle flag of the Grays reads “Sic semper tyrannis”); he was visiting Edwin’s house in New York City when the anti-draft riots happened (and apparently delighted in watching the city burn). Fowler makes clear that all of the Booth family thought of themselves as pro-Union Northerners, except for John Wilkes, and other than apparently suffering the mental illness and alcohol abuse that seems to run through the Booth family (Edwin says of his brother, “He has all of Father’s madness without the genius”), and some slightly different experiences at school (and particularly coddled at home), there’s no real explanation for how one of the Booths could become a murderer. But again: this isn’t really meant to be John Wilkes’ story; this is the story of America and how slippery the slope is towards considering your countryman your enemy once the drums start beating. What’s it like to love the most hated man in the country? Loving John is something the world simply will not have. Not loving John is something Rosalie and Asia simply cannot do. As I’m not an American, I had only a general knowledge of John Wilkes Booth and what Fowler writes about his background and upbringing (and particularly the stories of the more famous and celebrated acting Booths) was interesting and informative to me. And since the symbols of the United States aren’t emotionally affecting to me, it did take this whole, long novel and Fowler’s Author’s Note at the end for me to really understand what it meant for the Confederate Flag to have been “carried through the halls of the Capitol for the very first time” during the insurrection of January 6th, 2021: the events of that day were, naturally, shocking to witness as a non-American, but their meaning wasn’t really clear to me until now. It still felt like a bit of a slog — this is not at the top of my own Booker picks — but it wasn’t entirely a waste of time.

BOOTH will eternally evoke the name John Wilkes, the assassin of Abe Lincoln. All I knew about the family was that Booth was a stage actor. Actually, nothing about his family came to mind. But now, wow! I feel intimately close to his brothers and sisters, his parents. John Wilkes is not the main character in Fowler’s brimming character study of the Booths, and the author nailed it by choosing this way to deliver her story. There isn’t one family member that I don’t feel I can talk about with familiarity now, so deep did the author mine her story, her cast. Booth’s father was one of the most celebrated Shakespearean stage actors of his time, until one of his sons took up the mantle. The entire novel is Shakespearean, the way Fowler structured it, threaded throughout with lines from his plays showing up on the page in the exact right moments. This is a powerhouse of a great American novel. A great American tragedy. Another element that pulled me in was the old-fashioned third person POV, yet there was nothing fusty about this narrative. It felt fresh, with knowing parallels to today’s times, as well as particular character traits that almost had me believing that Fowler lived with the Booths! From Maryland, to Philadelphia, NYC, Richmond, London, and other settings, I felt that, no matter where the setting, I felt the insular, insulated feeling of the family, how the tight-knit brood kept others out, even when celebrated and well known in polite and high-toned society. There was a detached attitude to almost everyone outside the family; no matter how broad the travels and influence, the author showed how sequestered they were, how inside themselves they remained, no matter how social or cosmopolitan. The brothers and sisters—even Mother--had their favorites and expectations. Moreover, at their secretive heels, ghosts were constantly nipping. There were those that died as babies, and never stopped haunting Mary Ann, the matriarch. Births and deaths were momentous. One baby’s death: “There were no bouts of uncontrollable weeping, only an endless stream of silent tears. It was as if Frederick had taken her spirit along with him when he went, leaving only a Mother-shaped husk behind.” Or a birth: “Edwin is the family’s seventh child and…arrived with his caul still over his face. The caul has been saved in a small box in her mother’s cupboard. It has the feel of a well-worn handkerchief.” This is no saga—BOOTH is a momentous and character-driven story that will hold you in its grip from start to finish. Even history buffs will fall prey to the exciting and nuanced narrative, despite knowing the climax. But, is the assassination the only climax in this book? There’s more to this intrepid story than John Wilkes Booth, a peripheral character in his own story. Thank you for the free/gifted book from Putnam @PutnamBooks #partner

Reacting to the headline of a mass shooting, Karen Joy Fowler wondered about the families of the shooters. Did they struggle under the burden of notoriety? Were they stigmatized, or able to navigate in society? She realized she knew little about the family of the most notorious American shooter–the man who killed President Lincoln, John Wilkes Booth. As she researched extensively to understand the Booth family, she realized the relevance of this episode in American history, especially after the January 6 insurrection. In her new novel Booth, Fowler brings to life the nine children and parents of the Booth family, beginning with Junius Brutus Booth, a famous actor. He was also a deeply flawed man, a bigamist and an alcoholic. Junius abandoned his English wife and child when he met the beautiful Mary. He settled their family on a farm, scrambling to survive as their patriarch was on tour most of the year. As the boys came of age, they are tasked with being their father’s guardian and caretaker, endeavoring to keep him sober. The eldest son, June becomes an actor with a career in the West. Edwin had hoped for college but was next tasked with his father’s care; he falls into the same bad habits as his father, going on to forge his own acting career. The youngest son to go into acting is John Wilkes, beloved and handsome but demonstrating disturbing traits since childhood. He had little academic interest, joined a gang, and was swayed by extremist politics. The eldest daughter Rosalie experienced the death of younger siblings. She was plagued by physical handicaps, a limp and a curved spine, keeping her at home, a perpetual daughter and caretaker. Asia, strong willed and beautiful, settles for a comfortable marriage, but she remains devoted to her brother John Wilkes. These deeply flawed characters share family trauma of loss and poverty and alcoholism, revering their absent, unreliable father and idolizing their long suffering, beautiful mother. They move from the hard life of the farm to city luxury as the family fortunes rise. The family is apolitical, but Republican, but for John Wilkes who comes to hate abolition and defends slavery. Interspersed are chapters summarizing President Lincoln’s life, career, and speeches–which today seem prescient, referring to mobs and political division and populist leaders. Baltimore and Maryland’s political strife and division are central to the story. The political division in Maryland mirrors the entire country, then and now. Fowler’s story is deep and rich. The Booths seem like a family meant for fiction, encompassing such a broad swath of human experience. I received a free egalley from the publisher through NetGalley. My review is fair and unbiased.

Booth is superbly readable. The pages flow by even when nothing particularly thrilling is happening. Fowler paints intimate portraits of each family member, and the narration includes deft wink-nods to the reader and the future. I was most impressed by the way Fowler kept the day-to-day family drama in the foreground – it struck me as very realistic. My full review of Booth is up now on Keeping Up With The Penguins.

I've got a complicated relationship with Fowler, and I am relatively picky about historical fiction so I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed Booth. I was aided in having picked up from reviews I'd read before embarking on this novel, that it's not REALLY about John Wilkes Booth, but rather his family. This does feel like a bit of a bait and switch which is probably the fault of marketing rather than the novel itself. In this way, Booth is both sprawling and meditatively paced. Where I'd ordinarily find such sedate pacing over a pretty lengthy novel frustrating, I instead found this immersive. What I think Fowler does well is explore history through the eyes of those who sit in its periphery. Rather than looking at exceptional players, we see how shocking events are experienced by those adjacent to them. It is a thoughtful examination of the ripple effect of reckless and extreme actions, and what it means when someone you love turns out to be someone who does awful things. I found these characters, and this question thoughtfully compelling.
Unexpectedly riveting! Audio is the way to go with this one. More thoughts and book talk on my podcast, Book Talk, etc. https://www.booktalketcpodcast.com/

"What is it like to love the most hated man in the country?" Karen Joy Fowler tells us. We are introduced to Johnny as "the swimmer in Mother's belly", not as the firebrand breaking his leg as he leaps to a stage having committed the most heinous crime imaginable. The title Booth title refers to the entire family, with second-to-youngest son not being the central figure until his actions put paid to their future. Father Junius Brutus Booth was a star in his time, seeking his fortune in America after leaving Britain. That departure had more to it than anyone knew, and reasons are revealed in good time. Mother gives birth every other year, ten total with six surviving, and it is through the five siblings that the story is told, some more factual than others. As in David Eggers's What is the What, Fowler has cast this as a fiction, allowing herself the leeway to fabricate at will, most particularly in the words and character of Rosalie, eldest daughter and most obscure since little of her is available. Daily life as experienced almost 200 years ago is carried out with such attention to detail, so well researched and rendered that the reader is totally immersed. I found myself intrigued by the theatrical conventions of the time, life both urban and rural. Each section is tracked by a quote from Abraham Lincoln, a biographical timeline of his life running concurrently, giving a more complete picture of the times. Although this is not one of my favorite genres, I thoroughly enjoyed every page. Kudos.

This took some time to get into but in the end the effort paid off. It tells the story of the Booth family trying to make a life for themselves in 19th century America as Shakespeare actors with in the background the looming American Civil War. One of the sons goes on to kill Abraham Lincoln. It is by no means a flawless novel. The prose feels a bit clunky and doesn't sparkle. The structure is quite strange, often it is unclear who the narrator is and from time to time curious paragraphs pop up which seem written centuries later. I also had some issues with the Lincoln inserts in the text - on the one hand they provided valuable insight in the developing political situation, on the other hand it feels like the author selected them on the basis of the topic she was most interested in and not necessarily the Booth family (i.e. the abolition of slavery). But despite these flaws it worked very well for me as a historical novel and made me rediscover my love for historical fiction. It draws interesting parallels with the divided America we know today. How politics can divide families. How frustration can slowly turn into extremism. And how division can lead to civil war. But mostly this was just a fascinating family portrait of life in 19th century America. The characters felt very close and quite modern, and I was also surprised by how modern the US was already around 1850. Another one on the Booker list that would be on my shortlist, but that I would be very surprised to see as a winner.

The voice crafted for this story about the family Booth is very well done. It’s engaging and representative of different family members characterizations. It flies along the innocuous and the narration is great (say, 4/5 stars on that front, not incredible but better than average). What was a bit of a gamble for me, the premise that this whole family was interesting enough for this long a book, was more worth it than I expected, though still had what felt like superfluous content. The voice really does carry it at such times. In this case “truth” is stranger than fiction though, I bet, as the family is replete will all manner of foibles and wild occurrences and, as everyone expects: tragedy. Though they may not expect as many as are here. There’s also an authors note at the end that talks about fact and fiction in here, and where to go next if you want more Booth family drama. I appreciate that, since historical fiction for me is all fiction, unless otherwise stated. I think this would appeal to just about everyone - it is that dramatic and often presented in a melodramatic fashion that befits the predominate profession the family was known for. Certainly a bit of an Americana vibe, which I didn’t care much about, but I think would appeal to those folks. All around better than I expected but perhaps a bit overlong.
This well-written historical novel is told by Booth's family members and not by Booth. I felt sorry for them after he shot Lincoln because he left their lives in a big mess. None of them did well.

2022 BOOKER PRIZE LONGLIST CHALLENGE BOOTH by Karen Joy Fowler The Booth name has become villainous, synonymous with hatred and murder, its most recognized holder, John Wilkes, guilty of assassinating Abraham Lincoln just as the US Civil War was winding down. Karen Joy Fowler, previously shortlisted for unexpectedly wild WE ARE COMPLETELY BESIDES OURSELVES, delivers a much more down the middle work of historical fiction account of the Booth family, known for their work as thespians until the second-youngest of the family killed audience member Lincoln while performing My American Cousin. Providing altering accounts from each living sibling’s perspective, we get thrown into a family obsessed with Shakespeare, children trying to live up to the legacy of their famous father Junius Brutus Booth while trying to escape his shadow, all with a brewing national conflict coming to the break the family apart. This book has faced a lot of criticism and many readers have been bored by the content. At times, the multiple perspectives becomes tedious, but I was also fascinated by the themes explore. The novel feels like a brilliant fiction companion to James Shapiro’s SHAKESPEARE IN A DIVIDED AMERICA (which has a chapter on Booth and Lincoln and their relationship with The Bard’s works), introducing us to the first family of American theatre, a forum of art wedded deeply to popular consumption and participation at the time, where the larger fissures in the country would find their voice even in plays written centuries before. The character accounts are all intimate and very much focused on the personal conflicts inside the family but the larger events that were fundamentally transforming the nation at the time couldn’t help shape those family divisions. Maybe not gripping but still an excellent literary accomplishment. That said, I don’t expect it to appear on the shortlist. #bookerprize #bookerprizelonglist #bookstagram #bookstagramreadsthebooker #bookprizes #literature #novels #audiobook #libbyapp #americanliterature

A thorough exploration of the history and family dynamics that shaped infamous John Wilkes Booth. This novel follows the Booth family, largely involved in the Theater and other artistic pursuits, as they become more embroiled in the nation’s tumultuous political conflicts, until passions erupt with history-altering consequences. A solid glimpse into the ways in which our families build us up and tear us down, inspire us for good or for evil, and change the course of our identities as artists, activists, scandal makers, and criminals. With the detail and confidence of nonfiction but the poetic fluidity of a play script.

A story about an interesting family during an unsettling time. With ten children, it’s challenging to get to know all of them in full depth. We know how it will end, the buildup is slow and somewhat tedious. Characters are introduced then mentioned hundreds of pages later and it took me a moment to remember who they were. None of the characters are very like able. The plot just moves along. It is interesting how the Shakespeare plays mimic the themes in their lives. Still, it didn’t grab me as much as this authors other book. Thank you NetGalley for the ARC.

2.5 I found this novel somewhat "meh" hence the 2.5 stars. I listened to the audio which was nicely read by January LaVoy. I think I can safely say I now know far more than I ever wished to know about the family of John Wilkes Booth. Frankly I think Karen Joy Fowler set herself the near impossible task of writing a book about the family of John Wilkes Booth without making him the central character. It probably explains why the narrative jumped about all over the place encompassing all family members in the retelling of anecdotes about JWB. Karen Joy Fowler says there is a lot of written evidence but some of what she wrote was made up and some not. So my favourite piece of information (which I sincerely hope is not made up) was a letter from Asia written many years after the assassination in which she actually blames Lincoln himself for his own assassination because he should have stayed home that night or gone to church to pray for the souls of the many thousands killed in the war rather than going to the theatre to watch a play. She uses quite colourful language about the theatre which makes me suspect the veracity of the letter since her entire family made their money from acting. Either way it is this sort of evidence that reflects the book in that for the most part John is coddled and adored by his family and his brutal tendencies ignored or explained away. It is clear they were all a bunch of deluded idiots so far as their brother/son was concerned. The other part that I found hard to deal with was the huge cast of characters - quite a lot of whom seemed to change or share names- Junius, Jun, Joe, Johnny/John ... thank goodness the women didn't follow suit. It was like trying to follow the Kardashians singularly dull naming system. I know this has been a much lauded book but I found it circuitous, overlong and in need of a good edit. Not my thing at all.

Critically acclaimed and bestselling author Karen Joy Fowler returns almost a decade after WE ARE COMPLETELY BESIDE OURSELVES with BOOTH, an intimate yet kaleidoscopic portrait of the family behind one of the most hated men in American history: John Wilkes Booth, President Abraham Lincoln’s assassin. “What happens to love when the person you love is a monster?” writes Fowler in her author’s note. This question --- and the focus on this love rather than its recipient --- forms the heart of this ambitious, nearly 500-page novel. Like so many victim advocates have reminded us to do, Fowler sets her writerly gaze not on Booth, but on his victim and those victimized by his act: his loving, dysfunctional family. Presided over by Junius Booth, an esteemed Shakespearean actor, the Booth family’s history begins in 1822 on a secluded farm 30 miles northeast of Baltimore. Magnetic and mercurial yet undeniably talented, Junius is an eccentric: he considers eating meat a sin, he praises the “Hindoos” as the possessors of the only true religion, he believes that no man can be owned, and his penchant for liquor encourages him to act out these beliefs (and more) in varying states of inebriation and madness. The Booth matriarch, Mary, is a dark-haired beauty whose passion for Junius is eclipsed only by her tragic life as a mother. Between the two of them, the Booths conceive 10 children, only six of whom live beyond childhood. The children are Junius “June,” more brawn than brains, his father’s greatest disappointment; Rosalie, the family’s built-in nanny, who bears witness to the worst of her siblings’ deaths and her mother’s grief; Edwin, sensitive and quiet, with the most beautiful eyes; Asia, headstrong and stunning; John “Johnny” Wilkes, the apple of his family’s eye; and Joseph Adrian, nearly an afterthought. The youngest, Johnny and Joe, seem almost inconsequential, divided from their older siblings by four tragic deaths and years of grief and upheaval. Yet, as we all know, it will be Johnny who makes the family’s name synonymous with death. BOOTH contains six “books,” each of which is divided into chapters focused on one of the Booth children. Rosalie sets the scene in Book 1. Through her eyes, we watch as Junius Sr.’s career takes off in fits and starts, both propelled and halted by his alcoholism. Unstable and prone to angry outbursts, Junius is still beloved by his family, raising them with a love for nature so strong that to even pluck a flower on his property is akin to murder. But with his career taking off, Junius is gone for nine months each year, leaving Mary and Rosalie to nurture, parent and raise the remaining children. With Mary still reeling from the losses of four of her kids, Rosalie devotes herself to keeping the family together, becoming a sort of third parent to the young ones. Raised in a household steeped in Shakespeare, many of them dream of becoming actors, yet their father will hear none of it, demanding instead that they choose stable, honest careers. This dissonance is not the first of his idiosyncrasies to plague their mental and emotional states, but it is perhaps one of the most formative. The older children are much more like their father when it comes to spiritual and political beliefs. The younger ones have been raised in almost entirely different families, so changed were the Booths by wealth and access to better schooling, homes in the city and the loss of older siblings to guide them. June and Edwin become celebrated actors, while Rosalie turns into a spinster-fied version of their mother, and Asia is a budding flirt. As the older brothers venture farther away from the Booth home, Johnny and Joe grow up without the same influences. As a result, Johnny turns rebellious, while Joe is nearly forgotten at school. Johnny’s nature is a quiet current throughout the book, one that runs so naturally and unimpeded that his family cannot see it for the portent that it is until it’s far too late. Fowler never goes so far as to excuse John Wilkes Booth, but her writing of the historical context is so immersive and perfectly distilled that his actions seem inevitable --- if not because of the instability and difficulty with alcohol that binds his family, then for the tensions brewing nationwide over slavery, immigration and the rights of states. As war becomes a reality, Johnny starts siding firmly with the South on each of these issues. That he stands against the rest of his family is glossed over time and time again in favor of harmony, and with the constant refrain that “the war will be over soon anyway.” (If you’re hearing echoes of “He was always a quiet boy” or “We never could have expected this,” you’re on the right track.) BOOTH walks the fine line between immersive (at times unwieldy) historical fiction and searing contemporary social horror. The history is written beautifully and, at its best, does what only the strongest historical fiction can do: capture the details of a time vividly and place the reader in the mind of someone living in that time authentically. At its weakest, the prose can be a bit weighed down by cliché and information dumps. That said, the glory of the novel comes from Fowler herself, who does not write down to her readers by drawing overhanded parallels between the divide created by the Civil War and our current political climate. Early on, when setting the political scene, Fowler writes that Lincoln warned the public of two possible threats to the Republic: the lawless actions of the mob and the inevitable rise someday of an aspiring dictator. She tells us right from the start that “the gravest peril will come if the mob and the dictator unite,” thus setting the stage for both John Wilkes Booth --- radical and mad, but never not loved --- and political figures of our own time. That his family, and the Booth name, was also victim to his madness is an emotionally resonant point that reverberates through both 40 years of Booth history and centuries of America. Reviewed by Rebecca Munro

Everyone knows that John Wilkes Booth assassinated Abraham Lincoln; most people (I think) know that the murder happened at the theater, and that Booth jumped onstage and shot into the president's box. I also knew that Booth's brother was a famous Shakespearean actor. I didn't really know anything about him, or his family, and I can't say I ever stopped to wonder much about why he killed Lincoln, let alone what that meant to his family members. And that's the miracle of fine writers, like Karen Fowler (who is a friend). She explores the strange twists and turns of the Booth family from the marriage of John Wilkes' parents through the aftermath of the assassination. She couldn't do that well without exploring the times, which she does with her characteristic "ruminative irony" (phrase courtesy Jonathan Lethem's back cover blurb). Here's a snippet from Asia's point of view, when her oldest brother June brings home his wife, Hattie, and their filthy young baby. "Marion smells of urine and spoiiled food. Her dress is staind and clean cloths will have to be found to diaper her, since the ones Hattie brought, including the one she's wearing, all need a desperate washing. And yet, she's adorable, lots of hair and big brown eyes. "Asia's feelings for Hattie, who also has hair and eyes, are more complicated." I found the book absorbing, disconcerting, sometimes heart-wrenching. The primary point of view characters are Rosalie (the oldest sister, about whom least is known, requiring much more fictionalization on Karen's part), Asia, a younger sister with a very strong personality, and Edwin, the Shakespearean actor brother. Their father, Junius, was a leading Shakespearean actor in his generation, and three of four his surviving sons (June, Edwin, and John Wilkes) followed him onto the stage to various degrees, but it was Edwin who became one of the country's leading romantic figures. Historical fiction about real people is constrained by what actually happened, and this book does a far better job than most of foregrounding the history while keeping a strong narrative flow (some of that may be because the family was so interesting and the story is in fact a good one). It's not a story for the faint of heart--aside from the assassination itself, there are numerous accounts of childhood deaths, a great deal of alcohol abuse, family rifts, and the ongoing background of owned human lives. I devoured it; if it's your kind of book, I think you will too.

Could not put it down. A beautifully written exploration of the Booth family--not just John Wilkes, but the rest of this fascinating theatrical brood. And brood it was. Wilkes was one of ten children (six living) born to Junius Brutus Booth, an English actor who arrived in Maryland in 1821 with his new wife and his father, dropped them off at a rural cabin, and went on tour for most of the next several decades. Junius B. was one of the actors of his age and had a brilliant career until his alcoholism brought in an audience eager to see what he would do next as opposed to experiencing his Hamlet. Three of his sons, Junius Jr., Edwin, and John, would become actors, with Edwin becoming one of the most revered actors of the mid-19th century. Living on a farm in rural Maryland, the Booths worked side by side with Blacks, both enslaved and free. Junius B's father was part of the Underground Railway, the family gave money to Black friends to buy their children, and the Booths respected them more than their white neighbors. So what happened to John? Karen Joy Fowler believes his dedication to the cause of slavery came during a brief period when the family had enough money to send him to an elite boarding school where his charismatic personality made him the pal of boys from plantation families. Of all the handsome Booth boys, John was the most handsome and people loved him, even at his most erratic. Fowler creates a brilliant picture of an America divided, where people deny facts, alcoholism is rampant, and families are crushed by grief with the losses of loved ones from diseases now easily treated. The Civil War and the New York draft riots are drawn so skillfully that any reflection in today's events is completely terrifying. "Booth" is terrific reading. Thought-provoking, entertaining, and historically eye-opening, it is not to be missed.

Rec. by: Previous work Rec. for: Rival siblings We already know how the Booth family's story ends. It is a tragedy in the classical sense, both because we know and for what we know. We all know the story—or at least we think we do... but we have not previously been provided with the perspective. Karen Joy Fowler's historical novel Booth is a marvelous work that gives us that perspective. It is a tragedy of Shakespearean proportions (which is entirely appropriate; after all, the family's patriarch was the renowned Shakespearean actor Junius Booth, and several of his sons followed him into the theatre). The whole farm speaks in iambic pentameter. —p.239 This novel is more like Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, though, than Hamlet. Fowler focuses on the folks around John Wilkes Booth—his family and friends, and what they knew of him long before that fateful night in Ford's theatre. Booth himself does not even appear on the scene until page 59, and Abraham Lincoln appears only in brief establishing scenes throughout. This is all by design, and it's a measure of Fowler's confidence and determination that her sidelong gaze works so well. "Don't bring damnation on yourself by swearing to the truth of your anecdotes." —John Wilkes Booth, p.200 Booth is fiction, though, and Fowler cannot swear to the truth of all her anecdotes. This version is based on historical documents, but those are not comprehensive—especially when it comes to the eldest sister Rosalie and her role in raising her younger brother John. This is a good reminder that no one in the world is a reliable source for their own story. —p.98 I did find myself entertained by this description of Asia Booth's suitor Dan, which actually fits my son (who has the same name) eerily well... Dan {Scott} is thin and pale with excellent teeth and wild, curly hair, a thoroughly presentable young man. —p.223 Siblings can be problematic, to be sure. I know this myself—I have a beloved family member with whom I can only converse about innocuous topics ("butterflies and daffodils"), these days. Fowler understands this very well: I was in the midst of my final edits when, during the violent insurrection of January 6th, 2021, I saw the flag of the Confederacy carried through the halls of the Capitol for the very first time. Let it be the last. —Author's Note, p.466 Karen Joy Fowler is one of my favorite authors anyway, and I was eagerly anticipating Booth. I was not disappointed; Fowler's novel is a complex work with vivid characterizations and a plot that's both historical and extraordinarily timely. If I did not enjoy this one quite as much as I did We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves, that is—I am sure—my own failure, rather than hers. The novel itself is well worth reading, and I commend it to your attention.

Karen Joy Fowler’s newest novel, “Booth”, has been one of the year’s most anticipated books. “Booth” is the story of John Wilkes Booth and many other members of his family. Told in alternating chapters by individual family members, Fowler gives some time to Abraham Lincoln and his family. The Booth family was headed by Junius Brutus Booth, an English actor who absconded from London to Baltimore. He fled with his teenage lover, Mary Ann Holmes, leaving behind a legal wife and child. He settled in a farm outside Baltimore and began fathering children while touring as an actor for most of the year. The family here grew, despite losing children to various diseases. They lived an unsettled life, hidden away in the woods, but the male children followed their father on to the stage. They achieved success as actors before John Wilkes assassinated Abraham Lincoln. The Lincoln and Booth families had similar losses of children. The Booths lost four children, out of ten or eleven - and had six who reached adulthood. The Lincolns lost three out their four sons. Fowler does a wonderful job of comparing and contrasting the two…until the fatal meeting at Ford’s Theater in April, 1865. Karen Joy Fowler’s book is long at almost 500 pages, but it is a fascinating read.

A fascinating novel about a remarkable family. The Booths were an early American dynasty of acting talents who enjoyed a fair amount of celebrity, as well as scandal, in their day, but were eventually tarnished by infamy when John Wilkes assassinated Lincoln. Father Junius is barely ever at home, criss-crossing the nation on tour while his wife and children are mostly left at home in Baltimore and a farm nearby. The novel rotates in point of view from Rosalie, one of the older children of the family to survive infancy (she is, at times, on intimate terms with the ghosts of her deceased siblings), Edwin, who grows up to be at least as famous an actor as his father (you can easily find photos of him as Hamlet in an online search), and Asia, a younger daughter who is close to both Edwin and John. The historical details are fascinating, but if I had to summarize it in a phrase I'd describe this even more as fiction about family than historical fiction. I am drawn to stories about Lincoln (Lincoln in the Bardo, Courting Mr. Lincoln, movies like Young Mr. Lincoln) and Fowler peppers the novel with concise segments that give us brilliant flashes into his life in parallel to the Booths. I'm also drawn to fiction about Shakespeare (Hamnet) and love theater, so I was captivated by the details about actors of that era performing Shakespeare. But rest assured that Fowler keeps the focus on rich characters and the storyline, both handled superbly. (I've never read Fowler before, but looking over her past work I'm astounded by her range.) Ultimately, unavoidably, this comes down to John Wilkes Booth and the assassination of Lincoln. Fowler does an excellent job satisfying our curiosity about this event while keeping its impact on the Booth family at the center. As depicted here, the Booths were abolitionist and pro-Union in their sympathies (paterfamilias Junius was also vegetarian), and John's actions shake the family to its core. Like all the best historical fiction, it resonates with the events of our day as much as its own, but Fowler lets those parallels speak for themselves. I loved this story of a remarkable family experiencing both love and tragedy.

This fascinating new novel by Karen Joy Fowler tells the story, in fictional form, of the Booths, the 19th century theatrical family who produced two of America’s most acclaimed actors, as well as one infamous killer – John Wilkes Booth, the man who assassinated Abraham Lincoln. Although John Wilkes is, unfortunately, the best known Booth and probably the reason many readers will be drawn to this novel – to find out more about his background and what drove him to commit such a terrible crime – this is not just his story. In fact, he plays no bigger a part in it than several of the other Booths. For much of the first half of the book, the focus is on his father, the Shakespearean actor Junius Brutus Booth, who will have an important influence on the lives of each of his children – despite the fact that they rarely see him, as he spends so much time away on tour while the family stay at home on their farm near Baltimore. Junius Brutus is a talented and successful stage actor, but as the years go by his alcoholism and eccentric behaviour make him increasingly unreliable, damaging his reputation and his financial situation. Still, he remains the centre of his children’s lives, and when three of his sons – Junius Jr (or June), Edwin and John Wilkes – follow in his footsteps and become actors themselves, they face a lifelong battle to avoid comparisons with him and with each other. It is Edwin who emerges from his father’s shadow to become one of the leading actors of his time and it is from Edwin’s perspective that we see part of the story unfold. There are also two Booth daughters who survive to adulthood, Rosalie and Asia – and these are the other characters whose perspectives we see throughout the novel. Rosalie is the eldest and her viewpoint is particularly important early in the novel as she has experiences and memories that her younger siblings do not. As Rosalie grows into a sensitive woman who remains unmarried and close to her mother, she becomes known to the family as ‘poor Rosalie’, a sad and slightly tragic figure. Her younger sister Asia, a stronger personality who will become an author later in life, also offers some interesting insights into the dynamics of the Booth family; she has good relationships with both Edwin and John and feels caught in the middle as tensions begin to grow between the two brothers. The murder of Abraham Lincoln doesn’t take place until near the end of the novel and there’s not much time left after that to explore the impact this terrible incident has on the rest of the Booth family. Neither are we given any real answers as to what went wrong with John Wilkes Booth and what led him to carry out the assassination. It’s hard to say why, coming from a family who were loyal to the Union and largely anti-slavery, it is only John who ends up supporting the Confederacy and opposing abolition. All we can do is make our own assessment based on the information we are given, through the eyes of his siblings, about his childhood, his relationships, his education and his political views. The novel has clearly been thoroughly researched (although in her author’s note, Karen Joy Fowler explains that as there’s very little information available on Rosalie Booth, it was necessary to use her imagination to fill in the gaps where Rosalie’s character is concerned). However, the book is incredibly detailed and this does slow the plot down a lot, particularly in the middle. We are also given some biographical information on Abraham Lincoln himself and on the events that lead to the Civil War and his presidency. These sections are interspersed with the Rosalie, Edwin and Asia chapters and are presented as non-fiction, which I didn’t really like as I felt it disrupted the flow of the story. Despite the negative points I’ve just mentioned, I loved this novel. Even the use of present tense and heavy foreshadowing didn’t put me off. I enjoyed learning about a group of historical figures I’d previously known almost nothing about – I particularly liked the parts about the colourful theatrical careers of Edwin and Junius Brutus – and every time I picked the book up I looked forward to finding out what would happen to the family next. I haven’t read anything else by Karen Joy Fowler, not even We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves, but having enjoyed this book so much I’ll consider reading some of her others now.

Karen Joy Fowler is not an especially prolific author, but when she writes a book, she writes the heck out of it. (You may remember award-winning and Booker-shortlisted novel We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves.) In this book, the author explains that she was struck by the headlines about (yet another) mass shooting and began to wonder about the family of the perpetrator: What can they do with their love for someone who has done something so heinous? And then she thought, why not choose perhaps the most reviled killer in US history: John Wilkes Booth, assassin of Abraham Lincoln? All it took was a bit of research to convince her that she’d found exactly the right subject. Wilkes was one of 10 children (six surviving into adulthood) of famed tragedian actor Junius Booth, the most acclaimed Shakespearean actor of his time in the US. But to call the family shambolic hardly begins to cover it. Junius was a womanizer and prodigious alcoholic, earning great sums and pissing it all away, leaving his family close to starvation at times while he was away on lengthy tours. Edwin, one of the brothers, followed in his father’s acting footsteps, eventually achieving as much success as his father had. John Wilkes also tried acting, but he was wildly unreliable, drunk and erratic and unable to learn his lines. There’s much that is known about the family and much that is indistinguishable from rumour and myth, but Fowler does an amazing job of fictionalizing this entirely fascinating brood, placing John Wilkes Booth firmly in context as just a beloved member of a family and the beliefs and context that might have driven him to the fateful moment in the Ford Theatre. Brilliantly researched, imagined, and written. I found it hard to put the book down and was sad to leave its deftly drawn world.

In her historical novel “Booth,” author Karen Joy Fowler examines the family that gave America two of its most acclaimed 19th Century actors, Junius Booth and son Edwin; and spawned its most infamous villain: John Wilkes Booth. I’ve always wondered how such a family could simultaneously produce such great talents and so evil a malefactor; and how both Junius’s and Edwin’s reputations could survive their son and brother's great crime. In “Booth,” Ms. Fowler strives to give us the answers. The story she tells is an interesting albeit cheerless one, filled with alcoholism, mental illness, ambition, financial instability, pridefulness, guilt, divided loyalty, shifting alliances, and family dysfunction. Junius is a great actor, but an awful alcoholic. Edwin must be his “minder” on tour, making sure his father shows up to perform and fees are sent home, denying his own future. But then he deserts his father and becomes just as bad a drunk; then marries; then loses his wife in childbirth; then, guilt-driven, gives up drinking to concentrate on his career to financially support the rest of the Booth family. John Wilkes is handsome and charismatic and a family favorite, but, unlike the family, is devoted to the South and a terrible racist and classist who hates Lincoln for being both a “tyrant” and his social inferior. Mother Mary struggles to keep the family together and housed and fed. Daughter Rosalie suffers from scoliosis and shyness, is resigned to spinsterhood, and likes her nip of gin. Daughter Asia would like to run the family and have veto power over the women her brothers choose to marry. With all this and more, it’s a story that has a lot going on. It’s also a story filled with strange but true facts and coincidences. For example, two years before the assassination, Lincoln saw John Wilkes Booth in a performance at Ford’s Theater and liked it enough to invite the actor to visit him at the White House (an invitation which JWB refused). And sometime before the assassination, Edwin Booth saved Lincoln’s son, Robert Todd Lincoln, from being crushed by a train (although he didn’t know it was RTL at the time. Indeed, he only learned that through a friend who served with RTL on General Grant’s staff.) And it’s a story steeped in theater: Shakespeare’s “Richard III,” “Hamlet,” “MacBeth,” and “Othello;” Tom Taylor’s “Our American Cousin;” famous actors of the day, including Edwin Forrest and Laura Keene; Ford’s Theater, The Winter Garden Theater, Philadelphia’s Walnut Street Theater (each still open today)—all appear in “Booth.” So, there are some very, very interesting components to this novel—lots of history to discover. But I found the writing somewhat unconventional for a novel. It’s very expository with relatively few attempts to create actual scenes. There’s very little dialogue—almost none. Not much attention is paid to setting. I never really got the sense of what it was like to be in a 19th Century theater or in any of the cities (e.g., Baltimore, D.C., London, San Francisco) where the novel takes place--what they looked like, how they smelled, etc. And the third-person omniscient narrator is not shy about expressing their opinion or stepping out of the story’s present to tell us what happens in the future. All of this had the effect of distancing me from the novel. At times it seemed I was reading a history class lecture rather than fiction. Then again, I enjoy learning about history. Those similarly inclined, and especially those with an interest in 19th Century theater, Shakespeare, the Booth family, Abraham Lincoln, the Civil War, the period leading up to and following it, and Lincoln’s assassination, should find a lot to absorb them in “Booth.” My thanks to NetGalley, the author, and the publisher for providing me with an ARC. The opinions expressed above are independent and my own.

This is historical fiction at its best. Compulsively readable, gorgeously written, with fully alive and complex characters. Fowler had her work cut out for her, choosing to focus on the notorious Booth family; they were (in)famous before John Wilkes. The book is heavy on description and very light on actual dialogue, which adds to a sort of dreamy distance. The family was tormented by ghosts from the beginning, setting each of them up to be a tragic character. This is not to say that the book is wholly sympathetic to the Booths; they are deeply flawed, broken people trying to make life worth living. As noted by my shelves, I received an e-galley of this book in exchange for my honest review.

The children of Junius Booth grow up in the shadow of their father's fame as both a Shakespearean actor and a drunken eccentric. Most of the sons aspire to a career in the theater, and Edwin will eventually be heralded as a great actor. Rosalie aspires to leave the family home one way or another, but she's needed at her mother's side. Asia aspires to a life of beauty and purpose, and she loves her family with fierce intensity, especially her brother John. As the favored child, John Wilkes is indulged despite getting into frequent trouble, because it's understood within the Booth family that he's destined for greatness. This novel is a wonderful addition to one of my favorite genres, historical fiction that closely follows the known facts of a person or event, but gets to invent the small moments and interior lives of the characters. The fascinating Booth family provided plenty of material for Fowler to draw on, but she also had plenty of room for invention, and she portrays each family member with care and nuance. As always in Fowler's writing, the narrative is full of sharp observations and dry humor that conveys the humanity of these historical figures, even the infamous assassin. The tension of reading toward a historically inevitable outcome pulled me through the pages, but I also kept wanting to slow down and savor the well-crafted paragraphs. BOOTH was everything I hoped it would be, and then some.

Writing: 4/5 Characters: 4.5/5 Plot: 4/5 What an unusual book. It is a fictionalized history of the Booth family from 1822 to 1865 when its most infamous member — John Wilkes — shot Abraham Lincoln. John Wilkes is kept as an important but minor character throughout until his action at the end tears everything apart. The story is told from the perspective of three of his siblings: “poor” Rosalie, the eldest daughter who remains a spinster family caretaker for life; Edwin, who becomes the leading tragedian of the 19th century; and Asia, the youngest daughter and eventual poet and writer. Fowler is a fantastic writer — every book she writes is completely different and spans topics and genres easily. In this — her first fictionalized history — she brings the place and time to life in incredible physical, political, and every day life detail. Following their lives in rural Maryland, Baltimore, and later Philadelphia, New York, and then California (including a harrowing description of the trip across the 40-mile Panamanian isthmus, pre-canal) we are immersed in the attitudes and experiences of a very different time. Fowler doesn’t modernize sentiments — we are treated to multiple attitudes towards women, immigrants, and slavery. Having read a lot about the time period, I found them to be accurate and comprehensive. As examples, the family’s patriarch — Junius Brutus Booth (a famous Shakespearean actor of the time) — didn’t like slavery but had two slaves; John Wilkes declaimed frequently on the value of slavery and the tyranny of the North; and various speeches (including Lincoln’s, Douglas’ and others) offer additional viewpoints. I had to keep remembering I was reading a book which while novel-like had to adhere to actual history so while some details seemed extraneous to the plot, they were not extraneous to the lives of those living through them. For me it was a bit of a slow start — I let myself be unhappy that I was having to read a book about someone I did not want to know more about and of course, knowing what happens at the end, I had a kind of dread creeping up on me. However, if you can avoid the kinds of destructive thoughts I was having, it really is gripping reading, and the assassination and aftermath actually takes up a very small part of the end of the book.

Booth is not a story about John Wilkes Booth. Instead, it follows the entire Booth family, from its troubled patriarch, the heralded stage actor Junius, to the eldest surviving child, the quiet spinster Rosalie, to the stubborn and beautiful Asia, to the passionate Edwin struggling to assert himself as heir to his father’s theatrical legacy. John is just one of the many characters in this story, a volatile, handsome young man loved fiercely by his siblings even when he begins to fall from grace. Repudiating his father’s tolerant views and his family’s loyalty to the Union, John steeps himself in sympathy to the Southern cause, while the rest of his siblings wrestle with their own changing affections, burgeoning careers, blossoming families, and decades-old sorrows. Karen Joy Fowler creates an unconventional structure to the story, sprinkling vignettes of Lincoln alongside scenes from the Booths’ lives. There are moments where the text skips into the future and back again into its present, the narrative adopting a meandering, omnipresent quality as the Booth family endures both tragedies and triumphs. 3.5/5: A unique work of historical fiction that humanizes the infamous family and JWB himself without eulogizing or excusing his actions. It was a bit too slow-paced for me, partly because I knew it was heading for the inevitable conclusion of the assassination. Some characters are more compelling than others, but each of the Booths manage to emerge as holistic individuals rather than caricatured or hollow interpretations. Booth is more a collection of musings on the concept of family than a straight-forward historical fiction novel, something that is likely to appeal to many readers. I found myself seeking something more solid and structured, but I also appreciated the creative and measured approach to such a tricky historical subject. Many thanks to NetGalley and the publisher for an ARC in exchange for an honest review.

Also not at all hard to imagine that within federal programs, recruitment of neo Nazis and other whites supremacy groups have infiltrated organizations and branches from DHS to ICE to FBI. Popcorn entertaining thriller with quick chapters to keep you invested and a linear plot that’s easy to follow. The author’s decision to have 60 chapters in 322 pages makes this book really easy to fly though, but that also gives the illusion that it’s better than it is because you’re flying through 5 page chapters. Make no mistake, Edge of Honor is fun and entertaining, but there’s nothing profound or different/unique/special that pushes it into higher ratings. Author Brad Thor alludes to various political tropes in 2025/2026’s US political landscape which is cool, and it’s nice that he isn’t directly recreating real people with his characters but rather taking some but not all of their traits (that really helps the characters feel standalone), but there isn’t anything profoundly political here. It’s just a simple, intriguing thriller, with that topical political backdrop. The popcorn entertainment of it all reminds me of the movie Olympus Has Fallen. Fun. Good. But that 6/10 spot is where it belongs. Now, I had two key issues with the book. None of these are groundbreaking or dramatic, I just didn’t like them and feel they’re worth mentioning. First, this book is annoyingly masculine. And I can’t believe I’m saying this because more often than not books are geared towards gals and not guys (more gals read anyway so it makes sense), so I would’ve thought it’d be nice to get away from the constant “but I have to choose between my quest/career or relationship/family and because I’m strong I choose career even though there is literally nothing stopping me from having both besides this weirdly hypocritical feminist rhetoric telling me I have to reject the patriarchy and choose career-only to be ‘strong’, but then I tell myself it’s ‘society keeping women down’ and ‘sexism’ when I’m sad about my decision while everyone else in the book is like wtf is wrong with you, no one made you do that shit, bro is just a city official he can take care of the kids and the house while you go on work trips…but you’re the protagonist so we celebrate that you’re sooooo ‘relatable’” (I have very major beef with that trope and how it’s in damn near every fantasy book I picked up at Barnes & Noble today, needed to get that off my chest). Based on that completely random and highly peeved ramble, you’d think I’d want a more masculine read, but this book is just annoyingly so. Like we get it you’re a “man’s man” who has killed a ton of people, has a hot blonde badass foreign wife, and you hate driving a V4 car, and are rough and tumble, and eat gross things, and love America, and have all these cool guns and gadgets, and everyone’s like “wow Scot you’re so cool”, blah blah (so fucking drab). At some point you’re just annoyingly cliche and there’s nothing interesting about your character whatsoever. I found that I cared about the story and the implications of what was happening, but not any of the characters. Second was the use of torture. First, I dislike it because it’s such a lazy cop out narratively. The issue of how the protagonists get the admissible information they need from uncooperative detainees with an imminent threat is RIPE for heart pounding drama; but nope, let’s just torture this guy, and this guy, and “oh you don’t wanna answer my questions, you too buddy!” It’s just such a cop out to get to a conclusion in lieu of a clever plot, and that’s not even getting into the fact I don’t support torture so I don’t like reading it. It’s the absolute worst side of humanity, and seeing it glorified bothered me. Usually other books do a good job of showing that side of things as an ugly reality (which makes it far more tolerable because it’s acknowledging how horrific the act is) but this book just jokes around with it and there’s almost no pushback from other characters or obstacles to prevent the torture from occurring. Call me soft, but fuck that. I feel weird generally liking a book but having my review be predominantly a discussion of my negatives, but that’s what happens when the positives are pleasant but unremarkable, and the two negatives draw my attention more. Think I’ve been spoiled coming off of two books I absolutely adored. 6/10

## The Book in 1 Sentence Harvath and his new bride take on a cabal of insiders threatening the world order. ## Brief Review This is an extremely short book, but does trickle in some of the more recent concerns with [a threat from within](https://www.durbin.senate.gov/newsroo...), rather than an external threat. The action is well paced and very well described with the right elements to keep you involved. A weird place to start the series, but if it is going to quasi-reset, then it works. ## Why I Read this book New book in one of my favorite series ## In-Depth Review (Favorite Quotes) Lets start with the "bad." This book was short compared to the other more recent ones, like 60 pages shorter than average-ish. You kind of feel it in the fact that you feel it is missing something. Not anything of value per se, buy just something. The story is still full and make sense, but maybe it is the ending and just a good bit taking place "off-the-page." Even with that, the pacing is good. The story itself is really interesting. To be honest, I feel it is one of the more plausible stories he has had. Between ego, corruption, fear, and broken promises, there is a lot here that speaks to what is going on now. With that, I also see an underlying issue with government and that is the institutional bureaucracy within the US Government and all the issues that come with that. Especially when people feel cheated out supporting this party or the other. Brad Thor had a series, I think it was only one stand-alone book with a couple ties ins to others, called "The Athena Project." The description of the female operative is really well done and I think could be a place for him to revamp and revitalize that series. It has a place in the world he has built kind of like [[Lioness]]. ## [Rating](https://epicscreentime.com/rating-rules) This might be one of my favorite in the series. It was short, but well paced. I also just really like Harvath and Sylvie's story together and how they work with and for each other. This is an 8. I really hope the series continues like this. Want to get a hold of me? Email |

It is hard to believe that EDGE OF HONOR marks the 24th novel from author Brad Thor to feature American hero and patriot, Scot Harvath. For me, it feels like just yesterday that I was blown away by the first novel, THE LIONS OF LUCERNE --- still my favorite Thor title. Scot Harvath is a newlywed and he and his wife Solvi have just finished six months of globe-trotting purely for pleasure before returning to life in high-stakes spy service for their respective countries of the U.S.A. and Norway. During their lengthy honeymoon there is a new political regime running the U.S. in the form of a new President who has promised to clean up the political landscape and thus far has only heightened the level of criticism from his opponents and those that did not vote for him. Couple that with a series of deadly explosions outside the Vice-Presidential residence that Scot and Solvi were in the middle of, and you quickly realize that something big is in play. One of the decisions made by the new regime was to cut the secret service protection provided to members of the prior Presidential team. This has some of them on the run to the point where some dangerous and well-armed trained killers are hunting them down even invading the location where the Ambassador to Norway resides in Washington D.C. Solvi is called into action to help protect her home countries representatives while Scot is nabbed by the Carlton Group, his employers, to locate and find whoever is behind the very precise and personal attacks being made against current and former political figures in this country. Harvath builds a formidable team of trusted allies around him but is shrewd enough to see that there is a high-stakes conspiracy reaching the highest level of government that he may be working at counterpoint to. His loyalty is to his country and leaders, those who threaten it and are not used to being able to tell who the good guys are. Internal hate groups including many members of national White Supremist groups may be involved along with those who are obviously special forces trained and making up the bulk of the threat to the peace that Harvath must correct. There are not many authors in this genre who truly have their pulse on the machinations of the global political landscape like Brad Thor does. With both domestic terrorism, external threats from long-standing enemies like Russia, and a growing faction of online terrorism, Scot Harvath definitely has his hands full in a situation that is far more complex than he expected while still being firmly planted in the current world we all live in. EDGE OF HONOR delivers! Reviewed by Ray Palen for Book Reporter

Brad Thor's latest installment in the Scot Harvath series is another adrenaline-fueled ride that, while not my absolute favorite, is a highly enjoyable and worthwhile read for fans. I found myself tearing through the pages, a testament to Thor's knack for crafting a compulsively readable narrative. What truly stands out in this book is the masterful way Thor weaves in current-day issues. The plot feels eerily ripped from the headlines, creating a sense of urgency and relevance that has never been more effectively executed in the series. It's a powerful reminder of why we turn to thrillers—they often reflect the anxieties and complexities of our real world. The character dynamics were a high point for me as well. The new FBI duo was a fantastic addition, bringing a fresh energy and a compelling subplot to the mix. Their chemistry and contributions were a welcome change of pace and a highlight of the story. On the other hand, the book does fall into a familiar pattern. While I understand this is the core appeal of the genre—the reliable formula we've come to love from authors like Thor and Vince Flynn—it's also worth noting that the unbelievable, almost superhero-like feats of characters such as Scot Harvath are a bright-light reminder that this is fiction and pure escapism. I did feel that the main antagonist was a bit underdeveloped. The villain was, for lack of a better term, "meh," and didn't feel as menacing or memorable as some of Harvath's past adversaries. Despite this minor criticism, the book is a great addition to the series. It's a quick, entertaining read that will satisfy long-time readers and get them excited for what's next.

I’ll start with quoting the end of the review made by another contributor herewith, namely “thewanderingjew”, who also gave a 3 star rating. Quote: “ The story sometimes seemed contrived as Solvi and Scot were always thrust into the same dangerous situation, often appearing like super-heroes. Scot seemed like he was always racing to protect both Solvi and the country. The dialog also seemed trite and filled with needless details to fill pages. The book was in need of editing to make it less confusing, easier to follow, and more exciting. There were far too many characters and diversions to follow the story comfortably.” Now more of my own opinion. I praise Brad Thor and I have deeply enjoyed all his Scot Harvath series. However, this one displays way too many intertwined stories and characters, plus the need to now always have Sølvi to somewhat save the day, along with or besides Scot is a bit too much. BT is a skilled writer, but he loses himself, and the reader, in way too many useless context descriptions, the book would have gained to lose like 25% of “bad fat”. Also, I’ll never stress enough how much, when you have such a strong character as Harvath, at least 80%, if not more, of the book should be showcasing him. Please sir Thor, and every other story teller, take example on either Jack Reacher’s or John Puller’s books (no need to name the authors I guess…), those are the epitome of maintaining the reader’s focus and excitement from page one to the end. I’m just saying …

Another very good action read which has Scot Harvath and his new bride Solvi running for their lives most of this story by Brad Thor. Scott & Solvi return to America after a 6 month honeymoon traveling and relaxing in some of the most beautiful places in the world AND that's when the wheels come off and they are both stuck in the middle of a deceptive war of politics, egos, powerplays and retribution that is one of the deadliest plots I have read in a long time.
