The story is mostly concerned with the affairs of Collins Braithwaite, a leading proponent of the anti-psychiatry movement of the 1960s and at one point known as "Britain's most dangerous man." At the beginning, the author tells us that he has come into the possession of several notebooks written by a former patient of Braithwaite's, who believes that he was the leading cause of her sister's suicide. The book then splits into two separate narratives. One gives us a biography of Braithwaite - his troubled upbringing, his study of psychology, his hellraising ways. The second storyline looks at the nameless narrator's attempts to investigate her sister's death. She becomes a patient of Braithwaite's under a false name, Rebecca Smyth. She exaggerates Rebecca's fragile emotional state, in the hopes that he will continue to treat her, and she in turn can learn more about him. But she begins to enjoy this alter-ego a little too much, and it threatens to take over her whole life. Once again, Mcrae Burnet takes pleasure in blurring the lines between fact and fiction. I had to do a quick Google to verify that Braithwaite was not in fact a real person, so convincing was his description. But I must admit that I didn't enjoy this book as much as the author's previous efforts. Not all of the story's mysteries were satisfactorily concluded, in my opinion. The biographical sections about Braithwaite were a little dry and pedestrian, for my tastes. Rebecca's descent into madness became harder to fathom and my interest waned. As I turned the last page, I wondered about the point of it all. Something to do with the nature of identity, but I couldn't summon the enthusiasm to think any further about it.

If you're like me, you may have read the blurbs about this and thought to yourself: "Charismatic psychotherapist? Fake identities and suicide? Meditations on sanity and truth itself in a narrative where the reader can't be certain of anything? This sounds great and mysterious and it probably has a lot of twists and unique storytelling and it was Booker longlisted and I need to read it right away!!! Well I'm here to tell you to cool off a bit, jeez. This is a pretty standard novel that is solid but not really all that surprising, and I would suspect that if you read this and got to the end, you'd close the book and let out a sound that would equate to an audio version of a shrug. The novel bounces back and forth between a traditional biography of said charismatic psychotherapist and the journals of a woman who is seeing the psychotherapist to get some insight into why her sister (who was also a client) committed suicide. The biography sections are fairly typical: they cover this pretty annoying guy who thinks he's a genius despite never doing anything to make that kind of claim, and basically charms his way into sleeping with a lot of women while also pissing off every person he comes into contact with. An unsympathetic character for sure, although mildly interesting to read about in a train-wreck kind of way. The journal parts are a little more interesting, because the author is clearly going nuts herself, operating in at least two different personalities at war with each other. However she is also kind of a bore, mostly detailing her conversations with our psychotherapist and vaguely talking about being thrilled by sex and bondage, despite never letting herself enter any kind of situation where that might remotely be a possibility for her. (Even having a drink (!) with a man (!!) causes her to completely meltdown.) A qualified psychotherapist would certainly have a field day with such a person, but of course, there are none in this book. Anyway things kind of fizzle out towards the end in predictable fashion, and sure, there might be some surface-level stuff going on here about the nature of self, identify as performance, we all wear masks, etc etc etc, but it doesn't live up to the expectations of the book's setup (nor the book's marketing blurbs), and it's just kind of an ok time. You're likely going to find both characters unsympathetic, so really your enjoyment will depend on how much you have fun with the structure (fake biographies that seem like they're real are always kind of fun) and the writing style. And those things are pretty good! But not particularly "dazzling" or "inventive". ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

This started out very intriguingly but in the end it has left me somewhat disappointed, with quite a few question marks and a puzzling feeling of what the point has been. Or have I been duped and toyed with like the author GMB? The book explores the merits of psychiatry and essentially alternates between fragments from contemporary notebooks and a biography about the forgotten therapist Braithwaite. Disappointingly the notebooks and biography don't come together in the end, they sort of exist in parallel and the differences are too striking to decide what is 'true' (perhaps that was precisely the point?). I felt this needed a grand finale which didn't come. I had noted in his previous novels that GMB has a keen interest in and sharp eye for psychology - this is what lifted them above detective novels. Here, the focus is on psychiatry and the central theme appears to be that we we have a private self and a public self meaning we all play roles and try to see what story fits our personality best. This is an old theme and has been done better in my opinion (Gantenbein is a favourite of mine: at a certain point in life we all encounter a story we hold to be our own). I also found there was a strange disconnect between the Braithwaite of the notebooks and the Braithwaite of the biography. Socially skillful and arrogant as a therapist versus socially awkward and insecure in both his early and later life according to the biographer. I am not suggesting these conflicting traits cannot exist within the same person but it went beyond the believable. On a more positive note: I liked the tone and writing of the notebooks (Rebecca is a great character and fantastic unreliable narrator). I enjoyed the reading experience. I liked the 1960s setting. And the framing narrative once again worked very well to create tension even if the apotheosis was a letdown. But in the end I have to wonder what I have been reading. I also surely have missed some things as several questions remain unsolved for me, mostly regarding Veronica's suicide. As to the Booker, I find this less accomplished than its obvious companion 'Trust'...but neither experiment would make it to my shortlist.

I read Macrae-Burnet's Case Study as part of my catch up of books I hadn't got to that were longlisted for the 2022 Booker prize and caught my attention enough that I wanted to get to them, so this became part of my holiday reads pile in Jan this year. Set in 1960s England this pastiche style work plays with ideas of fiction, nestling within it various narrative forms, including historical documents, journals, psychiatric case studies, crime. It rifts throughout on RD Laing's anti-psychiatry movement, the history of psychology / psychiatry, philosophy etc. It encourages readers to speculate about the veracity of these various narrative sources as a 'story' is developed about an unnamed young woman,(with likely complex mental health challenges) approaching a psychotherapist, Collins Braithwaite, for sessions. Braithwaite is a somewhat disreputable character. We learn or at least initially assume that she's attending these sessions to explore her view that Braithwaite contributed to her sister's (Veronica) death (by suicide we presume), who was attending sessions with him. This story is recounted by a GMB (the initials of Graeme Macrae Burnet) who has got hold of this young woman's journal / note books (six of them) in which she recorded her account of these interactions with Braithwaite. GMB is interested in this as it contains allegations concerning Braithwaite and his practices and he's exploring the possibility of researching and writing a biography of Braithwaite in context of anti-psychiatry movement. Does he have in his hands source material that can give his study the edge he's been looking for? Some of my own research revals that GMB is also the 'writer researcher' of Macrae-Burnet's earlier work, His Bloody Project. So we get multi-layered representation, with nested fictions, all very metafictional / metatextual. To deceive Braithwaite this young woman takes on an identity as Rebecca Smyth, a confident even alluring young woman about town (very different from whom we understand to be this woman's unassuming life at home supporting / caring for her widowed father). So the metaficitonal games ramp-up with readers increasingly wondering who is this character, which is the 'real' version (whatever that means in the context of such a work); is 'she' a construction and fabricated to entice and trick GMB into trying to tell this tale, just as 'she' was seeking to entice and trick Braithwaite with her fabricated, performance of Rebecca Smyth. But is Rebecca Smyth perhaps really the core of this character's identity and being, her 'repressed self', and the more demure self the 'fake' that needs to be unmasked. And on it goes. How can we trust any of it as even in the journals she shares that she also kept 'fake journals/ diary' to deceive her mother, who she knew was snooping and reading them. So again, how do we know we readers, snopping over the shoulder of GMB, aren't being presented with a wonderfully elaborate and persuasive set of nested fakes? What if the notebooks are satire, playing with the gender stereotypes that proliferate through them (many entries are quite misogynistic, perhaps reflecting a young woman internalising that from 1960s culture). I don't mean to be totally dismissive of this. The metafictional architecture with its intricate narratives works quite well, I found it interesting to think my way through the various possible pathways. It holds-up in terms of a device to explore appearance and reality in context of psychiatry and 1960s England. It's well written and pulled me along, it had something of a psychological thriller feel to it as well, so also games here with genre. Maybe it was the reading mood I was in at the time, but I just didn't overly care enough about this one and where it ends up. Some reviewers have found it even funny and I see that quality, but I'm not convinced it brings anything much new to the table through the metafictional play (and I generally quite enjoy metafictional experiments). In my view many other far better books on the 2022 Booker Prize list.
all the characters think of themselves far too much but there were some great sentences in the jumble of it all

For me the star rating lands somewhere between a 4 and a 4.5. The full post is here: https://www.readingavidly.com/2022/08... I bought Case Study long before the announcement that it had been selected for this year's Booker Prize longlist, and like the vast majority of books that come into this house, I shelved it and promptly moved on to something else. That was October of last year; last week's above-mentioned announcement reminded me that it has just been sitting there and maybe it was time to read it, not because it landed on the longlist but because I've really enjoyed Graeme Macrae Burnet's previous novels. As was the case in those books, Case Study blurs the lines between fact and fiction, so much so this time around that I found myself spending way too much time doing google searches while reading. Set in 1960s England, Case Study unfolds in two parallel narratives, beginning with the author's ("GMB") receipt of an email from a Martin Grey in Clacton-on-Sea. As revealed in the Preface, in Glasgow's "notoriously chaotic Voltaire and Rousseau bookshop," "GMB" had run across a copy of a book written by Collins Braithwaite, who'd made an impression as "something of an enfant terrible" among those in the "so-called anti-psychiatry movement" of the 1960s. The book, Untherapy, described by GMB as "salacious, iconoclastic and compelling," collected case studies; Grey's email turned what was at first an interest in Braithwaite on GMB's part into a "properly aroused" curiosity. Grey explained that he had learned about GMB's interest in Braithwaite after reading a blog post GMB had written; he then claimed to have come into possession of a series of notebooks written by his cousin containing "certain allegations about Braithwaite" that GMB might like to read. At first refusing, GMB ultimately accepted the offer and the notebooks were sent to him. He was still not convinced, but after expressing his skepticism to Grey, he decided that since the notebooks "dovetailed" with his own research "it seemed too apposite to resist." The result is Case Study, which alternates between the content of the notebooks and GMB's biography of Collins Braithwaite. The author of the notebooks, as GMB discovers, is a young, unnamed woman whose sister Veronica, she was convinced, committed suicide two years earlier after several sessions with Braithwaite. After reading the psychologist's Untherapy and although he'd changed his patients' names, she discovered more than one link between a particular "Dorothy" and her sister. She'd thought she might go to the police, but realizing she had nothing to offer them, she decided instead to go directly to Braithwaite himself. As she says at one point, "Suicides make Miss Marples of us all," and eager to learn more about Braithwaite, her sister and the method "in Dr. Braithwaite's apparent madness," she decided that the only way to find out more about this man was to make an appointment with him. Realizing she can't go in as Veronica's sister, she took on another persona, an alter-ego if you will -- Rebecca Smyth -- who is quite literally everything our unnamed notebook writer is not and has gone forth with her mission in a quite naïve fashion, not knowing quite what to expect. Alongside the story, as the dustjacket cover notes reveal, the author brings out themes dealing with "the nature of sanity, identity and truth itself." More importantly, the idea of what actually constitutes a self runs throughout the book, with ongoing references to topics including doppelgangers and the notion of private vs. public persona. Despite the seriousness of these ideas, there are also some wickedly funny moments to be found here, and the ending found in the postscript was for me one of those rare out-loud "wtf" moments. I had great fun with this book, especially in trying to figure out what was real and what was fiction, which wasn't always easy, but this is the sort of out-there novel I tend to enjoy. Confession time: I admit that it wasn't too long into the book that I started googling Collins Braithwaite, and from what other readers have to say about this book, I wasn't alone. Case Study is cleverly constructed, very well written, and for me, insightful, but above all it was highly entertaining. It's a book I can certainly recommend with no hesitation.

This was a particularly excellent novel. Worth noting that the author published a blog post before this books release, in which he was effectively playing a narrative voice. I read it before even hearing of the book's release, I won't risk spoiling it, but this small detail I particularly love, signs that he is going above and beyond to make Case Study a compelling read. No irony is lost on Burnet. Well worth checking out on his Goodreads page before you read the book. The main narrative voice grated at first but I soon got used to it. A character study rather than a thriller, this will suit those interested in psychology, and novels which explore complexity of character, specifically around moral subjects, such as Crime and Punishment. The writer is open hearted and able to explore the inner lives of a wide variety of personality types. This book experiments with narrative voice, same as his other works, and is wickedly funny. What is done particularly well is the blend of fact and fiction. Some passages in the first 75 or so pages felt frivolous at first, however contained subtleties that were later built upon.

So I read this as a buddy read (which was immense fun) so the novel was split into 5 sections which I think really ratcheted the intrigue and tension up. For me this book is an absolute triumph and how it did let make it onto the Booker shortlist is simply incomprehensible. We are introduced to the book by the author who gives a brief explanation of how he came to have the notebooks that make up some of the narrative. The rest is a biography of the psychotherapist. It quickly becomes evident that Braithwaite, the psychotherapist, and the unnamed writer of the notebooks are maybe not quite who they seem to be. We then embark upon a roller coaster ride detailing the lives of both. I liked the end but opinions in the buddy read group were divided. However I loved this book. The writing and the premise are interesting and original. I immediately downloaded His Bloody Project by the same author. I'd highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys something a little different to a conventional story.

I'm very much in the minority with my low rating of this Booker Prize shortlisted title. Case Study opens with the author informing us that he is writing a biography of the radical psychiatrist Collins Braithwaite, who became a celebrity in the 1960s. The excerpts of CB's life story is alternated with six notebooks supposedly written by one his previous clients. I agree with everyone else that the author does a brilliant job in creating a non-fiction feel in this novel by immersing and surrounding the fictional character with people and events genuinely from the 60's. Some of his ideas on identity - Don't kill yourself. Kill your Self - was somewhat interesting. But mostly I felt bored while reading this. To be fair maybe it's just too clever for me.

The following reviews have been shared by Text Publishing - publisher of Case Study ‘An unparalleled joy.’ Fullers Weekly 'A thrilling investigation into sanity and identity.’ Bookseller 'Fun and funny, sly and serious, a beguiling literary game that manages to say more about the nature of the self than any number of more self-consciously solemn works.' David Szalay ‘A novel of mind-bending brilliance. Case Study was an interesting concept executed well, a story told through diary entries and existential observation with a central character who is intricate in her personality and intriguing to read. It is compelling on many levels but for me personally the writing was a little top heavy at times making the story a slow burn rather than highly addictive but it was beautifully done. Overall a good read that just took me a while to get through.

Case Study has an interesting premise. A young woman discovers a case study in a book by a psychotherapist, which she believes describes her sister who recently committed suicide. The novel itself is framed as a piece of non-fiction by 'GMB', which consists of the 'notebooks' left by the young woman interspersed with biographical sections written by GMB about A. Collins Braithwaite, the psychotherapist. Early on, the young woman explains that she believes that Collins Braithwaite had played a role in her sister committing suicide and that she decided to visit the psychotherapist in order to get further answers and ultimately to expose him. However, the rest of the 'notebooks' contain essentially no reference to these supposed aims. It becomes apparent fairly early that the young woman is an unreliable & unlikeable narrator who finds it very difficult to feel any empathy whatsoever for other people. In fact, she avoids feeling anything at all and sees herself, with her outmoded ways of doing things, as superior to those around her. Despite this, she enjoys creating a fictional self, initially in order to conceal her identity from Collins Braithwaite. The biographical sections about Collins Braithwaite also describe a fundamentally unreliable & unlikeable person, but from a third person perspective. Both the notebooks and the biography are quite conventionally written. In particular, the notebooks read more like a first-person novel than diary entries. None of the novel's initial questions really get answered, and the ending brings us back more or less to the place we started with a flash forward to the future tacked onto the end. There are some interesting explorations of psychiatric treatment in the mid-20th century and ideas of the self. The ending seems to want to say something about these ideas, but it feels rushed, like an afterthought.

I was excited to read this faux/factual narrative about an unconventional psychotherapist and a ‘patient’ investigating her sister’s suicide. As expected, nothing in this novel is as it seems on the surface. The conceit that blurs fact and fiction works less effectively than I’d hoped. Ultimately while I found both narrative threads separately interesting, even compelling, the clashing styles in which they are written made it challenging for me to find a rhythm in this reading experience. It might be more a sign of my pea-brain than an indictment of the book itself.

Huge fun, taking you back to the mid-60s and swinging London and the anti-psychiatry movement (RD Laing features heavily, I remember friends having copies of Knots in the early 70s), which proposes that mad people may be saner than their physicians (depicted as jailers). Lyons tea shops, corner pubs all jollily described, and engaging characters (particularly the monstrous Braithwaite), but I did feel it petered out a bit at the end, stories were not resolved (eg Tom the boyfriend) and this was the sort of book that needed resolution.

??? Brilliant and befuddling, a slow descent into the madness of self and attempting to grasp one's elusive identity as told through the eyes of two mentally ill characters. At least, I think that's what I read? This novel was so utterly compelling that I was glued to the pages with morbid curiosity, both loving and hating it at the same time. There is more than one unreliable narrator, and the only sane glimpses are from outsiders looking in, but since they are still told from these two narrators' POV, perspectives are constantly muddled. Yet, that's the whole point. First off, the question of "Rebecca"...is she simply pretending to pose as an alter ego when meeting with a charlatan psychiatrist to discover if he was responsible for his sister's suicide, or was she the Divided Self of a dissociative identity aka multiple personality? What was real? Rebecca meets and interacts with several men, but I honestly don't know if they were hallucinations or her warped sense of reality. Still, her explanation of wanting to act differently than the prison of her own making is actually a very freeing thought - there's always a part of us that wishes we could just act like an anonymous other for a day and be someone that we simply don't have the courage to be. So, I enjoyed this because I felt like I was living vicariously through her. But then, she has a total mental breakdown, and I realize I don't really want that persona all that much. Second, was the charlatan psychiatrist Braithwaite a full-on narcissistic con man or truly brilliant mad scientist? Burnet uses notebooks dropped into his lap and fleshes out Collins Braithwaite based on what he had scribbled and books that he wrote, piecing together pieces of a puzzle that are probably more bizarre than the actual truth. I suppose Braithwaite's character is part fiction/part truth, though I'm not sure which is which. Granted, Burnet inserts many sexual overtones which has always been the main focus of psychoanalysis, so things get unapologetically a bit spicy here and horrifically unethical for a therapist. If you want to stay away from some graphic scenes, suffice it to say this may not be for you. Nothing in this book, even from the first line, is as it seems, and honestly reminds me a bit of Plath's The Bell Jar with its dark undertones and mix of mental illness that is pervasive throughout but yet seems also so lucid and clear that I have no idea what to think anymore. This is one of the few books that I started to reread immediately to catch all the nuances and layers that I am certain I missed. I completely understand why this earned the Booker Prize, and I will certainly look out for Burnet in the future.

Case Study begins with Graeme Macrae Burnet telling the readers that he had acquired a series of notebooks belonged to a young woman who was a patient of the “untherapist”, Dr. Braithwaite. The owner of the notebooks is convinced that Dr. Braithwaite is responsible for her sister’s death and in order to find out the truth, she disguises herself as a “nutter” and poses herself as a patient. This is a pretty decent read. You know it was gonna be a fun reading experience when the first page of the book has you tilting your head in confusion and wondering if it’s based on a true story. Case Study is entirely fictional but the story is crafted like a biography that it had me google several individuals and incidents while reading it. I have to applaud the author for that. I find myself enjoying it although the second half of the plot didn’t work quite as well as the first. It was a little dry and repetitive for my tastes and I felt that like the story didn’t really go anywhere. The story was set in the 1960s in London but I didn’t find it particularly compelling and convincing. Overall, I think the concept of this book is wonderfully intriguing but I simply wanted more.

3.5 stars. Burnet is so clever at this style of novel (like His Bloody Project). Using ‘found’ documents to recreate a historical novel like this is very immersive and feels totally plausible. Braithwaite, his protagonist, is an extremely unlikeable character and it was difficult to feel any empathy for him. The star of this novel was his other protagonist, “Rebecca”. The humour her character imparts (a scene in a bar was particularly good) and her unraveling personality provide a perfect foil for the sparse matter of fact recount of Braithwaite’s rise and fall in the world of psychiatry. It almost felt like the psychiatric sessions caused “Rebecca” to descend into a mental health crisis that felt something like severe depression and a split personality rolled into one. This was an intriguing way to examine the ‘hit and miss’ development of psychiatry. There must have been a lot of casualties along the way.

this book expands the boundaries of fiction, i truly believed these characters were real throughout reading it. it’s certainly engrossing and humorous, the narrative voice of Rebecca Smyth is both naïve and cutting; i found her misplaced opinions on mental illness annoying at first, but i think that just shows how talented Burnet is at creating her character. this is a captivating study on psychoanalysis and identity, very well written.

Compelling yet fizzles towards the end. A mind-bending and bamboozling journey in the human psyche, Graeme Macrae Burnets Case study was longlisted for the Booker Prize 2022. I loved how the novel plays around with what’s fact and fiction, what exists and what doesn’t, and who’s mental and whos sane. The novel encourages you to look more closely and what’s fact vs fiction. At times, I found myself Googling if some of the events actually took place, forgetting that I was reading a work of fiction. Though halfway through, I did feel the novel fizzling out. What was once engaging, became repetitive and filled with huge chunks of exposition. Rather than continuing on to become a gripping thriller, the novel goes back and forth between different timelines/sections, losing its main focus. Unfortunately, by the end, I grew a bit bored and wanted the novel to end. Overall, the novel was alright, but I have to say, I’ve never read anything quite like it (in a good way).

At times compelling and thought-provoking, and at other times a bit too slow and tedious which caused me to loose interest but I'm pleased that I persevered because overall it's turned out a good read.

2022 BOOKER PRIZE LONGLIST CASE STUDY by Graeme Macrae Burnet The shortlist was announced last Tuesday and CASE STUDY did not make the final six. Burnet was previously shortlisted for his novel HIS BLOODY PROJECT and he once again entered the Booker fold with his follow up, a slick and tightly constructed psychological thriller of sorts that somewhat failed to close the deal. Doing something meta, Burnet projects himself in the novel, receiving an amateur manuscript from a mysterious source recounting the exploits of a charlatan psychotherapist Colins Brathwaite and his role in pushing his patients to suicide. The manuscript authored by an unnamed person whose nom de plum is Rebecca Smyth accounts how her sister took her life after seeing Brathwaite and Smyth deciding to see Brathwaite herself to find out if he played a nefarious role in her demise. Interspersed with the manuscript are Burnet’s own fictional research into the rise and fall of Brathwaite in the 1960s and 1970s. Although I liked CASE STUDY more than HIS BLOODY PROJECT it did not hold up for the entirety of its 276 pages. Initially feeling like one of those unreliable female narrator novels so popular a few years ago (think GIRL ON THE TRAIN and ELIZABETH IS MISSING) it nicely meanders through its plot, creating doubts about Smyth’s account while not revealing too much. However, the third act doesn’t come together as well as one would hope. One reveal felt predictable and the other much too cheeky. Burnet is a good writer but failing to seal the deal left me less impressed with the novel than I had found myself during the first 100 pages. CASE STUDY did not make the shortlist and I wouldn’t have placed it there but nonetheless a decent if somewhat disappointing work. #books #bookstagram #igbooks #bookerprize #bookerprize2020 #novels #unreliablenarrator #britishliterature #bookstagramreadsthebooker

‘Towards the end of 2019 I received an email from a Martin Grey of Clacton-on-Sea.’ After writing a blog post about the now forgotten and disgraced 1960s psychotherapist, Collins Braithwaite, the author receives an email from Martin Grey. Mr Grey has a series of notebooks written by his cousin which he considers might form the basis of an interesting book. While the author’s initial response is to decline, Mr Grey believes that there are certain allegations in the notebook which might interest him. The author had been contemplating a biography of Braithwaite but had received little enthusiasm thus far. The author receives five notebooks which he read in a day. The notebooks, written in 1965, allege criminal malpractice by Braithwaite. And so, the story begins. The diarist, a young woman, is convinced that Dr Braithwaite killed her sister Veronica two years earlier. Veronica had been consulting Dr Braithwaite and the diarist believes he is responsible for Veronica taking her own life. The diarist has read a case study in Braithwaite’s book ‘Untherapy’, ad is convinced the patient described is her sister Veronica. She assumes an alter ego, Rebecca Smyth, and presents as a client in Dr Braithwaite’s rooms. Macrae Burnet takes us on an interesting journey through a maze of delusions, secrets, and questions about identity. Braithwaite is egotistical and unlikeable while the diarist starts to assume (for real) the deeply troubled Rebecca she has chosen to present to Braithwaite. ‘She sometimes seemed to forget that without me she would not even exist, but (for once) we were getting on, it did not seem wise to remind her of this.’ References to the psychiatry practiced by R.D. Laing help ground this novel in the 1960s. The (is he fictional, or simply representative?) Braithwaite is jealous of Laing and Laing is contemptuous of him. The novel shifts between biographical details of Braithwaite and the five notebooks. What is real? What happens to the diarist? Braithwaite is a dangerous charlatan, and his end should come as no surprise — fiction can be wonderful sometimes. Once again, Macrae Burnett creates a story that feels so real that I want more information about Braithwaite. But I also want to know what happened to the diarist. I was intrigued by the story, fascinated by the characters, and finished the novel wanting (but not needing) more. Note: My thanks to NetGalley and Text Publishing for providing me with a free electronic copy of this book for review purposes. Jennifer Cameron-Smith

Given the monastic pacing of Charlotte Wood’s “Stone Yard Devotional,” I suppose it’s appropriate that we’ve had to wait patiently for it. Wood’s fellow Australians have been praising this story about a small abbey of nuns since the novel was published in 2023. Last year, it was a finalist for Britain’s Booker Prize. And now, as though publishing were operating by steam ship, “Stone Yard Devotional” has finally arrived in the United States. It’s just as extraordinary as the whispers from abroad suggested. But don’t recommend it to your book club because if some of your members don’t like it — and some certainly won’t — you may not have the stamina to tolerate them any longer. The unnamed narrator of “Stone Yard Devotional” is a woman of a certain age who’s joined a remote Catholic order — or, if not joined, at least moved in. With a caustic sense of wit and an unrelenting critical eye, she’s hardly the typical postulant. She’s troubled by “the savagery of the Catholic Church.” Shoveling compost is the closest she ever gets to prayer. She’s nauseated by sisters prattling on about how they “fell in love with Jesus.” Nobody asks, but she confesses that she’s an atheist. And yet, for all the narrator’s self-conscious rejections of religion, “Stone Yard Devotional” is a deeply spiritual novel. Marilynne Robinson’s Calvinist heart might protest, but this tale of sojourn among the nuns is founded on the same rock of introspection that anchors the “Gilead” series. It’s a years-long night wrestling with an angel capable of dislocating a thigh or a life. Wood’s narrator pursues fundamentally spiritual concerns: What is our purpose? Can we be forgiven for acts of callousness and neglect? Why are we here? Another navel-gazer, another endless musing best suited to a private journal or writing retreat. I long for crackling, sharp-edged writing that captivates and entertains instead of endless show-don’t-tell tactics and techniques.

Reader, I wanted to love it more than I did. Wood is an interesting author who is able to write compellingly obscure stories. However, the deeply reflective nature of this one didn’t work with the lack of narrative drive for me. There are some really interesting ideas here, about eschewing capitalism and the modern world for isolated introspection, and the role of ritual in helping us cope with, and/or avoid global and personal issues. I found moments of the consideration of these ideas interesting but this didn’t work for me as a whole.

'Nobody knows the subterranean lives of families'. Lying amid the stark, desolate surroundings of Monaro, is a place of quiet stillness: a cloistered community of nuns. Drawn to this austere, tranquility, so near to the town of her childhood, is a woman who has deliberately decided to delete her previous city life: her husband, friends, and job, 'I had a need, an animal need, to find a place I had never been but which was still, in some undeniable way, my home'. Being so near her old childhood home increasingly challenges her memories and beliefs. They erupt and multiply as drastically as the plague of mice invading their home and town, 'The mouse plague is infecting everything now: all sense of smell, of course, but even sound, even memory'. 'Stone Yard Devotional', is a contemplative story related in a series of short paragraphs, filled with reflection and wondering. The reader is never properly introduced to the main character, her name is never given and her past is only revealed in glimpses throughout. There really is no beginning and there is no end. However, the anonymity of the MC allows the reader to read the thoughts as their own. For me, it was the musing that made this story compelling. I have never read any of Charlotte Wood's previous books, but I did enjoy the desolation, the reflections, and the ruminations in this book. Overall, a compelling, contemporary book.
Watch out for this one. If there is one book that can take this year's Booker from Percival Everett's James, this is the one.

Longlisted for the Booker Prize 2024 I'm glad I went back to the audiobook and put aside my apprehension that this would be a s0-called "spiritual" novel. The Booker Prize longlisting of this short novel convinced me I should give it another chance. A middle-aged, childless woman leaves her job, interests, city life, her dying marriage, and moves close to where she grew up, in a small town. She somehow manages to move into a small Catholic monastery, inhabited by nuns. Interestingly enough, the narrator is not religious. The life is simple, preoccupied with survival, domesticity, and rituals. There's a horrendous mouse plague that lasts years (based on real-life events). Also, there is a famous nun coming to live at the monastery. Wood weaved seamlessly between the daily grind and the past, with little snippets of moments and events, showing how memory is so strange, certain seemingly small things we remember for decades. The back-and-forth examines life, sorrow, guilt, grief. The marriage and the relationships with men are brushed over, they're not analysed in great detail, which I guess is fair enough, I appreciate the author's choice of not centrering men in the character's life. This is a quiet, navel-gazing kind of novel that will appeal to some more than others. My appreciation of this novel was greatly enhaced by Ailsa Piper's beautiful narration.

Longlisted for the 2024 Booker Prize. For me this is a dark, ambiguous novel. Exploring the themes of grief and our own mortality. The narrator and protagonist of this novel is never named but you get a strong feeling that this narrator is the author or at least a vehicle used to express the author’s memories and experiences. We never truly find out why the narrator has left her husband, her job, her very way of life, and retreated to a religious community of nuns in the role of an oblate (I had to look up what an oblate is 😊). It cannot be for religious belief because she is an atheist. While not moving for religious reasons, it seems she may have moved for spiritual calmness and contemplation, enveloped in the nun’s world of prayer and routine. A way to stop and take stock of her life. Not long after the move, the nunnery is besieged by a plague of mice. This plague succeeds in creating a horrible claustrophobic atmosphere. As time passes the mice increase in number and eventually encroach on almost every facet of life for the community. I am not sure what this plague is meant to represent, if anything at all. I believe that Wood wrote this during the Covid pandemic, and the novel is set during this pandemic, so perhaps the plague is a representation of her feelings at the time. Or maybe they represent us, devouring everything in their path as they multiply uncontrollably trying to satiate an equally uncontrollable lust. Wood never lets the reader become bored, a distinct possibility with the setting, but fills the narrative with memories and flashbacks of the narrator’s life. She contemplates about the losses she has endured and the resulting grief. Meanwhile, the world outside the narrator’s thoughts is eventful. There is the mice plague, there is the arrival of a nun who turns out to be a woman that the narrator and friends bullied while at school. As you can imagine this nun adds to the narrator’s thoughts, primarily grief and guilt. No relationships are developed between the narrator and the nuns this book is very much about the narrator and her thoughts, memories, grief, reflection and contemplation.

Stone Yard Devotional strikes me as a very typical Booker book: chilly, elegant, balancing passages of banality against plainly stated emotion, with a pinch of oddness. I really liked parts of it, specifically the way the narrator discusses her relationship with her parents and enduring grief over their deaths. At its strongest, this narrative can be haunting. Overall, however, I’m left with the feeling that it’s less than the sum of its parts. (Probably should note, though, that I read this by switching between the ebook and audiobook, which may have magnified the sense that it was disjointed and/or overly digressive.)

Review to come, but for now: This started off very strong; middle was muddled; end section was great. Wish the whole book was like Part 1 and 3. But anyway, here’s a great quote for now: “But still, it has surprised me, over the years, to discover how many people find the idea of habitual kindness to be somehow suspect: a mask or a lie.”

(Book 4 of my Journey through the booker prize longlist ) 4.75 ⭐️ When I saw that the booker prize longlist came out I decided to challenge myself to read as much as I can before the shortlist was decided, I find it so exciting to be able to try and predict the winner, however; since there is 13 books on the longlist I know I will not be able to get through them all & I had to prioritise the books I think sound the most intriguing… along comes an Australian book Stone Yard Devotional “To find my parents, I had to recall the cold, unsheltered feeling I had - physically, I mean - at each of their funerals. There had been the sensation of too much space around me there, at the place where my father, then later my mother, were sent into their adjacent shafts of opened earth. (It seemed callous to me back then to lower a person into a hole in the ground using ropes and cords instead of arms)” Stone Yard Devotional was BRILLIANT. A story about a woman as she turns her back on her marriage and her life in Sydney and retreats to her hometown, where she resides with a group of catholic nuns. During the peak of covid she navigates her days introspectively and routinely. Doing chores and blending into the nuns daily structure, so much so she starts to just slowly fade and accept her new life, when suddenly a mouse plague infests the town. I can’t begin to tell you how incredibly captivated I was at this novel. The way it was written was so beautiful, with overall themes being grief and isolation. Following this main character as she just goes about her day to day duties, having to fight off the mice that plague her town, the exhaustion and dread of hearing them in the walls, never leaving. Seeing faces from her childhood and having to deal with old wounds and memories. Grappling with the grief of her parent’s death and the abandonment of her marriage, incredible! I finished this in 2 days. There isn’t a huge amount of plot, which seems to be the case with the past few books that I’ve read in the Booker prize longlist, such as Headshot & Orbital. Written like a diary, with an unnamed main character, I felt still incredibly connected and involved in this story. A great representation of Australian writing, from the first page until the end I loved it.

A core impacting novel. When I finished Stone Yard Devotional, I had many thoughts and ideas shooting off inside my mind. In fact my mind felt like it was caught in the middle of old west gun battle. Firstly, I don't know if I dreamt the setting for Stone Yard Devotional or had long conversations with my mum years ago, about visiting a NSW rural convent to have an immersive experience. For many years I've sprouted to friends and family, I'm the atheist nun. I've my reasons, beyond a fascination with ritual, sacrifice, and austere living. The question at the heart of Stone Yard Devotional is forgiveness, how does forgiveness work? Especially self forgiveness? A daughter - mother relationship that comes into its own, in analysis, analysis that leans into the stories that happen around us, and with us. The observations that are often only made many years later. Understanding that's only possible (perhaps) when time has past. As for grief - some of us are knitted with it. Grief is not other. Grief frames process, ways of living, and even choices. Solitude is a vehicle to understanding Solitude is the miracle Stone Yard Devotional is my favourite Charlotte Wood novel, to date. It will sit with me always, and it will live on my shelf - there anytime I need it.

I read this book quickly. It’s meditative and moody and I found myself going with the lack of explanations. It’s a book about forgiveness, death, memory, loss and despair which sounds really grim but it was quite a beautiful read. The narrator goes to stay with a small community of nuns even though she says she’s an atheist. Initially she visits for a five day retreat then returns to stay. She reveals some background to her life, that she’s broken up with her husband, that her parents died when she was young and some stories of her childhood and that she worked at a threatened species rescue centre. There’s a bit more to the story (like a mouse plague!) but I don’t think it’s a plot really. Strangely I didn’t mind, perhaps the reflections on life and the world just fit my own mood.
Brilliant. I will think about it for a long time.

Our unnamed narrator has retreated from her marriage and engagement with society and the environmental issues that filled her life, to a small religious order near the rural Australian community in NSW where she grew up. She is not religious, she doesn't pray, and the order does not have a "mission" such as nursing or teaching, so her days are filled just with quietly living, entering chapel every couple of hours, cooking and eating. The reader is left unsure about how her despair could have been so deep to drive her to this, but here she is. Shift to years later amid the Covid pandemic, and three events happen: the body of a missing nun of the order who went to Thailand to help exploited women is found, a celebrity nun of the order whom our narrator knew as a school girl is bringing her "home" for burial, and a plague of mice caused by drought has risen, with which the nuns and the whole area have to contend. This is a quiet story as you'd expect from the title, and the narrator's emotional life is not, what word is right, bounteous, but she's willing to give everyone the benefit of the doubt, generous enough to suspend judgment and assume good intentions of others, and humble in remembering her own failings or transgressions and not repeat them. Her life has become gentle and almost admirable, though personally I wouldn't appreciate the ultra processed foods the nuns bulk buy. It's not a utopian ideal, but it suits her and helps her go on. Living through a literary plague of mice certainly makes me hope I never have to live through one. What we are going to have to cope with due to climate change might be worse. There's a warning for us.
turns out i read this in one sitting too. a stunning mediation on life, loss, grief and trying to make sense of it all

Some interesting musings,but as a whole,it's rather aimless and weak. Starts from nowhere (which isn´t a bad thing) and goes nowhere. Definitively not Booker winner material,which this was shortlisted for.

3.5 stars I enjoyed this quiet book, and honestly thought it was a memoir until I was finished. After the fact, I found out by reading some articles about the book that it is indeed fiction. The unnamed narrator chooses to leave the city and her husband (it is hinted at why, but never fully explained by the author) to live at a monastery. The book is set in New South Wales. The Narrator reflects on different scenes from her life (the narrator is older, possibly 70s, it is not fully clear) those of which involves regrets, grief and forgiveness. She recalls different situations from her past, many involving her mother, her school friends and her childhood. Weaved into her reminiscing is her present day life which mostly centers around 2 main events. A horrible mouse plague that has taken over the monastery (and surrounding country) and the return of the remains of a deceased sister from the convent. I really enjoyed the slower pace and reflections found in this unassuming book. It is meandering, but in a good way, and the narrator is often troubled by her past. (Aren't we all?). Humor was sprinkled throughout to lighten the mood when the narrator would speak on the various circumstances surrounding the mouse plague. How horrifying. The author writes with clarity and ease, giving voice to an uncommon protagonist. Her thoughtfulness and care is evident throughout the book. Definitely recommend for lovers of : somewhat slower burns, literary fiction, grief and forgiveness related subjects, and those who aren't horrified by mouse plagues

After her husband leaves the country, our unnamed narrator spends a few days as a guest at a Catholic abbey, where she finds solitude and rhythm amongst the daily routines of prayer. Inexplicably (literally, we are never told why), she herself comes to live at the abbey years later, despite being an atheist and never taking religious vows. The abbey is located in dry and doer scrub and farmland in Australia, plagued by endless drought and increasingly, mice. Much of the book is spent detailing the killing of mice. This is not for the squeamish! If this wasn't enough for the half dozen nuns to deal with, the bones of a former sister, murdered in Thailand many years before are coming back to the abbey in the middle of the pandemic, along with a woman our narrator knows from childhood, now also a nun, but a worldly one. The bones sit in the nun's parlour for months as bureaucracy grinds on. Throw into this a friendship with a local farmer, our narrator's grief over the death of her parents and many other small plot lines. While Stone Yard Devotional is at times beautifully written I found it a confusing, disconnected and overly weighty story that didn't really go anywhere and lacked any kind of point. While is is stated at the beginning that the narrator is writing a diary, this is lost during the book and isn't played as it might have been. 2.5 stars.

Like a good number of the novels on this year’s Booker Longlist, the theme of spirituality features. Stone Yard Devotional does veer in this territory, It also be the more extreme one on the list. The book’s narrator goes to a convent as part of a retreat. She ends up feeling secure and moves in, despite being an atheist. There, she commits to chores. Then three things happen: The first is a plague of mice. The second is that the bones of a murdered nun are discovered and will be shipped to the convent. The third is that the person accompanying the bones is a person from the narrator’s childhood, and the memories of her aren’t particularly good. I would say that fourth is COVID-19 but I’m guessing the book takes place during the third lockdown where things eased up slightly. With all these happenings, the narrator feels existential dread but then this morphs into an exploration into grief, which is the book’s main theme. If I made this sound messy, it isn’t. Stone Yard Devotional is a quietly profound book which throws some surprises along the way. From spirituality to horror, the book throws a lot of things at a relentless pace. Oh and if you want someone to write a horrific mouse plague, Charlotte Wood is your person.

When I was a schoolgirl, I had to memorize William Wordsworth’s sonnet, The World is Too Much With Us, and throughout reading Stone Yard Devotional, the words ran through my head. This is the story of an unnamed Australian narrator – an atheist who leaves the city life and her marriage behind and takes her place in a small cloistered religious retreat. There she experiences the “unholy trinity” – an infestation of mice, the return of the bones of a nun who left the community to minister to abused women in Thailand and met an untimely death, and finally, the visitation of Helen Parry who has become a superstar activist. Unlike the narrator, Helen Parry is mentioned by both her names and brings back dark memories of the narrator’s unkind actions toward her a lifetime ago. The novel takes place in the early days of COVID, a time when Australia did indeed face a mouse plague, and when the outside world became even more frightening. Our narrator reflects, “I am filled with mourning…for all the extinctions and threats, flooded once again with the knowledge that nothing outside these abbey walls is well, and no manner of things shall be well. And I know that inside these walls, Helen Parry is the only one who will face that truth.” At a point of time when our nation – our world – is facing so many existential threats and so much cruelty, Charlotte Wood begs us to consider: is there any place, inside or outside of our mind, that we can truly take refuge? Is abdication of the world the answer or is it more likely that everyone who chooses the path of the narrator has hurt someone by coming? Can anyone truly forgive another who has hurt them badly, and how do we go about finding that shred of forgiveness? Is there meaning in suffering? And most of all, what does it mean to “be good”, given our human nature? How do we ever move from despair to hope? The mice, which gnaw through the pages of the book and eventually, our minds, are both literal and metaphorical. Not unlike humans, they destroy everything in their path, including their habitat, their deceased brethren, and even the face of a peace dove. This atmospheric and introspective novel deserves its short listing for the Booker Prize and is both profound and timely.

Another six star novel. Breathtakingly beautiful and fantastically read on audible. It took me a while to find my way in it (I had started it several times before) until I realised there was no way to be had and like some of the other novels I have read this year I needed to let go. I did and travelled with the narrator on her meditative journey about the past, forgiveness, grief and change. I need to get myself a hard copy but I would love to see how this was laid out - the paragraphs melted into each other. The narrator is an atheist but despite that she finds some kind of consolation in a religious community and in that sense it is a hopeful novel. It touched many nerves for me and made me smile many times. Compost and putting things back into the earth runs through the novel as a trope - I have been creating my own permaculture world this year and absolute joy of composting and creating a whole new cycle of material to grow from has been a highlight for me. This idea of the cyclical nature of life is so central to the book and so beautifully explored. Next morning. I have just woken up the next morning to something cold running up my arm. I had heard my cat and imagined she had brought something in - a frog or something. But no, it was a mouse. Managed to catch it and save its little life but what an appropriate gift Ludwig brought me today.
3.5 rtc. i’m writing a substack post on my thoughts on the booker shortlist & i have one book left…..so stay tuned

“All that was needed was time, and nature. Anything that had lived could make itself useful, become nourishment in death”. Stone Yard Devotional was complex and profound. This is a story about a woman who turned her back on her life in Sydney. She is drained, emotionally spent. She retreats to her childhood town, and seeks solace and a home among a group of Catholic nuns. She picks up the traditions of the nuns, even though she is not there to join the order. The rituals and traditions become second nature, like a structure that she was missing in her life, to reorder her thoughts and provide a space to contemplate and ask questions herself. “Visitant: a guest or visitor like Helen Parry, or a supernatural being, an apparition, like a saint. Like a delivery of bones, like a plague.” The mouse plague was a fascinating element to this book. It provoked anxiety, dread, panic: exhaustion. Different characters had different reactions; some resilient, and for others, it was the last straw. The fact that the mice stayed away from the ‘good room” had a miraculous or divine reverence about it. We are taken back to the woman’s childhood, and reminisce about her mother and school years. Observations and questions of the past permeate the present. We are privy to the woman’s thoughts, and what she is trying to unpack in her mind, and the whole process of how the unpacking is unfolding; almost like it was trying to break the fourth wall. I felt a sense of soundlessness and deliberation as the woman walked through the property owned by the nuns. Yet it was not entirely a monastic life: there was a renouncement of the outside world, yet so much conflict in adopting a devotion to the spiritual soul. It is hard, and that is right to be so; sacrifice is never easy. Thank you to #allenandunwin and #netgalley for the #gifted copy to read.

This book was a series of thoughts. You never know the main characters name and I swear 90% of it is about a mouse plague. It is set in a small religious community, where the lady decides to go and live to work through her grief of losing her mother and father but it’s not really about that at all… I’m disappointed because I saw so many good reviews but maybe this style of writing is just not for me.

I listened to this on audio & I’m not sure if that made it more difficult to enjoy - I’m not sure it was suited to audio. It felt like a memoir and, if I’m honest, I couldn’t really tell you what the point of it was. Charlotte Wood is a great writer, hence why I’ve given it 3 stars (and I absolutely adored The Weekend) but this one wasn’t really for me.

I loved this. I can't fully name why - but it absolutely has something to do with its simplicity, its depth, and its subtlety in handling big emotions. This was a quiet (except the mice, yikes) exploration of grief and of retreating and the backdrop of the religious community added to our character's exploration of purpose.

The unnamed narrator retreats once a year to a cloistered order of Catholic nuns located on the outskirts of the rural town in which she grew up. One year she decides to stay on. When the novel opens she has been living there for four years. She has abandoned her husband, her job, her home and her friends with no explanation, completely disconnecting herself from everything that was her life. She is an atheist, she doesn’t join the order but she forms a part of it. She is one of them. She follows the rituals and the routine of the nuns and finds solace in the physical labor and in the religious rituals of the place. Her retreat from the onslaught of life has given her a certain contentment although as we follow her stream of consciousness, she is very far from peaceful. This orderly and routine life is interrupted by three intrusions that breach the balance of the cloister and create havoc: The body of a nun of their order who was murdered while on a mission abroad is brought back for burial; Helen, a nun who is a global climate activist, is stranded at the cloister due to pandemic restrictions. She too grew up in the narrator’s home town and they share a troubled history. She carries out her mission not by retreating from the world as do the cloistered nuns, but by challenging it; The cloister and its surroundings are assailed by mice and it becomes a plague of epic biblical proportions. Throughout we are in the narrator’s consciousness as she reflects on her life, her choices and her relationships. Her retreat from life has given her the ability to take a critical look at it and to confront her actions and choices. We follow her on this journey of hers. Describing it seems banal but it's far from it. It completely works and it’s a well worthwhile read.

3.5 stars This 2024 Booker-shortlisted novel has been on my shelf for a while, and it turned out to be exactly the quiet, contemplative book it promises to be—sometimes to its benefit, sometimes to its detriment. The story follows an unnamed female character, possibly in her middle years, seeking refuge in a remote Australian convent. She’s wanting to retreat into the quiet rituals of the cloistered nuns. Wood’s writing is undeniably beautiful— spare, meditative, almost cleansing. Our narrator is not a believer, yet lives among nuns for four years. She finds solace in cooking and gardening, slipping into the abbey’s rhythms without looking for any type of spiritual awakening. But the tranquility is interrupted by unsettling events: the murder of Sister Jenny, a nun who worked with abused women in Thailand; the gruesome mouse plague sweeping the convent; and the return of Sister Helen Parry, an environmental activist/ heroine who the narrator knew from school. Helen Parry’s presence reminds the narrator that she was quite cruel to her back then and tries to atone. These quiet disturbances push the story forward. The novel’s stillness is deliberate, told through her words, and also reflects on the past. Then there are some fragmented stories that seep through. At times I didn’t feel fully engaged, but I personally connected to some of what she was going through. There are themes of grief, guilt, the climate crisis, and our obligations to one another linger. The atmosphere is serene, and the emotional weight is mostly subtle rather than sweeping. There are no big stakes here, no dramatic revelations, just a gentle nudge to look inward and perhaps connect with a protagonist whose hurts and regrets are relatable. It’s a book that may resonate more deeply if you’ve lived a bit.

I was not a fan of Wood’s ‘The Natural Way of Things’. The writing made me angry and I felt I’d been betrayed by hearing it was a strong feminist novel when I found it to be filled with anything but. So I went into Stone Yard Devotional with a little trepidation. But I am so glad I gave it a go. The unnamed narrator leaves her city life and husband and returns to the town she grew up in, moving onto a remote nunnery on the outskirts of the country town Monaro. There she reflects on loss, forgiveness, and what’s important in life. If you’re expecting much to happen beyond this you’d be disappointed but honestly it was the sparseness of the plot and the depth of thoughts that made this book utterly compelling. It was a beautiful contemporary literary novel. 4.5 stars.

I found this book absolutely stunning, and can only offer a series of disconnected thoughts in response. A middle-aged woman joins an order of nuns in the Australian outback near the small town where she grew up, and there, starts to reflect back on her own life and the lives of others she once knew - especially her mother's. Three visitations frame this account: a plague of mice, an unburied body, and a classmate from her past. Stone Yard Devotional is about grief, it's about treading lightly in the world, it's about faith and destruction, it's about finding a life that will let you breathe, it's about the conditions under which we can offer and accept forgiveness. Wood's prose has such deep clarity, and I'm not surprised that this was chosen by the Booker judges who picked Orbital, as I was immediately reminded of Samantha Harvey's writing, especially in Dear Thief. But I think this is even better than Orbital: the single narrator gives us a deeper and more complex internal world than is possible with a larger cast. The atmosphere and setting also took me right back to the disturbing Australian children's books about exclusion and cruelty that made their way to Britain when I was a kid - Libby Gleeson's Eleanor, Elizabeth, Robin Klein's People Might Hear You and Hating Alison Ashley - and to Jane Campion's directorial debut, the 1986 Australian film Two Friends.There's something a little otherworldly about this novel, cleverly signalled by the way the number of mice that ravage the community swells to impossible proportions, and I just loved it. 4.5 stars.

5 stars for tackling an extremely hard subject, death, and incredible use of symbolism and metaphor. Review will be posted at thereadersroom.org and posted here after Booker season ends. From thereadersroom.org: Here’s the unusual case where our rating system isn’t quite working for me. I actually LOVED this book. So if total enjoyment was weighted more heavily, it would have scored better. We don’t really have a score for great use of symbolism and metaphor. Underneath the surface, this novel is a meditation on death and our fears and anxiety surrounding it. It’s a deep, meaningful read that’s also very accessible. Really hope this makes the shortlist. Writing quality: 5/5 Originality: 5/5 Character development: 2/4 Plot development: 2/4 Overall enjoyment: 2/2

3.5 stars This is beautifully written and very meditative. I suspect I will need to sit with this for a while to appreciate it fully.

truly wonderful! paced so well and i loved my reading experience. overall it’s missing something for me personally, but i’ll read any book about an atheist nun (awesome) and i definitely would check out more of charlotte wood’s books in the future!

The Weekend, Charlotte Wood's previous novel, captivated me by her attention to the spaces around the narrative, changing dynamics seen through the actions of the protagonists. I found this novel had almost grown from that and for me was more about the space, the unvoiced than the central storytelling. The plot is almost incidental. Unnamed narrator leaves her life to enter a community of nuns. It appears, to the reader, that this self-imposed exodus has nothing to do with religious beliefs, she is an atheist. It provides her with "a" place in which to have some use whilst trying to make sense of global, climate realities. It played with the "stranger comes to town" trope, repeating this motif and using each, very subtly, as a different catalyst. She is the first of the "stranger" episodes as she retreats, then comes a mouse plague closely followed by a "celebrity nun" who brings with her the fourth element, the recently discovered bones of a former nun of this community. These all have a COVID backdrop. I found this an extraordinary novel. Curious content propelling the story with the cleverly carved space around this for constant introspection and contemplation of a much bigger picture. The beautifully crafted work juggled restraint, foreboding and challenge.

Such a strange story. I don’t know if I understood it the way I was expected to. It was a bizarre experience and I didn’t much care for the writing style, although it was beautiful in a way. I can’t tell if this was very clever or trying too hard to be.

Who hasn’t dreamed of walking out on their life and leaving all their responsibilities behind to go and join a nunnery….! I really enjoyed this quiet, thoughtful novel. But it does follow the current trend of stopping rather than ending.
Gorgeously quiet novel where the power of what is not said reverberates through the entire work.
Still not entirely sure what it’s about, but loved the slow rocking rhythm of it all. Feeling soothed.

went into the book with reviews of loved it and hated it so wasn't sure what to expect. thought it was very well paced and a great build up, i was satisfied at the end but also completely unsatisfied. exclusively read this while in the tasmanian wilderness, picture snuggled into a sleeping bag before bed, picture sunrise over dolerite cliffs. definitely hard not to enjoy a book here. also strongly feel the nun life is very similar to park ranger life. similar non linear structure to theory and practice but less essay-ey, which i think made me enjoy it more. love an aussie landscape. she kept talking about her dreams and all i wanted was her dream explanation book (gift idea!)

What I did love where the small things of how times bleeds into one another (when did she start praying?) and the clearness of the language. Will now be forever fearful of mice ruining my life
