This book ticked all my boxes for a fun rom-com: • Snarky, witty banter which had me laughing out loud more than once • Characters who love books and reading: Charlie, the likable hot guy who just so happens to be an editor and Nora, the city girl, who is a career-driven literary agent • Cozy small-town setting • Lots of bookish talk • Enemies to lovers • Steam but the door to the bedroom is closed with just a small crack. (Matter of fact I wanted them to get a room so they would stop lusting after each other like sex-hungry teenagers). We know where the story is going in a rom-com, so it is all about the journey, which I found engaging and fun. When Nora takes her sister, Libby, up on an offer to go on a month-long trip to Sunshine Falls, NC, Libby has a bucket list for her sister, built around familiar tropes in rom-coms, including falling in love with a lumberjack. Instead, Nora runs into Charlie, an editor from back in the city. Turns out Sunshine Falls is his hometown. Sparks fly immediately, but not romantic sparks. It seems they have a not-so-pleasant work history. I also liked the dynamic between the two sisters, Nora and Libby. They lost their mother at an early age and have some issues to work out that gave some depth to the story. I also liked the role reversal where it was the female lead who was the career-driven workaholic, and the author stayed true to the character throughout. I also liked all the bookish talk and book love. Julia Whelan, my favorite narrator, is the voice of Nora, and does so flawlessly. Timing is everything. This was a buddy read with Marialyce but do check out her review to see what she thought. The author’s book, Beach Read, wasn’t for me (pandemic brain?), but I loved The People We Meet on Vacation, and with this one, I’m officially a fan. It’s a perfect feel-good summer read.

No one writes like Emily. She has such an unique flow and a complex way of keeping things simple. She once again has won me over from page one, impressed me with the rhythm, the style, the humor, and she also impressed me with the banter. She is getting bold with her sex scenes and that is such a refreshing upgrade from her previous books. It is no secret that People We Meet on Vacation is one of my favorite book of all times, but we can't deny that it is because of the emotional weight of it and not because of that single sex scene. As cute as it is, Emily has always ran on the mild side when it comes to the finallys. Imagine my surprise when she creates these two characters and explores not only their mental chemistry but also their sexual chemistry more than once. I have never seen Emily be this descriptive this often, she has actually steered away from her usual slow burn with this book. It is still no extremely spicy book, but it delivered in everything else that mattered. They had chemistry, the book is the right length; it's funny, sexy, exciting, and relatable, like everything else she touches. Their flirting, their banter, their dirty talk, everything was measured, calculated to the perfect amount. None of it was cringy and this was so freaking fun! I couldn't put it down. She got a little bit lost at the end, I realized I don't enjoy vague happy endings as much as I thought I would. Emily tries way too hard to stay away from marriage and kids at the end of her books, which is something I am totally fine with. However, this one ended with something lacking. I can't pinpoint exactly what it is, but it felt like taking a bite out of a cupcake you thought was going to be frosted filled and it wasn't. She built the most incredible connection between these two characters, and this FMC is possibly my favorite female she has ever written, and that is why I think they deserved more at the end. She threw us a "happy ending" I couldn't quite grasp and it left me somewhat unsatisfied. Other than that, it is a very solid Emily book that will keep me glued to her next releases for a long time still.

“You’re perfect,” he rasps. “You’re fucking perfect.” This was such a cute and fun rom-com about love, acceptance, self-confidence and happiness. Nora Stephen is a literary agent from New York who works hard for her clients, but she is seen as cold-hearted by clients and people she meets. Nora first met Charlie, an editor, for a book deal but the meeting did not go well and Nora didn't like Charlie. Nora's sister, Libby begs Nora to go with her to a small-town in North Carolina to help her relax and learn that she can be a hero in her own life. In Sunshine Falls, Nora keeps running into Charlie around town instead of meeting a small-town guy. Soon they learn that they are heroes to each other. This book was so good! The pacing was well done and the plot was interesting. This story is told from Nora's point of view. I loved Nora, she is smart, hardworking, organized and even though she has a hard exterior once you get to know her she is caring and kind. I really like Charlie, he is responsible, sweet, smart, and dependable. I liked Nora's sister Libby, she is sweet and helpful, but there were times where I didn't agree with the decisions that Libby made. I also liked the side characters especially Nora's nieces, Brendan, and Charlie's mom Sally. I loved the banter between Charlie and Nora and the chemistry between them was amazing! I loved that Charlie and Nora understand each other and they had a lot in common including their love of reading. The ending was so good and heartwarming! I'm so glad it ended on a happy note and I liked seeing what happened to the characters a few months later. I would recommend this book to anyone who loves romantic comedies and great characters.

I wish I could give ‘The Five-Star Weekend’, a five-star review… Although the premise was exciting, I think I’ve just unfortunately read too many Elin Hilderbrand novels. At this point, every book just seems the same - same story, different cast. This book centers around Hollis Shaw. Hollis is recently widowed and grieving. So Hollis decides to have a five-star weekend at her summer home in Nantucket. For this weekend, Hollis invites four friends from all different stages in her life (which I actually love this idea). We have Tatum- her childhood best friend. Dru-Ann, her best friend from college. Brooke- her friend from when their children were growing up together. And Gigi- who was her favorite internet friend (Gigi follows Hollis’s blog). All these women have problems of their own, even though they put on a happy face to the rest of the world. There’s also some “friendship rivalry” going on, as some of them think they should be Hollis’s best friend. Hollis has her daughter Caroline, interview and film each of the women and tell their stories of how they all know Hollis. The five-star weekend ends up being so much more than what each woman thought it would be. So yes, there were some pretty good parts in this book. But, I found myself getting bored quite often as well. Once again, as with the past few books of Hilderbrand, I found that her books are nothing more than a walking (in this case writing) advertisement for Nantucket Island. Hilderbrand writes about all the hot spots to go to, which stores to shop at for all the latest fashion designers, and also which independent bookstore to shop at to purchase your books (I mean, there is no harm in being loyal). Hilderbrand also puts too much emphasis on what each character is wearing, and what designer handbag they’re carrying. We also have to hear about what each character ate for breakfast, lunch, and dinner!! If this was my first Hilderbrand novel that I read, it certainly wouldn’t be an issue, but at this point it’s just too redundant. Hilderbrand is always good for a nice summer, beach read 🏖️ However, for me personally I think it’s time to move on. I want a good story, less advertisements. I have heard that Hilderbrand is retiring from writing novels next year, in 2024. I will be sad to see her quit writing, but I wouldn’t be surprised if she comes out with a cookbook or two. She goes into great detail with her food descriptions in this book and some of her previous ones. That’s just my opinion…

Let's face it—it isn't a proper summer without the quintessential beach read. And Elin Hilderbrand's books have become a go-to for me in recent years. But unfortunately, The Five-Star Weekend didn't quite end up scratching that summertime itch. Hollis is grieving for her dead husband. She gets the idea to host a weekend get-together for her best friends, inviting one from each phase of her life, in the hopes that being surrounded by friends will help her heal and move on. But each of these women is battling her own issues and the weekend doesn't really turn out the way Hollis expects. Elin Hilderbrand's books always feel light and fun, and this one's no different. It's the sort of story I pick up when I need a distraction. It's easy to get sucked into the island of Nantucket, with all of its water, sunshine, and delicious food. But at the end of the day, something about this story just didn't click for me. Maybe it's because this feels more like a disjointed collection of stories about the different women rather than a cohesive whole. They're each having their own issues, and for the most part, they don't overlap. Hilderbrand could very well have written separate stories for each of them, and it would've still made sense. Or maybe I just don't buy into the premise. I can't imagine a former friend dropping everything to fly out and spend a weekend with me and a few others they don't know, just to comfort me. But perhaps that's me being cynical and this sort of thing really does happen. Or maybe it's because while the women's issues are real, the resolutions somehow end up feeling a bit shallow. Everything is wrapped up too neatly by the end of the book, whether the issue was medical, spousal, or work. Like the proverbial happily ever after, everyone gets one, even if the circumstances are too convenient or magical to be believable. Whatever the reason, this story just didn't quite rise to the level of beachy magic I usually associate with Elin Hilderbrand. Don't get me wrong, I still had fun with it. But I always hope for a memorable reading experience, and this one was all too forgettable. ~~~~~~~~~~~~ See also, my thoughts on: The Perfect Couple The Hotel Nantucket Swan Song ~~~~~~~~~~~~ ✧ Connect with me ✧ Instagram ✧ ✧ This was a pick for my BOTM box. 3⭐️ "The thing I love best about reading fiction is that it gives you a way to connect the experiences of your own life to the larger world." THE PLOT Hollis Shaw's life seems perfect. She has the perfect husband who is a heart surgeon, a beautiful, bright daughter, and a successful food blog. But one morning, when Hollis and her husband get into an argument, he leaves for the airport and is killed in a car accident. The cracks in Hollis's life begin to grow deeper. Then, she hears of an idea called the Five-Star Weekend, a weekend where she invites one best friend from each stage in her life to come together. As great of an idea this seems to be, it doesn't turn out rather ideal. All of her friends hold secrets that threaten to shatter the magic of this weekend, and may even change the way they are perceived all together. What was it like? It was like being suspended over a deep, dark endless hole knowing you were going to fall in and never get out. MY THOUGHTS I ended up having a good time reading this!! People weren't kidding when they said Elin Hilderbrand does a beautiful job of writing books that'd be perfect to read by the beach. The world of Nantucket is just described so beautifully and in so much detail. I could actually picture myself there on the island myself. This book is beyond beautiful and magical in it's descriptions and it's wording. I was captivated from the very start. I did find some parts of this book to be very slow, and I found myself reading slower in this just to take in the plot, characters, and world. I'm not saying this is a bad thing by any means! While I did have a good time reading this, something just didn't click for me. I didn't find myself wanting to pick this up constantly or obsess over reading this. It was fun and it was magical, but I just felt some connection...missing. Maybe it could have been that I couldn't fully relate to the characters and their dilemmas, but I just did not feel the urge to binge this. I found that once I put it down, it took a bit of effort to pick it back up. The characters themselves were so beautifully written as well. There was SO much character depth and backstory; the characters felt real. I could picture these characters as real people. These characters all had their own secrets and they were on a very wide scale from self-discovery to completely life-altering. I found it very easy to follow along with everyone and I didn't get overwhelmed by the amount of character information there was to know and remember. The journey of these characters just felt so raw and real, and I really liked it. Overall, this book was really fun to read, but also got deep and a little heavy at times. This book would mainly be about self-discovery after a traumatic loss, rekindling relationships, and finding love again. It had so many amazing, beautiful moments that I'd absolutely recommend you read, particularly a good summer read. ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ I am living for these summer reads lately they're hitting different 🤭

What can I say that hasn’t been said already about what an Elin Hilderbrand novel does to me, and for me? The Five-Star Weekend is her twenty-ninth novel, and every year Elin Hilderbrand proceeds to craft a book that is light, airy, fresh, easy to read, quick, full of wit and sharp humor, and just makes me so damn happy to read…..while at the same, being so layered and full of fully fleshed out characters with so many relatable issues in their lives. Her books get placed in a box and often written off as simply being a beach book; but they just do something to me every year when I read them, and for the last 5-6 years I’ve been lucky to enough to get them as ARCs, so my Februarys are always the time of year I look forward to most, when the typical reader has to wait til June for their summer to begin with Elin….my summer always starts early! And this year’s novel was no exception, what she has crafted in The Five-Star Weekend is a deeply intimate portrait of grief, resilience, and the bonds of female sisterhood; all sprinkled with fun, food, music, and ofcourse, some time at The Chicken Box ;) (If you haven’t been to Nantucket or read an Elin Hilderbrand book, I’m sorry that you don’t get that final reference 😅)

I have read several of Elin Hilderbrand’s books over the years. A few things that I have come to rely upon when I read one of Elin’s books is that they will transport me to a place that entertains, provides me with some drama and intersperses me among characters that I can escape with. I love that her books are set in picturesque Nantucket. The Five-Star Weekend was no exception. As soon as I began reading The Five-Star Weekend, I was whisked into Hollis Shaw’s life. I found myself transported into her everyday life. That included her interactions with her devoted followers from her food blog, Hungry with Hollis, the drama in her life that included her turbulent marriage with husband, Matthew, a prominent and respected heart surgeon who had been at her side for so many years, her relationship with her impressionable young adult daughter, Caroline and just her life in general. Hollis’s and Matthew’s marriage had been in a rut for some time. They seemed to be more like roommates than husband and wife. Somehow the magic had disappeared from their marriage and their relationship. Matthew was traveling a great deal and even when he was home Hollis and Matthew seemed to avoid each other. It was winter around holiday time and Hollis was planning their annual holiday party. Matthew informed Hollis that he would not be back in time for the party. He was traveling again. Harsh words were exchanged by both Hollis and Matthew before he closed the front door and headed to his car. Matthew’s last words to Hollis were, “You’ve changed. We’ve changed.” Hollis was still repeating that sentiment when the bell at the front door rang. She was positive that Matthew had returned to say he was sorry and that he would make sure he was home for their party but standing in front of Hollis were two policemen. Hollis was about to receive the worst news of her life. The policemen informed Hollis that Matthew had been in a fatal car accident. His car had hit a mother deer and her baby. Matthew had died instantly. Hollis became a widow that fateful day. She was so distraught that their last words they spoke to one another were in anger. When Hollis informed her followers of Hungry with Hollis that she would be stepping back for an extended period of time so she could mourn her husband’s death, one of her followers told her about how she hosted something called a “five-star weekend” and how it had helped her come to terms with her grief and how to proceed with the rest of her life. Hollis decided that that was what she would do. She would host a “five-star weekend “ in Nantucket at her home. Hollis would include a friend from every stage of her life. Tatum would represent her childhood friend, Dru-Ann, her college roommate would represent her college years, Brooke would represent the friend during the years she raised her daughter and lived in Wellesley and Gigi would represent her newest friend from her blog who had been there for Hollis when she needed someone to talk to. Hollis also decided to invite her daughter, Caroline, to film the weekend. Her ultimate goal for the “five star weekend” was for it to help Hollis through her grief of loosing Matthew. What better way than to be surrounded by your oldest, most devoted, and cherished friends! Needless to say, Hollis’s carefully planned weekend did not go exactly as planned. What would transpire? Be prepared for surprises and unexpected secrets. The Five-Star Weekend by Elin Hilderbrand was delightful and entertaining from start to finish. I enjoyed the relationships Hollis and her friends had forged. All the characters made me feel like I was included in their special weekend with Hollis. I loved all the yummy food that was mentioned throughout the book. The Five-Star Weekend could be your next beach read or just a moving yet fun book for now. I highly recommend this book. Thank you to Little, Brown and Company for allowing me to read The Five-Star Weekend by Elin Hilderbrand through Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. All opinions expressed in this review are completely my own.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (4/5 Fiction) It's not officially summer until I am lost in the (inevitably waterlogged) pages of Elin's latest novel. Elin Hilderbrand is the undisputed queen of the beach read, and somehow, 29 books later, she can still write a fresh & captivating story. In picking up this book, you are once again transported to the gorgeous island of Nantucket. Like all Elin books, this is chock full of the best kind of indulgences. Mouth-watering food, luxurious linens, frosty bottles of Sancerre, grand sailboats cutting through clear water. No book transports me quite as much as an Elin book. Our story is about Hollis Shaw, wife, mother, and creator of the wildly popular food blog, Hungry With Hollis. When Hollis' husband dies suddenly in a car crash, life as she knows it comes to a screeching halt. As she prepares for her yearly pilgrimage to the island of Nantucket and grapples with how difficult this summer will be, she learns about another widow who hosted something called a Five Star Weekend: a weekend filled with a friend from each chapter of her life. Hollis is inspired to round up a friend from high school, college, and early motherhood. Her friend for this chapter of life is unique in that Hollis has never met her! She's a Hungry with Hollis fan who has helped Hollis through some of her darkest days following the death of her husband. Each woman comes with their own literal and metaphorical baggage as they navigates this unique girls' weekend that will leave them forever changed. Elin has a knack for writing life-affirming novels that are happy and hopeful. Elin's books always leave me filled with joie de vivre. I splurged on a bottle of Casa Dragones, which graces the pages of many Elin novels, and I'm using it to make the watermelon margarita recipe (swipe for the recipe!). I've decided to rank my top 3 Elin books for fun. Please let me know yours! 1. 28 Summers (check out the playlist inspired by this book in my stories!) 2. Hotel Nantucket 3. The Blue Bistro

Summer wasn't over for me until I read one of the two Elin Hilderbrand books on my shelves. It is definitely a light summer read. It was Real Housewives level drama and Real Housewives level wealth and luxury. I liked the Nantucket setting, and the scenes she set were done quite well. So well, in fact, that I felt like I knew more about the house, what they were eating, what song they were listening to, and what everyone was wearing than I did any one of the single characters. And there were a lot of characters, too many. It is told in third person omniscient, so you know all the thoughts of all the characters, even down to the minor side characters present in one scene that don't ever have another role within the story. My last gripe is that there were way, way too many pop culture references. I don't know how many name brands and celebrities were mentioned, but this will not age well. I still will give it a 3⭐ for overall enjoyment and atmosphere. It is like sitting down and watching some real rich people drama on reality TV.

4.25 stars Oh my god I can't believe that I basically binged the last half of the book. Early in the book it was putting me into an slump but the audiobook as well as the plot getting interesting got me out of it. This book is a beautiful story of friendship, grief and love that I would recommend. It was so good. The five-star weekend is about Hollis Shaw and her four friends. Hollis seems to have the perfect life. She is the person behind the super popular food blog Hungry with Hollis, and has a doctor husband and a daughter in college who is on her way to becoming a filmmaker. But then her husband Matthew dies in a car accident shortly after having an argument with Hollis. Hollis's entire life changes in an instant. Her daughter Caroline comes back from college for Matthew's funeral but she constantly says cruel things to Hollis, and doesn't care that she's grieving too. For months Hollis has no idea what to do with her life. But then she hears about something called the five-star weekend, which is about a woman who went on a vacation to Nantucket with her four friends from each stage of her life after the death of her husband. Hollis decides to take inspiration from this and to do with four friends from the stages of her own life. These friends that she chooses are Tatum (her high school best friend), Dru-Ann (her best friend from college), Brooke (her mum friend from when Caroline was growing up) and Gigi (a fan from her blog who she's connected to but who's never actually met in real life). But all of these women have problems of their own. Tatum is terrified that she might have breast cancer after finding a lump on her breast, especially because she has a family history of this illness (her mother died from it when she was 18). Dru-Ann is facing a career crisis after a comment she made about her client's mental health goes viral, which even gets her cancelled from her very own successful sports show. Brooke has had enough after her husband and the father of her twins is being sued again for sexual misconduct at work, and is always struggling with her self-confidence. Gigi meanwhile is hiding a huge secret from Hollis-that she is the secret mistress that Matthew during the latter part of their marriage. Meanwhile Hollis manages to convince Caroline to film the five-star weekend for her blog in exchange for some money. Her daughter is happy to come back to Nantucket after ending her love affair with her filmmaker boss, who has a girlfriend. All of the women arrive there and it is not long before tension starts rising to the surface. Tatum and Dru-Ann still hate each other after meeting at Hollis's wedding 25 years ago. Brooke has finally dumped her husband but she still struggles low self-confidence and social awkwardness. Gigi still isn't telling Hollis that her dead husband was having an affair with her, but she's terrified that the truth will come out. Hollis is a little bit suprised by the drama that starts happening but she is hopeful that she can get the five-star weekend back on track. But this might be harder than she thinks it might be and during this time she is reunited with her high school boyfriend Jack Finnegan, who she still has feelings for and it seems that they are definitely reciprocated by him. Though Hollis still doesn't know how she feels about seeing Jack again. I really enjoyed this book. Some of the beginning was a bit slow for me but once I got past that I started getting really into the story, and I got through it a quicker. All of the characters were interesting, even though some of them were really annoying at times (which led me to sometimes kind of hate them lol), and I enjoyed reading their backstories and seeing how that shaped them into the women they are now. There wasn't that much romance but what it did have was sweet and beautiful. I would definitely recommend this book to literary fiction readers or if you just want to read a enjoyable and bingeable beach read.

Thank you to Elin Hilderbrand, Little, Brown and Company and Netgalley for the ARC of The Five Star Weekend. I rate this book 3.5. It had its perfect charm that Elin Hilderbrand books always do. You know exactly what you are going to get, and I love that. I always really enjoy the way Hilderbrand describes the settings so well, and this book had a lot of food in it, which was also described very well! I liked the characters for the most part, some were a bit annoying and I liked some more than others, but overall it was a fun novel with an interesting plot line. The reason I didn’t rate it higher was because I found the end a bit of a let down. Everything was wrapped up very neatly in a nice bow. For a book that built itself on setting up drama, nothing really major seemed to happen. The whole Electra plot line was kind of pointless and Brooke’s big reveal seemed to come out of left field. Overall this was a fun summer read and fun to escape to Nantucket again, it just wasn’t my favourite of Hilderbrand’s books,

Rounding up from 2.5 ⭐️ Audio: bland narration Nothing happened? I tried giving EH another chance after taking a 4 year hiatus from her books, but she’s still the same author. Characters, story, affairs, juvenile writing and youth slang usage, and an overall lukewarm feeling. I actually didn’t mind the story idea or development, but after the 60% point when I couldn’t keep the characters straight and nothing really happened, my rating just kept dropping.

3 stars - actually 2.5 rounded up! ⭐️⭐️⭐️ Well that plummeted quickly. Other than one of Elin Hilderbrand’s series that I’ve read, I have yet to find a stand-alone book of hers that I really enjoy. The cover (like all of her fun, summery covers) and the title really caught my eye. The blurb sounded awesome. However, once again the book didn’t live up to my expectations. The first half was really good. Towards the middle it started boring me. The last few chapters ruined it for me - for many reasons. I’ve read that this may be a Hilderbrand’s last book due to her retirement. I wish it would’ve gone out on a better note for me, but I doubt I’ll read any of her others.

I love traveling to Nantucket every summer through Hilderbrand’s books and all of her excellent descriptions! This story was filled with drama, friendships, romance, twists and so much more! The Hotel Nantucket remains my favorite book from this author but I still did enjoy this one! I will definitely be reading her last Nantucket book by the end of this summer!

The book is about a woman who goes through a tragic loss and decides to invite friends from all stages of her life for a healing girls weekend. To be honest, I didn’t love any of the characters. They all had pretty major flaws, but somehow it all worked. The flaws are what made it so interesting. Although I really don’t think any of these people went well together as friends. I guess that’s why they were friends at different points in their lives. There was so much going on in this book, it was packed with drama. I did love the ending and how everyone ended up exactly where they should be. I will say that one thing that annoyed me about this book was all the slang terms. It felt like this book was trying way too hard at times, but I was able to overlook it.

3.5 stars. This is why I love the GR choice awards. Every year I see an Elin Hilderbrand title in the fiction category, so this year I finally decided to give one of her novels a try, and I'm so glad I did. I love reading "lighter" books in between more literary ones. This normally means grabbing a whodunit or sometimes a romance, but what I enjoyed most about The Five-Star Weekend is that it may have some elements of these genres, but mostly it was an entertaining, uplifting story about 6 women and their backstories. The Story: The Five-Star Weekend is a lighthearted, engaging tale that takes you into the life of Hollis Shaw, a middle-aged successful food blogger who, after returning to her hometown of Nantucket, invites four friends, one from each stage of her life, to spend a weekend at her home on the island to help her come to grips with the recent loss of her husband and the strained relationship with her daughter she’s struggling to repair.

** spoiler alert ** My first review has disappeared. I really wanted to like this book. A nice summer read. But it was a Did Not Finish. I was disappointed in the usual plot… Poor girl, Hollis, from Nantucket married a wealthy surgeon. Many years later, she is upset as he will be in Europe, on a business trip and visiting a sick friend, at the same time she is hosting her big holiday party. They have words. He leaves for the airport and is killed in a accident on the way. Her young adult daughter is now not speaking to her, she is lonely and reaches out to an unknown stranger, who follows her blog. Hollis then decides to throw a ladies’ weekend, at her big house on Nantucket, with 3 friends, who do not know each other and the internet friend, who she has never met. Hollis’ daughter agrees to film it for a documentary. My rating is in the minority, but could not do another book about shopping and dining and the drama of the upper class.

The release of a new Elin Hilderbrand novel is a sure sign that summer is upon us. Her books are perfect summer reading, and The Five-Star Weekend is no exception. Set on Nantucket, this novel follows the recently widowed Hollis Shaw, a well-known food blogger, as she brings together four women from different stages of her life for a perfectly curated weekend of food, wine, shopping, and togetherness. These women have very little in common and all are dealing with conflicts in their own lives; will the weekend bring them together or end in disaster? I'll be honest, I didn't think this was Hilderbrand's best effort. I prefer her earlier books; her more recent works feel like an extended tourist advertisement for Nantucket, and her characters often feel disconnected from reality. I found myself most drawn to Tatum's character, a blue-collar year-round Nantucket resident. She seemed most down-to-earth and therefore was the most relatable. I had a hard time sympathizing with Dru-Ann's viral social media crisis or Brooke's struggles to remain plugged into wealthy local mommy society, and I definitely couldn't connect to Gigi, who harbors a secret that will destroy Hollis if/when it gets out. I don't want to say much else for fear of spoilers. If you love Elin Hilderbrand, you'll love this book. However, if you're like me and you long for a return to her earliest works, then you probably will find yourself disappointed by this novel. Hilderbrand plans to retire in 2024 and to be honest, after reading her past few works, I'm sad to say I'm not sure I'll miss her.

Since I have been reading the authors books once a year for many years now it almost feels like I’m getting my own sort of Nantucket vacation through her summer reads. She does such an incredible job at creating a sense of place you truly feel like you’re right beside the characters and this was no exception. She has a knack for describing food in the most mouthwatering and appealing way and I swear if I ever actually visited Nantucket for real it would be mostly for the food. Her characters are always so well drawn too, even though her books are the ultimate beach reads there’s always some depth because of her great characterization. This book had some super messy and relatable women in this group of “friends” and then you also get cameos from characters in previous books which is such a treat. If you haven’t had the pleasure of reading one of the authors books to get you ready for summer this is a great place to start!
not my favourite Nantucket book but it was fun for an audiobook even if it had too much sugar for my taste.

The Five-Star Weekend was a lovely story set, once again, on Nantucket and told only in a way Elin Hilderbrand can! Hollis Shaw is a famous food blogger, whose husband is suddenly killed in a one-car accident after a slight argument between them. Her whole world is torn to shreds, but 7 months later, she's determined to have a celebration of HER life with all the friends, "stars", from her various stages of life thus far. Enter the high school best friend. The college roommate. The mommy best friend. And the woman from her blog that has helped her piece her life back together following her husband's death. Will this friendship weekend get Five Stars despite the drama that will no doubt ensue amongst the five women...? Elin Hilderbrand brings back her signature Island-style writing and we're treated to a few cameos from several characters from previous novels (you won't need to have read any to enjoy this one). The story is written in a carefree, gossipy way that lures you in and doesn't let go until literally the very last page. The character growth in this book is HUGE. Each of the "stars" has personal drama that we follow and their development has you cheering for them the whole way. There's also enough conflict between the women to keep the story moving along and never, ever dull. Verdict: The Five-Star Weekend gets Five Stars from me!

4.5 ⭐️- Elin Hilderbrand knocked it out of the park again with this one! It’s a clever concept with a focus on female friendships, getting older, forgiveness, self discovery, and relationships of every kind. These five friend’s storylines blended together seamlessly. There was just the right amount of touching moments mixed with OMG moments and it had me hooked. And as always, Elin did an incredible job setting the scene with all of her descriptions of the food, locations, sounds (music via playlists), and smells. You really feel like a fly on the wall on Squam Road for this five star weekend 🤩
Her books are CANDY - I could not devour this fast enough. Loved it.

Spending a summer in Nantucket is something Elin Hilderbrand is so great at! I couldn’t wait for this book to come out and I was happy I got it so fast when it did! I read it in a day and couldn’t put it down! Another winner!
Another worthwhile book by the famous Nantucket author dealing with complicated relationships, between friends, mothers, daughters, lovers.
Elin is the queeeeen! As always. Also my dip is in this book, so yeah. I'm officially soaring.

Oh man so bummed not to have liked this one! Elin is normally one of my favorite authors for charming, quick and deeper than usual beach reads. Sadly, this one was a total miss for me - very unlikeable characters, such cliche tropes for everyone, no real drama or substantive issues amongst the women, and you really weren’t rooting for anyone. She was so name droppy about Nantucket and clothing brands that it became like an overdone advertisement for the island and expensive things. And all the talk about food and the ridiculous amount of detail she went into about each meal was just over the top. Overall this one was a miss for me but I’m sure folks who love Nantucket and a more light beach read will still be into it.

What I love about these books is the same thing I hate about them…they are incredibly easy to read and follow along to on audio. Admittedly, I don’t have much in common with or interest in Nantucket traveling, but I understand why Elin has such a big following, all of her books are great beach reads. I do feel like these authors get labeled as somewhat cookie cutter-ish, and while I don’t have a stance one way or the other, they have made reading enjoyable and accessible to a wider audience and that’s so cool!

I know I have said this about the great MKA (Mary Kay Andrews), but it is not really summer for me until I read a novel by Elin Hilderbrand, and I always look forward to my first of the year. I foolishly waited until August this time, but of course, I still enjoyed The Five-Star Weekend just as much had I read it in June. This one didn't capture me quite as much as The Hotel Nantucket did, but it still had all the elements I know and love from Hilderbrand books, such as the setting of Nantucket, wonderful characters, drama, a Peloton, and tearjerker moments. And we can't forget about the collective POV, which never lets me down. I had never heard of a "Five-Star Weekend” before, and it made for a wonderful concept for this story. Hollis was a strong female lead, as were the other female characters, and oh the drama that ensues when Gigi's secrets start coming out. The audiobook is again narrated by the talented Erin Bennett, and there is just a certain something about her that makes me love Hilderbrand books even more. She was able to fully capture every single character's personality with her narration, and this is an audiobook that truly cannot be missed. Hilderbrand tackles tricky subjects with ease and grace, and she manages to make every single woman in this book feel real and perfectly relatable in some way. The Five-Star Weekend would make for a great beach read, but even if you aren't on a beach I would highly recommend having a drink in your hand for this one. I don't know why but every single Hilderbrand novel feels like magic to me, and I can hardly believe this is her 29th book. I am hoping for many more to come, and if you are a fan of her at all you should definitely enjoy it. Reading this felt like coming home, and I enjoyed every minute of it.

Hollis Shaw's life seems perfect on the surface--a thriving food blog, a handsome surgeon husband, and a daughter in film school. But when her husband, Matthew, dies after a fight with Hollis, her perfect life is shattered. Her daughter, Caroline, blames Hollis, and their relationship is in tatters. Adrift, Hollis decides to host a "Five-Star Weekend," where she invites four friends from various decades in her lives--best friend from high school (Tatum); college (DruAnn); thirties (Brooke); and currently (Gigi). But when all the women arrive at Hollis' home in Nantucket, it's clear each has their own struggles too. This is typical solid Hilderbrand fare. Not one of my absolute favorites but an interesting read. There are some good twists, and the characters are interesting if not particularly deep or diverse. The thing about Hilderbrand is that she has a way of weaving a story that just pulls you in. I really liked Tatum, Hollis' childhood best friend, and Tatum and Hollis' backstories were more well-done. Each women is suffering from varying types of angst, even Caroline, Hollis' daughter. The Nantucket setting was enticing, as always, making you wish you were at the beach, if perhaps not suffering from the same woes as these characters. All in all, a quick, compelling read. 3.5 stars, rounded to 4 here.

HEY ALEXA PLAY LOOKOUT WEEKEND BY DEBBIE DEB! Lookout weekend ‘cause, here Elin comes Because Five-Star Weekend, was a dud! If you’ve been following me for some time, ya know I’m slightly obsessed with the Queen of Summer AKA Elin Hilderbrand! Her annual summer releases are the peak of my summer season and a cherished past time activity with Mama Rover! For six days leading up to pub day, I was feverishly stalking my local B&N, crossing my ears, eyes, tongue, AND TOES (!!!) that one of the angelic booksellers would place a copy of the highly anticipated The Five-Star Weekend on the shelves, days early (as they are wont to do.. BLESS!) Much to my dismay, my bookish treasure hunt did not end in a happy ending (no, not that kind of happy ending, get your head out of the Nantucket gutter!) and I had to wait until pub day to get my dirty paws on a copy! Did I immediately binge read The Five-Star Weekend? Yes! Was it a five star bookie wookie? NOPE! *siiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiigh* Hilderbrand’s 29th summer novel follows an iconic food blogger named Hollis Shaw, who is reeling in the aftermath of her husband’s sudden death. Nursing a broken heart, feeling the wrath of blame from her young adult daughter (ugggh), Hollis decides to organize a “Five-Star Weekend”. The concept is fab: gather women from each stage of her life and host a Nantucket-licious weekend doing all of the things! However… Hollis’s constant obsession over her followers, likes, and social media, were just… so cringe to me! The subplots of the women attending the weekend were also just… eeeeeeek! A PLETHORA of cancel culture (which I know EH drew from her own personal experience but the manner in which she handled it in this book was SO WEIRD), the wife of a man being accused of sexual misconduct, a handful of cheater-cheater-pumpkin-eaters… it was all just too much for me. Island vibes were lacking but per usual, the food descriptions were dynamite. ALRIGHT, OFF TO GO READ ONE OF ELIN'S BACKLIST BOOKS! BYEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE!

** spoiler alert ** Didn’t hate. Didn’t love. I know I have to suspend belief on a lot of beachy reads, but there were parts in this one that made me roll my eyes all the way up to my forehead. I loved the few Elin Hildebrand novels I’ve read so far, my fav being the summer of 1969 and Hotel Nantucket. I enjoy picturing Nantucket in the summer, the numerous references to my fav city Boston, and life on the storied East Coast in particular. I love her descriptions of beachy island days in the sun and nights spent drinking rosè and eating perfectly seasoned pomme frites. This one, however, was inconsistent. There were several times where I was genuinely questioning if I missed something or if the editor was drunk. A character coming out out of literally nowhere (seriously no small clues, no musings, no nothing, just all of a sudden, I’m gay! Should I announce on Facebook!) a character last name inconsistencies, several sentences that literally made no sense and did nothing for the plot. I don’t know. This one just missed the mark for me.

This book was actually a super cute beach read. We read it for my book club and it brough great discussion. We discussed which characters we related to most, which ones we felt the most sympathy for, etc. Interestingly, many of my book club members didn’t relate as much to Hollis, the main character.

Meh. Not bad but not too exciting either. The ending wrapped up a bit too conveniently, Jack (and Kyle) were creepy as hell, and frankly for a book about friendship, Hollis doesn’t seem like a good friend at all.

4.5 stars for this fantastic summer read! The setting was perfection, the details were swoon worthy, the foodie elements were mouthwatering & the relationships & characters hooked me right away. I loved all the twists & the narrative of female friendships. I need to read more Elin!
5 Summer Stars 👙🥂🐶🦀 loved everything about this the friendships, the food, the fun, the drama !
absolutely loved. I’m such an elin girlie. enjoy every single one of her books.

Tempted to give 5 stars but I am thinking I may settle at 4.5. Need to think for a bit before posting my full PUB DAY review on my bookstagram later today. REGARDLESS, I loved this one so much and Elin is forever a queen in my eyes. 🥹💙

What in the knockoff real housewives was this book? It took me so long to finish it was truly a chore. I’m relieved to never have to read about the sea shell driveway lined with hydrangeas again. This book had no substance other than wine moms sprinkled with desperate attempts at pop culture and brand name references. It was cheesy, flat and incredibly boring.
The worst book I've read in a long, long time. Trite, shallow, and just downright stupid.

A really interesting and complex story, however I felt as though the writing and structure was a little muddled. I found it hard to make sense of the timeline and how the characters related to Noenka. I thought Noenka as a character was great and I loved the sections which looked at her and Ramses. But I found myself getting confused too often to really enjoy it and I think this was down to how the book was constructed.

Thankfully, the Dutch texts out of Suriname are being translated into English. On a Woman's Madness by Astrid Roemer is such an amazing, seminal work that I regret not being able to speak Dutch so that I could have read this book much earlier in my life, and because I would be able to read the original, untranslated poetic mastery and craft of Roemer. The novel is nonlinear, as it takes the reader on a journey through the troubled life of Noenka, who faces tremendous adversity from her family, her community, and to a great extent, country. She is forced to deal with a problematic and unhealthy marriage to an abusive womaniser, while she traverses Suriname in search of true love. In this quest, she discovers the multicultural society that is Suriname and the tensions, suspicions and battles that go on among them as a result of being pitted against each other by the colonisers of Suriname. Noenka deals with having her heart in many places and with several individuals, as she is shattered by the death of one of her lovers. Roemer then takes the reader on a journey into the taboo (at least for the time this novel was written), as we discover that Noenka was bisexual and fell in love with Gabrielle who, in essence, helps her along the roads of mental illness, family drama, marital abuse, lust, and loss that she has to travel, as a woman who is seen as 'mad' by society. Gabrielle is not without her troubles, and Roemer does a beautiful job of ending the novel by creating doubt in the reader's (at least for me) mind of whose madness she referred to in the title of the novel. I absolutely loved this novel. It is traumatic, but necessary. It is graphic, but absolutely believable. It is historical, but contemporary. Roemer shattered many ceilings and bars when she wrote this novel in 1982. It was bold to publish a novel on abortion. It was bold to publish a novel on queer women. It was bold to challenge society's perception of mental illness. It was bold to challenge misogyny. It was bold to challenge authority.

A unique book. A woman’s book. A book from the point of view of a woman of color. It’s not madness, it appears like madness in the heteronormative world we live in, the world of the nuclear family, of colonialism and under the strict Christian laws of capitalism. Noenka rebels against this world like many before her. Noenka is finding her way in life, first through her mother and father, then through a black husband, then through a lover who dies and finally in Gabrielle. But they get caught in the system. They want each other. They want to live. But the world does not want them. The story is told poetically and non- linearly. It is well done. I learned about Suriname and the Native cultures of South America, of the terrible history, of how some survived. There is so much to learn about the world and women. And it is so complex. First published in 1982, Astrid Roemer wrote it in Dutch. It was translated into English by Lucy Scott. I wonder if it will ever be published in Sranan Tongo.

Recently, I felt that reading reviews ahead of reading UNDER THE EYES OF THE BIG BIRD led to increased expectations going in and then an eventual letdown by the unexciting revelatory chapters, whereas the opposite happened here. Reading reviews and others' thoughts on ON A WOMAN'S MADNESS before reading led me to have the lowest of low expectations. I expected an incoherent, opaque jumble of random mishmashed vignettes that would leave me feeling continually confused on the timeline and who was speaking. In a way, I'm glad I went in with these expectations because it made me enjoy the book all that much more when I realized this wasn't the case. I won't go so far as to say that it’s a totally undemanding read, but I never found it to be any more taxing than the many other literary novels that drop in nonlinear flashbacks here and there. What it is, though, is spectacular. I was surprised to be sucked in from page one. What we have here is a Creole Surinamese woman who refuses to be pinned down, to be trapped in the boxes that the norms of her time force on her. Her madness is no real madness at all, but instead an affliction caused by a mad society. Though considered a pariah by the other townspeople, her husband, siblings, her employers, doctors, etc., she constantly seeks liberation and fulfillment by any means possible. Time is spent with each of the three loves of Noenka’s life: her mother, her childhood beau turned lover, and her true love, Gabrielle. In the background, but really in the foreground, is the colonial and enslavement history of Suriname and its lasting effects, especially as seen in the divide between Noenka's parents, her mother adopting the colonists' religion and beliefs while her father descends from a family with Indigenous religious beliefs. Roemer’s writing is captivating, bringing to life the tropical setting with its lush greenery and violent wildlife; orchids and snakes are used as symbols throughout. The dialogue felt at some points a product of its time and at others astoundingly modern. It's a book filled with love, longing, and the desire to live a life of one's own. I'm so glad the International Booker got me to pick this one up!
Honestly, I have no idea what just happened. But it left me with a lot to think about, so.

Dense and intense, On a Woman's Madness is a novella that demands much of its readers. I struggled initially, but persevered by immersing myself into the beauty of the language passage by passage. The climax is sheer perfection, finally tying all that preceded it together.

On a Woman's Madness, is a poetic literary novel set in Suriname. We follow Noenka as she leaves her (awful) husband and tries to make her own way in life. Within these pages, we have some truly gorgeous writing. Sensual, philosophical prose that burrowed its way into my feels. Despite the delicious prose, the actual storytelling was all over the place! Disjointed narrative stops and starts, speeds up and slows down, jumps backwards and forwards in time. This book was difficult to follow and this took some of the sting out of its tail. Often, I was deeply moved, but a lot of the time I was simply confused. Every time I reached a pinnacle of frustration and bafflement, Roemer would hit me with a section of writing so powerful and beautiful that it would take my breath away. The ending, in particular, was annoyingly rushed. This book could either have worked better being drawn out into a family saga with more overarching clarity or been decluttered into a sparser work condensed into poetic chunks. Regardless, some stunning writing.

Wow. This story was dense but deeply moving. It’s a challenging read because the chronology is a little loose—time periods aren’t stated at the outset of a flashback, an important character is interacted with but not introduced, etc. A whole scene will unfold and its significance/what even happened is explained pages later. Still, i really enjoyed this novel’s exploration of 1980s Surinamese history, culture, and social dynamics and the use of poem/lyric/metaphor to build on the story. “I’m Noenka, which means Never Again. Born of two polar opposites, a woman and a man who pull even my dreams apart. I’m a woman, even though I don’t know where being female begins and where it ends, and in the eyes of everyone else, I’m black, and I’m still waiting to discover what that means.”

This is a very dense book that’s often hard to follow, but once you let go of the expectation of understanding every detail and just go with the flow, its rhythm sucks you in. It kept my attention all throughout, which is surprising for a book of that nature, as I usually get tired of being lost. It was a heavy read, not only in form but also in content. I loved following Noenka, a complex character who puts into sharp relief our unconditional need for love, freedom and belonging. A queer classic, its depiction of queerness was definitely rooted in the time and place it was set and written in, conditioned by religion, patriarchy and colonialism, but ultimately offered the sapphic yearning I was hoping for. The imagery was beautiful and I would love to reread this book to analyze it more, now that I understand where the story is going! Definitely a worthy pick for the International Booker Prize longlist. 🩷🐍🥀 "I loved him the way a sister loves a brother. Full of reservations and fear of him pulling me down into something that I was trying with all my might to rise above, the limitedness of my womanhood, of my blackness, and of my material powerlessness." "Was I only using other people as fertilizer for my growing individuality? Would I take the trouble to love these other people?" "Ever since you gave me life, you’ve been bleeding inside me, Mama." "I recognized you from the mosaic of my yearning."
reading around the world: suriname

Wow. Dense, poetic, chaotic, and just wow. There is so much in this book, such beautiful poetic flowing but dense writing, on top of a hell of a story, on top of the sensuality and life in there, on top of the history woven in, on top of the firy feminism. I’m in awe of Astrid Roemer. She won one prize?! She should have gotten them all.
wow…………incredible…………..am definitely going to read again……………not sure if i understood all of it but kind of didn’t need to?????? incredibly beautiful and sad
I didn’t really connect with this one, BUT there was some crazy stuff happening!

An utterly engrossing read! Roemer's novel is intense. With feeling, history, prejudices, identity, love, and relationships. Our main cahrater Noenka leaves her marriage and is shamed and blamed. She questions her capacity to love and how her very complicated bonds with both parents have shaped her own romantic views and expectations. She is afraid to give herself fully, keeping the most sacred part of herself locked away. The prose is rich yet sparse in some places, and the reader must pay close attention so that they miss nothing and are able to follow the change in time and place, which occur without warning. I love how poeticism emerges, woven quite seamlessly within dialogue and descriptions. The sensuality that is subtle yet so compelling when you come across it. There is passion, anger, betrayal, violence, and love within these pages, and for Noenka, just trying to live a life for herself is difficult. There is always the weight of expectations from family, society, even history. But she is not being completely honest with herself or her lovers and exists in a sort of maelstrom of undecidedness and torture.

2.5 stars. I don't want this rating to give the wrong impression. For its time, I'm sure this book was electrifying, but I suppose the synopsis gave me the wrong idea. I thought this would focus a lot more on a queer relationship than it actually did, which is my own biases and I can own that. Let's start with what I enjoyed. I hadn't ever read a book set in Suriname, so I loved learning more about the culture and history of this country. The writing, from a purely craft standpoint, was beautiful and definitely reflected the psyche of our main character. What little we did get of the relationship between Noenka and Gabrielle was lovely. There were lines in this book that I underlined and still so completely capture a burgeoning awareness of queerness. I do think that this represents a fantastic addition to queer literature in general and I'm glad it's accessible to English readers for the first time. The ending also took me by surprise. However, my experience was tampered by the fact that this book felt muddled and difficult to follow at times. Part of that is intentional, because Noenka's mental health is clearly affected by the cruelty and oppression that she's faced throughout her life. But as a reading experience I often lost the thread of the narrative. This book also focused a lot on Noenka's unhealthy and abusive relationships with the men in her life. While realistic, it's not my favorite subject to read and if I had known that was going to take precedence over the queer relationship I may have given pause to starting it. That said, I am glad I read this. I'd still recommend it especially if you're interested in learning more about Suriname and exposing yourself to more underrated and obscure queer fiction.

Longlisted for the 2025 International Booker Prize My longlist ranking #13 Translated from the Dutch “Over de gekte van een vroiuw” (1982) by Lucy Scott – the forty year gap from original publication being a record for the International Booker Prize which has no time limit on original publication. Published by Tilted Axis who in 2022 had no less then three books longlisted – “Happy Stories, Mostly”, “Love In The Big City” and “Tomb of Sand” which won the prize. The subject of this classic of Dutch Surinamese queer literature is Noenka – her mother a Christian, her father (descended from slave labourers) from a family notorious for their embrace of traditional religion. And in a society still steeped in racism and patriarchy, Noenka a primary school teacher, causes scandal when she walks out of her marriage – to Louis – after only nine days. The narrative style is extremely fragmentary – not least as each time Noenka meets someone in what its ostensibly the “present day” of the novel, her thoughts and the narrative immediately take in various past encounters with the same person (often from her childhood), so that as a reader I found myself often seemingly floundering, looking for a small piece of wreckage to cling on to. As an example, she stays with a childhood friend Emely (and her husband Emile) immediately after leaving Louis but this is bound up with fond childhood memories of Emely’s mother Peetje, recollections of a traumatic discovery (signalled by the presence of Vultures) at her house, a breach, a funeral, memories of sleepovers and so on. A later section brings in Lady Morgan, a close acquaintance of her mothers, who she stayed with as a child and her son Ramses (who was five when she first knew him) – both of whom play a key role in the middle part of the novel (Lady Morgan as a landlady, Ramses alongside his tennis coash friend Alek) and with Ramses Orchid’s collection providing some opening and then recurring imagery in the novel. Bit more than that at times the fragmentation turns into seeming choas. The effect is I think deliberate – much of the novel’s thesis (captured even in its protagonist’s name) is a rejection of conventional societal expectations, and I think its also represents the fissures both in Noenka’s life and in the society around her – but it does not make the reading experience a particularly fulfilling one. Further I rarely read English novels from 40 years ago – preferring predominantly contemporary and occasionally genuinely classical (ie pre 20th Century) literature – and it is perhaps no surprise I did not really warm to a translated novel originating from the same era. And it seems rather dated – as it progresses Noenka starts a lesbian relationship with Gabrielle (married, mother of two handicapped children and some 15 years her senior) – but for a queer classic the portrayal both of their relationship (and the cliched way in which they end up in a murder conspiracy) and of the condition of the children are both very much of their time. Interestingly, in a recent interview about the translation of her 2019 novel “Off White” and asked about how her writing had progressed over the 37 years she said “I’ve really deepened my humanity, and over time I’ve arrived at a comprehensive experience and understanding of my ethnicity, my female gender, my heterosexuality, my historicity as a Surinamese woman, and my membership in the human species. And above all, I’ve learned how to let go of those categories and become more open to our remarkable existence on this strange planet.“ So while its admirable that this novel was translated after so long it did not really work for me.

** spoiler alert ** It was hard to get into this book at the beginning as the writing style is very fluttery and disconnected but it does suck you in if you show patience and acclimate. The narration style of the protagonist is nonlinear and unconventional and aims to describe her marital estrangement and its aftermath with a jumbled temper of familial history, childhood reflections and dreams. You can tell Astrid Roemer dabbles in poetry by the strong poetic influences in the book. For people who appreciate that, it adds an almost ethereal, dreamy quality to the story. The nostalgia, romance and eroticism are magnified by poetic elements that revolve primarily around floral, maternal and feminine motifs. The setting of the novel and its story also filled me with intrigue about Suriname. It is a country that does not receive a lot of attention globally and the descriptions of the land and its cultural milieu pushed me to research it as a potential travel destination. Roemer takes you on the haunting, emotional journey of Noenka. I saw her as a renegade within her societal norms. She is a commentary against the idea of conventional femininity. She is not afraid to resist traditional, preset roles of women and their marital obligations towards their husbands. She abandons her husband Louis after just 9 days without hesitation and resists his constant advances to win her back. For this, she faces stigma and ostracism from her community and employers. She moves to a different city and has relations with other men, one of whom gets her pregnant. She willingly aborts the child, again displaying non-traditional femininity through unmaternal behaviour. She then falls in love with Gabrielle who is housing her. I see in this situation and the tenderness with which Noenka describes their moments and conversations, her latent 'mommy issues'. The most warm, intimate descriptions of her childhood are of her moments with her mother and the same stylistic language reemerges when she describes Gabrielle. Her attraction and subsequent relationship can be viewed as an actualization of that maternal bond. It is an irony considering how willingly she shirks a maternal opportunity of her own with an abortion. In fact, Noenka declares her love after her mother's death. It is almost as if pursuing a relationship with Gabrielle is a coping mechanism for her loss. As if, she can just replace that maternal warmth that is no more with the warmth of another woman. Having been coerced to move back with Louis, we see things come to a head as this is concurrent with a deepening relationship between Noenka and Gabrielle. They hatch plans to run away together to another place where they don't have to confront their traditional marital duties and where their courtship isn't taboo. However, in confronting the reality of their situation the novel rises to a dark crescendo in which Gabrielle murders Louis and is imprisoned.

'On a Woman's Madness' by Astrid Roemer. I chose this book as it was set in Suriname, a country I've never read anything from before. The author is Creole/Surinamese. The story is about Noenka, a young woman who struggles with mental health, maybe caused by her striving for empowerment and constantly being knocked back and made to realise she has none. I struggled a bit with this book because it seemed to jump around a lot and I often didn't really know what was going on. When I got on roll with it, it was great, but then it would suddenly take a turn and I was all confused again. I thought I was reading a new, modern release (it was long-listed for the international Booker in 2025) and only realised after I finished reading it that it was written in 1982. Maybe it's only recently been translated into English from the original Dutch? Now that I know when it was written, some of it makes more sense. It was a time of different values and expectations and the country was newly independent and still finding its feet. The book won prestigious prizes and in the context of when it was written I can understand why. It addressed issues that can still be problematic when addressed today, like mental health, lesbianism, disability, misogyny, suicide, abortion, racism, divorce, the influence of the church, the effects of slavery and colonialism ... an awful lot packed into just over 200 pages. A week after finishing the book, I'm still thinking about it, which I suppose is a sign of a good book. But at the same time, I remember how confused I was at times whilst reading it. So I'm sitting on the fence with it.

This was such a difficult but thought-provoking read. The writing style—preserved even in translation by Lucy Scott—was dreamlike and disjointed, which made it hard to follow. The lack of chapters and the constant shifts in time and place made me feel like I was drifting in and out of someone’s memories without direction. Still, I appreciate the themes Roemer explored: misogyny, oppression, feminism, sexuality, identity, and trauma. They’re powerful and still so relevant today. I empathized with Noenka’s pain, but I also struggled with her. She felt mentally fragile, easily swayed, and indecisive—especially in her relationships. Her bond with Gabrielle felt more like a reflection of her longing for maternal care than romantic love. However, I also understand that maybe these were shaped by a life where obedience was expected. In a society that denied her autonomy, it’s no wonder her sense of self became so fractured. Another character that truly stuck with me was Ramses. Despite societal norms, he genuinely adored Noenka. That’s why the abortion scene hit hard. While I understand the message about bodily autonomy and rebellion, I couldn’t help but feel it was unfair to Ramses. The baby was conceived from mutual desire, and considering Ramses’s own heartbreaking backstory, he at least deserved to know. This book left me conflicted, and maybe that’s the point. It doesn’t offer clear answers—it forces you to reflect on the messy truths of womanhood, survival, and the madness that comes with both.

After nine days of marriage, Noenka leaves her abusive husband and flees to Suriname’s capital Paramaribo… I really have anything particularly insightful to say about this one. Clearly, I did not get on with it at all - it was all over the place and I struggled to follow what was going on (and this is coming from somebody who normally quite enjoys fragmentary writing). Full disclosure: I did start it when I had a head cold, which certainly didn’t help, but I don’t think I can entirely blame my struggles on that. If I wasn’t specifically reading the entire International Booker 2025 longlist, I’d have DNFed it pretty quickly - there really was no need for it to be *so* opaque. Whilst it did eventually kind of come together, it was far too late for me, I just wanted the book to be over. I realise that it was progressive when first published in 1982, and it’s considered a classic of queer literature, but reading it 40+ years later was not an enlightening experience for me (evidently the International Booker judges disagree 🤷🏼‍♀️). An impenetrably fragmented story of searching for freedom whilst haunted by both society’s expectations and the legacy of colonialism in Suriname.

It took me quite a bit longer to finish this book than I had intended it to, some of that was my impatience with its nonlinear and fragmented style and some was the way in which this style often assailed the reader with things that can be triggering- particularly to those with sexual trauma, survivors of physical and psychological abuse, and those who endured manipulation and and gaslighting related to the patriarchal roles to which many women are pressured to conform. Death, loss, and grief are also a part of this book and while there is something of a resolution to Noenka's story the reader should expect to be all too aware it comes with a heavy dose of reality to go with it. It's an important book, one that discusses many aspects of how women suffer under the weight of societal, familial, and personal expectation, but it's also one that not all readers may be able tackle due to the subject matter being quite intense throughout.

4.25 stars “I loved seeing her like this. Wild, uninhibited, and so damn beautiful that it made my heart ache.” Finally, a good book in the KOS series! Honestly, I kind of gave up on this series after KOG, but Ana really surprised me with this book and Xavier and Sloane’s story. This book is totally different from what she usually writes, and I love how she’s experimenting with different characters and stories—ones that aren’t solely focused on romance but also on character growth and development. The storyline revolves around two things—Xavier and his new business venture, and their trial dating period. And somewhere in between, their attraction blossomed into love and something more. “Just shut up and follow me,” I snapped, wishing I had a wittier reply. “Yes, ma’am.” His cheeks dimpled. “I love a woman in charge.” Sloane Kensington is independent, responsible, and intelligent. She’s the woman everyone fears—cool and composed, never overreacting in any situation. Except when it comes to Xavier. He made her go bonkers with his antics, lol. She hides behind the façade of an ice queen because it protects her from potential hurt, and her fears were justified—her ex was an absolute asshole, and both he and her family gave her serious trust issues. People said she didn’t feel emotions or care, but Sloane felt everything—she just didn’t express it like others. She needed someone who would love and accept her for who she was, and Xavier did exactly that. I loved how she didn’t hold herself back when he asked her to go on a trip, how he challenged her, pushed her out of her comfort zone, yet always made sure she felt safe. She was also giving me Jules vibes with her comebacks. “You think you know me so well,” I whispered, even though he was right. “Only parts of you.” The gentle brush of his thumb against my hand unlocked a colony of butterflies in my stomach. “But we’ll get there.” Xavier Castillo is the epitome of a shameless flirt and effortless charm. But beneath all that is a man with raw vulnerability, scarred by his father’s treatment. I get why he was so stubborn and inconsiderate all these years, and I’m proud of him for finding his passion and working hard to make it a reality. He’s thoughtful and caring, and I love how much he paid attention to Sloane, he noticed everything about her. He’s so observant and stubborn when it comes to her. I fell for him in the very first chapter despite him being a playboy, and I liked that he wasn’t sexualising her every other moment like men in books usually do. Not once did he obsess over other women—Sloane was the only one who made him crazy and delusional. He’s so unhinged sometimes, always bribing people just to get to Sloane faster, but he’s also the sweetest, craziest person ever. The dates and outings he planned for her had me swooning so hard! He’s one of the best MMCs Ana has written and my favourite KOS series man. Period. “You would rather watch a rom-com about a witch and a plumber falling in love than attend a costume party with celebrities?” “One hundred percent. As long as I’m watching it with you.” Xavier and Sloane are absolute perfection. The romance was executed so perfectly—it wasn’t insta-love or insta-lust. It was about getting to know each other, giving a chance to the attraction that had been simmering between them for three years, slowly warming up to each other, breaking down the barriers they had built around their hearts, and falling in love in the process. It was simple, cute, and beautiful. Xavier and Sloane have opposite personalities, yet in some ways, they share the same fears and insecurities. Both were deprived of love and affection by their parents, but they loved each other with their flaws, not despite them. The way Xavier encouraged Sloane to step outside her comfort zone, and how she supported him at every step of his new business venture, was so endearing. “I don’t want a kiss or a one-night stand,” he said. “I want you. I want to know you outside work. I want to take you on real dates. And I don’t know if it’ll work out in the end, but I want us to at least try.” The ice queen x sunshine trope was executed so well. I loved their trips, their witty banter, the sexual tension, the dates Xavier planned (which were everything a girl deserves from a man), the effort they put into understanding each other, how they truly listened to each other’s stories, and their love confessions. Xavier and Sloane are the softest couple Ana Huang has ever written. “I needed her the way the ocean tides needed the moon, and I would give anything for her to feel a fraction of the same way toward me.” I loved Ana’s writing in this one; she included so many cameos from previous books, and my heart was full of happiness and nostalgia. This book also has some of the best love declarations at the end, and as unrealistic and dreamy as they were, my romantic heart loved every second of it. I loved how raw and relatable the characters were, watching them grow and step outside their comfort zones. The ending was the cutest! I seriously cried because I was so happy for these two idiot dorks. The third-act breakup was unnecessary as always—it’s Ana, so she had to throw it in. I would’ve loved for the mystery behind The Vault’s fire to be explained, but maybe it was left open for a future book. I really can’t wait for Ayana and Vuk’s book! I have a thing for broken, tortured heroes, so I already know I’m going to love it. ————— Pre-read review: Ice queen x sunshine boy trope never fails 😩 One of my most anticipated release of this year so pls ana dont disappoint me again

❝ whenever i was drowning, she was my anchor in the storm. ❞ just when i had officially given up on this series and was rotting in the ninth circle of romance hell, screaming "no more billionaire trauma dumps," ana guang yeeted king of sloth at my skull like a divine intervention and said "here, you ungrateful little raccoon, eat this." (she didn't actually say that but the vibes were there). after dragging my corpse through king of pride and king of greed (which felt like emotional waterboarding), i swore i was done. finished. retired from rich people feelings. but then the reverse sunshine trope whispered my name and my clown nose slid right back on like the weak, predictable gremlin i am. ₊˚꒰ 𖧷 ꒱ ⊹ i. plot and characters. ₊˚⊹ ꒱ sloane kensington is a publicist who could ruin your entire bloodline before her morning oat milk latte. to her elite clients she's a terrifying ice queen in a pencil skirt who weaponizes competence like it's a tactical nuke. but underneath that glacial resting bitch face is a very tired, very squishy woman who just wants to not be disappointed for once in her goddamn life. her armor is thick, her insecurities are loud, and when she goes feral? chef's kiss. i respect a girl who can be protective, petty, and ready to throw hands while still looking immaculate. xavier castillo is marketed as an international walking scandal and billionaire playboy, but on-page he's actually a dangerously observant, stupidly thoughtful golden retriever in human form. this man was in his emo "i don't care about anything" era, yet he was out here memorizing sloane's coffee order, tracking her micro-expressions like it was his full-time job, and cataloging her moods with the dedication of a man who has never heard of google calendar. i can't even get a situationship to remember my birthday without a formal evite and xavier is over here treating sloane's preferences like sacred scripture. be so fucking serious right now. and the cameos? delightful. all the previous rich traumatized idiots running around living their little happily-ever-afters like it's a billionaire reunion special. good for them. i'm happy for my silly little universe of walking red-flag collections. ₊˚꒰ 𖧷 ꒱ ⊹ ii. romance. ₊˚⊹ ꒱ this is reverse sunshine executed so perfectly i was straight-up feasting like a raccoon in a dumpster behind a five-star restaurant. grumpy ice-queen girl meets golden-retriever sunshine boy and i lost my entire mind. the romance is deliciously sloooow in the best way. they're learning each other's tells, picking up tiny details, and lowering their walls one molecule at a time like two emotionally constipated people who finally found someone worth the therapy bill. therre's no cheap trauma-dump bonding here. just two disasters actually getting to know each other while the plot gets gritty with heavier themes and messier backstories. it gave them texture, depth, and enough emotional baggage for a therapist to retire comfortably on. their connection actually felt earned instead of slapped on. ─〝 every version of my happily ever after will always include some version of you. 〞 ₊˚꒰ 𖧷 ꒱ ⊹ iii. conclusion. ₊˚⊹ ꒱ this book turned me into a giggling, feral mess more than once. i genuinely enjoyed it, against my will and better judgment. the longer length actually slapped for me; the extra page time gave space for the slow build, deeper character work, and maximum time to watch xavier be an absolute unhinged menace with a heart of gold. does it dethrone king of wrath for me? Considering the fmc “doesn't cry” she sure had a lot of moments where she was about to. Upcoming books in the series I do plan on reading the rest of the series. I am very excited about the next book with Vuk😚. But I am worried the quality is decreasing with this series😬.
