3 novellas in the usual John Grisham style, which I love. Homecoming - 4 * . All the familiar characters from the Jake Brigance series are back in this one. It is an extension of the short story 'Fish Files' (one of the stories in 'Ford County' collection).I liked it but the ending was abrupt. Mack's daughter was annoying Strawberry Moon - 5 * - Grisham's pet subject of death row. It was sad and also humorous. The young man who faces execution in a few hours discusses books with his benefactor. This gave an interesting insight into a few books. I feels sad that even an accomplice to murder (not pre-planned) can be executed in some states in the US. Sparring Partners - 5 * - This was fun. Love the intricate plot.

Three great stories packed into one book. From lawyers’ shenanigans to the viewpoint of a likely unjustly convicted death row inmate the tales told are intriguing and interesting. Characters both familiar and new are well drawn and developed. A thoroughly enjoyable read.
Grisham can write but his novels lack a decent plot lately. So, he tried his luck at three absolutely pointless novellas, again with no plot and, as an added bonus, no endings. 'Nuff said!

Having been told that John Grisham’s writing wasn’t particularly insightful, I approached “Sparring Partners” purely as a holiday read. I was completely unprepared to discover it was a collection of novellas rather than a single, cohesive plot. I was pleasantly surprised to discover that the writing is both compelling and effective at holding the reader’s attention. The novellas, despite their brevity, proved to be just as effective as a longer narrative. Of the three, “Homecoming” was interesting but felt like the weakest story, primarily due to its abrupt conclusion. Nevertheless, it held my interest until the very last sentence. “Strawberry Moon” was a very powerful and thought-provoking read. “Sparring Partners” was, without a doubt, the standout of the collection, and I felt a strong desire to re-read it immediately upon finishing. I truly enjoyed this book and am glad I gave this author a chance. It earns a rating of 4 to 4.5 stars in my opinion.

I love reading John Grisham but the short stories just make you miss how he lays out the story and shows you how the characters are when you read the whole book. Good book if you like shorts like this.

This is John Grisham’s latest book. It’s actually 3 novellas in one book. Story #1 was about Mack, a former lawyer who left the country and left his wife and kids behind. He comes back but everyone’s looking for him. Story #2 is about a 14 year old boy named Cody who was serving a life sentence for murder. He’s only 3 hours from execution and a 80 year old comes to visit him and come to find out, she’s the only person who has come to visit him the whole time he was in jail. Story #3 is about two brothers who hate each other and their dad is in prison for murdering their mother. I found myself easily confused in story #3 due to all the legal words. Overall, I give this book 3 stars.

This collection of three novellas begin with “Homecoming.” I am a long-time Grisham fan and was delighted to once again read about Jake Brigance and Canton, Mississippi. He is not doing his lawyering stuff, but he, Lucien Wilbanks and Harry Rex certainly have their hands full playing cat and mouse with the FBI. ***** “Strawberry Moon” focuses on a prisoner scheduled for execution. Cody has a few hours before his eventual punishment when he gets an unusual and amazing visitor. This book highlights many of the reasons the death penalty should be abolished.***** “Sparring Partners” was a bit of a disappointment for me. None of the characters were the least bit sympathetic. No wonder people hate lawyers.***

What a delightful sorbet. Three shorties from John Grisham, who never disappoints me, each with a point. The middle one, Strawberry Moon, as narrated by Ethan Hawke, gives an original take on the importance of books and the connections they forge. It also is a further examination of Grisham's stance against capital punishment. The one that made me laugh, however, was the titular entry. Sparring Partners, sly and hilarious, may have held a hidden take on the ability of power to pardon the guilty -- think tRump. Glad Grisham has not been wasting his time in lockdown.

This is a book of three novellas each very different from the others. They are all legal based. I thought the first one was an interesting story but was just a good story. The second story was better and more interesting and different with a good perspective on the subject of death row. The third one was the best. It grabbed you more and had some good twists and turns. A good read.
Seriously, does John Grisham need money this badly?

John Grisham has taking to publishing two novels a year lately. His usual legal thriller in the fall and some kind of change-up in the spring time. Those change-up books have included two involving Camino Island bookstore owner, Mercer Mann, and last year’s story of Sudanese basketball player, Samuel “Sooley” Sooleymon. This year, his spring-pushed-into -a-summer-release is “Sparring Partners”, a book of three novella’s that are focused on Jake Brigance and Ford County, the last hours on death row, and the fight between a father and two sons to control the future of their family law firm. “Homecoming” – our favorite small-town lawyer, Jake Brigance, from Ford County, gets a call from an old friend. Unfortunately, it is a notorious friend. A fellow lawyer, Mark Stafford, divorced his wife and ran away three years ago under mysterious circumstances. Word is that he stole money from his clients and left his family in bad shape. His former wife is now dying and his two daughters are in high school, and it appears that Mark wants to come home while trying to avoid any legal issues… “Strawberry Moon” - Cody Wallace is a young death row inmate is scheduled to be executed that evening for participating in murder with his brother when he was fourteen years old. His lawyer is working his last-minute appeals while the governor does not appear willing to grant clemency. Cody is facing his final requests… “Sparring Partners” – The once every successful Malloy family law firm, once run by a father now serving time in prison for killing his wife, is now led by competitive brothers – Rusty and Kirk – who are trying to keep it afloat. The problem is Rusty and Kirk despise each other, to the point that they avoid each other at all costs. Who will come out on top when the family war becomes a fight for the survival of the firm itself? For me, all three stories are an interesting dichotomy in why I liked them and yet was left feeling a bit empty. Let me explain why. What I liked – Let’s face it. John Grisham is one heck of a story teller. He can probably write a cookbook and make it come across as interesting and full of conflict. Even though I am going to provide some constructive complaints, I was still pulled in to each of the stories immediately and they kept my full attention throughout. Three’s no wasted words, just meat and story. For that I would give these stories 4 stars. What I didn’t like – This is a rare comment to make about a John Grisham book. There have only been two or three of his books (out of many) that I felt were too depressing. For me, “The Reckoning” was the one that I absolutely enjoyed the least. As a matter of fact, I will not read it again because nothing positive happened in the entire book. That was similar in several ways to these three novellas. All three of them were stories about bad people doing bad things and hurting the lives of others in significantly hurtful ways. Examples include a man who stole money and ran away from his wife and wo daughters. A man on death row who as been jailed since he was fifteen years-old and had a horrible upbringing. A family law firm, in which the father is in prison for killing his wife, while his two sons try to figure out how to take control of the business. The challenge I have is two-fold. Each story is sad and depressing (although, yes, I already said they were interesting- and they can both that and sad at the same time), and they ended incomplete. “Homecoming” set-up several sub-stories and then really kind of left things hanging. I could see another future novella to find out what happens next, because after some serious drama and conflict, mostly with selfish and uncaring characters, it felt like the story ended after act two than act three. “Strawberry Moon” ended okay for the most part, but it was awfully dang sad and depressing. That’s all I will say about that one. “Sparring Partners” was like a twisted version of “Dynasty” vs. “Dallas” with really unlikeable, superficial, and selfish-to-the-heart characters. Although, it was like watching a car wreck and you couldn’t turn away, the ending was so self-destructive and yet incomplete from a closure perspective, that I felt a bit frustrated and disappointed. As interesting as the novella’s were, they left a sad taste in my mouth. For that I would give them two to two-and-a-half stars. Overall, the three novellas were interesting and provocative, but came with a bad aftertaste. Still, John Grisham holds my attention and I give “Sparring Partners” three stars. I am sure that others will rate this higher than me and that’s okay. I may be in the minority when it comes to rating this one. That’s why “beauty is in the eye of the beholder”.

John Grisham has kept me turning pages for over 30 years, these three novellas were just as wonderful as anything he has written before. He has not “sold out” like some of the other popular writers. Homecoming stars Jake Brigance and another sneaky lawyer, who just defies the odds and does it his way! Strawberry Moon was the story of execution night on Death Row, very moving. It certainly makes you think twice about the death penalty. Cody Wallace, NO - Nikolas Cruz - YES. The Sparring Partners pits two warring brothers (lawyers not boxers!) up against one another. An intricate plot with a super ending. And I thought this book was going to be another sports story - don’t judge a book by it’s title!!
An entertaining read. I liked the way all three stories just "end". There are no fireworks.

Incomplete stories, disappointing! Three incomplete stories. Disappointing endings. A few good parts. Downer stories. Much preferred some of his olders stories. Would have preferred one complete story.
Classic Grisham writing. Three short stories in one book so they’re all wrapped up pretty quickly. I’ve always been a fan of John Grisham.

Sparring Partners is a collection of three novellas from John Grisham. In the first - Homecoming - A former attorney who had disappeared from Clanton, MS asked Jake Brigance to help him reconnect with his daughters. This is after the attorney had run off with clients' money and abandoned his family. And there may be an indictment. In Strawberry Moon, an inmate on Death Row reminisces about what got him there, In Sparring Partners, two brothers, who are partners in their father's law firm, try to find a way to keep their father in jail, while spending his recurring settlement. None of these characters are likable and they're all comitted some crime. Grisham tries to make them sympathetic but you just want to yell at them - "See what bad choices get you!" Maybe you feel for the man on Death Row, because it seems like he never got a chance at life. The stories are easy to read - like an old-school Grisham narrative. But they don't really end as much as drift away. Good pick if you want a shorter narrative. Grisham fans should enjoy these stories.
Loved all three stories even if they were cliff hangers

I liked the first story "Homecoming" the most of the three within the book; however, I definitely could have done without the repetitive sexualizing of Mack's 17 year old daughter, especially when he says how she flicks a cigarette out and lights it, blowing the smoke like a sexy Hollywood actress... eww and weird and just, no..

I admit that I didn't even bother to read the last two stories of this book because the first one was so horribly pathetic. The people who wrote the blurbs for this book and praising it must have their heads up their behinds or were handsomely paid to write what they did. What a disappointment and the last Grisham book I will bother to pick up.
3.5 stars. This book is made up of 3 short stories or novellas that are not connected. I didn't know this going in so it was an unpleasant surprise. All were decent but none were exciting.

This book is actually made of three novellas by John Grisham. They are continuing stories he had previously released at some point or wanted too. I feel if he would have put more work into the third story it would have made a great book!

Well, you probably already know that any Grisham book will be a good read - interesting story (or stories, in this collection of 3 novellas), smooth flow and engaging situations. Holds true for these as well. Think I enjoyed the Homecoming the most, tale of an attorney who ran out on his family with client funds and wants to return. Second would be the death row inmate with 3 hours to live in Strawberry Moon and Sparring Partners gets a bit clunky in places but it may be trying to blend a bit too much - office and external politics, crime and punishment, money laundering and tax issues, and of course the usual legalities. Certainly an interesting read!

I just saw this morning in the paper that this book was rated #1 on best seller list. Yikes!! I really did not think this book was "Grisham" quality. I think these were drafts of potential possible books that never got off the ground. Very light on every count you can think of. Talk about a summer read. This is the first time I have ever disliked any of his works. Too bad.

I’m not surprised this has already hit the bestseller list! I felt lucky to be one of the first to get it off the library book shelf. This book has 3 novellas. All 3 have one thing in common. Will it be obvious? The first, ‘The Homecoming’ has one of Grisham’s favorite character’s Jake Brigance, a small-town lawyer from Clanton, Mississippi who finds himself in the middle of an interesting ‘issue’ involving a divorced father who once fled the area who now wants to reconnect with his daughters. The only thing is, when he fled, did he break the law, and will his return create a problem for him? The question for us as readers is, who do we want to root for – the father or …? You don’t think I am going to give away spoilers do you?! In ‘Strawberry Moon’ we meet Cody Wallace a 28-year-old death row inmate who has only 3 hours left to live. He has been on death row since he was convicted at 14 years old. Yes, as readers we may have a reaction about the justice system, too. Cody has only one request to make – and as we patiently wait to learn what it could be – we learn of his back story that led him to a life behind death row bars. We also are reunited with many beloved books… (which you will find out what I mean, when you pick up this book to read on your own!). But, most of all, stay with Cody to the end, because the strawberry moon gives meaning to why it is the perfect title for this story. The third story is the same title as the book. I need to sigh here, because my question becomes, what happens when you don’t like any characters in the story? What are we waiting for? Knowing the author, there is always a catch, so what is it? The good news is, it is a short story. It doesn’t take long to get to the answer…but, it is somewhat painful getting there, knowing that there is nobody to root for…at least, in my mind. Or maybe, just maybe, there is one character to appreciate. And with that one, Mr. Grisham does the right thing, and makes reading the story worthwhile after all. Of course!

Was I entertained, yep. Were the stories great, nope. Were the stories satisfying, well that depends. I like John Grisham, but writing endings is not his strong suit and in this case, het gets three chances to improve. Did he? Nope. Did I feel like I wasted 9 hours, hell no. In reading a few reviews, most folks thought the last story, Sparring Partners was the best and the middle story, Strawberry Moon was the least of the three. I disagree, I thought Strawberry Moon was the best, mainly because it had the best ending. There is no doubt where Mr Grisham stands in the Death Sentence debate, and this story picks a completely ridiculous storyline to try and annul the death sentence. It is doubtful that in 1991 or so, that someone so young would be on death row, much less that a 14 year old would be convicted and sentenced to death under the events described by Mr Grisham. Never-the-less, the story was good and compelling and there is always hope.....

This book contains three novellas. I elected to listen to the first of the three novellas on a road trip with my 11 year old. The reader does a great job in the Audible edition but after 20 chapters in the book my kid looked at me and asked, "Is something going to happen?" I was wondering the same thing. Sadly, in the first two novellas not much happens. And the third one felt like an incomplete story that could have been developed into a full length novel, much like the Grisham novels of the 90's - edge of your seat kind of stuff, but instead it was very slow moving with a disappointing finish. If you loved the pace of Gray Mountain and The Rooster Bar this book may be right up your alley. For me, it was way too slow. I'm a huge Grisham fan, just struggling to enjoy his work from the past 5-6 years.

This was a book of supposedly short stories. It was really one short story and two not-so-short ones. All were excellent, but I enjoyed the two longer ones more. The book takes its title from the second of the two longer stories. The first was about JakeBrigance and his missing friend Mack Stafford. Mack tries to come home with varying results. The short story was about a man on Death Row who was convicted when he was only 15. The last story, also titled Sparring Partners, is far too complicated to get into without re-writing the story, which I am not about to do. Trust me, you'll like it. I'm not a short story fan, but did enjoy these. Well -- it's John Grisham.

Is there any writer to rival Grisham? His novels (or in this case three unrelated novellas)are like good buttered popcorn. They go down fast and easy. No, he'll never receive the Booker Prize, but who cares? Once you start a Grisham novel you can't put it down until you've finished. The stories here are interesting, well-plotted and not padded with fluff. The characters are relatable and believable. It's not "serious" writing, but damn he's entertaining. I've said it before, and I'll say it again, whoever decided to stop making Grisham's books into movies made a big mistake. Recommend.

3.5 stars. I enjoy Bennett as a writer, but I felt like this book didn't come all the way together. I wanted it to either be a more focused book with half the plot or to really go big and have more about all the characters. At first it feels like this book is going to be entirely about colorism and the strange town of Mallard, Louisiana where light-skinned Black people have effectively segregated themselves. The story begins here, with the story of twins Stella and Desiree, who grow up and then escape the town. Desiree returns after leaving her abusive husband with her dark-skinned daughter Jude. And at this point I thought this may be the real focus of the book. But then we seem to jump so quickly through time, which threw me somewhat off kilter. Desiree doesn't want to stay, but she does. And it is hard to understand why she stays knowing how unwelcome the town is for her daughter, but we gloss over it and start jumping ahead to when Jude finally leaves, moving into the other part of the story, set mostly in Southern California where Jude goes to college and then encounters long-lost Stella, who has cut off communication with her family and now passes for white. Then we have another section of the story, filling out those years of Stella's life, and this was much of the best of the book. Stella, always so afraid of being found out, develops a strange and complicated friendship with a Black family that moves in across the street in their wealthy subdivision. We get to see why Stella passes but all the ways in which it has complicated her life and her own identity. But then we push forward again, leaving just as a plot is really diving into what's interesting. The sections between cousins-but-also-strangers Kennedy and Jude are not as interesting as I wanted them to be, and didn't really dive very far into how different these women's lives are, race matters somewhat, but it's not clear what the daughters are here to tell us. I also have to note that I was frustrated and concerned by Jude's plot, which mostly centers around her relationship with Reese, a trans man. Almost all of the elements around Reese and queerness felt vague and fuzzy when many other things were given to us in such detail. Reese passes as a cis man so easily that after several years everyone wonders why Reese and Jude are still unmarried. Equating passing as a trans person with racial passing makes me feel very uncomfortable. They are not things that can and should be compared. So I had my hackles up almost immediately when Reese entered the story. And for much of Jude's first section, we get the typical kind of Trans 101 you expect when the cis character is the focus of the story and the trans character is a kind of window dressing. I was also confused by many of the details around Jude and Reese's social life, where they are out with groups of gay men and going to drag shows in the 70's. It isn't impossible, but spaces for gay men haven't exactly been open and friendly to trans men, and it would be unusual for a trans man with a girlfriend to be in that kind of space. (Yes, queer people have often been terrible and exclusionary and sexist and racist and plenty of other things.) The drag, again, seems to hammer in this idea of taking on a new identity as recurring theme, but again I am not sure that it really works. It is nice that Jude is so accepting but she's so accepting and they face no real repercussions to their relationship that sometimes it seems to almost invalidate the difficulties a trans man and his partner would have faced at the time. Without the queer issues, this would have still been a solid 4 stars for me, but I really couldn't get past it. Trans rep in fiction is certainly up, but there is so often this feeling that they aren't quite as fully real as other characters, that their trans-ness is there for some kind of message, and it really bothers me. I did this book on audio and it probably didn't help that I didn't like the reader.

What a tour de force Bennett has achieved with The Vanishing Half. Brilliant and complex, this story surpassed all my expectations and more. Twins Desiree and Stella couldn't wait to leave behind the small, black town they've grown up in. At sixteen, they finally seize their chance and run away. More than a decade later, the twins have lost touch with each other. One comes back to town with a black daughter, while the other lives across the country, passing for white while hiding her past. As time goes on, they and their respective daughters realize you can never quite cut the ties of the past. This book touches upon so many worthwhile topics. The themes of race and racism captured in this book are among the most nuanced and insightful I have come across. At its core, racism is the opportunity for one group to make themselves feel better by acting out to oppress another. There is no group that is immune to being the oppressor, including those that are oppressed themselves. The way the light-skinned colored people of Mallard act towards dark-skinned people both captures the insidiousness of racism (racism only begets more racism) and its pervasiveness in society. I appreciate the book's honesty on this, no matter how disheartening it is to think about. Another interesting theme captured over and over is whether someone can ever leave their past and heritage behind to make a clean start. The twins ran away thinking they could be the controller of their own destiny. But as they grow older and their paths diverge, it becomes apparent that their years growing up in Mallard continues to follow them. Even as they meet different opportunities and experiences, their past still contributes to shape their decisions and ultimately where they end up. It's possible to live separate lives through different decisions, as illustrated by the twins' dual contrasting paths, but they still remain within the parameters of their past. The twins' daughters are also molded by their mothers, yet they are a new generation, the first to break through the confines of their mothers' past. The daughters could truly say they are making strides when it comes to racism, having been given increased opportunities, which allow them to become more open and accepting than their mothers (as racism begets more racism, opportunities beget less). Another interesting point is that one daughter grew up with privilege and wealth, while the other grew up wanting. Yet, through choices and motivations, the one who grew up with less arguably ended up with more. And that is an encouraging thought. This story covers so much ground, both in terms of the strands of the twins' and their daughters' narratives, as well as its exploration of race, gender, identity, and belonging. The writing is beautiful and poignant, flowing smoothly along while guiding the reader from one insightful observation to another. What a powerful read, indeed. ~~~~~~~~~~~~ ✧ Connect with me ✧ Instagram ✧

Although the first 1/3 of the book was slow, once we start to see how two generations diverge and they connect later on, I became invested in each person's individual journeys as they grappled with race, loneliness, colorism, abuse, motherhood, and a sense of identity. I enjoyed reading about these women and also adored the male side characters (Reese makes me so soft!) It’s a poignant and lovely story that takes you through several lifetimes with empathy and hope.
Completely absorbing. Intricate prose. Deep characterization. Bennett exceeded my expectations with her second novel.

3.5 Two Black twins, so “light” they could “pass” for White. And, this story exploring “ PASSING” - a term I was not familiar with. One of the twins will choose to do just that-live life as a White woman. Her husband will never know the truth. She will not get to celebrate milestones with her twin sister or mother. She will not be able to share her heritage with her own daughter. I found this book to be profoundly SAD. IMAGINE believing that it would be worth LOSING all of that, to be WHITE? I enjoyed the first half of this book, when I learned about “Passing” and the story focused on the twin sisters..Desiree and Stella. The second half was not as strong for me, when the story shifted to their daughters, Jude and Kennedy, and the focus of race and “passing” became diluted with another theme, regarding a character named Reese. I understand it was another way to explore “Identity”. But, the book would’ve been more powerful for ME if the narratives had remained with the sisters-I wanted to spend more time with Desiree after she returned home- So we could see both her struggles and also the riches that she DID have- by having Adele, Jude, Early and the community of Mallard in her life. So that we could compare, and contrast, their two choices in more depth. To fully explore “PASSING”. I needed to feel more of the PAIN (of EACH sister) that resulted from Stella’s choice.. As I wondered how many women who chose to PASS, would choose that path again? Relevant Timely. Available now!! I'm not sure I have words for how excellent this book turned out to be, but terms such as "breathtaking, poignant, and ultimately hopeful" come to mind. I was constantly reminded of the golden oldie movie Imitation of Life (1959) in regards to the discussions surround race, class, and gender, while also featuring a plot thread where a light skinned Black teenager is living her life passing as white. Technically I would rate this 3.5 stars. This story is primarily centered on a set of twins born in Mallard, Louisiana. The twins run away from home to make it big in the city when one of the twins runs off and begins her life as a white person while the other twin goes through life as a black person. This story follows this set of twins through life as well as their daughters.
