"Easily pissed off and heavily armed." An apt description of Letty Davenport, daughter of Lucas, and the newest badass in John Sanford's literary arsenal. Just 24 years old, Letty has been working for a U. S. Senator, but due to boredom, tenders her resignation. The Senator, who has been duly impressed by her skill set and no-nonsense attitude, offers her a special position within the Department of Homeland Security, complete with a carry permit so she can be legally armed just about anywhere, anytime. Fans of the Prey series will recognize Letty (Lucas's adopted daughter) as having displayed preternatural ability with firearms in an earlier Prey novel, and so we now get to see her display that skill to great effect. The plot revolves around a militia group led by a woman who had served in the military and her plan to do something epic that will call attention to the problem she perceives at our southern border. Initially, the book centers on how the militia is raising money for their complex plan. This leads Letty, along with her assigned partner, John Kaiser, an ex-Delta Force soldier whose trust and respect she gradually earns, down to Oklahoma and Texas, where oil is being diverted and sold illegally. Along the way, Sanford takes great pains to focus on Letty's choice of sidearms (model, sights, caliber, holster) and her ability to compartmentalize emotions such that she will not hesitate to, nor be disturbed by, taking another's life. Both, of course, will come in handy as Sandford picks up the pace as Letty and John begin to close in on the cadre of militia members that are spearheading the project they are calling the next "Alamo." There is a considerable amount of time spent in cat and mouse mode, with limited action, but rather a lot of stage setting. The astute reader will probably suss out the plan well before the reveal, but that's really besides the point. What we have here is a young, female version of Lucas Davenport or, at least. the essence of that character. Cool, deadly, and fearless. My rating of 3.5 stars is rounded up because I'm a fan of the author and there are some very good scenes in the novel. But frankly, it really isn't a 4 star book, as there are several sections of the book that bog down and stretch credulity more than usual. Nevertheless, it's clear that Letty is going to be around a while, as there's already a second in this series. So, does this mean we'll see fewer Prey novels now or, heaven forbid, even fewer novels featuring "That f***ing Flowers?" I've no idea, but will certainly read on and hope for the best.

Letty Davenport is a chip off the old "Lucas Davenport" block in a spinoff of John Sandford's hugely popular crime fiction series. Daughter Letty is a smart, tough and courageous young Homeland Security Investigator and dynamic protagonist. Partnered with a former Delta Master Sgt., she's a fast gun shooter with deadly accuracy in this high energy thriller. I very much liked her character develop taking the lead in an investigation of stolen petroleum on the Texas border that morphs into a confrontation with a large right wing militia. In addition to her prowess as an investigator and shooter, she has a sharp sense of humor with a kick ass attitude. Unlike many authors of long running crime fiction series, author John Sandford has never "mailed in" a disappointing annual addition to the series and this wildly entertaining spinoff is no exception. I highly recommended it to my esteemed GR friends.

Lettie is basically Lucas with tits, which I expected, & there were enough nods to her sex to make her seem enough like a chip off the old block that the resemblance didn't become a burden. In this, I think he did a better job than Connelly has done with Renee, a female version of Harry. (I really like & read Connelly's books as soon as they come out.) The story was really good. I could certainly see the events depicted happening today. Hopefully we'll have a heroine & her trusty side kick available if they do. It's probably a question of when & I probably don't know about several attempts that have been stopped. It's that well done. He also did a good job of working Letty's back story in. That's tough to do. He didn't bore me with it & I've read every book in the series in order, but there's enough meat in the flashbacks & explanations that you'll get a good picture of her even if this is the first book you've picked up. Someone is stealing crude oil from smaller oil companies - not a lot , in fact, it could be written off as an accounting error if it wasn't noticed by veteran oilman Vermilion Wright. And he's not concerned about the loss which is minuscule by company standards but it is a vey large amount by most standards which means big bucks. He's is not so much concerned about the money but what the thieves (because it would require more than one to pull this off) are planning to do with it. He contacts Senator Colles, head of Homeland Security to investigate. Meanwhile,Letty Davenport, a junior aide to the Senator, has become bored with paper work and is ready to quit. To convince her to stay, the Senator offers her the chance to partner with Homeland Security agent John Kaiser to track down the thieves. Letty is looking forward to the chance for some excitement but it becomes apparent they are up against some very determined and well-trained thieves and soon she and Kaiser find themselves in a whole lot more danger than they could have imagined. What can I say about John Sandford's ability to provide the reader with some of the most exciting intelligent, timely an unputdownable thrillers around except to say, even after all this time, he never disappoints and his latest, The Investigator, is no exception. It is well-written well-plotted and with plenty of action. The characters are well-developed, especially Letty who is an extremely likeable new character. She may be Lucas Davenport's adopted daughter and she may have many of his characteristics - smart, complex, determined, and fearless - but she isn't just a female version of him. Although the story is mostly wrapped up and quite satisfactorily, there is a tantalizing cliffhanger left at the end and I look forward to see where Sandford takes readers in the future. Thanks to Edelweiss+ and GP Putnam's & Sons for the opportunity to read this book in exchange for an honest review

This is the first time in my entire life that I have rated a John Sanford book as a one. I looked forward to this book. The main character is Letty Davenport, after she finished college. He dad mentioned her name to a US Senator, and he hired her. Letty is bored with the work (this was my first clue because I was bored with this book); she works for Senator Colles and she quits. He puts her resignation in the shredder and gets her transferred over to Homeland Security. There are pages and pages of Letty getting dismissed or put down because she is female. She has to prove her value all the time. It starts with a shooting contest between Letty and her the DHS guy who is to take her for shooting practice. She beats him, of course, and she has a better gun than he has. The villains are soon introduced, and it becomes a contest between them and Letty. Guess who wins. Guess who has the better vehicles and the most assistance. I have never before read a dull Sanford book. I read it because I have read almost everything he has ever written. I read him before Letty. I read him during Letty growing up and sometimes getting in trouble. But enough is enough. Get me back to Virgil or Davenport.

This may be the WORST book I’ve read in years. It reads like a Sears manual. No surprises, no mystery, completely predictable. This book is also politically driven.. The lead character has NO PERSONALITY.. I forced myself through the book without gaining any enjoyment. The worst part of it is the Author is leaving it open for a sequel 😒 Don’t waste your time

I enjoyed The Investigator by John Sandford. It was a well-crafted story that easily held my interest and made me want to know what was going to happen next. I very much enjoyed the two primary characters (Letty and Kaiser). Not only were they well written and included just enough backstory to invest the reader in them (even with no foreknowledge from previous books), but they made a great pair. A good part of the success of the story was their partnership and interactions. Sandford has a long history of writing excellent books...this one is no exception and will not let you down. This is a great start to a new series--one that I will follow.

Too political. I don’t need the occasional left-wing jabs that are sprinkled throughout this book. I’ve loved most of Sandford’s previous books, and had high hopes for this book. If the right wing extremists come back for Letty in the sequel, you can keep it. I am looking forward to the next Prey book.

Yawn Terse, stilted dialogue. Boring topic. Lucas Davenport's daughter - the perfect woman but without any redeeming interesting facets. I quit. The father? Interesting stories and character. The daughter? Perhaps John Sandford hasn't found her voice yet. Call me when he succeeds
Best book of the year! I read this book about Lucas Davenport's daughter Letty in one day. I couldn't put it down. SPOILER ALERT: Is Jane Hawkes going to become Letty's Clara Rinker?

5 Stars. Did I ever like this book! A six although the max is five. We first meet Letty Davenport in 'Naked Prey,' #14 in the Lucas Davenport series. He bumps into her as a 12-year-old brat, smart and street-wise. She narrowly escapes death at least twice. Unfortunately her mother, an alcoholic who is more being supported by Letty than the reverse, is one of the victims. Lucas and Weather adopt her and realize that she likes detective work. She becomes a chip off the old block - a Lucas Two! Jump forward a dozen years and she's a Stanford graduate working for Senator Colles in Washington. But bored with a craving for field work and excitement, not a desk job. Colles arranges for her to be hired by Homeland Security and sends her to investigate the disappearance of small amounts of oil in Texas. His fear is that profits from the stolen oil could be getting into the hands of toxic militia groups. A well-placed concern. It leads to an illusive group called The Land Division, a showdown in Texas in a border town near El Paso, and attempts to stop a busload of Central Americans from entering the US. Letty's in the middle. It's so today. What a story. (July 2024)

In this latest John Sandford thriller, The Investigator (G.P. Putnam's Sons 2021), the star this time isn't Minneapolis' renowned crime fighter, Lucas Davenport but his brilliant and tenacious adopted daughter, Lettie. An old 24, graduated from Stanford and now working for a U.S. Senator, she is already bored of the government job she landed partly because of her famous father but just as much because of her own storied background. When the Senator offers her a change of venue, still investigating but in the field instead of an office, she wastes no time saying yes. With a mid-career former Marine as a partner, they are tasked with finding out why crude oil is being stolen from producers and what the huge amounts of money being generated by its sale is funding. Lettie proves she possesses her adoptive father's 6th sense for connecting the dots and quickly links the money to a female-run anti-illegal-immigration militia. The question is, what are they planning that costs so much? With instinct honed of years at the side of one of the best crime fighters in the Midwest, Lettie proves herself capable, clever, and smart enough to figure out what is going on. Why did I give it a 4/5 instead of the 5/5 it seemed headed for 80% of the story? A less than satisfying ending that didn't seem to quite fit with the facts. But I will read the sequel that is hinted at, and with relish.

A real let-down. I was excited to read a book where Lucas Davenport's daughter, Letty, had the starring role. But was very disappointed with the story. It read laboriously with too many superfluous details about guns and the oil business. Especially about guns. My god does it go into detail about weapons. I guess gun-lover might like it. A lot of people die, some of the criminals get caught and I think Sandford may have left the story line open for a sequel. Just wasn't my thing and since COVID started I've read dozens of other Sandford's novels and enjoyed them all. It was a Letty let-down all the way.

Please tell me we are going to get more Letty Davenport books I loved this one. The book starts pretty much the same way all of Sandford's books start but make no mistake Letty is her own character. It is really hard to believe at times that Letty is in fact not the biological child of Lucas - they are so alike it is eerie. This is a classis Sandford book so you are in for a faced paced mystery with some really great characters. No spoilers here but if you love Lucas, Virgil and Kidd you are going to love Letty.

"The Investigator" has all the hallmarks of John Sandford's best work: lots of action, fast pacing, decent writing, realistic dialogue, and good "good guys". I think it's a fine start to what might become yet another great series by one of my favorites. The Investigator opens with Lucas Davenport's adopted daughter, Letty, pulling the plug on a job her dad had pulled strings for her to get with a powerful US Senator. The senator doesn't want to lose her, so he rejects her resignation and assigns her to the DHS as a researcher. Her first gig in that role pairs her with an experienced DHS investigator, Kaiser, to try to determine who's 'stealing' oil from Texas fields, selling it, and doing lord knows what with the proceeds. Letty's background as a young, pretty, Stanford-educated non-law-enforcer tends to lead people who come into contact with her to underestimate her abilities. That's because in addition to the preceding, she's also Lucas Davenport's daughter and spent countless hours watching the legendary lawman work his magic, she actually grew up poor before being adopted and has a major chip on her shoulder due to that, she's a dead-eye shot who knows more about guns than most, and she'd already killed a couple (bad) people and didn't really have any remorse about doing so. She's also very handy with lock picks and knows many tricks of the trade. Letty and Kaiser travel to Texas, begin poking around, and develop an approach that helps them discover how the oil is being stolen and how it's transported. In some alternating chapters, the people who are the recipients of the funds from the stolen oil, a collection of militia types operating in the El Paso area, are planning some sort of big bang and are calling in like-minded folks from across the country to travel down to help make it happen. Letty and Kaiser eventually find themselves on the tail of the militia, but the militia leaders are cleaning up loose ends and their big bang in imminent. The Investigator is a solid beginning for the Letty Davenport character. I don't think she's fully fleshed out yet, though. I've always felt Sandford did a masterful job in bringing the Virgil Flowers character into the series as Lucas Davenport was transitioning to higher level positions, but Letty is sort of sprung out there as this almost fully-formed machine who, although new, acts like a 20 year veteran. It's a minor quibble, though, since I really enjoyed the book and look forward to more.

To begin with, I think it is only appropriate that I admit to being a fairly avid reader of John Sandford over the years, a fan of both of his Lucas Davenport “Prey” and Virgil Flowers series, which easily captured my imagination. Davenport and Flowers are perfect opposites, providing a great compare and contrast personalities, as well as approaches to investigative work. Now it’s time for Davenport’s adopted daughter, Letty, to step into the limelight and take a lead role. In “the investigator” Letty does just that… When we are reintroduced to Letty, she is twenty-four years old, graduated from Stanford university, and working in Washington D.C. for U.S. Senator Colles. When she gets the opportunity to look into a problem for him, she ends up an uncovering an issue for him and discovers she likes investigative work. Enough to quit her job with him and move on. However, the Senator is impressed with her skills and moxie, and offers her an opportunity to do investigation work fulltime with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). She’ll even get to carry a sidearm. Her first investigation involves something Senator Colles and his committee have been looking into. In Texas, several companies are reporting thefts of their crude oil. That’s the lesser problem. The bigger concern is what the thieves are doing with all of the money they are getting from selling the stolen oil. The worry is that a dangerous anti-government militia group appears to be involved with the criminal activities and who knows that chaos can come from that. Letty gets paired with an experienced DHS investigator and war veteran, John Kaiser, and they head on down to Texas to see what they can find. Following a trail of stolen oil isn’t easy, but it doesn’t take long before the two of them are discovering dead bodies and a link to a dangerous group of vigilantes who are preparing to do some serious life-threatening, explosive damage… There were some really good things to like about Letty’s first time in the lead role category. What worked best was how Sanford treated her as a complex, intelligent, and physically capable character, with depth and unique background that molded her into a strong female protagonist. Although she is still young and learning, Sanford gives her the perfect sidekick and mentor, in the older war veteran, John Kaiser. Someone that balances her aggressive approach by letting her go and supporting her actions, and yet gently pull her back and teach her things that she still needs to learn. I really enjoyed the development of their relationship in this book. In addition, Sanford provides Letty with opportunity for adventure and development. This was a good introductory story where she could get her feet wet, face dangerous enough opposition, and still learn the necessary lessons she needs along the way. The bad guys were bad, but not bad enough for her to outthink and strategically maneuver in her first investigation. And I really liked the flashback scenes that Sanford used to connect her past upbringing and survival to her current adult situation. I appreciated being reminded of things that happened throughout Letty’s life that I have forgotten over time. That was an excellent tough and well done. About halfway through, I realized that Letty is many ways Lucas Davenport version 2.0. She is her adopted father’s daughter in so many ways. His influences on her are so much stronger than I previously thought. They both have a strong hunger for justice, for hunting down criminals, and a willingness to bend the law if needed for a righteous cause. I must admit that I like watching another Davenport take center stage as a young pup and make her own future in law enforcement. It will be fun watching her blaze her own trail. On the other hand, there were some things that I didn’t like as much – there were a couple of things and at the top of that lit was the excessive political comments. Some were used as motivations for the bad guys, some were sarcastic jokes, and some were just plain unnecessary. I don’t know why, but it seems like over the last four or five Lucas Davenport novels, and now with Letty, the use of political references have just become way too much for me. Maybe other readers may feel differently, but they have become used way too much in my opinion. Along with those political comments, it seems that the bad guys have all become anti-government, political revolutionary-minded. Over the last several books, they have ranged from racist supremacists to downright hicks with hatred and guns. One of the problems that has arisen, is that these kinds of bad guys don’t come across as organized, financially backed, or powerful. Some of them comes across as just mean and stupid, which lowers the bar of opposition for the good guys, in this case, Letty. The best thing they have going for them is that they are willing to kill pretty much everything. Even if they are not that smart about it. Sanford’s writing style also involves is a lot of running around in the middle section of the book. Although I like how Letty was thinking and analyzing what was going on during the investigation, a lot of time was spent running from one location to another and jumping all around. I can’t say that I have an answer for it, but there sure was a lot of chasing around. Having said all that, I was going to give this 3.5 stars minus .5 stars for the excessive political dogma references. That is until the last 60 – 70 pages. That buildup to a hair-raising climax and ending was so good that I had to bump this up to 4 stars, and rightfully so. That last quarter of the book was strong, emotional, and set-up well for more Letty to come. A worthy 4-stars it is. I hope you enjoy it as much as I ended up doing. I can’t wait for more…

While I'm still enjoying the Prey novels with character Lucas Davenport as well as the Virgil Flowers series, both are starting to get a bit too familiar. OCEAN PREY was the recent exception. That team-up book with both Davenport and Flowers was excellent. With THE INVESTIGATOR, writer John Sandford has a fresh new subject to chronicle the adventures of, and he makes the most of it. This was a true page-turner, hard to put down (even though I did when other obligations called). This was new and exciting, especially not knowing the character's full inclinations just yet and where they might go and/or do. THE INVESTIGATOR has humor, suspense, plenty of action and shines a spotlight on current affairs. And, without editorializing too much. I thought the militia's point of view was presented fairly, even though I don't agree with the rationale and proposed solutions. I won't spoil the story any further. If you've been thinking about picking up a Sandford novel but unsure where to start, this would be a great place. There is enough back-story of Letty Davenport's history and upbringing to keep new readers informed. She's a true bad-ass. I can't agree with all her methods, but I certainly admire the spunk.

This is a perfect example of male authors not being able to write women. Letty came across as a wannabe Ryan Reynolds type cast character with breasts. The attempt at humor throughout this book was so cringeworthy I was regularly muttering out-loud "oh for fucks sake." Worse than that was the new male encounter formula that was repeated again and again. Letty meets new male character, man is condescending and distrustful of Letty, Letty demonstrates skill and/or knowledge of guns, man becomes both instantly impressed and aroused by this surprising revelation that a feminine looking woman enjoys handling ammunition. Just an exhausting read.

This book is very dragged I’d say. I find myself skipping a lot of pages, only reading the dialogues. Eventually I feel Letty’s character is too perfect for me to believe in. She bosses around everyone including the senator. She has that “I’m superior than everyone vibe” that I find hard to related to.

Synopsis: Several oil companies in Texas have reported thefts of crude. U.S. Senator Colles isn’t so much concerned with the oil as he is with the money: who is selling the oil, and what are they doing with the profits? Rumor has it that a fairly ugly militia group—led by a woman—might be involved. What they’re planning? I feel like I am late to the John Sandford game only just discovering him last year in book #32 of his Lucas Davenport series, Righteous Prey. I loved it so much and was thriled that he had a new series featuring Davenport's daughter. Bonus! I get to start on book 1 and not book #32. In the Investigator, I really enjoyed the relationship of Lettie and her partner, John Kaiser. Sandford creates ruthless, and realistic antagonists that we’re eager to root against. He uses multiple points of view so that we not only understand who the bad guys are but what they intend to do and why. I found Letty very likeable. She refuses to waste time and energy on being a people pleaser. Her efforts are far better spent on getting to the bottom of mysteries and foiling the bad guys. If that includes shooting murderers and not feeling any guilt about it, then so be it. I am looking forward to following along as she learns to kick more bad guy butt in future adventures!
Great! Letty Davenport is out in the world, trying to save lives and stop evil doers. Great fit with the Prey and Virgil Flowers series. I'm always ready for a new Sanford.

Letty Davenport at 24 years old has killed three people, one when she was just 14. The adopted daughter of Lucas Davenport is following in his footsteps. After graduating from Stanford, she accepted a job for Senator Colles. She finds the job boring and hands in her notice when the Senator presents her with a new opportunity as a hands on investigator in Texas. Oil companies in the Midland/Odessa have been experiencing thefts of crude oil, leading to the loss of a few million. The companies are not as concerned about the money, a pittance to them, they do want to know who is doing it, how and what do they intend to do with their profits. Letty is partnered with John Kaiser from DHS. The DHS investigator is skeptical over Leftys’ youth but a trip to the shooting range puts some of his doubts to rest. The two quickly rule out the missing oil/money as being an accounting error and rumors lead them to a secretive militia group led by a woman known only as Jael. Jane “Jael” Hawks and the three men in her inner circle have had enough of a country they believe is led by weaklings and cowards. Using the profits from the oil, the group is ready to take a stand and have amassed a large arsenal to use if anyone stands in their way. I have read the authors “Prey” series for years and this is another in which you watch the characters grow into adults. It took a bit longer than usual to get drawn into the story but it was not due to the writing or story and after a slow beginning I couldn’t wait to finish. I think some readers might find the slight political slant irritating but for me this was a human problem before politics. By the way the book ends we will definitely be seeing more of Jael and I look forward to the clash between the two women.

I have read a few of John Sandford's books in the Prey series featuring Lucas Davenport. This book is a literal offspring of that series. It's the first in a series featuring Davenport's adopted daughter Letty Davenport. Letty is in her mid-20s and a graduate of Stanford. She works for a U.S. senator named Christopher Colles in a desk job but she's bored with her assignments. Then the senator offers her a chance to go into the field as a liaison between his office and the Department of Homeland Security. In her first assignment in that position, she is sent to Texas along with DHS investigator John Kaiser to try to find out what is happening in regard to thefts of crude oil. The senator is not so concerned about the lost oil but wants to know where the money from its sale is going. Who is selling the oil and what they are doing with the profits? The suspicion is that a particularly nasty militia group led by a woman is involved. Letty and Kaiser head out to Texas, developing their working relationship along the way. From an unpromising beginning to their association they soon learn to trust and depend on each other. The two have different areas of expertise and their talents balance one another, making for a stronger partnership. In Texas, the two investigators find your basic nest of vipers and have to figure out how to deal with them. Sandford is a master storyteller and his descriptions of the Texas border towns and the people who live there rang true. He excelled at his world-building and at creating compelling characters. He told the story from different points of view which gave the reader a better insight into Letty's and Kaiser's stories as well as that of their antagonists. The story flowed well and the action came quickly and built to an exciting conclusion that made the book hard to put down. It seemed quite realistic as if it might have been plucked out of yesterday's headlines. It was a good beginning for a series that has possibilities for growth. Parenthetically, it reminded me quite a bit of Michael Connelly's series featuring female detective Renee Ballard as a spinoff from his Harry Bosch series. In this case, Sandford spins off of his Lucas Davenport series. Do I sense a trend among mystery writers developing here?

This book starts with a ridiculous storyline. Letty, a new Stanford grad, now works at DHS. First week in and she’s running field intelligence on a major terrorist attack. She yells at a General and tells a Delta how to run surveillance. This fantasy scenario can work if there’s a “wink, wink” attached, unfortunately the tone remains serious, even finds time for politics. Letty becomes a rogue hero with a know-it-all prickly bravado who breaks countless laws for the “public good” - hmmm, eerily like her adversary. The juxtaposition is jarring, uncomfortable and unintended. Letty’s nearly unlikeable, the plot holes are huge, the writing wanders. The audio book doesn’t help.

I read quite a few books early in J Sandfords "Prey Series"debut in the 1980's and quite frankley, was hooked. This is the first since then with the inclusion of Lettie Davenport which induced my curiosity. The Investigator had its pluses but also its minus's Lettie's companion an ex Delta force gent was a plus, but too much repetition on the terrain which was drawn out and a somewhat blunt ending which indicates a sequel on the horizon. Enough of a storyline to contain the outcome, but a 3 star rating was generous.

I have enjoyed all of the Virgil Flowers and the Lucas Davenport novels. I was anticipating a great new series, however I am sorry to say this isn’t it. We know Letty from the Davenport Prey series where she originated. She was a good character in those books, and she is a good character in this story. My issue with this story was it began so slow and I struggled with the over abundance of dialogue for 3/4 of the way through. The last quarter is very good, but getting to that point nearly had me bored to quit reading.

Wow!...Just absolutely thrilled to discover the first, of which I hope, will be many books in another John Sanford series...This one based on Lucas Davenports tough, brilliant, adopted daughter Letty who, after graduating from Stanford has gone to work as a staffer for a US Senator...She's bored, but the Senator gets her a gig as an investigator with Homeland Security, teaming her up with a "Sandbox" veteran security expert, who bond in their love of weapons...They're sent to investigate thefts of oil that leads them to a Texas militia's plan for a splashy headlines event...Loved it!

Lucas Davenport's adopted daughter has grown up and has joined the John Sanford book universe. I have been expecting a book with her as the main character for some time. Davenport is getting a bit old for the action stories he once stared. Letty's character needs a bit more polishing but I expect that will come with time if Sanford chooses to continue writing about her. I hope he doesn't give up writing about Virgil Flowers though. He is my favorite of the Sanford characters.
What a terrible time. I couldn't follow & I lost interest. It seemed to be all over the place 😕
A gun-fetishizing, man-writing-stereotypical-female-protagonist hot pile of garbage. I couldn’t even get halfway through listening to the audiobook. Sorry book club.

. The Investigator by John Sandford. A Letty Davenport novel, published in 2022 & about 400 pages. Overview: By age 24, Letty Davenport has seen more action and uncovered more secrets than many law enforcement professionals. Now a recent Stanford grad with a master’s in economics, she’s restless and bored at her D.C. desk job working for U.S. Senator Chris Colles (R-Floroda). Letty has decided to quit and gives two weeks notice, but her skills have impressed Colles, and he offers her a carrot: feet-on-the-ground investigative work, in conjunction with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Several oil companies in Texas have reported thefts of crude, Colles tells her. He and the DHS are not so much concerned with the loss of oil since it's a relatively small amount for major oil companies. However, the money made from selling stolen oil could be in the millions, a huge profit for a small group of thieves. Rumor has it that a border militia group might be involved. Colles wants to know if the money is going to them, and if so, what they’re planning. Letty is partnered with DHS agent John Kaiser, a 47 year old Army veteran who doesn't at first appreciate her abilities. They head to Texas and the case quicky turns deadly, they know they’re on the track of something bigger. The militia group (Land Division) has set in motion an explosive plan . . . and the clock is ticking down. - edited. . [Letty West first shows up in the book Naked Prey, number 14 in the long-running Lucas Davenport crime series. In that book young Letty's ne'er-do-well mom was murdered and two naked bodies were found hanging in the woods of northern Minnesota. Not a lynching of the interracial couple. Lucas, an agent with the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) was called in to investigate. Letty has mostly raised herself, setting a trapline to catch critters, hunting for dinner, scavenging, she can drive mom's Jeep and even shot a crooked cop with her .22 rifle. All this before Lucas and his surgeon wife Weather adopted the orphan girl who is now Letty Davenport The Investigator]. . Starts out with a young women, a blue-eyed burglar dressed in black, breaking and entering at an office building in Tallahassee, Florida where she accesses a computer and purloines a number of spreadsheets, looking for proof of stolen campaign funds. Later she followed the suspects, 2 lovers who drive to an out-of-state casino where she observes them gambling away the ill-gotten gain. There was no breaking involved. As the last person left the building for the night, the women kept the door ajar with a lenght of fish line and used a lock rake on the office door. An informant had already given her the location of the computer password. The talented young intruder is none other than Letty Davenport doing the first and only interesting job she's had working for her boss Senator Colles. Her dad, Lucas Davenport a US Marshal, didn't get her the job with the Senator, but he did put in a good word for her. Now she gives her two weeks notice and the Senator shreds her letter of resignation since he has something more to Letty's liking in mind. Throughout the story we get flashbacks of Letty's youth, her survival and hunting skills as she provided for herself and her mother, being adopted by the wealthy Davenports, killing two intruders that broke in to revenge-kill Lucas's family, her High School intern job at a TV station, developing a taste for fashion and the expensive just like daddy, a talent with handguns and apparently she's as bright and dangerous as her adopted father Lucas and just like dad, she bends the rules in pursuit of evidence. Agent Kaiser soon realizes, "You got a lot of cop shit from your old man." The Senator convinces Letty to stay on as a researcher working in conjunction with the DHS. She's given her own small office and a carry permit, allowing her to bring her gun almost anywhere and "she was pleased." Early on we get the details of the bad guys. Who they are and what they're up to is what Letty and agent Kaiser spend much of the book piecing together, interviewing known associates, stakeouts in the desert, clandestine searches of houses, tracing license tabs and cell phone numbers, GPS tracking, following suspects from a distance and much more. All this fact gathering can get a bit tedious at times, but for the most part the story remains interesting. Some details: Boxie and wife are missing and some speculate he might have been responsible for the oil thefts. Their cars are gone and so they may be on the run. When Lettie searches the house (the cops only looked in the windows) she finds both Blackburn's under the bed, plastic bags taped over their heads. Letty and some others enter the yard of Max the gun guy, but before they can ring the bell his pitbull attacks. Agent Kaiser grabs the dog and throws it over the fence and the wounded cop shoots it dead. Max is temporarily arrested and Letty pretends to lock up his house and give him back the keys. After everyone leaves, she searches the house, gets numbers out of his cell phone and destination locations from his truck's GPS - more leads to follow up on. Of course it's Letty who figures out they should look for a small oil outfit, a wildcatter, who has recently had a huge bump in production. That of course turns out to be the old crook Roscoe Winks and Letty overnights in the desert, watching his business from her small tent and sure enough a tanker truck of stolen oil arrives in the night. They follow the truck and soon learn where they keep it stored - more places to lock pick, B & E and illegally search for evidence. When Jane and her militia crew are done with old man Winks, Max the gun guy goes to his place and shoots him dead. Max doesn't know Letty is again staking out the little oil company and after a brief exchange of gunfire she kills Jane's pal with a bullet through the head. Jane Jael Hawkes is an honorably discharged, darknet propagandist with a big following. She's assembled a group of militia border guards who try to prevent illegal crossings at the southern border - assisting the Border Patrol whether they like it or not. They are mostly ex-military or criminals, gun nuts or vehemently anti illegal immigrant. Jane's inner circle consists of Rand Low a talented public speaker who also suffers from bouts of volcanic rage and is perpetually angry. Max Sawyer is the group's gun expert and owns a vicious pitbull named Rooter who gets shot for biting a cop. Terry Duran is ex Air Force and a bank robber. Victor Crain is a handsome veteran and all-around bad guy. We first meet Jane and some of her henchmen as they're driving to Midland, Texas to kill Boxie Blackburn and his wife. Boxie is an oil company accountant and apparently he figured out how the oil was being stolen and called the likely suspect Roscoe Winks. In fact Winks is the wildcatter oil guy who thought up the the oil theft scheme. Now Roscoe is panicked and Jane's gang kills Boxie before he can reveal his findings. Since, Roscoe is an untrustworthy loose end, they plan on killing him soon, but for now he's still needed as the seller of the filched oil. Jane and company have worked out a new plan, a symbol of resistance which involves like-minded militia folk from all over the country. Over a year ago a caravan of illegal aliens from Central America crossed the border bridge from Mexico to Pershing, Texas and were welcomed by the mayor and city council. Now another caravan is on the way and Jane and her militia are determined to stop them, no matter what. She isn't a racist. All nationalities are welcome in the militia. They are, however, against illegal aliens flooding into the country and displacing poor Americans. It's about wages. They also compare their plan to the Alamo. Fair warning - here's what's going on. As the caravan approaches the bridge on the Mexican side, the militia will blow it up. Jane plans to destroy only the bridge and not kill any of the illegals. However, perpetually angry Rand Low wants not only destruction but death and so changed the timer settings on the C-4 to explode after the caravan was on the very long bridge. It takes Letty and company nearly the whole book to figure out the bridge is going to blow, something the reader easily figures out. When an anti-immigrant militia has a hundred pounds of C-4, detonators and timers, and tested the explosive on a hunk of I-beam and have plans to stop a caravan from crossing a bridge into the USA, it's pretty clear they're going to blow up the bridge. Even though Letty warned the task force, somehow the warning didn't reach the caravan. Once the militia left the bridge and started driving out of the border town, the caravan started across the bridge. With John counting down the minutes remaining, Letty runs across the bridge to stop the immigrants, shouting in Spanish for them to go back. A bus full of kids starts backing up, but it's too slow. As it comes down to seconds, big John Kaiser picks up Letty, running her to safety on the Mexican side. The bridge blows, the bus of moms and children falls and Letty helps with the rescue. Since the group of some 1,500 illegals had just started crossing the 300 yard bridge, most were not harmed. Why this is such a monumental event for Jane and her militia, I don't know. She gathered 110 militia members from all over the country to take over the border town and blow up the bridge. Okay, but it won't stop them from crossing, since the Rio Grande River is just a trickle at that point - easily walked across. Perhaps a bigger spectacle would have been the militia members guarding the border against a huge mob of illegals and then they wouldn't be guilty of so many felonies and Jane wouldn't have to go into hiding. Letty and agent Kaiser got to the border town of Pershing before the militia arrived. After a get-together in the hills and a pep talk, the militia convoyed all in pickup trucks into town, fell a grove of trees to block the only road into town and guarded the roadblock with gunman. In town they forced the border patrol agents to give up at gunpoint; disarmed the tiny part-time police force; arrested and jailed the mayor and city council, locking them in the jail with plans for a show trial for treason. Remember the council invited the last caravan to invade the US a year-and-a-half ago. The militia blew up the cell phone tower and tried to assure the townsfolk - all who are heavily armed themselves - that they're not planning to hurt anyone and only plan to peacefully stop the upcoming illegal border crossing. People in town are invited to join them and are assured, as soon as the caravan has turned around - a day or two at the most - then they'll leave and hope for mercy from law enforcement. Worried that Jane and her militia may execute the city council for treason, agent Kaiser breaks them out of the town's jail and hides them in a cave, a tourist attraction not far from town. Once all hell breaks loose with the bridge blowing up, the militia start heading out of town, driving a rough back way across an Arroyo, then back roads to the highway. Jane has disappeared but the other leaders (Rand Low, Terry & Victor) are headed out last and Letty ambushes their truck, shooting as they drive by. Jane got a way, hitching a ride with another militia truck, assumes her new identity and is gone. She's alarmed to hear how quickly members of her militia are being rounded up since they had covered all the license plates to avoid being identified. She didn't know Letty had walked around town taking cell phone photos of license tabs and lots of the militia folks had been taking selfies with their masks off. In the end Letty and Kaiser meet up with the cops on the other side of the roadblock and are taken to the FBI task force in El Paso for debriefing. After some notoriety and interviews on various news shows, Letty is eventually back in her new little office and receives a surprise phone call from Jane. The women is PO'd that Letty wrecked her Land Division militia, killed her friend Max and the others and so promises, "We're coming for you." Of course Letty responds with, “Bring it on. Bring everything you fucking got.” THE END .. Mostly liked it. The story is similar to any of the Lucas Davenport Prey novels. It's kind of like the author just plugged in Letty as the new lead. Not necessarily a bad thing since I like the Lucas series. Sanford is a liberal leftist, anti-gun author and doesn't believe civilians should own guns. Something he has stated in the Prey series and continues in this book as well. Here he has his new protagonist Letty condemn gun owners and basically anyone using a rifle that shoots more than one bullet. So, why is Letty herself an armed to the teeth, gun nut? Because of all the gun-toting crazies out there. "Yet another reason, Letty thought, that all women should be issued guns at birth." The audio version is expertly narrated by Richard Ferrone. Why all the fame and hoopla over Letty and agent Kaiser? They didn't stop the bombing, close to twenty illegals died and many more were injured and the militia's leader, the kook who thought up this harebrained scheme, got away. Letty series: The Investigator (2022) Dark Angel (2023) . .

In THE INVESTIGATOR, John Sandford kicks off a new series starring Letty Davenport, the 24-year-old adopted daughter of Lucas and Weather Davenport. A graduate of Stanford with a master’s in economics, Letty is working for U.S. Senator Christopher Colles in a boring job that she hates. Her exceptional life experiences put her in a position of knowing how to solve cases and work with law enforcement and other professionals. But before she has a chance to quit, Colles offers her a job with the Department of Homeland Security investigating the theft of oil from Texas. The Senator is mostly interested in where the money from the oil sales is going and who is facilitating the thefts. Could a militia group be behind the scheme? If so, who are these people, and who are they supplying? What do they have planned for the oil and the money it generates? Letty is thrilled at the prospect of putting her investigative skills into a new career opportunity working with DHS investigator John Kaiser, who is not happy about being paired with her. But once he sees her skills with a gun, he changes his mind. The first job they tackle is to find Jane Jael Hawkes, a former soldier and the leader of an ugly militia group. Hawkes joined the Army to escape the hardscrabble life she lived with her “white-trash loafer, hard drinker, and sometime over-the-road truck driver” father. But she learned that “some things you are born with you can never escape.” Thus, she began to attract people to her group, ResistUS, and they labeled themselves “Jael-Birds.” Letty and Kaiser travel to Texas where the oil thefts are going into high gear. They meet with oilman Vermillion Wright, who tells them that he is concerned about the disappearance of Bradley “Boxie” Blackburn, one of his employees who is looking into the oil problems. They immediately drive to Boxie’s house and find him and his wife dead under their bed, clearly the victims of a homicide. Could Hawkes and her zealous followers be responsible for these killings, as well as the theft of the oil? While on a stakeout of the militia members, Letty and Kaiser stumble upon an abandoned shack, where they find an instrument used in the oil heist along with a pile of pamphlets hidden with Hawkes’ book. Between them, they come up with a plan to search out the leaders of the militia and inform Wright, who happens to be in the hospital recovering from surgery, and his colleagues about what they have witnessed and uncovered. With each piece of the puzzle falling into place, Letty and Kaiser begin to trust and respect each other. They realize that they have an opportunity to share their personal experiences solving complicated cases based on the various kinds of training each has had. Together, they assemble all the clues into a whole plan that gives them a clear picture of what the militia is about to pull off. The suspense builds as Sandford’s protagonists get to the town where the big event is going to take place. Readers will find themselves breathless until they reach the end, and they will look forward to the next Letty Davenport adventure. Reviewed by Barbara Lipkien Gershenbaum

I’ve been a John Sandford fan since the Prey series started in the late 1980s. Since then Lucas has aged almost gracefully into a seasoned manhunter with rather less graphic gore. The Prey books went seriously wobbly for a while but have recently improved – if that’s because Sandford now works with a writing partner (so the rumour goes) then I’m all for it. But I never liked Sandford’s ventures into other territories – the hacker Kidd and the news team in The Night Crew fell flat. Likewise, his adopted daughter’s earlier appearance as an adolescent in Gathering Prey felt forced and fake. She wasn’t a real character, just an awkward plot device. So I wouldn’t have bothered with The Investigator – the first book in a new series featuring that very daughter, Letty Davenport – unless it was on a seriously special offer. Which it was. So I grabbed it… …and was entirely gratified by how great it is. Sandford has created a credible niche for Letty as a politician’s agent, and given her the credentials of Homeland Security and a broad-ranging brief. The story takes her directly into the present political turmoil, referencing online conspiracy networks, citizens’ militias and the dark undercurrent of insurrection which appears to be tugging at America’s soul. It couldn’t be more timely. Letty feels eminently believable to me – and I like the notion of an independent young woman who is a capable and competent as her male counterparts, and who does not need to fall back on feminine wiles to achieve her aims. It helps that the plot barrels along at a rapid pace, without pausing for tedious domestic am-dram, and that Letty’s opponent is an equally interesting woman of strong will. Sandford also strategically fills in her back story for people who haven't read the earlier books (and to remind me, because I had forgotten large lumps of it!) So I’m converted. Roll on the next one! 8/10

The Investigator is a new series from John Sandford with Letty Davenport as the main character. Lucas Davenport is not named and is referred to as Dad. "Letty Davenport has graduated from Stanford with a Master's in Economics and is working for a Senator in DC. She is bored and ready to move on when the Senator convinces her to work as an investigator for Homeland Security. She teams up with John Kaiser, a former Delta operator. Their investigation into some missing oil turns up a bigger plot of possible domestic terrosism." I love that Sandford gives Letty has her own book. She is a character that is constantly underestimated but over-delivers. This feels a lot like a Prey book but Letty has a similar but different style to Lucas. There are flashbacks to her first appearance in the Prey series (Naked Prey) to give the casual reader some background. The story is fast-paced and I had a hard time putting it down. Sandford fans will love this book. Crime fiction/thriller fans should also enjoy this one. I hope we see a lot more of Letty Davenport.

I found John Sanford's Lucas Davenport series late and binged on all thirty-one mysteries. When he rescued and adopted a tough little girl named Letty, it was my favorite book of the series, so I'm glad Letty is grown up and has her own series. This is the first book. She is still a tough little girl, with the emphasis on tough! She's in her early twenties and small enough that men keep looking past her and over her to talk to her partner, even though the big guy stands behind her, where a junior partner belongs. Letty is more than tough, she's intelligent, well informed, well-connected, and a crack shot with any weapon. In this first story, she tackles a Texas miltia led by a disillusioned ex-military female. Fast action and fun to read.

I give this 4.75 out of 5. I have read all the Prey books, all the Kidd books, all the Virgil books and now the first Letty book and I have not read a book by John Sandford that I did not thoroughly enjoy. A lot of times I lose interest when the original characters are replaced by children or others. The story just doesn't appeal to me in the same way (maybe trying to get a new, younger audience. The Investigator was outstanding and Letty is fascinating in her own way to overcome the absence of her father. A great story with lots of action and interesting others. I really liked the sidekick Kaiser. I look forward to more books in this series.

Nice 1st entry in Sandford's new Letty series. It does a nice job laying the framework for Lucas's daughter working for a senator post college. He sets her up with a Homeland Security guy to investigate lost oil in the economy. Great interaction with the main characters and good action scenes.
I enjoyed this book, and would recommend it!

I love Sanford's other books. I rarely quit a book, but I quit this one. Letty, as a supporting character is just fine. Letty as a lead, is awful. She's arrogant and doesn't seem to realize she has her job because of her dad. She's a spoiled, unlikable brat. It pains me to write such a terrible review.

For me John Sanford books are always five stars. He is one my favorite authors, if not the favorite. I’ve read his Prey series three times, though the earlier Prey books have a bit more depth. Judgement Prey is back to form. This is not an action—running gun battle-kinda story. This is a whodunit with an emphasis on uncovering the “who” and the “why,” with Virgil and Davenport in pursuit of clues. Non-stop conflict on every page. In this story, the plot splinter’s off and creates a second heinous bad guy that causes confusion. Virgil and Davenport inadvertently forces this outlier into action, causes him to act. I haven’t seen this type of plot before, so it kept the story fresh. This secondary off-shoot is juggled and carried along without a loss of tension and forward motion on the main plot. Excellent. Another favored aspect of the Sanford books was (in earlier books at least) how he’d sneak in a particularly crass but funny joke. He’d keep the Davenport character clean by having a throw-away character do the honors. In one instance, the two meet on the steps of the police station and the throw-away character tells Davenport the joke. Those kinds of jokes are a little too dangerous to in today’s publishing world. So, instead in this book he did something different a little different. He winks at the reader without breaking the fourth wall of writing. Difficult to do. To set this up and blend it into the plot Virgil is a recently published novelist and writing a second one. This is truly hilarious. Lucas asks Virgil. “Where are you at in your new novel?” Virgil: “Halfway or a little more. Fifty-two thousand words.” Virgil says, “I went to a book signing once, and this famous author said books have three parts: The setup and the climax, and then, in the middle, the swamp. He said he wanders around in the swamp like a lost soul. I know where he’s coming from.” Davenport says, regarding their case: “If you are writing the Sand case where are we? In the swamp?” Virgil: “Yeah, we’re in the swamp, but we’re edging into the big build-up to the climax.” This happens in Judgement Prey at or about 52k words—in the actual swamp of this Prey book. And then, to double-down on the joke, the story goes into what I call, “Churning,” he did it on purpose to mimic being in the swamp. He describes something quickly and economically that has nothing to do with the story. The same as if Sanford at this point in his own novel is mired in the swamp wandering around like a lost soul. I liked his last three, but I enjoyed this one so much more. David Putnam author of the Bruno Johnson series.

Sandford’s Davenport and Flowers are at it again, solving curious crimes when the path to finding the killer is not curvy and crazy. The cold-blooded murder of a judge and his two kids is just heartbreaking as it is unthinkable. Getting Davenport back into the crime-solving saddle from his long recuperation from numerous bullet holes from his last engagement is a must. Has the wife committed this unbelievable murder, or is it the leader of a questionable non-profit? Or someone else? What I do love about Davenport and Flowers (and can be found in many other thrillers) is the sense of humor of these characters. They are always giving each other a hard time. What is otherwise horrific is blended with humor that makes each of these crime-fighters very human; the kind of human you wouldn’t mind hanging out with. This is a great read and if this is your first Sandford book, it will not likely be your last, as there are a least a dozen Prey books. -Tom L.

Sandy from the BCA and Elly Krueger, the childhood friend of Lucas got a brief mention.
