Special thanks to the person who confirmed the dog doesn't die in this. Jesus F*cking Christ this was a long book. Stephen King has written one of my favorite books of all times: IT. There is nothing like that book and those characters out there. I think he truly delivers magic when it comes to coming of age stories and he adds so much soul to mundane characters. This book feels like Stephen, but also doesn't at the same time. It's not quite a horror book, and it's not quite a fantasy book, it's somewhere in between. It was really easy to connect to Charlie during the first half. He is a young man with an alcoholic father. Charlie begged God to help his father sober up, and he did. And because of that Charlie became the most reliable person in the world, because he truly believed that if he broke his part of his deal with God, his dad would go back to the alcohol. He did great in school, at sports and helped his dad with work. Until one day, when walking back home from school, he hears his old neighbor's dog barking like crazy and once he checks it out, he finds the poor old man on the ground with a broken leg. The first half of this entire book had The Old Man and the Sea vibes. The grumpy old man falls in love with Charlie, and so does the dog. Charlie creates the most emotional routine with them, non-romantic love hits SO DIFFERENT. He takes the dog on daily walks, feeds him, and also helps Howard with his meds and keeps him company. It's the perfect recipe to make you bawl your eyes out. And I did cry about five times for the first half of this book. I don't want to drop you any spoilers here, because this book is SO LONG, and it really does carry 3 different stories all at once. 3 different worlds. Stephen was inspired by the old school Grimm tales and this turns into one, it was beautifully crafted, his writing is so so so great and honestly so satisfying to read, but unfortunately, the last 300 pages of this were unbelievably boring and slow. Basically, all you need to know about this book is: this is the story of a young man who fell in love with a dog, the dog is old and about to die, and he is willing to do WHATEVER it takes to make this dog stick around forever. That's where magic comes in, in this urban fantasy Stephen King tale. If you're ok with the slow pace of the book, you might actually love this one, because honestly? I'd also travel to an unknown world, talk to messed up creatures, make deals with the devil and face any kind of dangerous magic to make sure my dog lives forever.

An immersive beast of a novel. I fell into this world and didn’t want to leave. When Charlie sees his neighbour lying on the ground after a fall from a ladder, he takes it upon himself to look after the man’s dog - Radar. They form a kind of friendship and Charlie soon finds there is a world of secrets hidden in this grumpy man’s old house. The world Charlie discovers is full of terrors, curses and the fight between good and evil. He finds himself drawn to this world and their troubles, the people refer to him as the Prince that was Promised, and he can’t help but feel like he was meant to be there. A wonderful novel of epic scope. I thoroughly enjoyed this ride. *********************** Omg. library copy available for pick up I can’t believe this day is actually here!!! So freaking excited for this!!!

I can only tell that to me this book is just one more star to add to Stephen King's writing history. What's different? The fact there's magic involved and some legendary/mystical creatures, which make the story a Fairy Tale and this time the story is told by the main character in the story (Charlie Reade) who will do anything and everything to save Radar (his recently inherited female German shepherd left behind by late Mr. Bowditch), but drawn also by the curiosity it represents to step foot into a hidden world. Will Charlie succeed in carrying out what he intends? Being a Fairy Tale, what else will he find throughout his journey that may make his task difficult if not virtually impossible? What other characters will Charlie bump into who might make his journey easier or perhaps even more difficult than he thinks? Being a Stephen King novel, are we expecting a happy ending or...? As usual, there's just one way to find out.

My god, is there ANYTHING the "king of horror" cannot do? It doesn't seem to matter what kind of book SK writes, he always produces a wonderful story. Hero of Fairy Tale is Charlie, a 17-year-old who has been through hell ever since his mother was killed in a hit-and-run following which his father became an alcoholic. He's in a pretty good place at the beginning of this book, but he doesn't really trust it. Also, some stuff he's done in the past is haunting him. But when a dog alerts him to the plight of a reclusive neighbor, he does the right thing and helps. Charlie even becomes his caretaker. Eventually, Charlie not only becomes Mr. Bowditch's friend, but is told his secret and that opens a whole new can of worms. Not because Charlie is greedy - because he cares. In fact, caring is basically what this book was all about for me. Stephen King took the best elements of various Grimm fairy tales such as Jack and the Beanstalk (the original versions, not the Disney-esque ones) and combined them with the essence of portal stories like Narnia before turning the mix into his very own blend of fantasy and horror. There were many great references to pop culture as well as to other SK stories. The Crimson King definitely featured in here but if this is his origin story or just another example of him possessing and corrupting people and places, we can't be sure. I think the author is deliberately leaving that up to the reader. However, it is obvious that this book gives us another of the worlds of the wheel we were introduced to in The Dark Tower, which means we also get elements of gunslinging heroics and desolate worlds. Honestly, the worldbuilding was the best. In Charlie's world and the other. Though I also thoroughly enjoyed the growing relationship between Charlie and Mr. Bowditch. OK, Charlie's father was cool, too. My favorite character, however, was Radar. Hands down. Nobody beats the old girl. And her fate also kept me on the edge of my seat the most. The only problem was the difference between the first and second part of the book - the first definitely being better. As I said before, this is not one of my favorite SK books, not even top 3, but that is just because SK sets the bar so high and is producing so many incredibly fantastic books - this one was still enchanting and a wonderful adventure.
This was a slog to be honest. 2.5-3 stars

Seventeen year old Charlie is sort of in a good place after surviving the death of a loved one when he was a toddler; and surviving another loved winning their battle with addiction, so when he comes across a gnarly old-man in need, Charlie feels that he has to help him, snarky Mr Bowditch. There's something quite not right about Mr Bowditch, although he does have a wonderful, albeit aging and possible sick dog, Rader. As circumstances lead to Charlie getting told more and more of Mr Bowditch's secrets, he finds himself, beyond all reason, caught up in a genuine fairy tale! The problem with this actually interesting and at times compelling dark fantasy is that if you have read Stephen King's The Dark Tower series or say The Talisman you've seen the 'modern person' in a magical/strange environment with a dark history that has tainted it. I would say if you haven't read similar King reads this would be a worthwhile read, but for us Constant Readers, maybe a solid book taking us back to King's superlative creative past, but it neither feels original or innovative. I rated this as a 7 out of 12, strong Three Star read. Really though, I should just advise everyone to read it, it is ultimately a great dark fairy tale-like story, so I'll just keep my mouth shut. 2024 read

Omg I'm finally done with this dumpster fire of a book. What a huge let down and a drag! Thankfully this was not an anticipated read for me but I can't deny how much of a pooper this was! The first 200 pages is what King fans sink their teeth into the most, believable characters with strong relationships. This section could be a novella all on its own and would easily make fans happy. As a plot-driven reader, I found the first 200 pages to be more on par for the course in what to expect. Was it a stroke of genius or anything to rave about? Not to me, it was a decent slice of life section. If that was all this was it would be a solid ⭐⭐⭐. The last 400 pages of this wannabe Fairy Tale adventure was the most painful thing I've had the displeasure of ever reading. The title says it all in regards to the type of Fantasy this brick of wasted words contained. There is not a single ounce of originality to this at all. Charlie constantly always gives you the beat by beat of what kind of book this is. It mixes and matches various dark Grimm Fairy Tales, Ray Bradbury's, Something Wicked This Way Comes and if that wasn't enough King decides to add in a Lovecraft monster to boot. The reader is constantly hit over the head with pop culture references and nods to literally everything you would expect from this type of story that leaves a ton left to be desired. All the side characters are bland throwaways that you don't get anymore than a chapter or two with them to get attached. Even when they do return to the page it's not worth caring about. As a cherry on top as a personal dislike, there's a good 100 page chunk set in a Gladiator style trope that had me pull my hair out because of how much I can't stand it on top of everything else. Overall: I suggest that you skip this one and find something else to read. There are far better books than this.

4.5 stars! This was a brilliant and imaginative fantasy about family, love, courage, and the cost of power. Fairy Tale follows Charlie, a seventeen year old boy, who meets Howard Bowditch, a loner and his dog, Radar. After Mr. Bowditch falls and goes to the hospital, Charlie helps him around the house. When Bowditch passes away, Charlie listens to a tape that Bowditch left him and tells a story about a portal to another world inside the shed in his backyard that is actually true. This book was so good! The pacing in the beginning of the book was slow, but by the middle of the book I was completely swept away by this unique world. The world building is excellent, and I loved learning about the world that Charlie finds and the intriguing characters including night soldiers, giants, mermaids, giant crickets, and more. The characters are very complex and interesting. I really liked Charlie, he is brave, kind, helpful, strong and resilient. I love Radar, she is sweet, loyal, and so cute. I also really liked Leah, she is resilient, sweet, brave and loyal. The side characters were also great especially Iota, Eris, Claudia, Dora, and Jaya. The character development was excellent, I enjoyed seeing a different side to Charlie and he changed so much from the beginning of the book till the end. The writing and storytelling is awesome, the writing is so descriptive that I felt like I was transported into the story with the characters. The ending was so good and I'm glad it ended on a happy note. I recommend this book to anyone who loves fantasy, excellent world building and great characters.

I really enjoyed the first half, the part where it was focused more on Charlie, Radar, and Mr. Bowditch. In fact, I enjoyed it so much that I prefer the story to revolve longer around those three. The discovery of the parallel world can wait until the latter part of the book, in my opinion. I loved the suspense in the beginning and I felt like it was such a waste that it was revealed so early considering that this book is kinda long. Stephen King has already built a good reputation in literature so it is no wonder how his writing style captivates me. His description is so vivid it was like I'm with Charlie during his adventure. I adore his character very much, I just love how selfless he is. He is very dependable too. I think he sounded way too mature for his age, though. And, will I even forget Radar? She is so cute and I'm glad that Charlie was willing to go that far to keep this dog by his side. This book is basically a mixture of fairy tales most people are familiar with, hence the title. Sprinkled with dark stuff. Plus Hunger Games.

This book starts like many of King’s works, everyday people struggling with life’s challenges; financial problems, alcoholism, and loss of a parent. And again, like many of his novels, it flips over into fantasy and horror. At its heart, it’s a classic ‘heroes quest’ fable. It also borrows a bit from “Shrek” by using a sort of meta-fantasy worldbuilding. In other words, borrowing plot elements and characters from a long list of fantasy tropes. It leans heavily on Rumpelstiltskin and Jack and Beanstalk, but also at least references Goldilocks, Little Red Riding Hood, and several other classic fairy tales. There’s also a hint of connection to “The Wizard of Oz” and “Something Wicked This Way Comes,” suggesting that Authors’ Braum and Bradbury may have stumbled on at least a glimpse of this alternate reality. In addition, when things get dark, there is a strong association with H.P. Lovecraft and “The Call of Cthulhu.” And as King is so fond of doing, there are also references to his own works, such as “Cujo” and “The Dark Tower.” The book relies on King’s greatest strengths – character & relationship development and making fantastical elements feel real. I connected with the main character – Charlie and his relationships to his father, a strange old neighbor, and most fondly a dog named Radar. King is also adept at making his character’s reactions to fantasy elements feel authentic, a difficult trick! As with any book, I think you can find imperfections if you look hard enough. The main character’s flaws felt forced, and it seemed like King worked a little too hard to remind the reader that our hero wasn’t perfect. You might also argue that the worldbuilding is a little too derivative from classic fairy tales, but I enjoyed it the same way I enjoyed “Shrek.” King leans into this and made the connections overt and often amusing. As always, I also like the openness that King displays. My imagination sees King, tossing a stuffed monkey toy to his own beloved dog ‘Molly’ and mourning her declining health. He thinks about what he would do to magically turn back the years for her – what grueling journeys he would take, what giants he would fight, and what monsters he would face – just to give her another six to eight years. I also believe his politics shows through. He worries about political oppression and fears a leader that spreads hate and chaos for the sake of it. In this world, this oppression and hate spreads as a literal sickness, resulting in downtrodden people that are slowly becoming deformed and their skin turning grey. Ultimately, I enjoyed the tale, which admittedly takes elements from many of King’s past works and classic fairy tales, but results in an imaginative story that I was able to lose myself into, and that ability to fall into a tale, is one of my biggest gauges of a great book. A meta-fantasy fable told in traditional King fashion, that riffs on not only classic Aesops, but also on King’s own work. Five stars for richly developed character relationships and creative storytelling.

First of all, thank you to @simonandschuster and Stephen King for the opportunity to read this eGalley of the upcoming book “Fairy Tale”, releasing September 6, 2022. “Fairy Tale” is the story of Charlie Reade, a teenager who has dealt with a lot in his life: the death of his mother and the struggles of living with an alcoholic father. He crosses paths with a reclusive neighbor, Mr. Bowditch and his dog named Radar, who I will never ever forget. But Bowditch has a few secrets, and one that is revealed after Bowditch’s death will change Charlie’s world forever. King has described this book as the one he wrote to make him happy during the early days of the pandemic. And I am happy to report this book will make you happy too. “Fairy Tale” delivers in a way I never expected. The world building is masterfully done, and the characters will stay with me forever. First of all, Radar, the beloved dog of Mr. Bowditch and eventually Charlie, immediately found his way into my heart and revealed his love and loyalty throughout the story. Charlie is a young man, wise and mature beyond his years, who becomes a hero in ways he never knew were possible. Intermingled with the great fairy tales of our childhoods, “Fairy Tale” is a must read book this fall, and is another example of the absolute brilliance of the modern master himself, Stephen King.

This is a masterful dive into a world of dark fantasy and wonder, a departure from his usual horror fare, yet with all the mesmerizing storytelling that makes his work so compelling. The novel follows Charlie Reade, an ordinary boy thrust into an extraordinary world after discovering a hidden portal. The story starts slowly, with King expertly building the characters and the setting, creating a sense of quiet mystery before plunging the reader into a fantastical journey filled with strange creatures, dangerous kingdoms, and magic both wondrous and terrifying. What I loved most about Fairy Tale is the blend of classic fairy tale elements with King's signature darker touch. It's not your typical whimsical fantasy—there's an underlying current of dread, a sense that danger lurks around every corner, keeping the tension alive throughout. King's imagination runs wild here, and the world-building is rich and immersive. The layers of Charlie's character are carefully peeled back as the plot thickens, showing us a young man grappling with his own inner demons while navigating a strange and perilous world. At its core, this novel explores themes of bravery, sacrifice, and the thin line between good and evil, with King pulling readers into a coming-of-age story wrapped in a fantastical adventure. While the pacing can slow down at times, it allows for a deeper connection to the characters and a richer immersion into the world King has crafted. The climactic moments are truly gripping, and as always, King's ability to create emotional depth amid the fantastical shines through. Fairy Tale is both a nostalgic nod to the stories that have captivated our imaginations for generations and a fresh, thrilling take on the genre. Fans of Stephen King’s storytelling prowess will not be disappointed, and those looking for a blend of fantasy with a touch of darkness will find this novel hard to put down. blog instagram facebook twitter
The first 200 pages are absolutely fantastic, while the next 350 pages are 🥴 Probably my least favourite King book due to the plot structure.

I am not usually drawn to books written by Stephen King but there was something that was very intriguing for me about Fairy Tale that made me want to read it. After I started to notice that so many of the people I am friends with on goodreads had given Fairy Tale such high praise, I decided to give it a try. I decided that if I determined that it was not for me I had at least given it a try. Within just a few minutes I was completely immersed into the plot of Fairy Tale. Stephen King created engaging and likable characters for the most part. I listened to the audiobook that was brilliantly narrated by Seth Numrich and Stephen King, himself. Since I had Fairy Tale downloaded on my kindle, I also read certain parts as well. It was fast paced, so creative and well plotted. I was glad that I decided to read/listen to this book since in my opinion it was a creative gem. Fairy Tale was told in the first person by twenty-four year old Charlie Reade as he looked back on his life the year he had turned seventeen. Charlie had been an only child. He lived in Sentry, Illinois with his mother and father. One afternoon when Charlie had been seven years old, his mother had decided to walk to town to buy a bucket of chicken for dinner. His mother left Charlie and his father watching a baseball game on the television. After buying the bucket of chicken, Charlie’s mother started to walk home. She was eating an extra piece of the chicken while she walked. As she started to cross “that G D bridge” on her way home, a truck came out of nowhere, hit her and she died instantly. Charlie and his father were devastated as they learned about her death. The only way that Charlie’s father was able to cope with his wife’s death was by drowning his sorrows with alcohol. Before too long, Charlie’s father was a certifiable alcoholic. Charlie was forced to grow up very fast. He became the caregiver for his father. When Charlie’s father’s drinking problems became so severe, he was fired from his job. Charlie envisioned that he and his father could potentially become homeless or worse. It was then that Charlie started to pray that his father would stop drinking. Charlie made a promise to G-d that day. If G-d would make his father stop drinking, Charlie would pay it forward and help someone else in need. Just in the nick of time, Charlie’s father’s friend stepped in. His father’s friend became his sponsor in Alcoholic’s Anonymous. Taking one baby step at a time, Charlie’s father found his way to sobriety. There was a house at the top of the hill on the street that Charlie lived that was known by the neighborhood children as the “psycho house “. One day, Charlie was walking home and as he was passing that house he heard a dog barking frantically. The man who lived there was quite reclusive. No one knew a lot about him and he seldom left his home. One of Charlie’s friends had warned him that he had seen the dog that lived there several years ago and that it was quite vicious. Charlie pondered about what to do. He thought that something was wrong. Charlie decided to climb over the fence to see. When Charlie got to the backyard, he saw that the old man that lived there had fallen off a ladder and was hurt very badly. Charlie called 911 and got an ambulance to come and help the man. The man’s name was Mr. Bowditch. It was just Mr. Bowditch and his dog, Radar that lived in the house. Mr Bowditch did not have a wife, children or any living relatives. Before the ambulance took Mr. Bowditch to the hospital, Charlie offered to take care of Radar and feed him for Mr. Bowditch. That was the beginning of Charlie making good on the promise he made with G-d. Over the course of Mr. Bowditch’s recovery, Charlie became his caregiver and the two formed the most unlikely but beautiful friendship that anyone could have imagined. Mr. Bowditch was not your typical neighbor as you might have already surmised. He hoarded lots of things in his house and he was opposed to modern day conveniences and technology. His t.v. was probably as old as he was. It had rabbit ears and an antenna on the roof. He was not in the possession of a cell phone or a computer and he had no desire to own one either. One thing was apparent, though. Mr. Bowditch loved Radar with all his heart and the same could be said for Radar’s feelings towards Mr. Bowditch. When Mr. Bowditch came home from the hospital, he began to confide in Charlie about some things. Mr. Bowditch had to pay the hospital for his stay and the surgeries he had. Charlie learned about the gold that Mr. Bowditch was in possession of and that strange noises that could be heard coming from the padlocked shed on Mr. Bowditch’s property. Mr. Bowditch revealed information to Charlie on a need to know basis. One day, while Charlie was at school, he got a call from Mr. Bowditch. Charlie could tell that something was wrong. Mr. Bowditch was having a heart attack. He needed Charlie to know some very important things. Probably the most important thing Mr. Bowditch revealed to Charlie had to do with the shed on his property. Mr. Bowditch told Charlie that within the shed was a well that led to the “other world” where the sundial existed. Years ago, Mr. Bowditch had gone on the sundial to make himself younger. Mr. Bowditch had shared this information with Charlie already. As Charlie continued listening to the all that Mr. Bowditch had to tell him, tears welled up in his eyes. Charlie knew that Mr. Bowditch was dying. By the time that the ambulance got to Mr. Bowditch’s house, he was already dead. Charlie took Radar to his own house. Radar became his dog on that day. Unfortunately, Radar was also quite old and didn’t have long to live. That was when a plan started to formulate in Charlie’s mind. He could not loose Radar too. Charlie would do whatever he had to do to find the sundial and make Radar young again. The next part of Fairy Tale took place in the “other world” known as Empis. The fairy tale characters were very creative yet believable. Charlie’s adventurous journey was full of discovery, magic, dangers, good, evil and monsters. Some of the scenes were gruesome and unpleasant but for the most part they were well plotted and even uplifting. The ending was quite satisfying and it tied everything up quite nicely. I found myself thinking about the characters long after the book ended. Charlie was my favorite character by far. I am so glad that I took a chance and read Fairy Tale by Stephen King. I highly recommend it.

First, I want to thank Edelweiss and Simon and Schuster for this eGalley in exchange for an honest review! I got to read Fairy Tale a while back and found myself not being able to put it down, which, honestly, we all know goes without saying. It’s nice to *finally* talk freely about the excellent and meh elements (to which there are few, but whatever). 📖My favorite part of this book was the relationships. The relationship between Charlie and Howard is believable because cranky old men who refuse help and 17-year-old boys who are eager to help go hand in hand. However, the best relationship will naturally be between Charlie and Radar. Any quest worth taking requires a dog (or talking cat? just any animal here, honestly) to be a proper quest, right? I couldn’t think of a better companion to save the worlds than Radar ❤️ 📚It's acknowledged that saying the world-building and fantasy of any King work is a given, but I’m a huge fan of repeating things, especially if it’s going to make some neck beard super sad on the internet. 😂. The Dark Tower is present throughout most of King’s books, but it’s worth noting that its presence is strong in Fairy Tale. 📚Now for the one thing that was kind of meh was the 5,000,000 times breasts were mentioned. The main character is 17, so it makes sense, but it did pull me out of the story now and again. I can’t honestly remember disliking much of anything aside from that, though. So this was a 5-star read for me. Getting an eGalley of this book was like Christmas in April, so I’m beyond thankful for the opportunity to read/review so many fantastic titles.

I absolutely loved this book. In my opinion, this is the best Stephen King book in recent memory and it is easily my favorite read of the year, so far. Stephen King is known for horror, but I think some of his best works fall into other genres. Fantasy isn't necessarily my favorite genre, but If the author has "king" in their name, I'm going to read it (T. Kingfisher's Nettle & Bone is probably my second favorite read of the year). You'd expect a Stephen King fairy tale to be a close cousin to the Brothers Grimm, but it was surprisingly wholesome. It's no Disney tale, this is still Stephen King after all, but it was more hope and less horror. It was a fun hero's journey tale that I'm sure I'll re-read in the future. It's a new story, with hints of the fairy tales we're already familiar with. There are two things that King has been doing lately that I'm not a fan of. The first, is talking about Donald Trump way too much. The second, is self-referencing his other works, as works of fiction. He does both in this book, but restrains himself to just one of each. For King, this was a fairly short book at a little over 600 pages. In this case, I wouldn't have minded a few hundred more pages of story. The story was complete, I just wanted a lot more of it. I don't really think King left the door open for a direct sequel, but there's still a possibility for one.

This was quite a journey for me. I have immersed myself in horror fiction so completely in the last few years (I have King to thank for this passion) that it was hard to poke my head up out of that world and join King in this fantasy book. It came out in September 2022, but my mom and I decided to buddy-read it this Christmas. With all the hubbub of the holidays and reading other books at the same time, I was dipping in and out of this book for over a month. FAIRY TALE by Stephen King (other dark fantasy books: The Talisman & Black House with Peter Straub, The Eyes of the Dragon, The Dark Tower Series) Release Date: September 2022 General genre: Dark Fantasy Subgenre: Coming-of-Age (manhood. MC is a teen), Good & Evil, Man's Best Friend, Gateway/Portals, Secrets Writing Style: The first third of the book reminded me a lot of Mr. Harrigan's Phone. Classic Stephen King character-driven storytelling What you need to know: A teen boy, Charlie Reade (I love that his last name is READ), is passing by a neighbor's house when he hears someone crying out and a dog barking. He goes to investigate and ultimately saves an old man's life. Over the course of time, they become close, and Charlie develops a strong connection with the old man's ailing dog, Radar. The old man, Howard Bowditch, keeps his cards close to the vest but realizes he's not long for the world, so he trusts Charlie with some secrets. My reading experience: I'm biased. I wear rose-colored glasses when it comes to King's books. I can admit when I don't care for something, even go as far as to tell others I didn't like it, but at the end of the day, Stephen King is my all-time favorite author. His storytelling has been with me since I was barely a teen. That's over 3 decades of spending time in King worlds, falling in love with King characters, and elevating his work as the gold standard. So, I have a hard time disrespecting King's work. That being said, horror really and truly has ruined me for other books unless those other books are very, very dark. Fairy Tale is mostly sweet, it's nostalgic for his Constant Readers who have enjoyed his horror/fantasy genre mash-ups in the past...except this one is pretty light. It doesn't get as dark as The Talisman or the Dark Tower. The Territories and Mid-World plumb dark depths while Empis is a magical world that is the source of all our fairytales & fantasies. Charlie is your classic hero embarking on a hero's journey with King at the helm of that character arc. Sometimes, I felt like King was living out some of his own fantasies through Charlie...read it for yourself and see if you agree. Truth be told, I got impatient a few times while I was reading this. The set-up section of the story is sublime. The first 200 pages or so I zipped through and settled right in but then there are some long chapters in the middle before we get to Empis that made me restless. But once King hits his stride, I was right there with him, enjoying the gift. Fairy Tale is a gift and we're lucky to have it. My final recommendation: An enjoyable adventure with an open invitation to fall in love with Stephen King's remarkable ability to bring characters to life. His signature wheelhouse is character-driven storytelling. Fictional people who feel like friends that readers store away in their hearts. Charlie Reade and Radar will live there always and I would recommend this book to young people who have never experienced a King book, old people who have loved King's storytelling but don't enjoy horror anymore, and everyone in between. Comps: The Book of Lost Things by John Connolly, Every Heart a Doorway (Wayward Children Series) by Seanan McGuire, The Chronicles of Narnia by C. S. Lewis

This review and others @Bookerification Rating: 3 stars Cover: 🌟🌟🌟🌟 How pretty is this cover?! The gentle, pastel colours work wonderfully with the simple illustration to create a striking design. I also love that we have Charlie and Radar in the design, even though all we get is their outline. Writing: 🌟🌟🌟 As expected from Stephen King's reputation, his writing style is smooth and easy to follow. The narrative voice is confident and mature as the story is recounted by an older Charlie years later. While I found the world-building intricate and fascinating, the fantasy aspect seemed convoluted. On top of this, various elements within the parallel world are dismissed as part of the magical world. This simplistic explanation was not satisfying and dragged me out of the experience. “You’re only as sick as your secrets” Storyline: 🌟🌟🌟 The story begins with a gentle introduction to Charlie and his sad childhood. Charlie's connection with Mr Bowditch and his dog Radar is then established in a slow-paced, mundane account that takes up about a third of the story. While I was not captivated by this aspect of the story, it did allow me to form an emotional connection with the grumpy older man and his sweet dog. The pace gradually picks up once Charlie enters the parallel world and there is some action. Despite this, I could not bring myself to remain invested in Charlie's grand quest, as it took far too long to see where the story was heading. By the end, most loose ends are nicely tied without seeming too perfect or forced. Main character(s): 🌟🌟🌟 Seventeen-year-old Charlie Reade may seem like a typical good kid, but he also has a dark side because of his tragic childhood. However, besides the initial complexity and depth his character gets from this, Charlie experiences little growth during the story. This made it hard for me to connect and relate with him, even though I liked his character. "There’s a dark well in everyone, I think, and it never goes dry. But you drink from it at your peril. " Secondary characters: 🌟🌟🌟 The grumpy and suspicious Mr Bowditch took some time to grow on me, but he eventually melted my ice-cold heart. Bowditch's love for his dog Radar made him even more endearing, and I was impressed by how much personality King infuses into the dog. The remaining secondary characters are mainly from the parallel world. Sadly, I struggled to keep track of the large cast of characters, especially since most are given little depth and are unmemorable. Romance: 🌟 The little romance in this story caught me by surprise as the characters lacked a clear connection. What begins as Charlie's physical attraction to another character suddenly becomes love with little development shown. I would have preferred not to have this romance, as it adds very little to the story. It is clear that 'Fairy Tale' is not a story I found very gripping or engaging. Only a handful of the characters were memorable, and I struggled with the slow-paced, expansive storyline. However, I understand why other readers may enjoy this story, especially with the homage made to Grimms and Disney fairy tales. I would recommend The Invisible Life of Addie LaRue by V.E. Schwab for those who love this book.

I recently reread Fairy Tale, and I realized I never initially loaded a rating or review for this novel. It was extremely well received and has been reviewed and discussed so often, so I'll just quickly comment on it as a fan of his work. Far more a fantasy than a horror (though there are plenty of tense, frightening moments), Fairy Tale is one of my favorite books by Mr. King. There are multiple beautiful relationships between characters--between a boy and a dog, a boy and an elderly mentor, a boy and his father. If you appreciate character driven narratives that offer insights into the human condition, there's so much to love here. There are also hundreds of poignant lines that I felt the need to write down in my own journal just so I could continue to appreciate them later--I personally found this novel to be some of Mr. King's most exquisite writing. And of course characteristic of much of Mr. King's work, there is also a supernaturally bizarre element which forms the intrigue and mystery in the first half of the book, so I don't want to talk about it directly as finding out just what is going on is part of the thrill of it all. At it's core though, this is a coming of age story and an end of life story. It's a novel about the human condition--transitions, the relationships (non-romantic) we foster that help inform those transitions, and our acceptance of transitions. Time itself only becomes the antagonist when the characters try to deny its progression, but of course that too is a part of human nature. I know lots of readers who don't usually read fantasy or horror novels will miss out on this novel simply because of the association, but I wish everyone who has ever craved remarkable prose (in this case a stunning literary coming of age portrait of a compassionate young American teen who is just trying to be a decent guy and finding out what that--being decent--actually means in today's world) would give this book a chance. Yes, there's a element of the fantastical that serves as the plot vehicle during the second part of the book. But Fairy Tale is so much more than it's genre, and I have recommended it to readers who favor realism just as often. And even though the main character is a teenaged boy and the secondary characters are largely men, I also personally felt just as connected with the humanity of the story. So I recommend it just as often to women. There's something here for everyone--it's such a positive, life affirming novel, and though I have used the word beautiful far too often in this review, it's really the best fit. It is a beautiful fairytale.

This was a ride. I loved the journey with Charlie and Radar. Once I started, my first impression was how well Stephen King writes American casual vernacular speech. The inner monologue and the conversations are very effective at conveying place and character while appearing effortless and understated. He starts with windowpane prose. Later, as the fantasy story develops, he adds some carefully placed formal and sometimes archaic vocabulary to great effect. It's always done precisely and to benefit the progress of the story. The initial build up is slow but interesting. Then things get eerie. Then the adventure really starts. This is a top notch fantasy mystery survival adventure with good vs evil themes. The book frequently echoes actual fairy tales and fairy tale themes. I enjoyed the reminders of past experiences with fairy tales and fables. I believe the way it's handled would be a good introduction to fairy tales for someone who isn't familiar with those traditional stories, without interfering with their enjoyment of this book. There were times when the main character's inner voice and reflections sounded more like the elderly author than a boy of 17. That tendency gets a plot based explanation in the epilogue. I liked the book a lot regardless. If you like portal fantasy where the main character leaves ordinary life for a strange new world, read this book. If you like epic high stakes fantasy featuring good vs evil, read this book. If you like creatively drawn intimidating monsters, read this book. If you like coming of age adventures, read this book. If you like creative retelling of old stories, read this book. If you like adventures with brave loyal companions, read this book. The dog steals the show. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

"Here is something I learned in Empis: good people shine brighter in dark times." pg 250 Charlie is a typical teen- plays sports and helps his father out around the house. But one day, after helping a neighbor after an accident, Charlie enters a world that is not our own. And discovers an adventure that he wasn't looking for. The incomparable Stephen King has written a mammoth fairy tale (600 pages in my digital version!). I thought it was too long. Not that I mind long books. It sort of felt like King started the book thinking it was going to be about something different than it turned into. The reason I feel that way is because the first quarter of the book takes so long to establish Charlie's character and real world connections. I wanted to just get on with it. Then, when we finally made it to Empis, events went too quickly! King uses quite a lot of foreshadowing which was ok at first, but then it started to become too much. I realize he was trying to build tension- it was just over-used. "Remember when I said at the outset that no one would believe my story?" pg 494, ebook I enjoyed any part of the story that had Radar the dog in it. She was my favorite character. King really took his time developing her and her reactions to the world around her, which was fun. King is at his best when he's describing the eerie atmosphere of the other world and its unfortunate denizens. Like I said, those parts went too quickly. Other than my small gripes, this was a well-written story and worthy of its Good Reads nomination. Readers who like Stephen King for his horror should read a different book. This is definitely more fantasy than horror.
