3.5⭐️ for now rounding down, but I may change my mind the more I think about it. I have a lot to say, so this one is going to be a bit longer than usual. If you haven’t read this yet, I really recommend reading Quicksilver Bonus Scenes: Kingfisher’s POV first. It not only offers his point of view but also explains what happened at the Ajun gate, which I found really helpful to know beforehand. My thoughts are a little all over the place, much like the plot and pacing of this book. There was so much happening, yet at times it also felt like nothing was happening, if that makes sense, and threads that felt like they went nowhere. I will start with what I loved about Brimstone, which was mostly the characters. The bromance between Fisher and Carrion was pure perfection. Fisher and that mouth of his… sigh 😮‍💨. He is definitely one of my top-tier book boyfriends. Carrion remains an absolute highlight in this series and steals every scene he is in. He constantly makes me laugh, and I enjoyed seeing him take on a more active role, something I think will be even more important in the next book. Onyx the fox and Archer the fire sprite added a lot of charm as well. ❤️ While I enjoyed getting to know some of the new side characters, I was disappointed that a few of my favorites received very little page time (Ren and Lorreth). Even though I enjoyed this book overall, I had quite a few issues with it. Although I liked Saeris more here than I did in Quicksilver, she still comes across as immature and petulant at times. The spicy scenes were very spicy, which I am completely fine with, but outside the bedroom Saeris and Fisher barely communicate and I prefer romances with a bit more emotional depth. She did not even know his mother’s name, which was weird. And yes, Fisher is hot, but Saeris describing how hot he is over and over again started to feel like filler. The biggest issue for me was the overuse of “my mate” and “solar plexus.” It became annoyingly distracting and pulled me out of the story repeatedly. At 660 pages, cutting back on those phrases would have helped tighten the book considerably and made it feel far less repetitive. Overall, the story could have benefited from stronger editing. Even with all my complaints, I did enjoy the book. I just did not enjoy it as much as the first one, and in my opinion, it did not quite live up to what it could have been. I alternated between the physical book and the audiobook. The duet narration was really well done, and once again, Anthony Palmini’s performance as Fisher was absolute perfection. He could read me a menu and I would enjoy every second of it. **FINAL GRIPE IS A SPOILER SO STOP READING HERE IF YOU DON’T WANT TO KNOW.** I am struggling with Fisher’s name change, but what really pulled me out of the story was how Saeris instantly adopted his new name without a single slip. Not once does she call him Fisher or Kingfisher again, and that just does not feel believable.
Taking my rating off. Teetering between 4 and 4.5. Going to think on this weekend.

The author wrote so many scenes where the MC’s were physically apart that I question if she added a mind link just so she could slip in some spice. To each their own, but this kind of vampire spice where they drink each other like juice boxes just isn’t for me. I wanted to see more relational growth, but mostly what the author gave us was sex, sex, and more sex any time these characters shared a page. I do like that their relationship seems healthy and supportive, but the level of obsession they have for each other is a bit extreme when you consider that they barely know each other. People were joking about this developing into a romance between Fisher & Carrion, but that honestly didn’t seem that far fetched. If it weren’t for the fact that the word mate was used 180 times in this book… 180 TIMES, I might have really believed it was heading in that direction. Sigh… I’m sorry if this is coming out as a rant. I was just so genuinely excited for this and I wanted to love it so bad! It’s always extra sad when one of your most highly anticipated reads flops. 😔 And of COURSE this ended on a cliffhanger so now I feel like I might even continue the series despite wanting desperately to DNF this. 🫠 One thing’s for sure, these authors sure do know how to hook us. ✼ ҉ ✼ ҉ ✼ ҉ ✼ ҉ ✼ ҉ ✼ ҉ ✼ Pre-read: Let’s goooo!! ❝ because what was a book, if not a portal into another realm, another time, another life even. ❞ slipping back into the fae & alchemy universe with brimstone felt like waking up from a quicksilver hangover and immediately being handed a 600+ page war, three emotional crises, and a blood-soaked coronation. callie hart basically said, "you wanted more saeris and kingfisher? here’s trauma, desert politics, and a spiritual death march. have fun!" and honestly, i'm not going to lie, i kinda did. ₊˚꒰ 𖧷 ꒱ ⊹ i. plot and world. ₊˚⊹ ꒱ brimstone picks up after the absolute chaos of quicksilver. saeris fane is now queen of the blood court, which is hilarious because she very much did not apply for this job. she's also stuck as a fae–vampire hybrid whose skin does not vibe with sunlight, which is deeply inconvenient when your desert homeland, zilvaren, catches on fire politically and literally. she can’t go herself, so she sends kingfisher and chaos-smuggler carrion swift off to deal with it, while she stays behind in yvelia juggling court vipers, blood rituals, and the creeping darkness chewing through the realm. the worldbuilding absolutely goes feral in this one. deserts, frozen kingdoms, blood magic, war councils, portal lore, and an entire travel itinerary’s worth of alleyways, palaces, and battlefields. i loved the idea of it all: the widening scope, the sense that this war is so much bigger than saeris and fisher, the way their choices keep echoing through different corners of the world. there are some truly gorgeous, cinematic moments, too. but let’s be real. this book is thick. like, aggressively thick. sometimes the plot is sprinting, and other times it’s wandering in circles having a feelings monologue while i’m checking how many pages are left. there are stretches where it feels like second-book syndrome. there's lots of moving pieces, not as much payoff, and the war is always looming but rarely hitting that satisfying "oh shit" crescendo. ₊˚꒰ 𖧷 ꒱ ⊹ ii. characters and romance. ₊˚⊹ ꒱ saeris is still that girl. prickly, exhausted, powerful, and hanging onto her sanity with dental floss. i love that she doesn’t suddenly morph into a perfect queen. she’s tired, overwhelmed, and still very much learning how to wield both her crown and her alchemy without burning herself out (or, you know, the entire realm). her inner conflict feels heavier here. more responsibility, more guilt. the real glow-up in brimstone is kingfisher. we finally get his point of view, and callie hart really said, "what if we cracked his chest open and let you crawl around in there?" his chapters show a softer, messier version of him. more vulnerability, more self-loathing, more devotion so intense it borders on unhealthy in a way that’s, yeah, i’m not gonna lie, kind of delicious. he’s still the infuriating, morally grey disaster we signed up for, but now we get to see just how deep the obsession with saeris runs, and it is deep. septic, even. their romance in this book is like being in a relationship with a storm. there’s blood, power exchange, magically binding rituals, and constant push-pulls. some of their scenes absolutely slap, the intense, visceral, "we’re saving the world and also ruining each other emotionally" kind of slap. ₊˚꒰ 𖧷 ꒱ ⊹ iii. pacing. ₊˚⊹ ꒱ this book is vibes-heavy. war vibes. grief vibes. "i love you so much it might end us" vibes. sometimes it works beautifully and i was locked in, mentally gnawing on the bars of my own prison cell. other times it felt like the emotional beats were dragging the plot behind them like a dead body. the tonal mix of political intrigue, dark magic, and deeply horny blood rituals is absolutely my brand of unhinged, but i do think some tightening would’ve made the whole thing land harder. that being said, when brimstone hits, it hits. the set pieces are grand, the magic is fun and twisted, and the way saeris and fisher are constantly being forced to choose between each other and the world scratches a very specific angsty itch. i just wish the journey there hadn’t felt quite so long in places, with so many minor detours and side tangents muddying how sharp this book could've been. ₊˚꒰ 𖧷 ꒱ ⊹ iv. side gremlins. ₊˚⊹ ꒱ oh my god, yes, my little chaos gremlin. okay, let’s talk about him, because lowkey he's half the reason brimstone works at all. i need to dedicate one section just about carrion swift. if saeris and fisher are the main course, then carrion swift is the unhinged side dish you didn’t order but end up devouring anyway. in brimstone, he gets shipped off with kingfisher to zilvaren and basically spends the entire time carrying the book on his shoulders. every time the narrative wandered, he'd pop up again with some roguish one-liner, and suddenly i cared. MY BEAUTIFUL FLUFFY ONYX. special shoutout to onyx, the tiny white fox who has more plot armor and emotional impact than half the characters in this book. he’s a little white fox that saeris basically rescues from death, and then adopts like a feral emotional band-aid. he’s officially saeris’s fox, but let’s be so serious. he's also kingfisher's, even if fisher would rather chew glass than admit it. in quicksilver, onyx is mostly lurking adorably at the edges of scenes, being anxious and fluffy and watching all this fae–vampire–war nonsense unfold. then brimstone rolls in and callie hart decides it’s time for some real emotional damage. was it silly? was it overdramatic? meh. TRUST CALLIE TO MAKE THIS AN IMPORTANT PLOT POINT IN BOOK 3. ₊˚꒰ 𖧷 ꒱ ⊹ v. true name. ₊˚⊹ ꒱ oh my god, we also get fisher’s true name in this book. honestly, i kind of love that his true name reveal doesn't change the fact that i, personally, will continue calling him fisher like a disrespectful little peasant. ₊˚꒰ 𖧷 ꒱ ⊹ vi. conclusion. ₊˚⊹ ꒱ overall, brimstone feels like getting exactly what you asked for and then realizing you maybe should’ve asked for a slightly smaller portion. more fae politics, more blood court drama, more saeris/fisher intensity, more world-building, and also more pages, more circling, more emotional rinse-and-repeat. i liked it. i had fun. i highlighted unholy amounts of feral lines. but i also had to put it down a few times. still, for all my complaining, i’m invested, because that ending? i’ll absolutely be seated for book three, clown makeup on, ready to watch these two idiots and their friends save the world. — 3.5 stars. ⋆˚☆˖°.ᐟ .° ༘🎧ྀི⋆ favourite quotes 🖇₊˚ෆ ❛ every part. i love all of you. i'd spend the fortunes of the universe to protect you. i'd drain the seas dry. feel every tree. i would sacrifice the sun from the fucking sky and surrender the stars, too, if i could. But those things aren't mine to give. all I have is my life. It isn't much, but i'd spend it and consider the price small if it meant keeping you safe. ❜ ❛ so yes. i love saeris fane, because she's electric, and fierce, and loyal, and being around her brings the world back into focus. but i'm not in love with her, fisher. i tried. but my heart was just too full of sorrow to make room for her. ❜ ❛ i had no idea what you would mean to me. i had no idea what i would do to keep you safe. when i close my eyes, you are all i fucking see, saeris fane. i could be dead in the ground five thousand years and the frosts could have taken my bones, and still no other male will ever have loved another female the way that i love you. ❜ ❛ don't you know? there isn't much i wouldn't sacrifice to make you happy, osha. a little healing magic is the least of it. ❜ ⌗ started: dec. 19th, 2025. ⌝ ⌞ finished: jan. 7th, 2026. ✦ ₊˚⊹ ᰔ pre-review: ⤿ FINALLY FINISHED WITH MY FIRST READ OF 2026. An Oddly Fascinating… Yet Strangely Unfascinating Ride I’m convinced my experience with this book was a bit… unorthodox. It opened strong, and then suddenly I found myself trapped between endless 13-year-old-level fashion bickering, “high stakes—just kidding lol” moments, and a pacing style that occasionally wandered off for a coffee break… well, it pulled me right out. Here’s the wild part: 🎯 Everything that happened was actually interesting. Some plot threads did go a little poof for the sake of spotlighting two other big arcs, but honestly, that wasn’t the crime. The real crime? I was intrigued yet somehow… not. My brain said “gimme more,” while my heart said “I'm bored...” Make it make sense. 🤷🏻‍♀️ Around the 60% mark, I was firmly aboard the “please let this end soon” ship, waving politely at the plot as it went by. ⚔️ Character Glow-Ups & Half-Baked Moments I did enjoy seeing Saeris and Fisher finally step out of their “reluctant leader” / “professional martyr” personalities from book one. Very satisfying. Turns out having something to lose really tightens up a person’s priorities. And I appreciated the small-but-mighty side characters' contributions to the plot sprinkled throughout. But I’d be lying if I said some scenes didn’t feel like someone wrote half a paragraph, shrugged, and went “period. good enough.” ⚫ 🔄 A Future Reread? Sure... in the future. Even with the bumps, the core of the story is solid. The essence is there, and it's potent. So, I suspect I’ll pick this up again later to see if it hits differently. -- Pre-read: Okay. I am as ready as can be. LET's GO!🏁 -- Also, that new voice-over from Callie? No, it's not Carrion. I say Taladaius, I mean how could he not? But I guess I will see.

SPOILERS SPOILERS SPOILERS!!!! Stop reading it you don’t want SPOILERS! (Also includes spoilers for SJM books) Now, I’m not the most articulate reviewer, so I apologize if there is anything I missed while reading that may have been explained in my below cons/pros points. I did in fact read the bonus chapters for Quicksilver, but read them after I read Brimstone. While they were good chapters, and I wish I had read them/known about them before reading Brimstone, I don’t think having read the bonus chapters after held me back at all from enjoying this book. CONS -the fact that Kingfisher’s Mom was an Oracle and created a wardrobe of dresses for her is straight up a rip off of the ACOTAR series. Maybe other authors made this a big thing before SJM, but with her popularity in the romantasy genre, and the fact that ACOMAF was written well before Brimstone, it feels like a huge overall stolen plot point. While other romantasy books have the same tropes over and over again, this was too specific. Gotta take off half a ⭐️ for that alone. -Sigh…the Demon of the Desert, Joshin. So after I stopped laughing at the name (because seriously? Are you Joshin me with this name?), I did my own research, which consisted of like 10 whole minutes of google (so not extensive). The point of the research was to see if she either just made the most ridiculous name for a character, or if it was a demon from other lore, history, etc. the closest thing I came up with was a Naruto fanfic. But it doesn’t seem like she stole that from Naruto, so points for creativity! And if there is a demon out there, I *personally* agree it should be named Josh. (This is a safe place for Josh haters). My other issue with Joshin, is why is a demon that is killed by light in a world with 2 suns and where there is no nighttime? Zilvaren is a desert, so that matches the demons overall name, but he is known about in Yvelia, so why didn’t he just stay there, why did he go to a place that was known for its never ending day? If it was explained, I totally missed it. And why that locksmith guy (not worth remembering his name I guess) was working with Joshin to lure victims doesn’t ever seem to be explained either. If it was, it was so one dimensional I didn’t catch it. In this same scene, we learn about the Devils trap, which feels copied from supernatural, but no points taken from rating of the book for it because of course there is more lore and literature about devil traps. I only mention it since it seems like our girl Callie could be a big fan of things like ACOTAR and possibly Naruto, why wouldn’t she also be a fan of Supernatural? Okay continuing with cons. -I was personally hoping for a love triangle or something of the sort as well as some other readers, which didn’t happen (Kingfisher and Carrion at the same damn time). While that is totally fine it didn’t happen, 660 pages of Kingfisher and Saeris being sooooooooooooo in looooooooveeeeeeeee was such an overkill lol. I get it, they’re in love. I feel like a lot of pages could have better been used to wrap up other plot lines. -we walked away from this book with the ONLY plot line being wrapped up was Hayden being brought to Yvelia. Which is great he’s finally out of Zilvaren! But then we get basically no more information about what he was up to while Saeris was gone, and he and Saeris barely interacted when he got to Yvelia. Walking away with even more questions and plots felt kind of exhausting, but I understand it can pay off. It’s kinda giving me TOG vibes, not that Callie copied anything, but just in the sense of how exhausting of a read it can be and holding off a LONG time for any resolution. The ones who read TOG get it. -I love Archer, but could not open my heart fully to him because we all know how terribly it can go for loveable side characters (especially fire sprites, I’m still not over Lehabah). Of course something does end up happening to him. I won’t totally spoil it if you’re reading this even after the spoiler warnings. -Chapter 48, I cried like a baby. Don’t fuck with the fox. Another half of a ⭐️ gone -of course in the lead up to this book, I saw a lot of stuff on social media about Callie Hart saying “no one is safe in this book” and “book therapy after this”. But…why? We literally didn’t lose a single character except bad guys. And even those bad guys were one dimensional barely memorable. So meh. High stakes, but we lose no one? Idk seems like she overhyped it. Okay I’m done with the cons! PROS -CARRION SWIFT ADMITS HE LOVES SAERIS!!!! But not in love with her, at least not fully because he lost someone long ago? Interested to learn more about that. -Love the Kingfisher and Carrion adventure and banter so much. -Elroy is a fucking G. Love love love him. I hope to get more info than we already did in this book, and I hope he comes back up again in future books. -As we found out in book 1, Saeris was sterilized so she couldn’t have kids. I hope that doesn’t change in future books, I could enjoy a good fantasy series without a MFC pregnancy trope for once. Glad that wasn’t reversed in this book. -“Kingfisher” is DEAD! Yes I thought the name sounded ridiculous as well, I don’t totally love the new name either, but it’s a huge improvement nonetheless to not call him Kingfisher. Also, earlier in Brimstone it is explained that Kingfisher and Saeris cannot marry because he doesn’t know his true name. “Hell is empty and all the devils are here.” -Shakespeare Ever since I read Fifth Season I started paying close attention to the dedications written in books. It’s easy to read and forget them, but I’ve noticed that at the end of a story they hold so much more meaning. In my mind Callie is taunting us with this Shakespearean quote that speaks of chaos and trouble. And that is how I felt at times navigating the pages of Brimstone. There are threads of trouble dangling seemingly haphazardly throughout Yvelia and Zilvaren, and it’s difficult to see how they come together. Now this is not a criticism, I’m going to assume this is a deliberate plot move. I enjoyed the constructed chaos. My only criticism is that at times the pacing felt suspended. I’m not expecting constant battles and near death scenarios, I just found my mind wandering here and there. Just barely. It’s probably me. Now Saeris and Kingfisher: seeing them navigate their different challenges and always come back to each other was satisfying. Sometimes I wanted them to get a room. Jk! The spice is scorching and I would absolutely melt at Kingfisher’s feet. They are just a little gooey at times, like newlyweds. Carrion continues his role of comedic flirtation with everyone, allowing time to breathe whenever the situation gets too tense. So inappropriate, but that’s what we love about him. Onyx: if he doesn’t pull on your heartstrings in this one you must be part vampire. I’m curious to see what his role will be in the next book. I love how the side characters continue to play pivotal roles, especially Tal, Lorreth, and Archer. Some characters take a backseat to court politics and new faces, but in general Callie fleshes out a full cast. I think my favorite part might be that I have absolutely no idea where this story is headed. Those threads of chaos are so tangled that even the role of worst villain is up for grabs at this point. And that dumbfounding ending has me gleefully anticipating the next release. Callie definitely let all the devils out, or maybe they were there all along. BTW, if you don’t remember the dedication from Quicksilver read it and see what you think. 4⭐️’s audio & Kindle ———————————————————————- Planning on avoiding as many responsibilities as possibility in favor of Brimstone 🔥. Happy reading 🖤

** spoiler alert ** I went into Brimstone with cautious optimism. I thought Quicksilver was pretty mid, but FOMO convinced me to pick up Brimstone right at release, mostly to avoid spoilers. Unpopular opinion: Brimstone wasn’t worth the urgency. By the midpoint, I was so underwhelmed that I ended up listening to the rest of the audiobook at 3x speed. Why didn’t I DNF? Apparently I enjoy suffering. **SPOILERS BELOW** WHAT DIDN’T WORK FOR ME • So much happens and yet… nothing happens. The plot is constantly moving, but somehow feels like it’s going nowhere. Events happen, but impact? Stakes? Tension? Barely present. • Zero yearning. The FMC and MMC are SO in love that there’s no tension, no longing, no build-up. Even when they’re apart, there’s no emotional distance because they’re dreamwalking and having perfect sex scenes like it’s a sport. Which leads me to… • The sheer number of sex scenes. Normally I don’t mind spice, but these felt wedged in. If the couple is already blissfully in love, the constant scenes just became repetitive instead of meaningful. • The word “mate” was used so often it lost all flavour. At a certain point, I flinched every time it popped up. • ACOTAR déjà vu. From the vibes to certain plot elements, it felt like a watered-down version of something I’d already read. The Hasmax gave me total Suriel flashbacks. • The Kingfisher name change saga. We’re almost two books in and suddenly we’re supposed to call him by a new name AND a nickname? • Everything was too easy. Every dangerous situation had a simple, convenient solution. The lack of real stakes made it hard to care about the journey. • Hayden’s reaction didn’t make sense. They told him where Saeris had been and he just accepted it? But I thought she didn’t know what Yvelia was? The logic felt inconsistent. • Death is basically optional. Once again, loved characters can return from the dead with almost no struggle. When resurrection is that easy, emotional weight disappears. WHAT I LIKED • The narrators were great. Honestly, they’re the reason I made it through the book at all. The performance was engaging even when the story wasn’t. Overall, Brimstone had potential but ultimately felt like a repetitive, low-stakes echo of better fantasy romances. I wanted tension, emotional payoff, and meaningful conflict. Instead I got convenience and boredom. Ask me next year if FOMO convinces me to finish the series.

People complained about the Kingfisher name in the first book. Which fair, cause I hated it too. Besides, it really is awful. I don’t understand why anyone wouldn’t. But people need to complain about fucking everything, because apparently now, his real name isn’t good enough for people either. His real name is such a non issue, it’s like, go touch some grass to actually have something to do. There are books out there where characters have awful names, and no one mentions anything, because hello, it’s just a name. Now the name Kingfisher is an exception, because it’s KINGFISHER. But his true name isn’t completely weird, or ugly or anything. And yet people are all «ah I’m getting the ick». The ending was the perfect cliffhanger. It was enticing enough to keep my attention, but not horrific enough to actually have the opposite effect and make me not want to pick up the next book. Sometimes if the main characters are really in trouble. As in, is about to be tortured at the beginning of the next book trouble. And I have to wait a long time for the next book to come out, a hollow feeling will settle in my stomach. And by the time the next book comes out, that feeling will be the only thing I associate the books with, and I won’t want to read it at all. Yeah. I’m complicated. Now, there will be some spoilers. The plot was followed throughout the entire book, and I really liked the pace of the book. A few times there would be drawn out intimate scenes where I kind of wanted to skip ahead, but at the same time I was afraid to miss something important. My biggest issue with those scenes is that they didn’t really have a purpose. I’m used to scenes like this in romance books, but it isn’t something I crave in fantasy. One long smut scene is enough for me. The world stayed true to the whole Alchemical aspect which I was grateful for. I though maybe now that she’s both Fae and Vampire the story would lean more into the typical magic we meet in a lot of other fantasy books. Instead her being an alchemist was more relevant now than ever, and it seems like it will play a huge part in everything to do with The Rot spreading across the land. I was curious about how we would see Saeris step into her role as queen, and I loved how she didn’t know what she was doing, but managed to appear strong when it mattered. She never felt overconfident or prideful, but not naive and helpless either. Even though there weren’t a lot I really liked the connections she made with some of the people from the Vampire court. Mostly Taladaius and The Hazrax. I wanted her to get close to Taladaius just because I liked him from Quicksilver. And even though they aren’t a hundred percent as close as I want, I think they will grow to be closer friends. At least I hope they will. I think he needs a friend like her. The Hazrax I’m simply intrigued by. It doesn’t seem like a friend, but not an enemy either. I think it’s helping, maybe out of some goodness. But then Saeris will make a comment about how it’s mocking her. But I’m leaning more towards liking it rather than being concerned about it’s motives. Saeris’ relationship with Khydan - which yes, I will be calling him that rather than Kingfisher now - was a complete one eighty from when they first met each other. In some ways I absolutely loved it, especially the love he so openly showed her. In other ways he spent a lot of time talking about everything he would do for her in order to show us how deep his love ran. It would have been enough to just show instead of telling. Because it was shown. One huge declaration would have more than sufficed. I love all the side characters that we met in the first book. Lorreth is probably my favourite, but I feel like I know him slightly better. But I think I might love Foley even more depending on what we see of him in the next book. I just loved his background and complexity. I hate that witch. What was her name? Iseabail. In the beginning I thought we would see her and Lorreth have a little enemies to lovers story going on. And maybe that’s still in the cards, but the difference is I no longer like her. Just the whole ordeal with turning the vampire court back to what they were, and deceiving not only Saeris and Khydan, but also Taladaius who were helping her with the plan. I don’t necessarily hate that she did it. It was just her whole attitude around it. She was so confident and refused to apologise even though Saeris could have been killed immediately, and Taladaius almost died and a gate to hell or something was almost opened. But she had also lied to her fellow witches and made them believe the Vampire court had been willing. When really she used black magic which they forbid. And when Khydan wanted to send her back to them because he had figured that part out, and wanted her dead for endangering Saeris she was suddenly panicking. Served her right. I don’t have to say anything about Onyx rigjt? He is a sweetheart and thank god! I won’t say anything else about him. But just, thank god, honestly. I love Carrion. Nothing has changed about that from book one. He is really funny, but in a very subtle way, even though it comes across as the opposite…. It doesn’t feel over the top I guess. It’s just who he is, and it’s impossible not to love him. As for Hayden. I don’t really like Saeris’ brother. He has potential to be sure, but I just don’t think he’s a good brother. I was totally here for the absolute smack down she gave him. But still. She spent a lot of time worrying about him and all that time he was thinking she was traitor and never spoke up for her in Zilvaren when people were cursing her name after she almost died at the beginning of book one. Even her old mentor, the old guy took several beatings defending her. But no. Her brother just stood by. Prick. On a last note: Why did Saeris say Lorreth was with Carrion training when Carrion was in Zilvaren with Khydan at the time? This wasn’t her lying to someone. She mentioned it in her inner monologue, which leads me to believe it’s an editing error. I’m a little disappointed by this, because the first book made similar mistakes, and I would have thought, given that the author is now traditionally published, mistakes like this would be caught and fixed. And also. The names of literary everything and everyone in this book is making me sweat. It just sounds like jumble in my head whenever I come across any and all names! It really is a problem! Overall I really loved this book, and I’m itching to read the next one.

The older Stephen King gets the better his stories are. Here we have 12 outstanding pieces of fiction, shorter and longer ones. His characters often are old, near death, they look back on a long life full of experience and everyday horrors. You'll meet a man who dreamed of a dead body and found her in reality. An obsessed cop tries to prove he's the murderer. Then we meet Tad's father Frank again after so many years (do you remember King's Cujo?). Or we have The Answer Man. Dreams can be dangerous as we learn in the Mad Scientist story. Is this the right stuff for younger readers? Well, I have my doubts as whole lives pass by in most of the tales. The older you are the more you will like the stories offered here. Stephen King is on top of his game here. If you think one of the longer tales is over he surprises the reader with yet another twist. What can I say as a lifelong Stephen King reader since the 80s? One of his very best story collections. A true highlight. Even though a massive tome, it could have been longer is the only thing I can add to the title. Very impressive. Hard to beat highlight of the year!

I loved this book! Yes, it’s a bit slow in places, and some stories don’t shine as brightly as others, but overall, it’s a captivating read that keeps you hooked. My only gripe? I wished it was darker, but hey, I can still appreciate the thrills it delivered. One highlight for me was the sequel to Cujo but my absolute favorite, though, was “Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream.” It had me glued to the pages. So, thank you, Mr. King, for another sleepless night! You never fail to entertain, and I can't wait for more. If you're looking for a collection that offers a mix of chills and great storytelling, this one’s a solid choice.

Two Talented Bastids - 4⭐ The Fifth Step - 3⭐ Willie the Weirdo - 4⭐ Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream - 5⭐ Finn - 3.5⭐ On Slide In Road - 4.5⭐ Red Screen - 4⭐ The Turbulence Expert - 4⭐ Laurie - 3.5⭐ Rattlesnakes - 4.5⭐ The Dreamers - 5⭐ The Answer Man 4.5⭐ This was an excellent collection! Overall I am going to rate it five stars due to how much I enjoyed my favourites. The stories that I rated 3 stars were still enjoyable and they tended to be the shorter stories in the collection. My absolute favourite was Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream, which at around 150 pages is the longest in this collection. I would have been happy to pay the price of this book just for that story alone! I think Constant Readers will really enjoy this collection, the best he has done in years! I alternated between reading and listening to the audiobook and really enjoyed the narration by Will Patton and Stephen King. For the story Laurie, I listened and read at the same time and noticed that a lot of the words and phrases were different in the narration to the book in print, some sentences were missed out, some different ones added in. It was quite frequent, on almost every page of the story. I only did that with the one story, so not sure if it is the same for the rest of the book.

Stephen King really “nailed” it this time, straight into the coffin lid. As a huge fan of King’s short story collections, You Like It Darker might just be my new favorite. With twelve tales that creep under your skin and linger in the shadows of your mind, King delivers exactly what he promises: the darker side of life, both literally and metaphorically. Each story feels iconic, balancing terror, tragedy, and King’s signature surprises. My absolute favorite was "Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream", talk about a nightmare you don’t want to wake up from. One brief psychic vision turns dozens of lives upside down, especially poor Danny’s. It’s haunting in the best way, showing King’s unmatched ability to blend fate and catastrophe. The twists kept me guessing, and the ending stuck with me like a shadow at midnight. Close behind was "Rattlesnakes", a real “fang-tastic” sequel to Cujo. The return to that chilling universe had my heart racing. King proves that sometimes the past has more bite than we expect, especially when an unexpected inheritance comes with venomous strings attached. It was a brilliant mix of nostalgia and new terror, with that slow build dread King does so well. Other standout stories include "Two Talented Bastids," which peels back the layers of a long-hidden secret, and "The Dreamers," where exploring unknown corners of the universe might be a worse fate than staying home. And don’t sleep on "The Answer Man", or do, but don’t expect sweet dreams. It asks big questions about luck, fate, and whether knowing your future is a gift or a curse. King’s afterword says it best: “You like it darker? Fine, so do I.” And honestly, so do I, especially when it’s this good. This collection hits all the right notes: eerie, thought-provoking, and absolutely unputdownable. For fans of King’s short fiction, You Like It Darker is a must read. After all, when it comes to short stories, King is still the king. 👑👑👑👑👑- 5 out of 5 crowns, long live the King of Horror.

Initial Thoughts This is going to make me unpopular, but I hate those geeky labels that Stephen King fans come out with. Like 'constant reader.' But the funny thing is, I am without doubt one of those constant readers. In a two year span I read pretty much all his books. And what a glorious two years it was! A lot of King's books are absolute bangers, while some are just really good. But the guy writes at such a high level and in such an effortless way that even the ones that don't quite hit the mark are still a worthwhile read. But here's the thing you guys. Recently King has been branching off into areas I haven't been in a rush to read about. In fact I haven't even read his last two outings. Fairy Tale just didn't sound like my type of story and Holly, as well as being one of my least favourite characters of his, was way too focused on that virus that caused such a meltdown in 2020. Don't get me wrong, if I'd have heard reports that these two were must reads then I wouldn't have been able to resist. But that's just not the case. Maybe I'm just not the constant reader I thought I was. So it was with great relief that I discovered he was making a return to his dark and nasty routes with some spine chilling suspense and a little dash of horror. That's the horror that made him such a star in the eighties. And I, for one, am peeing my pants at the prospect of getting my gruby mits all over it. Believe you me, if it was a choice between this and Margot Robbie I'm choosing the book all day long. Plus, I'm a huge fan of these short story collections. Twelve stories makes up the book, with one of the longest being about ninety pages. So bring it on. Anyway, enough of the chit chat. It's time for you, me and the King to get acquainted. Let's go! The Stories Two Talented Bastids 4.25 ⭐'s - You Like it Darker gets off to a bang with a pretty fantastic tale of the son of a famous writer who has recently passed away. While digging through his office he discovers a document detailing the secret behind his father's success and how he went from a landfill owner to a world famous author. It centres around a hunting trip in the local woods and has strong vibes to another King novel, which I won't mention. But dare I say this one does it slightly better. The Fifth Step 4 ⭐'s - If the first entry wasn't exactly dark, this one certainly is as Stevie boy cranks it up a level. We have a random meeting on a park bench between an older gent, Harold Jamieson, and a recovering alcoholic. The younger man is working his way through the AA program, and you guessed it...he's on the fifth step. This one he can't do on his own and he needs help. And when Harold eventually agrees to help things are looking peachy. But with this being a Stephen King story, we'll...I'm saying no more about it. Willie the Wierdo 3.75 ⭐'s - This one felt very similar to a story from Skeleton Crew, not saying which one that is either. I'm evil like that. Not one to give the game away. Certainly not intentionally anyway. A ten year old boy, who's a bit of a weirdo...and funnily enough called Willie, is obsessed with his grandfather's war stories. Bloody, violent and a touch disturbing, who can really blame the young lad. We've all been there. The rest of the family thinks he's a bit of a misfit. Makes them feel a touch uncomfortable. But not grandpa. He sees something special in Willie. And you're going to find out exactly what that is. A bit like Danny De Vito, this one's a touch on the short side. But what's there is pretty decent with an air of suspense. Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream 5+ ⭐'s - The absolute star of the show. This one is worth the price of admission alone. It just has everything I look for in a King story. Suspense, great characters, a little bit of the supernatural and a touch of emotion all wrapped up in a gripping tale. Yeah, I liked it quite a bit. So what's this one about? Guess what? It starts with Danny Coughlin having a bad dream. One that shows him a location that's going to send him on a wild journey. He's your average working man, but his life is going to get anything but average. I honestly want to tell you what happens in this one, because it's so f'in good. But I won't, so pop along a read it right now! Finn 3.75 ⭐'s - I remember this one originally appeared on something called Scribd. But having absolutely no idea what that is I never got round to reading it. So believe you me, I was chuffed to see it appear in this collection. It's about a ridiculously unlucky teenager called Finn, who is on his way home when he predictably lands himself bang in trouble. Talk about wrong place, wrong time! There's a lot of people who say King doesn't know how to finish a story, and to be honest, sometimes that's true. I guess it comes with his style of not beginning with the end in mind and just seeing where the story takes him. Like here for instance. It did loose it's way a bit toward the end and fizzled out. However I loved the idea for this character and would love to see him in a feature novel. Rather than another Holly Gibney yarn. Another one of those planned apparently...bugger! On Slide Inn Road 4.25 ⭐'s - This one was really good and for me delivered on the darker part of the books title. Grandpa's family is driving to Derry, Maine, to visit his sister, when they take a detour down "Slide Inn Road." With this being a horror story they should have known better. We all know how these detours end up...badly. Grandpa is foul mouthed, not politically correct and a giant pain in the ass as far as his son is concerned. But boy are they happy to have him along for the ride. A good reminder not to discount the elderly simply because they seem out of touch. Red Screen 4 ⭐' s- This one is brief and a little bit on the vague side...but that doesn't put me off and I ended up really liking it. It follows a detective who's been having marriage trouble. And he's talking to a prisoner who confessed to killing his wife. But the reason is shocking! Could it be true? Guess you're going to find out. It's short but pretty intense. A bit like a night with yours truly. At least that's what I like to tell myself. The Turbulence Expert 3 ⭐'s - Probably my least favourite of the bunch. I'm not going to lie, it's a great idea. But it just fell a little bit flat. It starts with a guy getting a mysterious phone call about a job he wants no part of but is railroaded into taking. He ends up taking a flight, and guess what? There's going to be some turbulence. This one definitely could have done with being expanded on. I finished with the feeling of "is that it?" A crying shame because the potential was definitely there. Laurie 3.75 ⭐'s - More sentimental than dark, which isn't usually my cup of tea. But it was a well written and fairly enjoyable yarn. It chronicles an aging widower, who receives a new canine companion when his sister thinks it's the perfect antidote for his loneliness. At first he's far from impressed but a reluctant bond begins to form that blossoms into a heart warming friendship. For those of you that have hearts anyway. It's a nice story, but I'm not here for the nice stories. Plus I'm not a huge fan of dogs like everyone else seems to be. Including Stephen King. Which is why this story is included. Thats not saying I didn't enjoy it. But it certainly didn't blow my socks off. Or even my shoes for that matter. Rattlesnake 4 ⭐'s - This one's a sequel to another classic King story. Should I tell you what it is? I'll give you a clue and say it was one of those set in his fictional town of Castle Rock. This one isn't though and takes place in Florida. We follow Vic, who is looking to move on from past trouble while looking after an old friend's condo. It's set in 2020 and of course everything is in lockdown. The place is like a ghost town. But despite this Vic meets Allie Bell, a haunted woman who lives nearby. She has a bizarre habit involving the empty pram she pushes about. One that's going to get hold of Vic's life. It's tinged with sadness, with grief playing a big role. I'd have almost certainly scored it a little higher if it weren't for King's obsession with Covid running away with itself and distracting me from the main story at times. The Dreamers 5 ⭐'s - This was a goody. One of the darkest and most disturbing in the collection, with some fantastic imagery. A Vietnam veteran answers a job advertisement from the local rag involving conducting experiments with an affluent scientist. And what exactly are these experiments? Are you sure you really want to know? The vet soon learns that there are some corners of the universe best left unexplored as things are about to get a touch terrifying. This one could have been plucked straight out of the brain of HP Lovecraft. I loved it. The Answer Man 5 ⭐'s - So this collection finishes strongly with two bangers. Going out on a high is always a good idea. But where The Dreamers had you by the throat this one pulls at the heart strings just a little bit and really gets you thinking. A lawyer finds himself at a number of crossroads in his life, and just at those very moments a strange guy shows up to answer any questions he may have. And he has some big ones. But are you better not knowing some things? It's filled with tragedy, while still having a sense of hope. Can a life still have meaning when awful events come about? It's a fantastic story and a perfect way to end the collection. The Writing It's Stephen King. Of course the writing is bloody excellent. It's just so bloody effortless, while perfectly painting the picture my little brain needed to visualise these excellent stories. Honestly, this guy doesn't get enough credit amongst those snooty expert critics for how good he really is. But I digress. I could literally go on all day about it, but I've already talked enough. And my fingers are sore from all this typing. Final Thoughts Honestly, my reading performance has been absolutely diabolical in 2024. You know how it is when you have a lot of stuff going on with work and the family? Nothing negative, just not having a lot of free time to site down and read a good book. But I found myself making time for You Like it Darker. It was so bloody good. Best book I've read this year? Absolutely no doubt in my mind. It reminded me why I'm such a big fan of the King. It really is a sumptuous collection of short stories from one of the masters of horror and short fiction. Did you really expect anything else? Yes it does get dark at times, but not in a full on, balls to the wall way. It's certainly nowhere near the grimmest he's written. I'd go Pet Semetary for that. But it fully delivered on the suspense and fantastically written characters I was looking for. For me it contains some of King's best short stories. All of them are good but some are fantastic. Absolute belters. You'd be a fool to pass this one up. So you know what to do. In fact, why aren't you in that book shop right now? Thanks for read and....cheers!
i don't think a single one of these short stories had a decent ending. i don't understand how one can be considered the king of a genre if they can't write endings.

⭐️ ⭐️ ⭐️ ⭐️ Like a warm blanket on chilled flesh, King once again provides solace to an aching soul. This is just what I needed at this moment, and this stands out as one of his stronger short story/novella collections — maybe his best since Everything’s Eventual. Although not entirely congruous with its title, most of these stories were not in fact of a dark nature, but rather they were of a literary, introspective inclination. Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream is the standout among the bunch, but there are some incredibly memorable stories that can stand their ground among King’s best. Here is the definitive ranking, and I will accept no other order: 1. Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream 2. The Dreamers 3. The Answer Man 4. Willie the Weirdo 5. Rattlesnakes 6. Two Talented Bastids 7. The Fifth Step 8. Finn 9. Red Screen 10. Laurie 11. On Slide Inn Road 12. The Turbulence Expert And now we count down the days to Never Flinch…

A decent collection of King’s short fiction. A few standouts (Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream, The Dreamers, The Fifth Step, On Slide Inn Road), others not so much. Two Talented Bastids- considering the title, I expected the first story in this collection to be much darker (or at least somewhat dark). Nope, no darkness here. What do have is a very interesting tale of a young man discovering his father’s long held secret. Thoughtful and intriguing, it will grip you and have you reading straight to the end. Unfortunately, it is dated with references to Trump and Covid, but that is expected with King’s unending obsession with both. The Fifth Step - here we go! This one is short, quick, and dark! This’ll teach ya to talk to strangers. Willie the Weirdo - all families have their secrets. Some are darker than others, this family’s is one of the darkest. This one’ll have you guessing where it’s leading as you learn more and more of the family dynamics. Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream- one of the best so far. Full of tension, mystery and dread. This one sucks you in from the beginning wondering where it’s going to lead and you know it’s going to take you someplace dark. A few Covid mentions throughout seem pointless except to feed King’s obsession. Overall it’s a thoroughly enjoyable read. Finn- a story of a kid with bad luck. Not really sure what the point of this one is but at least it’s short. One Covid reference for those keeping track. :) On Slide Inn Road - a shortcut takes a dark turn for a family road trip. Red Screen - a detective’s interview with a man who killed his wife ends up having dark consequences for his own marriage. One random Covid comment seemingly thrown into the story for no reason. The Turbulence Expert - I’ll be checking out the middle seat off the starboard wing side of the plane next time I’m flying… Laurie - a grieving man receives a dog and has a very dark encounter. Interesting short story but doesn’t really seem to have a point. Rattlesnakes- the sequel to Cujo. Probably the reason so many were interested in this collection. It does have some truly creepy moments. However, the references to Cujo seem to be added after the fact as well as the various mentions of Covid. Neither were needed for the story. Honestly it would have been better without either. The Dreamers - this seemed very reminiscent of those 80’s horror films starring Jeffrey Combs based on Lovecraft tales. Specifically, The Beyond. I wouldn’t doubt that this will soon be optioned for a movie, if not already. The Answer Man - an interesting story. What if you could get answers to any question you asked. What would you ask and why? All in all a very melancholy ending to the collection.

I've been a Stephen King fan for a long, long time & although I haven't enjoyed much of his recent work I found You Like It Darker to be one of the best things he's written in years. These twelve short stories (some of them are quite long!) open with the superb Two Talented Bastids, which is a wonderful mix of small town life & science fiction. I won't go over each story here, as I'm sure my fellow readers will have already done this & far better than I could ever manage. All I will say is that there is one weak story in this collection, while the rest of them are nothing short of excellent. This really is old school writing from Stephen King, with excellent characterisation & tales that you can completely absorb yourself in. For me reading these King stories was an absolute joy....just like the old days!

12/5/2024 addendum: Winner of the 2024 Goodreads Choice Award for Best Horror I have found, as I get older, that what I found scary in my childhood is not what I find scary in my 50s. I realize that this is simply a part of maturity and aging. This is not to say that childhood fears ever go away. They simply change. Stephen King’s latest book of short stories, “You Like It Darker”, illustrates this point wonderfully. King’s early books of stories (“Night Shift”, “Skeleton Crew”, “Nightmares and Dreamscapes”) were exciting exercises in horror: things that lurk under beds, shapes in the shadows, haunted objects, creatures that have no right to exist in real life. Most of the stories were the literary equivalent of cinematic jump scares. It’s the cat leaping out of a closet. It’s the figure rising from behind the couch as the babysitter blithely watches TV. It’s the (insert here: rabid dog/possessed car/killer washing machine) that the hero must confront in the end. And, as anybody who loves horror movies knows, jump scares are great. But they aren’t very fulfilling. They get the blood flowing, sure, but they don’t linger in the subconscious the way true horror does. True horror is often subtle. It’s often more nuanced. It sneaks up on you, like old age. The stories in “You Like it Darker” are like that. Take, for example, “Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream”, the book’s longest (let’s be honest: this is definitely more of a novella than a short, but whatevs) and perhaps best story. In this story, Danny, an ordinary man, has an extraordinary psychic flash—-his first and only. He has a vision of a dead body and where it is buried. He decides to do the right thing and takes the info to the police. It turns out to be completely accurate. Unfortunately, the police now consider him the prime suspect. One of the detectives becomes obsessive in his quest to find evidence to convict Danny, beyond all reason. Now, Danny’s good samaritan deed is biting him in the ass as the psychotic detective slowly but surely destroys his life. I’ll be honest: if I had read this story thirty years ago, I probably wouldn’t have liked it. There is nothing really supernatural or scary about the story, other than the psychic flash, and that happens in the very beginning. It’s basically a noir thriller about an innocent guy being pursued by a psycho, who happens to be a cop. But I wasn’t really smart thirty years ago. Or, rather, my 20-something-year-old mind hadn’t fully developed. I was interested in self-gratification and the NOW. You don’t fully develop a sense of empathy and a worry for the future until you’re about my age. Hell, some people never develop it. Danny’s story is terrifying—-moreso at age 50 than 20-something—-because it works on the adult fears of aging: what have I done with my life? What kind of legacy am I leaving my kids? How do I know that what I’m doing is the right thing? You know: stuff a 20-something-year-old doesn’t give two shits about. And King tackles these themes in several stories throughout the collection. Standouts: “Laurie”: in which a widower who has given up on life finds hope in a new puppy. “On Slide Inn Road”: in which a disastrous family road trip is saved by the quick thinking of the only member of the family that nobody would have ever expected to be heroic—-grandpa. “Rattlesnakes”: a sequel to “Cujo”, in which the father who lost his son so many years ago to a rabid dog, is forced to deal with the ghosts of two other dead children who have latched on to his loneliness. Don’t get me wrong: I loved the other stories in this collection, too. And King still does a great job with those jump scares. But it’s clear that King’s fears have turned away from the childish fears of youth to the more nuanced and dread-filled horrors of those of us who worry less and less about the minor scares in life and more about the kind of world we’re leaving for our children.

BookTube channel with my awesome brother, Ed - The Brothers Gwynne My personal BookTube channel - William Gwynne The more King the better, so I dived into his latest release, You Like It Darker! It delivers on its title.... This is a fantastic short story collection. Stephen King still has it, and he demonstrates that seemingly with ease. His skill at crafting character and tension is just wonderful, from terrifying people who could be real in Willie the Weirdo, to exploring the supernatural with Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream, there is such an array of intriguing and engaging stories. There was only one that did not click with me, whilst all the rest were so enjoyable in different ways. Short story collections are perfect for dipping into when you have time, or when you want a little break from longer stories, and in You Like it Darker, King gives quality aplenty that you can dive into. 4.5/5 STARS

Perhaps one of the most difficult things a writer faces when writing is not knowing whether the final product will get to their audience and achieve the desired outcome on it. Being a great fan of SK's books, I feel this new short stories book really fulfilled what was expected from it. It made me imagine, smile, fear, empathize, feel sad...and more. It should be true that the first one to convince is oneself, the job of a writer is tough, even more so when what's been written is a work of fiction. But even if it's a work of fiction, it should all feel plausible by containing elements of true. A good writer must do their homework by doing research on what they are writing about so that when the book gets to their readers they can get to believe what their author has written for them. This is the first book on short stories I've read this year, and I really loved it. Throughout 12 stories SK covers a diverse series of topics. The ones I loved most were - Two Talented Bastids - Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream - Laurie - Rattlesnakes (Super fave) - The Dreamers...and finally... - The Answer Man Rattlesnakes has been by far my most favorite story as it incorporates Vic Trenton 40 or so years later. In the past it was Donna (his wife) and Tad (his son) who lived such an ordeal when attacked by a rabid St. Bernard (Cujo). It is now his turn to face some horror of his own. Will he defeat whatever is coming his way? But what about the other stories? Well, if you're really even a little interested, I'll let you be the judge to it by allowing you to read it and decide by yourself. In my opinion SK did a superb job and left me with the feeling of having read one of the best books this year (already on my favorites list).

Audiobook (20+ hours) narrated by Will Patton and the author, Stephen King Will Patton knocks this one out of the park! I wasn't expecting King to narrate more than the afterword. Just starting The Turbulence Expert and he narrates this one. Surprisingly there's a bit of a fuzzy type or grainy texture background noise. Not sure that explains it correctly, but it isn't as pin drop clear as Will's narrated stories. King also narrates Laurie, although the audio for this narration is pin drop clear. Both stories that King narrates had been previously published and released on audio, narrated by King. I suspect that these narrations were dropped in, rather than re-recorded. All other stories in this compilation are narrated by Will. The narration is fantastic! I highly recommend going with the audiobook for this read or pick up both if you like to follow along in print. Narration and audio are high quality, unless otherwise noted there are no distortions, erroneous noise or obvious edits. A good listening speed seems to be between 1x and 2.25x speed. Two Talented Bastids (2.5 hours) - 5 stars It seems fitting that the opening story takes place in the state of Maine. Will Patton, the narrator, may be from South Carolina, but he does a great job with the Maine accent. I'm from Boston and I believe him! The Fifth Step (21 minutes) - 5 stars Willie the Weirdo (26 minutes) - 5 stars A story about a grandson and his grandpa Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream (6+ hours) - 5 stars This story is stressful! At one point I was feeling deeply sad and anxious for Danny, at the verge of tears. Not finished with it yet. Fingers crossed. I mean it's King and all, but f... Yeah, I cannot tell you all how this one turns out, but it's pretty great. Finn (55 minutes) - 5 stars King mentions three BBC shows in this one, including Doctor Who. 5 stars for that alone! The stories are ordered perfectly, with larger and shorter stories laced together, some a bit of scare, others creep, mysterious, or a combination of. Some of the stories seemed that they had earned a pause before the next, for thoughts and reflections. Others demanded it, as the tales aftershocks or character shadows lurked and lingered until properly laid to rest with a few moments of contemplation, rumination, or perhaps a bit of celebration. Six or seven of the shorter stories were previously published, two in novels and the others in magazine publications. Overall this is a great piece of work by King and will be added to my favorites list, as I intent to revisit it every so often. I especially look forward to planning a re-read of Cujo, followed by a re-read of Rattlesnakes. Recommend, with a nod towards the audiobook, as stated about Will Patton didn't play around with this one. He came to win and it shows. ==== Addendum to my review (5/23/2024): After ruminating over this collection for several hours, there's a bit more that I want to say that I really wasn't sure how to make note of, without talking about one of the big fears of humanity that we, as a society, tend to not speak out loud as it pertains to those who we care about. Stephen King, one of the few Americans born a King. A name that would later be spoken as his status as an author for his skills and talents. This man, who walks around New England, as a regular guy, donating time to local libraries and the wellness and gift of being able to read and reading to those who cannot yet, or cannot any longer; is in his seventy-sixth year of a human life. One of the things that stood out in this collection, is a shifting focus towards older characters and end of life stories. It makes sense. As we age, if we remain open, we learn so much not just about the world but about ourselves, what makes us tick, perhaps why people do what they do. For those of us who 'people watch' as an interest in similarities and differences of how people act and react, trying to understand why some embrace the realness of our flawed selves that may include past mistakes which were, perhaps embarrassingly stupid, others pretend like that never happened. So much so that some people reject those who have done the same, perhaps punishing children or calling attention in big ways to those who would 'do such a thing.' King has a gentleness of his approach to some of these 'oddities' and realities of real life, even as he lays them in front of us in a way that can grip us from within. I theorize that while some of the things that have kept him awake for decades, like his known fear of flying, the new kid on the block is become darker and more pronounced as the shadow of death creeps nearer and nearer to his doorstep. This is something that I did not want to think about. King has been on this earth, hell living in my little corner of the world, for the entirety of my existence. The thing is that he is thinking about it. He is writing about it. In You Like It Darker, King doesn't shy away from contemplating about life itself. As you read through this collection of stories, you will read different ways that people physically and mentally struggle with the last laps. I was thinking about the darkness of his thoughts in his writing the entire time I was reading this. There's a lot of past themes that show up, some of them his personal fears raw with the lingering stench of reality, that can only come from those who understand it from the inside out, the outside in, red and sore from being tossed, turned and torn apart over and over again. There's just so much in this book to peel back. A lifetime, literally. While I think if I was a nicer, gentler individual, that last sentence would ideally be my last thought on the subject. I cannot stop myself from thinking: As much as this man who has shaped parts of my world and my perception of it through reading his words. As much as I believe that people should be able to have time for themselves and not work until they have taken their last breath. My greedy self isn't done with King. I do like it darker and I want more. Side note, if Mr. King ever were to read my review (not that he would but you know in my imaginative mind), Thank you.

As is the case with most short story collections, this to me was a mixed bag, with mostly good to excellent stories. The best two in the collection are the longest. Rattlesnakes is out-and-out creepy, and very visual - I could see a TV/movie adaptation of it being made. Ostensibly a sequel to Cujo, it has very thin ties to that book and is strong on its own. The masterpiece is Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream. A man trying to do a good deed is accused of rape and murder, and you wonder how - or if - he will get out of the bind he's in. The characters are sharply written and the suspense builds brilliantly to a tense finish. My favorite of the collection - also the longest, a novella at 152 pages. “The world is full of rattlesnakes. Sometimes you step on them and they don’t bite. Sometimes you step over them, and they bite anyway.” I can’t stress enough how much I adore Stephen King’s storytelling. The stories in this collection will make you want to settle into them at the end of each day. And I do mean "settle in" because many of the so-called “short” stories in this book actually could’ve been novellas. But that’s because King takes his time developing worlds that feel familiar and characters that feel real, be they the protagonist, the monster, or the one-scene side character. Throughout my experience reading this book, the stories simultaneously felt like a warm sunset and an ominous storm on the horizon. Yes, these stories are dark as the title of the book suggests, but they also carry themes of grief, obsession, human relationships, unanswered questions, mystery, and grappling with the unknown. In Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream, a man whose nightmare featuring a murdered woman turns out to be a psychic premonition, one that gets him in a world of trouble. (I was over-the-moon thrilled to discover this story was set in my home state of Kansas!) The Fifth Step opens with a man approached by an addict who claims he must share a story with a stranger as part of an AA recovery assignment (loved this one)! Two Talented Bastids begs the question of whether talent is something humankind naturally possesses or if the lucky ones are simply chosen by a supernatural fate. In Red Screen, a conspiracy theory leaves the protagonist and the reader uneasy about what to believe (this one was a personal favorite of mine). And we even get a sequel to Cujo in the story Rattlesnakes! Whether you end up loving every single story in this collection or simply find some of them to be lacking, what I know for certain is that there will be something in YOU LIKE IT DARKER that will stick with you and leave a lasting and haunting impression as King’s writing always does.

Mr King has hit the ball out of the park with this collection of stories! As with most collections, there are a couple which didn't quite sate my appetite but those that did were incredible feasts for my imagination. Below I have written my rating and thoughts for each story. I've kept each as short as possible and attempted to be as vague as possible about the details of each story. Two Talented Bastids ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ A tale told in typical Stephen King style. By using the word 'typical' I mean that it's amazing. It's hard to mention many details of this story without giving spoilers, so I'll steer well clear of that. Ufo, vivid, desires, ordinary, extraordinary, Profound!! The Fifth Step ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ In this extremely short story, we follow Jamieson, a retiree during his daily walk into Central Park, where he often sits and reads a copy of the Times. Here he notices a guy who decides to sit on his bench and soon asks if Jamieson could do him a favour. Yes, again King manages to cram so much into such a short yet distinct and punchy story. I loved this so much, especially the sharp and witty conversation. Willie the Weirdo ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ Yet another extremely short story which punches well over its weight. Willie is a ten-year-old, and most of his family thinks he's weird, I think he is weird, but will his curiosity and strangeness get him anywhere? An extremely snappy tale, with an interesting dynamic and plenty of obscure and dark humour. Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ My favourite story so far and one I will remember for some time, possibly one of my all-time time favourites. I love it!! This is storytelling perfection which would fit perfectly into the Hard Case Crime series of books. Danny is a regular guy, but one night he has a vivid nightmare. One that doesn't fade, one that he must go investigate. Finn ⭐️⭐️⭐️ I read this short story roughly three years ago. Back then I didn't think much of it and my opinion hasn't changed at all. In the most simple terms, this is a tale of mistaken identity. King's writing is great as usual, with a fair few humourous moments but for the most part, it didn't capture my attention. On Slide Inn Road ⭐️⭐️⭐️ I guess you could call this a road trip gone wrong. This is a tough one to rate, the story itself is okay but I've given it the benefit of the doubt just because of the witty conversation and the interactions between the different generations of the family. Red Screen ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ Wilson, a detective goes to visit a newly arrested suspected murderer. This murderer has a strange explanation of why he did what he did. I really enjoyed this, it's simple and very short but somehow managed to pull me into its web. The Turbulence Expert ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ This story is simple to explain, just read the title. I found this to be yet another enjoyable and witty story, the conversation feels natural, as do the character's actions and personas. Rattlesnakes ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ This one was a bit of a slow burn. We follow Vic who has travelled to the Florida coast to get a little R&R, a place to regroup and contemplate things. He meets a lady, she's strange in one particular way, but to find out about that you'll have to read this yourself. I loved how this linked to two of King's novels and in some ways gave potential for at least one to have a future. Quality storytelling, a tale of loss, pain and guilt, with a good pinch of existential dread thrown in for good measure. The Dreamers ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ A mean broody son of a bitch. Think cosmic wonders, eldritch horrors and a mad scientist. This was such a cool little story, take a little from each of the horror greats, mix it up and this beauty is born. The Answer Man ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ This one does exactly what it says on the tin. The story of a life, of our habitual need for confirmation and most of all our loves and losses.

King is back in old form I must admit that I had my reservations about the recent novels of King, with Fairy Tale being a big dissapointment and deciding to skip Holly all together, but given my appreciation for King's shorter works (such as Full Dark, No Stars) I definitely wanted to check this one out. ⭐ My Goodreads Review of You Like It Darker by Stephen King ⭐ I just finished You Like It Darker and… well… I think my neurons are still sizzling. Stephen King has once again proven he’s the undisputed master of messing with your head—in the best possible way. This collection is a mixed bag of horror, suspense, and a few moments where I nearly spit out my coffee laughing (and sometimes shrieking in terror). There’s something about King’s storytelling that feels like sitting around a campfire while a crazy uncle whispers creepy secrets into your ear. You know you should run, but you’re too hooked to leave. My top three favorites: 🐍 Rattlesnakes I’m gonna be honest: I hate snakes. I hate them with the fiery passion of a thousand suns. So naturally, Stephen King decided to write a story that’s not only about snakes, but also connects back to Cujo. Like I wasn’t traumatized enough by rabid St. Bernards as a kid. Now I have to worry about deep wells in Castle Rock and what might be slithering at the bottom. Thanks a lot, Steve. Seriously though, it’s a brilliant, tense story, and I couldn’t stop reading even while screaming internally. 🧢 Willie the Weirdo This one is such a wild ride. It starts off feeling like a sweet, slightly quirky coming-of-age tale, and I’m thinking, “Oh, this is cute, maybe like Stand By Me vibes.” And then… BAM. The last few lines flip the entire story on its head. I literally shouted “WTF?!” in my living room. Classic King—just when you feel safe, he pulls the rug out and dumps you in a pit of weirdness. I loved it. 😱 The Dreamers If there’s one story in this collection that screams classic Stephen King, it’s The Dreamers. It’s dripping with atmosphere, dread, and that unsettling sense that reality might be a fragile illusion. I was absolutely hanging on his every word, like I was with Duma Key (which, by the way, is one of my favorite King books, even though it’s completely bonkers). This story felt like a perfect distillation of King’s talent for making the ordinary terrifying and the cosmic deeply personal. Overall, You Like It Darker is creepy, funny, sometimes downright bizarre, and pure Stephen King. If you’re a Constant Reader, you’ll find plenty to love—and probably a few new phobias you didn’t know you had. And if you have ophidiophobia (aka a mortal fear of snakes)… maybe keep the lights on for Rattlesnakes. Or skip it altogether. I won’t judge. Highly recommended. Now excuse me while I check under my bed. And in any nearby wells.

If the name Stephen King makes you think, “Too scary!” or “Way too long!”—his latest short story collection, You Like It Darker, might just change your mind. The stories range from a quick 10 pages (The Fifth Step) to a novella-sized 150 pages (Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream). Out of the 12 tales, only a couple drift into spooky territory—and nothing that’ll have you sleeping with the lights on. What really stands out is King’s storytelling at its finest: a diverse mix of settings, characters, and situations that highlight just how wide his creative lens can go. And if you’re already a fan of King and his genre-jumping ways, don’t skip this one. You Like It Darker might just be your new favorite. ~Diana F. Find a Copy at Scottsdale Public Library
