Background – “You Like it Darker” was originally published in May 2024 in hardcover by Scribner. Length-wise - my hardcover lists it as 502 pages and my Kindle lists it as 504 pages. It is King’s seventh collection of short stories. The best stories include: “Two Talented Bastids” (previously unpublished) – Laird Carmody and Dave LaVerdiere, two middle-aged men who grew up in a small town, found huge success later in life as a writer and artist. Now, Laird’s adult son is about to find out their long-hidden secret as to how these two men mysteriously turned their struggling passions into skill works of art appreciated by many… "Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream" (previously unpublished) – Danny is a normal guy. He is the custodian at Wilder High school in a small Kansas town and lives in a trailer park. He is still friends with his ex-wife and has a current girlfriend (that although it’s not true love) that provides a steady physical connection. Then Danny has a nightmare, and not just any. This is a very bad and vivid dream that includes a half buried dead body in a deserted location, and Danny’s life is about to change in overwhelmingly dark and unimaginable ways… "Rattlesnakes" (previously unpublished) – Vic Trenton (previously seen in King’s 1981 novel, “Cujo”) is now in his seventies and a grieving widower, trying to recover for a few months at a friend’s mansion in the Florida Keys. However, everything takes an unexpected eerie turn when he’s introduced to the elderly neighbor, Allie Bell, who’s also suffered similar losses, including her twin baby boys many years ago from rattlesnake bites, and her husband from a heart attack shortly afterwards. Although Vic can relate, he has no idea of the trap being set for him… "The Answer Man" (previously unpublished) – Philip Parker has a serious decision to make, involving the woman he loves, their families, and his career path. And when he finds himself unable to figure things out, he meets The Answer Man, who promises to answer any question that Phil can ask, but at a cost of $25 and a five-minute limit… The good stories include: "The Fifth Step" (published 2020) – 68-year-old retired widower, Harold Jamieson, reads the New York Times each morning on a bench in Central Park. One day he is approached by a man attempting to complete step five of his AA program, and Harold’s life will never be the same again… "Finn" (published 2022) – Finn Murrie is the unluckiest 19-year-old alive. His bad luck - which includes having his little toe blown off at age five, breaking his arm at age nine, and suffering a concussion from a lightning strike at age 14 – is about to get desperately worse. Life threatening worse… "On Slide Inn Road" (published 2020) – The Brown family (parents and two children) are driving their Grandpop to visit his dying sister. However, the shortcut old country road they find themselves on leads them to a closed down inn and a life-threatening situation… "The Turbulence Expert" (published 2018) – Craig Dixon has a special job that few can perform. He is a turbulence expert that is afraid of flying, but trust that you want him on your flight if there are problems… The okay stories include: “Willie the Weirdo" (published 2022) – 10-year-old Willie is considered to be rather strange by his family and those who know him. He likes starring at clouds, dead birds, dead bugs, and empty space for hours at a time. However, Willie’s found another weirdo, someone close to him. His grandfather has very unusual personal stories from history, full of war and destruction… "Red Screen" (published 2021) – Did you hear the one about aliens coming to earth and inhabiting humans (mainly women) with the intent of an invasion? Their strategy is to be critical and irritable, wearing down their victims into submission… The lesser stories include: "Laurie" (published 2018) – Retiree Lloyd Sunderland is trying to move on following his wife’s passing away, and his sister thinks she’s helping him out by sticking him with a puppy to take care of. Lloyd has no idea what role his new pet, Laurie, will play when he’s faced with a life-or-death situation… "The Dreamers" (previously unpublished) – A returning Vietnam veteran gets hired to assist a man known as the Gentleman Scientist, who is planning to change the world by exploring the world of dreams. However, it may be that some parts of the psyche are meant to be left alone… Thoughts and Reflections – for me, this seventh collection of King’s short stories and novellas was probably one of the best ones when taken as a whole, and my personal favorite since King’s first set “Night Shift”. Most of the stories were pretty dang good or even better. Although some of the stories were more developed than others (“Willie the Weirdo” could have had more meat to it and “Red Screen” could have had more layers to enhance its ending reveal), there was only two stories that I would consider to be of lesser quality than the rest. Most of them were diverse, engaging, and explored different aspects of human life, including family, friendship, personal desires, and of course, the darker sides of human emotions. I will share one side note – I did not find “The Dreamers” to be as scary as King expressed in his public comments, which was a real surprise to me. That’s for sure. For me, the stories (regardless of which rating group I put them in) were fluid and easily immersive, gaining my interest quickly and keeping it throughout. They had elements of drama, horror, and some form of the supernatural, along with lots of scary suspense. but for the most part, they were just really good stories that tugged tightly on your emotional strings by a master storyteller still in his creative prime. My favorite story was "Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream" followed by " Two Talented Bastids", “Rattlesnakes”, and “The Answer Man”. Danny’s story was so tragically good that it made me stay up way too late reading on a work night. I found myself empathizing with his intent to do good and the hardships he suffered because of it. Bad events just kept mounting up against him and I was so immersed in wanting a hopeful outcome that I had to get through it at the sacrifice of other responsibilities. Each page held my rapt attention as the dramatic stakes built to a worthy climactic ending. Being sixty myself, I was also drawn to Laird Dave’s secret story of how their artistic talents developed during their later years in life. Although it was easy to follow the story’s direction, it was an interesting read that embraced King’s ability to capture the magical idiosyncrasies of small-town America and ordinary people being faced with the unimaginable. Vic Trenton’s return was superb and well delivered. No spoilers here, but I certainly understand why King chose Vic to lead this story and it made total creative sense. King found a way to link the past to the present in a personal way that made Vic’s presence and participation key to telling this particular story that felt like a perfect companion piece to King’s previous Florida based novel “Duma Key”. Philip Parker’s interactions with the Answer Man was also an interesting read that drew on my own life experiences and made me reflect on choices and decisions that influenced who I become. My professional career. My family. My achievements and my failures. And even my potential legacy. You can tell it this is a story that drives personal reflection and assessment, and raising questions like have I achieved what I want in life? Have I demonstrated a full committed to my family? And am I becoming the person that I want to truly be? This is the right story to end the book with. In addition, one of the interesting things that I noted was how easy it was as each story began to guess where you thought things were going. The interesting thing was that King was always ahead of you with surprises and different outcomes than expected. Several times he added new twists and angles that made the stories even more entertaining and enjoyable. Other Notes – The book includes a mix of new and previously published stories, including five new stories and the rest previously published in magazines, e-books, or on Stephen King’s website. Overall – Out of the seven short story collections written by King, this one was personal favorite, right along with “Night Shift”. Most of the stories (or novellas) were a gem worth reading (even the lesser stories) and exemplified a writer, who after fifty years of published works, is still in his creative prime and storytelling genius. In the author’s notes, King says “You like it darker? Fine. So do I, and that makes me your soul brother.” Amen, brother. Amen and keep them coming…

Twelve creepy, weird and brilliant short stories. Plenty here to get your teeth into and keep you up at night.

I read this collection of interrelated stories in one sitting; I didn't want to stop, and I was entirely unaware of the passing time--this is that sort of story collection--all great stories. I certainly have my favorites though. "Two Talented Bastids" and "Rattlesnakes" are just incredible. The first is a gorgeous story about a son's reflection on his father's writing talent with a slightly paranormal, alien twist. And "Rattlesnakes" is legitimately frightening as that title takes on new meaning and readers realize the rattle is literal, metaphoric, and in this case, also etheric. What you will notice early on is that each story has a very different emotional vibe. They range as widely as these two stories I mentioned. "Laurie" even includes a positive, healthy outlook on dog ownership, as a newly widowed man finds renewed meaning in life when he reluctantly adopts Laurie. All of the stories, however, center in some way around themes of aging, lost loved ones, and the many ways people cope with these human conditions. Absolutely worth reading and owning (I always debate this now as bookshelf space is so limited in our house), this is a solid collection.

The longer stories, "Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream," "Rattlesnakes," "The Dreamers," and "The Answer Man" all show that King still has it, he can manipulate your emotions and be creepy and disturbing when he wants to, even though DCBD, the longest in the collection, is one of his hard-crime/detective novels, not horror. Some of the shorter stories were fun, some were just so-so. That's to be expected. I guess I was really hoping to be bowled over, with this collection being a return to form for horror story-telling, since his last few big releases, "Holly," "Fairy Tale," "Billy Summers," etc., were good but really short on the horror, if at all. King is hte master of American horror for a reason, and we got some tastes of that here, especially with "Rattlesnakes," but I suppose I was hoping for more. Still, reading King always feels comfortable and inviting. And I especially like that some of these stories could have undergone the treatment of being padded out, made unnecessarily complicated, and spun into full length novels, but instead King was smart to keep them short, getting in and out and never overstaying their welcome. There are a lot of reflections on loss and grief in this collection, how to wrestle with a mortal life in the face of unknowable odds, and I appreciate the ruminating King provides. Not his best, and not my favorite, but another good collection and I am glad to keep reading them. (Rounded up from 3.5)

Several years ago, I began a chronological re-read of Stephen King's books and vowed not to read any of his new releases until I'd finished that project. But You Like It Darker made me break that vow, because how was I supposed to resist a sequel story to Cujo? That story, "Rattlesnakes," was my favorite in this collection, and it's a melancholy, haunting (in more ways than one) tale that I know will stick with me. Many of the stories, including "Rattlesnakes," are a meditation on growing older, looking back on a life full of joys and sorrows when you are reaching the end of it. It feels like an intensely personal perspective, so contemplative and weirdly gentle -- which I realize sounds strange for a book of horror stories but is in reality an often-overlooked trademark of King's writing. The other previously unpublished stories -- "Two Talented Bastids," "Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream," "The Dreamers," and "The Answer Man" -- were definitely the best in the collection. "Two Talented Bastids" is creepy and campy. "Danny Coughlin's Bad Dream" is, if a bit bloated, a fascinating exploration of belief in the face of extraordinary circumstances, and features an intriguing King villain. "The Dreamers" takes place on a level of the Dark Tower, I am 1000% convinced. And "The Answer Man" is a heartbreaking celebration of a life well-lived (and is also likely Tower-adjacent). And then there's "Willie the Weirdo" and "The Fifth Step," which read like a master class in how to write a perfect short horror story. You Like It Darker isn't my favorite of King's short story collections (I don't think anything will be able to unseat Night Shift for that title), but it is a phenomenal set of stories. It's incredible to me that an author as prolific as King can still give readers something new, and can still evolve as a writer, even after so many years. And yet, he always does.

Reading this feels cozy like visiting with old friends, the eccentric and properly mysterious kind. The fifth step: a nice morsel, delectable without feeling heavy. Willie the Weirdo: while I grant the twist is exciting, I dislike the story. However, it’s a hard to produce rendition of pure evil characters that I have to respect. Willie would feel at home with Apt Pupil’s Todd & Dussander. I could have done without this one. Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream I will eat my shirt if Danny Coughlin’s Bad Dream isn’t adapted for the screen! Hot take, but this is on par with The Body & Shawshank. This one feels a little like Children of the Corn mixed with a little 11/22/63 magic. I haven’t read the Bill Hodges Trilogy but I imagine there may be some similarities there too from a police procedural perspective. I mistook it for the Cujo Sequel at first glance, as a dog with an appetite for flesh takes up residence in the opening sequence.

Ah, Uncle Stevie, you spoil us! This collection features 12 stories, a new of which are novellas, others are short stories. I posted status updates after each one in case you want to get a glimse into what I thought about each of them. I'm not gonna give star ratings for each because I think that could influence future readers. Instead, let me say this: The first, fourth and tenth stories were novellas and definitely the gems of this collection. The others, short stories and novellas alike, were good, very good and extremely good. Not a single one was a stinker. Plus, even Uncle Stevie's worst is usually better than (almost) anything else out there. I loved that some stories gave definite nods to older works and had the vibe of some of SK's classics. Characterization has always been King's strong suit - as is showing the horror of the mundane, the "normal" and "everyday". These stories once again proved that. Creepy and highly atmospheric, sometimes with a strong dose of dark humour, sometimes full of tragedy or just warming your heart (yep, we got even that). Definitely, this indeed mostly was dark, as the title had promised. Wonderful collection / addition to my King shelf.

**Winner of the 2022 Goodreads Choice Award for Poetry** ‘To Begin again / Isn’t to go backwards, / But to decide to go.’ The poetry world was given quite a boost on Jan 20th, 2021 when poet Amanda Gorman took the stage at the Presidential Inauguration. ‘There is always light,’ she read ‘if only we’re brave enough to see it. / If only we’re brave enough to be it.’ While I was thrilled to see poets included in an inauguration again after being denied by the previous administration, it was also wonderful to see how many people were touched by her words and suddenly excited by poetry. I thought ‘welcome abroad, this is the good place.’ Call Us What We Carry is the first collection of poetry by 23 year old poet Amanda Gorman, which includes her inaugural speech and so much more as she addresses the social ills of racism, gun violence, greed, selfishness, and chronicles the grief of the pandemic years, asking for unity and cooperation instead of sticking our heads in the sand to decide something is ‘not your problem.’ Gorman is quite impressive, accomplishing so much already and this collection full of experimentation with form and bold accounting of the tumultuous present is the spark to a bright future of words and wisdom. ‘Hope is the soft bird We send across the sea To see if this earth is still home. We ask you honestly: Is it?’ Gorman’s poetry is a call to action amidst difficult times both nationally and globally. ‘This year the size of a sea / sick to its stomach’ she writes to describe the pandemic years still unfolding in the US where political tensions are at a tipping point egged on by bad faith rhetoric in the type of insidious lowest-common-denominator messaging that capitalism thrives on. Which is the perfect time for poetry to step in and make sense of it all, even if I may not exactly be ready for pandemic poetry. And Gorman uses the harsh truths as a reminder to come together in love and understanding, that moving forward through selfishness or ‘I got mine’ mentality will lead only to chaos. ‘As the world came / We have come together,’ she writes, ‘Only we can save us.’ It is all very hopeful and empowering, yet Gorman avoids coming across as saccharine by reminding us ‘there is no meek way to mend’ or that ‘at times even blessings will bleed us.’ Growth is hard, progress can be painful, but the alternative is worse. ‘The world still terrifies us. We’re told to write what we know. We write what we’re afraid of Only then is our fear Made small by what we love.’ Gorman has some delightful experimentation with style and form, such as poems constructed out of a questionnaire for migrants, poems in the shape of surgical masks, or the poem Monomyth written like the screenplay for a documentary of the past 2 years with each scene followed by the dates and events of the pandemic corresponding to her imagery. The poem reminds us ‘We are not all heroes, but we are all at least human,’ and in that reminds us that we have gone on a quest of events these past few years and have inevitably been transformed. At times the poetry feels a bit overly ‘Go USA’, which isn’t exactly a topic I enjoy in poetry, but I see the reasoning and it comes across as patriotic rather than nationalist and Gorman addresses many systemic issues that are plaguing the country. ‘What can we call a country that destroys / itself just because it can?’ she asks, and much of the book examines the way racism and violence has wormed its way into the heart of the country as she pleads with us to examine it and undo it. Something I particularly enjoy about her analysis is her attention to the way language and rhetoric become the barbs through which social ills latch on in order to infect. Poems like Vale of the Shadow of Death, which is structured in columns like a newspaper, discuss historical events like the “Spanish Influenza”, pointing out it did not actually originate in Spain (she mentions the Spanish called it the French flu). ‘To tell the truth, then, is to risk / being remembered by its fiction,’ she writes as the poem discusses how fearmongering and language are used to oppress and Other people. Jim Crow, the Chinese Exclusion Act and more are addressed in a poem that calls for speaking out, speaking true, and to respect the power of language. ‘Words matter, for Language is an ark. Yes, Language is an art, An articulate artifact. Language is a life craft. Yes, Language is a life raft.' -from What We Carry Language can harm, but it can also heal, and Gorman captures this duality well in her first collection of poetry. What We Carry is an interesting literary artifact of the present that chronicles the discourse and troubles of the United States over the recent years into a plea for better action, better times and better understanding. While it will inevitably be politicized on party lines because that's what trolls do in place of a personality, it doesn’t have to be and certainly doesn’t read that way. For newcomers to poetry who like what they see here I’d like to recommend some favorites such as Audre Lorde, Jericho Brown or the absolute greatest, Lucille Clifton, who you will certainly find more to examine and enjoy. Amanda Gorman is a bright young woman with a shining career ahead of her and I am happy to see it and watch how she has brought poetry into the hearts of many. 3.75/5 ‘That is to say, Love is justified by loving. Like you, we are haunted & human. You, like us, are haunted & healing.’

‘words matter, for language is an ark. yes, language is an art… language is a life craft. yes, language is a life raft.’ i, like most people, first heard and were inspired by AG when she delivered her inauguration poem, ‘the hill we climb,’ back in january. i was captivated by her words and was so excited to hear she would be releasing a collection. and let me tell you what. this collection is massive - there are 70 poems in this! and while reading, i discovered the same thing i always do when i pick up a poetry book - there are some entries that i adore and relate to more than others. some favourites: - compass - pre-memory - monomyth - what we carry - the hill we climb and also, with this collection specifically, i think i would have liked a lot more of the poems better had i listened to this, rather then read it. i think AGs poetry has power in her unique delivery. i feel like, because im missing out on the cadence and intonation of her words, a lot of the poems just didnt have a natural flow to them. so 4 stars for now, because i really did enjoy the content of the majority of her poetry. but i have a feeling once i get my hands on an audiobook, it will probably get a bump up. ↠ 4 stars

Wow! Words can't adequately describe my reaction to Amanda Gorman's poetry in Call Us What We Carry. Gorman is the youngest presidential inaugural poet in US history, and she stunned the world with her poem, The Hill We Climb, during the inauguration of President Joe Biden. The poems in her book capture the time, terror and feelings during the global pandemic (both during the Spanish Flu in 1918 and the COVID pandemic in 2020) and centuries of system racial discrimination including the tragic deaths of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor, and many others. Some of the memorable poetry passages include: * Unprecedented and unpresidented * Frayed and afraid * Our souls, solitary and solemn * Alive but alone * Our scars are the brightest part of us * Isolation is its own climate * Trauma is like a season; deep and dependable * Pre-memory determines who we are as a people * Storytelling is a way that unarticulated memory becomes an art * Grief is the grenade that always goes off * The Spanish influenza did not originate in Spain. The first recorded case was in Kansas. Spain was neutral in World War I. * Ignorance is a vine that sneaks up a tree and blocks out the light * Courage must cost something, or else it is worth nothing at all * Isolation is the first step in war and pandemics * A virus separates us from people * Hate is a virus * Hate only survives when hosted in humans * Never forget that to be alone has always been a price for some and a privilege for others * Who were we beneath our mask? * Language is a life craft. Language is a life raft. Highly, highly recommend!

I remember the first time I saw Amanda Gorman. I was not alone. Anyone who watched the inauguration of President Biden probably also experienced the artful amazing gorgeous intensity of her powerful poem, “The Hill We Climb.” “…when the day comes, we step out of the shade aflame and unafraid, the new dawn blooms as we free it, for there is always light if only we’re brave enough to see it, if only we’re brave enough to be it.” I can still feel the tears flowing listening to her. There was so much to appreciate about that day and her words. So, when I saw this book on the library book shelf on my weekly saunter for reading material, I happily grabbed it. It was a delight to read her. She has depth and soul. And, gratefully this beautiful poem is also included in this book. This book is eclectic in her expression of herself. Her poetry exudes discussion on a variety of topics and even atypical formats. And, she is not your typical poet. And, perhaps that is what makes her readable, and interesting. Would I have picked up her book of poetry had I not heard her on that important day and found myself in tears listening to “The Hill We Climb?” Maybe not. But I am glad I did. As an example, she talks about a fall in one poem. “Say our feet miss a step on a stair – …Sometimes The fall Just makes Us More Ourselves.” How many times have we been in this precarious position with our bodies? Is she not having us consider these moments in our lives? I like to open myself to different genres. Learn and grow and find myself stretching my mind to consider how other people think and feel. And, this author definitely does that. And, that is why if you are on a similar reading journey, you may just find this book worth your reading experience, too.

I was really looking forward to reading this, especially after all the hype from her presenting at the inauguration. What I found was a bunch of repetitive lines that could have been written by any of my students. I was surprised when I Googled her age and found her to be 23 years old. I had assumed she was in high school, which is why I didn't judge the poetry too harshly initially. This book is filled with too many previous accounts of past pandemics, from the Spanish Infulenza to slavery and wars, to be considered original content. She simply restates and lists historical documents and re-words them with a rhyme scheme. Any of my 8th grade students could do that. Maybe it's because I listened to the audiobook and didn't read the words printed on an actual page. I'll give it that, but I waited for four hours of "poetry" for even one line to stand out to me as quote-worthy or notable or deep or touching... and none ever did. With the way she is lauded, I was expecting something more akin to Jamaica Kincaid, Maya Angelou or Langston Hughes. What I got was a sloppy attempt at mashing words together with overused alliteration and unrhythmic lines. (for example: "This book is awake. This book is a wake." I mean... really?) There are plenty of good ideas in this book, and you can tell Gorman is authentic and has a genuine voice to her. However, it is evident that this book was rushed after her newfound fame, as a cash-grab. It feels very thrown together and haphazard. Reflections on a pandemic that is very much NOT over, feels a bit premature and assumptive. The entire first half was simply reciting statistics and facts that we are all too familiar with already. Like I mentioned previously, it's nothing new. In fact, it's weary and dull. It felt very much like a high school student desperately copy/pasting citations from Wikipedia to fulfill a word count limit. I tell my students all the time, I want to hear what YOU think, not what the internet thinks. Every other page was a constant interruption of thought to insert a definition or clarify what she meant. Rule number 1 in creative writing: Don't make the assumption that your reader is stupid. Say what you mean in any eloquent way you wish, and those who get it will "get it" and those who don't can go look it up themselves. Using way too many interruptions broke my interest and left me feeling frustrated that she felt the need to clarify things I already knew. Most of her literary references were fairly common and recognizable, yet she broke her poem's rhythm over and over just to "insert reference here just in case you didn't know what I was talking about." Put a footnote if you really want to educate your audience, but don't assume (as a 23 year old) that your readers won't have a clue what you're referring to. Many of these poems felt like responses to a creative writing college class prompt and not a fresh original idea naturally inspired. Her use of words like "Zoombies" is cringe-worthy in an era we are still living through and comes off as out-of-touch and juvenile. I wish I could like this, and went into it with relatively high hopes. Sad to see her publishers pushing for more content. I'd be interested in reading more natural work from her later in her career.

I admire Amanda Gorman's talent and I sincerely hope many young people start writing because of her. Having said that, I have to be honest to myself here and give 2.5 stars to her latest book. I admit that I like traditional poetry better than freeform poetry. That makes it difficult for me to get into contemporary poems. I used to write poems (in Japanese) and loved reading poems both in English and Japanese. What I learned these years was that you describe "beauty" without using a word "beauty" or "beautiful". You have to carefully chose every word. Get rid of every unnecessary word, etc. Every time I read "One Art" by Elizabeth Bishop I become tearful even though I have read it more than 100 times. To me, poems are like that. It just grabs my heart. Amanda's poems in this book are none of above. She wrote so many words such as "death" "love" "pain" but I didn't feel them. They failed to move me. Careless phrases like "The pain pulls us apart, Like lips about to speak" failed to give me a clear picture of what kind of image Amanda wanted to give us. She often states something like "That's what only words can do-- /Prod us toward something new / & in doing so, move us closer → together.", "Lost as we feel, there is no better/ Compass than compassion.", and these made me feel this book quite didactic. I wouldn't mind them if this book was collection of essays rather than poems. There are also so many Covid pandemic poems. We are still in the midst of it, but these poems feel outdated. I regard this book as an experiment of a young talented poet. She will one day look back and tell herself, "Oh I was so young...". My Japanese review: https://youshofanclub.com/2022/01/17/...

Amanda Gorman is a genius. I have said and written here many times that I'm really not particularly fond of poetry. Maybe that was always because I hadn't seen recently poetry of the type that Ms Gorman creates. It looks at us as we are and as we might be. It is full of life and full of hope. It is beautiful.

"Whoever said we never die in our dreams Obviously has never been Black." Amanda Gorman has captivated me yet again with poems about surviving the pandemic and being Black in America. Reaching back into the history of slavery and looking to the future with despair tempered by an unlikely yet resilient hope. This collection was stunning and profoundly moving, blunt and honest, real and raw, and incredibly insightful. "It's said that ignorance is bliss. **Winner of Goodreads Choice Award for Best Poetry** Ever since I saw Amanda Gorman at the inauguration, I've been passionately moved by her. Amanda Gorman's poetry in Call Us What We Carry exceeded my expectations. The book weaves together poems that reflect on our collective, and yet also unique, experiences as we navigate the year(s) of COVID - from March 2020 and forward - and also revisits history. Through her poetry, Gorman illustrates that we are not in truly “unprecedented times” as she ties the current state of (American) society to historical events such as the Essex disaster at sea in 1820, the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, the "Spanish" influenza in 1918, ongoing community issues such as AIDS, immigration, grief, and natural events like the behavior of animals in captivity and post memory. I wasn't expecting to LEARN and FEEL so much through Gorman's poems. This book is recommended for adult and teen readers even if poetry is not your usual genre. -Diana F.

In my view, Amanda Gorman was pressured by fame to put out a collection when she was not ready. Most of the poems included in this book are about the Covid-19 pandemic and although this is a fruitful topic, Gorman is too fixated on it and its general impact on a nebulous "society" for the poems to withstand attention. She fails to ground the poems in any concrete experience of the pandemic, and is reduced to vague generalisations abut how society was fractured and came together again. There are also just far too many "pandemic poems" and she fails to say anything new, or point a torch at a different element of the pandemic experience. The poetry itself was also not specific enough, and the images conjured were pedestrian and did not resonate. The second problem Gorman creates for herself is that she includes "found poems" as a great number of her work. These found poems are extracts from other (often better) writers work - from ordinary people to Lin-Manuel Miranda. These (plus the quotes from various texts which indicate section breaks in the collection) are of a far higher quality than Gorman's original work. Even when she cuts and obscures parts of sentences of another work, the result is to show the strength of the original, not the quality of the "surgeon-poet" cutting these apart. I dwelt far longer on the found poetry than I did on Gorman's own work, and, where presented with the full text of the original, I much preferred the original. The inauguration poem is the final poem in the book. Unfortunately, she had lost all my good will by the time I reached it. Other writers have articulated the African American experience, and the experience of "America striving" generally better than she has. The inauguration poem does not make the collection worth buying. It may have been better served as a standalone pamphlet, and Gorman could have been given more time to expand her range of subjects in the rest of her catalogue.

This is a beautiful collection! Lovely, lyrical writing. Speaking to the experience of living through the COVID pandemic and linking it back to the experiences of WWII soldiers with the Spanish flu. The poems range from the personal to the societal and feel very timely. Grief, identity, being Black in America, loneliness....but with hopeful undertones throughout. Amanda Gorman reads the audiobook herself and it's definitely worth a listen. I received an audio review copy of this book from the publisher. All opinions are my own.

We needed someone to give voice, texture, and meaning to our past few indescribable years. Amanda Gorman has stepped into this much-needed space. She begins by mapping where we are. Our recent experiences cannot be accurately described as a shapeless void, but rather as a murkiness with ragged borders, one which we've had to navigate at full-speed. Gorman uses accessible everyday speech to convey the remarkable, and to reveal what is hidden. Her poetry isn't just contemporary, but achingly present, an elegy for the living. If there's such a thing as meta poetry, this is an example of it, with a self-awareness and self-referential quality rarely seen in poetry. This poetry isn't simply a conduit for people and their experiences, but as a stand-in for them. We are the poetry, and the poetry is us, when we burst out of our confines to become more than we are. In no way, are we promised that this process will not be painful. Being is static. Becoming requires action. Even generational trauma, coded into the bones of descendants, persists, not because we've failed to leave it behind, but because we've failed a fully collective remembrance. There are many mind-expanding messages in this reverberant collection, yet the one which has echoed loudest for me has been this call to claim the fullness of historical memory. There is no way forward through repressive sublimation. This is a moving, living, breathing, testament to the power of words.

Thank you so much to Penguin Random House and Viking books for my ALC of Call Us What We Carry. I was so excited with we chose this for OC Books and Brunch this month. Amanda Gorman is a fantastic poet and she narrates this book which makes it even better. This is a collection of wonderful poetry about grief, memory, hope, identity, and healing. I found it intriguing that the first half of this book was about surviving the pandemic for the past two years. The second half focuses George Floyd, race in America, and a call to action. I love that this book ends with The Hill We Climb, because this is the poem that introduced the American people to Amanda Gorman and her amazing talent. I loved hearing the audio in her own words. If you really listen, the words are so meaningful and her inflection makes it special because it’s how the book was meant to be read. I loved the theme about the importance of words and and language and how what we say and how we say it matters. ‘To tell the truth, then, is to risk / being remembered by its fiction,’ “We’ve learned that quiet isn't always peace, and the norms and notions of what ‘just’ is isn't always justice.”

I appreciate Gorman’s prose poems and her creativity with form, but so many of these poems felt too on the nose, which made them seem a little trite. I most enjoyed the poems grounded in research and science and news.

"We lay down our arms so we can reach out our arms to one another We seek harm to none and harmony for all Let the globe, if nothing else, say this is true: That even as we grieved, we grew That even as we hurt, we hoped That even as we tired, we tried."

I don’t usually read or enjoy poetry all that much, but Amanda Gorman’s collection was eloquent and emotional in a way that I wasn’t expecting. Her words perfectly capture the spirit and emotions that pretty much everyone has felt at some point in the past few years and I can’t imagine anyone not finding at least one poem that will deeply resonate. Even if you don’t like (or enjoy) poetry, I still urge you to pick this up—you may be surprised how much you enjoy it. And if your curious, some of my faves were: At First The Shallows Lucent Fury & Faith The Truth In One Nation What We Carry (And of course) The Hill We Climb

I do not doubt that some of the work here will become required reading. The book is a viewfinder with faraway images of 2020. Gorman weaves together the climate crisis, racism, pandemics, and politics to consider what (or who) it is we carry with us through trauma. I was surprised how many times the word “to carry” appeared across poems. I thought about highlighting them all, but didn’t. A common verb, yes, but Gorman imbues it with its full spectrum of meaning. Her word play? 10/10. Her precision of diction? Makes reading feel like discovery. Words are jewels.

In reality I would probably give this 1.5 stars - and most of the positives were because she did have some good lines/metaphors here and there, some clever wordplay, but it was overshadowed by the way these poems came across as very know-it-all. The use of "we" throughout grated on me, especially as yes, we did all experience the pandemic, but we certainly didn't experience it in the same way and to present all of this as a universal experience felt false, especially since it's not over by a long shot. The collection didn't feel personal, and I feel like that is the most basic thing to get right about poetry, so I was pretty disappointed, especially since I watched her MasterClass and really admire her as a person. She is primarily a spoken-word poet, and I think she comes across better when performing than she does on the page, but she still sounds very childish in a lot of this book and it makes me glad I came to poetry at a slightly older age. "The Hill We Climb" is actually one of her best pieces in this book, and I thought she did a really good job with it, but she has a lot of maturing to do and I don't think this book should have been rushed to publication. Most of the poems are about the pandemic, and they are incredibly repetitive, using a lot of the images anyone could have picked up from the news rather than personal moments of her own. She does a lot of things I've been expressly told not to do because it comes across as juvenile and gimmicky - poems in the shapes of objects, using long words nobody knows, rhyming, and postulating. Part of me is envious of people who are so successful already that they can afford to release something really terrible/experimental - on the one hand it's refreshing to just read something terrible, because that person was able to just put whatever they wanted down, get it published, and get paid for it, and I think that should be all our right (to do what we love badly), but on the other hand, I think she will be embarrassed by this collection when she matures and looks back on it. It's very surface-level. The book was also incredibly liberal - it embodies the liberal experience of the pandemic and uses historical references to say how far we've come and how great it is now that we live in a post-racial society. I'm used to radical leftist poetry, and previously thought poetry was inherently subversive, so this was pretty off-putting. I found the footnotes and background information to be better-written and more interesting than the poems themselves, again not a great sign. This is a harsh review and I am sorry to write so harshly about someone so young, but she has a lot of potential and I just hope she matures and isn't too sucked in by her early fame.

Outstanding. Just like so many others, I was entranced by Gorman's poem and her reading of it at the inauguration. It was a high bar to set for this collection and she absolutely met it. I don't know that I am qualified to analyze/review poetry, so I'm just going to talk about what stood out for me. Each word in these poems feels so precisely chosen - for meaning, for pattern, for rhythm, for cadence. When you read it to yourself, you can almost hear it aloud. It's impressive to be able to craft a poem in such a way that the beauty of the language is so significant that it reads visually like an auditory experience. Since I mentioned craft - the variety of techniques and formats she used including concrete poetry - where the visual appearance of the lines matches the topic, integrating historical documents/journals into the structure of her poem and then expanding on them, integrating quotes and lyrics, and much more demonstrates an impressive mastery of the craft. Structurally, the poetry in the collection is varied, but each works perfectly for the images and message conveyed. The timeliness and timelessness of her subjects also stood out - much of the poetry in here reflects world experiences and events of the past few years, including the Pandemic and BLM. Within that exploration, though, she ties our experiences of today to the past and the future. If we had read poetry like this when I was in school, it wouldn't have taken me more than 20 years to be interested in it again.

Amanda Gorman established a name for herself, deservedly, with the seismic force of her inaugural poem “The Hill We Climb,” which is included as the coda to Call Us What We Carry. As her debut, full-length collection of poems, Gorman’s book exhibits her commitment to confronting America’s inequities and injustices, while she also uses her poetic vision to steer us towards a rational hopefulness for America’s potential of someday fulfilling its promise of inclusiveness and equality. Gorman has a unique ability to construct marvelous phrases and to seemingly bend the sounds of words to give them a potency that makes everyday language fresh and extraordinary. Although “The Hill We Climb” remains the paramount example of her talent and vision, her book also includes several pieces that showcase her creativity of experimenting with clever poetic styles and forms, such as when she employs her poems into the shapes of text messages, newspaper columns, famous buildings, the Earth itself, the American flag, and even a whale inspired by Melville’s Moby Dick. In its totality, Call Us What We Carry is a strong collection that keeps you gripped with eagerness to experience the immediacy Gorman’s poems, each of which reverberates with an urgency to enact change. For poetry reviews, I always feel best with allowing the poet’s voice to speak, so here are a few snippets that I think represent some of Gorman’s best from Call Us What We Carry: • From “& So”: Grief, when it goes, does so softy, Like the exit of that breath We just realized we clutched. Since the world is round, There is no way to walk away From each other, for even then We are coming back together. • From “Compass”: Lost as we feel, there is no better Compass than compassion. We find ourselves not by being The most seen, but the most seeing. • From “Alarum”: Our loss / colossal & blossomed / is never lost on us. Love the earth / like we’ve failed it. To put it plain / we have shipwrecked the earth / soiled the soil / & run the ground aground. / Listen. We are the loud toll / on this planet. / Our future needs us / alarmed. Man is a myth / in the making. • From “Pre-Memory”: Poke the scare until it speaks. This is how every memory starts. • From “Vale of the Shadow of Death or Extra! Extra! Read All About It!”: The oppressor will always say the oppressed want their overcrowded cage, cozy & comforting as it is; the master will claim that the slaves’ chains were understood, good, all right, okay—that is to say, not chains at all. • From “Back to the Past”: The closest we get to time travel Is our fears softening, Our hurts unclenching, As we become more akin To kin, as we return To who we were Before we actually were Anything or anyone— That is, when we were born unhating & unhindered, howling wetly With everything we could yet become. • From “War: What, Is It Good?”: A virus is fought inside us, While violence is fought amongst us. In both, our triumph is not in conquering others, But conquering the most destructive agents & instincts that we carry Within our mortal forms. Hate is a virus. A virus demands a body. What we mean is: Hate only survives when hosted in humans. If we give it anything, Let it be our sorrow & never our skin. • From “_ _ _ _ _ [Gated]”: Why it’s so perturbing for privileged groups to follow restrictions of place & personhood. Doing so means for once wearing the chains their power has shackled on the rest of us. It is to surrender the one difference that kept them separate & thus superior. • Also from “_ _ _ _ _ [Gated]”: Fundamentally, supremacism means doing anything to keep one’s sole conceit, Even if it means losing one’s soul. • From “America”: The fact of the matter is that our country seldom counts all who Matter. • From “Fury & Faith”: You will be told this is not a problem, Not your problem. You will be told now is not the time For change to begin, Told that we cannot win. But the point of protest isn’t winning; It’s holding fast to the promise of freedom, Even when fast victory is not promised. • From “The Hill We Climb”: And yes, we are far from polished, far from pristine. But this doesn’t mean we’re striving to form a union that is perfect. We are striving to forge our union with purpose, To compose a country committed To all cultures, colors, and characters, And conditions of man. And so we lift our gazes not To what stands between us, But what stands before us. We close the divide, Because we know to put Our future first, we must first Put our differences aside. • Also from “The Hill We Climb”: We will not be turned around Or interrupted by intimidation, Because we know our inaction and inertia Will be the inheritance of the next generation. Our blunders become our burdens. But one thing is certain: If we merge mercy with might, and might with right, Then love becomes our legacy, And change, our children’s birthright.

Not sure I’ve ever read an entire book of poetry and I actually listened to this one. The author recited the entirety of her book and it was fantastic. I doubt there is a single person here on Goodreads that has not heard at least a hint of the controversy surrounding this book. I’m also confident that nearly every reader has at least a basic idea of the synopsis of American Dirt. So, I’m not really touching either of those elements in my review. I am a white woman, living in upstate New York, thousands of miles from Mexico. I have no real personal experience regarding the Mexican migrant issue, and therefore cannot speak to whether or not author Jeanine Cummins writes a genuine representation of the crisis or not. I don’t even dare to attempt to do so. What I can write about, however, is my own reading experience of this novel. First of all, I was super excited to pick up this book. I lovingly cataloged it at my library when it first arrived. I put my name first on the list to get it on publication day. After all, it was hailed as “a new American classic” and was compared to the masterpiece The Grapes of Wrath. Naturally, this did give me pause, because both are tall orders to fill. Could this proclamation be true?! And it’s such a relevant topic! I need to read this book. I like to learn something when I read. Even if a book is labeled as fiction, I hope to garner some useful information regarding the topic surrounding a group of fictional characters. I want to feel as if I am in the shoes of a character or two, understanding what they are enduring for this short period of time we are together. To my disappointment, I was completely underwhelmed by American Dirt. It was far too melodramatic for my taste. It starts with a big bang right from page one. But for me it was too much. It seemed to be forced in order to provide the catalyst for the rest of the novel, an extravagant attempt to try to gain my sympathy. I felt an instant disconnection from the characters. I tried to remain hopeful about accompanying Lydia and Luca on their harrowing journey through Mexico towards their one glimmer of hope, the United States. And there were scenes that were charged with danger. Naturally, I hoped this pair and their fellow migrants would survive the risks. One additional thing that bothered me throughout – some characters were just not believable. I couldn’t help but think repeatedly “would so-and-so really act or speak this way in this situation?” One example would be too-wise beyond his years, eight-year-old Luca. I was further bothered by what seemed like an abundance of clichés. For example, the beautiful teenaged girl from Honduras – the threat of rape menaced her at every turn. Why not the arguably less stunning but perhaps still attractive mother of a little boy? Would not any migrant woman be at risk from such danger? I guess what I’m trying to say is that the characters were more like cut-outs, in my opinion. I missed the depth of characterization that I find so appealing in my favorite kind of novel. It doesn’t help that while reading this one, I also had the pure pleasure of another book that really did tick off all the boxes – including nuanced characters, equally relevant social and political issues, and perilous situations. I wouldn’t tell anyone they should not read this book. If it at all interests you, by all means, pick it up and make your own judgments. For me, the writing was mediocre and I was disappointed to remain a far-removed observer. None of the thousands of miles separating my home from the Mexican border were diminished after finishing the last page. But I truly hope it does get people talking about an extremely important issue. The best way to read this would be with a buddy, so you can bounce ideas off one another. I may not have made it to the end otherwise - muito obrigada, Pedro! I will continue my quest to become more educated on the topic. For an engaging write-up of this book, please visit my buddy's review here: https://www.goodreads.com/review/show...

What a mind blowing beginning of a book! A mother, Lydia and her little boy, Luca hid themselves in the bathtub for not being other victims of family massacre. The contract killers/ most dangerous drug-lord’s dirtbags kept looking for them, firing their guns, calling their names. And finally they thought they were not at the house so they left the place and 16 innocent victims behind. Now mother and her son have to leave the country for staying alive because one of the powerful men is chasing them and he is determined to finish his massacre that he already started. The man, Javier Crespo Fuentes, once upon a time he was her friend. They talked about books, shared their secrets, formed a close relationship till one day Lydia’s reporter husband Sebastian wrote an article about Javier…The day the article had published their life’s direction had also traumatically changed. So now, Lydia’s husband, mother, sister and her children are dead! Only she and her son stayed alive from vengeful attack of the cartel. And now their thrilling, heartbreaking, dangerous journey begins. They race against the time, authorities and killers at the same time. So keep still at the edge of your seats and take deep breathes to calm your nerves! This book will increase your heart rates and blow your mind by making you agitated, anxious but stop squirming nervously, just keep on reading, don’t you want to know what will happen to those innocent mother and her brilliant, smart son? Let me tell you something, they say: “destination not important but the journey” but this time it works quite opposite at this book because throughout this long journey, the mother and son walked, hid, slept in different places, ran from dangerous people, jumped into the trains, put their lives in danger, met with different people who had amazing experiences and life stories. This journey makes you up all night to read more, learn more, ache more, fists clenched, eyes filled in tears. You whisper prayers slowly to wish the characters can escape from the real monsters are living in our modern world. Not only mother and son but the people they’ve met especially the sisters helped them will always stay in my heart and soul forever because they’re so realistically developed, well-build characters who have heart-wrenching stories. I think instead of the beginning of this story, author’s note part is also impressive. It summarizes all those people including me who came to this land to chase their dreams, deal with our disappointments and learn from our mistakes to try again. On the border wall of Tijuana, there is wonderful piece of graffiti. When the author feel faltered or discouraged, she clicks to her desktop and look at those words: “On this side, too, there are dreams” Everyone has different dreams but sometimes making too many sacrifices and leaving your old lives and old selves behind might be too tough and compelling for you so sometimes you just procrastinate or give up on them. This book could be dedicated to the dreamers who are brave enough to leave, who have nothing to lose, make so much sacrifices and pay so many dues to fight with everything they have and finally reach their destinations! Maybe it is too early to say that but I think this will be one of the most stunning, impressive and fascinating readings of 2020. I wanted to read this novel because of the praise and high ratings by a number of my trusted Goodreads friends. Then just before I started to read it, I became aware of the criticisms in both the literary and press at large and I made the decision not to read any more of those articles until I finished the book. You’ll have to read the criticisms for yourself and decide whether you think the book is worth reading. In spite of everything said about the novel, I found it to be riveting, informative, suspenseful, heartbreaking and hard to put down . It’s 400 pages and I read it in two days. It’s the harrowing journey of migrants from Mexico, running for their lives, not to find a better life with more opportunity, but running to save their lives. There’s so much out there on this, you can easily find enough on the plot and characters, so I’m not going to talk about those here. I will say that the grief, the fear, the uncertainty, what people will do to save their loved ones and themselves was impactful. I found the last third of the book especially gripping. There are very few perfect books and few that meet up to the hype. While this isn’t one of them, I think this novel has a lot to offer. Some of the criticisms may certainly be valid, but they didn’t diminish the importance or relevance of the story, at least not for me. If nothing else, hopefully productive conversations and awareness will be generated about the issues that the critics raise, as well as the timely issue of immigration. I read this with Diane and Esil and I so much appreciated having them to discuss this with.

4.5 stars Is this the definitive immigrant experience? I’m not naïve enough to think so. This is fiction. Were there clichés or negative stereotypes? Not that I could see. Instead, this book destroyed the stereotypes. As the author notes in her epilogue the people are not “faceless brown masses”, an often quoted phrase by the naysayers taken totally out of context – it’s an image the author says she tried (quite successfully) to dispel. The people crossing into our borders are individuals with backstories and unique reasons for coming here. The humanitarian concerns of our fellow human beings touched my heart while delivering a page-turning thriller. As Lydia and her young son, Luca, fled for their lives, I felt I was in her shoes and quite literally held my breath more than once. This book puts a face to the plight of immigrants and the often harrowing journey they take to get here. It sent me to the internet to research for myself the conditions in Acapulco and what the drug cartels have done to make it one of the most dangerous places in Mexico. I read about “The Beast”, the train many migrants hop on, risking kidnapping, violence, and death in their long, hazardous journey to the U.S. I’m shocked and disheartened that the author is being vilified and subjected to threats of violence. Ugly, vile things have been said about her. Over fiction, people! This is nothing short of bullying and censorship. It’s a slippery slope when we have readers leave one star “reviews” of a book they haven’t read or change a 4 or 5 star rating to a one star after being “enlightened”. Readers are entitled to their opinions. The author, as stated, is a bridge. She spent four years researching the book and the epilogue left me with even more respect for her. Don’t we need as many voices as possible telling the story? Let the book open hearts and minds and start a civil discussion of the issues. I bought a hardback copy to support the author in the midst of this nonsense, and have no regrets. 4.5 Stars Lydia: My Heart Breaks for You and Your Strength Amazes Me. Lydia’s life changes in an instant. A bookstore owner, who cherishes her husband, Sebastian and her son Luca and the rest of her family. Everyday she goes into her store, pouring over beloved novels, spending time with customers and one in particular who, like she, loves to read. Little does she know, he is not who he seems. Then it happens. An attack. A bloodbath. Her entire family is gone, save herself and her son. Hot on her heels is the cartel. Lydia is then forced to flee from Acapulco, afraid for her life and that of her son’s. Her destination: America. Pulse pounding, terrifying, heart-wrenching, stunning and beautiful. An exploration of grief, friendship, family, survival and most of all love. “American Dirt” is, in my opinion, character driven literary fiction and it broke me. How could it not?! Though this is fiction (and should not be controversial as authors draw on real life to write fiction all of the time), it is based on events that happen each and every day to real people. While reading it, it felt as though my heart was ripping out of my chest. Luca: Brave, sweet, smart, kind Luca. Be still my heart. You brought such soul to this novel. My eyes fill with tears just thinking of you. Lydia: you are one heck of a mamma bear! All I have to say is you go! Soledad and Rebeca, you brought kindness to this book and you made my heart soar. Jeanine Cummins, this novel was beautifully written and brilliantly plotted and it will stay with me for a long time. To those of you who are considering reading this and have not, please disregard whatever you have heard and ignore the controversy and read it because you want to. Simply put, “American Dirt” is an incredible character driven novel about an important topic and that should be why you add it to your tbr and read it. I apologize for the controversy you have encountered regarding this book. You deserve awards, praise, kudos, champagne and so much more. Published on Goodreads on 4.12.20.

Lydia Pérez, bookshop owner and married to an investigative reporter, narrowly escapes a deadly life-destroying encounter with a drugs cartel in her home city of Acapulco. Lydia, alongside her son Luca, has no choice but to become one of the many people looking for a way to escape certain death (and/or torture) in their home country, by migrating north and getting their feet on some America dirt! This book is the story of their journey step by step, day by day, atrocity by atrocity, and act of kindness by act of kindness. The book captures the living on knife-edge 24-7 feeling, pretty good. This book, an in excess of a million copies bestseller, shines a light not only on a mother's love for her son, but, for me anyways, more importantly just how painful and dangerous being a migrant is, and reinforces my strong belief that people (especially women and children) wouldn't go through all this for solely economic reasons. The book gives a detailed back story of how Lydia and son Luca ended in the position they were in... essentially by chance, re-iterating the way maybe hundreds of thousands of people live on the edge of an abyss, that any chance gust of wind can blow them off and force them into becoming a migrant for survival. What I most liked about the book is that it shows that migrating would be impossible without the multiple acts of kindness migrants get from the many organisations and/or people they meet on their journies. It is however, hard to talk about this book, without mentioning that the writer is Puerto Rican - Irish, and that the book's familiarity and accessibility is in part due to us all (myself included) colluding, by accepting the many Mexican stereotypes and tropes in this book. It's easy to say with hindsight, but the moment this book was put on Oprah Winfrey's book list, Cummins' agent should have considered donating some of the proceeds to organisations that support migrants? I was hesitant to read this book, as I presumed that it would be back to back violence, peril and hopelessness, but began to look forward to reading it as I progressed, as it felt like it focused more on the logistics of the journey, and the reactions of the protagonists to what they saw and went through, as well as the people that they met. Still, the book is no picnic, and has quite a few gut wrenching and/or pretty dark moments in it... fair warning! 8 out of 12

What is there left to say about American Dirt? This novel was barely published a week ago and it has already generated such polarized reactions. I’m going to try to wave a white flag and give my own reaction to the novel divorced from the controversy... This is a harrowing story. It starts with the murder of Lydia’s whole family, except her son Luca, in Acapulco, and continues on as their perilous journey through Mexico to the United States. On their journey, they meet many people. It’s never easy to know who to trust and it’s not possible to survive without trusting some strangers. Early in their journey, Lydia and Luca meet two teenage girls, Rebecca and Soledad, who are also escaping violence, in their case from Honduras. Cummins keeps the tension and fear at a maximum from beginning to end. Survival is far from guaranteed, and even those who survive become different people. I’m not sure how realistic Lydia and Luca’s characters are as illegal migrants to the US. They come from a middle class intellectual background and Luca is a child prodigy. But I found it hard not to care about these characters, especially Luca and the teenage girls, and I appreciated the vivid picture Cummins painted of their journey. It’s not a masterpiece. One of the niggly things that bothered me is that, toward the end, the story suddenly shifted from only being told from Lydia and Luca’s points of view to being told from several other points of view. But is was a solid 4 star read for readability and emotional engagement. This was a monthly buddy read with Angela and Diane. I think we all had similar reactions. I’m really glad to have read this one as a buddy read.

American Dirt is the inevitable literary response to certain historical events. Notably June 16, 2015, the day Donald Trump announced his candidacy for president. In his announcement speech, Trump claimed Mexican immigrants were teeming with drugs, crime, and rapists. A sizeable minority of the American people shared this opinion, while the other side watched on in shock as a cult following grew around these xenophobic ideas. Not everybody watched silently, however. Jeanine Cummins, a successful but relatively unknown author, became obsessed with telling a more empathetic side to the immigration story. This passion ultimately led to her bestselling, albeit controversial, novel American Dirt. The novel centers around a middle class mother who narrowly survives a massacre designed to kill her entire family after her journalist husband spoke out against cartels. She has limited time to escape Mexico with her son before the cartel finds out she’s still alive and finishes the job. It’s a Hollywood-friendly, action-adventure type story that’s structured to entertain. Nevertheless, the adventure proves effective at painting a more diverse picture than the stereotypical image people have of undocumented immigration, on either side of the political aisle. Cummins’ strength lies in her charming, relatable characters. Lydia Quixano Pérez seems designed, almost at the microscopic level, to resonate with the average American reader, which is to say middle class and female. She even owns a bookstore, and her bookishness is the cream on top for readers to build a connection to her plight. The villainous characters are also well-drawn in their own way, showing a perspective that is not overtly evil but a kind of evil by desperation. Despite the dire circumstances, there's never too much graphic unpleasantness. Again, likely sculpted by design for that mass-market appeal. About halfway through, characterization takes a back seat and instead we’re tempest-tossed through a barrage of uh-oh moments as Lydia and her son make the dangerous journey across the border. It would seem Cummins researched every possible bad thing that could happen on such a trek and either crafts a scene out of it, or has the characters ponder the possibility of the bad thing happening. Before the global pandemic, American Dirt was one of the biggest dramas buzzing around social media. Much of the controversy stems from a tone deaf afterward by the author, where she essentially apologizes for being white and wishes “someone slightly browner than me would write it.” Naturally, authors much closer to the subject matter did not delay in saying we HAVE written this story, thank you very much. This further led to the issue of Oprah selecting Cummins’ book over a potential #OwnVoice author who might be better equipped to tell this story, and more accurately. I’ve been following this controversy with some interest, because it fascinates me. On one hand, I can’t think of a worse hell than a world where writers are only allowed to create characters identical to themselves. On the other, it’s true that depictions of minorities are often written by the majority, and that can be problematic. As an example, I read a lot of queer fiction and some of the most profound, deeply empathetic novels I’ve ever read have been by straight authors. Meanwhile, and probably more common through history, straight authors also have a habit of making queer characters suicidal, destined for unhappiness, or even rejecting their sexuality by the novel’s conclusion. If you only read queer characters crafted by straight authors, it’s possible to miss a critical side of the story. At the end of the day, responsibility will ultimately fall on readers to seek diversity in their book selections. And maybe some giants like Oprah can do a better job at promoting diversity, that’s certainly fair. I just hope we don’t see great writing passed over because of the author’s background, or create a culture where authors are scared to even attempt the deeply empathetic act of stepping into someone else’s shoes. As for American Dirt, from my perspective anyway, it succeeds in putting a face to families crossing the border. Faces which look very different from the hordes of rapists and murderers some politicians would prefer you believe. One member of my book club said this novel changed her point of view on the subject, which in these divided times is a profound accomplishment. Sometimes the best way to get people interested in a difficult topic is to create an easy-to-digest, mainstream adventure, and that’s exactly what this is. For better and for worse.
