In 1944, towards the end of WWII a rocket smashed into Woolworth’s in London killing 168 people including several children. The tragedy inspired Francis Spufford to write Light Perpetual, a reimagining of five crushed lives. We’re briefly introduced to the kids via an opening chapter that’s as bold, riveting and devastating as any you’ll ever read. ‘Shoppers, saucepans, ballistic missile. What’s wrong with this picture?’ And then whoosh … normality is restored in an alternative reality: a singing class that introduces us to the five and a sense of the future paths that might have been. Class bully Vernon ‘Vermin’, the poster-boy for Thatcherism; smart-talking defender of the underdog Alec the trade unionist; gentle Ben whose demons chart the developing science of psychiatry; and twins Jo and Val, one a passionate musician and the other, ‘always hanging around the boys’, who’s seduced into a chilling marriage. In 15-year leaps each shines a light on the social, political and economic transformation of 20th century London, their choices and pitfalls rooted in childhood personalities. This isn’t a glimpse into the world of great inventors, artists or leaders. This is a chronicle of folk stumbling through life navigating the complexities, the dramas and the everyday. Did their lives matter? You might as well ask, does any life matter? Spufford could have tantalised us with the knowledge that four of the five survived, prompting a race through the pages to find out who was the unlucky one . Or perhaps dealt the ultimate blow by revealing their childhood fate in an epilogue. Choosing to start the book with their deaths is a masterstroke. The power of the opening scene was in creating a more meditative experience: whenever I remembered they’d all died, came a secondary reminder that they never existed. A sense of loss upon loss. There’s a satisfying symmetry to the story. The torture of Miss Turnbull’s 1940s singing class contrasts beautifully to a later scene of reluctant teenagers coaxed into creating a moment of musical magic. Utterly glorious. In fact there are so many standout scenes, the forgettable scenes would make a shorter list. I loved this novel. Loved it.

A disappointing second novel by Spufford. The conceit is interesting: Spufford pretends that a handful of children killed in the Blitz of London during World War II in fact survived and lived for the next sixty years or so. The novel traces these lives, which very occasionally intertwine. Unfortunately, it therefore splinters into a number of generally unrelated novellas featuring in some cases some very unlikeable characters. There is no momentum. The one thing that is most interesting about these characters proves to be their death in the Blitz. It never becomes particularly clear why we should care about them, so the reader is constantly seeking the point of the story, turning the pages not on account of any suspense, but in a bewildered way, wanting to understand what point this collection of novellas is trying to make, other than the V2 rocket that killed them snuffed out a bunch of lives that could have gone in many different directions. That sense of potentiality, though, is snuffed out by the generally mediocre lives they in fact lead in Spufford's account. Not all is lost, to be sure. Spufford writes with a deft hand, and some of his characters (Alec, Val, Jo, Ben) are genuinely moving and even interesting and the cross-cultural character of London comes through loud and clear. But the fragments never add up to a whole.

The frame of this story – five children surviving the Blitz in 1944 unlike in real life – is interesting but, alas, remains undeveloped. Spufford rather focuses on developing individual, almost short story like segments that are poignant at best, yet my own readerly expectations looked forward to some sort of innovative treatment of the protagonists’ alternative futures. A good read that will unlikely stick to my mind.

I really wanted to give this book 5 stars because it is mostly a work of literary genius. It is the sort of book that if I was going to write a novel, I would want to achieve something as original, poetic and with the majestic impact Light Perpetual has. The opening chapter describing the atomisation of a ten thousandth of a second in time is jaw dropping and breath-takingly stunning. It is an opening I will never forget because it is beautiful, terrifying, powerful and so cleverly written. It immediately captures the reader's attention, arrests the mind and from thereonin you have no choice but to surrender to the wonder of Time itself and the intelligent way Spufford has portrayed alternative lives for the 5 children whose young worlds end in one bomb blast in Woolworths, in Bexford High Street, November 1944. The reason I could not award 5 stars was because in some parts I felt many readers could be lost if they do not share the passions the author himself does. Extensively researched or intimately known through personal lived experience, there are moments when some of the prose is a bit heavy going. This won't appeal to everyone. I was mostly simply swept away by the enormity of time and how the characters' imagined lives could have developed, however there was one notable section, about music, which even I found a little tedious. Sorry! The headings of the chapters show time as a very simple mathematical equation and the last heading and very last line of the book was perfect in my opinion, finishing the novel as powerfully as it started. There is plenty of nostalgia, lots of references to particular things found in certain decades that took me back and although I have never lived in London and very rarely visited the capital city, I could appreciate a social commentary which made landmarks of key events into a sort of political history. A constant turning, spiralling, spinning world where perpetial motion can lead to any destination at any point in time, Light Perpetual is a book I am so very grateful to have read and one I highly recommend to others. Thanks goes to the author, publisher, Pigeonhole and Netgalley for providing the opportunity to read a novel I so very nearly glanced away from. 4.5 stars.

2021 Booker Longlist The opening chapter of this book, describing a bomb exploding in the middle of a South London Woolworths (in a fictional Bexford), has to be one of the best opening Chapters I've ever read. "The light is grey and sullen: a smoulder, a flare choking on the soot of its own burning, and leaking only a little of its power into the visible spectrum. The rest is heat and motion......" then later moving into the sliding glass door moment Come, other future. Come, mercy not manifest in time; come knowledge not obtainable in time. Come, other chances. Come unsounded deep. Come, undivided light. Come dust. The children who's lives were to be snuffed out in an instant, instead are given time to grow and make their way through to the remainder of 20th Century London, into the next century, however, I never felt very connected to any of them. I never really felt emotionally invested, despite the brilliant writing and the interesting characterisation. So for me, all I wanted to do was get to the end of this book so I could read something I was more engaged with. Maybe it's me not the book. I did pause it partway through because I really wasn't connecting but that didn't really help either. I'm pleased I read it, maybe it would improve on a reread, however, back to the library with it now.

2023 has started off with a bang. As does this book, with a bomb that kills off all the main characters instantaneously leaving the rest of the novel to jump through snippets of their counterfactual lives decades at a time. Once I remembered who was who and didn’t have to keep flicking back to previous decades to check I really enjoyed this book that revelled in the monotony (bus journeys and run down flats) and the extremes (neo-nazi skinheads) of life in South London. That any fiction book gets you invested in characters you know aren’t real is impressive enough, the fact this one get you hooked on people who don’t even exist in the fictional world you’re reading about is next level. Francis. Doesn’t. Miss.

The five protagonists of Francis Spufford’s latest novel, Light Perpetual – Jo, Val, Vern, Alec and Ben – are all born in London around 1940. However, in 1944, these four-year-olds are looking at a new delivery of saucepans in Woolworths with their mothers when a German V2 bomb hits the store, incinerating them all immediately. Jo, Val, Vern, Alec and Ben are never going to hit or miss life ‘milestones’, or ‘transition’ into adolescence, adulthood or old age, because they are all dead. Here, Spufford steps in. He tells us what would have happened to these five people if they hadn’t been killed during the Second World War, jumping forwards in satisfyingly untidy intervals of time all the way up to 2009. For a while, I kept asking – and I think it’s a reasonable question – why did these people have to die in the first place? Spufford isn’t interested in playing with alternative timelines, at least not explicitly, so why not just trace their lives normally, without the interruption of a German bomb? However, by the end of the novel, I came to realise that its opening pages (slightly pretentious as their prose might be) are essential to Spufford’s project. None of the five protagonists change the course of history; the loss of these lives meant both nothing, and everything. As with Golden Hill, Spufford’s research is impeccable (and here I’m in a much better position to judge than I was with Golden Hill, because I’m a historian of post-war Britain). He shows how all five protagonists are restrained by class and gender and yet how their lives take them to places we might not have expected when we first properly meet them in a run-down primary school in Halstead Road. Musical, synaesthetic Jo becomes the temporary girlfriend of a rock star in America. Vern builds and loses several business empires. Val becomes mixed up with the fascist racism of the British Movement in the late 1970s. Ben and Alec’s lives seem most tied to their class destinies, in Alec’s case perhaps partly because of the way he sees class struggle; going into a ‘trade for life’ at the printworks, he faces his skills being made obsolete by digitisation. Meanwhile, Ben is also eventually phased out as a bus conductor but struggles terrifyingly in the meantime with schizophrenia, in a fragment that is one of the most immersive and horrific things I’ve ever read about mental illness. Light Perpetual is, notably, not that concerned with the dreams and promise of youth. More than three-quarters of the novel takes place after the protagonists are thirty-nine. This hugely refreshing choice pulls Spufford away both from the obsessions of the original cohort studies – what percentage get married? who is socially mobile? – and the concerns of most fiction of this kind, which, even if it follows the protagonists through their lives, tends to linger on the twenties and thirties and then race towards old age. It gives him space to explore how our lives still change, transform, explode or implode, even once we are seen as ‘middle-aged’. It feels like he’s telling us that we’re not always going to be defined by choices that felt so important when we were young. And as the characters get older, the book gets ever more beautiful and moving (yes, I cried a couple of times). I noted in my review of Golden Hill that Spufford seemed to have been influenced by George Eliot; here, it’s blatant. Eliot famously wrote in Middlemarch that ‘If we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life, it would be like hearing the grass grow and the squirrel’s heart beat, and we should die of that roar which lies on the other side of silence’. Here’s Spufford’s reinvention, through the eyes of Alec, who was possibly my favourite character: You couldn’t walk up a rush hour street, negotiate a bus queue, sit in a theatre, if you were constantly aware of the millionfold press of beings as entire and complicated as yourself… He’s still blundering among over-noticed faces when he boards his eastbound train, still ringed around as he sits down with his briefcase on his knee by eyes universally bright and significant because they are all of them the windows through which single souls are looking out. Riffing off such a famous passage is a pretty hard thing to get away with, but Spufford pulls it off here because he earns it. Golden Hill was brilliantly clever and thoughtful, but Light Perpetual is even better. It tells us that we are all important – even when we’re actually horrible, like Vern, or believe we’re horrible, like Ben – and that we’re all worth something. And somehow it does this, unlike most novels which try it, without ever being sentimental or obvious. What a book. I received a free proof copy of this novel from the publisher for review.

** spoiler alert ** This was a truly stunning novel based on five lives who never really were. In 1944 fourteen children were killed in a bombing of a Woolworths in London. Some were no older than infants. Spufford explores how five of their lives might have gone had they lived and it's not all pretty. One child grows up to be the beaten down spouse of a neo-Nazi; another, a hapless bus ticket collector, suffers from terrible bouts of mental illness but finds peace in an unconventional love in his later life. A third is a young woman who leaves LA on the edge of fame and wonders about her purpose for many years. The saddest of the group is a man who turns away from his questing soul to pursue a life scamming people and finally loses the only person who ever cared for him. The author here is saying that despite its trials and tribulations, recorded here in vivid painful detail, life is still worth living. It is true that Spufford identifies as a Christian so some might find his message corny and overly optimistic. But for those who still long to feel the sunlight on their faces at the end of a weary day, this book offers a kind of solace rarely found today.

I understand why Light Perpetual hasn't been for everyone, but it was definitely for me. I found it searing and touching and deeply true on people and all our flaws. The premise, inspired by a real bombing during the Blitz, is that a V2 bomb kills five children inside a Woolworths. We then get a counterfactual narrative: the stories of these five people had they not died. While some people think that the premise wasn't necessary, and that Spufford could have written a more straightforward story of Londoners in the post-war period, I thought the opening scene was effective. Firstly, wow, the detail is top notch. It also sets up the dichotomy of what the novel is all about: the interplay between the ordinary and the extraordinary in our lives. A bomb dropped during the Blitz—there are so many examples of that. Standard. But, for the families and individuals affected, it's quite literally life changing (or ending, rather). Spufford goes on to examine how the extraordinary and the ordinary coexist in our lives in so many other ways. As Jo, one of our five protagonists, observes of her students, "They long to hurry. Everything they are is oriented towards a future which they seem to themselves be having to wait for forever, enduring the great teenage boredom in which first kiss, first party, first love, approach at maddening snail's pace: but which if you're old enough to count time in decades you know is going to be on them in a flash, imminent, irresistible. In almost no time at all, possibility will be swapped for actuality." The novel is littered with so many elegant, accurate observations just like this, on honestly, so many things: white supremacy, class struggle, the value of work, familial bonds, divorce, mental health, and of course, life and death. The narrative structure is definitely different in that we get only one day of each character every 15 years, and it doesn't necessarily always make you desperate to turn the page. But, so much of reading for me is mindset, and I think reading this like you might read a collection of short stories is the best way to approach and enjoy the story.

Spufford's latest left me a bit puzzled. After setting up a dramatic prologue in which five children die during the Blitz bombing, he then goes on to tell these children's lives in episodes right up to the present. Sadly, it wasn't at all obvious to me, what the purpose of the prologue was. If he just meant to chronicle the nation's recent history through the biographies of a group of diverse people, why did they need to "die" in the Blitz first? The various biographies were grippingly written and very entertaining. However, only getting glimpses of their lives and jumping forward decades in between means that my understanding of the various chracters tends to be a bit sketchy. I enjoyed reading it, but ultimately I fail to see the point of some of the narrative decisions.

"Their part in time is done. They have no share, any more, in what swells and breathes and tightens and turns and withers and brightens and darkens; in any of the changes of things. Nothing is possible for them that requires being to stretch from one instant to another over the gulfs of time" Light Perpetual opens with a beautiful and masterful description of the V2 rocket hitting Woolworths store, London on 25th November 1944. As a backdrop, the V2 rocket attacks were launched by Hitler on several major cities in Europe when the Nazis' were losing World War II. The V2 attack on Woolworths resulted in 168 deaths. Of the 168 people who died, 15 were aged 11 or under. The lives of these children and their future were soon erased from that moment onwards. "They cannot act, or be acted on. Cannot call, or be called. Do or be done unto". Francis Spufford aimed to reimagine the lives of 5 children (Alec, Ben, Jo, Val, and Vern) but for the Woolworths V2 attack. The detailed description of the friction between atoms, matter, radiation, the bombing, and ultimately, its aftermath in the first chapter is so stunning and captivating. Subsequently, we then follow the alternate lives of the 5 children. Their lives were told at intervals of 15 years. The characters' lives, achievements, experiences, struggles were all fleshed out with different layers of complexity: Alec ventured into the printing industry and became the printer's union leader; Ben was schizophrenic and experienced nightmares of cannibalism, who ended up marrying a widowed black woman; Jo had a talent in music and songwriting who was then involved in a complicated relationship with a pop star; Val, Jo's sister, was involved in a relationship with a thug, Mike who was a racist with violent tendencies; Vern who was a bully in his school became a crooked property developer. Without a doubt, Spufford's writing is lyrical and poetic. He is able to pick up mundane particulars and transform such mundanity into something beautiful with his detailed descriptions. Glimpses of certain issues via Spufford's characters were offered: We get to know a little about the state of the printing unions in London in the 1970s through Alec's character; singing techniques, and songwriting process from Jo's character; racism, and white supremacy issues from Val's character; mental health issues from Ben's character; the real estate bubble from Vern's character. From the span of 1949 until 2009, Spufford managed to capture the entire reimagined lives of his 5 characters, from young, until death. The closing chapter is definitely impactful as the characters' frailty due to old age and dispassionate or melancholic attitude towards life, hope, and change are all condensed perfectly in that chapter. What troubles me deeply is the lack of reconciliation between Spufford's intention (in recreating the alternate lives of the victims of the Woolworths V2 attack) and the lives of his 5 characters. It seems to me that even without the Woolworths V2 attack premise, the story of the 5 characters can stand on its own. Apart from the first chapter, the V2 attack is no longer mentioned throughout the book. It appears that Spufford had missed the opportunity in his execution by linking up the characters with his interesting premise. It is a pity to give this a 3.8/5 star rating as I do think that Spufford's writing is distinctive. To me, Light Perpetual is speculative and experimental but lacked in execution.

Jo and Valerie and Alec and Ben and Vernon are gone. Gone so fast they cannot possibly have known what was happening, which some of those who mourn them will take for a comfort, and some won't. Five young children are killed in the 1944 bombing of a South London department store while their caregivers are looking at new saucepans. I was pleasantly surprised to read a largely unsentimental account of their sudden passing, and the equally unsentimental fabrication of all five lives as they might have been lived. The writing veered frequently from blunt and factual to wildly overblown and over-described, and occasionally I had no idea what the author was trying to get across. (It took me a double read of the first two pages to grasp that he was describing a bomb going off.) The best passages, for me, were about the children's classroom and their teacher, and the patriotic songs they sang. I even looked up a few of the songs and enjoyed Sandra Tucker singing "The Ballad of London River." Music is crucial to the story and worth the effort of thinking about and listening to as I went along. The characters were wonderful and I felt very involved in each of their lives over the years. In all, a very rewarding read and satisfying ending, with some lovely passages and some skippable ones. The author's acknowledgements at the end are a must-read.

Longlisted for the Booker Prize 2021. ‘Light Perpetual’ by Francis Spufford is a refreshing and original read. The premise of the story is an alternate reality in which a V-2 rocket doesn’t strike a Woolworths supermarket in the fictionalised London borough of Bexford. What follows is the story of five characters, starting from five years on from the moment the bomb wasn’t dropped, and continue in parts every fifteen years until 2009. _________ It’s rare for a novel to entice me from the very first page, but the strength of writing from Spufford sets up the grand scope of ‘Light Perpetual’ from the beginning of this story. The characters experience vastly different lives, of missed opportunities and moments of clarity and importance. There is a general sense of time and the inevitability of growing old in this novel, the reader naturally thinks of alternate realities themselves in writing that is simple yet effortless. _________ Overall, ‘Light Perpetual’ is a book deservedly nominated for the Booker Prize, perhaps one that would also make the shortlist. Spufford writes in a way that clicks with his characters and story, an author I’ll be reading more of after this.

Another excellent novel from Francis Spufford, much darker than Golden Hill but equally beautifully written. The opening, which recounts a WW2 bombing of a London suburb and introduces us to the novel's protagonists, is gripping, although I wasn't entirely convinced by the counterfactual premise of the story until I read the author's afterword which made it seem entirely appropriate. The novel traces the imagined lives of the children if they had not died and takes the reader through a social history of the second half of the twentieth century and I enjoyed the evocation of London and the period details. The very ordinariness of the characters made them seem somewhat sketchy and in some cases almost stereotypical, a vehicle for the description of social change - for example, Alec who is caught up in the radical changes in the newspaper industry and then becomes a teacher and Vern who becomes a fairly unscrupulous property developer but gets his eventual just deserts. But parts of their experiences were very vividly described. Ben's schizophrenic episodes are so poignantly written that I wondered if the author has had a similar experience. Although the sections set in LA and the music industry were less convincing, Jo's creative experience was also very credibly described and her reflections on teaching - the idea that you have to strip down your own knowledge in order to convey it to your students - resonated strongly with my own experience (although she doesn't add that the focusing process also enables you to extend your own understanding significantly). Val's story and her involvement with the violent side of skinhead culture was gripping and all too convincing. This is not a cheerful book but I found it compelling and thought provoking.

This is a really good story built around the idea of what might have happened to a group of (fictional) children had they not been killed in a V2 attack in 1944, aged 5. The story is set in the fictional borough of Bexford, which I think is really supposed to be Deptford with a bit of Brockley thrown in. I was going to downgrade it slightly as the mix of fictional and real jars horribly for me as a real resident of the real borough of Lewisham. There’s just enough to recognise then something will clang as not being right. I think I understand why he didn’t just call it Deptford but since the book makes clear its inspiration I don’t think it would have mattered if he had. It would be churlish to lower the rating for that though as it is a wonderful set of intertwined stories that really get you thinking about what was lost back in 1944. In that sense it is a fitting tribute to the victims of the real V2 attack in New Cross. I recommend you read it!

** spoiler alert ** A new book from Francis Spufford is always something to look forward to, as he's one of my favourite writers. From the blurbs, it sounded like this would be a better version of Kate Atkinson's Life After Life - an exploration of time, of the lingering effects of WWII, of the different paths lives can take. That expectation both over- and undersells the novel itself. Light Perpetual begins with the lives of a group of 4-year-olds being snuffed out, and goes on to imagine the might-have-been of those ordinary lives. However, the emotional impact of this framing is limited by the lack of sense of the children as people before they're killed. They're little more than tiny bundles of potential. Spufford then chooses not to reel the potential threads of their lives back in at the end of the novel, pulling them back into the epicentre of the explosion, cancelling out everything you'd read about them. This left me with the feeling that I'd read the lives of five fictional people as they panned out over the latter half of the 20th century, rather than the "might-have-been" cut off by a bomb in 1944. And because Spufford picks fairly ordinary, believable future-lives, though Ben, Val, Jo, Vern and Alec never have them, other people did, or something near enough as makes no difference (to a reader). People were a rockstar girlfriends, people had mental health issues, people unscrupulously profited from the booms and busts of those 50 years. So I think the sense of cataclysm, of the sheer waste and loss caused by an arbitrary split-second of time elapsing, which seems to have been what Spufford hoped to evoke, ultimately doesn't come off. That said, although the novel doesn't ever quite become more than the sum of its parts, those parts are absolutely fantastic. Spufford (as you'd expect from his non-fiction) has a voracious interest in everything, and in how things work. There are wonderful set-pieces on how type used to be set for London magazines, the semi-nocturnal life of an almost-famous group in LA, the rainy racist tension of a minor BF rally, the horrors of a mind dealing with schizophrenia. The people are real and their growth and relapses (the novel drops in on them all at 15-year intervals) are all brilliantly realised. It also highlights Spufford's twin faiths (music and Christianity). There isn't any overt god-bothering, but there is a sense of hope in the small things, in chinks of light peeking through, of small kindnesses, of a good vicar who says the right thing at the time, that point the way. The whole book is saturated in music (they should publish a combined kindle/audiobook that just soundtracks the chapters with the music mentioned). In many ways, this is a quiet, measured book - it certainly lacks the headlong plot of Spufford's previous novel, Golden Hill. The bangs tend to be noisier and more dramatic (the crashes, the breakups, the deaths, the voices inside Ben's head) and the moments of hope are quieter by comparison. Spufford is a subtle, tactful writer, and doesn't beat you about the head. An interracial couple, a remarriage, sisters reconnecting, two male vicars sharing a life as well as a vicarage - some key parts of the plot (such as there is), some mentioned only in passing. It's also, perhaps surprisingly, a melancholy book. Spufford says at one point that you can never go back, never go home, which is true, but he also makes clear that neither can you ever fully escape. People build things up and they fall apart; they start again. It's not a despairing book or grimdark, but there's a quiet melancholy that runs through it. The book is also that most appalling of things, a love letter to London. I usually hate any book described this way, but Spufford gets away with it. He clearly loves London and perhaps this is why no one really manages to 'escape' it (most don't manage to escape Bexford). This is in such stark contrast to the usual ideas of 'progress' that novels about this period try to encapsulate. No one goes to university, no one makes a ton of money and gets to keep it. The progress is those small moments of hope: a prescription for antidepressants; someone retraining later in life; grandchildren. As Spufford's previous novel, Golden Hill, was both a reproduction of, and a gentle sending up of, 18th-century novels, there's a suggestion that Light Perpetual is an example of modern litfic. After the first chapter, Spufford is swept away with his characters' lives, but that first chapter teeters between style and pastiche. (Is some of it meant to be ever so slightly funny? Perhaps it's just me and a crashing lack of taste and a morbid sense of humour: "But they can't see it. Nobody can. The image of the V-2 is on their retinas, but it takes far longer than a ten-thousandth of a second for a human eye to process an image and send it to the brain. Much sooner than that, the children won't have eyes any more. Or brains. This instant - this interval of time, measurably tiny, immeasurably vast - arrives unwitnessed, ends unwitnessed. And yet it is a real moment. It really happens. It really takes its necessary place in the sequence of moments by which 910 kilos of amatol are delivered among the saucepans.") Definitely a novel to savour and re-read, even if it doesn't quite achieve some of the grand literary claims being made for it.

What if? What if a V2 missile launched from The Netherlands during World War II didn’t hit London and killed five children in the process. What would’ve happened to those kids? This is the only connection these five storylines have over 60 years (and some mashups here and there). A book about the lives of five London people, living or no longer living in the big city. In a way it was even more impressive not to have the connection mentioned anymore after the first beautiful chapter, yet, I also missed “the connecting thread”.

5 children who were to die in a German bombing in 1944 at a Woolworth store survive. Then the novel revisits the characters every few years to look in on their lives. It was good but not as good as I’d heard.

4.5 Without a doubt, the beauty of this book is in the simplicity of the details. Beautifully written, nothing great, just the complexity of life that we sometimes take for granted. In parts it is very moving. The narrator is excellent.

There's some wonderful writing in this novel. Some individual stories that stand out. But I most struggled with the point of this novel. The premise is simple, this is the imagined lives of five children who were killed in an air raid during WWII. What would their lives have looked like in 15 years? 30? etc. For the most part, their lives are pathetic and sad. There's definitely a shot of realism to their stories, but not much hope. So is the author's intent to illustrate they were better off dying before they had to suffer? Or that living sucks? And in the end, there was no clarity for me, as a reader. These characters didn't live these lives because they'd died. So what? And what if they had lived these lives? Why does this story need to exist? I think this novel would've been more enjoyable without that initial detail clouding everything that came after.

It took me nearly half the book to get your invested and interested. 5 main characters… I barely liked 2 of them. The writing is a bit strange, overwrought with descriptions that don’t feel effortless and often redundant. This historical shifts were well done albeit one sided and a bit too Pollyanna for my taste.
Literary. Redemptive. Descriptive. Melancholic. Moving. Original. Harrowing. Memorable. Very good. Took a little time to get into the flow. Golden Hill was so very good it is a hard act to follow.

a booker prize longlisted fitzcarraldo edition? that's like an incantation to guarantee i'll read it. this has some moments of real brilliance, especially in dialogue, but ultimately this story of bereavement and punishment and loss and grief and travel and change gets too bogged down in attempts at subtly and mysteriously conveying all of it. i tried to work myself up to liking it as it crescendoed to its limp reveal, but the big swing of the final chapter knocked my chances out entirely. bummer. bottom line: this is a not-bad book, but it's a not-good one just as much.

The plot of One Boat is pretty scant. A woman visits a village in Greece when her mother dies and then revisits the same village nine years later when her father dies. She meets an assortment of characters and then revisits the same characters. The author brings two distincts strengths to the table: the beautiful descriptions and his philosophical discussions. Unfortunately, as a fan of more minimalist prose, I don't care that much about the former. And the latter felt a little too much like "telling" (as opposed to showing) to really light my fire, but I did find the topics and insights quite interesting. The ending chapter kind of has a "twist" to it, and I think that it was original and to me, as an avid reader, interesting. The book has many of the qualities I liked in Audition, a fellow nominee on the Booker longlist, but the setting and characters definitely didn't interest me as much and the suspense was not as high.

Longlisted for the 2025 Booker Prize. When her mother dies Teresa finds a small Greek town to mourn and grieve, but also to recollect and recenter, get her thoughts in order. A place that is “quiet, but not somnolent”. To do this she carries around a notebook with her and jots down thoughts and observations. Teresa does the same trip to the same town nine years later when her father dies. She even stays in the same hotel room. Teresa notes the changes that have taken place in nine years. As you read you are reading Teresa’s notes along with her actual thoughts. However, the narrative is in no way linear. It meanders along back and forth whimsically, much like memory itself and I suspect this is intentional. There are also dreams and at times you may be a little confused exactly where you are in the story. But it’s a short book and I found things clicked together much more smoothly on the second read making it more enjoyable. There is no real plot to the novel. Rather it is all about Teresa, documenting, remembering conversations, relations, with characters from the town. Exploring her grief through memories and anecdotes. Coming to terms with and reflecting on her losses. The characters and dialogue are great, the writing even better. An interesting sidenote which may mean nothing at all. The first trip Teresa brings a copy of “The Odyssey” with her and then on the second she brings “The Iliad”. Greece, Homer, but the poems read in reverse. Probably nothing, but you never know. :-) For some reason I think this is going to make the shortlist. :-)

I enjoyed this quiet, meditative novel which is more focused on philosophical observations about life and human relationships than it is any particular plot. Many comparisons have been made to Cusk and Levy, and I consider these valid although One Boat didn't reach quite those exquisite heights for me. One Boat is structurally sound, and beautifully written on a sentence level. I wasn't entirely sure I got everything that it was trying to do, but it was a lovely read.

3,5 I read this because of its Booker long listing - as others have noted: for fans of Rachel Cusk. It is about a British woman who travels to the Peloponnese on her own to contemplate the loss of her father and make time to think. She's visited the same little town 9 years earlier when her mother died, and she revisits that first stay based on the notebook she kept. She also looks for the people she met. I suspect the Booker-judge rooting for Katie Kitamura picked this one as well. It is a similar little book in that it creates a suspenseful atmosphere not by a spectacular plot but by withholding important background information. Some of it is never revealed. Buckley's work is more philosophical though, it explores big questions, and conversations are important to unpick them. Somewhat unfortunately, I was more impressed by the accessible way the ideas were described than fascinated by the philosophical ideas themselves. It was all quite enjoyable, but lost me a bit in the final chapters (except for the surprising final chapter!). Nice to have read it, but don't see this make the shortlist.
as soon as this was compared to rachel cusk’s outline it was curtains for me

I definitely often thought about Rachel Cusk's Outline and Katie Kitamura's A Separation while reading "One Boat" and not just because of the Greek setting. "One Boat" sets itself apart though by being a bit more complicated and varied in its form. The narrative is often nonlinear, with the narrator relaying events from her two different (and nine years separated) trips to this Greek coastal town, and this nonlinearity often occurs within the same chapter and sometimes even within the same paragraph. Occasionally entries and text from the narrator's journal are worked in and identified through italics. Like "Outline," a lot of the story is told through the narrator's conversations with other characters, though there's also plenty of the narrator's own internal recall and reflections throughout. Overall, I found this to be a very odd novel in terms of its execution, and I see how it wouldn't work for some people (it can sometimes feel glacial in terms of pacing; I've seen similar complaints about "Outline"). But ultimately, I found it to be a great introspective read, with a lot of cerebral delicacy that worked for me. 3.5 rounded up to a 4 I think.

If you’re drawn to the “observant solo woman rambling around town with a notebook in her hand” style of narrative (think Rachel Cusk), chances are you’ll like this. A woman who, 10 years earlier, visited a Greek village to mourn her mother’s death and flee her crumbling marriage, revisits the village following her father’s death. Intelligent and well-constructed fiction.

One Boat By Jonathan Buckley An interesting premise with the promise of a balmy Greek coastal village setting, however the author holds the reader at arms length, the language is practically tortured, and it's difficult to understand exactly what the story is actually about. A return to the place where Teresa previously sought haven to grieve her mother's death nine years ago, and this time it's her father's death she is mourning. There isn't much of a sense of grieving, and it's not clear exactly what she hopes to achieve by tracking down former acquaintances. The story feels directionless, the pace sags, my only points of interest being the sense of place. At times I was reminded of the mood and imagery I associate with Hot Milk and August Blue by Deborah Levy. The final two chapters don't feel connected to the previous twelve, and close with a reminder that there needs to be a sense of direction, momentum, to keep the destination in sight at all times, always be moving forward. Ahem! Languid, intriguing, confounding. Publication Date: pushed out from 13th March 2025 to 9th September 2025 Thank you ##Netgalley for providing an eGalley for review purposes.

tl;dr not much happens in One Boat, but it somehow feels like a stream of constant, plenteous inspiration There was little to be gained by further questions and much to be lost. I could know no more than I knew now, and as I was acceding to this conclusion I noticed, over to our right, to the north, on the horizon of the mountain, a thick smear of smoke sliding slowly away. On cue, another metaphor had been provided: the plot goes up in smoke. (p. 139) I don’t know much about the ancient Greek philosophers. Socrates, Plato, Aristotle; they’re all a-jumble in my brain. When I think of them I think: what a joy it must have been to just think for a living, (all historical context aside of course). They live in platitudes (thanks Plato) which ostensibly anchor the actions of individuals, but in practice really just seem to be retroactive justifications of “shit guys do”. I thusly turn to literature for perspective, as literature affords the closest thing to classic philosophy in our present day as anything, each novel a turn in the dialogue (thanks Socrates). I say this because Jonathan Buckley’s incredible novel One Boat, which tells of a woman’s quietly revelatory trip to Greece, felt distinctly Philosophical, yes, with-a-capital-P. It had the sense of a Socratic dialogue of memory, each recalled episode allowing itself to contribute to the whole of the picture. And in writing this, I feel like the protagonist Teresa, who throughout One Boat goes through notes that she made throughout this trip, doing her best to contextualize them in the narration; she humorously admonishes herself in her pursuit of the perfect literary phrase, in the same way I try to find a clever way of describing something to convince someone who, in the off-chance that they’re reading this review, to read this goddamn book. The internal tension of writing is that words often fail to fully capture the essence of something. We (the readers) inherit the role of conjuration-partner of the author. In One Boat, Teresa plays the conjuration-game by herself, which is a genius way of framing a novel that primarily concerns itself with memory. Writing is an act of capture, and the novel consists of her going through those writings, sometimes being impressed with them, other times seemingly laughing at herself at their inadequacy to the moment. To be unencumbered, I had left my phone in the room, with the notebook, so there is no visual record of that morning, and the verbal record is insubstantial, a thin summary of the remnant of what was seen: shallow pools of mist at the base of the mountain, and apricot clouds above – gold on the lagoon and on the slope below me – the sea lightly roughened: scribbles of white on the blue-black – mauve shadows behind the walls & thousands of small purple flowers – in all of that air, just one bird visible – an egret? – rising from the shore of the lagoon for a short skimming flight, then settling on the flank of a dune. (pp. 118-119). What gets me about this excerpt is that she’s apparently a bit embarrassed by her writing, but the way that Buckley has written these segments feels unpretentiously poetic, the start and stop rhythm of these sections feels genuine, like coming across something unexpectedly beautiful (just like one of the characters, who is unexpectedly and unpretentiously into writing poetry). Teresa is one of those friends wont to placate: I’m making art, but no, it’s not anything special, and then they show you and it’s one of the most incredible things you’ve ever seen. I truly think that Buckley disappears in this novel, having crafted something that feels wholly, authentically autofictional. Buckley (I keep wanting to say Teresa) has a way of propelling dialogue with the proper balance of character and those characters’ values. We take away deep and empathetic portraits of what each of these characters want and value, intensified by their ideological distinctions from Teresa. This is what I mean by a Socratic dialogue of memory – the whole of the world’s consciousness feels filled-in by these moments. (I just wrote this, and feel a bit silly like Teresa, but I SHALL keep it in) I found myself unexpectedly emotional at many points towards the end of One Boat, even moved to tears. Petros is one of the best characters I feel as though I’ve met in recent memory. His story, told somewhat in the empty space across the nine-year gap of Teresa’s visits, is incredibly affecting, and it’s clear why he’s adopted the simple-yet-profound philosophy that he has. In his thought-process, I found surprising amounts of closure in his acceptance of things-unable-to-be-known. Especially lovely were his “wisps of memory”, which feels in a vacuum perhaps like a hackneyed poetic phrase, but coming from Petros, is enlightening: It happens to everyone, said Petros. Wisps of memory, that was his phrase. Far from troubling him, they gave him great pleasure. They were gifts. The sunlight hits the path in a particular way, as the breeze rattles the leaves of a tree in a particular way, and suddenly, for a second or two, you’re taken to somewhere else. […] A shot of the past, he called it. (p. 140) The “wisps of memory” that float in-and-out of One Boat manifest in the novel’s free-floating structure. Teresa will move in and out through prior Greece visits, sometimes with very little warning or indication, with only character details to ground yourself in (which dog is Petros with? is Niko married at this point? is she getting texts from Tom or Patrick?). This caught me extremely off-guard at first, but the flow of memory felt holistic, as one. There are three layers of memory working here: the trip that she’s going over, the trip itself, and prior trips, and Buckley weaves them all together with deft, satisfying grace. This memory back-and-forth results in Teresa recalling a climb she made up an old fortress, which is one of the most stunning passages of the whole novel (which I won’t share here). It hits the characters too: when a character, including Teresa, is overcome by the story they’re telling, unable to stop, Buckley launches into long, unbroken paragraphs. In many other contexts, I might find this nigh unreadable, but I found myself unable to break away from these moments. Buckley’s sentence rhythm is mellifluous, even (or perhaps, especially) as they remain unbroken across pages. John is one such character who pops up early on, and in his monologue, we learn much about him as well as Teresa, and the darkness of his story serves as yet another mini Socratic dialogue for grief and justice. Between the lively, lovely writing style; living, breathing characters; a structure that plays with the nature of memory; and the absorbing conversation, reading One Boat feels like a constant, plenteous stream of inspiration, like an invigorating conversation: this is what the philosophers must have felt like. Through Teresa’s interlocutors, and in the observations big and small, I felt not like I was there, but rather that a sensation of fulfillment was being shared with me. What’s even more surprising about the sensation of reading this is that Teresa didn’t even have a clear motive for visiting this town in Greece. It was more just an impulse prompted by her father’s passing: a “decision” that “involved no deciding” (9). It had the feeling of being open to the world, to its people and its philosophies, and in being open, utterly transformed in the process.

One Boat is a quiet, meditative novel about a woman named Teresa who returns to a small Greek town in the aftermath of her father’s death. Years earlier, she had sought refuge in the same place after her mother died. Very little “happens” in the conventional sense; instead, Teresa gradually unpacks her grief through rigorous self-examination, documenting a detailed series of observations, memories, and conversations. Memory, for her, is something that can be messy, recursive, and unreliable, yet still essential to understanding who she is. By revisiting this town, she is also revisiting herself, searching for continuity in the wake of losing another parent. Her slow, contemplative journey toward some sense of closure gives the novel a circular shape, or rather emphasizes the somewhat circular process of solitude and reflection that allows her to reframe and reshape the myriad fragments of her past. For Teresa, the inherent instability of memory is not a flaw but a source of endless possibility. She patiently combs through her memories in an attempt to discover a more inhabitable emotional space that allows room for healing in the difficult, open-ended work of grieving.

Would I ever want to spend days in a small Greek coastal village talking amateur philosophy with the locals, gazing at the bay, exploring ruins, people watching at the cafe, getting tangentially involved in a case of blood revenge, and sleeping with the hot diving instructor? I can see a case for it! And that’s what this novel gives me, narratively speaking, in prose I enjoyed, and in a structure - two visits about a decade apart intertwined, and interspersed with added commentary in the form of critically analytical journal entries - I also enjoyed. Of course, there’s the fact that the general philosophical framework of this philosophical novel is antithetical to mine, Buckley writing for his character that “we know that the soul, if we can call it a soul, is not separable from the flesh, that when we die we die entirely. He paused to ascertain that he had not mis-intuited my position. We were in agreement.” The only character who would agree to the existence of the neshama is this one old guy with far right politics, obviously someone to frown on. Disappointing. Not a huge deal, but, something that affects my personal evaluation of the novel. And an absolute disgrace that this novel has a worse overall Goodreads rating than the limp, scared, and toadying fellow Booker longlisted novel The Rest of Our Lives.

One Boat is the first of this year’s shortlist that I have read and it’s also a first as it’s publisher Fitzcarraldo’s debut Booker Longlist entry. This publisher is known for their translations. Fitzcarraldo has been nominated 15 times for the International Booker, and in additional to their translations they publish a couple of non-translated titles every year: it looks like they got lucky with One Boat. One Boat’s main premise is simple: Teresa goes to visit a Greek island. There are a couple of reasons. One is to grieve her father’s death. The second is because she visited this island nine years earlier to grieve her mother’s death. Teresa then recounts events that happened during her first sojourn and there are flashes of her situation in the present day as she sees if anything has changed. During this personal odyssey, Teresa meets certain people. Each chapter consists of a meeting in the past or present, a philosophical discussion and some kind of lesson. One chapter is about a man whose nephew is murdered and his sister takes her life and that chapter is about depression, grief and loss. Another chapter is about her ex-lover diver who marries a beautiful woman, There’s the mechanic who moonlights as a poet. With each encounter, Teresa writes about her impressions. This is not a book for people who like closure. Instead, one sees meditations on all aspects of life: both good and bad. Within this structure One Boat manages to unearth a good number of intricate issues. Already One Boat as been compared to novels by Rachel Cusk and Deborah Levy and I can see that as both authors treat their novels as extended discussions although One Boat does not hit their heights (personally I think Cusk tries a bit too hard write about nothing and make it meaningful, but that’s another discussion) but it works as a novel. One Boat is also gorgeously written so there is the pleasure of soaking in Buckley’s erudite style. There is a lot more I could talk about : how the Odyssey and Iliad have their role to play in the book; the significance of Teresa writing her thoughts, or how love can turn up unexpectedly or equally how it can be deceptive – Jonathan Buckley throws a lot at the reader but as I said, his style makes all these thoughts flow, As the start of my Booker 2025 journey, I started strongly.

"The moment of the present becomes instantly the past, I wrote. The present was almost-nothing; I was almost-nothing – a momentary arrangement of energy. And when the time came for the arrangement of energy that went by my name to collapse, and become a different arrangement, barely anything would be changed. A slight readjustment of a few lives, for a while. Some after-life in the memory of a small number of people, for some of whom I was already nothing but a memory. Into the great indifference, I wrote, but the words caused a chill" A jack of all trades, Jonathan Buckley- University tutor,stage hand, builder, book manager- became a writer not out of passion but as a natural algamation of his academic background and later career as a writer of travel guides. "One Boat ", his Booker Prize longlisted novella, reads as travel guide revolving around its female protagonist. Languorous detailed descriptions of the Greek Town at the center are given priority over a protagonist that fails to be memorable. Buckley can bring Greece to life- it's smells, temperatures and culture but fails to make the story taking place captivating. Nor does he justify the notebook gimmick that has the character meditating on her present through turning her life into prose; the results are awkward quotables asynchronous to what surrounds it. Buckley's writing is inconsistent, dreary and uncomplicated at points- usually when narrating the present - but contrived and sentimental. I would have probably had a warmer reception to it had I not read a better book - five star book - earlier this year that hits the same beats and has a similar meta narrative where the character is attempting to turn their life into writing . That book, "Moon Tiger " by Penelope Lively, understood what grief meant . Aware of its location in our bodies and ambient drone thoughout our lives. Lively navigated the past and the present keenly aware of our blindness to both how it escapes us: present slipping into the past as the future runs out like water through cupped hands. "One Boat" attempts to be philosophical in that vein but is too conservative in its ambitions, satisfied with trite observations of unity and humanity as a group project, its title reflective of the adage "we're all on the same boat" . I needed it to go further, spread its legs and explore the world he's put to page. Let the relationships guide the narrative because as it appears, the book had plot points mapped out that he was writing to . Which becomes even more apparent when the meta twist (sort of) ending occurs during the last chapter . Where it is revealed that there is uncertainty and fiction to the aforementioned events and narrative added by Teresa for her book. Buckley didn't craft a detailed enough story for the reveal to be compelling, it's like telling me a secret about people I don't know then telling me that secret was a lie- ok? Idgaf . But if they had been well written I would have been compelled to figure out what changed but here I'm just relieved its over.

One boat tells the story of lawyer and aspiring writer Teresa as she returns to a Greek town to mourn her father, having visited years prior after her mother's death as well. The narrative explores themes of grief, memory, and identity through Teresa's observations and journal entries, blending her current experiences with recollections from her past trip. A place where she had met men like Petros ( a mechanic and an amateur poet ) and old flame Niko. Revisiting them offers varied perspectives to Teresa, which eventually becomes a part of her contemplative journey. She also meets John, a very infuriated local man whose life is overshadowed by the violent death of his nephew and the ways Teresa tries to understand his anger and reasons with him is engaging A book that was turning out to be a perfect read, just turned everything head over heels in that last one chapter. It was infuriating. But I think that was the whole purpose of writing it- to unsettle the readers, start conversation. I don't see any other reason otherwise for the author to write a one like that ( until and unless he is pumped up high on male ego) This book in its own different ways reminded me of a book by the famous Indian Author- Ladies Coupé. A book I have loved a lot. It's such an awe inspiring feminist story, where this 45 year old woman steps out to find answers to questions like - can a woman live alone the way she wants in this world. She travels alone and meets all women passengers in her coupe, where they all share their life story. In the end Akhila does find a man for her sexual liaisons but that also is a way for her to explore her sexual Freedom. Such a powerful book. Even though I love the ending but I still question it's need But one boat I think clearly has moved one step ahead, which feels like more than one, coz has been written by a male. But then I think it also mimics the actual world So maybe the author's plan was not to write an inspiring story but more like a reality check, which I hate but can't deny Further sharing thoughts of a fellow reader. I don't know their Goodreads ID so can't tag them "That final chapter, I thought it tied into that theme of revisiting (redrafting?) the past, & there’s that constant motif of her writing in her notebook & trying to find the right phrasing, painting the mundane in a literary way. I felt that what Patrick read isn’t the same version of the story we read, but her eventual novelisation of this experience. I would also argue that it ties in with the theme about the ‘correct’ way to produce art: symbolised by the attitudes towards the mechanic’s simplistic poetry, which itself is placed against Homer, & then you’ve got the narrator’s dual accounts- the straightforward & literary. So the final chapter kind of frames that- showing how her version is true to her, but not to her partner (who is perhaps biased by not only his own writing style and preferences, but also his distaste for hearing about her sexual attraction to the guy). So there’s all these layers of authenticity/control/manipulation going on." In all it is a challenging read.Not your comfort read. It makes me feel anguished. I would keep wishing for a different ending at the same time agreeing that different (read expected) ending wouldn't have challenged me as a reader. So basically I don't love this book but I love it

In the wake of her father’s death, a woman returns to the small Greek town where she mourned her mother nine years earlier. The narratives of her two trips are interwoven, and fragmented, making it difficult to follow at times. Buckley is vague about the location and the character of the narrator, as if he intends to wrongfoot the reader into making assumptions. It’s a complex novel that refers to Homer, and one in which I was never absolutely sure what was going on; the sort of thing Fitzcarraldo often publish, which, though I enjoyed parts of it, feels overdone and turgid, like it’s intended to be a mission to get through.

Teresa’s father has passed away and she returns to the same small town on the Greek coast that she spent time in nine years prior when she was mourning her mother’s death. This trip she reconnects with several of the town’s residents that she spent time with on the first trip. Unfortunately this was not the book for me. The two trips Teresa takes blur and often felt indistinct. I understand they were meant to be fragmentary and I often enjoy this approach in writing but not this time. I have no idea the purpose of the story. I didn't actively hate it but can't think of anything that I particularly liked. Actually possibly the only thing I didn't mind was the phrasing of Teresa's italicised words used to signify what she later wrote in her notebook about the events she experienced. These often had a lovely turn of phrase but this was certainly not enough to redeem this book for me. It definitely gave off Cusk and Levy vibes in its location and writing style. These are authors I’ve only dabbled in so I can’t tell if this type of writing is just not my thing or not. And for a short book this took me a long time to read! By the end the story descended into discussions of a philosophical nature which honestly lost me completely. The twist at the end didn't do it for me either. One Boat would be sitting last on my personal Booker ranking except for how much I really did not like Universality! Oh well onto the next book – trying to decide between Land of Winter or Seascraper?

Jonathan Buckley’s One Boat is a quiet, meditative novel that asks readers to sit with the ordinary and find meaning in its stillness. Buckley’s prose is elegant and deeply observant, sometimes to the point of obsession, but always with intention. The absence of heavy backstory gives the book a certain lightness, even if it occasionally leaves you wanting more to hold onto. What makes One Boat linger is the language itself. Buckley captures the smallness of life with stunning turns of phrase that seem to pause time. Like: “I am proficient, and so I don’t fall, but I am not in charge.” A beautiful contradiction tucked inside a quiet moment. Or: “The openness of the smile… made me flinch. Exit… into memory.” It’s a subtle, reflective read. One that rewards patience, even if it moves at the gentlest of paces.

There’s a dreaminess to this I can’t help but be drawn too. It slips between past and present, narration and journal. The Mediterranean coast with all its sounds and colours sprawling two trips to Greece a decade or so apart. The author asks us what it means to live. Not what makes a good life, but what is a life full stop. I found the philosophical back and forth entirely unrealistic - the kinds of conversations people think they’ll have on European summers with strangers after a glass of red wine. Still, I found the characters and their connections charming. An ending that feels a bit jarring, but drives home the absurdity of life. Can you cut up and edit your memories to change your past? If the past doesn’t exist, why not? 3.5 if Goodreads would let me. Booker #2.

3.5 A very well-written and thought-provoking book that touches on themes of self and memory. Though a bit navel-gazing, I think the philosophical musings were well placed. I fear that the disjointed timeline hurt the overall narrative, especially when placed alongside these aforementioned musings. We also have a dual timeline that I found difficult to distinguish. What made this distinction easier was the characters and the way each felt older. It's important to note that this is different from them feeling like they have changed because some of them do have qualities that have stayed the same - a highlight for me in this book. It takes a gifted author to write a static character and still make them feel as if they have lived a full life, and Buckley did just that! My biggest complaint with the book is the lack of clarity about some of the plot points. I feel as if there was an overall mystery - an inside secret - that was happening between the characters that I did not pick up on. A part of me wants to praise this feeling because it reflects how one may feel when coming back to a place they have not visited in a long time - a feeling our main character shares. Yet another part wants to ask why make everything so hard to see, if you're not willing to allow the sun to reveal what is being hidden?

One Boat is a quiet, meditative novel set in a Greek coastal village. Teresa visits the town after the death of her father to try to process her grief. The story moves slowly, focusing on conversations and reflections that explore mortality, desire, and the meaning of companionship. Much of the narrative is carried by dialogue, giving the book an almost philosophical tone. I really wanted to love this novel, but the long philosophical discussions between two of the main characters strained my patience. Do people really interact in this way? Not in my experience. While the setting and premise were intriguing, the extended exchanges felt artificial and pulled me out of the story rather than deepening it.
