Anyways, I liked this. The premise ("Two grad students travel to Hell to get a letter of rec from their dead advisor") is catchy, but Katabasis works best as a character study of Alice Law. Kuang's exploration of a woman dedicated to academia even when it rejects her reads as compelling and frustrating. Relatability is not something I usually seek out in books, but this was just such a book tailored for ME and what I like about dark academia. I've never seen my own attitudes towards grad school mirrored so honestly; I kept returning to Alice's realization that she pursued a PhD not because of any unique curiousity for her field, but because learning is something she liked and was good at it, and wanted commendation for. It's also nice to read an author who continues to dedicate herself to complex & potentially alienating characters. I think where Katabasis stumbles is the imbalance between promise of premise and execution. The beginning of the book centers Alice and Peter discussing how they will travel through Hell, how they will search for their advisor Jacob Grimes, and what challenges the respective circles of Hell will present. But the journey Alice takes is internal. She may be physically crossing from Wrath to Cruelty, but Katabasis isn't interested in overcoming that boundary except for what it means for Kuang to play around with landscapes and set dressing. This isn't a book about two people navigating Hell, it's about what it means for their relationship to academia once they get there. Thematically this is fine, and more interesting than the alternative, but at the end I'm left wondering why we spent so much of the first half of this book pretending otherwise. Why have Alice and Peter wander for so long through Pride? Why place so much weight on the difference between Greed and Wrath to have your characters speed by them? This is a book for people who are In On The Joke and who enjoy tangents about magic systems and debate clubs. I read entire sections out loud to my fiance, and I kept waiting for a Second Reviewer bit to hit. Katabasis is a book that's been recommended too widely-not because it's too "academic"/"smart" or that only a certain kind of person will understand it (we must be honest with ourselves, this is a very easy book to follow), but because it's so fine-tuned to an audience who /will/ care about the difference between magic chalk brands and linguistics jokes and Camus memes, or whatever. That doesn't necessarily affect whether the story is good or bad. Just if you are annoying enough to like it. Which I am. Thank you to the publisher for an advance copy. Opinions are my own.

«Katabasis» is a paradox: a book so desperate to be profound that it ends up saying absolutely nothing. Every page strains under the weight of its own cleverness, as though style alone could substitute for substance. Spoiler—it can’t. The prose is mock-academic to the point of parody, endlessly circling itself in self-referential loops. Characters are less people than megaphones, shouting Kuang’s arguments until the whole thing collapses into a lecture dressed up as a novel. The narrative, meanwhile, trudges along like it knows it doesn’t matter. Reading this was like watching someone congratulate themselves in real time—dense where it should be deep, smug where it should be smart. Kuang confuses paradox for brilliance, but the only true paradox here is how something so overwritten can feel so empty. One star, because even pretension should at least be entertaining.

I have been equally eager and daunted to read this since its release. No more waiting. The time has come to enter the underworld… 😈 ‘Katabasis, noun, Ancient Greek. The story of a hero's descent to the underworld.’ 🖤 I LOVED this book SO very much 😭 Having read Kuang’s other books, I had high expectations and I have to say: this is my FAVOURITE yet! It was incredibly readable and compelling. I couldn’t put it down, demolishing it in just over a day! I didn’t really have any preconceived ideas about the plot but I was NOT expecting this…it was FAR better than I could have imagined! 👏🏽 Katabasis takes us on a wonderfully dark and absorbing journey through Hell. As we follow 2 rival Cambridge academics, Alice Law and Peter Murdoch, on this compelling expedition we learn also of their past, both together and apart. This story is laced with fascinating insights and a heavy dose of mischief 😈 “Alice Law, you naughty girl. You’re trying to go to Hell.” Dark academia at its FINEST 🙌🏽 Alice Law has one goal: to become the greatest mind in the field of analytic magick. Only problem is she needs her advisor, Professor Jacob Grimes, to make this dream a reality and he is very inconveniently dead; in Hell to be precise. Her only solution is to go to Hell and bring him back. But not without her greatest rival, Peter Murdoch. He isn’t letting her go there alone. As their journey through Hell continues, the past unravels itself, creating a clearer picture of what has brought them both to this point. The question is: will they survive Hell together, or die trying? I enjoyed this SO much more than Babel! It was much easier to follow, perhaps because our focus was predominantly on 2 MCs. Alice Law. My girl. I feel so seen. Honestly, I can’t express how much I related to her character. As someone who spent many years in higher education, thriving off the buzz of approval from my professors, I saw my story written in words I could never quite find. Furthermore, (without spoilers) I too have experienced many of the traumatic events that she underwent, and found myself with a very similar mindset to hers. The depression representation was SO accurately portrayed. Watching Alice’s character develop over the course of the story was so captivating and rather emotional 🥹 ‘Rituals helped. Keeping herself busy helped. She was not one of the depressives who lay stinking in bed; she could not just lie there, the stillness hurt worse. Moving staved the agony.’ 🖤 Peter. Oh Peter. How I despised you in the beginning. You were Alice’s greatest enemy and so you were mine 👀 I apologise sincerely. I was wrong about this one. He became my brilliant and equally mischievous nerd 🧐 His character development was off the charts 📈 Over the course of the story, his character shows a wonderful mix of fierce intelligence and a surprising loyalty. And after learning about his chronic illness 🙂‍↕️ I die. I felt SUCH an emotional connection to him. I felt his pain so deeply. Peter - you deserve the world young man. There were also some great characters that we met along the way. Elspeth being my favourite, Jacob Grimes being my most loathed. For me, the highlight of this book was the middle section; so often not the case. I thoroughly enjoyed every page but I loved how Kuang dove deep into the personal lives of Alice and Peter. I could resonate with them both SO much, feeling the pain of both of their stories. As a female academic, I related so much to Alice, and as someone with chronic illness, I felt understood and respected so much of what Peter experienced. This combined vulnerability and relatability really sold the book for me. However, the plot as a whole grabbed my attention. I felt instantly sucked into the storyline and the world-building was rapid, yet vividly clear. I loved the academic rivals to lovers theme that was based on high-stakes; it was literally life or death. Their constant banter and mischievousness was balanced perfectly with their reliance on each other. It was a JOURNEY in more ways than one. Overall, this was a fantastic dose of dark academia. Every aspect of the book was so well done. The plot unfolded at a perfect pace, constantly leaving me on edge, excited to see what was next 👀 The characters were phenomenal; up there with the best of them. And the rivals-to-lovers romance subplot? 🤌🏽 Finally, I loved how the story was deep-set in a fantasy world, yet had me thinking about my real life choices…Highly recommend! ‘Wickedness felt better when you had a coconspirator; otherwise it was just you and your conscience.’ 🤭🖤✨ 5🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟

2.5/5 boring. flavorless. devastatingly average. i was lowkey fighting demons to make myself get through those last few chapters. so much of the plot felt like aimless meandering with philosophical interjections and reflections on the state of academia, the meaning of life, etc., but without any real substance or depth to it. i'm also shocked by how rf kuang was able to make Hell Itself appear so bland and lame and featureless - despite all the hullaballoo around the eight courts of hell, alice and peter pretty much just stroll through them. whatever little obstacles they face are easily resolved and it's only in the last third of the book that hell actually starts feeling dangerous. to be fair though, it's clear this book isn't about the journey through hell as much as it is a character study of our protagonist alice law - and the hell depicted here is obviously meant to reflect/challenge her own flaws, desires, nightmares, what she feels about academia and her place in the world. which makes it unfortunate that she just isn't that interesting of a character, at least to me. i didn't mind reading about her, i sympathized and hurt for her in many instances but ultimately, she didn't stand out to me and her motivations for going to hell just felt so flimsy. her relationship with peter was equally unconvincing, mostly because we only see the real meat of their relationship summarized in flashbacks instead of seeing it fleshed out in the moment. also, i think it's a bit misleading to label this book as a 'romance' or 'romantasy' (as i see goodreads has done). the romance isn't even a subplot here, it's really just crumbs. a couple of things i liked about this book: the magic system with magicians creating paradoxes to enact magic was fun, i always enjoy seeing a scientific, academic approach to magic. the writing style was solid and very readable, and i thought the ending was as satisfying as it could be.

“What Alice needed most then was a nice long holiday, and then perhaps institutionalization at some remote facility near the sea.” Rating: ⭐⭐⭐,5 This was as good as it was boring. Almost everything was amazing, exactly what anyone would expect from any R.F. Kuang book. The plot, the character arcs, the chemistry between the protagonists, ✨THE LORE✨, they were all so well thought out. There are only a few authors these days who could come close to Kuang's world-building and character development. She built a Hell that was entirely made up of the oldest and most famous stories and myths in literature, and it worked so well. She also created characters that were so irritatingly relatable. I wanted to be annoyed at the things they did, especially with Alice, but I couldn't because I knew I would most likely behave the same way. Not to mention that even though the romance was clearly the subplot, it was so well written that it could've stolen the spotlight had the main plot and lore not been so epic. However, it quickly became obvious that this should've been about 200 pages shorter. The chapters shifted from the present to the past, slowly revealing important plot points. I wouldn't have any problem with that whatsoever, had the chapters from the past been much shorter and didn't include such an overload of unnecessary information. It just took forever to get to the point, and at times, it made it almost impossible to stay focused. I think I would still recommend this book, regardless of "the filler chapters". They definitely annoyed me, but in the end, it was worth it to me. The story was just that good.

4.75⭐️ Thank you SO MUCH to the amazing Harper Collins and their wonderful team for gifting me an ARC in exchange for an honest review. [I will probably be editing this over time] This one is for the classic lit fans, the Greek and Roman nerds, for the dark academia lovers and most importantly, this book is for the GIRLS. Katabasis is everything that it was promised. A story about 2 post grad students, Alice and Peter, who go to hell to bring back their professor because they need him to write a recommendation letter for them to get a job. This story is written in RFK fashion. And we know this because of the brilliant writing, the vivid imagery and her thought provoking prose. The dark academia was dark academiaing in this book. But this is unlike anything she’s written before. This is a very ADULT book with real world ADULT problems. There are words used in here that made me say “REBECCA. DID YOU REALLY JUST FUCKING WRITE THAT?!” I was not expecting some of the lines she threw at me. She said this book was the most emotionally hardest books she ever written and it very much shows. In Alice’s POV, RFK shows us how HARD it is to be a woman of color in a male dominated field. How women have to work 2-3 more harder to get the recognition they deserve. And how toxic the relationship is between an older professor and a young woman of color in the academia world. Also the subtle SHADE that Rebecca threw in here was CHEFS KISS Example 1: “Most schools had stopped offering magicians tenure when it came apparent that their research were more interested in the trivial and esoteric than producing anything useful or profitable…” - On this specific page, RFK writes how the field of “magick” and being a magician is something that’s kind of frowned upon. To me, in this particular part, Alice resembles RFK as an author/ writer. How people scrutinize her as an POC author. We see a little bit of this in Yellowface (the shade I’m referring to)and how publishing only pushes out what’s profitable and what’s in trend. Example 2: Peter: “… I don’t know, taking into account when they were written, and the author’s social context, and such.” Alice: “historicalization Murdoch, that’s what we call it. What, do you just take everything you read at face value?” - TO ME. This was RFK throwing shade at TPW haters. Call me delusional. Now let’s talk about the beautiful romantic subplot that had me giddy. Peter and Alice’s banter was so mf cute my heart could not handle. Peter is such a hot nerd. I literally want him to slap my hand and tell me to rewrite his name 8000 times. Now I did end up giving it 4.75 stars. And that’s becaussseeee IM A PUSSY ASS BITCH YALL. but also yall knew that right?! I do NOT read or watch horror and my number one fear in life is death. You gave me a horror book about what happens after death?? Yeah. I was scared and uncomfortable for 75% of this book. But the pay off was extremely worth it. Because why focus on what happens AFTER DEATH when you can focus on the NOW? If you’re not finding the goodness in life then are you really living? If you’re not happy then what is the point? “There was no answer, only wondrous and inexplicable grace, and the only thing to do in return was to simply live.” Other than the horror elements and the essential crisis the book put me through. The pay off was extremely worth it. I am very happy with it. And I cannot wait for everyone to read it.

This isn't a book for readers, this is a book for pretentious asshats that think of themselves as 'scholars'. The hype for this book was real - I hadn't read any of this author's books before but The Poppy War is a favourite of my good friend Juliette so we were both hanging for this and were lucky enough to get ARCs from Harper Collins. So this was a Buddy Read with Juliette. A journey to Hell sounds like just my kind of premise, and this book started by taking us straight there with Alice Law and her fellow student/colleague, Peter. Magic(k) in this world mostly involves drawing pentagrams and reciting absurd paradoxes so a little of that and away we go. So let's get it out of the way: this book made a journey to Hell about as exciting as sitting through a lecture on the scientific properties of dry paint. Although, to be fair, science is much more interesting than this awful, bland blend of mathematics, linguistics and philosophy. Almost immediately, the narrative switches to flashbacks detailing how hard Alice worked as a student under Grimes, and goes on (and on, and on, and on ...) about word puzzles, paradoxes, mathematical properties and implications regarding Hell and all manner of pointless things in between. A little bit tested the brain so at the start I didn't mind so much, but as the book went on and all this extra stuff took precedence over the continuation of the story I became increasingly frustrated. We get about three chapters of this random, way-over-my-head crap for every chapter of actual journeying through Hell. The average reader is not going to be interested in this amount of superfluous speculation. GET TO THE GOOD STUFF ALREADY. Sadly, even 'good stuff' is a stretch because, Kuang's Hell? It's all flat, monotonous plains and other ridiculously dull iterations that I won't mention just for spoilers-sake. There is no kind of LIFE in her story - no demons or devils, no fire and brimstone, no pitchforks or pits or meaningful monsters. The creativity she does develop in this area is washed away easily by those other chapters of random stuff I mentioned, meaning there's really not much exciting about their journey at all. This is a book about a PHD student who is just the BESTEST STUDENT EVER. She's Not Like Other Girls because she doesn't mind being treated like a piece of crap by her advisor because it's all totally worth it: one day she's going to get A Really Good Job out of it. Honestly? The whole 'student life' she detailed was depressing AF but, with Kuang being a PHD student herself, I can only assume we're supposed to admire Alice's dedication to a life entirely devoid of anything other than her studies. I myself felt sorry for her lack of living, but that wasn't a subject that really made its way into this book the way it should have. So then we have the 'magick' which mostly amounts to a whole lot of nothing. It felt a stretch to refer to it as magic since it's just chalk drawings and paradoxes and there's no real decent explanation of how it all works. Basically, it's maths. 'Just be okay with it' is kind of the message here. Magic has never been less interesting to me. Finally, the whole reason for Alice and Peter going after Grimes was POINTLESS. Allow me to veer into SPOILER territory: (view spoiler) Essentially, this book had zero reason to exist because the premise thins to nothing as the book goes on. In the same line of thinking, a quick comment on the 'romance' this book is promoted as: what romance? There is some awkward smooshing of Alice and Peter's feelings here and there but nothing about their relationship feels organic. It's more like she threw in a little bit just so this book could cash in on the current trend of 'Romantasy.' I'm not even into romance and I found this relationship dull. And communication misunderstandings is one of my least favourite things in any book - JUST TALK TO EACH OTHER FFS. Don't get me started on the additional pointlessness of the fking CAT. This started out as a four star read for me, but dropped dramatically to a place of loathing. I wanted so badly for it to meet the high expectations I had for it, but it ended up turning me off Kuang completely. I've heard it mentioned that she believes people who don't like her books 'just don't get it' so I guess I'll happily admit she would think I'm a dumbass. Because this book was terrible. I'm throwing it a bonus star for keeping me curious for the first hundred or so pages, but it's more of a pity star and an apology to Harper for such a hate-filled review of a book they so generously provided. With thanks to Harper Collins for an ARC

While reading this book, I thought about RF Kuang. Not as a person, as an entity, a presence, a space in the wider conversation about books, genre, the concept of "having things to say", and so on. That's primarily because the book was too dull to provide engaging thought on its own, but I digress. This is the second of her big releases to focus on academia, and The Poppy War had a fair emphasis on it as well. Kuang has been a student for a long time. This seems only natural that she would have things to say about it, and while Babel was far from my favorite book, it had a point of view, things to say, concepts to engage with, prose that occasionally felt poignant, some measure of intrigue and stakes. So why does Katabasis regress in every category? Both of these books -strike that, all Kuang books- are filled with rage. That is the through line of every word of prose Rebecca Kuang has ever written - rage. But there comes a point during any outburst of rage where you no longer have new thoughts about the reason you're angry, you are merely working yourself up over and over again in different ways because your nervous system is not ready to relax, not ready to let it go, your rage has not been satiated or validated yet and so you grasp onto that famous phrase of the angry - "AND ANOTHER THING....!!!". Eventually, someone hands us a cup of tea or a beer or gives us a hug and says, "yeah, that really sucks". And you no longer need to tell us about another thing. Katabasis is the literary "and another thing" that has no clue what it wants to say, no coherence or cohesion, just blindly throwing things into the narrative with no larger picture of how to integrate these concepts. Rebecca. It really sucks that academia is so toxic. It sounds hard, and unfair, and sexist, and racist, and no doubt you and many other graduate students feel a giant ball of injustice in your chest when you think about how unfair it all is. Now can we move on? Katabasis is a metaphor made literal, with no shocking twists, no interesting concepts, no rehashing of older ideas in new ways, no compelling characters, no satisfying arcs or exciting challenges or really much of anything besides "academia is hell". Literally. And it occasionally tries to grapple with interesting topics, things that for just a brief moment, I was like, "oh, this new idea will be interesting", only for it to consistently choose the least interesting route. Alice, our MC, is one of the most insufferable characters I've ever read about, yet I am never left with an impression that I am supposed to dislike her, merely scold her gently for her worst traits (like hating those sluts who had the audacity to sleep with their professor, whom she also wants to sleep with) and accept that while rough around the edges, her goal of entering hell to rescue her professor so he can write a recommendation letter is a noble one. But don't worry, folks! Alice will be humbled by nice guy Peter. Humbled, simply by being in his presence for a large portion of this book and them both talking about random bits of philosophy or history or literature just to show that Kuang has read them too. There is no tangent too tangential to be included in "and another thing", that's what another things are for. This "enemies to lovers" is only that on the strictest, more bare bones of technicalities, mostly these two are together for them to both randomly get character growth without earning it. Another review said the book has "proximity dressed up as intimacy" and I have never felt a slam dunk of a line so keenly. These two bond and change simply because the narrative demands it. The book is first person from Alice's POV and reveals backstory in almost "throwing a dart"-esque fashion. There are so many valid ways to reveal information throughout a story, but the narrator telling you a small sliver of the story and then 200 pages later going, in internal monologue, "actually here's the rest of the story" which paints everything in a new light is boring and artificial. This isn't presented in an unreliable narrator type of way, simply "we are now a third of the way through the book, so I need to reveal more information about Alice's relationship with the professor" is so evidently the driving force that I was annoyed every time. This is not how internal monologues work. If I am thinking about why I like or dislike a person, I think about the biggest reasons in either direction first. I don't think "yeah, George is kinda shitty, he left my text on read last week" and then three days later remember, "oh yeah, George also shot my brother in the face". Also this book has lembas bread. Actually. Lembas bread, from Lord of the Fucking Rings. They go to hell, and say, man I'm hungry, lets eat some lembas. What in the absolute fuck is going on here. Did Kuang write the whole book, realize they never ate something, have two days to fix this in revision, and go, "screw it, lembas bread, as made famous in Lord of the Rings by most famous fantasy author of all time, JRR Tolkien, that will be fine"? This is absurd and I'm so infuriated that nobody else is talking about this. I demand an explanation. The resolution of this book is trite and unearned, every level of hell is the most boring, easy, uninteresting route. There is a cat, though, so not everything is pure misery. You could just watch the movie Whiplash instead of reading this book. Whiplash is two hours and handles the questions, "how far does one go in pursuit of being the absolute best, what do they give up to do so? How far does one go as an educator to coax greatness out of someone, how far is too far? What should be the consequences of either of these decisions?" much better than this book does and you might even feel some stakes or sense of tension in that movie instead of being lulled into your slow death by the 80th reference to Dante or Borges or Hume or whatever. AND ANOTHER THING!! The lembas bread!! You couldn't have just renamed it!? Keep it the same but call it Kuang Bread? Rage Bread? Sabmel bread? Anything!! 2/10

rfk please put down the textbooks and bibliographies, i’m begging you !! no one is more sad than i am that my most anticipated read for the last 3 years fell flat. this disappointment is perhaps partially my fault. my expectations for a new book from rf kuang were too high, and as you can see, i did not enjoy my time reading this book. i imagine what i experienced was akin to how it feels to crawl through hell one of my least favourite storylines in books is the quest trope: i hate making our way along a journey to retrieve an item (in this case a person) as i usually find my self dragging through the pages until we can finally get to the conclusion. it did not help that hell was made boring and monotonous. i was not attached to either alice or peter, especially not in the way i usually am to rfk’s characters. why this is extra damning, is that you spend the whole time with them. so if you aren’t clicking with your main characters, and there aren’t really any other characters to lock onto…who’s flying the plane? you don’t get any character depth, learn their motivations, backstories and history until very far in, so i spent way more than half of the book emotionally detached from them. one of my critiques with babel was the amount of info dumping not relevant to the story; somehow this book was even more excessive. the writing truly was so exposition heavy with the plot taking a back seat. i was frustrated because i could really feel this book’s length. i hate to say it, but this felt like rebecca’s weakest writing to date. the commentary on the way academia destroys you from the inside out - even more so as a woman of colour, written by someone as academically accomplished as rebecca, should have made this book a stand out. however, by the time these themes came into play, i was too detached to care after being inundated by a narrative that read 65% textbook. i sold my soul to rfk when i read the poppy war in 2020, which means i will read anything this woman writes. unfortunately, this one i will not remember fondly. in fact, i don’t believe that i will think of it again! but, hey, at least i will always leave an rfk book learning some obscure facts.

Alice Law wants to graduate in Magick with the highest honors and a recommendation from the greatest professor. That’s her golden ticket to success. Unfortunately, the professor died. And she was responsible for the accident that killed him. But just because he’s dead, that doesn’t mean her dream needs to be. She’s going to visit him in Hell. But her rival has the same idea. What a cool concept. This is a story that is basically one big criticism on elite academic institutions. But it’s not just about the institutions, it’s about the people there, or even better: how much people change because of those institutions. This is a character-driven story, but it’s worth mentioning that these aren’t the kind of people you’ll want to root for. Linda Ronstadt may have sung that it's so easy to fall in love, but R.F. Kuang proves that it’s also quite easy to dislike some fictional characters. The thing is that the main character Alice in particular has sacrificed so much of herself, that there’s barely anything left but unresolved trauma and an obsessive addiction to external validation. Part of that is the attitude of the scholars in general. They look down on anything that distracts from the life of the mind and they pride themselves on dedicating their lives completely to their research. And you can see that Alice discovers how wrong she’s been when she starts to question her idol, the professor she’s trying to find in Hell. For some reason, this book didn’t grab me as much as I was expecting it to. There is something to be said about the characters, but they’re supposed to be unlikeable. It’s a very complex read that requires quite a bit of academic knowledge to fully appreciate it, but that’s part of what makes this an interesting read. You could also say that there are quite a few flashbacks. Flashback always take you out of the story at hand for a bit, so it’s best not to use them too often. But honestly, everything is written well and serves a purpose. Objectively speaking, this story does a lot of things right. Subjectively speaking though, I just felt a bit bored and I never really cared about the characters. Maybe this is just not my kind of story. Overall, a unique concept with a strong but complex execution that makes it stand out. The characters are deliberately unlikable, but also interesting in their own right. Unfortunately, this never really grabbed me. Don’t let one reader’s opinion stop you from reading and enjoying this one though, as it has some cool things to offer.

Katabasis is a University English student's dream come true. If I were still in graduate school, I would have written about it. Yes, understanding the ideas in this novel might be a hiccup for younger or less experienced readers unwilling to type allusions into google. But come on, the day that an author can no longer count on readers to take two seconds to bloody well look up elementary allusions is the same day I'll lose interest in reading. You don't need a background in the western and eastern literary canons to enjoy a book with allusions--you just need to be willing to look up whatever you don't recognize. Brief Summary: Alice Law and Peter Murdoch, both Cambridge graduate students in the most challenging field of magical studies, transport themselves to Hell in order to rescue their deceased academic advisor, Professor Grimes. This particular professor is one of the most respected scholars in his field, and without him, both students feel that all of their academic toiling will have been wasted. So despite the steep price, they magic themselves into Hell. The majority of the novel details the various realms of Hell through which Alice and Peter must travel. Extended Metaphor, Wit & Humor: Surely by now, you are wondering if this book is an updated version of Dante. Nope. Of course Dante's works are referenced, but this novel is essentially a conceit--one giant allegorical metaphor--and it absolutely oozes the most delicious wit. When I first started, I had no idea that I was in for such fantastic hilarity. I hadn't read anything about the humor here at all. But the puns begin immediately, and it quickly becomes obvious that Kuang is making fun of everything we take too seriously. If as a student this ever applied to you, if you endured countless sleepless nights in service to your grade point average, if you poured over practice sites to obtain perfect standardized test scores and revised obsessively to win academic awards and scholarships; then this novel is your chance for catharsis...your chance to laugh. In Katabasis, Kuang takes on academia, the western canon, and even America. I laughed out loud at least once every three pages, and the moment I hit the last page, I flipped right back to the beginning for a reread. Style & Structure: Kuang's prose here is expertly sculpted. In fact, Katabasis represents an improvement over her prose style in Babel. She seems to have completely mastered organically allowing the sentence structure to imitate the tone and thus influence the reader's mood. Her diction, never high handed and never purple, is exquisitely measured and timed. One of my favorite opening sections details why our protagonist intends to make a quite dangerous rescue attempt. She introduces the local color of her magic system with several eclectic names for laws and principles, makes several subtly humorous allusions to Dante and TS Elliott. And then, at the end of the paragraph, Kuang adds bluntly and plainly, "this meant she had to go to hell, and she had to go today." It's the first time such simple diction has been used in this paragraph, and it's just the perfect touch. Another example of Kuang's evolved use of organic structure occurs when she uses repetition to emote exactly the opposite of what is said. To clarify, when Kuang offers exposition on Alice's conflict, she repeats the opening phrase of descriptive sentences. "No one saw" Alice's involvement in her professor's death, and "no one saw" when she took off her bloody clothes, and "no one saw" her incinerate them. The phrase "no one saw" is repeated multiple times throughout the paragraph. It's repeated so often that readers begin to doubt the validity of the phrase. They begin to understand that Alice is worried about just the opposite--that someone must have seen. Each time the phrase is repeated, the anxiety builds. Readers sincerely feel Alice's fear, her need to reassure herself, and the emotion is so much stronger because it is indirectly conveyed by structure instead of being merely stated. Kuang's prose depicts exactly the artistry possible when authors wield a mastery of grammar and form. There's nothing pedantic or even didactic in the descriptions. They are just as carefully crafted as the sentence structure. Ignore the one star reviews that say otherwise. This is the sort of novel that belongs on Locus Award nomination lists. Katabasis is literature. Further Thoughts: Kuang's books have always offered readers a carefully laid out symbology. But Katabasis is next level. Her motifs weave thematic layers upon layers so perfectly that the ending tapestry is a marvel. Bluntly, I can't even understand how brilliant one would have to be to pull off something like this. It's that sort of book--the sort you want to spend months deconstructing just so you can polish your own awe into language. I had not originally intended to write a review for this one, mainly because it's already so widely reviewed, but I have seen such a baffling smear campaign against what is essentially Kuang's most impressive work to date, that I felt compelled after a second reading to throw in my two cents. I really urge fantasy lovers, especially academic fantasy lovers, not to miss out. Of all the hardcovers on which I have spent far too much coin, this is one first edition I will never regret. This book is beautiful beyond its colorful jacket and sprayed edges. Bottomline: If you are a reader of literature, then you will love this book. If you are used to the average national bestseller, no problem--you can still love this book. Just go into it with a search engine at the ready and take your time. It's worth it.

੭୧ 5 stars . ۫ “ But why— ” He stopped himself, then rephrased. “ But then you came for nothing. ” “ Not nothing. I gained everything. ” It's not enough to just read Katabasis. I need it embedded in my matter 😣‼️ overall thoughts — This book is living proof that reading is subjective, because the fact that Katabasis - one of the most brilliant, deeply researched, and thought-provoking novels I've read to date - sits at a 3.78 rating, while a certain wildly popular novel Shatter Me, a 3.84, is unfathomable. Regardless, R.F. Kuang has clearly found her niche and perfected her craft!! With every release, I continue to be left in disbelief by her capabilities. It's impossible not to feel the blood, sweat, and tears that went into creating Alice and Peter's story. I believe this book makes for a better read by going in blindly, so I'll keep plot details short. Katabasis follows Alice Law and Peter Murdoch, two postgraduate students and academic rivals, who descend into Hell to retrieve the soul of their dead professor. We get to see Alice and Peter's journey through the 8 Courts of Hell, which resemble a university campus. One of the most honest things Katabasis says about academia is that the system only values the mind, and it treats the body as an inconvenience. In Alice's world, hunger is normal, exhaustion is expected, pain is ignored. The body is something to push through or sacrifice in the name of "brilliance." And the worst part is that no one explicitly forces this on her - she internalizes it. That mindset is exactly what turns academia into Hell. A lot of people criticize the novel by saying Hell was boring, it had no stakes, nothing dangerous really happens. But I think that misses the point. The tension in this book, to me at least, doesn't really present itself as "will they survive?" It's about watching Alice slowly realize that everything she's sacrificed her life for might be meaningless. As Alice and Peter go through Hell, rather than feeling exciting, it feels almost slow and draining. This to me perfectly mirrors academia because academia destroys people slowly, through exhaustion, pressure, and the constant feeling of never being enough. The next biggest complaint I've come across is that Katabasis is pretentious - R.F. Kuang spends so much time referencing + explaining different theories, writers, concepts, and in turn sacrifices the development of her characters (I'll comment on the latter below). First, if I went to Oxford, Cambridge, and Yale while writing 6 best-selling novels, I promise I would be infinitely worse. R.F. Kuang deserves to brag!! Being in academia is difficult as Hell (literally)!! And honestly, I am not ashamed to say there were so many terms and ideas I did not understand. It's a learning opportunity. Katabasis doesn't spoon-feed its readers, and that seems to be where a lot of frustration comes from. I don't know what non-Euclidean geometry is. What is a dialetheia? What is a syllogism? Having these unfamiliar ideas didn't ruin the experience for me. Maybe Google something. Maybe crack open a dictionary. I thoroughly enjoyed all the academic references and tidbits of knowledge. I think that's what makes the book unique and engaging. And what's more. Even if you strip away all the theory, all the references, all the philosophy - Katabasis is still fun. I laughed. I cried. I was invested the entire time. I loved the characters. I loved the ending. A book can be entertaining and enriching. The two are not mutually exclusive. I've always appreciated Kuang's ability to write characters who aren't morally perfect, and Alice is definitely her 2nd best example of that (Fang Runin is just unmatched). She's messy, obsessive, stubborn, and painfully sincere. Somehow, she's also incredibly likeable (contrary to what people say). Peter, too, I adored. Peter follows Alice to Hell partly out of obligation, partly out of guilt, and partly because he doesn't know how to stop orbiting her. Their romance is definitely not traditional (as the author mentions), but I personally felt their connection DOES NOT lack depth. A lot of their relationship is developed in Hell, and that choice makes sense because it is where they are able to mutually recognize and understand the toxic system that shaped them. Their relationship + the way it unfolded worked for me because it felt realistic for who they are: two deeply damaged people clinging to the only person who sees them clearly. I loved reading from Alice's perspective. I loved AlicePeter's interactions. My idiotic, crazy duo 😣😣 final thoughts — You don't need to be in academia to enjoy this novel. And again, I can't stress this enough: this book was fun. I never felt like I had to drag myself through the book - I wanted to keep reading. Obviously, reading is subjective, so what entertained me might not entertain others, but I think that a lot of reviews focus too heavily on this idea of pretentiousness and less on how Katabasis is a good book.
