“Some people charged toward the goal, running for all they had. Others stumbled. But it wasn't the speed that mattered. It was the direction they were going.” If I ever decide get a tattoo, it would say "Journey before destination." This quote sums up the series so well. I love my antiheroes, but the Stormlight Archive has made me realize that, after all these years, I am still a sucker for a straightforward hero's journey. Kaladin goes through so much growth in this book. He develops every book and with each new Ideal, but damn if this isn't the most he's ever struggled for the next step in his Radiant journey. He knows the words, has known them for a long time, but it is part of his character to resist them. Like Syl, I despaired at his spiraling depression and rejoiced as he found a new way to protect people: mental health care. (view spoiler). Moash is scum. That is all I'll say. Okay, I'll say a bit more. The main message of this series is: It's okay if you fuck up in life; what's important is you make amends and try to be a better person. Moash is the antithesis of that message and deserves to rot in Damnation. We finally recover all of Shallan's past in this book. All of the secrets she's carefully repressed. There are still a few small holes in her memory, but Shallan's character development matches Kaladin in terms of hefty growth. It is slightly frustrating that she harbors such self-hatred even after all this time, but trauma is not easily fixed, which is why Radiants must hold onto the mantra, "Strength before weakness." Small aside, but there's a little doodle of Pattern running in my hardback and it made me giggle. Dalinar is still important, but I think he takes a backseat to Navani this book. Through her POV chapters, we get a more nuanced perspective of the singers controlled by Odium and how their enemies have honor too. Navani has always claimed she's not a scholar out of repressed insecurity and her character arc is exquisite. We stan a queen. Well, two queens, including Jasnah. The fifth book can't come soon enough. My review of The Way of Kings My review of Words of Radiance My review of Oathbringer My review of Edgedancer My review of Dawnshard

The cosmere converges. I have read every Sanderson book in his cosmere universe and the convergence of characters, elements, worlds and magic is absolutely stunning. The pay off in Rhythm of War is enormous: Sanderson rewards the reader especially if they have read all the other books in the cosmere including Elantris, Warbreaker and Mistborn. I'm absolutely blown away at the forethought and organization that went into writing this latest installment in the Stormlight Archives. I say with little hesitation that the Stormlight Archive is my favorite fantasy series I've ever read, and I've read a lot of fantasy. Rhythm of War is different from the previous three books. There is less plot here but much more character and actual world development. In no other book in the cosmere are so many plot points and connections revealed. The character development is phenomenal, particularly for Kaladin, Navani, Venli, Adolin, Shallan and lesser characters like Rlain and many others. There is a HUGE focus on mental health in this book which I absolutely loved. Depression, self-loathing, anxiety and hopelessness are major emotions running through the pages. It was amazing to see how each character deals with their own demons and honestly inspiring to see how it could connect with the reader who is struggling with similar problems. The development of various villains was subverting and unexpected. You will not get any tired trops about good vs evil. No, there is depth and mystery behind all motivations which makes you just keep turning the pages. We get a much deeper peek into the parshendi and the complexity of their society and their subjugation to both humans and the Fused. Tantalizing information gets dropped on the reader about Wit, Szeth and Taravangian. There are just so many story elements that start stitching together and it was totally exhilarating to see thing start coming together. Of course, Rhythm of War is not a perfect book. My opinion mirrors those of others: there's a slog at the 3/4 mark and pacing goes stagnant. Some flashbacks aren't all that engrossing and some characters like Eshonai and Venli can be pretty stale. The Navani and Kaladin plot lines also get stagnant during this. There isn't a whole lot of action in this book compared to other Stormlight books and there seemed to be an inverse Sanderson avalanche. Most war action happens upfront and the ending has off stage action. Having said that, the reader is offered a tremendous amount of other content and development. I'd also like to offer my advice about reading order of the cosmere. I read the Stormlight Archive last and it really paid off. I think starting with either stand alone, Elantris or Warbreaker, is a good move. Then move to the first Mistborn trilogy. Then back to either Elantris or Warbreaker. I think after those, reading Arcanum Unbounded is the right move. After which, diving into the Stormlight Archive will really pay off. But of course, you can read any of these books in any order and it will work out. Love it! There's nothing more to say. This is one of the best, if not THE best, fantasy series ever written.

** spoiler alert ** This is... most certainly a book. A good book. A good, long book. I feel many will like it, many will love it. I am not one of those people. This book exposes the one chink in brandon's armor, the one weakness in his otherwise brilliant and commendable writing style, drive, and ambition. It highlights a concern that I've harbored for a time, but more on that later. First, I want to give this book its due praise. It consists of pretty much everything you might look for in a Sanderson book. We've got characters that are not only deep and interesting, but fun to read about. We have a superb world, built to hold under 'scientific' scrutiny. And of course we can't forget about the Sanderlanche, which made me write this review under the influence of sleep depravity, as i could not put it down until 3 am. I don't want to dive deeper into what made this book good, because those praises are very predictable, having been said a thousand times over. This book will arrive to the destination you expect it to get to, but as many characters are so fond of saying in this series; journey before destination. The journey in this case has exactly what you expect it to have, all the twists and turns in the road we have all became fond of. It makes the book predictable. Not quite boring, just unsatisfying and much less interesting. The strife of some characters, mainly Shallan and Kaladin just feel like they are going through the motions. Again. Collectively, at this point, the series consists of over four thousand pages. Each of these characters have gotten more page space than most main characters in more traditional fantasy stories. Those two have made a step forward, yes, they've been transformed. But every book seems like they make two steps forward and one step back. That's technically moving forward, but I have personally felt so fatigued and fed up with them that... I just didn't care as much anymore. Yes, in real life depression and DID doesn't just go away like that and their experience in this series is a realistic one. But there's a reason why fiction doesn't follow its real life examples to the letter. I can very much appreciate what Sanderson did and does for the depiction of mental illnesses for and in the fantasy community, as it expands the boundary of fantasy and with it, human imagination. It begs the question though, if this dynamic shifting back and forth, the struggle these characters show with their mental states, if it becomes constant and viewed over a longer period of time, does it not become monotone? A single note, played until it has far since overstayed its welcome? There is a way Sanderson could overcome this obstacle. The old nihilistic adage of what doesn't kill me makes me stronger, only applies as long as what doesn't kill me doesn't break me, as well. That is something Sanderson makes apparent not only through Kaladin, but the heralds and the Fused as well. And they are broken, but these heroes persist despite it all. They are in a way such traditional heroes, that their struggle feels like there are no stakes to them. I was never afraid for any of the characters, my lethargy to their conflicts was so strong that i couldn't even muster an eye roll at the predictable path and resolution they were walking towards. Navani is a bondsmith, no duh. The tower will survive, no duh. Kaladin will survive and regain his strength, saving the day, no duh. Shallan will stay, no duh. If Sanderson would kill of one of the main characters, or at least let Shallan leave, driving in the point above, it would build up the stakes to a similar height that they were in Oathbringer. Though I suspect that was never the point of this book, i feel it will be a big hurdle in the future because that d0es make the book boring. So what is the point of the book? In my honest opinion, Sanderson has a vision for how he wants the first part of this series to end, but in order to achieve it he needs to have certain concepts explained. This book essentially contains a myriad of small info dumps and really make the world come together. I was grateful for this, at first, because he has always been excellent at worldbuilding and it is one of the best parts of SA, but it quickly felt undeserved and, for the most part, unimportant. Roshar is a planet, and there are other planets! And the characters are all like, wow, that's cool, it totally shatters my worldview, but then they proceed as if nothing has happened. This is why i think Shallan of all people should have left with the ghostbloods, because her curious nature combined with the pain from her past could and should have driven her towards them. It just feels so cliche to have her reject that offer and choose the side love and honor and be a good little girl that knows her place. It would have raised the stakes for other characters, showing that Sanderson isn't afraid to stray from his own mould. Instead she slips back into her own monotony, a little better, more complete as a person overall (literally, in her case), but that's more of a narrative trick at this point, than anything else. Speaking of which, i think it's really ironic how he has Hoid spouting off about doing the kansas city shuffle, but then refuses to do anything but the most obvious for all of the characters. Well, with the exception of one. This is of course entirely subjective and maybe I have in my love for Sanderson's work got to know and understand him, at least the writer part. And so i can anticipate his next move. Perhaps that is the burden of knowledge, losing the excitement fueled by curiosity of the unknown. Though I very much hope that, like the Fused, like Raboniel, I too will be surprised. On the other hand, however, there are certain things you might expect from Sanderson that just aren't here. There have been a few theories that people have gone mad over since Oathbringer. The two main ones that i remember the most are that the Sibling is of both honor and cultivation and that it resides in Urithiru, and that the fourth ideal gives access to shardplate. Both of these things are confirmed so anticlimactically that i felt disappointed. Yes, Kaladin still has a pretty epic and emotional acquisition of it, but we all knew it was coming after it was so anticlimactically announced. I didn't expect Taravangian to become Odium. This is again very subjective but I didn't like that part. I mean, i did, i really did, but i didn't like how Rayse has been simply brushed off after three thousand pages, more, of building him up. Though I suppose the stakes have been raised because of it. It shows another problem that happens to a lot of characters where things just feel too convenient for them. From Adolin suddenly thinking of asking for a trial against the spren, to nightblood and taravangian being in the right spot at the right time. And i do understand that there are things involved here, like seeing the future and so on, but it just feels so damn convenient. Sanderson pretty much explains a lot of the world and the underlying principles of the cosmere, except the one that actually matters here, which is how was Taravangian able to draw nightblood without it killing him immediately AND transferring it into the spiritual realm to stab Rayse. It feels so fake to have both of these characters squirm and obsess with what they are going to do next, but then at the last moment they have this shining revelation. Which would be fine, except neither Adolin nor the sympathetic Taravangian fit this character type. Despite the fact that i stayed glued to the page for the last part of the book, I felt that Sanderson has been emotionally manipulating me, showing me the things I want to see, giving me my destination, but the journey felt empty. You can't spend time with characters and not care about them for this long, but this feels more like an old ex trying to play on your emotions to lure you into their embrace, which might feel good for a time, but as soon as the infatuation wears out, you see them for their true, empty self. That is how i feel towards this book. I could go on with describing the sometimes awkward dialogue, but that would be nitpicking, i feel. Though i mention it to further support this next point. Even this awkward dialogue, usually between two people discussing something very personal and intimate, used to serve in Brandon's benefit. In Mistborn it was endearing and kind of cute. Here it's sloppy. Rushed. And that is my main gripe with this book and my main concern, as i mentioned in the first paragraph. This whole book feels like that. It isn't as tight as some of his other works, and considering its his latest, it should be pretty high up on the list. But it's not. Now, I'm not demanding perfection every time, as i feel Oathbringer has been. My concern stems from some of the things Sanderson has said previously as well as on the release party video you can find on his youtube channel. He said that for every story that he tells, there are a thousand that he won't get to. And i think that scares him. Or at least gives him some sort of anxiety. I wholeheartedly empathise and sympathise with him, but i fear its starting to show on his work. Dawnshard was sloppy. Rhythm of War was sloppy. And i can only hope that it's not because of some Brandon's inner termoil, but because of outstanding circumstances. Such as covid-19. He has said that his team worked very hard to get this out this soon, and maybe they got a bit sloppy too. Maybe his speed of writing is making him rush to finish it and as many other stories as he possibly can. I think his team is both an asset and a hindrance for his works, because he is suddenly dependent on them to tell a good story. We have seen something like this influence his writing before, like when he postponed the continuation of Mistborn in favor of Skyward, because he wanted to give his other publisher something to publish. This is something that has been seen time and time again, mostly with big corporations, that as your influence expands you start to become dependent on other people, you start surrendering your power to them. I feel its unfair that Brandon gets all the love for the stories he writes, despite the fact that he does try very hard to get the people who have worked WITH him on them to get some of the recognition. But the more popular he gets, the bigger his team will get and his dependence on their performance increases. If he does not keep a tight grip on the reins, both for his team and for himself, i feel the coming stories will just get sloppier and more rushed. That is not to say that i think this more collective way of producing stories is wrong, quite the opposite. But it comes with a set of weaknesses as well, which one should be mindful of. All in all, I can not see into the future but only speculate on it, and in this world i have seen this same spiraling pattern too many times. Perhaps, and i hope that it will, my pessimism will hold no ground, but that is also the reason why i'm writing this long essay on the subject. I am eager to look at it in the future, seeing how my concerns held up. Perhaps this book is, at least to me, going to be a black sheep, a necessary sacrifice to bring the first half of the series to its spectacular conclusion. Whatever the case may be, i look forward to the next installments and despite my bad rating, this is very obviously a must read for a cosmere/Sanderson fan, and it is despite all its shortcomings, still a very good book. But it's just not a very good Sanderson book.

4.75/5 Stars Craaazyyyy I won't delve too deep into this because it is simply too vast to cover everything. This book was great! I liked it more than Oathbringer. It’s been a while. Time to shake off the cobwebs. 😅 Rando thoughts on the 4th Stormlight Archive Saga incoming: What really makes this installment stand out is how the weight of the war is carried by the characters we’ve grown to love. Kaladin’s journey hits especially hard this time; watching him battle his internal darkness while trying to revolutionize mental health care for his fellow soldiers—all while navigating complex connections with his family was incredibly moving. ---> Let me shoehorn a holy smokes moment here at the end of this thought: what an “ideal” way to showcase Kal’s wonderful “fourth” coming acceptance. You could say at this moment, I was “running” with the “wind” to finish the story. Even at the detriment of sleep. Who needs it anyhow? 😉 Okay, back at it... Adolin is the ultimate MVP. Even as he questions his place in the world, his unwavering loyalty and his shift from graceful brawn to negotiator during the trial in Lasting Integrity show that you don't need a formal bond to be a hero. It was a Sanderlanche story arc that didn't require swords, shields, or bridges. The research in the tower, spearheaded by Navani, was a fascinating plot device as well. Her back-and-forth with Raboniel and the many revelations discovered were major highlights, finally giving her the recognition as a scholar she has always deserved. On the political front, Jasnah is a total powerhouse in her new role, showing us exactly how terrifyingly effective she is on the battlefield. Meanwhile, Dalinar continues to hold the coalition together through sheer force of will and highly adaptable bond powers against the shifting shadow of Odium. It is impossible to list everything that makes this book so great, but I’ll mention a few other standouts. Seeing the world through Venli and the flashbacks of Eshonai added a tragic, beautiful layer of empathy for the Singers that changed how I view the entire conflict. Additionally, Shallan continues to face her truths with a courage that is both heartbreaking and inspiring; watching her battle her internal personalities was extremely satisfying. While some personas stay hidden and others shine, it’s always fun to see how they navigate the world and provide emotional resonance. I also have to mention one of my favorites, Lift, who provides a much-needed spark of light in the darkness. And, as always, Wit arrives at just the right moment with a story to remind us that even when the rhythm changes, the song goes on. (preferably by flute) Lastly, what really surprised me, was the last chapter (One Final Gift)—it was probably my favorite of the entire book. Reading this was a deeply personal journey. I laughed, I unapologetically teared up, and I cheered for every small triumph. It reaffirmed why I adore this series: its that special blend of colossal, world-scale conflict with intimate, human stories. I finished the book both devastated by its sorrows and delighted by its triumphs—an experience I’ll cherish until the next storm.
Did I finish this book or did this book finish me?

I received and ARC of this book through my former publisher as a favor, no promises to write an honest review required, but here's one anyway: There may be minor spoilers ahead, depending on what you consider to be a spoiler. Okaaaaaay, it's been a week since release, so I'll post a little more in-depth a review than "it was really good." First off there were a couple of things I didn't really care for in the book, so lets get those out of the way first thing. This book is longer than it needs to be. There are several scenes that could flat out be cut without any impact on story or characters, and dozens more that could be trimmed down considerably to greater effect than you get with them as they currently are. This book is long for the sake of being long, and not because it's necessary to the development of the plot, characters or world. It kind of feels like the editors might have been a little hesitant in suggesting things to be cut or condensed to Sanderson, as tends to start happening when an author reaches a certain level of popularity. Second, Sanderson tried somewhat to humanize Jasnah in this book, but failed at it. Hard. And even if he had succeeded, it's too little too late. This is book 4. She needed to be humanized in book 1. Even Elhokar, who was a pretty one-dimensional character in book 1 was shown to be a human being with flaws. I really, really dislike this character. Because she's not a character. She's a plot device. She exists within the story to be perfect at everything and to know everything. The fact that there's nothing more to her character than that has been grating on me since book 1. She is rarely, if ever, shown to have any sort of flaws. She is rarely, if ever, shown to work for her knowledge and skills. She never fails at anything. Because of that she is painfully uninteresting, and she's really kind of a dick on top of it. Okay, on to the good. This book has a bit of a change in format from the previous 3 in the series. First, there is a time skip between the previous book and this one of a year, where the first three books took place immediately after one another. And second, the flashbacks that feature heavily in the series do not begin until about halfway through this book, rather than right at the beginning like the other books. There are also far fewer flashback (and a few continuity errors in them with events in Words of Radiance, though I did read an ARC, so those may have been fixed before final publication.) The flashbacks are, in my opinion, the best of the series so far. Seeing how Eshonai began as a young girl with a burning curiosity about the world outside of her people’s chosen place of exile, and her desires to map the whole world, and Venli’s jealousy of her, and desires to outdo her older sister leading to the downfall of their people. Every step in the journey from nomadic people to those who summoned a dark god out of desperation is so logical and tragic. One of the themes of this series is the human cost of war, and I think that these flashbacks better illustrate that concept than any other part of this series. And Eshonai’s final scene is a bit of a tear jerker too, when you think of what she began as, what she became, and how it all ended for her. This book is really brutal to some of its characters, Kaladin and Shalan more than most others. You’d think that these characters had been through enough by this time, but they get dragged through it again, and much harder than they have before. This is a very dark and painful book for many characters, but these two especially. I won’t say how things turn out in the end for them, but lets just say that a lot of things these characters have been dealing with are resolved in one way or another. I will give this warning: As someone who suffers from PTSD myself, there are some extremely difficult sections of this book to get through, because it's like having a light shine down on all of the darkest, and hardest to face things in my life that resulted in my PTSD. I appreciate that Sanderson did his research, and so realistically portrays PTSD in this book, but as someone with PTSD, it's hard to get through. It was really painful to me, and if ever I choose to reread this book, I will probably skip those sections of it, because of how it made me feel, and what it made me remember. One of the most difficult things to accept about having PTSD is that it's alright to feel the way you do. It doesn't make you less of a person to have these horrible things in your past that have broken you. It's all right to accept that, and to move on. But acceptance doesn't make it go away, it just makes it easier to live with, and every now and then, you come across something like this book. And it drags it all back out of you again. The standout character in this book, for me, was Navani. She is fleshed out quite a bit in this book, and I really like what Sanderson does with her here, as a leader under occupation. She shows that she’s not just a wife of a prominent character and eccentric inventor, she’s her own character, independent of those she’s been attached to throughout the series. She makes some very interesting and profound revelations in the later third of the book that basically change everything. Sanderson continues to casually shatter my every expectation for this series. Adolin and Shalan make some very, very profound revelations in their storyline. Navani makes more. And holy crap that thing at the end with Odium! I bet NO ONE was expecting THAT to happen. By the end of the book, literally everything you know is wrong, or turned upside down in some way. I’ve always had a very strong dislike for Shalan. She was presented as one of the main viewpoint characters in the first book, and utterly failed to be relevant to that book in any way. It was a bad first impression. She was much more relevant to events in the second book, and I thought, hey, maybe I could get to like her if she kept on like this. Then she completely backtracked every shred of character development she’d made in the second book once the third one came along, and SO MUCH of that book was devoted to her that my strong dislike returned and grew deeper. This book does not do much to fix that. She’s worse in this book than she was in Oathbringer, but luckily her part is much, much smaller in this book than it was in the previous one, and led to some more profound revelations. HOWEVER when you find out what she’s been hung up on this whole time, you’re probably going to facepalm. It’s dumb. It’s really, really dumb. (view spoiler) I know she’s got her fans, and those fans will likely enjoy the conclusion to her story in this book, but it just solidified my dislike of her that much further. Another thing I have to complain about here is Kaladin. I totally understand why a lot of people don't like him. He's kind of whiny, and his constant depression gets old fast. But there are much bigger problems with his character than that. The biggest problem is that he only really gives the ILLUSION of developing as a character, while not actually developing as one. Shallan has the same problem. She'll deal with her shit, and then at the beginning of the next book, BAM, back dealing with THE EXACT SAME SHIT. Kaladin is the same. He has had THE EXACT SAME CHARACTER ARC IN EVERY SINGLE BOOK IN THIS SERIES. He's depressed. He finds the strength within himself to rise above it and endure. He moves on to the next stage of his life. But the problem here, is that the next stage of his life is ALWAYS the exact same stage of his life. He's followed this pattern in every single book in this series so far. It was actually a little underwhelming at the end of the first book, if I'm being honest. It was great at the end of the second book. But then the exact same thing happened in the third book. And then the exact same thing happened in the fourth book. He's gone on the exact same journey as a character FOUR FREAKING TIMES IN A ROW NOW!!! Don't get me wrong. It's GREAT character development. The problem is that every time he triumphs over his inner demons at the end of a book, he just reverts back completely at the beginning of the next book. He gives the illusion of making progress, but all he's doing is running on a freaking treadmill. After four books of this, it's really getting old. Can he PLEASE, for the love of god, HAVE SOMETHING ELSE TO DO IN THE NEXT BOOK OTHER THAN DEALING WITH HIS DEPRESSION YET AGAIN!!!!!!! So, all in all, this book is pretty good. I’d say it’s the second best of the series. My rankings go Words of Radiance > Rhythm of War > The Way of Kings > Oathbringer. It’s not without a few small flaws that are easily forgiven considering how good everything else in the book is. It has some very emotional moments, and literally turns everything on its head. Again. Definitely a must read for any Sanderson fan.

Full Video Review Here: https://youtu.be/0rywqezOoZg Spoiler Talk Here: https://youtu.be/0Ny6JtrDfzc Rhythm of War is the case of unreasonable expectations that haven't been seen since...well, 3 years ago when Oathbringer came out. Words of Radiance is one of my favorite fantasy books ever written, so my hopes were through the roof and Oathbringer didn't quite hit them. So I went into RoW with tempered expectations. And even with that in mind, it was still a mixed bag in this fourth rolling storm through Roshar. The biggest hindrance to this book for me is two-fold; first I never was able to connect with the flashback character, Venli, or her backstory. Again, the bar was very high after Kaladin, Shallan, and Dalinar prior to this one. But the flashbacks also being so heavily centered towards the middle of this book made the second act a slog to get through at times. Part III of this book is my least favorite Part of any Stormlight book up to this point. But it was mostly a structure thing, as I feel if the flashbacks had been more spread out evenly over the book as Sanderson had done previously it might have landed better. My second issue is that unless you have a PhD in science, you're going to glaze over many of the Navani chapters. It's all very important information and it has a purpose in being here, it just doesn't make for a very exciting read when you feel like you're taking a trip back to college for that science credit you never received. Thankfully, the rest of the book is mostly par for the course from Sanderson and that means he shows why he's still arguably the best in the game right now. The arcs for Navani, Kaladin, and Shallan in this book met every expectation and even exceeded them in some cases. Taravangian finally gets a central part of story I've been begging for since book 2. Parts I, II, and V are everything you'd hope for in a Stormlight adventure. This book does feel its length many times and it does have those moments where you'll question if Sanderson is fluffing things up to ensure that it was as long as the previous book. Truly, a lot of this story I felt he did better the first time he wrote them. Back then they were called The Gathering Storm and Towers of Midnight. Those who know...know. In the end, this is my least favorite Stormlight book yet. However I think the worst Stormlight book is better than most series best book. The Willshaper order and Venli/Eshonai/The Singers just really never moved the needle for me. But with book 5 closing this arc and focusing on Szeth and the Skybreakers, I'm every bit as excited for the next trip to this universe as I ever was. Rhythm of War has more good than bad and I mostly enjoyed it and think you will, too.

Check it out here. *** 3 stars **Although this is a spoiler free review (spoilers are hidden), there may be spoilers for previous books in series (scroll down)** “Integrity doesn’t stop men from killing, Brightness, ... It just makes them use different justifications.” Rhythm of War definitely went in a way that was unexpected to say the least, though I believe many people will enjoy this new direction, it caused me to not fall in love as much with this instalment as I did with the other ones. I loved so many segments in this book, but truth is, these POVs were rare as the focus was on two characters that I really didn't feel like following most of the time... but we'll get into that later. Still. I really really liked this book and once again am in awe of Sanderson's storytelling abilities. The major aspect of this book that I didn't enjoy as much as the others was that we spent so much time with Navani and Kaladin. Shocker, I know. Despite loving the epic Kaladin/Navani moments towards the end, I just didn't want to spend the majority of the book focusing on them. Since The Way of Kings Navani put a bad taste in my mouth, and frankly I did not care about her in any other book (and then she was rude to Evi so...), meanwhile Kaladin just steals the spotlight all the time and I wanted to really get more of Venli (this was supposed to be her/Eshonai's 'book')... but she is overshadowed by Kaladin. Again, I feel like a lot of people will like this because Kal is a fan favorite, but it was just tiring for me. I felt like Venli had so much potential, and while Sanderson did deliver, I kind of wished we would have gotten more her, less Kaladin. The aspect in which this book shone was the world expansion. Note: although it isn't necessary to read Sanderson's other works, I would definitely say read Mistborn ERA 1 (Era 2 reveals something about the Ghostbloods and their mission), and Warbreaker at least. (I would also encourage people to read Sixth of the Dusk, Elantris, and White Sand volumes 1-3, but these aren't as prevalent as Era 1 and Warbreaker). Without this knowledge, I think the story is still very much enjoyable, but having that extra knowledge really kept me on the tip of my toes wondering about what different connections meant. Intrigue was really high in this novel, but most of it relied on Navani... and I just don't care about Navani. The most enjoyable segment in my opinion is the Adolin/Shallan segment as they travel into Shadesmar for reasons. Although I usually find Shallan tiring, I really liked her in this book (most of the time). I liked seeing her and Adolin supporting each other and figuring their way through the world of spren, their traditions, politics, secrets, etc. It was great, can't really say more without spoilers, but shame that we got so relatively little of it... because of Kaladin/Navani. The last group of joined POVs are Dalinar/Jasnah, and they were in this book much less than I thought they would be. Usually, Dalinar steals the show in my mind, but Jasnah's moments were epic. Seeing her become the queen and try to break the gender stereotypes of Roshar was really interesting. Her relation to Wit also opened a doorway for world expansion (which was much more enjoyable that Navani might I add) and I was just really amazed at her. Come to think of it, there are things in Jasnah's past that we don't exactly know about, and I really wish we'd get more from her in book 5. I'd also like to give a few spoiler-free thoughts on the beginning/ending. Whereas a lot of people rave about the fast-paced beginning, I must admit I liked the ending more, despite there not being a Sander-avalanche occurring. Then again, this might be because Kaladin/Navani really take the book by storm in the beginning... but they're basically done by the end. TL;DR? Great story, but too much Kaladin/Navani for my taste. This is the fourth instalment in The Stormlight Archive series. Dalinar Kholin and his Knights Radiant are engaged in a seemingly unwinnable war. Time passes, little changes, and more lives are lost. They need to find an advantage to fend off their enemies and Navani Kholin might just be the one to unearth it. So much was revealed here that made reading the previous three, epic series instalments feel like scaling a mountain and reading this book feel like cresting the clouds and finally reaching the peak. I'm not sure if I was breathless from the thin air or from my open-mouthed awe at all Sanderson delivered! The final chapters were not only thrilling and well executed but they each incorporated a series of perspectives, whereas most previous ones only contained one or two viewpoints. The quick shifts between them kept the pace high, my intrigue piqued, and the suspense at a maximum. I honestly had no idea what would occur, and which characters would be lost during each scene, but loved the path that was taken. A conclusion to this story arc was granted but there was also a future hinted at for many of the characters. It left me excited to continue on with them, in new adventures and new settings, and to see what else Sanderson can reveal about his epic and awe-inspiring Cosmere creation.

Rhythm of War is the fourth entry of the great stormlight archives saga from Brandon Sanderson. The first time I read a book from Brandon Sanderson was in 2007 and although many years had passed his talent had never dwindled. In 2015 I read the way of kings and Words of radiance in a row and needless to say WOR was for me the perfect fantasy book my favorite by far. Alas I found Oathbringer a letdown. Although Oathbringer is a good book by my standards it didn’t live up to my expectations and the level set by WOR. I had high expectations for ROW and Brandon Sanderson deliver not only a great sequel but a book whose quality excelled WOR. The force of ROW is the change of POV. The first three books evolved mainly and too much for my taste around Shallan. Needless to say I was happy to see her less. Yes she’s a great character but I think it was time to see something else and Sanderson did it. He brought in light some background characters and it was a great move. Navani Kholin is Dalinar’s wife but also the head of the scholars. ROW is the path where she had to decide if she becomes true to herself or let others decide in her place. Adolin Kholin is the elder son of Dalinar and unlike his little brother isn’t radiant. After some unfortunate events he needs to prove his value to his father. Dalinar will give him a difficult task convince the honorsprens to work again with the humans. An almost impossible task especially after the recreance when thousands of sprens died. Venli is Eshonai’s sister or more accurately the last listener. After betraying her people , Venli is working with the gods her people had run away from long time ago. She struggles between two paths , her legacy and the new way with the fused. She hid a secret from everyone and maybe it will become her salvation. ROW is a powerful entry in the stormlight books, fast paced and everything is relevant. I won’t add more because I’m too afraid to spoil but I’m looking forward to read the last book of the first arc.

"You can bear it. You can remember it. Our weakness doesn't make us weak. Our weakness make us strong. For we had to carry it all these years." Rhythm of War reminded me of why the Stormlight Archive series was always where I looked to when I needed to be inspired, its characters were whom I turned to when I was in need of remembrance of what strength and courage really was. It was somewhat different from the previous books, especially from Oathbringer. In Oathbringer I got my mind blown over and over by the continuous revelations, the actions and events was an avalanche of overwhelming tensions. But in Rhythm of War, the revelations lead to pile and pile of questions, the world of Roshar had exploded by the cosmere convergence, because from now on we were officially trodding on the scale of universe and its enormous mysteries. If one had to acknowledge every aspect of a book, Rhythm of War granted was slower in pace, there were some parts that dragged and slogged its way on. This fourth book was where fantasy met science, where magic, technology and art blended into something truly wonderful. Yeah maybe Navani's part was a tad too technical at times, though personally I enjoyed it, I found the whole explanation of the mechanism of fabrials, to be very intriguing even when I didn't understand it. The whole part with the concept and properties of light and music, and how Navani discovered, invented the Rhythm of War and other lights was one of my favorite in the whole series. I was totally struck and stunned by how amazing, how brilliant a mind Sanderson had. I always loved how his magic system had sense, in each and every book he had written, the magic system was a conjuration of imagination and science, it was always crafted masterfully with absolute care. Rhythm of War was also distinct from the predecessors due to its weighty topic of mental illness. The portrayal of depression, PTSD, loneliness, personality dissociative disorder was handled in a very thoughtful, in depth with the perfect amount of balance. It didn't only show readers how life was for people who struggled through it but also how was it for the family and friends who watched their loved ones fought through it, who couldn't do much directly. Personally in this case, Kaladin's struggle through his darkness was pretty relatable to me. The truth was some things could only be understood by people who had gone through the same thing in their life. Depression despite being one of the mental illness suffered by quite the amount of people in the world was still misunderstood and judged with lots of misconception, even intolerance, unkind or direct hostility. It tore relationships because family and friends were helpless and unable to understand. Sometimes acceptance was more important than understanding, that sometimes, really, the presence of support, love and patience, of being there was everything and enough for the person who suffered MI to know and have. This was a very delicate and sensitive issue as people could be so judgmental, and Sanderson did a very impressive job of juggling the balance. Shallan's MI and Adolin's genuine love and support was so moving and inspiring. The characters development was not limited to the characters who fought traumatic events though, but also the other POVs and side characters. This fourth book was the heaviest one in personal development yet. It's all about choices, the ability to change, to grow, about potential, about redemption. It's about overcoming challenges, weaknesses, the past, keeping moving, taking the next step, even just one step at a time, it's about journey before destination, strength before weakness, life before death. "No man can judge another man's heart or trials, for no man can truly know them." The Stormlight Archive series was simply something else for me. I wouldn't say that every book written by Sanderson was my favorite. In fact, some of his books despite being brilliant in every way technically, didn't truly connect with me. But with Stormlight Archive, it just touched me in a very fundamental way, the world and all the characters were so, absolutely significant to me, I was beyond invested, it was always able to leave such impact. And Rhythm of War was simply a perfection. It was just truly dazzling in its powerful, meaningful themes; majestic in its grand scale of plots and vast stories, its complex world-building; remarkable in its meticulous, painstaking details, the way the lines and points met; marvelous in its endless mystery, the way it never stop to amaze, to surprise, magical in its genuine; heart-wrenching way to provoke, inspire emotions, breaking and healing hearts; radiant in its prompting, coaxing to make us think, question, ponder about everything. "This is life, and I will not lie by saying everyday will be sunshine. But there will be sunshine again, and that's a very different thing to say. That is the truth." "If we can choose, we can change."

I received a free advance copy from NetGalley for review. Ocean Spray? What kind of a name is that for a book? What’s it about? The history of the drink? Or is it a biography of the guy who made the viral video of him skateboarding and drinking Ocean Spray while he lip synced that Fleetwood Mac song? I mean, that was cool and all, but how are you gonnna do a whole book about… What’s that? It’s not Ocean SPRAY, but instead it’s Ocean PREY? Well, that sounds like a John Sandford title. Oh. It is a John Sandford novel. That makes a lot more sense. A Coast Guard patrol runs across what appears to be drug runners doing a pick-up of previously submerged dope out of the ocean using a scuba diver off the coast of Miami. A shootout ensues that leaves several Coast Guard guys dead while the bad guys got away. Months later the FBI and local cops still have no clue as to who was behind it, and the prevailing theory is that there’s still a fortune in drugs waiting to be picked up once the heat dies down. US Marshal Lucas Davenport gets asked to join the investigation by one of his political patrons in DC, and he quickly starts leaning on local dealers trying to get a lead on who might have been involved with the drug ring. As usual in a Davenport case, things start to get sticky, and when Lucas needs more help he turns to his old buddy, Virgil Flowers (a/k/a That fuckin’ Flowers.) to help him crack the case. I’ve written so many Sandford reviews that I can’t think of a single new thing to say about why this one is another great crime thriller from one of my favorites in the genre. As usual, there’s solid plotting and tension mixed with just enough real world verisimilitude regarding police work and the political factors behind it to make it feel grounded and believable despite a plot that could easily turn into an action movie from the ‘80s. All the things I love about Sandford’s novels are on display here. However, there are some very different things in this one. For one, ever since Sandford shifted Davenport from a Minnesota state cop to a US Marshal, he’s been sending Lucas on assignments across the country, and that has enabled him to do some different things with this series while still sticking to the parts that made it popular to begin with. Moving from typically land locked Midwestern settings to a Florida one that has a lot to do with boats and scuba diving makes it feel like Sandford is doing new things rather than just repeating himself. That’s just the window dressing though, and the biggest difference from previous Prey novels comes in the structure itself. In the past, Lucas was the star of the these books, and then there was the spin-off series featuring Virgil Flowers as the lead. They existed in the same universe with some crossover between them, but generally one of the characters was the focus with the other being a supporting player. However, in this Lucas is the focus in the first third with Virgil taking over the next part, and the last act shifts between them both. I assume that this is because Sandford has said that he’s only going to do one book a year from now on*, and it seems like he folded Virgil into Davenport’s story much like Robert Crais began splitting time between Elvis Cole and Joe Pike in his novels. That gives this book a hybrid feel in that it doesn’t entirely seem like a Davenport novel, and yet it’s not exactly Virgil’s book either. It’s a little odd. Not bad, just different. Sandford is in his late 70s now, and he’s written about 50 novels after a career as a Pulitzer Prize winning journalist. If he had decided to retire completely, he’d have more than earned the right to do so at this point. So if I can get some more of his stories because he’s cutting his work load and figuring out a way to combine his two most popular characters, you won’t hear me complaining about it. Aside from all that, if someone had never read another Sandford book and just picked this one up, I think they’d find it an entertaining crime novel with some great twists as well as an interesting premise with the angle of the bad guys trying to find a way to retrieve a fortune in drugs from the ocean. *Correction: I originally said that Sandford would only be doing the Davenport series from now on, but apparently plan is for him to scale book to one book a year while alternating the Prey and Virgil Flowers books.

John Sanford brings investigation, action, surveillance, and suspense to the latest book in the Prey series. An off-duty Coast Guardsman, Barney Hall, and his family are fishing off the coast of Fort Lauderdale when he calls in suspicious activity to the watch officer. A boat appears to be picking up a lone diver in the middle of the ocean. When the three guardsmen sent to investigate are killed, the FBI is called in. However, when its investigation stalls, a U.S. Senator from Florida convinces Lucas Davenport, a U.S. Marshall, to become part of the task force and resolve it. Lucas partners will Bob Matees, another Marshall, to assist the investigation. Later on, Virgil Flowers, who used to work for Lucas at the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, joins the task force as well. What were the diver and the men in the boat that murdered the guardsmen doing? Two fantastic characters come together when Lucas Davenport and Virgil Flowers team up. Their personalities and approaches to an investigation are very different. However, both have depth. Lucas is a character whose methods I sometimes disagree with. He has plenty of good qualities and always tries to do the right thing. Virgil pursues a legal solution and he also has the ability to think like a criminal. The story is part investigation and part action thriller. The opening is strong, intriguing, and impactful. This disturbing event hooked me and immediately drew me into the novel. A suspenseful narrative provides plenty of opportunities for things to go wrong. The first dive scene was especially impactful, visual, and somewhat nerve-racking. The story takes readers from Florida, New Jersey, and Washington D.C. Sandford’s writing is always great, but his world-building in the dive scenes in this novel was fantastic. He’s a superb storyteller who kept me on the edge of seat as the investigation and action unfolded. The dialogue deepened the conflict and pulled this reader into the inner world of the characters. There was a strong sense of place causing me to feel transported, as though living the events alongside the characters. The final action scenes are riveting and high-powered, and the epilogue does a great job of tying up the loose ends. Overall, this was suspenseful and action packed with compelling characters that kept me turning the pages. It’s a great series and I’m looking forward to reading the next one in both this series and the Virgil Flowers series. PENGUIN GROUP Putnam, G.P. Putnam's Sons and John Sandford provided a complimentary digital ARC of this novel via NetGalley. This is my honest review. Opinions are mine alone and are not biased in any way. Publication date is currently set for April 13, 2022. This review was originally posted at Mystery and Suspense Magazine. ----------------------- My 4 star review will be posted 3-4 days after it appears in Mystery and Suspense Magazine.

I first started listening to John Sandford’s Prey series of books some ten years ago, I would say that JS provided my introduction to audiobooks as my local library seemed to stock a whole bunch of his titles. The front man is a smooth but tough Minnesota lawman called Lucas Davenport who is equally likely to admire your English leather shoes or punch you in the gut – whichever takes his fancy. This is the 43rd book in the series (if you include books featuring his sidekick Virgil Flowers) and you might expect it all to start feeling tired by now. But Sandford has managed to keep it fresh by regularly updating the cast of support characters, by expanding the role of Lucas – so that now he operates across the whole of the United States rather than just statewide – and finally by keeping each story largely standalone he allows easy access to the series without the incumbrance of having to know (or learn) a whole bunch of carry-over baggage. Here Lucas and Virgil team up to hunt down a gang of drug smugglers who have shot and killed three Coast Guard Officers down in South Florida. In truth, the first half of this tale is somewhat lumbering as the groundwork is set for the action to come. I found myself crying out for Lucas to go and intimidate someone or maybe even shoot them – it’s what he really does best. But eventually it all takes off, and once the action starts it’s unremitting. I won’t go into the detail of it – why spoil the fun for future readers – but I will say that there’s a good deal of scuba diving (a new skill developed by Virgil), some great interplay between the undercover law enforcement officers and the criminals and finally the tension is racked up sky high as the inevitable climax approaches. If I were new to this author I wouldn’t start here – it’s not actually his best book and it’s really worthwhile getting to know Lucas and Virgil when they were younger and a little greener – but equally it really is accessible as a first read. I enjoyed it, as I always do with this writer, and I’ll be definitely be dialling back in for book 44 in due course.

This one had me worried. So much excitement at the end. Also, this one was heartbreaking. Did I shed a tear or two...absolutely! A Coast Guardsman is fishing with his family when he notices a suspicious boat. Since he is off duty, he calls it in. When three Guardsmen come to take a closer look, they are all murdered. The FBI starts an investigation but the trail fizzles out. So when the FBI can't find find anything, Lucas gets involved but he won't go in alone. Rae, Bob, Virgil, Jane Chase, and Louis Mallard all make an appearance. We also get new characters including Andres Devlin and Dale Weaver who were both a good addition to the cast. Finally, after 3 years and 31 books, I'm finally caught up with this series just in time for Righteous Prey. Cliffhanger: No 4/5 Fangs MrsLeif's Two Fangs About It | Facebook | Twitter | Instagram

Overall, a good police detective novel featuring Lucas Davenport and Virgil Flowers, evidently recurring characters separately in series by the author, together in this one. [Warning: some spoilers possibly] The book caught my interest since it involved an effort to solve a case involving the deaths of 3 Coast Guardsmen during a counter narcotics vessel boarding gone awry. After months of a Federal task force fruitless in their efforts to solve the crime and bring the murderers to justice, Davenport and Flowers are brought in at the request of one of Florida’s senators. Since this novel is one in the middle of a series of them involving both characters, it doesn’t go much into detail on their backgrounds, assuming readers are already familiar with them. Not a barrier to enjoying this book, but, for example, both seem to be from the Minnesota Department of Investigations, a state agency yet both are quickly deputized as US Marshals to join the task force. Seems odd, but there’s probably a back story to this that’s not explained in the novel. The first third of the book gets a little slow as Davenport and associates do the less glamorous work of investigation and evidence gathering. From there , it picks up as he finds leads in the investigation that eventually lead to introducing Flowers and another Marshal, Rae, a black woman, to work undercover as lowlifes on the wrong side of the law with Flowers having unique skills needed as a professional diver desired by the Mafia to recover contraband lost during the repelled Coast Guard boarding. I thought the character, Rae, was an interesting one. In reality, a proficient Federal LE agent, she artfully played upon the bad guys’ premises about black women from hood, speaking in its vernacular and building a back story that gets them to lower their guard around her, allowing her to extract important information from them leading to cracking the case. She would eventually use this act to save both her and Flowers’ lives when her mafia counterparts are ordered to kill them. As a retired Coast Guardsman, since the case revolves around the murders of some of my colleagues, I’d have liked it if Coast Guard Intelligence (CGI) could have been more involved in the plot since these have jurisdiction in such a situation. There’s some but it’s fairly peripheral. However, given the number of characters already in the plot, it’s understandable that not more are introduced . Overall, a good detective novel. I recommend it for those who enjoy this genre.

One of the most boring books I’ve read. A textbook with dialogue. I’ve given it two stars because it’s well written and follows Sandford’s basic plotting system — i.e., the reader knows who the criminals are from the beginning, and the cops do too. There is no mystery. The story is in the chase. But I remember John Sandford’s earlier books as being ironic — full of wit. In this one, except for a bit of banter between Virgil and Rae, there was no humour. I remember the crooks being dumb and getting caught because they were greedy. These Mafia criminals are not dumb. They are eventually caught due to collaboration among major U.S. law enforcement agencies. The story was so boring that I read a few other book between chapters. I just couldn’t continue without major stops. And one of those books that I perused was The Best American Mystery Stories of 2020 (still haven’t read all of it). Behold, in this short story book was one by John Sandford — Girl with an Ax — one of the best stories in it. Great. Classic Sandford. So what went wrong with “Ocean Prey”? Is Sandford tired of the series and/or characters? In a couple of places, he writes that Davenport looks old for his age, and Davenport is Sandford’s alter ego. Was Ocean Prey ghost-written?

As always, Sandford delivers an engrossing and entertaining book. Having read all of the books in the Prey series and the Virgil Flowers series, I feel like I am deeply acquainted with each of the characters and have a vested interest in their lives. You would expect at some point that the stories would become rote or redundant, but not at all. Very enjoyable read.

Two of my favorite characters in the same book? No way this one won't be a winner, I said to myself as I happily opened it on my Kindle. And in no way was I disappointed. Well, maybe a titch in one respect; mostly because of asthma and a little bit of claustrophobia, I'm not a fan of putting my head under water at all - not even in the shower. So, the mere thought of scuba diving gives me hives. That's a big part of this story, so I was on the edge of my seat throughout, trying not to hold my breath and hoping that no human would be harmed in the process (close calls, however, not only are acceptable, but expected). The two characters are Lucas Davenport, now with the U.S. Marshal's Service, and his buddy Virgil Flowers, an agent with the Minnesota Department of Criminal Apprehension. They've had books all to themselves for years (with the occasional cameo appearance by one in the other's), and I'm pretty sure I've read them all. This time out, the balance of power gives a slight edge to Lucas, but Virgil certainly makes his often irreverent presence known. The story begins in Florida, after three National Guardsmen are murdered by what appear to be drug smugglers. Lucas gets called in, agrees to investigate, and convinces Virgil to join his team of expert cohorts. That leads to some serious confrontations, at least one of which doesn't turn out well. The trail leads from Florida to New Jersey and back again, putting both Lucas and Virgil on dangerous ground (well, in Virgil's case, that would be in water). In between are the usual quips and one-liners that never fail to make me chuckle - here, it's double the fun - and plenty of excitement as the rush is on to identify and catch the bad guys before they get away. All told, another great adventure with double the usual appeal - highly recommended! Many thanks to the publisher, via NetGalley, for the opportunity to read and review a pre-release copy.

Think of having desert. Not just any desert, but your favorite desert: Strawberry Shortcake, or Apple Pie, or a Chocolate Sundae. That is how I think of a John Sandford book. This isn’t about nutrition; it is just for enjoyment. It is not like I learn anything or am inspired to anything. (Actually that would be rather scary given the plots of these books.) It is just simple enjoyment, or indulgence. These books are just to be enjoyed. Turn the pages and find out what happens next. The Sandford books come in two series, one featuring Lucas Davenport and the other featuring Virgil Flowers. Both characters are based in Minnesota and occasionally their path cross, but in this book you get a double treat as both Davenport and Flowers are featured each with their own story line. Now that Davenport is a U.S. Marshall his investigations have taken him to other parts of the country. This one is set in Miami and involves drug smuggling. Flowers is recruited by Davenport to help with the investigation. I recently read and reviewed a book about WWI and mentioned the horrific body counts after many of the battles. The body count in this book is not quite as high, but there are some people killed. It does pain me to say anything negative about a Sandford book, but some of these killings are of innocent people, and Davenport may have been the reason for their deaths. Davenport has been known to take justice into his own hands on occasion, and no one can object too much to a bad guy being killed. But here he is so focused on getting to the head of a drug ring that he ignores the danger that he is exposing to some of the people he questions. The writing is sparse, almost Hemingwayesque and the tension is taut. It is one of those reads where you think, “Just one more chapter.” I missed two afternoon naps and read past my bedtime a few nights. Almost everyone, I’m sure, has their favorite authors. Sandford is mine. My favorite desert is a Banana Split.

Okay, a couple of confessions first. 1) I’m starting to like Virgil more than Lucas. 2) After this…I kind of want Virgil and Rae to get together and make beautiful babies. (Yes, I know…not the point, but still!) So I have to admit that I wasn’t all into the crime in this one. While it was interesting enough, our baddies weren’t charismatic and the crime itself wasn’t a particularly exciting one. I need baddies you love to hate. These were…baddies I was apathetic about. However, I did love our character interactions, found myself very curious about exactly how some of our characters would get out alive, and even had my heart broken in one particular scene. While not my favorite book in the series, I did like it and will happily read the next book in the series (and the next and the next and the next). It’s a solid read, if not the most exciting for me. *ARC Provided via Net Galley

Another excellent entry in the Prey series as Lucas and Virgil take on organized crime from Florida to New York. Exciting, very well plotted and Rae adds a lot of interest to the story. Well done. Recommended.

This book delivers believable though fantastical action in the world of law vs drug criminals, and we get to spend satisfying time with Lucas as well as Virgil - two great characters. I highlighted so many passages that I loved and was entertained by...maybe I could share a couple. Nope, I won't do that as I wouldn't wish to rob anyone of the pleasure of reading this book and finding their own favorite segments. Yes...somehow Marshalls are needed and wanted by the FBI - to work with, that is!

5 Stars. I was skeptical when opening page one. How could this be a joint Davenport, Flowers novel? It's a "Prey" title isn't it? I enjoy both, with a lean to Virgil, so I thought I'd probably love this new approach anyway. Having read it, Flowers and Davenport do deserve equal billing, and I loved it as expected. In baseball, batting one for two is a good day. Sandford goes two for two. Rather than #31 and #13, it truly is "Davenport & Flowers #1." We get right into it. An astute Coast Guard officer, Barney Hall, out fishing on his day off, spots something strange. A lone scuba diver far from shore suddenly gets picked up by a speedboat. After suggesting a boat inspection to the on-duty team, Hall watches in horror as three Coast Guard men are shot. Soon the FBI are all over the Miami / Port Everglades scene but results are meagre. These drug gangs are professional - modern Mafia out of New York and New Jersey. They make few mistakes. That's the case until Davenport and Flowers begin chipping away. Lucas first asks, "How much does a wet suit weigh?," and then Virgil gets serious about deep sea diving. Suspense galore. It's taut and tense. (May 2021)

Just when you thought Sandford had no where to go with this series he pulls Ocean Prey out of his - well you know where I am going with that. Virgil and Lucas together in the one novel with a major shock that I was not expecting at all. This book had it all. Let's hope that rather than one book on alternative years for our boys we get more of them together. The story itself was extremely compelling, and once I started listening I could not stop. There is not much that I can say that I have not said before, I simply love these books and characters. If this is a series you have not read, or if it a series you have been waiting to start don't delay its more than worth it.

At this point, Davenport is so boring and defanged, he might as well be the dad in a sitcom. With all his rough edges sanded down, this character has never been less interesting. Long gone are the days of interesting villains. Decades after reading them, I can still recall the baddies from Eyes of Prey, Winter, night and Mind Prey. Absolutely terrifying and remorseless, those guys were some of the scariest and most interesting put to page. For the life of me, I can't remember the last bad guy that made any kind of impression on me; instead, for decades, we've been given a group antagonists as boring and interchangeable as this series book titles. Back in Davenport's salad days, his coworkers and friends and fellow cops were as a whole, the second most appealing aspect of the classic Prey novels. Those friendships and relationships provided some of the highlights of this series. They were funny when they wanted to be and provided real drama when put in danger. I get that Lucas has changed jobs a few times over since the good old days and that someone doesn't work with or stay in touch with even the closest friends but no one of much noticed has ever stepped in to replace the old crew. Lately we have had Bob and Rae but Sandford doesn't seem interested in the least of filling out either character. In fact, here in Ocean Prey, we get hints that he's already growing tired of them. Plot-wise, we get one or two action scenes propping up pages and pages of the good guys not doing much of anything. And then they have meetings and admit to each other they still have nothing. Eventually, Davenport will talk to someone who knows someone who might know something and then finally, a finale. As far as actual stories go, there's just not much here. Sandford always had great skills when writing thrillers and even in dud after dud, these books are very easy reads and I keep up with them not only out of pure nostalgia and the hopes that the author may some day get his groove back and start caring again but also because even when nothing's happening, they're still so damn easy to read. Like that imaginary sitcom I can picture Lucas starring in as a befuddled, clueless dad, a Sandford Prey novel is still somehow comforting to me. Unfortunately, I couldn't recommend this one less. Gosh, do I miss Kidd and Luanne.

In Ocean Prey, Sandford's latest in the wildly-popular Prey detective series, three Coast Guards are gunned down while investigating a suspicious ocean craft and then the boat is burned, killing Lucas' girlfriend who is also a high-ranking FBI officer. When the FBI fails to solve the mystery, Lucas and Virgil Flowers get involved and quickly come up with threads to pull as only they can. It is unusual for both Davenport and Flowers to be the main characters in a story but in this story, it works brilliantly. The story is fast-moving and clever, the scenery well-defined, and the characters vintage. Sandford has a way of writing these stories that I don't find in other novels, a little like a police procedure but not so technical. Here’s an example. “We’ve still got twenty-five minutes on the movie,” Bob said, when Weaver rang off. They watched the movie to the end and a few minutes of a sports talk show, and then Bob went back to his room to catch some sleep. Lucas was a night owl and spent an hour reading a Lee Child thriller.” Detail about life beyond the explosive moments that occupy all cases. Sandford's writing style is to create characters that are sharp, clever, and human. For example: "Where do we find the guys whose toes we’re going to step on?” "I never even saw your name in the newspapers.” “There’s still newspapers?” “Hell hath no fury like a woman yanked out of La Perla . . .” One annoyance: For the first time I can remember, Sandford got a little preachy. Virgil was annoyed at Lucas because Lucas tends to shoot bad guys to save his own life. Virgil didn’t think Lucas always tried all other available options while Lucas was sure he did. This came up three or four times in the book, enough to tell me Sandford was trying to make a point, and enough to annoy me. One more annoyance: Every book in this series includes a character saying "F***** Flowers” (if you read the series, you know exactly what I mean--like Clive Cussler cameoed in every book he wrote). Not in this one and I looked for it--even did a search for the phrase! The closest I got was Virgil saying, "F*** me." I don't know if that counts... Luckily, Sandford is a magnificent storyteller so I recovered from my angst. Overall, an excellent read--as usual.

When the killing of three Coast Guard officers by drug smugglers finds no suspects, U.S. Marshal Lucas Davenport is called in to get results. Using hard edged police tactics, he and his team quickly zero in on the drug runners, but now they must prove it. From the beaches of Florida to hard streets of New York, this realistic chase is complex and mesmerizing. With more action, shooting and suspense to equal a dozen books, the author creates a memorable story. This is the 31st book in the series and I plan on searching out others. As an author, I could appreciate the author’s comments concerning mistakes found in manuscripts and the work that goes into bringing together a novel.

I would give this book 100 stars if I could! Besides one MAJOR DAMMIT happening, the book was beyond my expectations. I loved the banter between all the characters in this book. And for the most part it was banter :) Each person has a unique sense of humor and wit and Sandford employed it to the max. I think being from Minnesota helps with the Sandford written dialogue as it is SO Minnesotan :) YOU ROCK! The only problem is the long wait for the next book. No one does books better.

Oh, John Sandford! You have gone and done it again. How do you keep writing such wonderful books? One would think that you would run out of ideas, but (thankfully) no, they just keep coming! Thus, another couple of sleepless nights spent devouring it! This time Sandford's intrepid detectives, Lucas Davenport and Virgil Flowers, team up on an adventure in Florida. Drug running, the Mafia, murder, it's all here. And told in the exciting and fast-paced way that the author masterfully employs. Of all the authors in this genre, I truly believe that Sandford is one of the best. I was particularly pleased at the way this novel wrapped up. I found it much more satisfying than some of his others (readers of his books know to what I am referring, Davenport's penchant for vigilante justice). As I have come to expect, Sandford drops hints at possible future adventures for his characters. I, for one, am eagerly awaiting the next one! Thanks to NetGalley for an advance reading copy of this book.

Starts off fast & keeps on going. Interesting diving stuff & generally a lot of fun as Lucas kicks butt. Then Virgil Flowers joins in about halfway through to add icing to the cake. There's some interesting diving stuff, but it's pretty typical of the series & one of the better ones. There is an afterword by Sandford about how errors can get into a novel. He points out several such as a safety on a Glock. Turns out the pistol had originally been a Barretta, but he found out just before the novel went out that the police had changed policies, so he changed the pistol to a Glock. He missed the bit with the safety, though. Oops! Another time he wrote that Lucas had a 40mm pistol instead of a .40 caliber. He's well aware of the difference & not sure how such a goof managed to get through all the proofreads, but it did. Anyway, it was one of the more entertaining afterwords I've read in a while. Well narrated & highly recommended.

A huge cache of drugs is submerged in the ocean and while recovering it, the criminals are spotted by the Coast Guard. In the resultant shoot out, 3 Coast Guard officers are killed. For months, the FBI investigates and makes no headway. Enter ✨Lucas Davenport, and his prodding stirs the hornets nest. The hunters now become the hunted!
